en.abajar:
Spanish ~abajar~ is ~bajar~ (“to lower, to go down”) carrying the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”). ~bajar~ descends from Old Spanish ~baxar~, from Vulgar Latin *~bassiāre~, a verb built on Late Latin ~bassus~ (“low, short”), a word of uncertain deeper origin that is sometimes traced to an Oscan-Umbrian source. It is cognate with Italian ~abbassare~, French ~baisser~ and Portuguese ~abaixar~.

Both ~abajar~ and ~bajar~ once meant “to bring down” or “to descend,” but the bare form prevailed and ~abajar~ faded into archaic and regional use, still heard in some rural and Latin American speech. The idea of lowness radiated into a large family: the adjective ~bajo~ (“low”), the adverb ~abajo~ (“below”), the noun ~bajada~ (“descent, slope”) and the verb ~rebajar~ (“to reduce, to lower”).
en.aballar:
Spanish ~aballar~ (“to drive or move livestock; to shake”) is of disputed origin. Some etymologists derive it from Late Latin ~ballāre~ (“to dance”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~βαλλίζω~ (ballízō, “to dance, to jump about”); others, including the Spanish academic tradition, judge the verb to be of uncertain origin and decline to fix a Latin source. It survives in the northwest: compare Asturian ~aballar~ and Mirandese ~abalhar~ (“to leave, to set off”).

The word names the herdsman's task of stirring up and driving animals along, and by extension “to shake” or “to get moving.” If the derivation from ~ballāre~ is correct, ~aballar~ would share its root with ~bailar~ (“to dance”) and ~balada~ (“ballad,” in origin a dancing-song) — but because the very origin is disputed, that kinship remains conjectural. The verb dropped almost entirely out of standard Spanish, lingering in Asturian, Leonese and older texts.
en.abandonar:
From French ~abandonner~, from the Old French phrase ~a bandon~ (“at one's discretion, under one's control”), from ~a~ (“to, at”) and ~bandon~ (“power, jurisdiction, permission”). ~bandon~ goes back to Late Latin ~bannum~ (“proclamation, ban”), a borrowing from Frankish *~ban~, from Proto-Germanic *~banną~ (“proclamation, command”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰeh₂-~ (“to speak”). Cognate with English ~abandon~ and, through the Germanic root, with English ~ban~ and ~banns~.

The phrase ~a bandon~ meant “under someone's control,” hence “left to another's will.” A medieval feudal formula, ~mettre à bandon~, meant to throw one's forest open — to let anyone freely graze or cut wood there — so “to place at everyone's disposal” slid into “to give up, relinquish, forsake.” Spanish borrowed the fully formed French verb rather than inheriting it directly. The same Germanic root of “proclamation” gave ~bando~ (“edict; faction”) and ~bandido~ (“outlaw,” one proclaimed against).
en.abarcar:
From Vulgar Latin *~abbracchicāre~ (“to embrace, clasp in the arms”), a verb built on Latin ~bracchium~ (“arm”), which Latin had borrowed from Ancient Greek ~βραχίων~ (~brakhíōn~), from Proto-Indo-European *~mreǵʰ-~ (“short”). Cognate with Spanish ~brazo~, Italian ~braccio~ and French ~bras~, and — through the same noun — with English ~brace~, ~embrace~ and ~bracelet~; through the “short” root it also meets English ~brief~ and Greek ~brakhýs~.

The image is bodily and vivid: to ~abarcar~ was first to throw one's arms around something, to encircle it, and from that embrace the sense widened to “to take in, encompass, span, include” — an area, a subject, a whole field of study. The proverb ~Quien mucho abarca, poco aprieta~ (“who grasps at much squeezes little”) preserves the literal arms-full picture while warning against overreach. Spanish keeps a close doublet in ~abrazar~ (“to embrace”), from the same ~bracchium~ by a slightly different Vulgar-Latin route, alongside ~brazo~, ~abrazo~, ~brazalete~ and ~braza~.
en.abatir:
~abatir~ joins the prefix ~a-~ (Latin ~ad-~, “to”) to ~batir~ (“to beat”), which comes from Latin ~battuere~ (“to strike, to beat”). ~battuere~ was rare in classical Latin and is of uncertain origin — possibly Gaulish, and often connected to an onomatopoeic root *~bʰat-~ (“to hit”), though this remains unproven. It is cognate with French ~abattre~, Italian ~abbattere~ and Portuguese ~abater~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~abate~.

From “to beat down,” ~abatir~ came to mean “to knock down, to fell, to demolish,” and figuratively “to dishearten”: someone ~abatido~ is cast down or dejected. The same ~battuere~, through its frequentative and derivatives, seeded a broad Spanish family, including ~batir~ (“to beat, to whisk”), ~batalla~ (“battle”), ~combatir~ (“to fight”) and ~batería~ (“battery, drum kit”).
en.ablandar:
~ablandar~ is formed from the prefix ~a-~ and the adjective ~blando~ (“soft”) with a verbal ending, meaning literally “to make soft.” ~blando~ descends from Latin ~blandus~ (“soft, tender, caressing, flattering”), traced to a nasalized Proto-Indo-European *~mland-~, a variant of *~meld-~ (“soft, weak”) and kin to Latin ~mollis~ (“soft”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~melt~; English ~bland~, by contrast, is a direct borrowing of ~blandus~.

Where ~blandus~ in Latin leaned toward “flattering, ingratiating,” Spanish kept the physical sense, and ~ablandar~ means “to soften” — a hard surface, a tough cut of meat, or a person's resolve or anger. From the same adjective come ~blando~ (“soft”), ~blandura~ (“softness, gentleness”) and ~reblandecer~ (“to soften, to make soggy”).
en.abolir:
From Latin ~abolēre~ (“to destroy, efface, do away with”), a compound of the prefix ~ab-~ (“away from”) and, probably, a verb *~oleō~ (“to wipe out, destroy”), though the details are uncertain. By this account the root goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₃elh₁-~, making ~abolēre~ a distant cognate of Ancient Greek ~ἀπόλλυμι~ (apóllymi, “to destroy utterly”). The verb passed intact into the Romance languages: Spanish ~abolir~, Portuguese ~abolir~, Italian ~abolire~, and French ~abolir~, the last of which English borrowed as ~abolish~.

The Latin sense of erasing or annulling narrowed in Spanish to the legal and political abolishing of laws, institutions, and customs, as in the abolition of slavery. For centuries ~abolir~ was famously defective: speakers used only the forms whose ending began with ~-i-~ (~abolimos~, ~abolía~, ~abolió~, ~abolir~) and avoided the rest, so one never said *~abole~. Modern grammars now admit the full conjugation, but to many ears the old gap still sounds more natural. From the same Latin stem Spanish keeps ~abolición~, ~abolicionismo~, and ~abolicionista~.
en.abonar:
~abonar~ was formed within Spanish from the prefix ~a-~ plus ~bueno~ (“good”), which descends from Latin ~bonus~ — Old Latin ~duonus~ — ultimately from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to show favor or esteem. The literal idea is “to make good.” Cognate with French ~bon~, Italian ~buono~ and Portuguese ~bom~, and — through ~bonus~ — with English ~bonus~ and ~bounty~.

From “to make good” the verb fanned out: to vouch for someone (make their word good), to credit or pay a sum (make a debt good), and to fertilize land (make soil good and productive) — the “fertilizer” sense that gives the noun ~abono~. A second, disputed strand feeds the subscription meaning: the reflexive ~abonarse~ (“to subscribe,” and its noun ~abono~, “season ticket”) is widely traced to French ~abonner~, itself from Old French ~bonne~ (“boundary”), a different word only later merged with the “good” family. The kin group also holds ~bueno~, ~bondad~, ~bonito~ and ~bono~.
en.abordar:
Spanish ~abordar~ is formed from ~a-~ (“to, toward”) and ~bordo~ (“the side of a ship; on board”), plus the verbal ending. ~bordo~ comes from ~borde~ (“edge, border”), and that from Frankish *~bord~ (“plank, board, ship's side”), a Germanic word from Proto-Germanic *~burdą~ (“board, plank”). So this is a Germanic root that entered Romance through the Franks. It is cognate with English ~board~ and ~border~, German ~Bord~, and — as a nautical borrowing — with Italian ~abbordare~ and French ~aborder~.

The literal sense is nautical: to come up alongside a ship's ~bordo~ — its side or planking — hence to board a vessel, and by a natural extension to approach or accost a person. From there Spanish developed the figurative meaning that now dominates everyday speech: to ~abordar~ a subject, a problem, or a task is to take it on, to tackle it head-on. English preserves the same maritime image in “to board” a ship and in the adverb “aboard.” From the Germanic ~bord~ Spanish also keeps a nautical and edge-related family: ~bordo~, ~borde~, ~bordear~ (“to skirt”), ~abordaje~ (“a boarding”), and ~francobordo~ (“freeboard”).
en.abrazar:
From ~a-~ plus ~brazo~ (“arm”) plus ~-ar~ — “to take into one's arms.” ~Brazo~ descends from Latin ~bracchium~ (“arm, forearm”), which Latin borrowed from Ancient Greek ~brachíōn~ (“arm”). ~Brachíōn~ was traditionally read as a comparative of ~brachýs~ (“short”) — the “shorter” upper arm — though that inner link is not certain and is best offered as the traditional account rather than settled fact. The Latin word spread through Romance: French ~bras~ and ~embrasser~ (“to kiss”), Italian ~braccio~ and ~abbracciare~, Portuguese ~braço~ and ~abraçar~; through Latin it also gave English ~brace~, ~bracelet~ and ~embrace~.

The verb is transparent once you see the noun inside it: to ~abrazar~ is to put your ~brazos~ around someone. Spanish widened it figuratively too — one can ~abrazar~ a cause, a faith, or an idea. From the same ~bracchium~ Spanish keeps ~brazo~, ~abrazo~ (“a hug”), ~brazalete~ (“bracelet”), ~abrazadera~ (“clamp, bracket”) and ~braza~, the “fathom” once measured by the span of two outstretched arms — and the breaststroke swum with them.
en.abrevar:
~abrevar~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~abbiberāre~, a compound of ~ad-~ (“to”) and Latin ~bibere~ (“to drink”), from Proto-Indo-European *~peh₃-~ (“to drink”). Spanish inherited ~bibere~ directly as ~beber~ (“to drink”); the prefixed ~abbiberāre~ gave the Romance verbs for watering animals — Italian ~abbeverare~, French ~abreuver~ and Portuguese ~abeberar~.

Where ~beber~ is simply “to drink,” ~abrevar~ means “to give (animals) water to drink,” and by extension “to water” or “to irrigate.” The place a herd is led to is an ~abrevadero~ (“watering trough”). From the same ~bibere~ come the everyday ~bebida~ (“drink, beverage”) and the more colorful ~brebaje~ (“brew, concoction”), the latter borrowed back through Old French.
en.abreviar:
~abreviar~ is a learned borrowing of Late Latin ~abbreviāre~ (“to shorten”), from ~ad-~ (“to”) plus ~brevis~ (“short”), which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~mréǵʰus~ (“short”). Through that root ~brevis~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~βραχύς~ (brakhús, “short”) and, more distantly, with English ~merry~; the same borrowed ~brevis~ also gave English ~brief~ and, by the popular French route ~abréger~, English ~abridge~.

Because Spanish took it straight from Latin rather than inheriting it through everyday speech, ~abreviar~ kept its learned shape and its plain meaning, “to make shorter, to abbreviate.” From the same ~brevis~ come ~breve~ (“brief, short”), ~brevedad~ (“brevity”) and ~abreviatura~ (“abbreviation”).
en.abrir:
From Latin ~aperīre~ (“to open, uncover”), which reached Spanish through Vulgar Latin *~operīre~ and Old Spanish ~abrir~. The deeper origin is debated. By the standard account ~aperīre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~apweriō~, analyzed as Proto-Indo-European *~h₂epó~ (“off, away”) plus *~h₂wer-~ (“to cover, shut”) — so “to un-cover” — which would make it a near-mirror of its opposite ~operīre~ (“to cover, close”). This decomposition is plausible but not certain, and other explanations have been proposed. Cognate Romance forms include Italian ~aprire~, Portuguese ~abrir~ and French ~ouvrir~.

Whatever its ultimate source, ~aperīre~ meant “to open” throughout its history, and Spanish ~abrir~ carries that unbroken. Its past participle is the irregular ~abierto~, and from the Latin verb and its relatives Spanish draws ~abertura~ and the learned ~apertura~ (“opening,” as of a chess game or a session), ~abridor~ (“opener”) and ~aperitivo~ (“aperitif” — literally something that “opens” the appetite before a meal). Through French, the same Latin verb gave English ~aperture~ and ~overt~ (from Old French ~ouvert~, “opened”), so an ~overt~ act is, etymologically, an opened one.
en.absorber:
From Latin ~absorbēre~ (“to swallow up, gulp down”), from ~ab-~ (“away, off”) plus ~sorbēre~ (“to suck, sip”), from Proto-Italic *~sorβeō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~srebʰ-~ (“to sip, slurp”). It is cognate with Italian ~assorbire~, French ~absorber~, and Portuguese ~absorver~, and — through the root — with Ancient Greek ~ῥοφέω~ (rhopheō, “to gulp down”) and Lithuanian ~srebti~ (“to slurp”). English ~absorb~ is a parallel borrowing of the same Latin verb.

The meaning has barely drifted in two thousand years: ~sorbēre~ was to suck liquid in, and ~ab-~ added the sense of drawing it fully away, so to ~absorber~ is still to soak up. The humblest relatives are the most vivid: Spanish kept ~sorbēre~ alive as everyday ~sorber~ (“to sip, slurp”) and the noun ~sorbo~ (“a sip”), so a ~sorbo~ of coffee and a sponge that soaks up water are close kin. From the same root Spanish also draws ~absorción~, ~absorbente~, and ~resorber~ — and, figuratively, a book that ~absorbe~ the reader swallows attention just as a sponge swallows water.
en.aburrir:
From Latin ~abhorrēre~ (“to shrink back from, shudder at”), from ~ab-~ (“away”) plus ~horrēre~ (“to bristle, tremble, dread”), from Proto-Italic *~horzēō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰers-~ (“to bristle”). English borrowed the same Latin verb as ~abhor~, so Spanish ~aburrir~ and English ~abhor~ are, remarkably, the very same word. Through ~horrēre~ it is also kin to ~horror~ and ~horrible~, and — through the root — to Latin ~hīrtus~ (“shaggy”) and Sanskrit ~hṛṣyati~ (“bristles, thrills”).

The emotional history is a long cooling-off. ~abhorrēre~ meant to recoil in loathing; Old Spanish ~aborrir~ still meant “to hate,” a sense its twin ~aborrecer~ keeps to this day. But in the reflexive, the fierce recoil faded into mere weariness: to ~aburrirse~ is no longer to loathe the world but only to be bored by it. The bristling root also stood a hedgehog’s spines on end — Latin ~ericius~ gave Spanish ~erizo~ (“hedgehog,” literally “the bristly one”) and ~erizarse~ (“to stand on end,” of hair) — so boredom and a hedgehog’s prickles trace back to the same shudder.
en.acabar:
Spanish ~acabar~ was formed within Romance from the noun ~cabo~ (“end, tip, extremity”), with the prefix ~a-~ and the verbal ending ~-ar~; the reconstructed Vulgar Latin form is *~accapāre~. ~cabo~ comes from Latin ~caput~ (“head”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kaput-~ (“head”). That root is cognate, by Grimm’s law (k → h), with English ~head~ and German ~Haupt~; from ~caput~ itself came English ~capital~, ~captain~, and ~chief~. French ~achever~ (“to complete”) and, borrowed from it, English ~achieve~ rest on the same image.

The metaphor is bodily: the ~cabo~ is the “head” or far tip of a thing, so to ~acabar~ is to carry something to its extremity — to finish it off. Spanish put the verb to hard work: ~acabar de~ + infinitive means “to have just” done something, while the phrase ~el acabóse~ names an utter end or a disaster. From ~caput~ the language also drew ~cabeza~ (“head,” via ~capitia~), ~cabecera~ (“headboard, head of a table”), ~cabo~ (the “cape” of a coast and the military “corporal”), ~capital~, and ~capitán~. One Latin word for “head,” then, tops off a Spanish verb for “to end” — and is quietly cognate with the English ~head~ you nod.
en.acaecer:
~acaecer~ descends from a Vulgar Latin *~accadēscere~, an inchoative reshaping of Latin ~accidere~ (“to fall to, to befall”), itself ~ad-~ (“to”) plus ~cadere~ (“to fall”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱad-~ (“to fall”). Spanish inherited ~cadere~ as ~caer~ (“to fall”); through the same root the learned Latin stock gave English ~cadence~ and ~chance~, the latter through Old French, literally a “falling” of the dice.

To “fall to” someone was to happen to them, and ~acaecer~ settled into the meaning “to happen, to occur, to come to pass,” now a literary or archaic word beside suceder and pasar. The falling metaphor runs through the whole family: a ~caso~ (“case, occurrence”) is something that “falls out,” an ~accidente~ is an unlucky fall, ~decaer~ is “to decline,” and even ~occidente~ (“the West”) names the quarter where the sun goes down.
en.acampar:
~acampar~ was borrowed from Italian ~accampare~ (“to pitch camp”), a verb built on ~campo~ (“field”), from Latin ~campus~ (“open field, level ground”). The deeper source of ~campus~ is uncertain: it is sometimes traced to a Proto-Indo-European *~kh₂emp-~ (“to bend, to curve”), but the irregular match with Greek forms led others to suspect a borrowing from a pre-Latin substrate. From ~campus~ Romance drew a wide range of military and rural words, among them French ~camper~ and English ~camp~.

The word began as soldiers' language — to settle an army on open ground — and only later broadened to the peaceful modern sense, “to camp” for pleasure. Spanish keeps the whole field beside it: ~campo~ (“field, countryside”), ~campamento~ (“camp, encampment”) and ~campaña~ (“campaign,” once a stretch of open country, then a season's military operations, now any organized effort).
en.acceder:
From Latin ~accēdere~ (“to approach, go toward, be added”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~cēdere~ (“to go, move, yield”). The origin of ~cēdere~ is debated: it goes back to Proto-Italic *~kezdō~, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱyesdʰ-~ (“to drive away, go away”), though some instead build it from *~ḱe~ (“here”) plus *~sed-~ (“to sit”). It is cognate with French ~accéder~, Italian ~accedere~, and Portuguese ~aceder~, and with English ~accede~ and ~access~.

Since ~cēdere~ meant “to go” or “to yield,” ~accēdere~ was “to go toward” — and from approaching came both “to assent” and “to gain entry.” Spanish ~acceder~ still carries both: to accede to a request and to access a place. The computing sense “to access” is a modern loan from English. The root threw off a large family — ~ceder~, ~conceder~, ~proceder~, ~suceder~, ~preceder~, ~retroceder~ — plus the nouns ~acceso~ and ~proceso~, its close relatives.
en.accionar:
Spanish ~accionar~ is a modern derivative of the noun ~acción~ (“action”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-ar~. ~Acción~ descends from Latin ~actiōnem~, the accusative of ~actiō~, itself built on ~actus~, the past participle of ~agere~ (“to drive, do, act”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, lead”). The same Latin verb underlies Italian ~azionare~ and French ~actionner~, and — through ~agere~ — the English cognates ~act~ and ~agent~.

Where ~agere~ meant “to set moving,” ~accionar~ narrowed to the mechanical sense of activating a lever, switch, or mechanism, and in law “to bring an action.” The prolific root *~h₂eǵ-~ seeded a broad Spanish family, among them ~acto~, ~actor~, ~agente~, ~agenda~, ~agitar~, ~examinar~ and ~exigir~.
en.acelerar:
From Latin ~accelerāre~ (“to hasten”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~celerāre~ (“to quicken”), from ~celer~ (“swift”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *~kel-~ (“to drive, set in motion”), probably cognate with Ancient Greek ~κέλης~ (“racehorse, runner”) and ~κέλλω~ (“to drive on”). English borrowed ~accelerate~ and ~celerity~; the Romance cognates include Italian ~accelerare~ and French ~accélérer~.

The prefix ~ad-~ here is intensive, so ~accelerāre~ is essentially “to add speed to,” to make something already moving move faster. The Greek link is offered by the sources as probable rather than certain, so it is best held lightly. From ~celer~ Spanish keeps the learned adjective ~célere~ (“swift”) and the noun ~celeridad~ (“speed”), and from the verb it forms ~aceleración~ (“acceleration”) and the everyday ~acelerón~ (“a burst of speed”).
en.aceptar:
From Latin ~acceptāre~ (“to receive willingly, accept”), a frequentative of ~accipere~ (“to receive, take to oneself”), which is ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), from Proto-Italic *~kapjō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~kap-~ (“to grasp, seize”). English ~heave~ is a native cognate of that root; the verb itself came into English as ~accept~, into French as ~accepter~ and into Italian as ~accettare~.

A frequentative denotes repeated or intensive action, so ~acceptāre~ was, strictly, “to keep receiving” — and the willingness in “accepting” grew out of that habitual taking-toward-oneself. Spanish ~aceptar~ narrowed it to agreeing to receive: one ~acepta~ a gift, an offer, a fate. The prolific ~capere~ root fills the language — ~aceptación~, ~captar~, ~capaz~, ~cautivo~, ~concebir~, ~recibir~, ~percibir~ and ~excepto~ — everywhere the idea of taking or holding persists.
en.acercar:
A parasynthetic verb built from ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”), the adverb ~cerca~ (“near”), and the ending ~-ar~ — literally “to make near.” ~cerca~ comes from Latin ~circā~ (“around, round about”), an adverb bound to ~circum~ (“around”) and the noun ~circus~ (“ring, circle”). ~circus~ was most likely taken from, or shared with, Ancient Greek ~kríkos~ / ~kírkos~ (“ring”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)ker-~ (“to turn, to bend”); by one account English ~ring~ belongs to the same root.

The semantic hinge is neat: what lies “round about” a spot is precisely what lies “near” it, so Latin ~circā~ “around” slid into Spanish ~cerca~ “nearby,” and the causative ~acercar~ came to mean “to bring closer.” The same word ~cerca~, as a noun, also means a “fence” — that which rings a field — beside the verb ~cercar~ “to encircle, to besiege.” Other kin of the turning-root include ~círculo~, ~circo~, ~circular~, ~cerco~, and the learned dating word ~circa~ itself.
en.acertar:
Spanish ~acertar~ (“to get right, hit the mark”) was formed from ~a-~ + the adjective ~cierto~ (“certain, sure”) + ~-ar~. ~cierto~ comes from Latin ~certus~ (“settled, sure”), originally the past participle of ~cernere~ (“to sift, separate, distinguish, decide”), from Proto-Indo-European *~krey-~ (“to sieve, separate”). The root reaches English ~certain~, ~discern~ and ~secret~, and — through Greek ~κρίνειν~ (~krínein~, “to judge, separate”) — ~critic~ and ~crime~.

The hidden picture is agricultural: ~certus~ literally meant “sifted out” — what is sure is what has been separated from the chaff and decided. Spanish ~acertar~ moved from “to make certain” to “to hit what you aim at, to guess right,” its noun ~acierto~ meaning a “right answer, good call” and its opposite ~desacierto~ a “blunder.” The same ~cernere~ family fills modern Spanish — ~certeza~ (“certainty”), ~certero~ (“accurate, well-aimed”), ~concertar~ (“to arrange, concert”), ~discernir~ (“to discern”) and even ~cribar~ (“to sieve”), from the related ~cribrum~ (“sieve”).
en.achacar:
Spanish ~achacar~ was borrowed from Arabic ~šakā~ (“to complain, to make an accusation”), most likely through a derived intensive form: the Spanish ~ch~ points to Maghrebi Arabic ~tšakka~, from Classical Arabic ~tašakkā~, the reflexive-intensive of the same root. The exact path is disputed — some sources instead connect the word to the Arabic noun for « complaint » by way of Spanish ~achaque~ — but the Arabic origin itself is secure.

The original sense of « complaining » narrowed in Castilian to « imputing a fault »: to ~achacar~ something to someone is to lay a defect or blame at their feet, often unfairly. The same Arabic root gave Spanish ~achaque~ (“chronic ailment; pretext”) and the adjective ~achacoso~ (“sickly”), a reminder that the word once lived close to the language of illness and grievance. Its Semitic ancestry sets it apart from most Spanish verbs, whose roots run back to Latin; ~achacar~ belongs instead to the large stratum of Arabic borrowings absorbed during the centuries of al-Andalus.
en.aclamar:
Spanish ~aclamar~ comes from Latin ~acclāmāre~ (“to shout at, cry out to, applaud”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~clāmāre~ (“to shout, call out”). The verb ~clāmāre~ traces back to Proto-Indo-European *~kelh₁-~ (“to shout, call”). Through Old French ~clamer~ the same Latin verb reached English as ~claim~, and within Spanish it is the learned twin of the fully inherited ~llamar~ (“to call”), which descends from that very ~clāmāre~ by ordinary sound change.

The sense stayed close to the Latin: to ~aclamar~ is to greet or hail someone with collective shouting — of approval, victory, or praise — so a crowd may ~aclamar~ a champion or a king. The productive Latin family around ~clāmāre~ seeded a whole cluster of Spanish words that all carry the idea of raising the voice: ~clamor~ (“outcry”), ~reclamar~ (“to demand, claim back”), and ~exclamar~ (“to exclaim”). What began as the plain act of shouting became, in ~aclamar~, the formal language of public acclamation.
en.aclarar:
From ~a-~ plus the adjective ~claro~ (“clear, bright”), from Latin ~clārus~, which in Vulgar Latin already spawned a verb ~clārāre~ (“to make bright”). ~Clārus~ derives from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱelh₁-~ (“to shout, call out”), the very root behind Latin ~clāmāre~ (“to cry out”) and ~calāre~ (“to summon”) and Ancient Greek ~καλέω~ (“I call”). English took the descendants as the borrowings ~clear~, ~declare~ and ~clarion~.

Here is the surprise: ~clārus~ first described sound, not light. Its earliest sense was “clear-sounding, loud, ringing” — fitting a root that meant to shout — and only afterward did it slide to “bright” (of light), then “transparent” (of water), then “evident” (of an idea). Spanish ~aclarar~ inherited that whole fan of senses: you can ~aclarar~ a doubt, ~aclarar~ the rinse water, or watch the sky ~aclarar~ at dawn. The family is large — ~claridad~, ~clarear~, ~aclaración~, ~declarar~, ~clarín~ and the given name ~Clara~ — every one a ripple from an ancient act of calling aloud.
en.acoger:
From Vulgar Latin *~accolligere~, from Latin ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~colligere~ (“to gather, collect”). ~colligere~ is ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~legere~ (“to gather, pick, read”), from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather”). Cognate with French ~accueillir~, Italian ~accogliere~ and Portuguese ~acolher~.

At heart ~acoger~ means to gather someone to yourself — hence “to welcome, take in, shelter.” Its Latin base ~legere~ is one of the great word-factories of Spanish, yielding ~coger~ (“to take”), ~escoger~ (“to choose”), ~recoger~ (“to collect”) and, learned, ~colegio~, ~colección~ and ~elegir~. Most strikingly, ~legere~ also meant “to read,” and by that path it gave Spanish ~leer~ — so welcoming a guest and reading a book trace back to the same gesture of gathering.
en.acometer:
Spanish ~acometer~ is built from the prefix ~a-~ and the verb ~cometer~, which descends from Latin ~committere~ — itself ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~mittere~ (“to send, let go”). The Latin ~mittere~ has an uncertain deeper history but is usually traced to Proto-Indo-European *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, remove”), whose sense of « exchange » drifted through « give up » to « let go, send ». English borrowed the same compound as ~commit~.

Where ~cometer~ kept the notion of « committing » an act (a crime, an error), ~acometer~ added the directional ~a-~ and specialized to « launching oneself at » something: to attack, to charge, or — figuratively — to undertake a hard task with energy, so one may ~acometer~ an enemy or a project alike. The noun ~acometida~ (“assault; the connection of a utility line”) preserves both the martial and the practical sides. From the same ~mittere~ Spanish also inherited ~meter~ (“to put in”), ~someter~ (“to subdue”), and ~prometer~ (“to promise”).
en.acomodar:
~acomodar~ comes from Latin ~accommodare~ (“to make fit, adapt, adjust”), from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~commodare~ (“to make suitable, to lend”), which rests on the adjective ~commodus~ (“fitting, convenient”). ~commodus~ is transparently ~com-~ (“with”) plus ~modus~ (“measure, due measure”), from Proto-Indo-European *~med-~ (“to measure, take fitting measures”) — so something ~commodus~ is, literally, “in keeping with the measure.” Cognate with Italian ~accomodare~, French ~accommoder~ and English ~accommodate~.

To ~acomodar~ is to put things in due measure — to arrange, to fit in, to make comfortable; reflexively, ~acomodarse~ is to settle in or, less flatteringly, to grow complacent. The core idea of “right measure” radiates outward: from ~commodus~ Spanish drew ~cómodo~ (“comfortable”) and ~comodidad~ (“comfort”), and English the ~commode~. From the underlying ~modus~ came a whole toolkit of measure and manner — ~modo~, ~moda~ (“fashion”), ~modelo~, ~módulo~, ~moderar~ and ~molde~ (“mold”) — every one turning on the Roman instinct that the fitting thing is the thing kept to measure.
en.acompañar:
From the prefix ~a-~ on ~compañero~/~compaña~, the family goes back to Late Latin ~companio~ (accusative ~companiōnem~), “companion, mess-mate,” a compound of ~com-~ (“with”) and ~pānis~ (“bread”) — literally one who shares bread. This ~companio~ is generally taken as a calque of Proto-West Germanic *~gahlaibō~ (“mess-mate”), first recorded in the Lex Salica, while ~pānis~ itself is traced — with some caution — to Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂-~ (“to feed, protect”). Cognates: Italian ~accompagnare~, French ~accompagner~, English ~accompany~ and ~company~.

The heart of the word is a homely image: a ~companio~ is a “bread-fellow,” the person with whom you break bread. Spanish keeps that warmth in ~compañero~ and ~compañía~, and ~acompañar~ is simply to go alongside someone, to keep them company. The bread at its center, ~pānis~, lives on directly as Spanish ~pan~, and spreads through ~panadería~ (“bakery”) and ~empanada~ (something “breaded,” wrapped in dough).
en.acondicionar:
Spanish ~acondicionar~ is a built-up verb: the prefix ~a-~ and the suffix ~-ar~ wrapped around ~condición~ (“condition”). ~condición~ descends from Latin ~condiciō~ (“agreement, terms, condition”), a noun from ~condīcere~ (“to agree upon, arrange”), itself ~con-~ (“together”) + ~dīcere~ (“to say”), from Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, point out”). That root runs through English ~condition~ and ~dictate~ and German ~zeigen~ (“to show”).

The Latin noun first meant a mutually spoken agreement — a “saying-together” — and only later the general sense of the state or terms something is in. Spanish ~acondicionar~ pushed that into the practical: to put something into good condition, to fit it out, and in the modern compound ~aire acondicionado~ (“air conditioning”) to condition the air itself. From the same ~dīcere~ Spanish inherited a broad family — ~decir~ (“to say”), ~dicción~ (“diction”), ~índice~ (“index”), ~dictar~ (“to dictate”) and ~bendecir~ (“to bless,” literally “to say well”). A quiet footnote: the classical spelling ~condiciō~ was later reshaped as ~conditiō~ by scribes who wrongly linked it to ~condere~ (“to store, found”).
en.aconsejar:
From ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”) plus ~consejo~ (“advice”), which descends from Latin ~consilium~ (“deliberation, counsel”), a noun linked to the verb ~consulere~ (“to consult, take counsel”) and to ~cōnsul~. The ultimate source of ~consulere~ is uncertain, and etymologists disagree about how it was formed. Through ~consilium~ the word is cognate with French ~conseil~ and Italian ~consiglio~, and — borrowed into English from Old French — with ~counsel~ and ~council~.

Latin ~consilium~ named a body deliberating together; Spanish made a verb of the noun by prefixing ~ad-~, so ~aconsejar~ is literally “to bring someone toward counsel.” The family stayed close to both public office and private wisdom: ~consejo~ still means both a piece of advice and a governing council, and ~consejero~ is at once an adviser and a board member. English preserves the same split its speakers still muddle — between ~counsel~, meaning advice, and ~council~, a deliberating body.
en.acordar:
From Vulgar Latin *~accordāre~ (“to bring hearts together, agree”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~cor~, stem ~cord-~ (“heart”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱḗr~, *~ḱerd-~ (“heart”). That root is the direct ancestor of English ~heart~ and German ~Herz~, and the source of Ancient Greek ~καρδία~ (“heart”) and Latin's own ~cordiālis~. Italian has the parallel ~accordare~.

Classical Latin never had *~accordāre~; Vulgar Latin coined it on the model of ~concordāre~ (“to be of one heart”), and Spanish drew from it both ~acordar~ (“to agree, resolve”) and the noun ~acuerdo~ (“agreement, accord”). The heart here is no idle metaphor: to Romans and medieval Spaniards the ~cor~ was the seat of memory as much as feeling, which is why the same organ underlies ~recordar~ (“to remember,” literally to bring back to the heart) and ~acordarse~ (“to recall”). Around them gather ~corazón~, ~cordial~, ~concordar~, ~cordura~ (“good sense”) and ~misericordia~ — a whole life of the heart.
en.acortar:
Spanish ~acortar~ joins the prefix ~a-~ to the adjective ~corto~ (“short”) with the verbal ending ~-ar~. ~Corto~ descends from Latin ~curtus~ (“shortened, cut off, mutilated”), which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)ker-~ (“to cut”). The same root, through Germanic, surfaces in English ~short~, while English also borrowed ~curtus~ directly, learnedly, as ~curt~ (“brusquely brief”).

The metaphor at the core is physical cutting: to ~acortar~ is to make something shorter — a hem, a route, a speech — as if a length had been cut away. Spanish kept a rich family from this root: the plain verb ~cortar~ (“to cut,” from Latin ~curtāre~), ~recortar~ (“to trim, cut out”), and the noun ~acortamiento~ (“shortening”). Because the prefixed ~acortar~ stresses reaching a shorter result rather than the act of cutting itself, one may ~cortar~ a rope but ~acortar~ a journey — the deed versus its diminishing effect.
en.acostar:
Spanish ~acostar~ is formed from the prefix ~a-~, the noun ~costa~ (here in its old sense “rib, side”), and the ending ~-ar~; literally it means to lay someone or something down on its side. Latin ~costa~ (“rib, flank”) has an uncertain prehistory — it is traditionally compared with Old Church Slavonic ~kostĭ~ (“bone”), but that link is disputed and some scholars reject it. From the « side » sense come the English cognates ~accost~ (originally “to come up alongside”) and, more distantly, ~coast~.

The body-on-its-side image explains the reflexive ~acostarse~ (“to go to bed, to lie down”): one settles onto one's ribs. Spanish kept several descendants of ~costa~: ~costilla~ (“rib”), the coastal ~costa~ itself, ~costado~ (“side, flank”), and ~cuesta~ (“slope,” the inherited doublet, since a hillside is the land's « side »). What ties them together is the notion of the flank or edge — the part of a thing that lies alongside — so to ~acostar~ a child is simply to bring that upright little body down to rest on its side.
en.acostumbrar:
Spanish ~acostumbrar~ is built on the noun ~costumbre~ (“custom, habit”) with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~) and the verb ending ~-ar~. ~Costumbre~ descends from Latin ~consuētūdinem~, accusative of ~consuētūdō~ (“custom, usage”), a noun on the verb ~consuēscere~ (“to accustom”), from ~con-~ plus ~suēscere~ (“to grow used to”), itself tied to ~suus~ (“one’s own”) and the Proto-Indo-European reflexive root *~swe-~ (“oneself”). It is cognate with English ~custom~, French ~coutume~, and Italian ~costume~.

The Latin abstract suffix ~-tūdō~ that closes ~consuētūdō~ surfaces in Spanish as ~-dumbre~, the ending of ~servidumbre~ (“servitude”) and ~muchedumbre~ (“crowd”). ~Acostumbrar~ therefore means “to make (something) a habit,” and its participle ~acostumbrado~ means “accustomed, usual.” The verb ~suēscere~ also underlies ~mansedumbre~ (“meekness”), from Latin ~mansuētus~, literally “accustomed to the hand,” and the same family gave the literary term ~costumbrismo~, the nineteenth-century vogue for depicting everyday customs and manners.
en.acotar:
Spanish ~acotar~ combines the prefix ~a-~, the noun ~coto~ (“enclosed reserve, boundary”), and the ending ~-ar~. ~Coto~ descends from Latin ~cautus~ (“guarded, protected”), the past participle of ~cavēre~ (“to be on guard, take heed”), from Proto-Italic *~kaweō~ and ultimately Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kewh₁-~ (“to observe, heed”). The same root shows up in Ancient Greek ~koéō~ (“to perceive”), Sanskrit ~kaví~ (“seer, sage”), and — through Germanic — English ~show~, whose oldest sense was « to look at, to observe ».

A ~coto~ was land set under guard, its limits legally marked, so to ~acotar~ became to mark off, delimit, or reserve a space — and, by extension, to annotate a text with boundaries or measurements. The idea of watchful protection persists in the learned doublet ~cauto~ (“cautious”), and in ~cautela~ (“caution”) and ~precaución~ (“precaution”), all from the same ~cavēre~. So the surveyor who draws a line to ~acotar~ a field is, etymologically, standing guard over it.
en.acreditar:
~Acreditar~ was formed in Spanish from the prefix ~a-~ and the noun ~crédito~ (“credit, trust”), on the model of French ~accréditer~. ~Crédito~ comes from Latin ~crēditum~ (“a loan, a thing entrusted”), the past participle of ~crēdere~ (“to believe, to trust”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱred-dʰeh₁-~, literally “to place one’s heart.” Cognate through ~crēdere~ with Italian ~accreditare~ and, in English, with ~credit~, ~creed~, and ~credo~.

That Proto-Indo-European compound is quietly vivid: *~ḱred-dʰeh₁-~ joins *~ḱerd-~ (“heart”) with the root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place”), so to believe was, at root, “to put your heart into” something. The first element is the same *~ḱerd-~ that surfaces in Latin ~cor~, ~cordis~ (“heart”) and, through Germanic, in English ~heart~. ~Acreditar~ carries the trust sense in several directions — “to accredit, to vouch for, to prove.” Its Spanish relatives keep the belief and lending threads side by side: ~creer~ (“to believe”), ~creencia~ (“belief”), ~crédulo~ (“credulous”), ~increíble~ (“incredible”), and ~acreedor~ (“creditor”).
en.activar:
A learned verb: from the adjective ~activo~ (“active”) with ~-ar~ — reinforced by French ~activer~ — going back to Latin ~āctīvus~, from ~āctus~, the past participle of ~agere~ (“to do, drive, act”), from Proto-Italic *~agō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”). The root is old and far-flung: cognates include Ancient Greek ~ágō~ (“to lead”), Sanskrit ~ájati~ (“drives”), and Old Norse ~aka~ (“to move”). From the same Latin ~agere~ English draws ~act~, ~agent~, and ~agile~.

~agere~ became one of Latin’s most productive roots — “to drive” widening into “to do, act, conduct.” ~activar~ itself means to set something in motion or switch it on. The family in Spanish is enormous: ~acto~, ~acción~, ~actor~, ~actuar~, ~actividad~, ~agente~, ~agencia~, ~ágil~, ~agitar~, ~exigir~, and ~reaccionar~. A hidden relative is ~examen~ (“exam”), from Latin ~exāmen~, originally the needle of a balance — the thing that “drives out” a true weight — so every test still faintly recalls a weighing-scale.
en.actualizar:
A modern coinage, ~actual~ plus the verb-forming suffix ~-izar~. Spanish ~actual~ comes from Late Latin ~āctuālis~ (“active, practical”), from ~āctus~ (“a doing, an act”), the participle of ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, to lead”). Cognate with English ~act~, ~agent~, and ~actual~, and with French ~actualiser~.

Here a false friend hides in plain sight: Spanish ~actual~ does not mean English “actual” (real) — it means “current, present-day,” the time that is now being enacted. So ~actualizar~ means “to make current,” that is, to update — a nuance the software age made everyday. From the same ~agere~ Spanish keeps a large family: ~acto~ (“act”), ~acción~ (“action”), ~agente~ (“agent”), ~actuar~ (“to act”), ~agenda~ (“things to be done”), and even ~examen~ (“examination,” from ~exigere~, “to weigh out, drive out”).
en.actuar:
From Medieval Latin ~actuāre~ (“to put into action, to carry out”), formed on ~actus~ (“a doing, an act”), the past participle of ~agere~ (“to drive, to lead, to do”). ~agere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~agō~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, to set in motion”), one of the most fertile roots in the whole language family — source also of Greek ~ágō~ and, in the north, of English ~act~, ~agent~, and ~agile~. Its Romance siblings are Italian ~attuare~ and Portuguese ~atuar~.

In Latin, ~agere~ meant to drive cattle, to conduct business, to plead a case, to spend time — an enormous fan of senses all radiating from “setting something in motion.” The derived ~actuāre~ meant to make actual, to realize; Spanish ~actuar~ kept that and added the theatrical sense of “to act, to perform” and the legal sense of a court's “proceeding.” The past participle ~actus~ seeded an astonishing crowd of Spanish words — ~acto~, ~acción~, ~actor~, ~actividad~, ~actual~ (which in Spanish means “present-day,” not “real”), ~agente~, ~ágil~, and even ~agitar~ and, more distantly, ~examen~ (through ~exigere~, “to drive out, to weigh”). Few Latin roots left so wide a footprint.
en.acudir:
The origin of ~acudir~ is debated, but the account favored by Corominas derives it from Old Spanish ~recudir~ (“to rebound, respond, pay back what is owed”), with the original prefix ~re-~ later reshaped to ~a-~. ~recudir~ comes from Latin ~recutere~ (“to strike back, cause to rebound”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back”) and ~quatere~ (“to shake, to strike”). ~quatere~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kʷeh₁t-~ (“to shake”). Through ~quatere~ and its participle it is cognate with English ~percussion~, ~concussion~, ~discuss~, and ~rescue~.

The thread that ties the senses together is response: ~recudir~ meant “to rebound” and then “to respond to a call or pay what one owes,” and from “responding to a summons” came the modern ~acudir~ — “to come when called, to show up, to turn to someone for help.” One still ~acude a~ an appointment, a call, or a person in need. Its clearest surviving cousin is ~sacudir~ (“to shake”), from a sibling compound of ~quatere~; the learned line of the same root gave Spanish ~discutir~ (“to discuss”) and ~percutir~ (“to strike, percuss”). A verb of coming, then, that began life as a verb of shaking and rebounding.
en.acumular:
From Latin ~accumulāre~ (“to heap up”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~cumulāre~ (“to pile up”), from ~cumulus~ (“heap, mass, surplus”), traditionally traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱeuH-~ (“to swell”). Latin ~cumulus~ survives unchanged as the meteorologist’s ~cumulus~ cloud; the verb gave Italian ~accumulare~, French ~accumuler~, and Portuguese ~acumular~.

~Acumular~ is a learned borrowing, taken straight from written Latin with its shape intact. Latin ~cumulus~ also traveled a rougher, popular road into Spanish, where sound change reshaped it: through metathesis and vowel loss it became Old Spanish ~colmo~ (“the heaping top, the very brim”), source of the verb ~colmar~ (“to fill to overflowing, to fulfill”) and the everyday exclamation ~¡el colmo!~ (“the last straw!”). So the tidy Latin ~cumulus~ split into two Spanish lines: the bookish ~cúmulo~ and ~acumular~ on one side, the homely ~colmar~ on the other — both, at heart, about a pile heaped past its edge.
en.acusar:
From Latin ~accūsāre~ (“to call to account, to accuse”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~causa~ (“cause, reason; lawsuit, legal case”). The literal sense is to call someone toward a causa — to summon them to answer a charge in court. Spanish ~acusar~ is a learned borrowing that preserves the Latin form. It is cognate with Italian ~accusare~, French ~accuser~, Portuguese ~acusar~, and English ~accuse~, and — through ~causa~ — with English ~cause~.

The origin of ~causa~ itself is uncertain within Latin, so the chain of ~acusar~ reaches back confidently only to that noun and no further — a reminder that even a common verb can have a firm middle and a hazy floor. From the courtroom sense the verb broadened: Spanish ~acusar~ means to accuse, but also to acknowledge (~acusar~ recibo, “to acknowledge receipt”) and, tellingly, to reveal or betray — a face may ~acusar~ fatigue, letting a hidden state show. From the same ~causa~ root come ~causar~, ~acusación~, ~excusar~ (from ~excūsāre~, “to free from a charge”), and ~recusar~.
en.adaptar:
Spanish ~adaptar~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~adaptāre~ (“to fit to”), from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~aptāre~ (“to fit, adjust”), a frequentative of ~apere~ (“to fasten, attach”); its participle ~aptus~ (“fitted, suitable”) is the form that survives. The root is Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ep-~ (“to grasp, take”). Cognates run through Italian ~adattare~, French ~adapter~, and Portuguese ~adaptar~, and through ~aptus~ to English ~adapt~, ~apt~, and ~aptitude~.

The simple verb ~apere~ was already so old in Rome that it survived mainly in grammarians’ notes; the living forms were the participle ~aptus~ and the frequentative ~aptāre~. A charming offshoot is ~attitude~: through Italian ~attitudine~ and Late Latin ~aptitūdo~, an “attitude” was first the fitting posture of a figure in a painting. Spanish keeps the family in ~apto~ (“apt, fit”), ~aptitud~ (“aptitude”), ~adaptación~ (“adaptation”), ~inepto~ (“inept,” “not fitted”), and ~adaptador~ (“adapter”) — the last now most often a plug between incompatible devices, still doing exactly what the root means: making one thing fit another.
en.adecuar:
Spanish ~adecuar~ was borrowed from Latin ~adaequāre~ (“to make equal, to level”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to”) and the verb ~aequāre~ (“to make even”), which was built on the adjective ~aequus~ (“equal, level, fair”). The further origin of ~aequus~ is uncertain, so the chain is secure only back to Latin. The Latin verb gave learned, late-borrowed forms across Romance rather than an inherited popular one, so beside ~adecuar~ stand the parallel loans French ~adéquat~ and English ~adequate~, all reflecting the past participle ~adaequātus~. The same ~aequus~ also yielded Spanish ~igual~ (“equal,” through Vulgar Latin) and the openly learned ~ecuación~ and ~ecuador~.

The core idea is “to make one thing match another,” to bring it to the same level; adapting comes from equalizing. That is why ~adecuar~ today means “to adapt, fit, suit,” as in fitting a text to its audience — one levels the register to the reader. A small surprise lives in the present tense: usage divides between the older ~adecuo~ (stress on the ~a~) and the analogical ~adecúo~ (stress on the ~u~), and the Real Academia now admits both. Kin of ~aequus~ crowd the vocabulary of fairness and measure — ~igualdad~, ~ecuánime~, ~equidad~, ~equinoccio~ (“equal night”), and ~adecuado~ (“adequate, suitable”) itself — every one of them still turning on the notion of two things brought level.
en.adelantar:
From ~adelante~ (“forward, ahead”), formed with the directional prefix ~a-~ on ~delante~ (“in front”), which comes from Latin ~dē~ (“from”) plus ~in ante~ (“in front”), where ~ante~ means “before,” from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ent-~ (“front, forehead”). The Latin ~ante~ is cognate with Greek ~antí~ (“against, opposite”) and Sanskrit ~ánti~ (“before, facing”), and, through the ~and-~ element it preserves, with English ~answer~.

Layer by layer the word piled up spatial prefixes: ~ante~ (“before”) became ~in ante~, then Old Spanish ~denante~ and ~delante~, then ~adelante~ (“forward”), and finally the verb ~adelantar~ — to put or move something forward. Hence its modern senses fan out from a single image of “forward”: to advance, to overtake on the road, to pay in advance, to run fast (of a clock). Kin in Spanish include ~delantero~, ~antes~, ~antaño~ and ~adelanto~.
en.adentrar:
A parasynthetic verb built in Spanish from the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad~, “to, toward”) + the adverb ~dentro~ (“inside”) + the verb ending ~-ar~ — literally “to put or go inside.” ~dentro~ descends from Latin ~dē intrō~ (“from within”), where ~intrō~ (“inward, to the inside”) belongs with ~inter~ (“between, among”) and ~intrā~ (“within”), all resting on Proto-Indo-European *~h₁en~ (“in”). Through that root the word is distant kin to English ~in~ and ~inn~, German ~in~, and the ~inter-~ of countless borrowings. Portuguese has the parallel ~adentrar~ and Italian the related ~entrare~; Spanish itself inherited ~entrar~ from Latin ~intrāre~.

~adentrar~ means to go or penetrate deep into something — a forest, a subject, a mystery — and is most alive in its pronominal form ~adentrarse~ (“to venture into, delve into”): el explorador se ~adentró~ en la selva. It doubles the sense already carried by ~entrar~ (“to enter”) but adds the flavour of going further in, past the threshold. The same ~dentro~ underlies ~adentro~ (“inside,” as a direction) and the noun phrase los ~adentros~ (“one’s innermost self”). From the wider ~inter~/~intrā~ family Spanish holds ~interior~, ~íntimo~, ~entrada~, and ~internar~ — every one a way of naming what lies within.
en.adherir:
From Latin ~adhaerēre~ (“to stick to, cling to”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~haerēre~ (“to stick, cling, be fixed”). ~Haerēre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~haizēō~, whose deeper origin is uncertain; it has been tentatively linked to Proto-Indo-European *~gʰeys-~ (“to adhere, stick”), though even this is problematic, and cognates are scarce — Lithuanian ~gaišti~ (“to linger, be slow”) is one proposed relative. Italian ~aderire~, French ~adhérer~ and Portuguese ~aderir~ are the Romance parallels.

The physical sense of sticking fast broadened into the figurative one that dominates today: to ~adherir~ is to attach oneself to a cause, a party, or an agreement — one ~se adhiere~ a un partido or a un tratado. The related noun ~adhesión~ names both a physical bond and an act of joining; ~adhesivo~ is glue. From the same ~haerēre~ Latin also formed ~inhaerēre~ and ~haesitāre~ (“to stick, hesitate”), which is why English ~hesitate~ — literally to keep sticking — is a distant cousin of ~adherir~, along with ~adhesive~ and ~cohere~.
en.adiestrar:
Spanish ~adiestrar~ is formed from the prefix ~a-~, the adjective ~diestro~ (“right-handed; skillful”), and the ending ~-ar~. ~Diestro~ comes from Latin ~dexter~ (“on the right; skillful, favorable”), from Proto-Indo-European *~deḱs-~ (“right, right-hand”). Cognates include Ancient Greek ~dexiós~, Sanskrit ~dákṣiṇa~, and — learnedly borrowed into English from the same Latin — ~dexterous~ (“nimble, adroit”).

Across many Indo-European cultures the right hand was the deft, favored one, so « right-handed » and « skilled » were long a single idea; ~adiestrar~ therefore means to make someone ~diestro~ — to train, drill, and render capable, whether a horse, a soldier, or an apprentice. The same root gives Spanish the noun ~destreza~ (“skill, dexterity”) and the adjective ~ambidiestro~ (“ambidextrous,” literally « right-handed on both sides »). Even the wariness of the « left » survives beside it, for where ~diestro~ prized skill, its counterpart ~siniestro~ came to mean « sinister » — the old bias of the hands preserved in the vocabulary of training.
en.adir:
A rare, strictly legal verb, ~adir~ comes straight from Latin ~adīre~ (“to go to, approach; to enter upon, take possession of”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and the verb ~īre~ (“to go”). ~īre~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”), one of the oldest and most widespread verbal roots, the same one that surfaces in Latin ~ire~-derivatives across the Romance languages. Italian preserves a matching legal ~adire~ (“to apply to a court; to accept an inheritance”), and the plain Latin ~īre~ is the ancestor of Spanish ~ir~ itself, whose paradigm was later patched together from three different Latin verbs.

In Roman law ~adīre hereditatem~ meant to step forward and formally take up an inheritance, and it is exactly this narrow sense that Spanish preserved: to ~adir~ is to accept an inheritance, expressly or tacitly, before a notary. The verb survives almost only in the fixed phrase ~adir la herencia~, a fossil of legal Latin that most Spanish speakers never meet. The same ~īre~ root, by contrast, is everywhere once disguised: ~éxito~ (“success,” from ~exitus~, a “going out”), ~tránsito~ (from ~transitus~), ~ambición~ (from ~ambitus~, a “going around” to canvass votes), and ~súbito~ all carry the ancient step of *~h₁ey-~ inside them.
en.adjudicar:
From Latin ~adiudicāre~ (“to award by judgment”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~iudicāre~ (“to judge”), the verb of ~iūdex~ (“judge”). That noun is itself built from ~iūs~ (“law, right”) and a root form of ~dīcere~ (“to say, pronounce”) — so a judge is, literally, one who “speaks the law.” ~dīcere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, point out”). Cognate with Italian ~aggiudicare~ and French ~adjuger~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~adjudicate~; English ~judge~ comes from the same ~iūdex~.

In Roman law ~adiudicāre~ was a courtroom term: the judge “adjudged” a disputed thing to one party, assigning it by verdict. Spanish preserved that juridical core — to ~adjudicar~ is to award something formally, a public contract, a prize, an inheritance — while the reflexive ~adjudicarse~ came to mean to claim or carry off (a victory, a title). From ~iūdex~ Spanish also has ~juez~, ~juzgar~, ~juicio~ and ~judicial~; from ~dīcere~ it drew a large family including ~decir~, ~dictar~ and ~bendecir~.
en.administrar:
From Latin ~administrāre~ (“to manage, direct, serve”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~ministrāre~ (“to serve, attend”), from ~minister~ (“servant, attendant”). ~minister~ was built on ~minus~ (“less”) — a servant is the “lesser” one — with a suffix mirroring its antonym ~magister~ (“master”), built on ~magis~ (“more”). ~minus~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~mei-~ (“small, less”). Cognate with Italian ~amministrare~ and French ~administrer~, and, through the same Latin stock, English ~minister~ and ~administer~.

A ~minister~ was originally a servant, the one who waits on another, so to ~administrar~ was to serve something to someone or to manage affairs on their behalf. The etymology holds a quiet irony: an administrator, and a government ~ministro~, is by origin a “lesser one,” a servant — the exact opposite of a ~magister~ or master. That same ~minus~/~magis~ (“less”/“more”) contrast surfaces in everyday Spanish as ~menos~ and ~más~. From ~administrāre~ Spanish keeps ~administración~, ~administrador~, ~ministro~, and ~ministerio~; and from the root ~minus~ come ~menos~, ~minúsculo~, and ~minoría~.
en.admirar:
From Latin ~admīrārī~ (“to wonder at, marvel at”), from ~ad-~ (“at, toward”) plus ~mīrārī~ (“to wonder”), a verb built on ~mīrus~ (“wonderful, astonishing”), from Proto-Indo-European *~smey-~ (“to smile, to laugh”). It is cognate with Italian ~ammirare~ and French ~admirer~, and — through ~mīrus~ — with English ~admire~, ~marvel~, ~miracle~, and ~mirror~; through the deeper root *~smey-~ it is a distant cousin of English ~smile~.

That root connection is the surprise: the Latin family of wonder and the Germanic word for a smile spring, by the standard reconstruction, from one Indo-European root for gladness and laughter — so to admire is etymologically to be moved to a smile. Latin ~mīrārī~ gave Spanish two verbs: the everyday ~mirar~ (“to look at,” its wonder worn down to plain seeing) and the learned ~admirar~ (“to admire”). The same root also yields Spanish ~milagro~ (“miracle,” from ~mīrāculum~), ~maravilla~ (“marvel,” from ~mīrābilia~), ~mirada~ (“look, gaze”), and ~admirable~ (“admirable”).
en.admitir:
From Latin ~admittere~ (“to let in, allow to enter”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~mittere~ (“to send, let go, release”), from Proto-Indo-European *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, remove”), an extension of *~mey-~ (“to change”); its past participle ~admissus~ gives the Spanish noun ~admisión~. English carries the borrowings ~admit~, ~mission~, ~permit~ and ~message~.

The semantic path is neat: from “exchange,” the verb ~mittere~ moved to “give, let go” and finally “send,” while ~admittere~ layered on a sense of direction — to send toward and let across the threshold — hence “to admit, allow in,” and by a short moral step “to accept, concede as true.” Spanish keeps both senses in ~admitir~. From the same ~mittere~ comes a sprawling family: the plain verb ~meter~ (“to put in”), plus ~prometer~ (“to promise”), ~comprometer~, ~permitir~, ~remitir~, ~someter~ and the noun ~mensaje~ (“message”) — all, at bottom, acts of sending and letting go.
en.adobar:
Spanish ~adobar~ was borrowed from Old French ~adober~ (also ~adouber~, “to dub a knight, to equip, to arm”), which goes back to a Frankish verb reconstructed as *~dubban~ (“to strike, to push”) — the same Germanic source that English ~dub~ comes from, as in dubbing a knight with the flat of a sword. Because the Frankish form is a reconstruction, that deepest step is proposed rather than firmly attested.

The sense traveled from « equipping » a knight to « preparing, arranging, dressing » in general, and from there to the kitchen and the tannery: modern ~adobar~ means to marinate or season food, and also to tan or dress leather. Its everyday descendant is ~adobo~, the seasoning paste or marinade. Beware a tempting false friend, though: the building material ~adobe~ (“mud brick”) is not related at all — despite the near-identical shape, ~adobe~ came instead from Arabic ~aṭ-ṭūb~ (“the brick”). So ~adobar~ carries a Germanic warrior's kit all the way into a bowl of marinade, while its look-alike belongs to a wholly different language.
en.adoptar:
From Latin ~adoptāre~ (“to choose for oneself, to take by choice, to adopt”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~optāre~ (“to choose, to wish for”). The origin of ~optāre~ is uncertain; De Vaan links it to Proto-Italic *~opeje-~ (“to choose, to grab”) and a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to choose, to seize,” comparing Hittite ~ēpzi~ (“takes, seizes”) — but the reconstruction is debated. Cognate with Italian ~adottare~ and French ~adopter~, and with English ~adopt~, ~opt~, and ~option~.

In Roman law ~adoptāre~ was a precise term: the formal act by which a paterfamilias took an outsider — often an adult male — into his family as a legal heir, a practice so central that emperors chose their successors this way. The core verb ~optāre~ simply meant “to choose,” and the prefix ~ad-~ points the choosing toward oneself. Spanish carries both the legal sense (adopting a child) and a figurative one (to ~adoptar~ a measure, a posture, a custom). From the same ~optāre~ come Spanish ~optar~ (“to opt”), ~opción~ (“option”), ~optativo~ (“optional”), ~adoptivo~ (“adoptive”), and ~cooptar~ (“to co-opt”).
en.adorar:
Spanish ~adorar~ comes straight from Latin ~adōrāre~ (“to address, entreat, worship”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and the verb ~ōrāre~ (“to speak formally, plead, pray”). Roman grammarians derived ~ōrāre~ from ~ōs~ (genitive ~ōris~, “mouth”) — literally “to use one's mouth” — but this may be folk etymology; a competing view links ~ōrāre~ to an inherited root of solemn, ritual utterance, seen in words for prayer in Greek and Sanskrit. The question is genuinely unsettled, so the “mouth” story is best flagged as the traditional guess, not fact. Either way the descendants are plentiful: English took ~adore~, ~oration~, ~oral~ and ~oracle~ from the same stock, and French has ~adorer~.

In classical Latin ~adōrāre~ was a public, almost legal act — to address a god with the correct words, to entreat, to venerate; the swooning hyperbole of ~te adoro~ (“I adore you”) for mortal affection is a later, Romance softening. The ~ōrāre~ core seeded a whole vocabulary of speech and worship in Spanish: ~orar~ (“to pray”), ~oración~ (“prayer,” and in grammar “sentence”), ~orador~ (“orator”), ~oráculo~ (“oracle”) and ~perorar~ (“to hold forth”). A caution for the curious: ~adornar~ (“to adorn”) looks like kin but is not — it belongs to ~ōrnāre~, not ~ōrāre~. From a root whose very beginning — the mouth or a rite of solemn speech — remains in doubt, Spanish built its words for prayer, eloquence, and love.
en.adquirir:
From Latin ~acquīrere~ (also ~adquīrere~, “to acquire, get”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~quaerere~ (“to seek, look for, ask”). The deep origin of ~quaerere~ is uncertain, and no secure Proto-Indo-European root is established for it. Spanish ~adquirir~ is a learned borrowing that kept the Latin ~-quir-~ stem visible; the same verb gave French ~acquérir~, Italian ~acquisire~, and English ~acquire~.

The Latin verb meant literally “to seek in addition,” to get something over and above what one already had, and that sense of gaining by effort survives in modern ~adquirir~. Its everyday sibling in Spanish is ~querer~, also from ~quaerere~: where the acquisitive prefix pulled one branch toward “getting,” the bare verb drifted from “seeking” to “wanting” and “loving.” From the same ~quaerere~ family Spanish also inherited ~cuestión~, ~requerir~, ~inquirir~, ~pesquisa~, ~exquisito~, and the noun ~adquisición~.
en.aducir:
From Latin ~addūcere~ (“to lead or bring toward”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~dūcere~ (“to lead”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to lead, draw”). The native English cognates of that root are humble ones — ~tow~ and ~tug~ — while Latin handed English the loftier borrowings ~duke~ and ~duct~ and ~adduce~ itself; Italian shows the compound in ~addurre~. Spanish inherited the verb twice over: in Old Spanish it lived on as a popular, patrimonial word ~aduzir~ meaning simply « to bring », with an irregular past participle ~aducho~ from Latin ~adductus~. That homely medieval verb faded, and the modern ~aducir~ (“to adduce, cite as evidence”) is a later learned re-borrowing straight from the Latin, which is why its sense stayed close to the courtroom and the argument rather than the everyday « bringing » of its older self.

The Latin ~dūcere~ was a workhorse of word-building, and its prefixed compounds seeded a whole Spanish family: ~conducir~ (“to drive, conduct”), ~producir~, ~reducir~, ~traducir~ (“to translate,” literally to lead across) and ~inducir~, alongside the nouns ~ducto~ and ~acueducto~ and even ~duque~ (“duke,” the leader). Semantically ~aducir~ narrowed elegantly: from physically leading something toward you to figuratively bringing forward reasons, proofs or examples in support of a claim — the sense that English ~adduce~ shares. So when a speaker ~aduce~ un argumento, the underlying image is the old Roman one of a commander leading his forces up to the line: the evidence is marched into position.
en.advertir:
From Latin ~advertere~ (“to turn toward, direct one’s attention to”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~vertere~ (“to turn”); Spanish shifted it into the -ir conjugation. ~vertere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~wertō~ and from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wert-~ (“to turn, rotate”), a highly productive root that surfaces across the family. Through Latin it gives Spanish and English a legion of “turn” words; through Germanic the same *~wert-~ yields English ~-ward~ (“turned toward,” as in toward, forward) and the verb ~worth~ in the archaic sense “to become.” Romance cognates of the verb itself include French ~avertir~ and Italian ~avvertire~, both, like Spanish ~advertir~, meaning “to warn, notify.”

The literal image behind ~advertir~ is turning: to “turn toward” something is to notice it, and to make another person turn toward it is to warn or point it out. Spanish holds both halves of that logic at once — ~advertir~ means “to notice, perceive” and “to warn, caution,” so context decides whether you have spotted the danger or flagged it for someone else. The English doublet ~advertise~ took the “make others turn toward” sense down the commercial road to mean “publicize.” From the same *~wert-~ Spanish is thick with descendants: ~verter~ (“to pour”), ~convertir~, ~invertir~, ~divertir~ (literally “to turn aside”), ~advertencia~ (“a warning”), ~verso~ and ~versión~, and the borrowed ~universo~ — the whole “turned into one.”
en.afanar:
The Spanish verb ~afanar~ derives from the noun ~afán~ (“eagerness, toil, exertion”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-ar~. The deeper origin of ~afán~, however, is genuinely uncertain and disputed. One proposal traces it to Arabic ~فَنَاء~ (fanāʔ, “annihilation, passing away”), a term steeped in Sufi mysticism; another set of accounts favors a Vulgar Latin source. The sources hedge, and no single etymon is settled. What is clear is the Romance company it keeps: Spanish ~afanar~ is a close cousin of Italian ~affannare~ (“to leave breathless, to vex”) and Catalan ~afanyar~, all sharing the notion of panting, anxious effort.

Whatever its birth, ~afán~ in Old Spanish meant hard, anxious toil, and ~afanar~ meant to work oneself to exhaustion — the reflexive ~afanarse~ (“to strive, to toil away”) still carries exactly that breathless striving. A vivid modern twist runs the other way: in colloquial Spanish, especially in parts of Latin America, ~afanar~ also came to mean « to swindle » or « to steal », as if the thief were the one doing all the strenuous « work ». The most quotable detail — the Arabic Sufi ~فَنَاء~, self-annihilation, lurking behind a word for daily grind — is precisely the disputed one, so it is best enjoyed with caution rather than asserted. Related everyday words include the adjective ~afanoso~ (“laborious, eager”) and the adverb ~afanosamente~.
en.afectar:
From Latin ~affectāre~ (“to strive after, aim at”), the frequentative of ~afficere~ (“to influence, affect”), itself ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~facere~ (“to do, make”). ~facere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~fakiō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, do”). Spanish took the learned ~afectar~ straight from written Latin, yet the very same ~affectāre~ also travelled the popular, spoken road and surfaced as the doublet ~afeitar~ (once “to adorn, to make up,” today simply “to shave”). Cognate with Italian ~affettare~, French ~affecter~, Portuguese ~afetar~, and English ~affect~.

The frequentative sense — to do something repeatedly or pointedly — is why ~afectar~ still splits two ways in Spanish: to affect or influence (« la sequía afectó la cosecha ») and to feign or put on airs (« afectar indiferencia »), the latter preserving the Latin idea of studiously aiming at an effect. The shared root *~dʰeh₁-~ is one of the most fertile in the language, and beyond ~facere~ it seeded ~hacer~, ~hecho~, ~fábrica~, and — through ~afficere~ — the nouns ~afecto~, ~afición~, and ~afectación~.
en.afinar:
Spanish ~afinar~ was built on native soil from the prefix ~a-~, the adjective ~fino~ (“fine, refined”) and the verb-forming suffix ~-ar~ — literally « to make fine ». ~Fino~ itself goes back through Old Spanish ~fin~ (“end”) to Latin ~fīnis~ (“boundary, limit, end”), the idea being that something « fine » is brought to its utmost limit or finishing point. The Latin noun spread across Romance — French and Italian ~fin~ and ~fino~ and, borrowed into English, ~fine~ and ~finish~ — and English even preserves an archaic verb ~affine~ (“to refine”) that parallels ~afinar~ almost exactly. (The ultimate pre-Latin root of ~fīnis~ is itself uncertain, so the trail stops honestly at Latin.)

The semantic journey is a pleasing one. To ~afinar~ is to bring something to a fine point: to refine metals, to sharpen or perfect a skill and above all — in music — to tune an instrument, adjusting each string until its pitch is exactly « right » and no more. From the same ~fīnis~ family Spanish drew a crowd of common words: ~fin~ (“end”), ~final~, ~finalizar~, ~finar~ (“to die,” to reach one's end), ~definir~, ~confín~ (“boundary”) and ~refinar~. The reflexive ~afinarse~ can even mean to become more polished or genteel — a person, like a violin, brought into tune with the finer register around them.
en.afincar:
Spanish ~afincar~ formed from the prefix ~a-~ and the verb ~fincar~, borrowed from Old Galician-Portuguese ~fincar~. That verb descends from Vulgar Latin *~fīgicāre~, a frequentative built on Latin ~fīgere~ (“to drive in, fix in place”), from Proto-Italic *~feigʷō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeygʷ-~ (“to stick, set up”). The very same PIE root, through Germanic, gave English ~ditch~ and ~dike~ and German ~Teich~ (“pond”) — all of them things dug or driven into the earth. Within Spanish, ~fincar~ has a well-known doublet, ~hincar~ (“to drive in, thrust in,” as one ~hinca~ a stake into the ground), the two forms splitting from the same frequentative.

The core sense was concrete: to fix oneself firmly in a place. From « being fixed in the ground », ~fincar~ and ~afincar~ moved naturally to « to settle, to establish oneself, to take up residence » — to plant one's roots somewhere. That is exactly the sense preserved in the modern ~afincarse~ (“to settle down, establish residence”): someone ~afincado~ en Sevilla has driven his stakes into that city. Much of the property vocabulary of Spanish sprang from the same image of fixed, immovable land: ~finca~ (“a piece of real estate, a farm or estate”) is ground one is fastened to, and ~afincar~ shares its whole family with ~fijar~ (“to fix”), ~fijo~ (“fixed”) and ~hito~ (“landmark, milestone”).
en.afirmar:
From Latin ~affirmāre~ (“to make firm, strengthen”), from ~ad-~ + ~firmāre~ (“to make firm”), from ~firmus~ (“firm, strong, steadfast”), from Proto-Italic *~fermos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰer-~ (“to hold, support”). Cognate with French ~affirmer~, Italian ~affermare~, Portuguese ~afirmar~ and English ~affirm~; through the root, with Sanskrit ~dharma~ (“that which upholds, law, duty”).

To affirm is literally “to make firm” — to hold a statement steady. Latin ~firmus~ gave Spanish a broad family: ~firme~, ~firma~ (a signature, what one holds to), ~firmar~ and ~confirmar~. The negative ~infirmus~ (“not firm, weak”) yielded ~enfermo~ (“sick”), so the sick person is, etymologically, one who has lost firmness. The PIE root *~dʰer-~ also underlies the Indian ~dharma~, the cosmic order that “holds” all things in place.
en.afrontar:
Spanish ~afrontar~ descends from a Vulgar Latin ~affrontāre~ (“to strike against, face”), a compound of Latin ~ad~ (“to, against”) and ~frontem~, the accusative of ~frons~ (“forehead, brow, front”). Literally it meant to bring one's ~frons~ up ~ad~ another's — to go face to face. It is cognate with Italian ~affrontare~, French ~affronter~, and English ~affront~ and ~confront~.

Spanish inherited the word twice, in a learned and a popular form: ~afrontar~ (“to face, to confront”) and the doublet ~afrentar~ (“to insult, to shame”), whose noun ~afrenta~ (“affront”) keeps the sharper edge of the original “blow to the face.” The etymon ~frons~ itself has, in De Vaan's words, “no plausible etymology” — a proposed derivation from a Proto-Indo-European *~bʰren-~ (“to project”) is rejected as semantically weak, so no deep root should be asserted. From ~frons~ Spanish also drew ~frente~ (“forehead; front”), ~frontera~ (“border”), ~frontón~, ~enfrentar~ (“to confront”), and ~confrontar~. To ~afrontar~ a danger is, at root, to turn your forehead toward it.
en.agarrar:
From ~a-~ (a verb-forming prefix, from Latin ~ad-~) plus the noun ~garra~ (“claw, talon”) and the ending ~-ar~ — literally, to take hold of something with the claws. The origin of ~garra~ itself is disputed: by one account it descends from a Vulgar Latin *~garra~ borrowed from Gaulish *~garrā~ (“leg”), from Proto-Celtic *~garros~, comparable with Old Irish ~gairri~ (“calves of the legs”); by another it comes from Andalusian Arabic ~gārfā~ (“handful”). The sources hedge on both, so the deeper root is best left open.

Whatever its ancestry, ~garra~ meant the claw of a beast or a bird, and ~agarrar~ carried the ferocity of that image: not merely to take, but to seize and clamp down, as a hawk grips its prey. Over time it softened into the everyday Spanish word for grabbing, catching, or clutching — one can ~agarrar~ a rope, a bus, or an opportunity — and across much of Latin America it has largely displaced ~coger~ for “to grab, to take.” From the same noun Spanish keeps ~garra~ (“claw,” and figuratively “grit, fighting spirit”), ~agarre~ (“grip”), ~agarrón~ (“a sudden grab, a scuffle”), and ~agarrado~ (“clutching; stingy”).
en.agotar:
From Vulgar Latin *~eguttāre~ (“to drain to the last drop”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out, off”) and ~gutta~ (“a drop”). The verb should by rights have begun with ~e-~ — Old Spanish had ~egotar~ — but the initial vowel was later reshaped to ~a-~, by confusion with the countless verbs in ~a-~. Latin ~gutta~ is of uncertain deeper ancestry, but its Romance children are everywhere: Spanish ~gota~ (“drop”), French ~goutte~, Italian ~gotta~, and — through medieval medicine — English ~gout~.

The literal image is a spring or a well emptied drop by drop, and from “to drain dry” the verb passed to “to use up completely, exhaust” — a mine, one's patience, one's strength. A book or an edition that is ~agotado~ is “sold out,” drained to the last copy. The English cognate ~gout~ carries a vivid fossil of old physiology: the disease was named from ~gutta~ because doctors imagined it caused by drops of corrupt humor falling into the joints. From the same “drop” Spanish keeps ~gota~, ~gotear~ (“to drip”), ~gotera~ (“a leak”), ~cuentagotas~ (“dropper”), and ~agotamiento~ (“exhaustion”).
en.agradecer:
Spanish ~agradecer~ builds on Old Spanish ~gradecer~ (“to be thankful”) with the prefix ~a-~. The base descends from an inchoative Vulgar Latin *~grātēscere~, formed on Latin ~grātus~ (“pleasing, thankful”), from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷerH-~ (“to praise, welcome”). The adjective ~grātus~ also gave the noun ~grātia~ (“favor, thanks”), whence Spanish ~gracia~, English ~grace~, and — via ~ad grātum~, “to one’s liking” — English ~agree~.

The ~-ēscere~ ending marked an inchoative, “to come to find pleasing,” which in Spanish settled into the everyday “to thank.” Its most useful quirk is that ~agradecer~ takes the thing as object — one thanks a favor, ~agradezco tu ayuda~ — where English needs a preposition. The same root spread widely: ~gratitud~ (“gratitude”), ~agradable~ (“pleasant”), ~grato~ (“agreeable”), ~gratis~ and ~gratuito~ (“free of charge”), and ~congratular~ (“to congratulate,” literally “to rejoice together”).
en.agravar:
From Latin ~aggravāre~ (“to make heavier, weigh down”), from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~gravāre~ (“to burden”), built on ~gravis~ (“heavy, grave”). ~gravis~ rises from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷreh₂-~ (“heavy”), a root shared by Sanskrit ~guru~ (“heavy,” the spiritual “weighty one”) and Greek ~barýs~ (“heavy”). Cognate through Latin with Italian ~aggravare~, French ~aggraver~ and Portuguese ~agravar~, and with the English borrowings ~grave~ and ~gravity~.

The literal Latin sense — to pile weight on — became figurative early: to make a matter heavier is to make it worse, hence ~agravar~ (“to aggravate, worsen”). Spanish inherited the same verb twice: the learned ~agravar~ and the popular ~agraviar~ (“to wrong, offend”), where the “weight” laid on someone is an injustice. The ~gravis~ family runs deep — ~grave~, ~gravedad~, ~gravamen~, ~gravitar~ and ~agravante~ — and even the imported ~guru~ is, at root, simply “heavy.”
en.agraviar:
Spanish ~agraviar~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~aggraviāre~, a reshaping of Latin ~aggravāre~ (“to make heavier, to burden”), itself ~ad-~ (“to”) plus ~gravāre~ (“to weigh down”), from the adjective ~gravis~ (“heavy, weighty, serious”). ~Gravis~ traces to Proto-Italic *~gʷraus~ and Proto-Indo-European *~gʷréh₂us~ (“heavy”), a root of distinguished pedigree: it is cognate with Ancient Greek ~βαρύς~ (barús, “heavy”) and Sanskrit ~gurú~ (“heavy; venerable”). English received the same Latin stock in the borrowings ~grave~, ~grief~, ~aggravate~ and the near-twin ~aggrieve~.

The metaphor at the heart of ~agraviar~ is that a wrong is a weight laid unjustly on someone. Where the doublet ~agravar~ kept the literal sense « to make heavier, to worsen » (an illness ~agrava~, it grows worse), ~agraviar~ specialized into the moral realm: « to offend, to wrong, to injure someone's honor », to burden a person with an injustice they did not deserve. The deverbal noun ~agravio~ (“offense, grievance, wrong”) names exactly that injury, and English legal ~grievance~ carries the identical image. From the same heavy root Spanish gathered ~grave~ (“serious, grave”), ~gravar~ (“to tax, to encumber”), ~gravedad~ (“gravity, seriousness”) and ~gravamen~ (“lien, burden”).
en.agregar:
From Latin ~aggregāre~ (“to add to a flock, gather together, join”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~gregāre~ (“to herd, gather into a flock”), the verb of ~grex~ (genitive ~gregis~, “flock, herd”). The noun goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~ger-~ (“to gather, come together”), which also gave Greek ~ageírō~ (“I gather”) and ~agorá~ (the gathering place, the marketplace). Through the Latin ~grex~ branch, ~agregar~ is cognate with a cluster of English words — ~gregarious~, ~congregate~, ~aggregate~, and ~segregate~. Italian ~aggregare~ and Portuguese ~agregar~ match it directly.

The whole family is about the flock. To ~agregar~ is to add one more to the group — the plainest modern sense, “to add.” Spanish keeps the herd-image alive in ~grey~ (“flock; congregation of the faithful”), ~congregar~ (“to congregate”), ~segregar~ (“to separate from the flock”), and ~disgregar~ (“to scatter, break up”). The most vivid relative is English ~egregious~: Latin ~egregius~ meant “out of the flock” (~ex~ + ~grex~) and so “outstanding, distinguished” — a compliment in Latin that soured in English into ‘outstandingly bad.’ Spanish preferred the neutral path: an ~agregado~ is simply something added, or an embassy’s attaché.
en.agrupar:
A denominal verb: ~a-~ (“to, toward”) + the noun ~grupo~ (“group”) + ~-ar~, so literally “to form into a group.” Spanish ~grupo~ was borrowed from Italian ~gruppo~ (“knot, cluster, bunch”), which came from a Germanic source, Proto-Germanic *~kruppaz~ (“rounded mass, lump”). The same Germanic word, via French, gave English ~group~ and is related to English ~crop~ (originally the rounded top of a plant).

Italian painters used ~gruppo~ for a cluster of figures massed together in a composition; French took it as ~groupe~, and from there the word spread across Europe as the ordinary term for any set of things gathered as one. Spanish ~agrupar~ simply verbalized that noun, “to gather into a group.” From ~grupo~ Spanish also formed ~agrupación~, ~agrupamiento~ and ~subgrupo~, while the Germanic root left a second, more physical trace in ~grupa~ (“the croup or haunches of a horse”), borrowed through French ~croupe~.
en.aguantar:
The favored account derives ~aguantar~ from Italian ~agguantare~ (“to seize, grip; to hold fast a rope”), a term of the sea, itself from ~guanto~ (“glove”), from a Frankish *~want~ (“glove”) — so the Spanish word is ultimately kin to ~guante~, its own word for “glove.” The origin is debated and the sources hedge (the RAE writes “perhaps from Italian ~agguantare~”), but the nautical borrowing, first attested around 1587, is the account most etymologists favor.
