By this account the picture is a gloved or gauntleted hand closing firmly on something: from “to grip” the verb passed, in sailors' speech, to “holding a rope or a ship steady against the strain of wind and wave,” and from resisting that force to the modern “to endure, bear, put up with.” If the glove etymology is right, ~aguantar~ and ~guante~ are the same image twice over — the hand that grips and the leather that clothes it. From the same family Spanish keeps ~aguante~ (“stamina, staying power”) and ~guantelete~ (“gauntlet”).
en.aguardar:
Unlike most of its neighbors, ~aguardar~ has Germanic blood. It is ~a-~ prefixed to ~guardar~ (“to guard, keep, watch over”), which Spanish took from a Germanic *~wardōn~ / Proto-Germanic *~wardāną~ (“to guard, watch”) — brought in by the Visigoths and reinforced through Frankish, which Medieval Latin borrowed as ~wardāre~. The ultimate source is Proto-Indo-European *~wer-~ (“to perceive, watch out for”). The Germanic word is a cousin of English ~ward~ and ~warden~ and, by a French detour from the same Germanic stock, of English ~guard~ itself; German ~warten~ (“to wait”) is a strikingly close semantic match, since it too slid from « watching » to « waiting ».

The path from « guarding » to « waiting » is the heart of the story. To watch over something attentively is to keep your eyes on it and abide — and from that watchful abiding ~aguardar~ took its modern meaning « to await, to wait for », the patient cousin of the plainer ~esperar~. Where ~guardar~ kept the sense of keeping and protecting (~guardar~ un secreto, to keep a secret), ~aguardar~ specialized in expectant waiting: one ~aguarda~ el momento oportuno. The same Germanic root fanned out across Spanish into ~guardia~ (“guard, watch”), ~guardián~ (“guardian”), ~guarida~ (“lair, refuge”), ~resguardar~ (“to shelter”) and ~aguardo~ (a hunter's hide, the place where one waits).
en.ahondar:
Spanish ~ahondar~ was formed on native ground from the prefix ~a-~, the adjective ~hondo~ (“deep”) and the suffix ~-ar~, though it was also inherited nearly whole from Vulgar Latin *~affundāre~. Its base ~hondo~ comes from an older ~fondo~, from Latin ~fundus~ (“bottom, base, foundation”) — the Castilian change of initial Latin f- to a silent h- is what turned ~fondo~ into ~hondo~. ~Fundus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~fundos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~bʰudʰmn̥~ (“bottom”), a venerable root that also produced English ~bottom~, Ancient Greek ~πυθμήν~ (puthmḗn, “bottom of a vessel”) and Sanskrit ~budhna~. Portuguese preserves the exact cognate verb ~afundar~.

The metaphor is transparent: to ~ahondar~ is « to go to the bottom of » something, and so the verb means both « to deepen » literally — to dig a hole deeper, to sink a channel further down — and, figuratively, « to delve into, to go deeply into » a subject: uno ~ahonda~ en un problema. That double life, physical and intellectual, mirrors ~hondo~ itself, which describes both a deep well and a deep sorrow (~un pesar hondo~). The same ~fundus~ family filled Spanish with ~fondo~ (“bottom, background, fund”), ~hondura~ (“depth”), ~profundo~ (“profound, deep”), ~profundizar~, ~hondonada~ (“a hollow, a dell”) and ~desfondar~ (“to knock the bottom out of”).
en.ahorrar:
The verb ~ahorrar~ was built from the adjective ~horro~ (“freed, free of obligation”) with the prefix ~a-~, from Hispanic Arabic ~ḥúrr~, from Classical Arabic ~ḥurr~ (“free, freeborn”). The word entered Castilian during the centuries of Al-Andalus. It has kin across Iberia: Portuguese and Galician ~aforrar~, and the related Portuguese noun ~alforria~ (“the freeing of a slave”).

The semantic journey is remarkable. Because ~ḥurr~ meant “free,” to ~ahorrar~ first meant to grant freedom — to manumit a slave or release a captive. From “to free a person” it broadened to “to free someone of something,” a burden or an obligation, and then to “to spare oneself” a trouble or an expense. From sparing an expense it slid to its modern sense: to save, to set money aside. So, etymologically, to save money is to free oneself of the spending — the coin is “liberated” for later. The everyday noun ~ahorro~ (“saving, savings”) rides along, together with ~ahorrador~ and ~ahorrativo~ (“thrifty”), and the old adjective ~horro~ still lingers in legal and dialectal use meaning “free, exempt.”
en.aislar:
From ~isla~ (“island”), formed with the prefix ~a-~ and the verb-ending ~-ar~; ~isla~ descends from Latin ~insula~ (“island”), a word of uncertain origin — perhaps « in salō », “in the open sea,” from ~salum~ (“the deep”), though it may equally be a loan from some lost language. Cognate with Portuguese ~ilha~, Italian ~isola~ and French ~île~, and — through the same Latin word — with English ~isle~ and, via Italian ~isolare~, the learned twins English ~isolate~ and French ~isoler~.

The verb began quite literally: to ~aislar~ was to make something into an island, to ring it with water, and only later did it broaden to the figurative “to separate, cut off, set apart” that dominates today. A spelling curiosity sits in plain view: where the noun is ~isla~, the verb shows ~ai-~, because the ~a-~ prefix and the initial ~i~ of ~isla~ fused into a diphthong. English took the same idea by a different road, borrowing Italian ~isolato~ as ~isolated~ in the eighteenth century. From the ~insula~ family Spanish also keeps ~isleño~, ~islote~, ~insular~, ~aislamiento~ and ~aislante~.
en.ajuntar:
Spanish ~ajuntar~ is the prefix ~a-~ added to ~juntar~ (“to join, put together”), a verb formed from the adjective ~junto~ (“joined, together”), which comes from Latin ~iūnctus~, the past participle of ~iungere~ (“to join, yoke together”). Behind it stand Proto-Italic *~jungō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~yewg-~ (“to join, yoke”) — one of the great Indo-European roots, formed with a nasal infix. It is cognate with English ~yoke~ and, through Latin and French, with ~join~ and ~junction~; with Latin ~iugum~ (“yoke”) and Ancient Greek ~ζυγόν~ (zugón); and even with Sanskrit ~yóga~ (“union”), the very ~yoga~ of the meditative discipline, a yoking of body and mind.

~Ajuntar~ is essentially a colloquial or regional doublet of ~juntar~, and the prefix ~a-~ adds little beyond emphasis — in the standard language ~juntar~ (“to gather, assemble, join”) does the everyday work, while ~ajuntar~ survives in dialect and in the children's playground taunt ~ya no te ajunto~ (« I won't play with you anymore »). The root's harvest in Spanish is enormous: ~junto~ (“together”), ~junta~ (“a board, a junta,” an assembled council), ~juntura~ and ~coyuntura~ (“a joint; a juncture”), ~conjunto~ (“a set, an ensemble”), ~adjunto~ (“attached, adjunct”), ~yunta~ (“a yoke of oxen”) and ~yugo~ (“yoke”) — all of them, at bottom, things joined.
en.ajustar:
Formed within Romance from the prefix ~a-~ and ~justo~ (“just, exact, right”), from Latin ~iūstus~, itself from ~iūs~ (“law, right”), a noun of debated Indo-European origin. The Late or Vulgar Latin verb is reconstructed as *~adiūstāre~ (“to make right, fit exactly”). Cognate with Italian ~aggiustare~, French ~ajuster~, and Portuguese ~ajustar~; English ~adjust~ was borrowed through Old French from the same verb.

The thread of meaning runs through “right, exact”: to ~ajustar~ is to bring a thing into just proportion — to fit two parts so they meet exactly, to tighten a screw, to settle an account, to agree on a price. From the same ~justo~ Spanish built a broad family: ~ajuste~ (“adjustment, settlement”), ~ajustado~ (“tight, close-fitting”), ~reajustar~ (“to readjust”), and, sharing the deeper root, ~justicia~ (“justice”), ~justo~ (“fair; exact”), and ~ajusticiar~ (“to execute a condemned person,” literally to do justice upon). The financial ~ajuste de cuentas~ (“settling of accounts”) preserves the original sense of making two sides balance exactly.
en.alabar:
From Late Latin ~alapārī~ (“to boast, to brag”), a verb whose deeper origin is genuinely uncertain. Etymologists connect it only tentatively to Latin ~alapa~ (“a slap, a box on the ear, a blow with the open hand”), so that step is best treated as probable rather than settled. Already in the comedies of Plautus this family of words lived in a world of physical gesture. Catalan later took its own ~alabar~ as a loan from Spanish, and the verb stayed largely confined to the Ibero-Romance sphere.

How a word for striking came to mean “to praise” is not clearly explained by the sources, and — because the tie to ~alapa~ is itself only probable — it is wise not to invent a tidy tale of applause or acclamation to bridge the gap. What is secure is the medieval Castilian outcome: ~alabar~ settled firmly into the sense “to praise, to extol,” and from it Spanish built the everyday noun ~alabanza~ (“praise, commendation”). The verb keeps a faintly formal, even liturgical ring — one ~alaba~ a God, a hero, or a fine meal — which is why it turns up so often in prayers, dedications, and old chronicles.
en.alargar:
A Spanish formation, ~a-~ (a prefix from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”) plus ~largo~ (“long”) plus the verb ending ~-ar~ — literally “to make long.” ~Largo~ descends from Latin ~largus~, whose own deeper origin is uncertain and disputed: it has been linked to a Proto-Indo-European *~leh₂y-~ (“fat, grease”), but De Vaan finds the long vowel awkward and other scholars suspect a Mediterranean substrate word, so no PIE root can be stated with confidence. Cognate with Italian ~largo~, French ~large~ and, as a borrowing through French, English ~large~.

The meaning traveled a striking distance: Latin ~largus~ meant “abundant, copious, generous” (the sense kept in English ~large~ and in ~largesse~), but in Spanish ~largo~ shifted to “long” in space and time, leaving the old “abundant” idea mostly to relatives like ~largueza~ (“generosity”). ~Alargar~ therefore means to stretch out in length or duration — one can ~alargar~ a rope or ~alargar~ a meeting. Same family: ~largo~, ~largura~, ~alargamiento~ and the nautical ~largar~ (“to let out, cast off,” as of a sail or line).
en.albergar:
From Old Occitan ~albergar~, from a Germanic *~heriberga~ (“shelter for the army, lodging”), a compound of *~hari~ (“army, host”) + *~bergō~ (“shelter, protection”). Cognate with Italian ~albergare~ (~albergo~ “hotel”), French ~héberger~ (~auberge~ “inn”), German ~Herberge~ (“hostel”), and — from the very same Germanic compound — English ~harbour~/~harbor~.

The image at the root is martial: a *~heriberga~ was the place where a war-band sheltered, and the word softened from military billet to any lodging as armies gave way to travelers. Spanish ~albergar~ thus means both to lodge or shelter guests and, figuratively, to harbor something — a building ~alberga~ a museum, a heart ~alberga~ hopes. From it comes the noun ~albergue~ (“hostel, shelter”). The Germanic *~hari~ (“army”) behind the first element also lies under English ~harbinger~ (first a person sent ahead to arrange lodgings) and army-names like ~Herbert~.
en.alborozar:
A denominal verb, from the noun ~alborozo~ (“great joy, elation”) plus ~-ar~. The noun descends from Hispano-Arabic ~alburúz~, from Classical Arabic ~burūz~, a term for the military review or parade held before an army set out on campaign — the etymology accepted by the Real Academia and by Corominas. Portuguese ~alvoroço~ (and its verb ~alvoroçar~) share the same Arabic source.

The leap from a troop inspection to sheer delight lies in the scene itself: the pre-campaign parade was greeted with shouts and cries of joy, and Castilian kept the emotion while dropping the soldiers. Care is needed with the neighboring word ~alboroto~ (“uproar, commotion”): the two look like twins, but Corominas argued they are not — deriving ~alboroto~ instead from Latin ~volūtāre~ (“to roll, to tumble about”) on the strength of its Catalan and Provençal spread — so their common origin is disputed rather than established. From ~alborozo~ Spanish also formed the adjective ~alborozado~ (“overjoyed, elated”), still a warm, slightly literary way to describe delight.
en.alcanzar:
The origin is debated, but the favored account traces ~alcanzar~ to a Vulgar Latin *~incalciāre~ (“to tread on someone's heels, to pursue”), a verb built on Latin ~calx~ (“heel”). Old Spanish had ~alcanzar~ beside a more transparent ~encalzar~, and the shift of the prefix to ~al-~ is itself uncertain — it may reflect the influence of Latin ~ad~, of the Spanish contraction ~al~, or, by one hypothesis, of the Arabic article ~al-~. Whatever reshaped the head, the Romance kin agree on the body: Portuguese ~alcançar~, Galician ~alcanzar~, and Catalan ~encalçar~ all point back to the same heel-chasing verb.

The image behind the word is vivid: to ~alcanzar~ was first to chase so close that you trod on the runner's ~calx~, his heel — and then, naturally, to catch him, to reach him, to attain your goal. Spanish kept the whole arc of that metaphor, from physical overtaking (« alcanzar la meta ») to abstract achievement (« alcanzar un acuerdo ») to sheer sufficiency (« el dinero no alcanza »). From the same Latin ~calx~ come ~calzar~ (“to put on footwear”), ~calcetín~ (“sock”), ~coz~ (“a kick”), and ~recalcar~ (“to stress, to press down on”).
en.alegar:
From Latin ~allēgāre~ (“to send on a mission, adduce, cite in support”), formed from the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward,” assimilated to ~al-~) and ~lēgāre~ (“to depute, commission”), itself a denominal verb from ~lēx~ (stem ~lēg-~, “law, statute”). ~lēx~ is probably from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, collect”) — a body of law as a gathering of binding rules — the same root as ~legere~ (“to gather, read”). Spanish ~alegar~ is a semi-learned inheritance; cognate with Italian ~allegare~, French ~alléguer~, and English ~allege~.

In classical Latin ~allēgāre~ meant to send someone as an agent and, in speech, to bring something forward as evidence or authority. Spanish kept the second, forensic sense: to ~alegar~ is to plead, to cite a reason or a law in one's defense, which is why the courtroom noun ~alegato~ (“argument, plea”) sits right beside it. The parent ~lēx~ passed into Spanish twice over — as the popular ~ley~ (“law”) and in a swarm of learned kin: ~legal~, ~legítimo~, ~legislar~. From the verb ~lēgāre~ came ~legar~ (“to bequeath”), ~delegar~, ~relegar~, and the noun ~legado~; from the related ~collēga~ came ~colega~. To ~alegar~, then, is to lay a rule on the table.
en.alegrar:
Spanish ~alegrar~ (“to gladden, cheer”) was formed from the adjective ~alegre~ (“happy, cheerful”) plus ~-ar~, matching a Vulgar Latin *~alecrāre~. ~alegre~ goes back through Vulgar Latin *~alecris~ to Latin ~alacer~ (also ~alacris~), “lively, brisk, eager.” The deeper origin of ~alacer~ is genuinely uncertain: it has been tentatively linked to a Proto-Indo-European root of movement — variously reconstructed, roughly “to wander” or “to drive” — but no derivation is secure, so it is best left as debated. Its Romance cousins are clear enough: Italian ~allegro~, French ~allègre~ and Portuguese ~alegre~.

The sense traveled from Latin “brisk, animated” to Spanish “cheerful, glad,” and ~alegrar~ makes that transitive — to make someone glad. The Italian form took a different road into music: ~allegro~ marks a brisk, lively tempo, and it entered English as a musical term with exactly that value, still faithful to the old “lively” sense. In Spanish the family stays warm and everyday — ~alegre~, ~alegría~ (“joy”) and the reflexive ~alegrarse~ (“to be glad, rejoice”). Because the root itself is disputed, these words are among the rare common verbs whose ultimate ancestry the dictionaries decline to pin down.
en.alejar:
A Spanish formation from the prefix ~a-~ and the adverb ~lejos~ (“far”), with the verbal ending ~-ar~. ~Lejos~ descends from Latin ~laxius~ (“more loosely, more widely apart”), the comparative adverb of ~laxus~ (“loose, slack, wide”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sleg-~ (“to be slack, to be languid”). Through that root ~laxus~ is cognate with English ~slack~ and ~lax~, and within Spanish with ~laxo~, ~relajar~ and ~dejar~.

The image hidden in ~lejos~ is spatial slackness: Latin ~laxius~ meant “more loosely, more spread out,” so to be far away was, literally, to be more loosely spaced — and ~alejar~ is to make something take up that slack distance, to move it away. From the same “loosen” idea Spanish also built ~dejar~ (“to let go, to leave”), from Latin ~laxāre~ (“to loosen, to release”), so that letting go and being far apart are quietly the same gesture. Nearby in the family stand ~lejano~, ~lejanía~, ~alejamiento~, ~relajar~, ~laxo~ and ~laxante~ — a cluster all turning on the idea of looseness and release.
en.alentar:
Spanish ~alentar~ (“to encourage; to breathe”) goes back to Vulgar Latin *~alenitāre~, an altered form of *~anhelitāre~, frequentative of Latin ~anhēlāre~ (“to breathe hard, to pant”). The learned doublet of the same Latin verb is ~anhelar~ (“to yearn, to long for”): one word came down the popular road with metathesis and softening, the other was borrowed straight from the books, so ~alentar~ and ~anhelar~ are twins from a single source. Compare Portuguese ~alentar~ and the shared kin ~hálito~ (“breath”).

The semantic thread runs from breath to spirit: to give someone ~aliento~ (“breath”) is to give them heart, and so ~alentar~ shifted from “to breathe” to “to inspire, to encourage.” The reverse, ~desalentar~, is “to dishearten” — literally to take the wind out of someone. From the same breathing-family Spanish keeps ~aliento~, ~anhelar~, ~exhalar~ and ~inhalar~. The precise deeper ancestry of Latin ~hālāre~/~anhēlāre~ is uncertain, so it is best to stop the firm chain at Latin rather than force a root onto it.
en.alertar:
From the noun and adjective ~alerta~, borrowed from the Italian phrase ~all'erta~ (“on the watch”), literally “to the height.” Its core is ~erta~ (“a steep slope, high ground”), from Latin ~ērecta~, the feminine past participle of ~ērigere~ (“to raise, set upright”) — itself ~ē-~ (“up, out”) plus ~regere~ (“to keep straight, direct”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, rule”). Cognate through that root with English ~erect~ and ~right~, and borrowed onward into French ~alerte~.

~all'erta~ was a soldier's cry — “to the high ground!” — the order to a sentinel to take the heights and watch. Univerbated, it became the noun ~alerta~ (a state of readiness), and Spanish coined the verb ~alertar~, “to put on guard.” The buried image is a lookout standing erect on a hilltop. The same PIE root seeded a broad Spanish family: ~erigir~, ~regir~, ~dirigir~, ~corregir~, ~recto~, ~regla~ and ~rey~.
en.alimentar:
From the noun ~alimento~ (“food, nourishment”) plus the verb-forming ~-ar~; ~alimento~ descends from Latin ~alimentum~ (“nourishment”), a derivative of ~alere~ (“to nourish, feed, rear”). ~Alere~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂el-~ (“to nourish, grow”), a root that grew a remarkable family: Latin ~altus~ (“high, tall” — literally “having grown”), ~adolēscere~ (“to grow up”), and English ~old~ (“that which has grown up”), ~adult~, and ~alumnus~ (originally a “nursling, foster-child”).

The core idea was causative: to ~alere~ was to make something grow by feeding it — a child, a herd, a crop, a fire. Spanish ~alimentar~ keeps this exactly — “to feed, nourish” — and stretches easily to machines and abstractions: a stove is fed with wood, a database with data, a hope with small encouragements. The noun ~alimento~ means “food,” ~alimentación~ means “nutrition, diet; food supply,” and ~alimenticio~ means “nutritional.” From the same growing root Spanish also inherited ~alto~ (“tall”), ~adolescente~, and ~adulto~ — all, at bottom, words about having been nourished into size.
en.alinear:
From ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”) + ~línea~ (“line”) + ~-ar~. Spanish ~línea~ descends from Latin ~līnea~ (“linen thread, string, line”), the feminine of ~līneus~ (“of flax”), from ~līnum~ (“flax, linen”), whose deeper origin is uncertain — likely an ancient Mediterranean culture-word rather than a secure Indo-European inheritance. Cognate with French ~aligner~ (from ~à ligne~, “into line”), Italian ~allineare~, and — through ~līnum~ — English ~line~ and ~linen~.

A ~līnea~ was first a “linen thread” — the taut cord a builder or surveyor stretched to mark a straight edge — so ~alinear~ means literally “to bring things onto the line,” to set them in a row. The verb probably followed the model of French ~aligner~. Spanish uses it of troops and teams (~alineación~, a starting lineup) and, figuratively, of political alignment. The ~líne-~ family is broad: ~lineal~, ~delinear~, ~alineación~, ~lino~ (“flax, linen”), and ~lienzo~ (“canvas,” the popularly inherited descendant of Latin ~līnteum~).
en.aliviar:
From Latin ~alleviāre~ (“to lighten, relieve”), from ~ad-~ (“to”) plus ~levis~ (“light in weight”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light, nimble”). Cognate with Italian ~alleviare~ and Portuguese ~aliviar~, and — through the same root — with English ~light~ (not heavy) and, as a learned borrowing, English ~alleviate~.

To lighten a load became, figuratively, to ease pain or grief: ~aliviar~ lifts weight off body or spirit. From ~levis~ Spanish keeps a broad family — ~leve~ (“light, slight”), ~liviano~, ~aligerar~, ~elevar~ and ~relevar~ — all turning on the idea of lightness or lifting.
en.allegar:
Inherited from Latin ~applicāre~ (“to attach to, to bring near”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to weave”). The same root surfaces in English ~ply~ and ~pleat~, in French ~plier~, and in Spanish ~plegar~ (“to fold”). Spanish kept several reflexes of ~applicāre~ side by side: the popular ~llegar~, the semi-learned ~allegar~, and the fully learned ~aplicar~.

The most striking fact is that ~allegar~ and the everyday ~llegar~ (“to arrive”) are the same word twice over: ~applicāre~ meant “to bring one thing up against another,” and in nautical use “to bring a ship to shore” — from which ~llegar~ took its sense of arriving. The heavier ~allegar~ stayed closer to the literal “to draw together,” hence “to gather, to collect, to amass” (money, followers, evidence). It has an old-fashioned, formal flavor today. From the same ~plicāre~ family Spanish also has ~pliegue~ (“fold, crease”), ~aplicar~, and, through cognate compounds, ~emplear~ (“to employ”).
en.almacenar:
From ~almacén~ (“warehouse, storehouse”) plus the verb-forming ending ~-ar~. ~almacén~ came into Spanish from Andalusi Arabic ~al-makhzan~ (“the storehouse”), from the definite article ~al-~ and ~makhzan~, a noun of place from the root ~khazana~ (“to store up, hoard”). The initial ~al-~ that opens so many Spanish words is the fossilized Arabic article, absorbed whole during the centuries of al-Andalus. Cognate — through the Arabic plural ~makhāzin~ — with Italian ~magazzino~, French ~magasin~ (“shop”), and English ~magazine~.

The word's later career is one of the great surprises of etymology. The Arabic ~makhzan~ (“storehouse”) travelled two ways out of the Mediterranean. Into Spanish it stayed concrete: ~almacén~ is a warehouse or, in much of Latin America, a grocery shop, and ~almacenar~ is simply “to store, stockpile.” But Italian ~magazzino~ and French ~magasin~ carried it to English ~magazine~, which first meant a military store for gunpowder, then — figuratively, a “storehouse” of writings — the periodical you read. So a Spanish speaker who ~almacenar~ stores data and an English reader leafing through a ~magazine~ are touching the same Arabic root for a place where things are kept. Modern computing revived the concrete sense: to ~almacenar~ is now most often to save files.
en.almorzar:
A denominal verb, from ~almuerzo~ (“lunch, midday meal”) plus ~-ar~. The noun goes back to Vulgar Latin *~admordium~, from Latin ~admordēre~ (“to bite into”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“at, into”) and ~mordēre~ (“to bite”), from Proto-Italic *~mordeō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~(s)merd-~ (“to bite, to sting”). Through ~mordēre~ Spanish also has ~morder~, matched by French ~mordre~ and Italian ~mordere~; through the same PIE root come English ~smart~ (first “to feel a sharp pain”) and ~mordant~.

Despite the Arabic-looking ~al-~, ~almuerzo~ is not an Arabism at all — that ~al-~ is a development of Latin ~ad-~, not the Arabic article, a neat trap for the eye. The literal sense was simply “a bite”: to breakfast or to lunch was to “take a bite,” and Castilian fixed the verb on the midday meal. The same ~mordēre~ family is rich in Spanish — ~mordisco~ (“a bite, a nibble”), ~mordaz~ (“biting, sarcastic”), and, most vividly, ~remordimiento~ (“remorse”), literally a “biting again” of the conscience.
en.alojar:
From Catalan ~allotjar~ (“to lodge, quarter”), from Medieval Latin ~laubia~ (“shelter, gallery”), taken from Frankish *~laubja~ (“arbor, shelter of foliage”), from Proto-Germanic *~laubjō~, a relative of *~laubą~ (“leaf”). The Spanish verb — first at home in the military language of billeting troops — prefixed the noun with ~a-~. It is cognate with Italian ~alloggiare~ and French ~loger~, and, through the same Germanic word, with English ~lodge~, ~lobby~, and ~loge~, and with German ~Laube~ (“arbor, bower”). Through the “leaf” root it also touches English ~leaf~ and German ~Laub~ (“foliage”).

The charming detail is that origin in foliage: the ancestral *~laubja~ was a leafy shelter, a bower of branches, and only later a built lodging — so to lodge a person was first to shelter them under leaves. Spanish narrowed the sense to “to house, quarter, put up a guest,” giving the noun ~alojamiento~ (“lodging, accommodation”) and the antonym ~desalojar~ (“to dislodge, evict”). For all its tidiness, the modern hotel word still carries, in its deepest root, the memory of a shelter woven from leaves.
en.alquilar:
From the noun ~alquiler~ (“rent, hire”), a borrowing from Andalusi Arabic ~alkiráʼ~, from Classical Arabic ~al-kirāʼ~ (الكِراء, “the hire, the lease”), the verbal noun of the root ~k-r-y~, “to hire out.” The ~al-~ is the Arabic definite article, fused into the word as in so many Spanish Arabisms. Portuguese ~alugar~ (“to rent”) comes from the very same Arabic source, making it alquilar’s closest cognate.

The word’s shape records a small drama of sound change. In Andalusi Arabic ~kirāʼ~ was pronounced with imāla, roughly ~kiré~, giving early Spanish ~alquilé~; the first ~r~ then dissimilated to ~l~ (a common Romance shift), and finally a parasitic ~-r~ reattached at the end, yielding ~alquiler~ — from which the verb ~alquilar~ was back-formed. Spanish uses it in both directions: a landlord and a tenant both ~alquilan~. From the same borrowing come ~alquilado~, ~alquilador~, ~subalquilar~, and ~realquilar~ (“to sublet”).
en.alterar:
~alterar~ descends from Late Latin ~alterāre~ (“to make otherwise, change”), coined from the adjective ~alter~ (“the other of two”). ~alter~ is itself ~al-~ (“other, beyond”) plus a contrastive suffix ~-ter~ that sets one of two things against the other, exactly as in ~uter~ and ~neuter~. The base goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂el-~ (“beyond, other”), which also yielded Latin ~alius~ (“another”) — ancestor of Spanish ~otro~, French ~autre~ and Italian ~altro~ — and, in Germanic, English ~else~. Through that root ~alterar~ is also related to English ~alias~, ~alien~ and ~alternate~.

Where Latin ~alter~ simply meant “the other,” ~alterāre~ took on the dynamic sense “to turn something into something other” — to change it — and by the seventeenth century Spanish had darkened that further to “to disturb, upset, agitate,” as in ~alterarse~ (“to get worked up”). The neutral change sense survives in ~alteración~ and ~inalterable~. The same root *~h₂el-~ runs through a large Spanish family of otherness: ~alternar~, ~alternativa~, ~alterno~, ~adulterar~ (literally “to make other,” to corrupt) and — by way of French ~autrui~ — ~altruismo~, the impulse to live for the other.
en.aludir:
From Latin ~allūdere~ (“to play with, jest at, refer to playfully”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~lūdere~ (“to play”), the verb of ~lūdus~ (“game, sport, school”). Cognate with English ~allude~ and, through the same ~lūdere~, with English ~illusion~, ~elude~, ~prelude~ and ~ludicrous~; Italian has ~alludere~. The deeper origin of ~lūdus~/~lūdere~ is disputed: some trace it to a Proto-Indo-European *~leyd-~ (“to play”), while others hold it to be a borrowing from Etruscan — so the root is best left open.

The Latin verb wandered from “to frolic” toward “to touch on in passing, hint at,” and Spanish ~aludir~ kept only that last sense: to refer to something indirectly, without naming it. Its noun is ~alusión~. From the same ~lūdus~ Spanish gathered a playful cluster — ~ilusión~, ~eludir~, ~preludio~, ~interludio~, ~lúdico~ and ~ludopatía~ (“compulsive gambling”) — a reminder that behind so much talk of pretense and play lies one Latin word for a game.
en.alzar:
From Vulgar Latin *~altiāre~ (“to raise”), a verb coined from the Latin adjective ~altus~ (“high”). ~altus~ was originally the past participle of ~alere~ (“to nourish, feed, rear”), so “high” first meant “grown, well-nourished.” The root is Proto-Indo-European *~h₂el-~ (“to grow, nourish”). The Romance sisters kept the coinage: Italian ~alzare~, Portuguese ~alçar~ and, with a different suffix, French ~hausser~.

The buried metaphor is lovely: to ~alzar~, “to make high,” rests on a word for “nourished into growth.” From ~altus~ Spanish keeps ~alto~ (“high, tall”), ~altura~ (“height”), ~altivo~ (“haughty”) and ~realzar~ (“to enhance”), while the deeper root through ~alere~ feeds ~alimento~ (“food”) and ~adulto~ (“adult,” literally grown-up). Through Latin ~altus~ English is cousin in ~altitude~, ~exalt~ and ~haughty~ (via French).
en.amanecer:
From Vulgar Latin *~admānēscere~, an inchoative verb built on ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~mānēscere~ (“to grow light, to become morning”), from Latin ~māne~ (“in the morning, early”). ~Māne~ in turn is tied to the old adjective ~mānus~ (“good”) — the morning being, literally, the “good” or auspicious early hour — and is related to English ~matins~ and ~mature~. From the same ~māne~ Spanish also drew ~mañana~ (“morning; tomorrow”).

The inchoative ending *~-ēscere~ carries the idea of “beginning to be,” so ~admānēscere~ meant “to start to be morning,” that is, to dawn — used impersonally, as in ~amaneció~ temprano (“it dawned early”). Castilian then stretched it in a very human direction: to ~amanecer~ somewhere is to be there, or to wake there, when day breaks — ~amanecí~ en el tren (“I woke on the train at daybreak”). It pairs neatly with ~anochecer~ (“to grow dark, to reach nightfall”), the same word-shape applied to the other end of the day, and both keep the impersonal, atmospheric flavor of describing the sky rather than a subject.
en.amansar:
A causative verb, from ~a-~ plus the adjective ~manso~ (“tame, gentle, meek”) plus ~-ar~. ~Manso~ descends from Vulgar Latin *~mānsus~, a shortening of Latin ~mānsuētus~ (“tame, domesticated”). That word is wonderfully concrete: it is ~manus~ (“hand”) joined to ~suētus~, the past participle of ~suēscere~ (“to grow accustomed”) — so a tame creature is literally one “accustomed to the hand.” Italian ~mansueto~ and Portuguese ~manso~ preserve the same adjective.

The verb thus means “to make hand-tame,” to break in an animal or, figuratively, to soothe and soften a person’s temper — one ~amansa~ a wild horse or a hot temper alike. The hand-image at its core is the memorable heart of the word: taming as the slow work of the hand. From the same ~manso~ family Spanish keeps ~mansedumbre~ (“meekness, gentleness”) and the learned ~mansueto~, while the ~suēscere~ side of the compound reappears, through ~consuēscere~, in ~costumbre~ (“custom, habit”) — habit and taming being, at root, two kinds of getting-accustomed.
en.amar:
From Latin ~amāre~ (“to love”), inherited directly and preserved across Romance: Italian ~amare~, Portuguese ~amar~, Catalan ~amar~, and Old French ~amer~ (surviving in modern ~aimer~). Beyond Latin the origin is genuinely uncertain. One traditional view treats ~amāre~ as a nursery or affectionate word, alongside ~amita~ (“aunt”) and ~amīcus~ (“friend”), from a Lallwort root *~am-~ of the babbling type also seen in “mama.” A different proposal, favored by de Vaan, connects it to a Proto-Indo-European *~h₂emh₃-~ (“to seize, take hold of”), so that “to love” would have grown from “to take by the hand.” The sources disagree; treat the deep root as debated.

Whatever its ultimate source, ~amāre~ named the warmest and most voluntary kind of love, distinct from the desire of Latin ~cupere~; Latin ~amor~ passed intact into Spanish ~amor~. Spanish kept ~amar~ as the elevated, literary verb for love — one ~ama~ God, a country, or a beloved in poetry — while everyday affection is carried by ~querer~ (“to want, to love”). From the same stem flow a large and tender family: ~amor~, ~amante~ (“lover”), ~amado~ (“beloved”), ~amistad~ (“friendship,” through ~amīcus~), ~amable~ (“kind”), ~amigo~, ~enamorar~ (“to make someone fall in love”) and ~desamor~ (“lovelessness”). French ~amateur~ — one who does a thing for love of it — reached Spanish and English from this same root.
en.amargar:
From Late Latin ~amāricāre~ (“to make bitter”), a verb built on Latin ~amārus~ (“bitter”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eh₃m-~ (“raw, bitter”). The root’s older sense of “raw, unripe” survives in its cognates — Ancient Greek ~ōmós~ (“raw”) and Sanskrit ~āmá~ (“raw, uncooked”) — a reminder that the bitter and the unripe were long felt to be the same flavor. The adjective ~amārus~ gave Italian ~amaro~, French ~amer~, and Portuguese ~amargo~.

Where most of Romance kept the plain adjective, Spanish inherited the derived ~amāricāre~, so that from a flavor it made a verb: ~amargar~, “to taste bitter” and then, figuratively, “to embitter, to spoil, to sadden.” One can ~amargar~ a coffee or, crueller, ~amargar~ la vida a alguien (“to make someone’s life bitter”). The whole family stays close and productive: ~amargo~ (“bitter”), ~amargor~ and ~amargura~ (“bitterness,” the second usually of grief), all tracing back to that single Latin ~amārus~ and its idea of a sharp, raw taste on the tongue.
en.amasar:
A denominal verb, from ~a-~ plus ~masa~ (“dough; mass”) plus ~-ar~. ~Masa~ comes from Latin ~massa~ (“lump, mass, wad of dough”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~mâza~ (“barley-cake”), a noun tied to the verb ~mássō~ (“to knead”). Beyond that the trail is uncertain: the Greek is usually traced to Proto-Indo-European *~maǵ-~ (“to knead”), but sources flag that reconstruction as tentative. The Latin ~massa~ also gave Italian and Portuguese ~massa~ and, by borrowing, English ~mass~.

A ~masa~ was first a worked lump of dough, and ~amasar~ meant simply “to knead” — the motion a baker makes, and, as Spanish cheerfully notes, the motion a cat makes on a blanket. From the physical kneading grew a financial one: to ~amasar~ una fortuna is “to amass a fortune,” exactly the metaphor English keeps in ~amass~ — wealth gathered and worked together like dough. The same ~masa~ seeds a small pantry of words: ~amasijo~ (“a mix, a jumble”), ~masilla~ (“putty”), and the physicist’s ~masa~ (“mass”), the abstract quantity still wearing the name of a lump of bread.
en.amenazar:
~Amenazar~ goes back to Vulgar Latin *~minaciāre~, from Latin ~minācia~ (“threats”), an abstract of ~minax~, genitive ~minācis~ (“jutting, menacing”), from ~minae~ (“projecting points, threats”), akin to the verb ~minārī~ (“to jut out; to threaten”). The prefix is ~a-~ (from ~ad-~). The Latin family traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~men-~ (“to project, stand out”). It is cognate with English ~menace~, French ~menacer~, and Italian ~minacciare~.

The oldest sense of ~minae~ was concrete: the “overhanging points” of a wall or cliff, things that loom — only later did looming become “threatening.” The same root *~men-~ “to jut” produced Latin ~mons~, ~montem~ (“mountain”), and through it Spanish ~monte~, ~montaña~, and ~promontorio~, plus the “standing-out” family ~eminente~, ~prominente~, and ~inminente~ (what “juts toward” us). So a threat and a mountain are, at root, the same gesture of jutting out; the noun ~amenaza~ preserves it.
en.amparar:
Spanish ~amparar~ goes back to a Vulgar Latin *~anteparāre~ (“to set up a defense in front of”), from ~ante~ (“before, in front”) plus ~parāre~ (“to prepare, provide”), from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to produce, procure, grant”). The compound lost its interior vowel and the cluster ~-ntp-~ simplified to ~-mp-~, giving ~amparar~. Strikingly, a matching compound survives in the ancient Umbrian ~amparitu~. Cognate with Portuguese ~amparar~ and Catalan ~emparar~.

The literal image is a soldier raising a barrier before himself; from “defending” the sense softened to “to shelter, protect, help.” In Spanish law the noun ~amparo~ names a landmark remedy — the ~recurso de amparo~, the constitutional writ by which citizens shield their fundamental rights, most famous in Mexico's ~juicio de amparo~. From the same ~parāre~ Spanish also has ~parar~, ~preparar~, ~reparar~, and the opposites ~desamparar~ and ~desamparo~ (“to abandon; abandonment”).
en.ampliar:
From Latin ~ampliāre~ (“to widen, enlarge”), a verb built on the adjective ~amplus~ (“large, spacious, ample”). Where ~amplus~ itself comes from is uncertain. De Vaan sets out the leading proposal — a derivation from Proto-Italic *~amlo-~ (“seizable, graspable”), tied to a noun ~ampla~ (“handle, grip; opportunity”) and ultimately to a Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂emh₃-~ (“to take hold of”), the same root proposed behind ~amāre~ (“to love”) — but he flags weaknesses in it, so the origin is best treated as unresolved rather than settled. Spanish took ~ampliar~ from Latin as a learned word; its everyday cousin ~amplio~ (“wide, roomy”) descends from the same ~amplus~, as do French ~ample~ and English ~ample~.

The meaning has stayed remarkably close to home: ~ampliar~ is simply “to make ~amplio~,” to widen, extend, or enlarge — a room, a business, a photograph, a body of rights. Spanish uses it where English splits the job among “expand,” “extend,” “enlarge,” and “broaden.” The photographic sense gave the noun ~ampliación~ (“an enlargement,” both the act and the enlarged print). The adjective ~amplio~ carries the spatial idea into everyday speech, and the adverb ~ampliamente~ means “widely, amply, at length.” If De Vaan’s tentative link to *~h₂emh₃-~ (“to take hold of”) is right, there is a quiet irony in it: a word now all about opening things up would share its deepest root with ~amāre~, “to grasp” having drifted toward both embracing and enlarging.
en.analizar:
From ~análisis~ (“analysis”), a verb back-formed (via French ~analyser~) from the noun, which came through Latin ~analysis~ from Ancient Greek ~análusis~ (“a dissolving, a loosening-up”). That word joins ~aná-~ (“up, throughout”) to ~lúsis~ (“a loosening”), a noun of ~lúō~ (“to loosen, release, dissolve”), from Proto-Indo-European *~lewh₁-~ (“to cut off, separate, free”). English ~loose~ and ~-less~ are native cognates of that root.

The Greek image is chemical before it is logical: to analyse is to dissolve a whole into its parts, to loosen the knot. Spanish ~analizar~ carries that from laboratory to reasoning — one ~analiza~ a compound or an argument alike. From the same ~lúō~ root, borrowed through Greek, Spanish holds a technical family in which the “loosening” is still visible: ~diálisis~ (a dissolving-apart), ~parálisis~ (a loosening beside, i.e. disablement), ~catálisis~ and ~electrólisis~. The relatives ~análisis~, ~analista~ and ~analítico~ complete the set.
en.andar:
The origin is debated. Spanish ~andar~, like Italian ~andare~ and French ~aller~ (all meaning “to go”), descends from Vulgar Latin, but no single source is agreed. The most widely favored account derives it from Latin ~ambulāre~ (“to walk, travel about”): Corominas proposes that ~ambulāre~ was reduced in casual speech to *~amlāre~ and then to *~andāre~. A competing account starts instead from a Vulgar Latin *~ambitāre~ (a frequentative of ~ambīre~, “to go around”), which some hold explains the Spanish, Portuguese, and Italian forms better than ~ambulāre~ does.

Whatever the exact etymon, the deep sense is “to go about, walk around,” and Spanish ~andar~ kept a wide range: to walk, to function (a clock ~anda~ or not), and to be in a state (~andar~ cansado, “to go about tired”). If ~ambulāre~ is the source, ~andar~ shares its root with the borrowings ~ambulancia~, ~ambulante~, ~deambular~, and ~preámbulo~, and with English ~amble~ and ~ambulance~ — though, given the dispute, that kinship holds only under the ~ambulāre~ hypothesis. From ~andar~ itself Spanish built ~andén~ (“platform”) and ~andanza~ (“fortune, adventure”).
en.animar:
From Latin ~animāre~ (“to give life to, enliven”), a verb formed on ~anima~ (“breath, air, soul, life”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂enh₁-~ (“to breathe, blow”). Italian ~animare~, French ~animer~ and Portuguese ~animar~ share the same descent, and through the root ~anima~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~ἄνεμος~ (“wind”) and Sanskrit ~ánila~ (“wind, air”). The learned English ~animate~ and the everyday ~animal~ (originally “a breathing being”) come from the same Latin family.

The metaphor was already alive in Latin: to ~animāre~ someone was literally to breathe life or spirit into them, and Spanish kept that thread — to ~animar~ a friend is to put ~ánimo~ (“spirit, courage”) back into them. The reflexive ~animarse~ means to cheer up or to work up the nerve to do something. From ~anima~ Spanish inherited a remarkable pair of doublets: the learned ~ánima~ (“soul in purgatory”) and the popular, everyday ~alma~ (“soul”), whose ~l~ arose from the same Latin word by regular sound change. The root fanned out into ~ánimo~, ~animoso~, ~unánime~ (“of one mind”), ~magnánimo~ (“great-souled”), ~desanimar~ (“to dishearten”) and ~reanimar~ (“to revive”).
en.anotar:
From Latin ~annotāre~ (“to note, mark down”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~notāre~ (“to mark”), itself built on the noun ~nota~ (“mark, sign, letter”). Spanish took the word in as ~anotar~, keeping the sense of setting a mark or a few words beside something. It is cognate with French ~noter~, Italian ~annotare~, Portuguese ~anotar~, and — through the same Latin noun — with English ~note~ and ~annotate~.

The deep origin of ~nota~ is disputed. It was traditionally referred to the verb ~nōscere~ (“to know”), as though a ~nota~ were a “means of recognition,” which would tie it to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know”); but that connection is contested — De Vaan judges the word to have no credible etymology, so the link to “knowing” is best presented as a proposal, not a fact. Whatever its ultimate source, ~nota~ proved enormously productive: from it Spanish inherited ~nota~ itself, along with ~notar~, ~notable~, ~notario~, ~notorio~, and the modern derivative ~anotación~ (“annotation, note”).
en.anticipar:
From Latin ~anticipāre~ (“to take beforehand, act in advance”), from ~ante-~ (“before”) plus ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”). Through ~capere~ it is cognate with English ~capture~ and ~capable~; through ~ante-~ with Greek ~ἀντί~ (“against, opposite”). Italian keeps the verb whole as ~anticipare~.

The Latin sense was literally to “take before” — to seize a thing, a moment, or an advantage ahead of time — and Spanish keeps exactly that, from anticipating an event to paying an ~anticipo~ (“advance payment”). The root ~capere~ was extraordinarily productive: from it Spanish drew ~capturar~, ~recibir~ (“to receive”), ~concebir~ (“to conceive”), and — least obviously — ~caber~ (“to fit”), since what fits is what a space can “take.” The prefix ~ante-~ likewise seeded ~antes~, ~anterior~, and ~antaño~ (“long ago”), so anticipar carries a “before” at each end of its Latin skeleton.
en.antojar:
Spanish ~antojar~ derives from the noun ~antojo~ (“whim, sudden craving”), which most authorities trace to an Old Spanish phrase ~ante ojo~ (“before the eye”): Latin ~ante~ (“before”) plus ~oculum~ (“eye”). The word for eye goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₃ekʷ-~ (“to see; eye”), the root behind Spanish ~ojo~, Italian ~occhio~ and French ~œil~, and — through Germanic — English ~eye~, alongside the learned borrowing ~ocular~.

The etymology paints a vivid picture: a desire is something that springs up « before your eyes » and seizes you on the spot. Fittingly, the verb is almost always used pronominally — ~se me antoja~ means roughly “I have a hankering for it,” with the craving treated as an outside force acting on you. From the same family come ~antojo~ (a whim, and specifically a pregnant woman’s craving), ~antojadizo~ (“capricious, whimsical”), and, in Mexico, the affectionate ~antojitos~ — literally “little cravings,” the street snacks one suddenly longs for.
en.anular:
From Late Latin ~annullare~ (“to bring to nothing”), from Latin ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~nullus~ (“none, not any”). ~nullus~ itself decomposes into ~ne~ (“not”) and ~ullus~ (“any”), a diminutive of ~unus~ (“one”) — so at the bottom of the word lies the idea of “not even one.” Cognate with French ~annuler~, Italian ~annullare~ and Portuguese ~anular~.

The verb means to make a thing legally void — a marriage, a contract, a result — reduced, etymologically, to zero. A neat trap for learners: Spanish has a second, unrelated ~anular~, the adjective and noun for “ring-shaped” and the “ring finger,” which descends instead from Latin ~anulus~ (“little ring”); the two words converged in spelling by pure coincidence. From ~nullus~ come the transparent modern relatives ~nulo~, ~nulidad~ and ~anulación~.
en.anunciar:
From Latin ~annuntiāre~ (“to announce, report, bring word”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~nuntiāre~ (“to report, make known”), the verb of the noun ~nuntius~ (“messenger; message, news”). The deeper origin of ~nuntius~ is disputed. An old and appealing account contracted it from *~noventios~ and tied it to ~novus~ (“new”), making the messenger a bringer of news; de Vaan rejects that derivation on formal grounds and tentatively prefers a Proto-Indo-European root *~newH-~ (“to shout, cry out”), which would make ~nuntius~ literally “the one who calls out.” Either way, the Spanish verb ~anunciar~ comes down from ~annuntiāre~ through regular sound change.

Whatever its ultimate root, ~nuntius~ was the ordinary Roman word for the bearer of a message, and its verb ~nuntiāre~ spawned a whole prefixed set that Spanish inherited almost intact: ~anunciar~ (“to announce,” to bring word toward someone), ~denunciar~ (“to denounce,” to report against), ~pronunciar~ (“to pronounce, declare forth”), and ~renunciar~ (“to renounce,” to report back that one gives something up). The noun lives on as ~anuncio~ (“announcement, advertisement”) and, in the Church, as ~nuncio~ (“nuncio,” the pope’s ambassador — still, faithfully, a messenger). English ~announce~, ~denounce~, ~pronounce~, and ~renounce~ mirror the Spanish set step for step.
en.apagar:
From Vulgar Latin *~appācāre~ (~ad-~ “to” plus ~pācāre~ “to pacify, appease”), from ~pāx~, ~pācis~ (“peace”), from Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂ǵ-~ (“to fasten, fix”). Cognate with Portuguese ~apagar~, and — from bare ~pācāre~ — with Spanish ~pagar~ (“to pay”) and, by the same path through French, English ~pay~.

~pācāre~ meant “to make peaceful, appease,” and in medieval Spanish ~apagar~ and ~pagar~ alike first meant “to satisfy, content.” One branch specialized toward settling a debt — restoring peace between creditor and debtor — and became ~pagar~ (“to pay”); the other specialized toward quieting a fire or a light, and became ~apagar~ (“to put out, switch off”). It is a striking pair: to ~pagar~ a bill and to ~apagar~ a lamp are, at root, the same act of bringing something to peace. The extinguishing sense of ~apagar~ developed chiefly in the Peninsular languages; from the same ~pāx~ Spanish also has ~paz~, ~pacífico~, ~apaciguar~, and ~pacto~.
en.aparecer:
From Latin ~appārēscere~, an inchoative (“to begin to appear”) built on ~appārēre~ (“to appear, to become visible”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~pārēre~ (“to come forth, to be visible”). The ultimate Proto-Indo-European source of ~pārēre~ is uncertain, with more than one reconstruction proposed. Cognate with French ~apparaître~, Italian ~apparire~, and English ~appear~ and ~apparent~.

Latin ~pārēre~ had a second, everyday meaning — “to obey,” to present oneself when summoned — and it seeded a nicely paired set of Spanish verbs. From the plain inchoative ~pārēscere~ came ~parecer~ (“to seem, to appear to be”), while the prefixed ~appārēscere~ gave ~aparecer~ (“to appear, to show up”): to seem is to be merely visible; to appear is to arrive into sight. The family also includes ~aparición~ (“appearance, apparition”), ~aparente~ (“apparent”), and the formal ~comparecer~ (“to appear in court”) — where the old sense of presenting oneself on command still lingers.
en.aparejar:
Spanish ~aparejar~ is built from the prefix ~a-~ and the adjective ~parejo~ (“even, matching”), which comes from Late Latin ~pariculus~, a diminutive of Latin ~par~ (“equal, a pair”). The same ~par~ yielded French ~pareil~ (“similar”) and Italian ~parecchio~, and, borrowed into English, the doublet ~pair~ and ~peer~ as well as the bare ~par~ of “on a par with.”

To ~aparejar~ was first “to make things equal or matched,” then “to fit out, make ready” — you paired an animal with its gear, or a ship with its tackle. That nautical sense dominates the noun ~aparejo~ (“rigging, tackle, harness”), the block-and-tackle a sailor rigs to hoist a sail. In the building trades an ~aparejador~ is a quantity surveyor or clerk of works, and ~aparejado~ survives in the phrase « llevar aparejado » (“to entail, carry with it”), where one thing comes matched to another.
en.apartar:
A Spanish formation: the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”) on ~partir~ / ~parte~, ultimately from Latin ~pars~, ~partem~ (“a part, share, portion”), from Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to grant, allot”). The verb ~partīrī~ (“to divide, share”) lies directly behind Spanish ~partir~. It is cognate with English ~part~, ~portion~ and ~parcel~, with French ~part~ and Italian ~parte~ — all sharing the idea of a piece assigned out of a whole.

The literal build is “to set toward a part,” hence to put to one side, separate, move away. The family is everywhere in Spanish: ~parte~, ~aparte~, ~repartir~, ~partición~ and even ~apartamento~ — a “set-apart” suite of rooms. The most striking descendant, though, traveled abroad: the Romance ~aparte~ / French idea of à part passed into Dutch and Afrikaans and produced ~apartheid~, literally “apart-hood,” the state policy of forced separateness — a grim monument built, at root, on the same small word that lets you gently ~apartar~ a curtain or step aside from a crowd.
en.apasionar:
From the prefix ~a-~, the noun ~pasión~ and the verbal suffix ~-ar~. ~pasión~ derives from Latin ~passiō~, from ~passus~, the participle of ~patī~ (“to suffer, endure”). The root is uncertain: it is usually referred to Proto-Indo-European *~peh₁-~ (“to hurt”), though some prefer *~pet-~ (“to fall”), with a sense drifting from “to befall” to “to suffer.” It is cognate with Ancient Greek ~πῆμα~ (“suffering”) and underlies the English borrowings ~patient~ and ~passive~.

The original idea is endurance under suffering — the sense preserved in the religious ~Pasión~ (“the Passion of Christ”). But ~apasionar~ took the emotional charge of “passion” in its warmer direction: to fill with ardor, to thrill, so that a subject ~apasiona~ its enthusiasts and ~apasionarse~ is to be swept up. From the same root Spanish keeps ~paciente~ (“patient”), ~padecer~ (“to suffer”), ~compasión~ (“compassion,” literally “suffering-with”), ~pasivo~ (“passive”) and the vivid adjective ~apasionante~ (“thrilling”).
en.apear:
Spanish ~apear~ goes back to Vulgar Latin *~appedāre~, from the phrase ~ad pedem~ (“to the foot”): the prefix ~ad-~ (assimilated to ~ap-~) plus ~pes~, ~pedem~ (“foot”). That noun descends from Proto-Indo-European *~pṓds~ (“foot”), source of Spanish ~pie~, French ~pied~ and Italian ~piede~, and — through Germanic — English ~foot~, along with the learned English pair ~pedal~ and ~pedestrian~.

The oldest recorded sense is surprisingly specific: to ~apear~ an animal was to hobble it, tying its feet so it could not stray. From “securing the feet” the verb slid to “setting one’s own feet on the ground,” and so to today’s core meaning, “to dismount” or « get down » from a horse, carriage, or car. Related uses branch out: to ~apear~ a tree is to fell it at the foot, and the reflexive « apearse de » means to give up a notion or climb down from a position. The little station-word ~apeadero~ (“halt, wayside stop”) is the place where you get off.
en.apedrear:
Spanish ~apedrear~ is transparently ~a-~ plus ~piedra~ (“stone”) plus the iterative ending ~-ear~. ~piedra~ comes from Latin ~petra~ (“rock, crag”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~πέτρα~ (~pétra~, “rock”); the Greek word is of uncertain, possibly pre-Greek origin, so no secure Indo-European root can be claimed. Cognates include French ~pierre~, Italian ~pietra~ and Portuguese ~pedra~, and, through the same ~petra~, English ~petrify~ and ~petroleum~ and the name ~Peter~ (Spanish ~Pedro~).

The ~-ear~ suffix makes the verb iterative and forceful: ~apedrear~ is not to place a stone but to pelt with a hail of them — to stone someone, a punishment as old as the word. By a natural leap the verb turned meteorological: in many regions ~apedrear~ is used impersonally for “to hail,” when the sky flings stones of ice. From the same root grow ~pedregal~ (“stony ground”), ~pedrada~ (“a blow from a thrown stone”), and ~empedrar~ (“to pave with stones”).
en.apegar:
Spanish ~apegar~ is ~a-~ prefixed to ~pegar~ (“to stick, glue”), which comes from Latin ~picāre~ (“to coat with pitch”), a verb from ~pix~, ~picem~ (“pitch, tar”). That noun goes back through Proto-Italic *~piks~ to Proto-Indo-European *~pik-~ (“pitch”), the source also of Spanish ~pez~ (“pitch”), French ~poix~ and Italian ~pece~, of Ancient Greek ~píssa~, and — borrowed straight from Latin — of English ~pitch~.

The metaphor is tactile: pitch is the stickiest of substances, so ~pegar~ meant “to make things adhere.” ~apegar~ carried that adhesion into the heart — ~apegarse~ « a algo » is to grow attached, to cling emotionally, and the noun ~apego~ names fondness or attachment. Spanish took the physical root in a second, violent direction too: ~pegar~ also came to mean “to hit,” as if a blow were something you stick onto someone. Other descendants of the pitch-word include ~pegamento~ (“glue”), ~pegajoso~ (“sticky, clingy”), and ~empecinarse~ (“to dig in stubbornly”).
en.apelar:
~apelar~ comes from Latin ~appellare~ (“to address, call upon, name”), generally taken as a variant of ~appellere~ “to drive toward,” from ~ad-~ (“to”) plus ~pellere~ (“to drive, push, set in motion”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pel-~ (“to thrust, drive”). Cognate with Italian ~appellare~, Portuguese ~apelar~ and French ~appeler~ (“to call”), and — through Old French ~apeler~ — with English ~appeal~. The same ~pellere~ underlies a cluster of Latin verbs of pushing that Spanish inherited as ~impeler~, ~expeler~, ~compeler~ and ~propulsar~.

In Rome ~appellare~ was to call on someone by name — to accost, to summon, and in law to call one's cause up to a higher judge. Spanish keeps exactly that legal gesture: to ~apelar~ a ruling is to “call it upward” for review, and figuratively to ~apelar a~ someone's conscience is to call on it. The surprise is a homely cousin: ~apellido~ (“surname”) descends from the frequentative ~appellitare~ (“to call repeatedly”) — the family name once shouted to muster or identify a man — so the word for a legal ~apelación~ and the word for your last name spring from the very same act of calling out.
en.apellidar:
Spanish ~apellidar~ descends from Latin ~appellitāre~, a frequentative (“to call again and again”) of ~appellāre~ (“to call, address, appeal”), which is ~ad-~ plus a form related to ~pellere~ (“to drive, push”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pel-~ (“to drive, set in motion”). It is thus a sibling of Spanish ~apelar~ and English ~appeal~ and ~appellation~, and of French ~appeler~ (“to call”).

The noun ~apellido~ tells a martial story. In medieval Castile it did not mean “surname” but the ~apellido~ — the war-cry or summons to arms by which a lord mustered his men. Only later, as growing communities needed to tell apart the many named Juan or Pedro, did ~apellidar~ settle into “to call someone by name,” and ~apellido~ into the modern “surname.” To be ~apellidado~ « X » is to bear X as a family name. The same *~pel-~ root also underlies ~impeler~ (“to impel”) and ~propulsar~ (“to propel”).
en.aplicar:
From Latin ~applicāre~ (“to attach to, to bring toward, to fold onto”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). ~plicāre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to fold”), an enlargement of *~pel-~ (“to fold”). It is cognate with Latin ~plectere~, Ancient Greek ~plékō~ (“I plait”), and, through Germanic, English ~fold~ and ~ply~. The compound survives in Italian ~applicare~, French ~appliquer~, and Portuguese ~aplicar~.

The literal image is of folding one thing onto another; from “laying on” came the figurative “to devote oneself to” and “to put into practice.” The humble root hides a surprise: ~plicāre~ also meant to fold up a ship's sails on nearing the coast, and Vulgar Latin turned that “coming to shore” into a general verb of arrival — the direct source of Spanish ~llegar~ (“to arrive”) and Portuguese ~chegar~. Relatives of the fold-root abound in Spanish: ~plegar~, ~pliegue~, ~plegaria~, ~explicar~, ~complicar~, ~replicar~, and ~emplear~ (from ~implicāre~).
en.apoderar:
Spanish ~apoderar~ is the prefix ~a-~ joined to ~poder~ (“power; to be able”) and the ending ~-ar~. ~poder~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~potēre~, a regularized reshaping of Latin ~posse~ (“to be able”), originally ~potis~ (“able, powerful”) plus ~esse~ (“to be”). ~potis~ reflects Proto-Indo-European *~poti-~ (“master, lord”), the root behind English ~power~ (through Old French), ~potent~ and ~possess~, and even Greek-derived ~despot~.

To ~apoderar~ someone is to vest them with power — to authorize them to act in your name. Hence an ~apoderado~ is a legal proxy, an attorney-in-fact, and in bullfighting a matador’s manager. In the reflexive, ~apoderarse~ « de algo » swings to the opposite pole of power: to seize it, to take possession or control. The same rich root gave Spanish ~poderoso~ (“powerful”), ~poderío~ (“might”), and ~potente~ (“potent”), a whole vocabulary of capacity and command.
en.aportar:
Two originally distinct verbs fell together in ~aportar~. One is nautical: ~aportar~ (“to reach port”), from Latin ~portus~ (“harbor”). The other is the modern everyday sense, “to contribute,” from ~apportāre~ — ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~portāre~ (“to carry”) — literally to carry something toward someone. But the two are cousins, not strangers: ~portus~ (“harbor”), ~porta~ (“gate, passage”), and ~portāre~ (“to carry”) all descend from Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to cross over, pass through, bring across”). Through the Germanic branch of that root run English ~ford~ and ~fare~; through Latin come English ~port~ and ~portable~.

The shared image is movement across a threshold — a harbor, a gate, a load carried over. From the ‘carry’ sense Spanish built a broad family: ~portar~ (“to carry, bear”), ~aportación~ (“contribution”), ~transportar~, ~importar~, and ~exportar~. From the ‘harbor’ sense come ~puerto~ (“port”) and, by regular diphthongization, ~puerta~ (“door”). A quiet gem is ~oportuno~ (“opportune”): Latin ~opportūnus~ meant ‘(a wind) driving toward the harbor,’ hence favorable — so an ~oportuno~ moment is one that, like a good wind, carries you safely in. To ~aportar~ today, whatever the harbor, is still to bring your share across.
en.apostar:
Spanish has two verbs ~apostar~ that fell together in sound, and dictionaries still list them apart. The first, “to bet, wager,” was built on the notion of the stake set down: it rests on Latin ~appōnere~ (“to place beside,” ~a-~ + ~pōnere~ “to place”) and its participle ~appositum~, and is bound up with ~apuesta~ (“a bet”), the sum ~puesta~ — “placed” — on the table. The second, “to station, post,” was formed on the noun ~posta~ (“a relay station”), from Latin ~posita~ (“things placed”), which reached Spanish through Italian ~posto~ as ~puesto~. So the two are homonyms in form, yet both descend, by separate paths, from Latin ~pōnere~ — one places money, the other places a sentry.

The second sense opens onto history: along the old royal roads, fresh horses and riders were stationed at each ~posta~, and from that relay network came the postal service and the modern ~poste~ (“post, pole”). A soldier ~apostado~ behind a wall and a gambler who ~apuesta~ his wages are doing, etymologically, the same thing — putting something in a chosen place. The wider family is enormous — ~poner~, ~puesto~, ~posición~, ~componer~ — all of it, at bottom, about placement.
en.apoyar:
Spanish ~apoyar~ was probably borrowed from Italian ~appoggiare~ and reshaped around the native ~poyo~ (“a stone bench”); it is first attested in 1496. The Italian verb goes back to Vulgar Latin *~appodiāre~, a compound of ~ad-~ (“onto”) and ~podium~ (“raised platform, support”), which Latin itself had taken from Ancient Greek ~pódion~ (“little base”), the diminutive of ~poús~ (“foot”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ped-~ (“foot”). Literally, then, to ~apoyar~ is “to set something on a footing.” It is cognate with French ~appuyer~ and Portuguese ~apoiar~, and — through the foot-root — with English ~foot~ and ~pew~, the last of these having reached English from that same ~podium~ by way of Old French.

The picture behind the verb is bodily: to ~apoyar~ is to lean one thing against another so that it will not fall — to give it something to rest on. From that physical leaning Spanish widened the meaning to “to back, endorse, second,” so that today one may ~apoyar~ a friend, a motion, or a candidate. The Greek “foot” at the root is still visible in the noun ~poyo~ (“stone seat built against a wall”), a homely doublet of the learned ~podio~. Other relatives include ~apoyo~ (“support”) and the musical ~apoyatura~ (“appoggiatura, a leaning grace note”), which Spanish and Italian both built on the same idea of leaning. And the same Indo-European *~ped-~ (“foot”) underlies a whole crowd of words, from Spanish ~pie~ and ~peatón~ to English ~pedal~.
en.apreciar:
From Late Latin ~appretiāre~ (“to value, set a price on”), from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~pretium~ (“price, value, worth”), from Proto-Indo-European *~preti-~, from *~per-~ (“forward, against, in exchange”), with a core notion of equivalence or recompense. Cognate with Italian ~apprezzare~, French ~apprécier~, and Portuguese ~apreciar~. English ~appreciate~ comes from the same Late Latin verb; and from ~pretium~, by various routes, English also has ~price~, ~precious~, ~prize~, and ~appraise~.

The starting point is commercial — ~appretiāre~ meant to appraise, to fix a price — and Spanish ~apreciar~ still holds both a measuring sense (“to appraise, gauge, perceive a difference”) and an affective one (“to value, esteem, be fond of”): we appraise a jewel and cherish a friend with the same verb. Its opposite is built transparently as ~despreciar~ (“to despise,” literally to price down). The family includes ~precio~ (“price”), ~aprecio~ (“esteem”), ~apreciación~ (“appreciation, assessment”), ~apreciable~ (“appreciable, considerable”), ~precioso~ (“precious, lovely”), and ~preciar~ (“to prize”), with the reflexive ~preciarse de~ meaning “to pride oneself on.”
en.apremiar:
The origin of Spanish ~apremiar~ is disputed. Some derive it directly from Latin ~apprimere~ (~ad-~ “to” + ~premere~, “to press”); others, following Cuervo and Corominas, from the prefix ~a-~ plus the Old Spanish noun ~premia~ (“constraint, compulsion, urgency”), itself a derivative of ~premere~. Either way the ultimate source is ~premere~, from Proto-Indo-European *~pres-~ (“to press”), beside English ~press~ and ~print~, French ~presser~, and Spanish ~oprimir~ and ~exprimir~.

Whichever path is right, the sense is the same: to ~apremiar~ is to press on someone, to urge or hurry them, to leave no room for delay. The noun ~apremio~ means “urgency, pressure,” and in legal Spanish a « mandamiento de apremio » is a court order compelling payment — the law’s way of pressing you. From the same ~premere~ come a whole press-gang of Spanish words: ~prensa~ (“press,” including the news media), ~imprimir~ (“to print”), ~comprimir~ (“to compress”), and ~expresar~ (“to express, press out”).
en.aprender:
From Latin ~apprehendere~ (“to seize, grasp”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~prehendere~ (“to grasp, take hold of”), itself ~prae-~ (“before”) plus a ~-hendere~ from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰend-~ (“to seize, take”). Cognate with French ~apprendre~, Italian ~apprendere~ and Portuguese ~aprender~; through the same root, with Ancient Greek ~khandánō~ (“to hold, contain”) and — via Germanic — English ~get~.

The mental leap “to seize with the mind” happened already in Latin: ~apprehendere~ moved from grabbing physically to grasping an idea, and by Old French ~aprendre~ that figurative sense was the only one left. So to learn is, etymologically, to “get hold of” knowledge. The learned doublet ~aprehender~ preserves the literal “seize, arrest” meaning. From the same root: ~aprendiz~, ~aprendizaje~, ~comprender~, ~emprender~, ~sorprender~ and ~prender~.
en.apretar:
From Vulgar Latin *~appectorāre~ (“to press to the chest”), a compound of Latin ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~pectus~ (“chest, breast”). Old Spanish already had the verb, and it is cognate with Portuguese ~apertar~ (“to tighten, to squeeze”). The noun ~pectus~ gave Spanish ~pecho~ (“chest”) — its Latin ~-ct-~ softening to the ~-ch-~ of Spanish by the regular Castilian sound change — while the more learned adjective ~pectoral~ preserves the original consonants intact.

The literal image is vivid: to ~apretar~ something was once to clasp it against the ~pectus~, the chest — the tightest, most secure hold a person can manage. From that embrace the verb generalized to any act of pressing, squeezing, or making fast: one can ~apretar~ a knot, a button, a fist, or a schedule. Spanish keeps a rich family from the same ~pectus~: ~pecho~ itself, ~pectoral~, ~apretón~ (“a squeeze; a handshake”), ~aprieto~ (“a tight spot, a jam”), and the participle ~apretado~ (“tight, packed”). The chest also survives, faintly, in English ~expectorate~ (“to cough up from the chest”), a distant cousin through the same Latin noun.
en.aprobar:
From Latin ~approbāre~ (“to approve, to sanction”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~probāre~ (“to test, to try, to find good”), itself from the adjective ~probus~ (“good, upright, honest”). Through Proto-Italic, ~probus~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European, joining ~pro-~ (“forth, in front”) with the root *~bʰuH-~ (“to be, to grow”) — roughly “growing well, standing straight.” Its Romance kin include Italian ~approvare~, French ~approuver~, and Portuguese ~aprovar~, and through the same Latin stock it matches English ~approve~, ~prove~, and ~probe~.

In Latin ~probāre~ first meant “to test the quality of” a thing, and only by extension “to judge it good.” That double sense survives in Spanish ~probar~, which still means both “to taste, to try” and “to prove.” The prefixed ~aprobar~ narrowed to the favorable verdict — to pass a student, to ratify a law. The same family seeded ~prueba~ (“proof, test”), ~probable~, ~comprobar~ (“to verify”), ~probeta~ (“test tube”), and ~aprobación~. English keeps the fork too: to ~probe~ is to put to the test, while to ~approve~ is to bless the result — the two halves of one Latin idea, trying a thing and finding it worthy.
en.apropiar:
From Late Latin ~appropriāre~ (“to make one's own”), from ~ad-~ (“to”) + ~proprius~ (“one's own, particular”). ~Proprius~ is perhaps from the phrase ~prō prīvō~ (“for the individual”), from ~prīvus~ (“single, one's own”) — an origin the sources offer only tentatively. Cognate with Italian ~appropriare~, French ~approprier~ and English ~appropriate~.

~Appropriāre~ meant to take a thing as ~proprius~ — as one's own — and Spanish ~apropiar~ keeps exactly that: to appropriate, and reflexively ~apropiarse de~ (“to seize, take possession of”). The adjective ~proprius~ gave Spanish ~propio~ (“own”), and from it a wide family: ~propiedad~ (“property”), ~propietario~ (“owner”), ~impropio~ (“improper”) and ~apropiado~ (“suitable”). Through the same ~prīvus~, Latin ~prīvāre~ (“to deprive”) gave Spanish ~privar~ and ~privado~ (“private”) and English ~private~ and ~deprive~.
en.aprovechar:
From ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “toward”) plus the noun ~provecho~ (“benefit, profit”) and the verbal suffix ~-ar~. ~Provecho~ descends from Latin ~prōfectus~ (“progress, profit”), the past participle of ~prōficere~ (“to advance, make headway”), itself ~pro-~ (“forward”) plus ~facere~ (“to make, do”). The Latin cluster ~-ct-~ regularly palatalized to ~-ch-~ and the ~f~ voiced to ~v~, so ~prōfectus~ became ~provecho~. Cognate with English ~profit~ and French ~profit~.

The verb ~aprovechar~ means literally to “put to profit,” to turn a thing or a moment to good account, and the reflexive ~aprovecharse~ took on the pointed sense of taking advantage of someone. The toast ¡Buen ~provecho~! at table — “may it do you good” — preserves the older, wider meaning of ~provecho~ as benefit rather than mere money. From the same ~facere~ Spanish drew a huge family, among them ~hacer~, ~afición~, ~perfecto~, and ~aprovechamiento~.
en.aproximar:
From Latin ~approximāre~ (“to draw near to”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~proximāre~ (“to come near”), a verb built on ~proximus~ (“nearest”), the superlative of the adverb ~prope~ (“near”), itself usually traced to a Proto-Indo-European base *~pro-~ (“forward, in front”). Cognate with English ~approximate~ and ~proximity~, Italian ~approssimare~, and Portuguese ~aproximar~.

The double comparison inside the word is easy to miss: ~proximus~ is already a superlative (“nearest of all”), so ~aproximar~ means, literally, “to bring toward the nearest.” Older and legal Spanish kept a concrete spatial sense — moving one body toward another — while modern usage leans figurative: an estimate that is ~aproximado~ (“approximate”), or two people who grow closer (~aproximarse~). The same family gave Spanish ~próximo~ (“next, near”), ~proximidad~, ~aproximación~, and the adverb ~aproximadamente~.
en.apuntar:
From ~a-~ plus ~punto~ (“point, dot”), which descends from Latin ~punctum~ (“a prick, a puncture, a point”), the neuter past participle of ~pungere~ (“to prick, to pierce”). ~pungere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~pewǵ-~ (“to prick, to punch”). It is cognate with Italian ~appuntare~ and French ~pointer~, and — through ~pungere~ and its participle — with English ~point~, ~puncture~, ~pungent~, and ~poignant~, all of them sharp in one way or another.

The core idea is making a point or mark, and ~apuntar~ fanned out from it into a startling spread of senses: to aim a weapon (to bring it to a point on a target), to point at something, to jot down (to set a point of ink on paper), and — in the theatre — to prompt an actor, which is why a prompter is an ~apuntador~. From the same ~punctum~ Spanish also drew ~punto~ (“point”), ~punta~ (“tip”), ~puntual~ (“punctual”), ~puntería~ (“aim”), ~apunte~ (“note”), and ~puntuar~ (“to punctuate”). The tiny prick of ~pungere~ thus points, notes, aims, and punctuates all at once.
en.aquejar:
The transitive ~aquejar~ (“to afflict, to distress”) is the prefix ~a-~ added to the older verb ~quejar~ (“to complain; to afflict”), which descends from Vulgar Latin *~quassiāre~, a reshaping of Latin ~quassāre~ (“to shake violently, to batter”), itself the frequentative of ~quatere~ (“to shake”). That verb traces to Proto-Indo-European *~kʷet-~ (“to shake”). Spanish shares the word with Portuguese ~queixar-se~ and, through Latin borrowings, with English ~quash~.

The thread runs from the physical to the mental: what ~quassāre~ once “battered” came to torment and oppress, so ~quejar~ and ~aquejar~ drifted from “to batter” toward “to afflict” and “to lament.” The same root left a broad Spanish family, among them the noun ~queja~ (“complaint”) and — from ~quatere~ through its compounds — ~sacudir~ (“to shake off”) and ~discutir~ (“to discuss,” originally “to shatter apart”).
en.arar:
Spanish ~arar~ comes straight from Latin ~arāre~ (“to plough”), from Proto-Italic *~araō~, from the Proto-Indo-European verb *~h₂éryeti~, from the root *~h₂erh₃-~ (“to plough”). It is one of the oldest farming words in the language, shared with Portuguese ~arar~ and Italian ~arare~, cognate with Greek ~ἀρόω~ and with the archaic English verb ~ear~ (“to plough”).

The same root ploughed a deep furrow through the lexicon: Latin ~arātrum~ (“plough”) gave Spanish ~arado~, and the adjective ~arable~ describes land fit for tilling. Where English generalized other roots for the field, the Romance languages kept the inherited verb almost untouched, so a Roman farmer’s ~arāre~ and a modern one’s ~arar~ are, in form and sense, nearly the same act two thousand years apart.
en.archivar:
From ~archivo~ (“archive”), from Latin ~archīvum~ (also ~archīum~), from Ancient Greek ~ἀρχεῖον~ (~archeîon~, “public office, town hall”) — the building where a magistrate kept official records — from ~ἀρχή~ (~arkhḗ~, “beginning; rule, magistracy”). Cognate with Italian ~archiviare~ and French ~archiver~, and — through Greek — with English ~archive~.

The chain hides a small irony: to ~archivar~ a document is, etymologically, to lodge it in the ~ἀρχή~, the seat of power, so filing was once an act of governance, not of forgetting. Modern Spanish has bent the word the other way — ~archivar~ un asunto now often means to shelve it, to let it lie. The Greek ~ἀρχή~ carried two senses, “beginning” and “rule,” and Spanish harvested both: from the first came the ~arqui-~/~arce-~ prefix of ~arquitecto~ (“chief builder”) and ~arzobispo~ (“archbishop”); from a related stem, the ~-arca~ of ~monarca~ and ~jerarquía~. The noun ~archivo~ now also names a computer file.
en.arder:
Spanish ~arder~ (“to burn”) descends from Latin ~ārdēre~ (“to burn, to blaze”), which is bound up with ~ārēre~ (“to be dry”) and the adjective ~āridus~ (“dry”), all from a Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eHs-~ (“to be dry; to burn”). The verb survived intact across Iberia and Italy, giving Portuguese ~arder~ and Italian ~ardere~; through Latin borrowings it is cousin to English ~ardent~ and ~ardor~.

The link between dryness and fire is the heart of the word — what is parched is what catches flame. Through its participle ~ārsus~, the same verb produced Old French ~arson~ (“a burning”), borrowed into English as ~arson~, the crime of setting fire. In Spanish the root still blazes in ~ardor~ (“ardour, heat”), ~ardiente~ (“burning, ardent”), and — from ~āridus~ — in ~árido~ (“arid”).
en.argumentar:
From Latin ~argūmentārī~ (“to argue, adduce proof”), from ~argūmentum~ (“evidence, proof”), from ~arguere~ (“to make clear, prove, demonstrate”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂erǵ-~ (“bright, white; to shine”). Cognate with Italian ~argomentare~ and French ~argumenter~, and — through the same root — with English ~argue~ and ~argument~.

The root meant brightness, and Latin ~arguere~ began as “to make bright,” hence “to make clear, to prove” — so to ~argumentar~ is, at bottom, to bring a matter to light. The most vivid relative hides in plain sight: from the same *~h₂erǵ-~, “the shining metal,” Latin named silver ~argentum~ — which gave Spanish ~argén~ and, by way of the silver-freighted Río de la Plata, the country name ~Argentina~. Greek preserved the root in ~ἄργυρος~ (~árgyros~, “silver”). Spanish also keeps ~argumento~, ~argüir~, and the participle-noun ~arguyente~ from this bright, argumentative family.
en.armar:
From Latin ~armāre~ (“to arm, equip with weapons”), a denominal verb from ~arma~ (“weapons, tools, equipment”). ~arma~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂er-~ (“to fit together, join”), via a form *~h₂(e)rmos~ (“that which is fitted”) — so weapons were, literally, the things fitted together, the gear. The root is richly attested: cognate with Ancient Greek ~ararískō~ (“to fit together”) and Sanskrit ~áram~ (“fittingly”). Within Latin it also produced ~ars~ (“skill, art”) and ~artus~ (“joint, limb”). The Romance verbs run parallel: Italian ~armare~, French ~armer~, Portuguese ~armar~.

The core image never left: to ~armar~ is to fit pieces together, and Spanish keeps that concrete sense vividly — one can ~armar~ a bookshelf, a tent, or an argument, not only an army. From the sense of fitting and joining, the vocabulary of skill and order also grew: the same root underlies ~arte~ (“art”), ~artículo~ (“article; joint”), ~armonía~ (Greek for “a fitting-together”) and ~arma~ itself. Colloquial idiom pushed the “assemble” sense toward chaos, too: ~armar~ un lío or ~armar~ un escándalo is to kick up a fuss — to assemble a mess. From ~armāre~ come directly ~armario~ (“wardrobe,” a place to store gear), ~armada~ (“fleet”) and ~armadura~ (“armor”).
en.arraigar:
Spanish ~arraigar~ (“to take root”) comes from Vulgar Latin *~arradicāre~, that is ~ad-~ (“to”) plus ~rādīcāre~ (“to take root”), a derivative of Latin ~rādīx~ (“root”), from Proto-Indo-European *~wréh₂ds~ (“root, branch”). Old Spanish had ~raigar~, later reanalysed as ~a-~ plus the stem; the verb is shared with Portuguese ~arraigar~. Through that same PIE root it is a distant cousin of English ~root~.

The image is the agricultural one made abstract: a plant sends down roots, and so do customs, families, and people. Spanish kept the metaphor vivid in ~raíz~ (“root”), ~raigambre~ (“roots, deep-seated tradition”), and the legal-social ~arraigo~ (“rootedness, established residence”). From the learned side of the same ~rādīx~ come ~erradicar~ (“to eradicate,” literally “to root out”) and ~radical~.
en.arrancar:
The origin of ~arrancar~ is genuinely disputed, and the sources agree only that no single etymon is secure. By the account Corominas favored, it descends from an Old Spanish *~esrancar~, formed on Old Occitan ~ranc~ or Old French ~ranc~ (“row, rank of soldiers”) — the Germanic-derived word that also gave English ~rank~ — with the idea of tearing a fighter out of the line. A rival account derives it from Latin ~ēruncāre~ (“to weed out”), perhaps crossed with ~ērādīcāre~ (“to uproot”); Romanian ~arunca~ (“to throw”) and Sicilian ~arruncari~ are cited in its support. An older guess tracing it to a Gothic *~wrankjan~ (“to twist”) is rejected on phonetic grounds.

Whatever its source, the verb fixed on the image of wrenching something loose from where it sat rooted — pulling up a plant, yanking out a tooth, tearing off a strip. From that violent tug came its everyday modern senses: a car ~arranca~ when its engine is jolted into motion, and a sprinter ~arranca~ bursting from the line. The noun ~arranque~ names both an engine’s “ignition” and, figuratively, a sudden “fit” of temper or generosity — a surge that grips you as abruptly as a root torn from soil.
