Nearby forms include ~arrancada~ (“a sudden spurt, a lurch forward”) and ~arrancador~.
en.arrastrar:
Spanish ~arrastrar~ (“to drag, haul”) is a prefixed formation: ~a-~ + ~rastrar~ (from ~rastro~) + the suffix ~-ar~. ~rastro~ (“rake; trail, trace”) descends from Latin ~rastrum~ (“rake, hoe”), an instrument noun from ~rādere~ (“to scrape, scratch, shave”), from a Proto-Indo-European root reconstructed as *~reh₁d-~ (“to scrape, scratch”). English ~erase~ (from Latin ~ērādere~) belongs to the same verb, and Spanish keeps ~raer~ (“to scrape off”) and ~arrasar~ (“to raze, level”) beside it.

The image inside ~arrastrar~ is vivid once you see it: a rake — ~rastrum~ — is a tool dragged along the ground, so ~rastro~ came to mean both the rake and the trail it leaves, and the verb came to mean pulling something across the ground the way a rake is pulled. Madrid’s famous flea market, ~El Rastro~, is named for that same “trail” sense, reputedly the trace of blood dragged from a nearby slaughterhouse. From the same root Spanish keeps ~rastrear~ (“to track, trace”), ~rastrillo~ (“rake”) and the noun ~rastro~ itself.
en.arrear:
Spanish ~arrear~ (“to drive on, to urge livestock forward”) is built from the interjection ~arre~ (“giddy-up!”), the cry with which herders spur their animals, plus the verb-forming ~-ar~. The interjection is an expressive word of uncertain, probably imitative origin, so the verb rests on a sound rather than on a Latin etymon. It gave the trade name ~arriero~ (“muleteer”) and the noun ~arreo~ (“a droving”).

A different, homonymous ~arrear~ — “to harness, to adorn” — has a separate source: Vulgar Latin *~arredāre~ (“to arrange, to equip”), of Germanic stock, from which come the noun ~arreo~ (“trappings”) and, in other languages, English ~array~ and French ~arroi~. The driving verb, though, stays tied to that shouted ~arre~: to arrear is, at heart, to keep saying ~arre~ until the mule moves.
en.arrebatar:
Spanish ~arrebatar~ (“to snatch, to seize violently”) is ~a-~ plus ~rebatar~, from the noun ~rebato~. Corominas, following Oliver Asín, traces it to Andalusi Arabic ~ribāṭ~, from the Arabic root ~r-b-ṭ~ (“to tie; to be garrisoned at a frontier post”). A ~ribāṭ~ was a fortified frontier convent, and by extension the sudden raid or alarm launched from the border.

That military suddenness is the whole story of the word: ~rebato~ came to mean a surprise attack or the alarm bell that announced it, and ~arrebatar~ took on the sense of carrying something off in a violent rush. The same emotional suddenness lives in ~arrebato~ (“fit of rage, rapture”) and in ~arrebatador~ (“captivating, ravishing”), where being snatched away is a thing one welcomes.
en.arredrar:
Spanish ~arredrar~ (“to intimidate, to daunt”) derives from the old adverb ~arredro~ (“backward, behind”) plus ~-ar~, from Vulgar Latin ~ad retrō~ (“to the rear”), from Latin ~retrō~ (“backward, behind”), itself built on ~re-~ (“back”). Old Spanish also had ~arriedro~. Portuguese preserves a sibling in ~arredar~ (“to move away”).

The logic is spatial turned psychological: to ~arredrar~ someone is literally to push them backward, to make them fall back — and from retreat in space came retreat in spirit, that is, fear. The same ~retrō~ runs through Spanish ~retroceder~ (“to back away”) and ~retaguardia~ (“rearguard”), and reached English as ~rear~, borrowed through Old French ~rere~.
en.arreglar:
Spanish ~arreglar~ is a prefixed derivative — ~a-~ plus ~regla~ (“rule, ruler”) — parallel to Late Latin ~regulāre~ (“to regulate”), from ~regula~ (“a straight rod, rule”), from ~regere~ (“to keep straight, guide, rule”). The root is Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, direct”). It is one of the most productive roots in the family: through ~regula~ it gives English ~rule~ (via Old French) and ~regular~; through ~regere~ and ~rēx~ (“king”) it gives ~regent~, ~royal~, and ~correct~; and the Germanic branch of the same root gives English ~right~.

To ~arreglar~ something is to bring it back into line with the ~regla~ — the straight measuring rod — hence to set it right, put it in order, adjust, or repair it. Old Spanish also had the barer ~reglar~; the ~a-~ form won out for everyday “to fix.” The root’s Spanish harvest is large: ~regla~ (“rule, ruler”), ~reglamento~ (“regulation”), ~regular~, ~regir~ (“to govern”), ~rey~ (“king,” worn from ~rēx~), ~región~, ~recto~ (“straight”), ~corregir~ (“to correct”), and ~dirigir~ (“to direct”), all sharing the idea of the straight line.
en.arremangar:
Spanish ~arremangar~ (“to roll up one’s sleeves”) is ~a-~ plus ~remangar~, itself ~re-~ plus ~manga~ (“sleeve”) plus ~-ar~. The noun ~manga~ goes back to Latin ~manica~ (“sleeve, long glove”), a derivative of ~manus~ (“hand”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *~méh₂-r̥~ (“hand”). The Latin word spread widely, giving Italian ~manica~, French ~manche~, and Portuguese ~manga~.

The image is concrete and universal: to free the hands for work you push the ~manga~ up the arm, so ~arremangar~ (and its variant ~remangar~) quickly gained the figurative sense of buckling down to a hard task. From the same ~manica~ English has ~manacle~ (“handcuff,” borrowed through Old French), while ~manus~ underlies a crowd of learned words — ~manual~, ~manuscrito~, ~maniobra~.
en.arremeter:
From ~a-~ + ~remeter~, the latter from ~re-~ + ~meter~, and ~meter~ from Latin ~mittere~ (“to send, let go, throw”), from Proto-Indo-European *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, remove”). The prefix ~a-~ (Latin ~ad-~) adds a sense of motion toward a target, so the whole is literally to fling oneself forward again and again. Cognate with French ~mettre~ and Portuguese ~arremeter~, and — through the same Latin root — with English ~mission~.

Where plain ~meter~ means simply “to put in,” ~arremeter~ specialized to the violent, repeated lunge of a charging bull or an attacking soldier, giving the modern sense « to charge, to rush at ». The image is of a body hurled bodily against an obstacle. From the same ~mittere~ Spanish also drew ~someter~ (“to subdue”), ~prometer~ (“to promise”), ~remesa~ (“remittance, shipment”) and ~misión~ — a whole family built on the idea of sending or letting go.
en.arrendar:
From ~a-~ + ~renta~ (“rent, income”) + ~-ar~. The noun ~renta~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~rendita~, an alteration of Latin ~reddita~, the feminine past participle of ~reddere~ (“to give back, render”), itself ~re-~ + ~dare~ (“to give”), from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Cognate with French ~rente~, Italian ~rendita~ and English ~rent~ (borrowed through Old French).

So to ~arrendar~ is, at root, to hand something over in exchange for a yield that is “given back” periodically — a lease. Curiously, Spanish has a second, homonymous ~arrendar~ meaning « to tie a horse by the reins », built instead on ~rienda~ (“rein,” from Latin ~retina~); the two verbs look and conjugate alike but come from unrelated words. From the same ~reddere~ came ~rendir~ (“to yield, surrender”), ~renta~, ~arrendamiento~ and ~arrendador~.
en.arrepentir:
From ~a-~ + Old Spanish ~repentir~ (“to repent”), attested in the thirteenth-century Cantigas de Santa María, from Vulgar Latin *~repaenitēre~, a reinforced form of Latin ~paenitēre~ (“to cause regret, to repent”), itself linked to ~paene~ (“almost, not quite”) — regret pictured as the nagging sense that something fell short. Cognate with French ~repentir~, Italian ~pentirsi~ and English ~repent~ (borrowed through Old French), and more distantly with ~penitent~ and ~penance~.

The regular Castilian sound-change would have voiced that intervocalic consonant to /d/, yet the medieval form held onto ~repentir~; Spanish later wrapped it in a prefix and the reflexive to give today's ~arrepentirse~. From the same ~paenitēre~ come ~penitencia~, ~penitente~ and the noun ~arrepentimiento~ — all circling a regret that keeps coming back.
en.arribar:
From Early Medieval Latin *~adrīpāre~, from Latin ~ad~ (“to, toward”) plus ~rīpa~ (“shore, riverbank”): to ~arribar~ was, at first, to bring a ship to the ~rīpa~ — to reach land. The deeper origin of ~rīpa~ is uncertain; it has been tentatively connected to a Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁reyp-~ (“to tear, cut”), the bank being the cut edge where water bites into the land, but this is proposed rather than settled. The Romance sisters are transparent: Italian ~arrivare~, French ~arriver~, Catalan ~arribar~, and, borrowed through Old French, English ~arrive~.

The nautical picture is the surprise inside the word: to arrive was to make landfall, and only later did ~arribar~ generalize to reaching any destination — though in Spanish it still keeps a seafaring flavor, often used of ships putting into port. From the same ~rīpa~ Spanish inherited ~ribera~ (“riverbank, shore”), ~ribazo~, and the place-name element ~riba~; and, most tellingly, the everyday adverb ~arriba~ (“up, above”) is the very same phrase ~ad rīpam~, “toward the [high] bank” — so that to head ~arriba~ and to ~arribar~ are, at root, the same journey to the water's edge.
en.arriesgar:
From ~a-~ plus ~riesgo~ (“risk”) plus ~-ar~ — literally “to put into risk.” The noun ~riesgo~ is of debated origin, and the sources are careful. The Spanish Academy once posited Arabic ~rizq~ (“provision, one's lot, fortune”), but Corominas rejects that and favors a link to ~risco~ (“steep crag, cliff”): the peril of the sharp rock gave the abstract sense of danger. Both ~riesgo~ and ~risco~ would then go back to a Vulgar Latin *~resecum~ (“that which cuts”), from ~resecāre~ (“to cut off”), ~re-~ plus ~secāre~ (“to cut”). None of this is settled — the medieval “riesco” the dictionaries presuppose is barely attested — so treat the crag story as the favored account, not proven fact.

Whatever its source, ~riesgo~ spread across the western Mediterranean of medieval maritime trade, with kin in Italian ~rischio~, Portuguese ~risco~, Catalan ~risc~ and French ~risque~ (a borrowing from Italian). Spanish ~arriesgar~ came to mean “to expose to danger, to venture,” and its participle ~arriesgado~ describes both a risky undertaking and a bold person. If Corominas is right, the same ~secāre~ (“to cut”) family includes ~segar~ (“to reap”), ~sierra~ and ~sección~ — making a risk, at root, a place where things are cut.
en.arrimar:
Of uncertain origin. The standard etymological dictionaries mark ~arrimar~ as « de origen incierto », and no ancestor has been securely established; various Latin and Germanic sources have been proposed, but none is accepted. What is clear is only the Romance company it keeps: Portuguese and Catalan also have ~arrimar~, with the same core sense of drawing one thing up against another.

Whatever its source, ~arrimar~ settled into the meaning « to bring close, to lean against » — to prop a ladder against a wall or, reflexively, to draw near to someone for shelter and support. It has a rich idiomatic life, as in « ~arrimar~ el hombro » (“to put one's shoulder to the wheel,” to pitch in). From it Spanish formed the noun ~arrimo~ (“support, shelter”), the phrase « al ~arrimo~ de » (“under the protection of”), and ~arrimadero~ (“something to lean against”). Given the disputed origin, the honest summary is that a very common verb carries an unknown pedigree.
en.arrojar:
~arrojar~ has no classical Latin ancestor of its own; the standard account, advanced by Menéndez Pidal and endorsed by Corominas, derives it from an unattested Vulgar Latin *~arrotulāre~ / *~rotulāre~ (“to send rolling”), from ~rotulus~ (“little wheel, roller”), the diminutive of ~rota~ (“wheel”). ~rota~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~Hret-~ (“to roll, run”), the root also behind German ~Rad~ (“wheel”) and, in Latin, ~rotāre~. So ~arrojar~ belongs, by this account, to the wheel-and-roll family that also gave Spanish ~rueda~, ~rodar~ and ~rótulo~.

If that etymology is right, ~arrojar~ began as something concrete and physical: to set a thing ~rotulāre~, rolling downhill, and hence to hurl or fling it. First recorded in the fourteenth century, it broadened from the literal throw to a wide arc of casting-out senses — to throw, to give off, to yield: a ledger ~arroja~ a balance, a report ~arroja~ results, and colloquially a queasy stomach ~arroja~ (“vomits”). From the same act Spanish drew ~arrojo~ (“boldness, daring” — the spirit of one who throws himself forward) and the adjective ~arrojado~ (“bold, rash”), where the old rolling stone has become a headlong courage.
en.articular:
From Latin ~articulāre~ (“to divide into joints; to utter distinctly”), from ~articulus~ (“small joint”), a diminutive of ~artus~ (“joint, limb”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂er-~ (“to join, fit together”). It is cognate with Italian ~articolare~ and French ~articuler~, and was borrowed into English as ~articulate~. The same root surfaces in Greek ~ἄρθρον~ (~árthron~, “joint,” whence the word arthritis) and in Latin ~ars~ (“skill, art”) — something well fitted together.

The metaphor runs from anatomy to speech: where bones meet at a joint, breath is likewise jointed into distinct sounds, so ~articular~ came to mean both to connect and to pronounce clearly. Spanish keeps both threads: ~articulación~ names a knuckle and a crisp enunciation alike; an ~artículo~ is a jointed “little member” of a text or a law; and ~arte~ preserves the older notion of fitting things aptly together. To articulate an argument is, at heart, to set its joints in the right order.
en.asar:
From Latin ~assāre~ (“to roast”), from the adjective ~assus~ (“roasted, dried by heat”). The adjective belongs to the vocabulary of cooking over fire rather than boiling in water, and it is generally connected with the idea of dryness and scorching. Cognate with Portuguese ~assar~ and Catalan ~assar~; Old Galician-Portuguese already had ~assar~ in the thirteenth century.

The verb has stayed close to its literal meaning — to cook by dry heat — but also drifted figuratively to « to be sweltering », as when one says « me ~aso~ de calor » (“I'm roasting with heat”). Its most famous descendant is the noun ~asado~, the roast, and in the Southern Cone the ~asado~ is the barbecue itself, a whole social institution of grilled meat. Spanish also keeps ~asador~ (“spit, rotisserie, grill-cook”) and ~asadura~ (“offal, pluck”) from the same ~assāre~.
en.ascender:
From Latin ~ascendere~ (“to climb up, mount”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~scandere~ (“to climb”), from Proto-Indo-European *~skend-~ (“to climb, dart, leap”). Cognate with Italian ~ascendere~ and Portuguese ~ascender~; through the same root, with English ~ascend~, ~descend~ and ~scan~, and — more distantly — with Welsh ~esgyn~ (“to ascend”).

Latin ~scandere~ named physical climbing and, in verse, the “climbing” of metrical feet — the origin of English ~scan~. Prefixed with ~ad-~, it became “to climb toward,” hence to go up; Spanish kept both the literal sense of climbing a height and the figurative ones (to be promoted, to rise in rank). From the same Latin verb Spanish drew ~ascenso~ (“ascent, promotion”), ~ascensor~ (“elevator”), and ~ascendiente~/~ascendente~ (“ancestor; ascending”); the prefixes ~de-~ and ~trans-~ yielded ~descender~ and ~trascender~, and ~con-~ gave ~condescender~.
en.asegurar:
From ~a-~ plus ~seguro~ plus the verbal ending ~-ar~ — literally “to make secure.” ~seguro~ comes from Latin ~sēcūrus~ (“free from care, safe”), a compound of ~sē-~ (“without”) and ~cūra~ (“care, concern”). Cognate with French ~assurer~ and ~sûr~, and with English ~secure~ and ~sure~ — the latter two a famous doublet, ~secure~ borrowed straight from Latin and ~sure~ worn down through Old French.

So to assure or ensure is, at root, to remove someone’s cares. The Latin ~sēcūrus~ described a mind at peace, untroubled; from that inner calm the word drifted toward outward safety and reliability. Spanish keeps both threads in ~seguro~, which is at once “safe,” “sure,” and (as a noun) “insurance” — the contract that buys freedom from worry. Relatives include ~seguridad~ (“security”) and, from the same ~cūra~, the verb ~curar~ (“to cure, to care for”) and the noun ~cura~ (“cure,” and also “priest,” the one charged with the care of souls).
en.asentar:
~Asentar~ formed in Old Spanish from the prefix ~a-~ and ~sentar~ (“to seat”), and is often traced to a Vulgar Latin *~assedentāre~. ~Sentar~ itself goes back to Vulgar Latin *~sedentāre~, from ~sedentem~, the present participle of Latin ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sed-~ (“to sit”). Cognates run deep: Italian ~sedere~, French ~asseoir~, and — through the same root — English ~sit~, ~seat~ and ~settle~.

The image is concrete: to ~asentar~ something is to make it “sit” — to set it down firmly, so the verb came to mean “to steady, establish, or put in writing,” and reflexively “to settle,” as a people settles a land (whence ~asentamiento~). From *~sed-~ Spanish also drew ~asiento~, ~sede~, ~sedimento~, ~sedentario~, ~presidir~ and ~residir~.
en.asesinar:
The verb ~asesinar~ was formed from the noun ~asesino~ (“assassin, murderer”), which came through Italian ~assassino~ and Medieval Latin ~assassīnus~ from Arabic ~ḥaššāšīn~, a name given to the Nizari Ismaili sect of Syria and Persia in the era of the Crusades. Cognate with French ~assassin~, English ~assassin~, and Portuguese ~assassinar~.

The traditional account, popularized by Marco Polo, reads ~ḥaššāšīn~ as “hashish-users,” from Arabic ~ḥašīš~ — the story being that the sect's members were drugged before their killings. That etymology is disputed: there is little evidence the Ismailis used hashish, and the label appears to have been a slur coined by rival Muslims; a competing account instead ties the name to their founder ~Ḥasan~ ibn al-Ṣabbāḥ, whose followers would be “Hasan's men.” Either way, the sect's reputation for targeted political killing is what fixed the word's meaning: through Italian it came to mean a hired killer, and Spanish ~asesinar~ is simply to murder — especially by treachery or for hire. Modern relatives: ~asesino~ and ~asesinato~ (“murder”).
en.asesorar:
From the noun ~asesor~ (“adviser”) plus ~-ar~. ~Asesor~ comes from Latin ~assessor~ (“one who sits beside; an assistant judge”), an agent noun of ~assidēre~ (“to sit beside, attend”), from ~ad-~ (“beside”) and ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sed-~ (“to sit”). That immense root also yielded English ~sit~, ~session~ and ~sedentary~, French ~asseoir~ and — straight from the same Latin word — the English legal ~assessor~.

The etymology is a posture. In a Roman court the ~assessor~ was the jurist who literally “sat beside” the magistrate to advise him on the law — counsel embodied as a seat — and from that image Spanish drew ~asesorar~ (“to advise professionally”) and ~asesoría~ (“advisory office”). The same “sitting” root sits inside many other Spanish words: ~asiduo~ (“assiduous,” one who sits at a task), ~sesión~, ~residir~ and ~presidir~.
en.asignar:
From Latin ~assignāre~ (“to mark out, allot, assign”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~signāre~ (“to mark”), from ~signum~ (“sign, mark, standard”). The deeper root is disputed: ~signum~ is traced either to Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut,” a mark cut in) or to *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow,” the standard a legion follows), and the sources do not settle which. From ~assignāre~ come Italian ~assegnare~, Portuguese ~assinar~, and French ~assigner~; from ~signum~ itself, English ~sign~.

To assign was originally to mark something out and set it apart for a purpose — a plot of land, a duty, a share. Spanish shows the usual split between a popular and a learned line from ~signum~: the inherited ~seña~ and ~señal~ beside the bookish ~signo~, ~signar~, and ~designar~. A charming descendant is ~asignatura~ — a school “subject,” literally something “assigned” to be studied — and ~insignia~, ~consigna~, and ~diseñar~ (“to design,” to mark out a plan) belong to the same clan. Whether the root first meant a cut or a thing-to-follow may stay unresolved, but either way ~asignar~ has always been about marking one thing off for another.
en.asir:
The origin of ~asir~ (“to grasp, seize”) is debated. The favored account, defended by Corominas, derives it from the noun ~asa~ (“handle”), from Latin ~ansa~ (“handle, grip”), so that ~asir~ meant literally to take something by its handle. A rival proposal traces it to Old French ~saisir~ (“to seize”), but Corominas rejects this: the old voiced ~-s-~ of Castilian and Portuguese argues against it, Catalan never had the word, and ~saisir~ was chiefly a legal term for taking formal possession, whereas ~asir~ is thoroughly physical. Latin ~ansa~ itself goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂enseh₂-~ (“handle”), with cognates in Lithuanian ~ąsa~ (“jug handle”) and, more distantly, Ancient Greek ~ἡνία~ (hēnía, “rein”).

If the ~asa~ etymology is right, ~asir~ carries a homely image at its core: to grip a pot or basket by the very part made for holding. The verb kept the sense of firm physical seizing and extended to abstract grasping, as in ~asirse a una esperanza~ (“to cling to a hope”). Its conjugation preserves a telltale irregularity, the ~-g-~ present ~asgo~ / ~asga~ (like ~tener~ → ~tengo~), but in practice speakers tend to shun those forms, reaching for synonyms such as ~agarrar~ or ~coger~. From the same ~asa~ come ~asidero~ (“handhold”) and the participial adjective ~asido~ (“clutched, held fast”).
en.asistir:
From Latin ~assistere~ (“to stand by, take one’s place beside”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~sistere~ (“to cause to stand, to take a stand, to halt”). ~sistere~ is a reduplicated form built on ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — the same root behind ~estar~. It gave Italian ~assistere~, French ~assister~, and English ~assist~; and through ~sistere~ it is cognate with English ~exist~, ~insist~, ~resist~, ~consist~, and ~persist~.

To “stand beside” someone is to be there both for support and as a witness, and ~asistir~ split along exactly that line. In Spanish (as in French ~assister~) it chiefly means “to attend, to be present”: one ~asiste a~ a class or a concert. But it also keeps the “stand-by-to-help” sense in ~asistir~ (“to assist”) and in ~asistencia~ (“assistance; attendance”) and ~asistente~ (“assistant”). English ~assist~, by contrast, narrowed to helping alone — a tidy false-friend trap. The ~sistere~ family stands tall across Spanish: ~existir~, ~insistir~, ~resistir~, ~consistir~, ~persistir~, ~desistir~, and ~subsistir~, every one of them, at root, a way of standing.
en.asociar:
From Latin ~associāre~ (“to join to, unite with”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward,” assimilated to ~as-~) and ~sociāre~ (“to join, ally”), the verb built on ~socius~ (“companion, ally, partner”). ~socius~ meant literally “a follower” and descends from Proto-Indo-European *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”) — the same root that gave Latin ~sequī~ (“to follow”). The cognate web is wide: through ~sequī~ English took (by borrowing) ~sequence~, ~sequel~, ~second~ (“the following one”) and ~pursue~. The learned Romance descendants of the compound include Italian ~associare~, French ~associer~ and Portuguese ~associar~.

The logic is transparent: companions are those who follow together, and to associate is to make someone a ~socius~, a fellow-goer. From ~socius~ Spanish keeps ~socio~ (“partner, member”), ~social~, ~sociedad~ (“society”), ~asociación~ (“association”) and ~asociado~ (“associate”). The deeper root *~sekʷ-~, through ~sequī~ and its participle ~secūtus~, fanned out enormously: ~seguir~ (“to follow”), ~seguido~, ~secuencia~ (“sequence”), ~consecuencia~ (“consequence”), ~perseguir~ (“to pursue”), ~ejecutar~ (“to execute, follow through”) and even ~segundo~ (“second,” the following one). To associate ideas, then, is to let one “follow” another — companionship written into cognition itself.
en.asolar:
Spanish has two verbs spelled ~asolar~, and they pull in different directions. The first, « to raze, to devastate », is a compound of ~a-~ + ~suelo~ (“ground, floor,” from Latin ~solum~) + ~-ar~ — literally to bring something level with the ground, to lay it flat in ruins. The second, « to scorch, to parch », is ~a-~ + ~sol~ (“sun,” from Latin ~sōl~, from Proto-Indo-European *~sóh₂wl̥~) + ~-ar~ — what drought and blazing sun do to a crop.

The two are held apart partly by conjugation: the devastate-verb diphthongizes (~asuela~, like ~contar~), while the sun-verb often stays regular (~asola~), though usage wavers and the senses bleed together, since a scorched land is also a devastated one. From ~solum~ Spanish also has ~suelo~, ~solar~ and ~subsuelo~; from ~sōl~, the cognate of English ~sun~, come ~sol~, ~solar~ and ~solsticio~ — two roots meeting, by accident, in a single troublesome verb.
en.asomar:
From ~a-~ + Old Spanish ~somo~ (“top, summit”) + ~-ar~. The noun ~somo~ descends from Latin ~summus~ (“highest, topmost”), a superlative that also gave ~sumo~ and ~suma~; ~summus~ itself goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~upo-~ (“up from under”), the root behind ~super~ and English ~up~ and ~over~. English ~summit~, borrowed through Old French, is a cognate of ~somo~.

The literal force of ~asomar~ was “to show the top (of the head),” to bring just the crown of something into view over an edge — and from that narrow image the verb generalized to « to show, to begin to appear, to peep out ». One ~asoma~ the head through a doorway, and dawn ~asoma~ over the hills. Reflexive ~asomarse~ means to lean out — « asomarse a la ventana », to lean out of the window. The same field gives the noun ~asomo~ (“a hint, a trace,” as in « ni por asomo », “not in the slightest”).
en.aspirar:
From Latin ~aspīrāre~ (also ~adspīrāre~, “to breathe upon, breathe toward”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~spīrāre~ (“to breathe”). Cognate with Italian ~aspirare~ and French ~aspirer~, and — through ~spīrāre~ — with English ~aspire~, ~respire~, and ~conspire~; the noun ~spīritus~ (“breath, spirit”) came down to Spanish as ~espíritu~.

The origin of ~spīrāre~ is uncertain: it has no secure cognates, and de Vaan judges it probably onomatopoeic, an imitation of the very sound of breathing; an older proposal tied it to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)peys-~ (“to blow”). ~Aspirar~ began as “to breathe toward” and, by way of the breath one draws in longing, took on the figurative “to aspire, yearn for.” Its concrete senses stayed close to the lungs — “to inhale,” “to aspirate” a consonant, and colloquially “to vacuum” (hence ~aspiradora~). The breathing family is large: ~respirar~, ~espirar~, ~suspirar~, ~inspirar~, ~conspirar~, ~expirar~, and ~aspiración~ all trace back to that single Latin breath.
en.asumir:
From Latin ~assūmere~ (“to take up, adopt, claim”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~sūmere~ (“to take up”), itself ~sub-~ (“up from below”) plus ~emere~ (“to take, buy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁em-~ (“to take, distribute”). It is cognate with French ~assumer~, Italian ~assumere~, and Portuguese ~assumir~, and with the Latin-derived English ~assume~; through ~emere~ it is also kin to English ~example~ and ~exempt~.

In Latin ~emere~ first meant “to take” and only later specialized to “to buy” — a shift from grasping a thing to grasping it by purchase. Its compound ~sūmere~ kept the “take up” sense, and ~asumir~ today means to take something on: a duty, a role, a cost. The ~sūmere~ line gave Spanish ~consumir~, ~presumir~, and ~resumir~, while the older ~emere~ surfaces in ~ejemplo~ (from ~exemplum~, “a sample taken out”), ~redimir~, and ~eximir~. What unites them all is the plain, physical act of taking.
en.asustar:
~Asustar~ is built from the prefix ~a-~, the noun ~susto~ (“fright, scare”) and the verb-forming ~-ar~ — literally “to give someone a fright.” The origin of ~susto~ itself is disputed. By one account, favored by the Spanish Academy, it goes back through a hypothetical *~sustar~ to Latin ~suscitāre~ (“to rouse, stir up”), from ~sub-~ plus ~citāre~ (“to set moving”), the frequentative of ~ciēre~ — from Proto-Indo-European *~keyh₁-~ (“to set in motion”). Corominas, by contrast, rejects a clear etymon and judges ~susto~ probably imitative, from the hiss ~¡sst!~ of a startled breath.

Whichever account is right, the word is a relative latecomer, documented only from the early 17th century, and ~susto~ and ~asustar~ seem to have grown up side by side rather than one straightforwardly from the other. If the Academy's ~suscitāre~ is correct, then ~asustar~ shares its deep root with ~excitar~, ~incitar~, ~solicitar~ and ~resucitar~, all carrying the sense of “stirring” something into motion. The imitative account, by contrast, leaves ~susto~ without cousins, an isolated echo of a gasp.
en.atacar:
From Italian ~attaccare~ (“to attach, to join,” and in ~attaccare battaglia~, “to join battle”), taken into Spanish in the sixteenth century as a military term. The Italian verb is generally linked to a Germanic word for a stake or post — Gothic *~stakka~, also the source of Spanish ~estaca~ — the idea being to fasten one thing to another; but the details of that descent are disputed. From the same Italian source come French ~attaquer~ and, as doublets, English ~attach~ and ~attack~.

The journey from a fence post to open warfare runs through the idea of fastening: to ~attaccare~ was to fix things together, and ~attaccare battaglia~ was to “knit” two armies into combat. Spanish borrowed only the martial sense, so ~atacar~ came to mean purely “to assault,” while the older “fasten” meaning stayed abroad in English ~attach~. If the stake origin holds, the native Spanish cousin is ~estaca~, and with it ~destacar~ (originally “to detach a body of troops,” now “to stand out”) and ~estacada~. It is a striking case of one Germanic post branching, through Italian, into fastening, detaching and attacking.
en.atajar:
From ~a-~ + ~tajar~ (“to cut, slice”), and ~tajar~ from Vulgar Latin *~taliāre~ (“to cut, split”), from Latin ~talea~ (“a cutting, a slip or rod taken from a plant”). It is a doublet of ~tallar~ (“to carve”). Cognate with French ~tailler~, Italian ~tagliare~ and Portuguese ~talhar~, and — through French — with English ~tailor~ and ~detail~.

The prefix turns “to cut” into « to cut off, to head off, to cut short » — one ~ataja~ a fire, an argument, or a fugitive by cutting across its path. The intransitive sense « to take a shortcut » gave the everyday noun ~atajo~ (“shortcut,” literally a cutting-across). From the same ~talea~ Spanish grew a large family: ~tajo~ (“cut, gorge”), ~tajar~, ~tajada~ (“slice”), ~talla~ (“size, carving”), ~tallar~ and ~detalle~ (“detail,” a thing cut small).
en.atar:
From Old Spanish ~atar~, from Latin ~aptāre~ (“to fit, to adapt, to make ready”), the frequentative of ~aptus~ (“fitted, suited, apt”), from Proto-Italic *~aptos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ep-~ (“to join, to fit”). It is a doublet of the later, learned borrowing ~aptar~, and cognate with English ~apt~ and ~adapt~ and with Spanish ~apto~ — all carrying the idea of things fitted neatly together.

The semantic slide is quietly logical: what fits together can be bound together, and Latin ~aptāre~ (“to fit”) narrowed in Spanish to ~atar~ (“to tie, to bind”). The ~-pt-~ cluster simplified to a single ~-t-~ in the inherited word, which is exactly how you tell it apart from the bookish ~aptar~, borrowed centuries later with the consonants intact. The PIE root *~h₂ep-~ (“to grasp, to reach, to fit”) also underlies Latin ~apiscī~ (“to grasp, to attain”), and from the same broad family Spanish draws ~apto~, ~aptitud~, ~adaptar~, ~adepto~, ~inepto~, and the everyday ~atadura~ (“a tie, a bond”) and ~desatar~ (“to untie, to unleash”).
en.atañer:
From Vulgar Latin ~attangere~, a variant of Classical Latin ~attingere~ (“to touch, reach, border on”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~tangere~ (“to touch”). The root is Proto-Indo-European *~teh₂g-~ (“to touch, handle”). Spanish inherited two verbs from ~tangere~: ~tañer~ (“to pluck, play” an instrument) directly, and ~atañer~ (“to concern, pertain to”) from the prefixed ~attingere~. The same root gives Italian ~tangere~ and, as learned borrowings, English ~tangent~ and ~tangible~.

~atañer~ narrowed from physical touching to the figurative sense of touching upon someone's affairs, that is, to concern or be one's business. That semantics made it defective: it is used almost only in the third person, typically with an indirect object, as in ~en lo que a mí me atañe~ (“as far as I am concerned”) or ~eso no te atañe~ (“that doesn't concern you”). It has no imperative, for one hardly commands a matter to concern someone. From the same fertile root *~teh₂g-~ Spanish draws a wide family: ~tacto~, ~tangente~, ~tangible~, ~contacto~, ~contagio~, and ~intacto~, all of them, at bottom, about touching.
en.atender:
From Latin ~attendere~ (“to stretch toward, direct one’s mind to”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate with Italian ~attendere~ and — with a telling shift of sense — French ~attendre~ (“to wait”) and Portuguese ~atender~; through ~tendere~ it is kin to English ~tend~ and ~tension~.

The Romans pictured attention as a physical reaching: to ~atender~ was to stretch the mind toward something. Spanish kept the engaged senses — to heed, to look after, to serve — so that in a shop a clerk ~atiende~ a customer, a false friend for English speakers who expect it to mean simply to be present. The same ~tendere~ left a homely trace: Spanish ~tienda~ (“shop,” earlier “tent”) began as a stretched-out awning of cloth. Related descendants include ~atención~ (“attention”), ~tender~ (“to spread, hang out”), ~extender~ (“to extend”), and ~tenso~ (“tense”).
en.atener:
From Latin ~attinēre~ (“to hold to, pertain, concern”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~tenēre~ (“to hold”), from Proto-Italic *~tenēō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate with Italian ~attenere~ and Portuguese ~ater~, and — through the same root — with English ~tenant~ and ~tenacious~.

The Latin sense of holding fast narrowed in Spanish to the reflexive ~atenerse~, above all ~atenerse a~ (“to abide by, to stick to”): to hold oneself to a rule, a decision, or its consequences. The old idea of stretching and holding seeded a large family: ~tener~ (“to have”), ~contener~, ~detener~, ~mantener~, and the adjective ~tenaz~ (“tenacious”).
en.aterrar:
Spanish ~aterrar~ is really two verbs that fell together. The first, “to terrify,” comes from Latin ~terrēre~ (“to frighten”), from an earlier *~tersēō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~tres-~ (“to tremble”); the second, “to fell, to throw to the ground, to cover with earth,” is ~a-~ + ~tierra~ (“earth, land”), from Latin ~terra~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ters-~ (“dry”). The two roots are wholly distinct despite the identical modern form.

So the same string means both “terrify” and “demolish,” disambiguated only by context — a striking homonymy born of two unrelated Latin words. From ~terrēre~ Spanish also drew ~terror~, ~terrible~, and ~aterrorizar~, sharing the root of English ~terror~ and ~deter~; from ~terra~ came ~terreno~, ~territorio~, ~enterrar~, and ~aterrizar~ (“to land [an aircraft]”), kin to English ~terrace~ and ~terrain~.
en.atizar:
From Vulgar Latin *~attitiāre~, a verb built on Latin ~titiō~ (“firebrand, burning stick”) with the prefix ~ad-~. Cognate with Portuguese ~atiçar~ and Galician ~atizar~. The ultimate root of ~titiō~ is uncertain; it has been linked to a Proto-Indo-European root for burning, *~teyh₁-~, but the connection is not secure.

The primary sense stayed close to the firebrand: to ~atizar~ a fire is to poke, feed, and stir it so it burns hotter — which is why the verb turned figurative so easily, letting one ~atizar~ hatred, a rumor, or a quarrel. From the same ~titiō~ Spanish keeps ~tizón~ (“firebrand, ember”) and ~tizne~ (“soot”), and the agent noun ~atizador~ names the poker itself.
en.atormentar:
From ~a-~ + ~tormento~ (“torment, torture”), from Latin ~tormentum~ — originally a twisted rope, a torsion catapult, and hence an instrument of torture — a noun formed from ~torquēre~ (“to twist”) with the suffix ~-mentum~. Latin ~torquēre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~terkʷ-~ (“to turn, to twist”). Cognate through that root with English ~torque~, ~torch~, and ~thwart~.

The mechanical image — a rope or a body wrenched under tension — passed straight into the emotional sense of ~atormentar~, “to torment,” to twist someone with suffering. The same ~torquēre~ gave Spanish ~torcer~ (“to twist”), ~torno~ (“lathe, winch”), ~tornillo~ (“screw”), and ~tormenta~ (“storm,” the sky wrung and churned), while learned ~tortura~ and ~torsión~ were later borrowings from the same Latin stem.
en.atraer:
From Latin ~attrahere~ (“to draw toward”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~trahere~ (“to draw, drag, pull”); Spanish reshaped it on its own inherited ~traer~ (also from ~trahere~). The deeper origin of ~trahere~ is uncertain — De Vaan reconstructs a possibly non-Indo-European root *~trāgʰ-~, perhaps shared with Celtic, and a much-debated link to Proto-Germanic *~draganą~ (source of English ~draw~ and ~drag~). Romance cognates include French ~attraire~, Italian ~attrarre~, and Portuguese ~atrair~, while English ~attract~ comes from the Latin participle ~attractus~.

The metaphor is purely physical: to “draw something toward” you, whether by a magnet or by charm. From ~trahere~ Spanish inherited a large, productive family — ~traer~ (“to bring”), and the prefixed ~atraer~, ~contraer~, ~extraer~, ~distraer~, ~sustraer~, ~retraer~, and ~abstraer~. Alongside these run the learned ~-tract-~ nouns and adjectives: ~tractor~ (“one that pulls”), ~tracción~, ~atractivo~, ~contrato~, and ~retrato~ — a portrait being, quite literally, a face “drawn again.”
en.atrapar:
Either from ~a-~ + ~trapa~ (an old Spanish word for a snare), or taken from French ~attraper~ (“to catch in a trap”), from Old French ~trape~ (“trap”), ultimately from a West Germanic *~trappa~ (“snare”). The Germanic word belongs to a family meaning “to tread, step,” which surfaces in English ~trap~, German ~Treppe~ (“staircase”), and Middle Dutch ~trappe~. Its earliest written trace is the Late Latin ~trappa~ recorded in the Frankish Lex Salica. Cognates include Italian ~trappola~, Portuguese ~trapa~, and French ~trappe~.

The meaning moved from the concrete device — a pit or spring-snare that shuts on an animal — to seizing or catching anything, and then figuratively to “catching” a person in a lie or a promise. The link to treading recalls the hunter's trap triggered underfoot. From the same Germanic stock Spanish keeps ~trampa~ (“trap; cheat”), ~trampear~ (“to swindle”), ~trampolín~ (“springboard”), and ~atrapamoscas~ (“flytrap”).
en.atravesar:
Spanish ~atravesar~ is ~través~ with the prefix ~a-~, and ~través~ comes from Latin ~transversus~ (“turned across, lying crosswise”), the past participle of ~transvertere~, from ~trans~ (“across”) plus ~vertere~ (“to turn”). ~Vertere~ rests on Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (“to turn”), which also gave English ~-ward~ and, through Latin, ~verse~ and ~convert~. French built ~traverser~ from the same participle, the twin of English ~traverse~.

The image is bodily: to ~atravesar~ something is to move through it along the “turned-across” line — to cross, span, or pierce it. The stem ~través~ still means “aslant,” and the derivative ~travesía~ names a crossing or voyage. Most striking is ~travieso~: literally “lying crosswise,” it drifted from “wayward, contrary” to the affectionate modern “mischievous, naughty” said of a restless child. From the same ~vertere~ Spanish also draws ~verter~, ~convertir~, ~invertir~, ~verso~, ~universo~ and ~aniversario~.
en.atrever:
By the received account, from Latin ~attribuere~ (“to assign, attribute”) — specifically the reflexive ~attribuere sibi~, “to grant oneself (the power to do something)” — a compound of ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~tribuere~ (“to allot, assign”), from ~tribus~ (“tribe”), whose deeper origin is uncertain (one proposal analyzes it as ~tri-~, “three,” plus a form of “to be”). Cognate — through ~tribuere~ — with English ~tribute~, ~attribute~, ~contribute~ and ~tribe~.

The semantic path is neat: to grant oneself the capacity for a bold act is, in the end, to ~atreverse~ — to dare. The origin is not undisputed, however: struck by the Old Spanish variant ~estreverse~, Cuervo proposed instead a Germanic source, Old High German ~strëben~ (“to strive”), but that account has been rejected in favor of ~attribuere~. Spanish keeps the daring branch in ~atrevimiento~ (“audacity”) and ~atrevido~ (“bold, cheeky”), while the ~tribuere~ root also gave ~atribuir~, ~contribuir~, ~distribuir~, ~tributo~ and ~tribu~.
en.atribuir:
From Latin ~attribuere~ (“to assign, allot”), which is ~ad-~ (“to”) plus ~tribuere~ (“to allot, grant”), literally “to distribute among the tribes”. That verb rests on ~tribus~ (“tribe, a division of the Roman people”), whose own origin is unclear: by one traditional account it is built on ~trēs~ (“three”) — the three original tribes of early Rome — perhaps with an element from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰuH-~ (“to be, grow”), though this is contested, not settled. It is cognate with English ~attribute~ and ~tribute~.

The bookkeeping image never quite left: to ~atribuir~ is to assign a quality, cause, or credit to someone, as a share is allotted to a tribe. The Latin noun surfaces plainly as Spanish ~tribu~, and the verb radiated into a whole administrative vocabulary — ~tributo~ (“tribute, tax”), ~contribuir~, ~distribuir~, and ~retribuir~ (“to pay back, reward”) — each about apportioning something out to its recipients.
en.atribular:
From Late Latin ~tribulāre~ (“to press, to oppress, to afflict”), taken into Spanish with the prefix ~a-~. The Latin verb derives from ~tribulum~ (“threshing sledge,” the studded board dragged over grain), from ~terere~ (“to rub, to wear, to thresh”), from Proto-Indo-European *~terh₁-~ (“to rub, to turn”). Cognate through the root with English ~tribulation~, ~trite~ (literally “worn down”), and ~detriment~.

The metaphor is agricultural and vivid: to be afflicted is to be threshed, crushed under the sledge like grain — a figure that Christian Latin embraced for spiritual suffering, which is how the learned ~atribular~ entered Spanish. Tellingly, that very same Latin ~tribulāre~ also descended, by ordinary sound-change, into ~trillar~ (“to thresh”), so Spanish holds a doublet: ~atribular~ afflicts the soul while ~trillar~ still beats the wheat. The abstract noun ~tribulación~ belongs to the same family.
en.atronar:
From ~a-~ + ~tronar~ (“to thunder”), from Latin ~tonāre~ (“to thunder, to resound”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)tenh₂-~ (“to thunder”). The intrusive ~r~ of ~tronar~ (against ~tonāre~) is a Romance development. Cognate through the root with English ~thunder~, with the Norse thunder-god ~Þórr~ (Thor), and echoed in the Roman epithet ~Tonans~, “the Thundering,” for Jupiter.

The prefix in ~atronar~ is intensive: where ~tronar~ simply thunders, ~atronar~ is to deafen, to fill a space with thunderous noise. The same ~tonāre~ yielded the noun ~trueno~ (“thunderclap”) and the adjective ~atronador~ (“deafening”), while the compound ~detonāre~ returned as the learned ~detonar~ (“to detonate”) — an explosion being, etymologically, a thunder flung outward.
en.aullar:
From Latin ~ululāre~ (“to howl, to wail”), an imitative verb echoing a cry, ultimately from a reduplicated onomatopoeic Proto-Indo-European root. It gave Old Spanish ~ullar~, later ~aullar~ with an added initial vowel. Cognate with Italian ~urlare~, French ~hurler~, and Portuguese ~uivar~, and — as a direct learned borrowing of the same Latin verb — with English ~ululate~.

Because the word merely imitates the sound, it has always meant the long cry of wolves, dogs, and the wind. Spanish preserves a doublet: popular ~aullar~ beside the learned ~ulular~ (“to ululate, to hoot”), both from ~ululāre~ — the first worn down by centuries of speech, the second lifted straight from Latin. From ~aullar~ comes the noun ~aullido~ (“howl”), and the wind or a siren can equally ~aullar~ in Spanish.
en.aumentar:
From Latin ~augmentāre~ (“to increase”), from ~augmentum~ (“growth, increase”), from ~augēre~ (“to increase, enlarge”), from Proto-Italic *~augeō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ewg-~ (“to grow, increase”). Cognate with Italian ~aumentare~, French ~augmenter~, Portuguese ~aumentar~ and English ~augment~; through the root, with English ~eke~ and — via Germanic — ~wax~ (“to grow”).

The PIE root *~h₂ewg-~ was extraordinarily productive in Latin. Beyond ~aumentar~ it gave ~aumento~ and ~auge~ (“peak, height”); through ~auctor~ (“originator, one who makes grow”) came Spanish ~autor~; through ~augustus~ (“consecrated, majestic”), the month ~agosto~ and the name ~Augusto~; and through ~auxilium~ (“help, reinforcement”), ~auxilio~. Even the diviner’s ~augurio~ may belong to this family. To increase is, at bottom, to make something grow.
en.autorizar:
From Medieval Latin ~auctorizāre~ (“to give authority to”), from Latin ~auctor~ (“originator, promoter, author”), an agent-noun of ~augēre~ (“to increase, to make grow”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ewg-~ (“to increase”). The growth-root is prolific: cognate with English ~augment~, ~auction~ (Latin ~auctiō~, “an increasing” of bids), and ~august~, and — through Germanic — with the archaic English ~eke~ (“to add to, to increase”).

An ~auctor~ was one who caused a thing to grow — who originated, backed, or vouched for it — so to ~autorizar~ is to lend one's authority to an act and let it stand. At the center of the Spanish family sit ~autor~ (“author”) and ~autoridad~ (“authority”), joined by ~aumentar~ (“to increase”), ~auge~ (“peak, boom,” a high point of growth), and ~augusto~ (“august, majestic”), the imperial epithet of ~Augusto~ (Augustus) that also named a month.
en.avalar:
From ~aval~ (“a guarantee, an endorsement”) plus ~-ar~. Spanish took ~aval~ from French ~aval~, a term of commercial law — but the origin of the French word is genuinely disputed, and the sources will not settle it. By one account it is ~à val~ (“downward, at the foot”), because the guarantor once signed at the bottom of a bill of exchange; on this reading it belongs with Latin ~vallis~ (“valley”), Spanish ~valle~. By another, it comes from Arabic ~ḥawāla~ (“a transfer of debt, a bill of exchange”), a core term of medieval Islamic finance. Both accounts fit the mercantile setting, and neither is proven — so it is safest to present the two side by side rather than pick one.

Whatever the source, the meaning is clear and consistent: an ~aval~ is a signature by which one party guarantees another's obligation, and ~avalar~ is to give that backing. From the ledger the word spread into ordinary speech, where to ~avalar~ a person, a claim or a theory is to vouch for it, to lend it one's credit. The agent noun ~avalista~ names the one who so guarantees. Its narrow, technical birth makes ~avalar~ a good reminder that everyday words often begin life on a banker's page.
en.avanzar:
Spanish ~avanzar~ (“to advance”) goes back to Vulgar Latin *~abantiāre~, a verb built on Late Latin ~abante~ (“forward, in front”), itself the univerbation of ~ab~ (“from”) and ~ante~ (“before”). The ~ante~ half rests on Proto-Indo-European *~h₂énti~ (“in front, before”). It is cognate with French ~avancer~, Italian ~avanzare~ and Catalan ~avançar~ — and, through Old French, with English ~advance~. That English ~d~ is a historical mistake: scribes wrongly read the ~av-~ as if it held the prefix ~ad-~ and inserted a ~d~ that never belonged there. The war-word English ~vanguard~ (from French ~avant-garde~, “fore-guard”) comes of the same ~abante~.

The etymology is a picture of forward motion: to ~avanzar~ is to move “from the front,” to push the front line onward. In Spanish the verb serves every kind of progress — an army, a project, an argument, a clock all ~avanzan~. It kept, too, a quieter commercial sense of “to advance” money, to pay ahead. Its Spanish family marches in the same direction: ~avance~ (“advance, progress; a film trailer”), ~avanzado~ (“advanced”), ~avanzada~ (“outpost, vanguard”) and ~avanzadilla~ (“advance party”). And the ~ante~ at its heart is everywhere in Spanish — in ~antes~, ~anterior~, ~antaño~ and ~delante~ — the little Indo-European word for “in front” still doing its work.
en.avenir:
From Latin ~advenīre~ (“to arrive, to come to”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷenjō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to go”). Cognate with Italian ~avvenire~ and French ~advenir~, a doublet of the learned Spanish ~advenir~, and — through the same root — with English ~come~ and the English ~advent~ and ~adventure~.

“To come to” shaded into “to fit, to agree,” and modern ~avenir~ lives mostly in the reflexive ~avenirse~ (“to get along, to come to terms”) — two parties whose wishes at last arrive at the same place. Hence the noun ~avenencia~ (“accord, settlement”) and its negative ~desavenencia~ (“discord”). The same ~venīre~ underlies ~venir~ (“to come”), ~convenir~ (“to suit, to agree”), ~prevenir~, and ~porvenir~ (“future,” literally “what is to come”).
en.aventar:
Spanish ~aventar~ was built from the prefix ~a-~ and ~viento~ (“wind”, from Latin ~ventus~) plus the verb-ending ~-ar~. Latin ~ventus~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂weh₁-~ (“to blow”). The same coinage surfaces in Portuguese and Galician ~aventar~ (“to air, to ventilate”), and through that shared root Spanish ~viento~ is cognate with English ~wind~ and, more distantly, with ~ventilate~ and ~vent~.

The verb first named winnowing: threshed grain is tossed upward so the ~viento~ blows away the light chaff while the heavy kernels drop back. From there it spread to “fanning” a fire and “airing out” a room. In much of Latin America, and especially Mexico, ~aventar~ slid toward the plain sense “to throw, to hurl”, and the noun ~aventón~ came to mean a free ride or a lift. Numerous relatives descend from the same root, among them ~viento~, ~ventilar~, ~ventana~ (a “window”, originally an opening for air) and ~vendaval~ (a strong wind).
en.aventurar:
Spanish ~aventurar~ is a verb built on the noun ~aventura~, which comes from Vulgar Latin *~adventūra~ (“things about to happen”), a substantivized form of Latin ~adventūrus~, the future participle of ~advenīre~ (“to arrive, to happen”). That verb parses as ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”), which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to step”). Spanish ~venir~ descends from the same ~venīre~, and through the root the word is cognate with English ~come~ and, by a parallel Latin route, with ~adventure~.

The medieval noun ~aventura~ first meant “chance, luck, what fate sends” — the events “coming toward” a person — before it narrowed to a risky or exciting exploit. To ~aventurar~ was thus to entrust something to chance, and reflexively ~aventurarse~ still means “to dare, to risk oneself”. The same family gathers ~ventura~ (“fortune, luck”), its opposite ~desventura~ (“misfortune”), the ~aventurero~ (“adventurer”) and ~porvenir~ (“the future”, literally “what is to come”).
en.averiguar:
From Medieval Latin *~advērificāre~ (“to verify”), from ~ad-~ plus ~vērificāre~, itself from ~vērus~ (“true”) and ~facere~ (“to make”), the root ~vērus~ going back to Proto-Indo-European *~weh₁ros~ (“true, trustworthy”). Cognate — through that root — with English ~very~ (originally “true”) and German ~wahr~.

So ~averiguar~ means literally “to make true,” that is, to establish the truth of something — to ascertain or find out. The road from ~vērificāre~ to ~averiguar~ ran through a chain of sound changes: the ~-f-~ voiced to ~-v-~ and the ~-c-~ to ~-g-~. From ~vērus~ Spanish keeps ~verdad~, ~veraz~, ~verídico~, ~verosímil~ and ~verificar~.
en.avisar:
From Vulgar Latin *~advīsāre~ (“to advise, notify”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + the past participle ~vīsum~ of ~vidēre~ (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”). It reached Spanish through Old French ~aviser~. Cognate with Italian ~avvisare~ and French ~aviser~, and — through French — with English ~advise~ and ~advice~.

The word grew from a Romance idiom, ~m’est vis~ (“it seems to me,” from Latin ~mihi est vīsum~): an ~aviso~ was first an opinion, a view laid before someone to see, and only then a warning or piece of notice. Spanish ~avisar~ thus means to put something before another’s eyes — to notify, alert, warn. The root *~weyd-~ is one of Indo-European’s most fertile: through Latin ~vidēre~ Spanish holds ~ver~, ~vista~, ~visión~, ~previsión~, and ~improvisar~; through Greek it stands behind ~idea~ and ~historia~; through Germanic, behind English ~wit~ and ~wise~.
en.avivar:
Spanish ~avivar~ is a causative verb formed from the prefix ~a-~, the adjective ~vivo~ (“alive”, from Latin ~vīvus~), and the ending ~-ar~ — literally “to make alive”. Latin ~vīvus~ comes from Proto-Italic *~gʷīwos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷeyh₃-~ (“to live”). The same coinage exists in Portuguese and Catalan ~avivar~, and through the root ~vivo~ is cognate with English ~quick~ (in its old sense “living”, as in “the quick and the dead”) and with ~vivid~ and ~revive~.

The verb means to make something more ~vivo~ — to brighten a color, sharpen the wits, quicken a pace and, above all, to stoke a fire, feeding it so the flame leaps back to life. Its reflexive ~avivarse~ in several American varieties means “to wise up, to look sharp”. From the same fertile root Spanish drew a whole cluster of everyday words: ~vida~ (“life”), ~vivir~ (“to live”), ~vivo~, ~revivir~ (“to revive”) and ~vívido~ (“vivid”).
en.ayudar:
From Latin ~adiūtāre~ (“to help, assist”), the frequentative of ~adiuvāre~, itself ~ad-~ (“toward”) plus ~iuvāre~ (“to help, please”), a verb of uncertain deeper origin. Old Spanish had ~aiudar~ before settling on ~ayudar~. It is cognate with Italian ~aiutare~, Portuguese ~ajudar~ and French ~aider~, and — borrowed through Old French — with English ~aid~ and the learned ~adjutant~.

The frequentative ~adiūtāre~ conveyed repeated or earnest helping, and it is this intensive form, not plain ~iuvāre~, that the Romance languages inherited. Because ~iuvāre~ has no secure Proto-Indo-European pedigree, prudence forbids attaching it to a root here. Within Latin it kept lively company: it was linked to ~iūcundus~ (“pleasant, agreeable”), the source of English ~jocund~. In Spanish the same stem gives ~ayuda~ (“help, aid”), ~ayudante~ (“assistant”) and the learned ~coadyuvar~ (“to contribute, cooperate”), which preserves the ~-iuv-~ that popular ~ayudar~ wore away.
en.ayunar:
Spanish ~ayunar~ comes from Late Latin ~iēiūnāre~ (“to fast”), from the Latin adjective ~iēiūnus~ (“fasting, hungry, empty”), whose own origin is uncertain. The initial ~ie-~ smoothed to Spanish ~ay-~, giving Old Spanish ~ayunar~. The Latin word was borrowed straight into English as the rare adjective ~jejune~ (“meagre, dull”) and named the ~jejunum~, the stretch of small intestine anatomists usually found empty in dissection.

The verb kept its narrow sense: to abstain from food, especially as religious observance. Its most useful descendant is ~desayunar~ (“to breakfast”), built with ~des-~ (“un-, reverse”) on ~ayunar~ — literally “to un-fast”, to break the night’s fast — which yielded the noun ~desayuno~ (“breakfast”), an exact parallel to English ~breakfast~ and French ~déjeuner~. The plain noun ~ayuno~ means “a fast”, and the set phrase ~en ayunas~ means “on an empty stomach” or, figuratively, “clueless”, still in daily use.
en.azotar:
Spanish ~azotar~ is formed from the noun ~azote~ (“whip, lash”) plus ~-ar~. The noun was borrowed during the Muslim centuries in Iberia from Andalusi Arabic ~as-sawṭ~ (“whip”), in which the article ~al-~ had fused onto the noun ~sawṭ~ — the same agglutinated ~a-~ that begins so many Spanish arabisms. Portuguese ~açoitar~, from ~açoite~, took the identical path from the same Arabic source.

Literally the verb means to flog or lash, and it kept that harsh core through the colonial period. But it also went figurative early: a storm, a plague or a war can ~azotar~ a region — “to batter, to scourge” it — and ~azote~ came to name any devastating calamity, as when Attila was called ~el azote de Dios~ (“the Scourge of God”). Related forms include the noun ~azotaina~ (“a spanking”) and ~azotador~ (“one who whips”). It is a small window onto the roughly four thousand Arabic-derived words that Spanish absorbed.
en.añadir:
Spanish ~añadir~ comes, through Old Spanish ~eñadir~ (also ~añader~), from a Vulgar Latin *~innaddere~ or *~inaddere~ — Latin ~addere~ (“to add, put to”) reinforced with the prefix ~in-~. The doubled ~nn~ of the reconstructed form is what Spanish needed to yield the ~ñ~. ~addere~ is itself ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~dare~ (“to give”): literally “to give to, put to.” ~dare~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”), one of the most widespread roots there is — source of Latin ~dōnum~ (“gift”) and Spanish ~dar~, Greek ~dídōmi~ (“I give”), and, via Latin, English ~date~, ~donate~, and ~add~ — the last from ~addere~ itself, the very verb that ~añadir~ elaborates.

The quiet lesson of ~añadir~ is redundancy: Latin ~addere~ already meant “to add” (its ~ad-~ = “to”), yet Vulgar Latin piled a second directional prefix, ~in-~, on top — a doubling-up of “to it” that is exactly what adding feels like. The word’s ~ñ~ is a fossil of the assimilated ~in-~ + ~n~ cluster. Spanish also inherited ~addere~ by the learned road as ~aditar~ (“to add, annotate”) and the nouns ~adición~ (“addition,” including the arithmetic operation) and ~aditivo~ (“additive”). From the broader *~deh₃-~ root come ~dar~, ~dado~ (“die; given”), ~dádiva~ (“gift”), ~donar~, ~perdonar~, and ~dosis~ (from Greek ~dósis~, “a giving”).
en.bailar:
By the usual account, from Late Latin ~ballāre~ (“to dance”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~βαλλίζειν~ (ballízein, “to dance, jump about”); the Real Academia marks the descent as only probable (~quizá~). Corominas argues the Spanish word is not a direct heir but an adaptation of Old Occitan ~balar~, and he leaves the puzzling ~i~ of ~bailar~ unexplained — possibly a crossing with a homonym ~bailar~ (“to rock, sway”), from Latin ~bāiulāre~. So the deep origin is genuinely disputed. Cognate with Italian ~ballare~, French ~baller~, and Portuguese ~bailar~.

Whatever the exact path, the whole European family of dancing and dance-events flows from ~ballāre~: English ~ball~ (a formal dance) and ~ballet~ both trace to it, and even ~ballad~ began as a song to dance to. Spanish keeps a lively cluster — the noun ~baile~ (“dance”), ~bailarín~ (“dancer”), and ~bailable~ (“danceable”) — so that a modern ~baile~ still, distantly, jumps to a Greek beat.
en.bajar:
From Vulgar Latin *~bassiāre~ (“to lower”), from Late Latin ~bassus~ (“low, short, thick”). Old Spanish had ~baxar~, later reshaped to ~bajar~ as its old sh-sound hardened into the jota. Cognate with French ~baisser~ and Italian ~abbassare~; the same parent adjective surfaces in English ~base~ (“low, mean”) and the musical ~bass~ (“low in pitch”).

The engaging part is the disputed source of ~bassus~ itself. Classical Latin used the word only rarely, mainly as a personal name, and its origin is genuinely uncertain; the sources hedge. By competing accounts it was borrowed from Oscan, or from a Celtic word, or connected to Greek ~bathýs~ (“deep”) — none settled, so the adjective is best labeled “of uncertain origin.” Whatever its root, ~bassus~ flourished in Spanish, yielding ~bajo~ (“low; under”), ~bajada~ (“descent”), ~rebajar~ (“to lower, reduce”), ~abajo~ (“below”), and ~bajón~ (“slump”).
en.balbucir:
From Latin ~balbutīre~ (“to stammer, stutter”), a verb built on the adjective ~balbus~ (“stammering, lisping”). ~balbus~ is transparently imitative, an onomatopoeia for the halting ~bal-bal~ of blocked speech, and philologists reconstruct a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European *~balb-~ / *~balbal-~ (“to stammer”). The same babbling root surfaces across the family: Sanskrit ~balbalā~ (“stammering”), Lithuanian ~balbė́ti~ (“to babble”), Ancient Greek ~βαμβαίνω~ (bambaínō, “to chatter”), and Italian ~balbo~ (“stammering”), whose derivative ~balbettare~ still means “to stutter.”

~balbucir~ came to describe not only stammering but the sweet, half-formed speech of infants and lovers. Curiously, the verb is defective: Spanish shuns its would-be first-person present (there is no *~balbuzco~) and its present subjunctive, and speakers plug the gap with the fully regular ~-ear~ verb ~balbucear~, which has all but eclipsed the older form in everyday use. Both live on beside the noun ~balbuceo~ (“babbling”) and the adjective ~balbuciente~ (“faltering, halting”). The imitative instinct behind ~balbus~ is the same one that gives many languages their words for unclear speech: the mouth reaching for a sound it cannot yet manage.
en.barrer:
Spanish ~barrer~ was inherited from Latin ~verrere~ (“to sweep, to drag along the ground”). Regular Castilian sound-change turned the initial ~v~ into ~b~, so ~verrere~ became ~barrer~, while Portuguese and Galician kept the older consonant in ~varrer~. Latin ~verrere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~wers-~ (“to drag, to wipe”), a root also reflected in Latvian ~vārsms~ (“a heap of threshed grain”, the very stuff a broom gathers).

The core sense stayed put — to clean with a broom — but Spanish gave it a vivid figurative life. A team or a party can ~barrer~ its rivals (“to sweep them aside, to trounce them”), and the idiom ~barrer para dentro~ (“to sweep inward”) means to look after one’s own interest. The everyday family includes ~barrendero~ (“street-sweeper”), ~barredora~ (“sweeping machine”) and ~barredura~ (“sweepings”). It is a good example of a plain, inherited Latin verb that survived intact where flashier borrowings came and went.
en.barruntar:
The origin of Spanish ~barruntar~ (“to sense, to suspect, to have a foreboding”) is uncertain, and the sources hedge. The most cited account, from Corominas and echoed by the DLE, derives it from the noun ~barrunte~ — whose oldest meaning was “spy” — and traces that word, tentatively, to an old Basque ~barrunti~ (“the inner part, interiority”), a derivative of Basque ~barru(n)~ (“inside, interior”). On this proposal the semantic thread runs from “what is within” to “penetrate” to “spy out” to “sense in advance”. The Basque link is offered as probable, not proven, so it should be carried as a hypothesis.

However one weighs the etymology, the modern meaning is settled: to ~barruntar~ is to guess at something hidden, to feel a hunch — often of trouble coming, as when a peasant ~barrunta~ a storm from a change in the air. The noun ~barrunto~ means “an inkling, a foreboding”, and ~barrunte~ survives in the same orbit. It is a quietly poetic word, more at home in literary and rural registers than in bureaucratic prose.
en.basar:
From the noun ~base~ (“base, foundation”) plus the verbal ending ~-ar~; ~basar~ is a denominal verb, coined rather than inherited. ~base~ comes from Latin ~basis~ (“base, pedestal”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~βάσις~ (“a step, a stepping, base”), a noun built on the verb ~βαίνω~ (“to go, to step”). That verb descends from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to go, come”) — the same root that, on the Germanic side, produced English ~come~. Romance preserved the Latin noun broadly: Italian ~base~, French ~base~, Portuguese ~base~.

Because ~basar~ was formed on the noun, its story is really the story of ~base~, which moved from the concrete “pedestal, that on which a thing stands” to the abstract “foundation, grounds”; the reflexive ~basarse~ means “to rest on, be grounded in.” A pleasant surprise: the modest Greek ~βαίνω~ (“to step”) also hides inside ~diabetes~ (Greek for “a passing through”) and ~acróbata~ (one who “walks” on the heights). Spanish relatives of ~base~ include ~básico~, ~basamento~, and the chemistry term ~base~.
en.bastar:
From Old Spanish ~bastar~, from Vulgar Latin *~bastāre~ (“to bear, carry a weight”), generally traced to Greek ~βαστάζειν~ (~bastázein~, “to lift, carry, bear a load”). It is cognate with Italian ~bastare~, Portuguese ~bastar~, and Catalan ~bastar~, all sharing the sense “to be enough.”

Medieval Spanish kept meanings much closer to the Greek: ~bastar~ could mean to endure, to hold out, to reach as far as, to last, or to bear a weight. From “to be able to sustain something” it slid to “to be sufficient,” the sense that prevailed — what suffices is what can carry the load. The same root feeds ~bastante~ (“enough, quite”), the exasperated interjection ¡~basta~! (“enough!”), and the family ~abasto~ and ~abastecer~ (“to supply”), from the idea of providing enough. So the modern accountant's “that will suffice” still carries, faintly, the Greek porter's burden.
en.batir:
From Latin ~battuere~ (later ~battere~) “to beat, strike,” a verb whose deeper origin is disputed: Corominas and others judge it probably borrowed from Gaulish (Celtic), comparing Welsh ~bathu~ (“to strike, coin”) and Irish ~bata~ (“stick, cudgel”), rather than inherited from Proto-Indo-European. Whatever its source, it swept through Romance: French ~battre~, Italian ~battere~, Portuguese ~bater~ and Catalan ~batre~ all descend from it, as does — through Late Latin — English ~battle~ and ~batter~.

From the plain sense “to strike” Spanish ~batir~ branched widely: to beat eggs, to flap wings, to pound a coastline, to beat down (~abatir~). The martial line is especially rich — ~batalla~ (“battle”), ~batallón~, ~combatir~, ~rebatir~ (“to refute”) and ~debate~ (originally a “beating down” of an argument) — while ~batería~ gave both the artillery “battery” and the drum kit, and ~batuta~, the conductor’s baton, reached Spanish from Italian. Even ~abatir~ keeps the image of striking something down.
en.bautizar:
From Latin ~baptizāre~, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~baptízein~ (“to dip, immerse, baptize”), an intensive of ~báptein~ (“to dip, dye”). What lies behind ~báptein~ inside Greek is uncertain, so the trail is best followed only that far. Because the word spread with Christianity, it has close cognates across Romance: Italian ~battezzare~, French ~baptiser~, and Portuguese ~batizar~, alongside English ~baptize~ and ~baptism~ — all resting on the same Greek verb of dipping.

The core image is immersion in water. Early Christian baptism was administered by dipping, and the Greek verb of dipping became the technical term for the sacrament; from the rite the meaning spread to the naming that accompanies it, so ~bautizar~ also means “to christen, give a name to.” Spanish keeps a playful extension too: ~bautizar el vino~ means to water down wine — to “baptize” it with a secret splash of water. The family in Spanish includes ~bautismo~ (“baptism”), ~bautizo~ (“christening ceremony”), and ~bautista~ (“Baptist,” as in Juan el ~Bautista~), the last preserving the Greek agent form almost unchanged.
en.bañar:
Spanish ~bañar~ was inherited through Vulgar Latin *~baneare~ from Late Latin ~balneāre~ (“to bathe”), from the noun ~balneum~ (“bath”). Latin itself had borrowed ~balneum~ early from Ancient Greek ~balaneîon~ (“bathhouse”), whose own origin is pre-Greek and uncertain. The loss of the ~l~ in the Vulgar-Latin form left ~bañar~; its siblings across Romance kept more of the cluster — Portuguese ~banhar~, Catalan ~banyar~, French ~baigner~ and Italian ~bagnare~.

Beyond the bathtub, the verb spread by metaphor. A river or a sea can ~bañar~ a coastline (“to wash, to lap against” it), light can bathe a room and — most deliciously — food is ~bañado~ in something: ~bañado en chocolate~ (“coated in chocolate”) or ~bañado en oro~ (“gold-plated”). The everyday family is large: ~baño~ (“bath; bathroom”), ~bañera~ (“bathtub”), ~bañador~ (“swimsuit”) and ~bañista~ (“bather, swimmer”), all built on the same imported Greek word for washing the body.
en.beber:
From Latin ~bibere~ (“to drink”), from Proto-Italic *~pibō~ — a reduplicated present — from Proto-Indo-European *~píph₃eti~, from the root *~peh₃-~ (“to drink”). Cognate with Italian ~bere~, Portuguese ~beber~ and French ~boire~, and — through the same root — with Sanskrit ~píbati~ and the English Latinisms ~potable~ and ~potion~.

The root's initial ~p~ became ~b~ in Latin, most likely under the pull of the second ~b~ — an assimilation that leaves ~bibere~ looking nothing like its ~p~-initial cousins. Spanish carried it through Old Spanish ~bever~ to modern ~beber~. From the same verb come ~bebida~ (“drink”), ~bebedor~ (“drinker”) and ~biberón~ (“baby bottle,” by way of French), while the past participle ~bibĭtus~ (“having drunk”) yielded the adjective ~beodo~ (“drunk, tipsy”).
en.bendecir:
Spanish ~bendecir~ comes from Latin ~benedīcere~ (“to speak well of, to praise”), a compound of the adverb ~bene~ (“well,” from ~bonus~, “good”) and ~dīcere~ (“to say, speak”), from Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, point out”). The verb ~dīcere~ gave Spanish ~decir~, and its root also underlies English ~token~ and ~teach~. Cognate with Italian ~benedire~, French ~bénir~, and Portuguese ~bendizer~.

Classical ~benedīcere~ meant simply to speak well of someone; Christian Latin repurposed it as a calque of Greek ~εὐλογεῖν~ (“to bless,” literally “to speak well”), itself rendering Hebrew ~בָּרַךְ~ (bārakh), and so the word acquired its sacred sense “to bless.” Its irregular participle ~bendito~ still lives alongside the regular ~bendecido~; the personal name ~Benito~ (and learned ~Benedicto~) come from the same ~benedīcere~. Its exact antonym is ~maldecir~ (“to curse,” from ~male~, “badly”), and the family includes ~bendición~.
en.beneficiar:
~beneficiar~ is built on ~beneficio~ (“benefit”), from Latin ~beneficium~ (“a kindness, favor, service”), a compound of ~bene~ (“well”) and ~-ficium~, from ~facere~ (“to do, make”) — literally “a well-doing.” The adverb ~bene~ belongs to ~bonus~ (“good”), from Old Latin ~duenos~, of debated further origin; ~facere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, do”), the root of English ~do~ and German ~tun~. Romance kept the verb: French ~bénéficier~, Italian ~beneficiare~, Portuguese ~beneficiar~.

In Latin a ~beneficium~ ranged from a personal good turn to an official grant of land or office — the feudal “benefice” that let a churchman live off an endowment. Spanish ~beneficiar~ thus spans “to benefit, do good to” and the technical “to work, process” (to ~beneficiar~ ore or a hide is to render it useful). The reflexive ~beneficiarse~ is “to profit from.” Kin include ~benéfico~, ~beneficencia~, ~benefactor~, and — from ~bene~ alone — ~bendecir~ and ~benévolo~.
en.besar:
From Latin ~bāsiāre~ (“to kiss”), from the noun ~bāsium~ (“a kiss”). The word swept through the West: Italian ~baciare~, French ~baiser~, Portuguese ~beijar~ and Catalan ~besar~ all descend from it. The origin of ~bāsium~ itself, however, is genuinely uncertain — often proposed as a Celtic or expressive nursery formation, but not securely established, so any deeper root is best left open.

Classical Latin had other words for a kiss — the decorous ~ōsculum~ (“little mouth”) and the amorous ~sāvium~ — and ~bāsium~ was originally the tender kiss of family and lovers; Catullus begged his Lesbia for a thousand of them. By one debated account ~bāsium~ belongs to an expressive root also glimpsed in English ~buss~, but the sources hedge and it should not be stated as fact. In Spanish the word settled comfortably into ~beso~, ~besar~ and the playful ~besuquear~ (“to smother with kisses”).
en.bloquear:
One of the newer verbs in this set. Spanish ~bloquear~ comes from French ~bloquer~, derived from ~bloc~ (“a block, solid mass”), which French borrowed from Middle Dutch ~bloc~ (“trunk of a tree, log”), of Germanic origin (compare Frankish *~blok~), from Proto-Germanic *~blukką~ (“block, log”). Beyond that the trail grows faint: many trace it to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰl̥ǵ-~ (“thick plank, beam”), though the deep root is uncertain. It is cognate with English ~block~, German ~Block~ and Dutch ~blok~.

The image behind the word is concrete: a felled log or heavy block set down to obstruct a passage. From “to close off with blocks” the sense fanned out to block, blockade, jam, and — in modern finance and computing — to freeze an account or lock a screen. Spanish took it comparatively late, largely through French military and naval usage, alongside the noun ~bloqueo~ (“blockade”) and ~bloque~ (“block,” including a political ~bloque~ of nations). The reversible ~desbloquear~ (“to unblock, unlock”) is a purely modern coinage. It is a small Germanic word that grew up to run the world's networks.
en.bogar:
Spanish ~bogar~ (“to row”) is not a native inheritance from Latin but a borrowing: it came through Old Italian ~vogare~ into Old French, and ultimately from a Germanic source, Old Saxon ~wagon~ (“to float, to move like waves”). It is cognate with Italian ~vogare~, Catalan ~vogar~ and Portuguese ~vogar~, and it is related to French ~vogue~ (“wave; fashionable currency”) and its verb ~voguer~ (“to sail along”). An older, now less-favored account instead derived the word from Latin ~vocāre~ (“to call”), imagining the commanding voice of the rowing master who set the stroke; the sources mark this as the weaker hypothesis.

Within Spanish, ~bogar~ has always belonged to the vocabulary of the sea, meaning “to row” or “to sail,” and today it keeps a literary, slightly archaic flavor, everyday speech preferring ~remar~. From the same Mediterranean family comes the noun ~boga~, which names both the act of rowing and — exactly as in French — a passing vogue or fashion, preserved in the set phrase “estar en boga” (“to be in vogue”). The nautical and the fashionable senses, surprisingly, share one root: what is “in vogue” is, etymologically, moving briskly along on the water.
en.borrar:
From ~borra~ (“coarse wool, flock”) plus the verbal ending; ~borra~ itself descends from Late Latin ~burra~ (“shaggy wool of little value”), a word of uncertain further origin. The shift from Latin ~u~ to Spanish ~o~ is regular (compare ~bucca~ → ~boca~). Cognate with Italian ~borra~ and French ~bourre~ (“stuffing, flock”); from that French word, through the coarse cloth ~burel~ that once covered writing tables, English drew ~bureau~ and hence ~bureaucracy~.

Why a word for cheap wool came to mean “erase” is charmingly literal, though not beyond doubt: the favored account is that a wad of ~borra~ was the cloth used to wipe chalk from a slate, so to ~borrar~ was to rub something out with wool; a rival account points instead to the sediment or dregs of ink. Either way, the modern family is tidy — ~borrador~ means both “eraser” and “rough draft,” ~borrón~ is a blot or crossing-out, and ~borroso~ means “blurred, smudged.”
en.brillar:
From Italian ~brillare~ (“to shine, sparkle”), from ~berillo~ (“beryl”), from Latin ~bēryllus~, from Ancient Greek ~βήρυλλος~ (“beryl”). The Greek gem-name was itself borrowed from an Indian source — Prakrit ~verulia~, Pali ~veḷuriya~ — and by one proposal from a South Indian place-name, though that final step is not certain. Sibling Romance verbs include French ~briller~ and Portuguese ~brilhar~.

The surprise is that “to shine” began as the name of a gemstone: to ~brillar~ is, at root, to glitter like a polished ~beryl~. The very same ~bēryllus~ took a different path through German, where lenses first ground from beryl gave the word ~Brille~ (“eyeglasses”). In Spanish the family sparkles on in ~brillo~ (“shine, gloss”), ~brillante~ (“brilliant,” and also “a cut diamond”), ~abrillantar~ (“to polish, make shine”) and ~brillantez~ (“brilliance”). The chemical element ~beryllium~, isolated from beryl, keeps the same shining stone at its origin.
en.brindar:
Unlike its Latinate neighbors, ~brindar~ is a Germanic import. It derives from the noun ~brindis~ (“a toast”), which Spanish borrowed in the sixteenth century from the German toasting phrase ~bring dir’s~ — a running-together of ~(ich) bring dir’s~, “I bring it to you.” The verb behind it is German ~bringen~ (“to bring”), cognate with English ~bring~, both from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~. The little words matter too: ~dir~ is “to you” (dative, cognate with English ~thee~) and the clitic ~’s~ is ~es~ (“it”). Italian ~brindare~ and Portuguese ~brindar~ borrowed the same festive word from Spanish.

The story behind the word is vivid and, unusually, well documented: when the Landsknechte — German mercenaries in the service of Charles V — sacked Rome in 1527, they are said to have raised their cups crying ~bring dir’s~, offering the drink to a companion. Spanish soldiers carried the custom and the cry home, and by the early 1600s ~brindar~ and ~brindis~ were common enough that Covarrubias recorded them in his 1611 Tesoro de la lengua castellana. The meaning then broadened gracefully: from “to drink someone’s health” to “to offer, to provide” in general — today one can ~brindar~ apoyo (“offer support”) or ~brindar~ una oportunidad (“provide an opportunity”), a generosity still audible in that original “I bring it to you.”
en.bullir:
Spanish ~bullir~ comes from Latin ~bullīre~ (“to bubble, to boil”), a verb built on the noun ~bulla~ (“bubble, blister, stud”). The deep origin of ~bulla~ is uncertain: it is tentatively traced to a Proto-Indo-European root, perhaps *~bew-~ (“to swell”) or alternatively *~bʰel-~ (“to blow, to swell”), and the sources hedge on both. ~bullir~ is cognate with French ~bouillir~, Italian ~bollire~ and Catalan ~bullir~, and — through the same Latin verb, borrowed via Old French — with English ~boil~.

The imagery is delightfully physical: a boiling pot throws up ~bulla~ after ~bulla~, so “to bubble” naturally became “to boil,” and then, figuratively, “to seethe, to teem, to swarm.” Spanish keeps all these layers — a street can ~bullir~ with people just as water ~bulle~ on the stove. The same root gave Spanish ~ebullición~ (“boiling; ferment”), ~bullicio~ (“bustle, hubbub”), ~bullanguero~ (“rowdy, boisterous”) and the frequentative ~rebullir~ (“to stir, to begin to move”). Even the little ~bulla~ (“racket, uproar”) survives as a noun in its own right, the etymological bubble now made of noise.
en.buscar:
Inherited from Old Spanish ~buscar~, but of genuinely uncertain origin — Corominas and the DLE alike label it « de origen incierto ». Several hypotheses compete, none settled. By one account it is tied to ~bosque~ (“forest”), the earliest sense being to beat the woods for game; by another it descends from a Celtic *~boudi~ (“gain, victory”), compared with Old Irish ~búaid~ and Welsh ~budd~. It shares its mystery with cognate Portuguese ~buscar~ and Italian ~buscare~ (“to scrounge, wangle”).

Whatever its source, ~buscar~ had by the medieval period already generalized to “to look for, seek,” and it remains one of the plainest, most frequent verbs in the language. The hunting-in-the-woods story is memorable but rests on the unproven ~bosque~ link, so it is best told as one guess among several rather than as fact. The verb is productive in its own right: it yields ~búsqueda~ and ~busca~ (“search”), ~buscador~ (“search engine; seeker”), ~rebuscar~ (“to search thoroughly”), and the old noun ~buscón~ (“petty crook”), immortalized in Quevedo's picaresque novel ~El Buscón~.
en.cabalgar:
Spanish ~cabalgar~ descends from Late Latin ~caballicāre~ (“to ride on horseback”), a verb formed from ~caballus~, the Latin word for a workhorse or nag — as opposed to the noble ~equus~.
