The origin of ~caballus~ itself is uncertain: it is most often taken as a borrowing from Gaulish, and possibly an old Wanderwort shared across many tongues, with look-alikes in Ancient Greek ~kabállēs~, Proto-Slavic *~kobyla~ and Persian; the sources are careful to flag this as unsettled. Cognate verbs appear in Italian ~cavalcare~, French ~chevaucher~ and Portuguese ~cavalgar~.

Because the humble ~caballus~ — not ~equus~ — won out across Vulgar Latin, nearly every Romance word for “horse” and “horseman” grows from it: Spanish ~caballo~, ~caballero~ (“knight, gentleman”) and ~caballería~ (“cavalry; chivalry”). Through French and Italian the same root reached English as the borrowings ~cavalry~, ~cavalier~ and ~chivalry~ — so the ideals of knighthood trace, etymologically, to a plodding packhorse. ~cabalgar~ keeps its literal sense (“to ride”) and lends a vivid figurative one, ~cabalgar~ over waves or over centuries, plus the noun ~cabalgata~ (“cavalcade, procession”).
en.caber:
From Old Spanish ~caber~, from Latin ~capere~ (“to take, seize, hold, contain”), from Proto-Italic *~kapiō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kap-~ (“to grasp, seize”). Cognate with Portuguese ~caber~ and — through the same Latin verb — with the borrowings ~capaz~ and ~captura~; English has ~capture~ and ~capable~ from ~capere~, and, from the same PIE root, the native ~heave~.

The meaning shifted from grasping to spatial room: Latin ~capere~ meant “to take” or “to hold, contain,” and Spanish narrowed the “contain” side to “to fit, have room for” — a box ~cabe~ on the shelf, five people ~caben~ in the car. The irregular present ~quepo~ (“I fit”) preserves Latin ~capiō~ under metathesis, and the preterite ~cupe~ reflects a Vulgar Latin perfect *~capuī~. From ~capere~ Spanish also drew ~capaz~, ~cabida~ (“capacity”), ~caudal~, and the shared-root ~recibir~ and ~concebir~.
en.caer:
From Latin ~cadere~ (“to fall”), from Proto-Italic *~kadō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱad-~ (“to fall”). The intervocalic ~-d-~ dropped away, giving Old Spanish ~caer~. Cognate with Italian ~cadere~, Portuguese ~cair~ and the now-archaic French ~choir~.

Latin’s ~cāsus~ (“a falling”), the past participle of ~cadere~, became a metaphor for whatever “befalls,” hence Spanish ~caso~ (“case, chance”) and ~casualidad~ (“coincidence”), and grammatical “case.” The setting sun falls: ~ocaso~ (“sunset, decline”) and ~occidente~ (“the West”) come from ~occidere~ (“to fall down, to set”). English borrowed the same verb widely — ~cadence~, ~accident~, ~occasion~, ~decay~ and ~cascade~. Other Spanish descendants: ~caída~, ~decaer~, ~recaer~ and ~cadencia~.
en.calar:
Spanish ~calar~ goes back to Late Latin ~calāre~ (“to lower, to let down”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ~χαλάω~ (~khaláō~, “to slacken, to loosen, to lower”). It is cognate with Portuguese ~calar~ and Catalan ~calar~. The starting sense was thoroughly nautical: to ~calar~ was to lower sails, nets or a sounding line into the water.

From “to lower into the water” the meaning slid to “to sink in, to penetrate, to soak through” — rain that ~cala~ your coat, a look that ~cala~ someone’s intentions. Spanish preserves a whole cluster from this root: ~cala~ (“cove, inlet”; also the “core-sample” cut into a melon), ~calado~ (“draft of a ship; openwork lace”), ~caladero~ (“fishing ground”) and the reflexive ~calarse~ (“to get soaked,” and, of an engine, “to stall”). The image throughout is of something let down and going deep — from a slackened Greek rope to the drizzle working its way to the skin.
en.calcar:
Spanish ~calcar~ is inherited from Latin ~calcāre~ (“to tread, to trample, to press with the heel”), a verb built on ~calx~ (“heel”). The origin of ~calx~ is uncertain — it has been linked, tentatively, to a Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)kel-~ (“to bend”), but a non-Indo-European (possibly Etruscan) source has also been proposed, and the sources leave it open. It is cognate with Italian ~calcare~ and Portuguese ~calcar~.

The leap in meaning is memorable. From literally treading or pressing down, ~calcar~ came to mean pressing a design through a sheet onto the surface below — hence “to trace,” and, by extension, “to copy slavishly, to imitate exactly” (a plan ~calcado~ on another). Both senses live on: one can still ~calcar~ a plant underfoot and ~calcar~ a drawing on paper. From the same ~calx~ Spanish drew ~coz~ (“a kick,” its native reflex), ~calcetín~ and ~calceta~ (through the neighboring word for footwear), ~recalcar~ (“to stress, to emphasize,” literally to press again) and ~calcar~’s learned relatives in the vocabulary of tracing and copying.
en.calcular:
From Latin ~calculāre~ (“to compute, reckon”), from ~calculus~ (“a pebble”), the diminutive of ~calx~ (genitive ~calcis~, “limestone, small stone”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~khálix~ (“small pebble, gravel”). The ultimate origin is unknown — Beekes finds no convincing etymology for the Greek word. Cognate with Italian ~calcolare~, French ~calculer~ and Portuguese ~calcular~.

The homely detail is that a ~calculus~ was a counting-pebble: Romans “placed pebbles” (~ponere calculōs~) on a reckoning board to add and subtract, so to ~calcular~ is, at root, to push stones around. From ~calx~ English also drew ~chalk~ and ~calcium~, and the medical ~calculus~ is still a “little stone” in the body. Spanish keeps ~cálculo~, ~calculadora~ and ~recalcular~.
en.calentar:
From Vulgar Latin *~calentāre~, from Latin ~calēns~ (accusative ~calentem~), the present participle of ~calēre~ (“to be warm, be hot”), from Proto-Italic *~kalēō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱelh₁-~ (“warm”). The root surfaces in English ~calorie~ and, by a longer road through French, in ~nonchalant~ — literally “not warming oneself,” hence unconcerned.

Spanish did not build the verb on the infinitive ~calēre~ but on its participle ~calentem~, which is why we say ~calentar~ and ~caliente~ rather than a form closer to ~calor~. The same warm root spread through a wide family: ~caliente~, ~calor~, ~cálido~, ~caldo~ (“broth”), ~caldera~, ~escaldar~ and ~calefacción~. What began as the plain sensation of heat now covers warming food, warming up muscles before sport, and, figuratively, warming tempers.
en.calificar:
~calificar~ comes from Medieval Latin ~quālificāre~ (“to endow with a quality”), a compound of Latin ~quālis~ (“of what kind”) and ~facere~ (“to make, do”) — literally “to make of a certain kind.” ~quālis~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European interrogative-relative stem *~kʷo-~ (source also of ~qué~ and ~cuál~), while ~facere~ goes back to *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, do”), the root behind English ~do~ and ~deed~ and German ~tun~. The same coinage spread as Italian ~qualificare~, French ~qualifier~, and English ~qualify~.

The scholastic Latin verb meant “to attribute a quality to,” a technical sense still alive in “to qualify” a statement with reservations. Spanish specialized it toward judgment and assessment: a teacher ~califica~ (“grades”) an exam and gives it a ~calificación~ (“grade, rating”). The neutral “assign a quality” lingers when we ~calificar~ a remark as rude or brilliant. Kin from the ~facere~ half include ~fácil~, ~hacer~, ~facción~, and countless ~-ificar~ verbs; from the ~quālis~ half come ~cualidad~ and ~cualitativo~.
en.callar:
Of debated origin. The account favored by Corominas derives ~callar~ from a Vulgar Latin *~callāre~ (“to lower, let down”), a borrowing of Ancient Greek ~χαλᾶν~ (~khalân~, “to slacken, loosen, let down”). The sense passed from “lowering” a physical thing to “lowering the voice,” and thence to falling silent — a shift that reappears in Italian, where ~calare~ still means “to lower.” Because the descent runs through Greek rather than an inherited Latin verb, the sources present it as the probable, not the certain, etymology.

If the Greek origin holds, ~callar~ is a striking case of a nautical or commercial word — “to strike, to lower (a sail, a load)” — narrowing into a verb of silence, as though hushing were letting one's voice down like a sail. The everyday imperative ~calla~ (“be quiet!”) and the emphatic ~cállate~ are among the first phrases a learner meets. From the same “lowering” source Spanish kept ~calar~ (“to soak, to penetrate, to see through”) and the noun ~cala~ (“a cove, an inlet”), where the sea “lowers” into the land. The link between ~calar~ and ~callar~ is itself part of the debated reconstruction, so treat that tidy family as proposed rather than proven.
en.calmar:
From the noun ~calma~ (“calm, stillness”), which Spanish, like Italian ~calma~ and French ~calme~, took from Late Latin ~cauma~ (“the burning heat of the day”). That in turn came from Ancient Greek ~kaûma~ (“heat, burning”), a noun from the verb ~kaíō~ (“to burn”). English ~calm~ is a cognate, borrowed through the same Romance chain. One puzzle: the expected Latin form would give ~cau-~, not ~cal-~; by one account the word was reshaped under the influence of Latin ~calor~ (“heat”) and ~calidus~ (“hot”), which is why Spanish has ~cal-~.

The semantic journey is vivid. ~kaûma~ named the oppressive heat of the Mediterranean midday — and at that hour the sea often falls windless and flat. Sailors transferred the word from the heat itself to that dead stillness of the becalmed sea, and from there to calm of any kind, including the inner tranquility we mean today. The verb ~calmar~ (“to calm, soothe”) was formed on the noun, and the maritime sense survives in the phrase ~calma chicha~ (“dead calm”). Spanish relatives include ~calmante~ (“sedative, painkiller”), ~calmoso~, and ~encalmar~. It is worth marking that the ~calor~/~calidus~ influence is a proposed explanation for the ~cal-~ vowel, not a documented certainty.
en.calzar:
Spanish ~calzar~ descends from Latin ~calceāre~ (“to put on shoes”), a verb formed from ~calceus~ (“shoe”), itself from ~calx~ (“heel”), a word of uncertain origin. It is cognate with Italian ~calzare~, Catalan ~calçar~ and Portuguese ~calçar~, the last documented in the thirteenth-century Cantigas de Santa Maria.

Where English says one puts on shoes, Spanish ~calzar~ treats footwear as something you clothe the feet with, and the verb reaches well beyond shoes: one can ~calzar~ gloves, a wedge under a wobbly table, or a tool with a metal edge, and a shoe size is the number you ~calzas~. The old noun ~calza~ (“hose, stocking”) gave the plural ~calzas~ and then ~calzones~ and ~calzoncillos~ (“breeches; underpants”), while ~calzado~ is the general word for “footwear.” From the wedge sense come ~calzo~ and ~calza~ (“chock, shim”). All of them circle back to the Latin heel — ~calx~ — that once anchored the whole family.
en.cambiar:
From Late Latin ~cambiāre~ (“to exchange, barter”), a term of Gaulish (Celtic) origin, traced to a Gaulish ~cambion~ and a Celtic *~kambos~ (“curved, crooked”), reflecting Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kamb-~ (“to bend, curve”). It is cognate with Italian ~cambiare~, Portuguese ~cambiar~ and French ~changer~, and — through Old French — with English ~change~.

The verb began as commercial jargon: ~cambiāre~ first surfaces in Apuleius, and the noun ~cambium~ (“exchange”) appears only later, in medieval Latin banking. The tie to the Celtic root is engaging but wants care: by one account the sense moved from the physical “to bend, turn” of *~kambos~ to the abstract “to give one thing and turn it into another,” yet this semantic bridge is a proposal, not a documented step. What is secure is the family the verb seeded in Spanish: ~cambio~ (“change, small coin”), ~intercambiar~, ~recambio~ (“spare part”) and, borrowed back through Catalan and Occitan, ~canje~ (“exchange, swap”).
en.caminar:
From ~camino~ (“road, path”) plus the verbal suffix ~-ar~; ~camino~ descends through Old Spanish from Vulgar Latin ~camminus~, a word Latin borrowed from Gaulish (Celtic), ultimately from Proto-Celtic *~kanxsman-~ (“step, pace”), an action-noun built on *~kengeti~ (“to step”). Being Celtic rather than Latin, it is cognate not with a Latin verb but with Welsh ~cam~ (“step”). The Romance family kept it everywhere: French ~chemin~ and ~cheminer~, Italian ~cammino~ and ~camminare~, Portuguese ~caminho~ and ~caminhar~.

The Celtic loan spread precisely because road-building and road-travel were where Gaulish vocabulary left its deepest mark on Latin; ~camminus~ eventually displaced native Latin words for “road” across much of the West. The verb ~caminar~ simply means “to walk” or “to travel a road,” and Spanish elaborated the family richly: ~caminante~ (“traveler, wayfarer”), ~caminata~ (“a long walk, hike”), ~encaminar~ (“to set on the right path, direct”), and the pilgrim’s ~Camino~ de Santiago. The English ~camino~, now used for that pilgrimage route, is a direct borrowing of the Spanish noun.
en.cancelar:
From Latin ~cancellāre~ (“to cross out, cancel”), literally “to mark with a lattice of crossing lines,” from ~cancellī~ (“a lattice, grating, crossbars”). ~cancellī~ is a diminutive form related to ~cancer~ / ~carcer~ (“an enclosure, lattice, prison”). Cognate with English ~cancel~, and — surprisingly — with ~chancel~ and ~chancellor~, discussed below.

A Roman clerk voided a document by drawing a grid of crossing lines over it — a little lattice, ~cancellī~ — so ~cancellāre~ meant “to lattice through,” i.e. to strike out. The same word for a lattice screen took a different route: the ~cancellī~ that railed off part of a church gave English ~chancel~ (the screened-off area near the altar), and the official who stood at that lattice barrier became the ~cancellārius~ — English ~chancellor~ and Spanish ~canciller~. From the lattice sense Spanish also keeps ~cancel~ (“a screen, storm door”) and ~cancela~ (“a wrought-iron gate”), while the “strike out” sense lives on in ~cancelación~ (“cancellation”).
en.cansar:
By Corominas’s account, Spanish ~cansar~ came from Latin ~campsāre~ (“to round a headland, tack, turn aside from a course”), a nautical term the Romans had taken from Greek ~κάμπτειν~ (“to bend”), aorist ~κάμψαι~. The Latin verb is scantily attested, which is why the derivation, though standard, is drawn from the Greek. Portuguese ~cansar~ is the direct cognate.

The path of meaning is the memorable part: from “to double a cape, change course” the verb slid to “to abandon the course one is on,” then to “to give up an effort,” and at last to “to grow weary” — so a word for tiredness set out as a sailor rounding a headland. The reflexive ~cansarse~ is “to tire oneself.” Spanish built more on the stem: ~cansancio~ (“weariness”), ~cansado~ (“tired”) and, with the reversing prefix ~des-~, ~descansar~ — literally “to un-tire,” that is, “to rest.”
en.cantar:
From Latin ~cantāre~ (“to sing”), the frequentative of ~canere~ (“to sing”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂n-~ (“to sing”). It passed unchanged in shape to Portuguese ~cantar~ and Italian ~cantare~, and became French ~chanter~; through the same root it is cognate with English ~chant~ and ~accent~, and even with English ~hen~ (originally “the singing bird”) and German ~Hahn~ (“rooster”).

~Cantāre~ began as an intensive of ~canere~ — not just to sing but to sing repeatedly — and it so thoroughly displaced the plain verb that every Romance language sings with the frequentative. The root *~keh₂n-~ radiated widely in Spanish: ~canto~, ~cántico~, ~cantante~, ~encantar~ (“to enchant,” literally to sing a spell over someone) and, borrowed back from French, ~chantaje~ (“blackmail”).
en.capacitar:
A learned formation from ~capaz~ (“capable”) plus the verb-forming ~-itar~. ~capaz~ descends from Latin ~capāx~ (“able to hold much, roomy”), from ~capere~ (“to take, hold, grasp”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp, seize”). Cognate through that root with English ~heave~ (Old English ~hebban~) and, through Latin ~capere~, with English ~capable~ and ~capacity~.

~capāx~ meant literally “holding a lot” — a roomy vessel — so ~capaz~ first described capacity, then a person “able to hold” a task, i.e. competent. ~capacitar~, built on that, means to make someone capable: to train, qualify, or empower. Latin ~capere~ was extraordinarily fertile in Spanish, which changed its vowel and kept the plain verb as ~caber~ (“to fit”); the same root yields ~captar~, ~capturar~, ~recibir~ (from ~recipere~), ~concebir~ (from ~concipere~), and ~ocupar~. So ~capacitar~ and ~caber~ — “to enable” and “to fit” — are cousins under one Latin verb of holding.
en.captar:
From Latin ~captāre~ (“to try to seize, catch at”), a frequentative of ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), formed with the iterative suffix ~-tāre~. The verb goes back to Proto-Italic *~kapiō~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kap-~ (“to grasp, seize”). Cognate with Italian ~captare~ and French ~capter~, and — through the same root — with English ~have~ and ~heave~ and German ~haben~.

Spanish inherited ~captāre~ twice over. Its popular, orally worn-down form became Old Spanish ~catar~ (“to look at, examine”), which survives in ~acatar~ (“to obey”) and in ~catar~ (“to taste”); ~captar~ is the later, learned re-borrowing that preserved the Latin cluster. Its senses radiate out from “seizing”: to capture a signal or an image, to grasp an idea, to win over an audience, even to collect rainwater. From the wider ~capere~ family Spanish also drew ~captura~, ~cautivo~, ~capaz~, ~caber~ (“to fit”), and ~recibir~ (“to receive”).
en.capturar:
From Latin ~captūra~ (“a catching, seizure”), a noun from ~captus~, the past participle of ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp, seize”). Cognate with Italian ~catturare~ and French ~capturer~, and — through the same root — with English ~capture~, ~captive~, and even ~have~ and German ~haben~, which descend from the same grasping root through Germanic.

Latin ~captūra~ named the act of catching game or fish; Spanish kept that concrete, hunterly edge, and ~capturar~ still suggests seizing a live, resisting thing — a fugitive, an animal, a piece on a chessboard. It is a learned re-formation: the same ~capere~ had already come down through popular speech, worn smooth, as ~caber~ (“to fit”) and, via the frequentative ~captāre~, as ~catar~ (“to taste, examine”) and ~cazar~ (“to hunt”). The prolific root *~keh₂p-~ also gave Spanish ~cautivo~, ~capaz~, ~caza~, ~recibir~, ~concebir~, and ~aceptar~.
en.caracterizar:
Spanish ~caracterizar~ is formed from ~carácter~ plus the verb-forming suffix ~-izar~. ~carácter~ comes from Latin ~character~, a borrowing from Ancient Greek ~kharaktḗr~ (“an engraving tool; the mark it stamps; a distinctive imprint”), from the verb ~kharássō~ (“to scratch, to engrave, to sharpen”). The Greek noun first named the stamp on a coin or the brand cut into a surface, then the distinctive mark it left, and finally a person's stamped-in nature. Spanish ~caracterizar~ is a learned formation. It is cognate with Italian ~caratterizzare~, French ~caractériser~, Portuguese ~caracterizar~, and English ~characterize~.

The metaphor buried in ~caracterizar~ is the engraver's: to characterize something is, at root, to press a distinguishing mark into it, to say what stamp it bears. Spanish uses it in two live senses — to describe the defining traits of a thing (“what characterizes this region”) and, in the theatre, to make oneself up and dress for a role, to ~caracterizar~ a character on stage. The Greek ~kharássō~ (“to engrave”) sits behind the whole family: Spanish ~carácter~, ~característica~, ~caracterización~, and the typographic sense of ~carácter~ as a written sign — the “characters” of an alphabet, still literally little marks stamped onto a page.
en.carecer:
~Carecer~ comes from Latin ~carēscere~, an inchoative in ~-scere~ built on ~carēre~ (“to lack, be without”). The deeper origin is disputed: one proposal derives ~carēre~ from Proto-Italic *~kazēō~ and a Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱes-~ (“to cut,” hence “to be cut off from”), but de Vaan rejects it as semantically strained, and the ultimate root remains uncertain. It is cognate with Portuguese ~carecer~ and French ~carence~, and it survives in English ~caret~.

The inchoative ~-sc-~ gave ~carēre~ a “coming-to” nuance: ~carecer~ is not just to lack but to fall into lacking. The most charming descendant is the proofreader’s mark ~caret~ (^), which is simply Latin ~caret~, “it is lacking” — the third-person present of the same verb, flagging a spot where a word has been left out. Spanish keeps the plainer relatives ~carente~ (“lacking”) and ~carencia~ (“shortage, deficiency”). De Vaan even wonders whether ~caries~ (“decay”) belongs here too, though that link, like the root, is far from settled.
en.cargar:
From Vulgar Latin *~carricāre~ (“to load a wagon”), a verb built on Latin ~carrus~ (“wheeled vehicle, wagon”). ~carrus~ was itself borrowed from Gaulish ~carros~, a Celtic word, and traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱers-~ (“to run”), the same root behind Latin ~currere~ (“to run”). In its passage to Spanish the double consonant softened, the ~-i-~ dropped, and the second ~c~ voiced to ~g~, giving ~cargar~, already attested in the twelfth-century Poem of the Cid. It is cognate with Italian ~caricare~, French ~charger~, Portuguese ~carregar~, and English ~charge~ and ~cargo~.

The image at the root is concrete: to pile a load onto a ~carrus~, a Gaulish cart — so ~cargar~ began as a teamster's word for loading a wagon and then generalized to loading of every kind: a ship, a rifle, a battery, a debt, an emotional weight. English shows how far the ~carrus~ family traveled — “car,” “carriage,” “career,” “cargo,” and “charge” in its electrical sense all descend from the same Celtic-Latin cart. In Spanish the family is large: ~carga~, ~carro~, ~cargo~, ~cargamento~, ~descargar~, ~encargar~, ~acarrear~, and ~ferrocarril~.
en.casar:
Spanish did not inherit its everyday verb for marrying from Latin's marriage vocabulary; it built one at home. ~casar~ comes from the noun ~casa~ (“house”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-ar~ — literally “to set up house” or “to become a member of the household.” The noun descends from Latin ~casa~ (“hut, cottage, cabin”), a humble word of uncertain further origin. The same household-based verb arose across Ibero-Romance: Portuguese ~casar~ and Catalan ~casar~ likewise mean “to marry.”

Where Latin framed marriage with ~mātrimōnium~ and stately legal phrases, Iberian Romance reframed it as founding a house — a domestic fact as much as a rite. That image survives in the reflexive ~casarse~ (“to get married”) and in ~casamiento~ (“wedding”), and echoes in ~casero~ (“homely; landlord”) and the diminutive ~casilla~ (“box on a form, cubbyhole”). Beware a look-alike: the legal ~casar~ (“to quash a judgment”) is a wholly separate verb, from Latin ~cassāre~ (“to annul”), from ~cassus~ (“empty, void”); the two merely fell together in spelling. From the same ~casa~ also come ~caserío~ (“hamlet”) and, borrowed worldwide, ~casino~.
en.castigar:
From Latin ~castīgāre~ (“to set right, chastise, punish”), a compound of the adjective ~castus~ (“pure, chaste”) and a reduced form of ~agere~ (“to drive, to make”) — so, roughly, “to make pure.” Old Spanish ~castigar~ long carried the milder senses “to advise, admonish, teach a lesson,” closer to the Latin notion of correcting someone. It is cognate with Italian ~castigare~ and Portuguese ~castigar~, and — by way of Old French ~chastier~ — with English ~chastise~ and ~chasten~; the later learned borrowing ~castigate~ came straight from the Latin. English ~chaste~ descends from the same ~castus~.

The drift from “make pure” to “punish” went through the idea of correction: to castigate was to purify conduct, first by reproof and then by penalty. The instructive sense lingered in older Spanish, but modern ~castigar~ is firmly punitive. From ~castus~ Spanish also built ~casto~ (“chaste”), ~castidad~ (“chastity”), and ~incesto~ (“incest,” literally “not chaste”). The deeper prehistory of ~castus~ is debated — by one account it belongs with a root meaning “to cut off, separate,” whence “set apart, pure” — so that step is best left marked as uncertain.
en.castrar:
Spanish ~castrar~ comes from Latin ~castrāre~ (“to castrate, to geld”), traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱes-~ (“to cut, to slaughter”), perhaps by way of a lost instrument noun *~ḱos-trom~ (“cutting tool, knife”). A striking cognate is Sanskrit ~śastra~ (“sword, dagger”). It is cognate with Portuguese ~castrar~, Catalan ~castrar~ and Italian ~castrare~; English ~castrate~ is a later borrowing straight from the Latin.

Sources note that it is not certain whether ~castrar~ was inherited without a break or partly re-borrowed as a learned word, and that in everyday medieval speech the synonym ~capar~ was more common; some Romance reflexes even show metathesis or crossing with ~crista~. If the ancient *~ḱes-~ root truly underlies it, then ~castrar~ belongs to a grim little family of “cutting” words. The related Latin ~castus~ (“cut off from fault, pure”) — the source of ~casto~ (“chaste”) and ~casta~ (“caste, lineage”) — may spring from the same notion of separation, though that link is itself debated.
en.catalogar:
A modern denominal verb, coined in Spanish from the noun ~catálogo~ (“catalogue”) plus the verbal ending ~-ar~. ~catálogo~ comes from Latin ~catalogus~, from Ancient Greek ~katálogos~ (“a list, register, enrolment”), from ~katalégein~ (“to list, recount, enrol”), a compound of ~katá~ (“down, thoroughly”) and ~légein~ (“to gather, pick out, say”). That Greek verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, collect”). Cognate with English ~catalogue~ and French ~cataloguer~.

The Greek ~légein~ first meant “to gather or pick up,” then slid to “to pick out words, recount, say” — the same leap from gathering things to gathering speech that shaped so much of our vocabulary. A ~katálogos~ was, literally, a “counting-through” list, run down item by item. The root *~leǵ-~ seeded an enormous family: through Greek ~lógos~ come ~lógica~, ~diálogo~, and ~catálogo~ itself; through Latin ~legere~ (“to read, gather”) come ~leer~, ~lección~, ~elegir~, ~colección~, and ~legión~. To catalogue, then, is at root to gather and lay down in order.
en.catar:
Spanish ~catar~ comes from Late Latin ~cattāre~ (“to look at, to watch”), from Latin ~captāre~ (“to try to seize, to try to catch — including with the eyes”), the frequentative of ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”). ~capere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~kh₂p-~ (“to grasp”), which also gave, through Germanic, English ~have~ and ~heave~. Cognate verbs from ~captāre~ include Portuguese ~catar~ and Old Galician-Portuguese ~catar~.

The original Spanish sense was “to look at, to examine,” and it survives in fixed phrases — ~catar~ meaning “to inspect” or, negatively, in “sin ~catar~” (“without so much as looking”). From “to examine (closely)” the meaning narrowed to examining with the mouth: “to taste, to sample,” especially wine, which is the everyday sense today, along with the noun ~cata~ (“a tasting”) and ~catador~ (“taster”). The old “look” sense is still visible in ~acatar~ (“to obey, to comply,” once “to heed, to regard”) and in ~recatar~ / ~recato~ (“modesty, caution,” from watchfully keeping something back).
en.causar:
From Latin ~causāre~ (“to cause, to give as a reason”), a verb built on the noun ~causa~ (“cause, reason, legal case”). It is cognate with Italian ~causare~, French ~causer~ and Portuguese ~causar~, and with English ~cause~, taken through Old French. The ancestry of ~causa~ beyond Latin is genuinely uncertain: it goes back to Old Latin ~caussa~, but no secure Proto-Indo-European source is agreed, and some scholars have proposed a non-Indo-European — possibly Etruscan — origin.

In Roman usage ~causa~ leaned heavily toward the courtroom — a “case, suit, legal matter” — and Spanish still keeps that legal sense alongside the ordinary one, so a ~causa~ can be either a cause or a criminal case. The noun's most startling descendant, though, is utterly ordinary: in Vulgar Latin ~causa~ (“matter, affair”) weakened all the way to “thing,” giving Spanish ~cosa~, French ~chose~ and Italian ~cosa~. From the same Latin stem come ~acusar~, ~excusar~, ~recusar~ and ~causante~.
en.cavar:
From Latin ~cavāre~ (“to hollow out, dig out”), a denominative verb built on the adjective ~cavus~ (“hollow, concave”), from Proto-Italic *~kawāō~ and, ultimately, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱówHwos~ (“hollow, cavity”). Cognate with Italian ~cavare~ and Portuguese ~cavar~, and — as a later loan — with English ~cave~.

The original Latin sense was not so much “to dig” as “to make hollow,” to open out a concavity; Spanish narrowed it to the gardener's and gravedigger's labor of turning and opening the earth. The same root gave Spanish ~cava~ (“cellar, wine-cave”), ~caverna~ (“cavern”), the learned ~excavar~ (“to excavate”), and the adjective ~cóncavo~ (“concave”). A vivid idiom preserves the old force: ~cavar~ su propia tumba, “to dig one's own grave.”
en.cazar:
From Old Spanish ~caçar~, from Vulgar Latin *~captiāre~, a reshaping of Latin ~captāre~ (“to try to seize, chase after”), the frequentative of ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”). Cognate with Portuguese ~caçar~, French ~chasser~, and Italian ~cacciare~, and — through the same Vulgar Latin verb — with English ~chase~ and its doublet ~catch~.

The root sense is repeated, insistent grasping: not a single seizure but the pursuit that precedes it, which is exactly hunting. From ~capere~ Latin built a whole vocabulary of taking that Spanish still shows in the relatives of ~cazar~: ~caza~ (“hunt, game”), ~cazador~ (“hunter”), and ~cacería~ (“hunting party”). The same PIE root *~keh₂p-~ surfaces far afield in the Germanic family, in English ~have~ and ~heave~. Spanish keeps a curiosity here: the everyday ~cazar~ and ~casar~ (“to marry”) are near-homophones in seseo dialects, a trap for learners.
en.cebar:
From Latin ~cibāre~ (“to feed, give food to”), a denominative verb from ~cibus~ (“food”), a noun of uncertain, possibly non-Indo-European origin. Cognate with Portuguese ~cevar~ and Galician ~cebar~.

The Latin verb meant simply “to feed,” and Spanish preserved that core while fanning it out into a surprising range of specialized senses: to ~cebar~ is to fatten livestock, to bait a hook or a trap, to prime a firearm or a pump — and, figuratively, to feed a passion or stoke a fire. The shared image is supplying something with what makes it grow or go. From the same ~cibus~ come the everyday ~cebo~ (“bait; feed”), ~cebada~ (“barley,” originally fodder-grain), and ~cebador~ (“primer, feeder”). The mate-drinker's ~cebar~ el mate — repeatedly refreshing the gourd with hot water — keeps the “feeding” metaphor alive in daily South American speech.
en.ceder:
From Latin ~cēdere~ (“to go, withdraw, give way”), traced to Proto-Italic *~kesd-o-~ (“to go away”) and the Proto-Indo-European root *~ked-~ (“to go, yield”). Spanish ~ceder~ is cognate with Italian ~cedere~ and French ~céder~, and — through the same verb — with English ~cede~; its frequentative ~cessāre~ (“to hold back, leave off”) gave both Spanish ~cesar~ and English ~cease~.

The core sense “to go, move off” narrowed to “to give up one’s place, yield” — what one does by stepping back. Latin loved compounding ~cēdere~ with prefixes, and Spanish inherited the whole set: ~conceder~, ~acceder~, ~preceder~, ~suceder~ (“to follow; to happen”), ~exceder~, ~proceder~ and ~retroceder~. From the past participle ~cessus~ came a matching crowd of nouns — ~cesión~, ~proceso~, ~acceso~, ~exceso~ — and ~antecessor~ (“one who goes before”), which through French reached English as ~ancestor~.
en.cegar:
From Latin ~caecāre~ (“to make blind”), a denominative verb from the adjective ~caecus~ (“blind”), from Proto-Italic *~kaikos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kéh₂ikos~ (“one-eyed, blind”). The adjective is cognate with Gothic ~haihs~ (“one-eyed”) and Old Irish ~cáech~, a well-reconstructed Italo-Celtic-Germanic match.

Spanish inherited both a literal and a figurative force. To ~cegar~ is to blind or to dazzle, and reflexively ~cegarse~ is to be blinded by rage or love. A second, concrete branch means “to block up, stop up”: one can ~cegar~ a well, a window, or a pipe — sealing an opening as if putting out an eye. The adjective lives on as ~ciego~ (“blind”), and the family includes ~ceguera~ (“blindness”) and the learned ~obcecar~ (“to blind the mind, make obstinate”).
en.celar:
Spanish ~celar~ in the sense “to watch over, guard jealously” has a genuinely disputed origin. The dictionaries of the Academia derive it from Latin ~cēlāre~ (“to hide, conceal”); other authorities instead connect the jealousy sense to Late Latin ~zēlāre~ (“to be zealous or jealous”), from ~zēlus~, a borrowing of Ancient Greek ~ζῆλος~ (~zêlos~, “zeal, ardent rivalry”). The sources hedge, and so should we: the watching-out-of-jealousy sense may descend from either line, or from a blend of the two.

Both ancestors left clear marks in Spanish. If from ~cēlāre~ — from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱel-~ (“to cover, hide”), cognate with English ~conceal~ and ~occult~ — the underlying image is guarding by keeping hidden. If from ~zēlāre~, the relatives are ~celo~ (“zeal”), ~celos~ (“jealousy”), and ~celoso~ (“jealous”), tied to English ~zeal~ and ~jealous~. A separate homonym ~celar~ (“to engrave, chase metal”) comes from Latin ~caelāre~ and is unrelated to either.
en.celebrar:
From Latin ~celebrāre~ (“to frequent, throng, honor, solemnize”), from ~celeber~ (“much-frequented, crowded, populous; famous”). Cognate with Italian ~celebrare~, French ~célébrer~, Portuguese ~celebrar~ and English ~celebrate~. The deeper origin of ~celeber~ is uncertain; it has been linked to ~celer~ (“swift”), but that connection is unproven and the sources leave the root undetermined, so it is best treated as disputed.

The core image is a crowd: a ~celeber~ place was one thronged with people, and ~celebrāre~ first meant “to fill, to frequent in numbers,” then “to honor with a gathering,” and finally “to solemnize.” A festival is still, etymologically, a well-attended event. The same family gave Spanish ~célebre~ (“famous”), ~celebridad~ and ~celebración~. The oft-repeated claim that ~celeber~ comes from ~celer~ “swift” is appealing but not established — by most accounts the origin remains unknown.
en.centrar:
From Spanish ~centro~ (“center”), from Latin ~centrum~ (“center of a circle; the fixed point of a compass”), itself a borrowing of Ancient Greek ~κέντρον~ (~kéntron~, “sharp point, goad, the stationary leg of a compass”), from the verb ~κεντέω~ (~kentéō~, “to prick, goad”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱent-~ (“to prick”). Cognate with Italian ~centrare~, French ~centrer~ and Portuguese ~centrar~; English ~center~ descends from the same Greek word.

The Greek noun first named the sharp point of a goad and then the fixed pivot around which a compass sweeps a circle — the geometric sense Latin took over. From that idea of a central point Spanish built the verb ~centrar~, “to place at the center,” whose senses branched into balancing, aligning and, reflexively, focusing: ~centrarse en~ means “to concentrate on.” The same root seeded a broad family in Spanish, among them ~centro~, ~céntrico~, ~concentrar~, ~excéntrico~ and ~centímetro~.
en.cercar:
From Late Latin ~circāre~ (“to go around, traverse in a circuit”), from Latin ~circā~/~circum~ (“around”), from ~circus~ (“ring, circle”), itself likely borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κίρκος~ (~kírkos~, “ring”); the family reaches back to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)ker-~ (“to turn, bend”). Cognate with Italian ~cercare~ and French ~chercher~ — and, borrowed through Old French, with English ~search~.

Here the Romance languages split the sense of “going around” in two directions. Iberian Spanish and Portuguese took ~cercar~ toward encircling — to fence in, surround, or lay siege to — while Italian and French took ~cercare~/~chercher~ toward searching, going around looking for something. Spanish shows the concrete side in its relatives ~cerca~ (“fence; near”), ~cerco~ (“ring, siege”), ~acercar~ (“to bring near”), and, borrowed straight from Latin, ~circo~ (“circus”). The learner's trap is real: a Spaniard who ~cerca~ a town besieges it, while a Frenchman who cherche it is merely looking for it.
en.cerrar:
Spanish ~cerrar~ comes from Late Latin ~serāre~ (“to bolt, lock, close”), a verb derived from the noun ~sera~ (“a bolt, bar, or lock for a door”). The classical form ~serāre~ appears already in Varro and Tibullus (~serāre forēs~, “to bolt the doors”). Two changes reshaped it in the mouths of speakers. First, the ~-r-~ doubled to ~-rr-~ through confusion with ~serra~ (“saw”) and ~serrāre~ (“to saw”) — an entirely different word — so a Vulgar Latin *~serrāre~ arose, still living as Italian ~serrare~, French ~serrer~ (“to tighten, squeeze”), and Portuguese ~cerrar~. English ~serried~ (as in “serried ranks”) is borrowed from the French. Second, the initial ~s-~ became ~c-~ in Castilian — a shift Corominas attributes to the pull of the near-synonym ~cercar~ (“to enclose”).

So the word’s history hides a small comedy of errors: a verb for locking a door got tangled with the unrelated verb for sawing wood, borrowing its double ~r~, and then swapped its opening consonant under the influence of a synonym. The s-to-c shift is Corominas’s proposal, not a certainty, and is best held as the favored account rather than settled fact. Meaning stayed stable — to shut, close, seal — and Spanish grew a rich brood: ~cerradura~ (“lock”), ~cerrojo~ (“bolt”), ~cierre~ (“closure, zipper”), ~encerrar~ (“to lock up, enclose”), ~cerrado~ (“closed; dense; unintelligible”), and ~cerca~ (“fence,” and the adverb “near”). Beware the false friend: Spanish ~cerrar~ (“to close”) and ~serrar~ (“to saw,” from that same ~serra~) are separate verbs that merely sound alike.
en.certificar:
From Late Latin ~certificāre~ (“to make certain, attest”), a compound of Latin ~certus~ (“sure, settled”) and the combining form ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make, do”). ~certus~ is the past participle of ~cernere~ (“to sift, separate, distinguish, decide”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~krey-~ (“to sift, discriminate”). It is cognate with French ~certifier~, Italian ~certificare~, and English ~certify~ and ~certain~.

The underlying image is agricultural: to be ~certus~ is to have been “sifted” — passed through a sieve until the matter is settled, just as grain is separated from chaff. The same root surfaces in the Greek cognate ~κρίνω~ (~krínō~, “to separate, judge”), which gave English ~crisis~ and ~critic~, and in Latin ~cribrum~ (“sieve”) and ~crīmen~ (“verdict, charge”). Spanish keeps a wide family from ~cernere~: ~cierto~ (“certain”), ~certeza~ and ~certidumbre~ (“certainty”), ~discernir~ (“to discern”), ~cerner~ (“to sift”), and — through ~crīmen~ — ~crimen~. To ~certificar~ is thus, at root, to sift a matter until it is sure.
en.cesar:
From Latin ~cessāre~ (“to hold back, leave off, be idle”), a frequentative of ~cēdere~ (“to go, withdraw, yield”), whose past participle ~cessus~ furnished the frequentative stem. The root is Proto-Indo-European *~ked-~ (“to go, yield”). Spanish ~cesar~ is cognate with French ~cesser~ and — by way of Old French — English ~cease~; and, through ~cēdere~ directly, with English ~cede~ and ~cession~.

A frequentative names a repeated or drawn-out action, so ~cessāre~ was “to keep withdrawing, go slack,” which slid easily into “to stop, cease.” Spanish inherited a whole family from ~cēdere~: ~ceder~, ~conceder~, ~exceder~, ~proceder~, ~suceder~ and ~acceder~, plus the nouns ~suceso~ and ~proceso~. A tempting false friend to disarm: the name ~César~ (Caesar) is unrelated. Its origin is genuinely uncertain, and the old story linking it to ~caedere~ (“to cut,” from a supposed birth “cut” from the womb) is a folk etymology the sources treat with doubt. When something ceases, it yields and steps aside — no emperor required.
en.charlar:
From Italian ~ciarlare~ (“to chatter, to prattle”), a word most likely of expressive, onomatopoeic creation rather than inherited descent. Spanish adopted it in the sixteenth century as ~charlar~. The Italian verb is itself hard to pin down: by Corominas's account it is an expressive formation, perhaps an alteration of an older ~ciarrare~ under the pull of ~parlare~ (“to speak”). Because the root imitates the sound of rapid, empty talk, the sources hedge — the origin is expressive, not a clean chain back to Latin.

In Spanish ~charlar~ settled into the friendly, informal sense “to chat, to talk idly,” without the pejorative edge of mere gossip. The same Italian family gave Spanish ~charlatán~: the expressive ~ciarlare~ appears to have contaminated ~cerretano~ (a hawker of fake relics and cure-alls, named for the town of Cerreto), yielding the word for a smooth-talking fraud. From ~charlar~ Spanish also draws ~charla~ (“a chat”) and ~charlador~. English ~charlatan~, French ~charlatan~ and Italian ~ciarlatano~ share that second thread.
en.chocar:
The origin of ~chocar~ (“to collide, clash, shock”) is genuinely debated. The most widely cited account derives it from French ~choquer~ (“to strike against”), attested from the 13th century and itself probably of Germanic origin. But Corominas stresses that the matter is uncertain: he notes that an onomatopoeic origin — the word imitating the very sound of a blow — cannot be ruled out, and may even have arisen independently and in parallel across Germanic and Romance. No secure Indo-European root can be assigned, precisely because a sound-imitating coinage need not descend from one.

Whatever its birth, the meaning is vivid and physical: two things striking each other. From the literal collision Spanish extended ~chocar~ to the figurative — ideas, opinions or people that ~chocan~ — and to the social gesture ~chocar~ la mano or ~chocar~ los cinco (“to high-five”). The colloquial ~me choca~ can mean “it startles me” or, in Mexico, “it annoys me.” Related words include the noun ~choque~ (“crash, shock, collision”) and ~chocante~ (“shocking, off-putting”). English ~shock~ shares the same debated Germanic-or-echoic background, which is why the two words feel like cousins.
en.circular:
From Latin ~circulāre~ (“to form or move in a circle”), from ~circulus~ (“little ring, circle”), the diminutive of ~circus~ (“ring, circle, circular arena”). ~Circus~ was borrowed from Ancient Greek ~kírkos~ (“ring,” and also the name of a circling hawk), and both go back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)ker-~ (“to turn, bend”) — the same root that, through its Germanic branch, produced English ~ring~. Latin ~circus~ also lives on directly as English ~circus~ and ~circle~.

To ~circulāre~ was to go round in a ring, and the verb kept that turning motion: Spanish ~circular~ means “to circulate, move around” — of blood, of money, of traffic, of rumours — and, as an adjective, simply “circular, round.” When William Harvey described the blood’s ~circulación~ around the body in 1628, he was drawing on exactly this image of a closed ring. The diminutive lineage is rich in Spanish: ~círculo~ (“circle”), ~circo~ (“circus”), ~circuito~ (“circuit”), and — worn down through Vulgar Latin — ~cercar~ (“to encircle, fence in”) and even ~cerca~ (“near,” from Latin ~circā~, “around”).
en.citar:
From Latin ~citāre~ (“to summon, call forth, set in motion”), a frequentative of ~ciēre~ (“to move, rouse, stir”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱey-~ (“to set in motion”). Cognate with French ~citer~, Italian ~citare~, and — as learned borrowings — English ~cite~ and ~excite~.

The frequentative ~citāre~ meant to summon repeatedly or insistently, and that legal-sounding “call before a court” underlies the modern “quote an authority.” It also explains a happy Spanish ambiguity: ~cita~ means at once a “quotation,” an “appointment,” and a “romantic date” — all of them a calling-together at an agreed time. Kin from the same root abound: ~incitar~ (“to incite”), ~excitar~ (“to excite”), ~recitar~ (“to recite”), ~solicitar~ (“to request”), and vividly ~resucitar~ (“to resuscitate”), literally to stir back to life.
en.clamar:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~clāmāre~ (“to shout, cry out”), a denominative built on a noun *~klāmā~ (“a shout”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kelh₁-~ (“to shout, call”). Its inherited, popular doublet is ~llamar~ (“to call”), which underwent the regular Spanish shift of initial ~cl-~ to ~ll-~; ~clamar~ instead re-entered the language straight from Latin, keeping the cluster. Cognate with French ~clamer~, Italian ~chiamare~ (“to call”), and Portuguese ~chamar~, and — through Old French — with English ~claim~ and ~clamor~.

The same PIE root *~kelh₁-~ is unusually productive: it gave Latin ~clārus~ (“clear,” originally “clear-sounding”) and Ancient Greek ~καλέω~ (~kaléō~, “to call”). In Spanish the ~clam-~ family clusters around raising the voice — ~clamor~ (“clamor, outcry”), ~reclamar~ (“to claim, demand”), ~exclamar~ (“to exclaim”), and ~proclamar~ (“to proclaim”). The verb keeps a solemn, rhetorical color: one uses ~clamar~ not for coffee but for justice, and ~clamar~ en el desierto (“to cry out in the wilderness”) marks a plea that goes unheard.
en.clasificar:
A learned compound coined from Latin ~classis~ (“a division, class, fleet”) plus the combining form ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”) — literally “to make into classes.” ~Classis~ came from Proto-Italic *~klāssis~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kelh₁-~ (“to call, shout out”), and so is kin to Latin ~calāre~ (“to call”), ~clāmāre~ (“to shout”) and ~clārus~ (“clear”), and to Ancient Greek ~kaléō~ (“I call”). Cognate formations include Italian ~classificare~, French ~classifier~ and Portuguese ~classificar~.

The startling turn is that a ~classis~ began as a military summons: by De Vaan's account the sense ran from a “calling out” of citizens to arms, to the ~classis~ or body of soldiers so called, to the property classes into which Servius Tullius sorted Roman citizens, and finally to any “class” or category. ~Clasificar~ therefore means to sort things into ranks first drawn up by a herald's cry. Related Spanish words are ~clase~, ~clásico~ and ~clasificación~.
en.cobrar:
From Old Spanish ~cobrar~, an aphetic (head-clipped) form of ~recobrar~ (“to recover, get back”), from Latin ~recuperāre~ (“to regain, recover”), related to ~recipere~ (“to take back, receive”). Some scholars instead posit a Vulgar Latin *~cuperāre~, a back-formation drawn out of ~recuperāre~, which would make ~cobrar~ old rather than merely clipped — the point is debated. Whatever the route, Latin ~recuperāre~ also survives as the learned Spanish doublet ~recuperar~, and gave Italian ~ricoverare~, French ~recouvrer~ and English ~recover~ and ~recuperate~.

The starting sense was “to get back what was lost,” and Spanish ~recobrar~ and ~recuperar~ still carry it. The clipped ~cobrar~, though, drifted toward money: its dominant modern meaning is “to charge, to collect payment, to get paid.” It keeps older senses too — a hunter ~cobra~ (retrieves) downed game, and a feeling can ~cobrar fuerza~, “gather strength.” The family includes ~cobro~ (“collection, charge”), ~cobranza~, ~cobrador~, ~recobrar~ and ~recuperar~.
en.cocinar:
Spanish ~cocinar~ was built from the noun ~cocina~ (“kitchen”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-ar~. ~cocina~ descends from Latin ~coquīna~ (“kitchen”), a nominalization tied to ~coquere~ (“to cook”), from Proto-Italic *~kʷekʷō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~pekʷ-~ (“to cook, ripen”). The same root produced Italian ~cucinare~, French ~cuisiner~ and Portuguese ~cozinhar~, and — through the Latin verb directly — Spanish ~cocer~ (“to boil, cook”). English ~cook~, borrowed early from Latin ~coquus~ (“cook”), belongs to the same family.

The meaning has stayed remarkably steady: to prepare food, especially with heat. The surprising twist is phonetic. In Latin the initial p of *~pekʷ-~ assimilated to the following labiovelar, turning the root into ~coquere~ — which is why the Romance words for cooking begin with a hard c/k rather than the p the root would lead you to expect. From the same source Spanish also keeps ~cocinero~ (“cook”), ~cocido~ (“stew,” literally “cooked”) and ~bizcocho~ (“sponge cake, biscuit”), from ~bis~ (“twice”) + ~coctus~ (“cooked”) — literally something baked twice.
en.coger:
From Old Spanish ~coger~ (first attested around 1140), from Latin ~colligere~ (“to gather, collect”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~legere~ (“to gather, pick, read”). ~legere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, collect”), the root that also gave Ancient Greek ~légō~ (“to gather, to say”) and hence ~lógos~. Sister forms of ~colligere~ include Italian ~cogliere~, French ~cueillir~, Portuguese ~colher~, and Catalan ~collir~.

The journey from “to gather up” to plain “to grasp, take, catch” was gradual, and Spanish generalized ~coger~ into one of its handiest everyday verbs — coger el autobús, coger un objeto, coger fruta. But the meaning kept drifting regionally: across much of the Americas (Argentina, Mexico, and beyond) ~coger~ acquired a vulgar sexual sense, so speakers there favor ~agarrar~ or ~tomar~ for the neutral idea. From the same ~legere~ root Spanish also holds ~colegir~ (“to infer,” to gather a conclusion), ~recoger~, ~escoger~, ~coleccionar~, and the learned ~colección~ — a whole cluster around the image of gathering things together.
en.coincidir:
From Medieval Latin ~coincidere~ (“to fall together, occupy the same place”), a learned compound of ~co-~ (“together”) and ~incidere~ (“to fall upon, into”), itself ~in-~ (“on, into”) plus ~cadere~ (“to fall”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱad-~ (“to fall”). English carries the borrowings ~coincide~, ~incident~, ~accident~ and ~cadence~.

Unlike the inherited verbs, ~coincidir~ was assembled by scholars — first for geometry, where two figures “coincide” by falling exactly onto each other — and only later widened to the everyday “to agree, to happen at once.” The parent ~cadere~ left Spanish an enormous progeny: the plain ~caer~ (“to fall”), ~caso~ (“case,” a “falling-out” of events), ~casualidad~ (“chance”), ~decaer~, ~ocaso~ (“sunset, decline”), ~incidente~, ~accidente~ and even ~cadáver~ — the Latin ~cadāver~, literally “the fallen one.” To coincide, then, is for two things to fall onto the very same point.
en.colaborar:
From Latin ~collaborare~ (“to labor together”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together, with”) and ~laborare~ (“to work, to toil”), which derives from the noun ~labor~ (“work, effort, hardship”). Spanish took it as a learned borrowing rather than by unbroken oral descent. It is cognate with English ~collaborate~, Italian ~collaborare~, French ~collaborer~, and Portuguese ~colaborar~, all reflecting the same late-Latin formation.

In classical Latin ~laborare~ carried a note of toil and hardship, not just activity; the prefix ~com-~ added the sense of shared effort toward a common end. That cooperative meaning stayed remarkably stable, though the twentieth century gave ~colaborar~ a darker political shading in the sense of aiding an occupying enemy. From the same root Spanish keeps ~labor~, ~laborable~, ~laboratorio~, ~laborioso~ and ~elaborar~, all turning on the old idea of work.
en.colgar:
From Latin ~collocāre~ (“to place, set, arrange”), an emphatic ~com-~ prefixed to ~locāre~ (“to put in place”), from ~locus~ (“place”). Spoken Latin carried ~collocāre~ into Romance twice over: the inherited, sound-worn form became Spanish ~colgar~, while a later learned borrowing of the same word gave the doublet ~colocar~ (“to place, position”). French took its own descendant as ~coucher~ (“to lay down, put to bed”), and English borrowed that as the noun ~couch~; Portuguese has ~colgar~ beside ~colocar~.

Where Latin ~collocāre~ meant to set a thing anywhere, Spanish ~colgar~ specialized upward — to place something so it dangles from a hook or nail, that is, to hang it. The learned twin ~colocar~ meanwhile kept the neutral “to place,” so the two verbs split the labor between them. Modern relatives cluster around the base ~locus~: ~local~, ~localizar~, ~lugar~ (“place,” worn down from ~locālis~), and, back in the ~colgar~ branch, ~descolgar~ (“to take down, unhook”) and ~colgadura~ (“hanging, drapery”).
en.colocar:
From Latin ~collocāre~ (“to place together, to arrange, to set in order”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together, with”) and ~locāre~ (“to place”), from ~locus~ (“place”). ~locāre~ and ~locus~ go back, through Old Latin ~stlocus~, to an uncertain earlier form, but the family is unmistakable in Romance: Italian ~collocare~, Portuguese ~colocar~, and — by inheritance rather than borrowing — French ~coucher~ (“to lay down, to put to bed”) and English ~locate~ and ~couch~ all spring from the same Latin verb.

Spanish inherited ~collocāre~ twice over. The popular, orally transmitted line — its pretonic vowel lost and its consonants worn smooth — yielded ~colgar~ (“to hang”), while a later learned borrowing taken straight from the books gave ~colocar~ (“to place, to position”). The two form an etymological doublet: a single Latin word that entered Spanish by two different roads. From ~locus~ the language also draws ~local~, ~localizar~, and ~lugar~ (the fully popularized reflex of ~locālis~). And from the French ~coucher~ branch came the borrowed ~colcha~ (“bedspread”) and ~colchón~ (“mattress”) — so that a sleeper's mattress and the tidy verb ~colocar~ are, at a great distance, the very same word.
en.combatir:
From Vulgar Latin *~combattere~, an intensive ~com-~ (“with, together”) prefixed to Late Latin ~battuere~ (“to beat, strike”). That base looks foreign to Latin — genuine Latin words rarely begin with b — and is widely thought borrowed from Gaulish (compare Welsh ~bathu~, “to strike, to coin”), perhaps going back to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰau-~ (“to strike”); this Celtic route is probable but not certain. It is cognate with French ~combattre~ and English ~combat~ and ~battle~.

The soldierly sense was there from the beginning: to ~combatir~ is to “beat against” an enemy. The plain descendant of ~battuere~ is Spanish ~batir~ (“to beat, whisk, pound”), and the same base spread widely into ~batalla~, ~combate~, ~debatir~ (originally “to thrash out”), and ~abatir~ (“to knock down, to dishearten”).
en.combinar:
From Late Latin ~combīnāre~ (“to join two by two”), from ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~bīnī~ (“two at a time, in pairs”), a distributive of ~bis~ (“twice”) that traces back to ~duo~ (“two”) and ultimately to Proto-Indo-European *~dwóh₁~ (“two”). English borrowed the same verb as ~combine~, and the ~bīnī~ element survives in ~binary~.

The word's whole logic is pairing: to combine is to set things two by two until they hold together. Late Latin coined ~combīnāre~ precisely to name that yoking of pairs, and Spanish kept the sense intact in ~combinación~ (“combination”), which can mean a chemical union, a subway connection, or a woman's slip. The numeral core shows up wherever “two-ness” is at stake — in ~binario~, ~combinado~ and the mathematics of ~combinatoria~. Far older, that same *~dwóh₁~ underlies Spanish ~dos~, ~doble~ and ~dúo~, making combine and its cousins a distant echo of the plain word for two.
en.comedir:
From Latin ~commētīrī~ (“to measure out, measure together”), a compound of ~com-~ (“with, together”) and ~mētīrī~ (“to measure”), from Proto-Indo-European *~meh₁-~ (“to measure”). The simple verb ~mētīrī~ descended into Spanish as the everyday ~medir~ (“to measure”); ~comedir~ is its prefixed relative. The root is widely spread: it gave Ancient Greek ~μέτρον~ (~métron~, “measure”) and, through Latin ~mēnsūra~, English ~measure~.

The metaphor is quietly beautiful: to ~comedirse~ is to take the measure of one's own conduct, to keep within bounds. Spanish uses this reflexive ~comedirse~ (“to restrain oneself, act with moderation”) and its most common face is the adjective ~comedido~ (“moderate, courteous, considerate”). In parts of Latin America ~comedirse~ took an appealing turn, coming to mean “to offer to help unbidden.” The same measuring root underlies ~mesura~ (“restraint, poise”) and ~medida~ (“measure, measurement”).
en.comentar:
From Latin ~commentārī~ (“to consider thoroughly, study, discuss”), a deponent verb linked to ~comminīscī~ (“to devise, contrive, think up”), formed with ~com-~ (“together, thoroughly”) on the root of ~meminī~ (“to remember”) and ~mēns~ (“mind”), from Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to think”). ~Comentar~ therefore shares its deepest root with ~mencionar~. It is cognate with Italian ~commentare~, French ~commenter~, Portuguese ~comentar~ and English ~comment~, and — through *~men-~ — with English ~mind~ and ~mental~.

The literal sense is “to have thoroughly in mind” — to turn something over in thought — and from that came the ideas of studying a text and remarking on it. The Latin noun ~commentārius~ meant a notebook or memorandum, a set of things thought over; Julius Caesar titled his war memoirs ~Commentāriī~, and the English “commentary” descends straight from it. Modern Spanish keeps the reflective streak: to ~comentar~ is to offer one's considered remark, and the ~comentario~ can range from a scholarly gloss to a passing aside. Related through *~men-~ are ~mente~, ~memoria~, ~mencionar~ and ~mentar~.
en.comenzar:
From Vulgar Latin *~cominitiāre~, a compound of intensive ~com-~ and ~initiāre~ (“to begin, initiate”), the verb of ~initium~ (“a beginning”). ~initium~ comes from ~inīre~ (“to go in, enter”), from ~in-~ (“in”) plus ~īre~ (“to go”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”). Cognate with French ~commencer~, Italian ~cominciare~, Portuguese ~começar~, and Catalan ~començar~; English ~commence~ was borrowed from the Old French form.

The literal core is quietly logical: to begin is to “go into” a thing — ~inīre~ — and ~initium~ named the threshold, the point of entry. Late Latin stacked an intensifying ~com-~ onto ~initiāre~ to make the everyday “start,” and that doubled form, not classical ~incipere~, is what the western Romance languages inherited. Spanish paired the popular ~comenzar~ with the noun ~comienzo~, while borrowing the learned doublets ~iniciar~ and ~inicio~ straight from ~initium~. The same PIE *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”) also underlies ~ir~ itself and words such as ~éxito~ (“exit” of effort → “success”) and ~tránsito~.
en.comer:
From Latin ~comedere~ (“to eat up, to consume”), an intensive compound of ~com-~ (here a strengthening prefix) and ~edere~ (“to eat”). ~edere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁ed-~ (“to eat”), one of the oldest words humans can reconstruct — the same root that gave English ~eat~ and ~edible~, German ~essen~, and, through the image of “the biter,” even the ~tooth~ (from *~h₃dónts~, “the eating one”). Portuguese shares the choice exactly: ~comer~.

Here Spanish went its own way. Classical Latin's plain ~edere~ (“to eat”) was short and riddled with irregular forms, so it faded; where French, Italian, and Romanian reached instead for ~mandūcāre~ (“to chew, to munch” — originally a slangy, comic word, and the source of French ~manger~ and Italian ~mangiare~), Spanish and Portuguese kept the older, more dignified ~comedere~, worn down to ~comer~. So a Spaniard still “eats” with a verb Cicero would recognize, while a Frenchman “chews.” From the same root Spanish holds ~comida~ (“food, meal”), ~comestible~ (“edible”), and ~comilón~ (“big eater, glutton”).
en.comercializar:
Spanish ~comercializar~ is a modern verb from ~comercial~ (“commercial”) with the suffix ~-izar~, and ~comercial~ rests on ~comercio~ (“commerce, trade”), from Latin ~commercium~ (“trade, traffic”). That noun is ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~merx~ (stem ~merc-~, “merchandise, goods”). Cognate with French ~commercialiser~ and English ~commerce~, ~merchant~, and ~mercantile~; the same ~merx~ gave Spanish ~mercado~, ~mercader~, and ~mercancía~.

The origin of ~merx~ is contested: de Vaan links it — together with the god-name ~Mercurius~ (Spanish ~Mercurio~), patron of merchants — to a layer of trade vocabulary he suspects is Etruscan, while more recent scholars have proposed Indo-European derivations instead; no account is settled. From ~merx~ Latin also formed the verb ~mercārī~ (“to trade”), whence ~mercado~ (“market”) by way of ~mercātus~. ~Comercializar~ is the youngest branch, coined for the modern economy in the sense “to bring to market, commercialize,” beside ~comercio~, ~comerciar~, and ~comercialización~.
en.cometer:
From Latin ~committere~ (“to bring together, join; to entrust; to commit”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, let go, release”). ~mittere~ most likely goes back to Proto-Italic *~meitō~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, remove”), itself an extension of *~mey-~ (“to change, exchange”) — the same root that gives Latin ~mūtāre~ (“to change”) and ~commūnis~ (“common”), and, through Germanic, English ~mad~ (“insane,” originally “changed for the worse”). Spanish inherited ~cometer~ in a somewhat worn shape (Old Spanish also had ~cometre~), while keeping many learned relatives. Romance cognates of the compound include French ~commettre~ and Italian ~commettere~.

The semantic path is memorable. ~committere~ first meant “to join, bring together” — Romans used it for “to join battle,” to commit troops to the fight — and from “to put together, engage in” it slid to “to bring about, perpetrate.” Spanish ~cometer~ inherited that darker end: one “commits” an error, a crime, or a sin. The noun ~cometido~ means “a task, assignment” — what one has been entrusted with. Around it stand a crowd of ~mittere~-derived words: ~comisión~ and ~comité~ (both, through French, from the same ~committere~), ~comprometer~ (“to compromise, commit”) and ~compromiso~ (“commitment, obligation”). English ~commit~, ~committee~, and ~commission~ are the same verb’s English harvest.
en.comparar:
From Latin ~comparāre~ (“to couple, match, place side by side”), a verb built on ~compar~ (“equal, a match”), itself ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~par~ (“equal, a pair”). The comparison sense thus rests on the idea of setting equals together. Cognate with Italian ~comparare~, French ~comparer~, and Portuguese ~comparar~, and with English ~compare~ and ~pair~.

Latin ~comparāre~ carried a broad range — to pair, to furnish, to procure — and Spanish drew two different verbs from it. The ordinary inherited outcome was ~comprar~ (“to buy,” from the sense “to procure, get together”), while ~comparar~ (“to compare”) was reborrowed later as a learned form closer to the Latin spelling; the two are doublets from one source. From the same root ~par~ Spanish keeps ~pareja~ (“couple, partner”) and ~impar~ (“odd, unequal”), and the family branches into ~comparación~ and ~comparativo~.
en.compartir:
A prefixed compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~partir~ (“to divide, to split”), which comes from Latin ~partīre~ (also deponent ~partīrī~, “to divide, to share out”), from the noun ~pars~, ~partis~ (“part, portion”). ~pars~ descends from Proto-Italic *~partis~; its deeper Proto-Indo-European root is disputed, usually tied to *~per-~ in a sense of apportioning and to the root behind Latin ~pariō~ (“to bring forth”), but no single reconstruction has won out. Compare Italian ~compartire~ and Portuguese ~compartir~, alongside English ~part~ and ~portion~.

Latin ~partīre~ meant to cut a whole into shares; Spanish kept that (“to divide”) but also, through the idea of separating oneself from a place, developed the everyday ~partir~ “to set off, to depart” — the same journey French ~partir~ (“to leave”) completed. Prefixed with ~com-~, the verb means to divide something in common, and so “to share.” The teeming ~pars~ family in Spanish includes ~parte~, ~partido~, ~partícula~, ~partida~, ~repartir~, ~impartir~, and ~apartar~.
en.compensar:
From Latin ~compēnsāre~ (“to weigh against, to balance, to offset”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together, mutually”) and ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh carefully, to ponder”), the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to hang”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull, to stretch, to spin”). It is cognate with English ~compensate~ and ~pension~ and, through the root, with ~pendant~ and ~ponder~.

The metaphor is the balance-scale again: to ~compensar~ is to add weight to the lighter pan until the two even out — to offset a loss, to make up for a wrong. The delightful twist is in the parent verb ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh”), which Spanish inherited twice: once as ~pesar~ (“to weigh”), keeping the literal scales, and once as ~pensar~ (“to think”), because to think is to weigh ideas against one another. So ~compensar~, ~pesar~, and ~pensar~ are all siblings. From the same ~pendere~/~pēnsāre~ stock Spanish also holds ~pensión~, ~peso~, ~dispensar~, ~suspender~, and ~pendiente~ (“pending; a pendant; a slope”).
en.competir:
From Latin ~competere~, originally “to come together, to meet,” and hence “to be fit for, to be suitable,” a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~petere~ (“to seek, aim at, strive toward”). ~Petere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~peth₂-~ (“to fly, rush at”), which makes ~competir~ a distant cousin of English ~feather~ and Greek ~pterón~ (“wing”), as well as of the ~petere~-derived borrowings ~petition~, ~appetite~, and ~impetus~.

Latin split ~competere~ into two currents. One, “to be fitting, to fall to someone’s lot,” gave Spanish ~competer~ (“to be someone’s responsibility or business”); the other, “to strive together for the same thing,” gave ~competir~ (“to compete”) — rivals literally seeking the same prize side by side. The two verbs are doublets, one letter apart. The noun ~competencia~ neatly preserves both threads, meaning at once “competition/rivalry” and “competence/authority,” and ~competente~ and ~competitivo~ branch off from there. From the same ~petere~ Spanish also draws ~apetito~, ~petición~, ~ímpetu~, and ~repetir~.
en.complementar:
From ~complemento~ (“complement”), from Latin ~complēmentum~ (“that which fills up, completes”), from ~complēre~ (“to fill up, complete”), which is ~com-~ (intensive) plus ~plēre~ (“to fill”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”). Through that root it is cognate with Latin ~plēnus~ (“full”), with the Latinate English ~complete~, ~plenary~, and ~plenty~, and — in the Germanic branch — with plain English ~full~.

A complement is what fills a thing out to completeness, and ~complementar~ is to supply that finishing measure. The filling-root left an unusually rich Spanish harvest, including a striking doublet: the learned ~pleno~ (“full, plenary”) beside its inherited twin ~lleno~ (“full”), both from ~plēnus~. From the verb ~complēre~ itself Spanish drew two more — ~completar~ (“to complete”) and, by a quieter road, ~cumplir~ (“to fulfill, keep a promise”) — so that finishing a task and keeping one’s word share a single Latin verb about filling something to the brim.
en.completar:
From Latin ~complētus~ (“filled up, complete”), the past participle of ~complēre~ (“to fill up, finish”), a compound of ~com-~ (intensive “thoroughly”) and ~plēre~ (“to fill”). ~plēre~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill; full”), one of the great word-families of the language. Through Latin it gives ~plēnus~ (“full”) and ~plēbs~ (“the multitude”); through Germanic the very same *~pleh₁-~ yields English ~full~ (“full”) and ~fill~ (“to fill”); and it also stands behind English ~plenty~ (“abundance”) and ~plus~. Romance built a fresh verb on the participle: Spanish ~completar~, Italian ~completare~, and — reborrowed through French — English ~complete~ all rest on ~complētus~ rather than directly on the old verb ~complēre~.

The image is of filling: to complete something is to fill it up until nothing is missing — hence ~completar~ “to complete, finish, fill in.” Spanish preserves a beautiful doublet here. Alongside the learned ~completar~ (from the participle), the very same verb ~complēre~ came down by unbroken popular speech as ~cumplir~ — “to fulfill, carry out, keep (a promise); to turn (a given age); to come due.” Learned and inherited, ~completar~ and ~cumplir~ are two Spanish reflexes of one Latin verb, worn to different shapes by different histories. The wider family fills a page: ~completo~ (“complete, full”), ~complemento~, ~cumplido~ (“courteous; a compliment”), ~cumplimiento~, and — straight from ~plēnus~ — the everyday ~lleno~ (“full”), plus ~llenar~ (“to fill”).
en.complicar:
From Latin ~complicāre~ (“to fold together, roll up”), from ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to fold, to plait”). Cognate with Italian ~complicare~, French ~compliquer~, and Portuguese ~complicar~, and with English ~complicate~; through the same root it is kin to English ~ply~ and ~pleat~ and to German ~flechten~ (“to braid”).

The image is concrete: to complicate a thing was to fold it over on itself until its parts no longer lay flat and separable — the opposite of ~explicar~ (“to explain,” literally “to unfold”). Spanish preserves the whole folding family from ~plicāre~: ~plegar~ (“to fold”), ~desplegar~ (“to unfold, deploy”), ~aplicar~ (“to apply, fold onto”), and the adjective ~complejo~ (“complex, folded-together”). Even ~emplear~ (“to employ”) belongs here, through Latin ~implicāre~ (“to enfold, involve”).
en.componer:
From Latin ~compōnere~ (“to put together, arrange”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, place, set down”). ~pōnere~ itself was ~po-~ (a reduced form of *~apo~, “off, away”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, leave, allow”), so its literal image was “to set down and leave.” ~compōnere~ gave Italian ~comporre~, Portuguese ~compor~, and — reinforced by French — English ~compose~ and ~component~.

In Spanish ~componer~ kept “to compose” and “to put together,” but also became the everyday word for “to fix, to mend” — to put the broken pieces back in order — and the reflexive ~componérselas~ means “to manage, to get by.” A tidy false friend lurks here: the ~-pose~ of English ~compose~, ~propose~, and ~impose~ does not in fact descend from ~pōnere~ but from Latin ~pausāre~ (“to rest, pause”) by way of French ~poser~ — the two families simply merged in meaning. From ~pōnere~ Spanish drew a great crowd of verbs: ~poner~, ~disponer~, ~exponer~, ~imponer~, ~proponer~, and ~suponer~, plus ~componente~, ~compuesto~, and ~composición~.
en.comportar:
From Latin ~comportāre~ (“to carry together, collect”), from ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~portāre~ (“to carry”), from Proto-Italic *~portāō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to pass through, go forth”). Cognate with Italian ~comportare~, Portuguese ~comportar~, and French ~comporter~, and — through the same verb — with English ~comport~. The root *~per-~ also underlies Latin ~portus~ (“harbor”) and ~porta~ (“gate”).

The Latin verb meant to haul things together. Spanish keeps a faint sense of “to carry along, entail” (una decisión que comporta riesgos), but the verb lives mostly as a reflexive: to ~comportarse~ is literally to “carry oneself” in a given way, so a child who ~se comporta~ bien is, etymologically, one who carries himself well. From the same ~portāre~ Spanish drew a wide family — ~portar~, ~puerto~, ~portal~, ~portátil~, ~importar~, ~exportar~ — and the noun ~comportamiento~ (“behavior”).
en.comprar:
Spanish ~comprar~ descends from Latin ~comparāre~ (“to procure, prepare, get”), through a Vulgar Latin variant *~comperāre~. This ~comparāre~ is ~com-~ (“together, wholly”) plus ~parāre~ (“to prepare, procure, furnish”), which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to grant, allot”) — the root also behind Latin ~pariō~ (“to bring forth”) and Sanskrit ~pṛṇā́ti~ (“he grants”). The Romance family is unanimous: Portuguese and Catalan ~comprar~, Italian ~comprare~, Romanian ~cumpăra~.

Here lies a genuine trap. Latin had two verbs spelled ~comparāre~: one from ~parāre~ (“to procure”), which became ~comprar~ (“to buy”); the other from ~pār~ (“equal”), meaning “to pair, to match, to compare,” which Spanish later re-borrowed intact as ~comparar~ (“to compare”). The everyday “buy” and the bookish “compare” are thus look-alikes from different Latin bases, not one word split in two. From ~parāre~ Spanish also draws ~preparar~, ~reparar~, ~separar~, ~parar~ (“to stop”), ~aparato~, and the agent noun ~comprador~ (“buyer”); the plain noun ~compra~ (“purchase”) rounds out the set.
en.comprender:
From Latin ~comprehendere~ (also ~comprendere~), “to grasp, seize, take in together”, a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~prehendere~ (“to seize, grasp”). ~prehendere~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰed-~ (“to seize, take”), which — surprisingly — makes it cognate with English ~get~ and with Ancient Greek ~χανδάνω~ (khandánō, “to hold, contain”).

The metaphor is the familiar one that turns holding into knowing: to seize a thing bodily became to “grasp” it mentally, and Spanish ~comprender~ means “to understand” as well as “to comprise”. The verb ~prehendere~ was extraordinarily fertile in Spanish: ~prender~ (“to seize, to catch fire”), ~aprender~ (“to learn”, literally to grasp), ~emprender~ and ~sorprender~, plus ~preso~ and ~prisión~ from the same root. English harvested ~comprehend~, ~apprehend~, ~comprehensive~ and, through Old French, ~prison~ — all ways of taking hold, like the humble cognate ~get~.
en.comprobar:
From Latin ~comprobāre~ (“to approve fully, to confirm, to prove”), from ~com-~ (“together, thoroughly”) + ~probāre~ (“to test, to prove, to approve”), from ~probus~ (“good, upright, honest”). ~probus~ derives from Proto-Indo-European *~pro-~ (“forward”) + *~bʰuH-~ (“to be, to grow”) — literally “growing well, turning out well.” Cognate with Italian ~comprovare~ and Portuguese ~comprovar~, and — through ~probāre~ — with English ~prove~, ~probe~, and ~approve~.

At the root sits ~probus~, “good” in the deep sense of “growing forward, turning out well” — the same *~bʰuH-~ (“to be, to grow”) that underlies English ~be~ and the Spanish preterite ~fui~ (“I was”). To ~probāre~ was to test whether a thing was truly ~probus~, genuinely sound; the ~com-~ prefix adds thoroughness, so ~comprobar~ means to “check right through,” to verify. The family is large and thoroughly everyday: ~probar~ (“to try, to taste, to prove”), ~prueba~ (“proof, test”), ~aprobar~ (“to approve, to pass an exam”), ~probable~ (“probable,” literally “provable”), and ~probeta~ (“test tube”).
en.comprometer:
From Latin ~compromittere~ (“to make a mutual promise, to submit to arbitration”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~promittere~ (“to promise”), which is itself ~pro-~ (“forth”) plus ~mittere~ (“to send, to let go”). Spanish ~comprometer~ thus rests on the image of sending forth a word together. It is cognate with English ~commit~ and ~compromise~, Italian ~compromettere~ and Portuguese ~comprometer~.

In Roman law ~compromittere~ meant that two parties jointly promised to abide by an arbiter’s ruling, and that double edge survives: ~comprometer~ can mean to commit or pledge oneself, but also to compromise in the sense of endangering or implicating — to leave someone exposed. The reflexive ~comprometerse~ is the ordinary verb for getting engaged to marry. From ~mittere~ Spanish draws a huge family, among them ~meter~, ~prometer~, ~someter~, ~admitir~, ~misión~ and ~mensaje~.
en.comulgar:
From Latin ~commūnicāre~ (“to share, to communicate”), from ~commūnis~ (“common, shared”), from Old Latin ~commoinis~, from Proto-Italic *~kommoinis~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱom-moy-ni-s~, built on the root *~mey-~ (“to change, to exchange”). Through that root it is cognate with Latin ~mūnus~ (“duty, gift”) and, by way of Proto-Germanic *~gamainiz~, with English ~common~ and ~mean~ (in the sense “held in common”).

~comulgar~ is the inherited, popular doublet of the learned ~comunicar~: both descend from ~commūnicāre~, but the church word travelled the worn road of everyday speech, where the shift of /n/ to /l/ is irregular — the expected outcome would have been *~comungar~. Its meaning narrowed from the general “to share” to the specifically religious “to receive Communion,” to partake of the shared body of Christ; figuratively, to ~comulgar~ con una idea is to be in deep agreement with it. From the same ~commūnis~ Spanish also drew ~común~, ~comunidad~, ~municipio~, and ~comuna~.
en.comunicar:
From Latin ~commūnicāre~ (“to share, make common, impart”), from ~commūnis~ (“common, shared”). ~commūnis~ goes back through Old Latin ~commoinis~ to Proto-Italic *~kommoinis~ and Proto-Indo-European *~ḱom-moy-ni-s~, built on the root *~mey-~ (“to change, exchange”) — the same element seen in Latin ~mūnus~ (“duty, service, gift”). Cognate with French ~communiquer~, Italian ~comunicare~ and English ~communicate~; and, through ~commūnis~, with English ~common~ and, via ~mūnus~, ~immune~ and ~municipal~.

Etymologically, to communicate is to “make common” — to put something into the shared pool, which is why the word covers passing on news, connecting rooms and receiving Communion alike. The ancient root *~mey-~ carried the idea of reciprocal exchange: a ~mūnus~ was a service or gift given with the expectation of return, and one who owed no such service was ~immūnis~, “exempt.” From this stock Spanish keeps ~común~, ~comunidad~, ~comunión~, ~municipio~, ~inmune~ and ~remunerar~, all circling the notion of shared obligation.
en.concebir:
From Latin ~concipere~ (“to take in, take together, conceive”), from ~con-~ (“together”) + ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”). Cognate with Italian ~concepire~ and French ~concevoir~, and — through Old French — with English ~conceive~ and ~concept~.

Latin ~concipere~ meant to gather up, and from “taking together” it branched two ways that Spanish still keeps in one verb: the womb ~concibe~ a child, and the mind ~concibe~ an idea — both a “taking in.” The change from ~-cipere~ to ~-cebir~ is the regular Old Spanish treatment of ~capere~ compounds, seen also in ~recibir~ (~recipere~) and ~percibir~ (~percipere~). The participle stem gave the learned nouns ~concepto~ (“concept”) and ~concepción~ (“conception”). Behind them all stands the same grasping root *~keh₂p-~ that produced ~capturar~, ~caber~, ~cazar~, and ~aceptar~.
en.conceder:
From Latin ~concēdere~ (“to yield, give way, grant”), from ~con-~ (intensive here) and ~cēdere~ (“to go, withdraw, yield”). The deeper origin of ~cēdere~ is disputed: by one account it comes from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱe-~ (“here”) plus *~sed-~ (“to sit”) — “to sit down, then go” — while another connects it to a root *~ḱyesd-~ (“to drive away”); the sources do not settle the question. Cognate with Italian ~concedere~, French ~concéder~, and Portuguese ~conceder~; English ~concede~ comes from the same Latin verb, and English ~cede~ from ~cēdere~ itself.

The image is spatial: ~concēdere~ is to step aside, to give ground — and from yielding physical space came the sense of yielding a point, then granting a favor or a right. Spanish ~conceder~ still means “to grant, concede, award,” whether a prize, a loan, or an argument. The noun ~concesión~ covers both a concession in debate and a commercial franchise. ~cēdere~ seeded one of Spanish’s most productive verb families through its prefixed compounds: ~ceder~ (“to yield”), ~acceder~ (“to agree; to access”), ~exceder~ (“to exceed”), ~preceder~ (“to precede”), ~proceder~ (“to proceed”), and ~suceder~ (“to happen; to succeed”), plus their nouns in ~-cesión~ and ~-ceso~.
en.concentrar:
