Around the plain verb ~culpar~ (“to blame”) Spanish arranged a tidy set of prefixed opposites: ~inculpar~ (“to incriminate”) against ~disculpar~ and ~exculpar~ (“to excuse, to exonerate”), while the adjective ~culpable~ names whoever bears the guilt. English ~exculpate~ echoes the very same formation.
en.cultivar:
From Medieval Latin ~cultīvāre~ (“to till, cultivate”), from Late Latin ~cultīvus~ (“cultivated”), from Latin ~cultus~, the past participle of ~colere~ (“to till, tend, inhabit, worship”), from Proto-Italic *~kʷelō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kʷelh₁-~ (“to turn, move around, dwell”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~wheel~ and Greek ~kúklos~ (“circle”) and ~télos~ (“end”). Romance kin include Italian ~coltivare~, French ~cultiver~, and Portuguese ~cultivar~.

Latin ~colere~ carried two senses at once — the farmer's “till the soil” and the worshipper's “tend a god” — so its participle ~cultus~ seeded both ~cultivar~ (agriculture) and ~culto~ (“worship; cultured”). Late Latin built the adjective ~cultīvus~ and from it the verb, which Spanish took up by the fifteenth century. The metaphor spread easily: one cultivates land, but also friendships, talents, and the mind. From the same PIE root Spanish keeps ~cultura~, ~colono~ (“settler”), ~colonia~, ~agricultura~, and ~inquilino~ (“tenant,” from Latin ~inquilīnus~).
en.cumplir:
From Latin ~complēre~ (“to fill up, complete, fulfill”), from ~com-~ (intensive) plus ~plēre~ (“to fill”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”). Medieval Spanish had ~complir~ before ~cumplir~ prevailed. It is cognate with Portuguese ~cumprir~ and, through the same Latin verb, with English ~complete~, ~comply~ and ~compliment~; the bare root surfaces in English ~full~ and ~fill~.

The sense ran from “to fill up” to “to fulfill, discharge, carry out (a duty).” Two byways are memorable. First, the phrase ~cumplir años~ (“to complete years”) produced ~cumpleaños~ (“birthday”). Second, the courtesy sense of ~complēre~ passed through Italian ~complimento~ to give both Spanish ~cumplido~ and, back in English, ~comply~ and ~compliment~ — once, to ~comply~ was simply to be gracious. From the same root Spanish keeps the popular ~lleno~ (“full,” from ~plēnus~) beside the learned ~pleno~, along with ~completo~ and ~complemento~.
en.cundir:
A rare survival from the Visigoths: Spanish ~cundir~ (“to spread, to go far, to yield abundantly”) descends from Gothic ~kundjan~ (“to propagate, to multiply”), one of the small stock of Germanic verbs that entered Ibero-Romance during Gothic rule. The Gothic word grew from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to beget, to produce”), so ~cundir~ is a distant cousin of Old English ~cynn~ and ~gecynd~ (whence English ~kin~) and of Ancient Greek ~γένος~ (génos, “race, kind”).

The original sense was reproductive — to breed, to multiply — and Spanish generalized it to any rapid spreading: rumors, panic, oil stains, and rice that ~cunde~ (“goes a long way”) in the pot. A separate ~cundir~ meaning “to season food,” heard around Salamanca, is unrelated: that one comes from Latin ~condīre~. Because ~cundir~ arrived through Germanic rather than Latin, it has almost no Spanish word-family of its own — yet through the same PIE root it is kin to the whole Latin-derived clan of ~género~, ~generar~, and ~genio~.
en.curar:
From Latin ~cūrāre~ (“to care for, attend to, look after”), from the noun ~cūra~ (“care, concern”), Old Latin ~coira~. Cognate with Italian ~curare~, French ~curer~, and Portuguese ~curar~, and with a surprising English crowd all built on ~cūra~: ~cure~, ~curate~, ~curious~, ~procure~, and — inside ~sēcūrus~ (“free from care”) — ~secure~ and ~sure~.

Latin ~cūra~ (Old Latin ~coira~) is of uncertain origin, with no secure Indo-European etymology. ~Cūrāre~ meant “to take care of” in every register, medical care included, so “to cure, heal” grew naturally out of “to care for”; the priest charged with the ~cūra~ of souls became simply the ~cura~. A nice trap for the etymologist: Spanish ~cuidar~ (“to look after”), so close in sense, is not from ~cūra~ at all but from ~cōgitāre~ (“to think”). Genuine kin of ~cūra~ include ~curación~, ~curador~, ~curioso~ (from ~cūriōsus~, “careful, inquisitive”), ~procurar~, and ~seguro~ / ~asegurar~ (from ~sēcūrus~).
en.cursar:
From Latin ~cursāre~ (“to run to and fro”), the frequentative of ~currere~ (“to run”), whose past participle is ~cursus~; from Proto-Italic *~korzō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). Through that root English ~car~ is a distant cognate (via Latin ~carrus~, a Gaulish loan), as is Welsh ~car~; French ~courir~ and Italian ~correre~ continue ~currere~ directly.

The noun ~cursus~ meant “a running, a course, a route,” and it is the running that survives in ~cursar~: to “cursar” a subject is to travel its course of study, to take the class. The same verb also means “to be under way” — an illness that ~cursa~ with fever runs its course — and, in officialese, “to dispatch” a document, sending it on its way. From *~ḱers-~ Spanish keeps a crowded family: ~correr~, ~curso~, ~carrera~ (“race; career”), ~corriente~, ~ocurrir~, ~discurso~, ~concurso~, ~socorro~ (“help,” literally a running-to-aid), and ~carro~.
en.danzar:
From Old French ~dancier~ (“to dance”), which passed into Spanish as ~danzar~ and into English as ~dance~; Italian ~danzare~ and Portuguese ~dançar~ share the same Romance source, a Vulgar Latin *~dantiāre~. Where that verb itself came from is genuinely uncertain: a Frankish (Germanic) origin has often been proposed — some cite a form like *~dintjan~ (“to move to and fro”) — but the reconstruction is disputed and the sources leave it open, so it is safest to call ~dantiāre~ simply of unknown origin.

Whatever its root, the word spread across medieval Europe as the name for the new courtly step-dances, gradually displacing older native terms in several languages. In Spanish the base verb anchors a small family: the noun ~danza~ (“dance,” often the formal or ritual kind), the performer ~danzante~ or ~danzarín~, and the couple-figure ~contradanza~, a Romance reshaping of the English country dance.
en.dar:
Spanish ~dar~ descends straight from Latin ~dare~ (“to give”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”) — one of the most stable meanings in the whole family. The same root shines through Latin ~dōnum~ (“gift”), Greek ~dídōmi~ (“I give”), and Sanskrit ~dádāti~. Italian ~dare~ and Portuguese ~dar~ kept the plain verb, but French abandoned it for ~donner~ (from ~dōnāre~, “to make a gift”), leaving Spanish among the languages that still simply “give” with ~dare~.

For so short a verb, ~dar~ carries an enormous idiomatic load in Spanish, while its root branches out into a whole family of giving. The language has ~dádiva~ (“gift”), ~don~ (“gift, talent”) and ~donar~ (“to donate”), and, through the Latin participle, ~dado~ (“given; a die”) and ~dato~ (“fact, datum”). Even English ~date~ and ~data~, borrowed from the same Latin participle ~datum~ (“given”), belong to this quietly generous root.
en.datar:
From the noun ~data~ plus the suffix ~-ar~. ~data~ comes from Latin ~data~, the feminine participle of ~datus~, from ~dare~ (“to give”), from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). The root is cognate with Ancient Greek ~δίδωμι~ (“I give”) and Sanskrit ~dádāti~ (“gives”), and underlies the English borrowings ~donate~ and ~date~ itself.

The noun preserves a scribal habit: Roman and medieval letters were closed with the formula ~data~ — “given (at Rome, on such a day)” — where ~data~ agrees with an understood ~epistula~ (“letter”). That first word of the dating clause became the Romance noun for a calendar date, and ~datar~ the verb “to assign a date to.” Spanish keeps a rich cluster from ~dare~: the everyday ~dar~, the noun ~dato~ (“a datum,” plural ~datos~, “data”), ~dádiva~ (“a gift”) and ~don~ (“a gift, a talent”). Tellingly, the common Spanish word for “date,” ~fecha~, comes not from “given” but from ~facta~ (“done”) — a parallel idiom in the same clause.
en.dañar:
From Latin ~damnāre~ (“to condemn, to fine, to inflict loss on”), from the noun ~damnum~ (“loss, damage, a penalty”), from Proto-Italic *~dapno-~ and Proto-Indo-European *~dh₂pnom~ (“expense, what is paid out”). Most etymologists tie this to the root *~deh₂p-~ and to Latin ~daps~ (“a sacrificial feast”), the shared idea being ritual expenditure — a loss given up — though the exact PIE reconstruction is debated. Cognate, through Old French, with English ~damn~ and ~damage~, and with the learned ~condemn~ and ~indemnity~.

Latin ~damnum~ was first the legal “loss” or “fine” a court imposed, and ~damnāre~ meant to sentence someone to such a loss. Popular Spanish narrowed the verb to plain physical harm — to ~dañar~ is to injure or spoil — while the courtroom sense went to the learned doublet ~condenar~ (“to condemn”). From the noun come ~daño~ (“harm, damage”) and ~dañino~ (“harmful”), and the loss-averting ~indemne~ (“unharmed”) — one who has been kept free of ~damnum~.
en.debatir:
From Old French ~debatre~ (“to fight, contend”), which joins ~de-~ (“down, completely”) to ~batre~ (“to beat”), from Latin ~battuere~ (“to beat, strike”). The deeper origin of ~battuere~ is genuinely disputed: rare in literary Latin yet common in speech, it is often taken as a loan from Gaulish (compare Welsh ~bathu~, “to beat, coin money”) and traced to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰedʰh₂-~ (“to stab, dig”), while other scholars judge it simply onomatopoeic — the sources do not settle it. Spanish ~debatir~ is cognate with French ~débattre~ and English ~debate~, ~battle~ and ~batter~.

The sense moved from literal blows to verbal ones: “to beat down” an opponent became “to argue, contend, discuss.” The ~battuere~ family is large in Spanish: ~batir~ (“to beat”), ~combatir~, ~abatir~, ~batalla~ and ~batería~. The memorable thread is that a debate is etymologically a fight — parties still “trade blows” and “hammer out” a question — and the very same root supplies the ~batería~ that powers a phone, named from the notion of guns “beating” a target. The pen may be mightier than the sword, but ~debatir~ never forgot the sword.
en.deber:
Spanish ~deber~ comes from Latin ~dēbēre~ (“to owe”), which began as a contraction of ~dē-~ (“from, away”) plus ~habēre~ (“to have”): to owe was “to have something from someone else,” held but not truly one's own. So ~deber~ is, at root, a compound of ~haber~. Its Romance siblings share it: French ~devoir~, Italian ~dovere~, Portuguese ~dever~. English ~debt~ and ~due~ come from the same Latin verb, borrowed through French, so they are cousins rather than natives.

From “owe,” ~deber~ grew a second, modal life: to owe an action is to be obliged to do it, so ~deber~ came to mean “must, ought” — ~debo irme~ (“I must go”). The noun ~deber~ means “duty,” and ~deberes~ are a schoolchild's “homework,” obligations owed. The financial thread survives in ~débito~ (“debit”), ~deuda~ (“debt”), and ~debido~ (“due, owed”) — the whole family circling the idea of something held that must be given back.
en.debilitar:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~dēbilitāre~ (“to weaken, cripple”), from ~dēbilis~ (“weak, feeble, crippled”), from ~dē-~ (“un-, away”) + a root *~bel-~ (“strength”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bel-~ (variant *~bol-~, “strong”). Cognate — through that root — with Sanskrit ~bala~ (“strength”), Ancient Greek ~beltíōn~ (“better”), and Russian ~bolshoi~ (“big”). Spanish ~débil~ (“weak”) sits at its heart.

The paradox sits in the word: ~dēbilis~ joins ~dē-~ (“away from”) to a root meaning “strength,” so “weak” is literally “un-strong,” vigor taken away. The everyday ~débil~ is the learned adjective, ~debilitar~ the learned verb, ~debilidad~ the noun. By one account the same “strong” root surfaces far afield in Russian ~bolshoi~ (“big, grand”) and ~bolshevik~ (“one of the majority”) — but these Slavic ties are a cross-family cognate claim offered by the reconstruction pages, not settled Spanish scholarship. Homegrown kin stay close: ~débil~, ~debilidad~, ~debilitamiento~.
en.debutar:
A late borrowing from French ~débuter~ (“to make one’s first appearance”), which entered Spanish in the 19th–20th centuries and was long frowned on as a Gallicism. ~débuter~ was formed from ~but~ (“target, goal”); the ~but~ was the mark aimed at in games of bowls, so ~débuter~ first meant to make the opening throw. The origin of French ~but~ is disputed — traced to a Germanic source, whether Frankish *~būt~ (“stump, log”) or Old Norse ~bútr~ (“log, butt”).

From “to make the first move” the sense broadened to any first public appearance — an actor’s, a player’s, a singer’s. Spanish borrowed the whole family together: the noun ~debut~ (“debut”), ~debutar~ and ~debutante~. The English ~debut~ comes from the same French word.
en.decaer:
A prefixed compound of ~caer~ (“to fall”): Spanish ~decaer~ continues a Vulgar Latin *~decadere~, the intensive prefix ~de-~ added to Latin ~cadere~ (“to fall”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱad-~ (“to fall”). The Romance reflexes run parallel — Italian ~decadere~, French ~déchoir~ — and through Latin ~cadere~ the family reaches English ~decay~ and ~decadence~ as well as ~cadence~, ~cadaver~, and even ~chance~ (“a falling of the dice”).

The metaphor of falling drives the whole sense: to ~decaer~ is to fall away — to lose strength, health, prestige, or spirits. Old Spanish used it for the literal decline of the day and of dynasties alike, and the noun ~decadencia~ became the standard word for cultural or moral decline. The base ~caer~ anchors a large family: the noun ~caída~ (“a fall”), ~recaer~ (“to relapse”), ~ocaso~ (“sunset, decline,” from the sun’s fall), and ~accidente~, literally “a befalling.”
en.decidir:
From Latin ~dēcīdere~ (“to cut off, to determine”), from ~dē-~ (“off, away”) plus ~caedere~ (“to cut, to strike down”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kh₂eyd-~ (“to strike, to cut”). Cognate with French ~décider~, Italian ~decidere~, and English ~decide~ and ~decision~.

The metaphor is a blade: to decide is to cut off deliberation, severing every alternative but the chosen one — the mental equivalent of slicing through a knot. ~caedere~ was a violent, physical verb, and it left a bloody trail across Latin: it is the ~-cide~ of ~homicida~ (“murderer”) and ~suicidio~, literally acts of cutting down. Gentler siblings survive in Spanish too: from ~praecīdere~ (“to cut in front”) came ~preciso~ and ~precisar~ (“precise,” cut to exact measure), and from ~concīdere~ came ~conciso~ (“concise,” cut short). Every ~decisión~, then, is a small cut.
en.decir:
Spanish ~decir~ comes, through Old Spanish ~dezir~, from Latin ~dīcere~ (“to say, to tell”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”) — saying imagined first as pointing something out. That root of showing gave, on the Germanic side, English ~teach~ and ~token~, and in Greek ~deíknymi~ (“I show”). The Romance reflexes stayed close: Italian ~dire~, French ~dire~, Portuguese ~dizer~.

The step from “point out” to “speak” is the whole story of the word, and the pointing sense lingers in its relatives. Spanish keeps the past participle ~dicho~ (“said; a saying”) and builds ~contradecir~ (“to contradict”) and ~bendecir~ (“to bless,” literally “to say well”). From the same root come ~dictar~ (“to dictate”) and ~dictado~, the legal ~edicto~ (“edict”), and ~índice~ (“index, forefinger”) — the very finger that points.
en.declarar:
From Latin ~dēclārāre~ (“to make clear, reveal, announce”), formed from an intensive ~dē-~ and ~clārāre~ (“to make clear, brighten”), a verb from the adjective ~clārus~ (“clear, bright, loud”). ~Clārus~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~kelh₁-~ (“to shout, call out”), by way of *~kl̥h₁rós~ (“loud”). Spanish ~declarar~ is cognate with Italian ~dichiarare~, French ~déclarer~, Portuguese ~declarar~ and English ~declare~ and ~clear~; through *~kelh₁-~ it is kin to Latin ~clāmāre~ (“to shout”) and even to German ~hell~ (“bright”).

Here is the memorable twist: ~clārus~ began as a word for sound, “loud, ringing,” and only later crossed over to light and sight, “bright, clear” — the ancient mind treating the spreading of a shout and the spreading of light as one image. ~Dēclārāre~ rode that shift, moving from making a thing audibly plain to making it visibly clear, and finally to the modern “to declare,” to state openly. From ~clārus~ Spanish drew ~claro~ (“clear”), ~aclarar~ (“to clarify”), ~clarear~, ~claridad~ and ~clarín~ (“bugle”); and from the same root *~kelh₁-~, through ~clāmāre~, came ~clamar~ and the everyday ~llamar~ (“to call”).
en.decorar:
From Latin ~decorāre~ (“to adorn, embellish”), from ~decus~, ~decoris~ (“ornament, grace, honor”), related to ~decēre~ (“to be fitting, become”), from Proto-Indo-European *~deḱ-~ (“to take, accept; be fitting”). Cognate through that root with English ~decent~ and ~decorum~, and — more distantly — with ~dignity~ (from ~dignus~) and the ~docēre~ family (~doctor~, ~doctrine~).

The core idea of *~deḱ-~ is fittingness — what is accepted as becoming or graceful — so ~decus~ was “that which becomes one,” an ornament or honor, and ~decorāre~ was to add such grace. Spanish keeps ~decoración~, ~decorado~ (“stage set”), ~decoro~ (“decorum, propriety”), and ~decente~. A curious footnote: the Spanish ~decorar~ that means “to learn by heart” is a different word, from the phrase ~de coro~ (“by heart”) built on Latin ~cor~ (“heart,” once thought the seat of memory) — an accidental twin of the ornamental ~decorar~, not a descendant of ~decus~.
en.decretar:
From the noun ~decreto~ (“decree”), a learned borrowing of Latin ~decrētum~ (“a decision, a decree”), the neuter past participle of ~decernere~ (“to decide, settle, resolve”). The verb resolves into ~de-~ (“off, apart”) plus ~cernere~ (“to sift, separate, distinguish”), from Proto-Indo-European *~krey-~ (“to sift, separate”). Along that root ~decretar~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~krī́nō~ (“to separate, judge”), the source of ~crisis~ and ~criticism~; the Latin verb itself passed into Romance as French ~décréter~, Italian ~decretare~, and English ~decree~.

The picture behind ~decretar~ is judicial: to decree was to separate truth from falsehood, sifting a dispute down to a settled ruling — a ~decreto~ is, quite literally, something “sifted out.” Latin ranged the verb beside its relatives ~discernere~ (“to discern”), ~secernere~ (“to set apart,” the root of “secret”), and ~concernere~ (“to concern”). Modern Spanish preserves the whole clan: ~decreto~, ~discernir~, ~cerner~ (“to sift”), and even ~crimen~ (originally a “sifting,” a judicial charge) and ~crítica~ all lead back to the same Indo-European idea of separating in order to decide.
en.dedicar:
From Latin ~dedicāre~ (“to consecrate, to dedicate, to proclaim”), from ~de-~ (“completely, down”) + ~dicāre~ (“to proclaim solemnly, to consecrate”). ~dicāre~ is a first-conjugation relative of ~dīcere~ (“to say”), and both go back to Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”). That root surfaces in Ancient Greek ~deíknumi~ (“I show”), German ~zeigen~ (“to show”), and English ~teach~ and ~token~. Spanish took the learned ~dedicar~ from Latin. Cognate with Italian ~dedicare~, French ~dédier~, and Portuguese ~dedicar~.

The root idea is pointing: to ~dicāre~ was to point something out with words, to proclaim it — and to ~dedicāre~ was to point it out entirely, to set it apart by solemn declaration, as a temple was dedicated to a god. Modern ~dedicar~ keeps that sense of setting time or effort apart for a purpose. The pointing root *~deyḱ-~ is astonishingly productive in Spanish: ~decir~, ~índice~ (“the pointing finger”), ~dedo~ (“finger”), ~juez~ and ~juzgar~ (“to point out the law,” ~ius~ + ~dicere~), ~predecir~, and ~dictar~.
en.deducir:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~dēdūcere~ (“to lead down, to lead away, to derive”), a compound of ~dē-~ (“down, from”) and ~dūcere~ (“to lead, to draw”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to lead, to draw”). The same ~dūcere~ gave Spanish the productive ~-ducir~ family, and the root is cognate with English ~duke~, ~duct~, and ~educate~, and with German ~ziehen~ (“to pull, to draw”).

Latin ~dēdūcere~ literally “led down” — a general could march troops down from the hills, a writer could derive one point from another. Roman logicians borrowed the physical verb for the movement of thought, leading a conclusion down from its premises, and that is the sense Spanish ~deducir~ inherited: to infer, to conclude — and, by a second thread, to subtract (to “lead away” an amount). Because it entered Spanish through the learned channel rather than by ordinary speech, ~deducir~ kept its Latin shape almost untouched. Alongside it stands the whole ~dūcere~ clan: ~conducir~, ~producir~, ~reducir~, ~traducir~, ~inducir~, and ~seducir~, plus nouns like ~ducto~ and ~acueducto~.
en.defender:
From Latin ~dēfendere~ (“to ward off, protect”), from ~dē-~ (“away, off”) and a bound root ~-fendere~ (“to strike, push”), from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷʰen-~ (“to strike, kill”). The same root gave ~offendere~ (“to strike against”). Cognate with Italian ~difendere~, French ~défendre~, and — as borrowings — English ~defend~, ~fend~, and ~offend~.

Curiously, ~-fendere~ never stood on its own in Latin: no simple verb “to strike” is attested, only the compounds ~dēfendere~ (to strike the enemy away) and ~offendere~ (to strike against — hence to give offense). French pushed ~défendre~ in a legal direction, so it means both to defend and to forbid, while Spanish ~defender~ held to protection. Descendants in Spanish include ~defensa~ (“defense”), ~defensor~ (“defender”), ~ofender~ (“to offend”), and ~ofensa~ (“offense”).
en.definir:
From Latin ~dēfīnīre~ (“to set bounds to, limit, define”), formed from the prefix ~dē-~ (“off, completely”) and ~fīnīre~ (“to limit, bring to an end”), itself built on the noun ~fīnis~ (“boundary, border, end”). The deeper origin of ~fīnis~ is uncertain: one proposal links it to ~fīgere~ (“to fix, fasten, drive in”), as if a boundary were a stake fixed in the ground, but that connection is disputed and far from secure. Spanish ~definir~ is a learned borrowing, cognate with Italian ~definire~, French ~définir~ and Portuguese ~definir~; and because ~fīnīre~ passed through Old French, English ~finish~ belongs to the same family.

In Latin ~dēfīnīre~ meant to mark out the limits of a thing, whether a field or an idea; from drawing those edges came the abstract sense of saying precisely what something is — the modern “to define.” The noun ~fīnis~ was extraordinarily productive in Spanish, yielding the everyday ~fin~ (“end”), together with ~final~, ~finalizar~, ~confín~, ~finito~, ~infinito~ and, of course, ~definición~. The legal ~finiquito~ (“final settlement”) and the verb ~afinar~ (“to tune, refine”) descend from the same source, all preserving the core idea of bringing something to its edge or its end.
en.degollar:
From Latin ~dēcollāre~ (“to behead”), a transparent compound of the prefix ~dē-~ (“off, away”) and ~collum~ (“neck”) — literally “to take off at the neck.” ~collum~ is traditionally linked to a Proto-Indo-European root *~kʷel-~ (“to turn”), the neck imagined as the pivot on which the head turns, though that connection is not certain. The Latin verb is the source of Portuguese ~degolar~ and of the rare English ~decollate~ (“to behead”), while ~collum~ itself lives on in English ~collar~ and French ~col~.

Spanish ~degollar~ kept the grim precision of the Latin — it means specifically to cut the throat or sever the head, not merely to kill. The neck-noun ~collum~ became Spanish ~cuello~ (“neck”) and, through a diminutive, ~collar~ (“necklace, collar”); the act itself yields the noun ~degüello~ (“slaughter, throat-cutting”), famously the bugle call meaning “no quarter.” The related ~collado~ (“hill, a saddle between peaks”) preserves the older geographic sense of a “neck” of land.
en.dejar:
From Old Spanish ~dexar~ (also ~lexar~), from Latin ~laxāre~ (“to loosen, slacken, let go”), the denominative verb of ~laxus~ (“loose, slack”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)leg-~ (“to be slack”). Cognate with Portuguese ~deixar~, French ~laisser~, and Italian ~lasciare~, all of which kept the original ~l-~; through the same Latin verb English acquired ~relax~, ~release~, and ~lease~, and through the same PIE root the native English ~slack~.

Latin ~laxāre~ first meant to slacken a rope or relax the limbs; in Ibero-Romance the sense drifted to “let go,” then “leave behind, allow.” The startling feature of the Spanish form is its initial ~d-~: by one commonly cited account, the expected ~l-~ shifted to ~d-~ under the pull of ~dar~ (“to give”), a neighbor in both meaning and grammar — a swap that sets ~dejar~ apart from its ~l-~-keeping cousins. First documented around 1140, it later spread from “leave” into “stop” and “let.” The same Latin verb seeded the learned Spanish ~laxo~, ~laxante~, and ~relajar~ (a bookish doublet of ~dejar~), plus ~dejadez~ (“lassitude, neglect”).
en.deleitar:
From Old Occitan ~deleitar~ — a borrowing rather than a direct inheritance — which ultimately goes back to Latin ~dēlectāre~ (“to charm, to please”), the frequentative of ~dēlicere~ (“to allure, to entice”), itself from ~dē-~ plus ~lacere~ (“to lure, to ensnare”). Cognates include French ~délecter~, Italian ~dilettare~, and Portuguese ~deleitar~; through the same Latin verb, English ~delight~ is a distant relative.

The telltale diphthong -ei- betrays the Occitan route: Spanish took the word from the medieval troubadour world rather than inheriting it directly, which would have produced a quite different form. Its meaning has stayed close to the Latin sense of intense pleasure or charm. From the same family come the noun ~deleite~ (“delight”), ~deleitoso~, and ~deleitable~, while the closely related Latin ~dēliciae~ (“delights”) gave Spanish ~delicia~ and ~delicioso~.
en.demandar:
From Latin ~dēmandāre~ (“to entrust, to commit to one's charge”), from ~dē-~ (here intensive) plus ~mandāre~ (“to order, to entrust”). ~mandāre~ is traditionally analyzed as ~manus~ (“hand”) plus ~dare~ (“to give”) — literally “to give into someone's hand” — from Proto-Indo-European *~man-~ (“hand”) and *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Cognate with French ~demander~, Italian ~domandare~ and Portuguese ~demandar~; English ~demand~ arrived through Old French.

Latin ~dēmandāre~ meant “to entrust, to put in another's charge.” Across Romance the sense slid toward simple asking — French ~demander~ still means merely “to ask” — but Spanish ~demandar~ kept a firmer edge, “to demand,” and took on the courtroom sense “to sue, to file suit.” From the same ~mandāre~ come ~mandar~, ~mandato~, ~mandamiento~, ~comandar~, ~recomendar~ and ~encomendar~, while the older ~manus~ survives plainly in ~mano~. The image beneath all of them is a thing placed, quite literally, into a waiting hand.
en.demostrar:
Spanish ~demostrar~ comes from Latin ~dēmōnstrāre~ (“to point out, indicate, prove”), a compound of ~dē-~ (“fully, from”) and ~mōnstrāre~ (“to show, point out”). ~mōnstrāre~ is a denominal verb from ~mōnstrum~ — originally “a divine omen, a portent” — which in turn derives from ~monēre~ (“to warn, advise, remind”). ~monēre~ reflects Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to think”), the vast root behind Latin ~mēns~ (“mind”) and English ~mind~, ~mental~, and ~mean~. English took ~demonstrate~, ~monster~, ~monstrance~, and ~monitor~ from this branch. Italian ~dimostrare~, French ~montrer~ / ~démontrer~, and Portuguese ~demonstrar~ are the Romance parallels of ~demostrar~.

The buried surprise is ~mōnstrum~: a monster was first not a beast but a sign — something shown by the gods as a warning, from ~monēre~ (“to warn”). A ~mōnstrum~ was a portent that pointed to something, and ~mōnstrāre~ meant to point it out; ~dēmōnstrāre~ intensified this into showing thoroughly, and thence proving. Spanish split the inheritance: popular ~mostrar~ evolved by regular sound change, while learned ~demostrar~ was reborrowed closer to the Latin. From the same ~monēre~ / *~men-~ family Spanish keeps ~mostrar~, ~muestra~ (“sample, sign”), ~monstruo~, ~amonestar~ (“to admonish”), ~mente~, and ~mención~.
en.demudar:
A prefixed compound of intensive ~dē-~ plus ~mudar~ (“to change, to move”), the latter inherited from Latin ~mūtāre~ (“to change, to exchange”), from Proto-Indo-European *~mey-~ (“to change, to exchange”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~mutate~ and ~mutual~, with ~molt~ (an old reflex of ~mūtāre~), and with Italian ~mutare~ and French ~muer~.

Where plain ~mudar~ means simply “to change,” ~demudar~ specialised: in medieval and literary Spanish it describes above all a sudden change in someone’s face — the colour draining, or the features altering with emotion. The intensive prefix lends it that abrupt, visible quality. The same PIE root *~mey-~ seeded a broad family, among them ~muda~, ~mutación~, ~mutuo~, ~permutar~, and — through Latin ~commūnis~ (“shared”) — ~común~.
en.denegar:
From Latin ~dēnegāre~ (“to deny, to refuse”), a compound of intensive ~dē-~ plus ~negāre~ (“to say no, to deny”), built on the negative particle seen in ~nec~ and ~neg-~ and ultimately on the Proto-Indo-European negator *~ne~ (“not”). Cognates include Italian ~denegare~ and French ~dénier~; through ~negāre~ itself, English has ~deny~ (via Old French ~denier~), ~negate~, and ~renegade~.

Spanish inherited both the simple ~negar~ and the reinforced ~denegar~, and over time they divided the labour: ~negar~ stayed the everyday “to deny, to refuse,” while ~denegar~ narrowed to a formal, largely legal register — to reject a petition or request handed up to authority. From the same root grew ~negación~, ~negativo~, ~renegar~, ~abnegación~, and the noun ~denegación~.
en.denominar:
From Latin ~dēnōmināre~ (“to name, designate”), formed from ~de-~ (here intensive) and ~nōmināre~ (“to name”), from ~nōmen~ (“name”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁nómn̥~ (“name”). It is cognate with French ~dénommer~, Italian ~denominare~, and Portuguese ~denominar~, and with the Latin-derived English ~denominate~. Straight from *~h₁nómn̥~ come English ~name~, German ~Name~, and Greek ~ónoma~.

Latin ~nōmen~ left Spanish two lines: the patrimonial ~nombre~ (“name”) and the learned ~nominar~ and ~denominar~ (“to name, designate”). A quiet gem sits in arithmetic: the ~denominador~ of a fraction is literally what “names” its parts — in three-fifths, the fifths are the name and the count. The same family gave ~nómina~ (“payroll,” once simply a list of names), ~nomenclatura~, ~denominación~ (as in the wine label ~denominación de origen~), ~renombre~ (“renown”), and the grammatical ~pronombre~ (“pronoun”).
en.denostar:
From Old Spanish ~denostar~, from Latin ~dehonestāre~ (“to dishonour, to disgrace”), a compound of privative ~dē-~ plus ~honestāre~ (“to honour”), from ~honestus~ (“honourable”), from ~honōs~ / ~honor~ (“honour”). It is thus, in origin, a near-twin of the learned verb ~deshonrar~, which reached the same idea by a different path.

The form is a small monument to sound change: the four-syllable Latin ~dehonestāre~, “to strip of honour,” lost its medial -h- and contracted until the very word “honour” disappeared from view inside ~denostar~. Now literary and formal, it means to revile or vilify. The related noun ~denuesto~ (“insult, affront”) keeps the diphthong that the verb levelled out. From ~honor~ also descend ~honesto~, ~honestidad~, ~honrar~, ~honra~, and ~deshonra~.
en.denunciar:
From Latin ~dēnūntiāre~ (“to announce officially, give notice, proclaim, threaten”), from ~dē-~ (“down, fully”) plus ~nūntiāre~ (“to announce”), a verb built on ~nūntius~ (“messenger, message”). The origin of ~nūntius~ is uncertain: it is usually traced to Proto-Indo-European *~newH-~ (“to shout, cry”), with possible cognates in Sanskrit ~návate~ (“cries, sounds”) and Old Irish ~núall~ (“a loud cry”), while an older derivation from ~novus~ (“new”) is now rejected. Cognate with Italian ~denunciare~, French ~dénoncer~ and Portuguese ~denunciar~, and with English ~denounce~.

In Latin the word was formal and legal — to serve official notice, lodge a public declaration, even proclaim war. Spanish ~denunciar~ preserved that accusatory edge: to report a crime to the authorities or to condemn a wrong in public, a sense the noun ~denuncia~ carries in everyday legal Spanish. The ~nūntius~ family branched widely: ~anunciar~ (“to announce”), ~pronunciar~ (“to pronounce”), ~renunciar~ (“to renounce”) and ~nuncio~, the papal envoy who is, etymologically, simply a “messenger.”
en.departir:
A compound of ~dē-~ plus ~partir~ (“to divide, to split”), from Latin ~partīre~ / ~partīrī~ (“to share, to divide”), from ~pars~ (“part, share”). Cognates include French ~départir~, Italian ~dipartire~, and Portuguese ~departir~; through ~pars~, English has ~part~ and ~depart~.

The oldest meaning was concrete — “to divide, to separate,” as in dividing a kingdom. From “to divide up” it drifted to “to distinguish and discuss the parts of a matter,” and finally to “to converse,” which is the sole surviving Spanish sense, now formal and faintly archaic — used of friends passing the time in unhurried talk. English ~depart~ kept only the spatial branch of the same tree. From ~pars~ also come ~parte~, ~partición~, ~partido~, ~repartir~, and ~departamento~ (borrowed back through French).
en.depender:
From Latin ~dependēre~ (“to hang from, to hang down”), a compound of ~dē-~ (“down from”) and ~pendēre~ (“to hang, to be suspended”). ~pendēre~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull, to stretch, to spin”). The verb is thoroughly Romance — Italian ~dipendere~, French ~dépendre~, Portuguese ~depender~ — and through the same Latin root it matches English ~depend~, ~pendant~, ~pending~, and ~suspend~.

The metaphor is beautifully literal: to ~depender~ is to “hang from” something, exactly as a ~pendiente~ (“earring, pendant”) hangs from an ear. What hangs from a support is held up by it and cannot stand alone — so “hanging from” became “being contingent upon,” relying on. The same ~pendēre~ family gave Spanish ~pender~, ~pendiente~, ~suspender~, ~depender~, and ~independiente~. And here is the surprise: the frequentative ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh carefully”), from the same root, split into two Spanish verbs — ~pesar~ (“to weigh”) and ~pensar~ (“to think”) — because to weigh an idea in the mind is to think it over. So ~depender~, ~pesar~, and ~pensar~ all hang, in the end, from the same thread.
en.deportar:
From Latin ~dēportāre~ (“to carry away, to transport, to banish”), from ~dē-~ (“away”) plus ~portāre~ (“to carry”), from Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to cross over, to carry through”). Cognates include French ~déporter~, Italian ~deportare~, and Portuguese ~deportar~; through ~portāre~, English has ~port~, ~portable~, and ~transport~.

Here is the surprise: in Old French and Old Spanish the noun ~deport~ and the reflexive verb meant “amusement, pastime” — to carry oneself about for pleasure. That sense crossed the Channel into English as ~disport~, soon clipped to ~sport~. Modern Spanish later rebuilt the noun ~deporte~ on the very same root for “sport,” even as the verb ~deportar~ hardened into the grim legal sense “to banish, to deport.” The family also holds ~deportivo~, ~deportista~, ~portar~, ~portador~, and ~transportar~.
en.depositar:
From Latin ~dēpositāre~ (“to lay down, deposit”), a frequentative built on ~dēpositum~ (“something laid down, a deposit”), the neuter past participle of ~dēpōnere~ (“to put down, lay aside”), from ~dē-~ (“down, away”) + ~pōnere~ (“to put, place”), itself a contraction of ~pō-~ + ~sinere~ (“to let, set down”). Cognate with English ~deposit~ and ~depose~, Italian ~depositare~, and French ~déposer~.

The idea under ~depositar~ is entrusting something by setting it down in a safe place — which is why one word covers laying sediment, placing money in a bank, and reposing trust in a person. Latin ~dēpōnere~ was likewise the verb for laying down an office and for giving sworn testimony, a legal echo still heard in ~deposición~ (“deposition”) and ~deponer~ (“to depose, testify”). The prolific ~pōnere~ seeded a vast Spanish family: ~poner~, ~poste~, ~posición~, ~depósito~, ~componer~, ~exponer~, and ~posar~.
en.derivar:
From Latin ~dērīvāre~ (“to lead or draw off [water]”), from ~dē-~ (“from, away”) + ~rīvus~ (“brook, stream, channel”). ~rīvus~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reyH-~ (“to flow”). Cognate with Italian ~derivare~ and French ~dériver~, and — through ~rīvus~ — with English ~derive~ and ~rival~.

The literal image is hydraulic: to ~derivar~ water is to lead it away from its main channel into a side one — exactly what an irrigation engineer does. From that physical sense grew the abstract one still dominant today: one thing “flows from” another, so a word, a right, or a conclusion is ~derivado~ (“derived”) from its source. The most charming relative is ~rival~: in Latin a ~rīvālis~ was literally someone who shared the same ~rīvus~ — a neighbor drawing water from the same stream — and since people who share a water source tend to quarrel over it, the word came to mean “competitor.” Spanish kept the whole watery family: ~río~ (“river,” straight from ~rīvus~), ~riachuelo~ (“little stream”), ~derivación~ (“derivation”), and ~deriva~ (“drift,” as in a boat going adrift).
en.derramar:
Spanish ~derramar~ is built on ~dē-~ plus ~ramo~ (“branch,” from Latin ~rāmus~) plus the verb-forming ~-ar~, reflecting a Vulgar Latin *~dērāmāre~. The tie to “branch” is agreed across the sources, and the same base yielded Italian ~diramare~ (“to branch out, to ramify”), Portuguese ~derramar~, Romanian ~dărâma~, and Old French ~deramer~.

What is not transparent is the leap from ~rāmus~, “branch,” to the Spanish meanings “to spill, to pour out, to scatter.” It is usually explained as an original notion of spreading out like branches, or of lopping branches so they fall and scatter — but this should be taken as a plausible reconstruction of the semantics rather than a documented step. That Italian ~diramare~ kept the concrete “to ramify” sense makes the Spanish drift toward liquids all the more striking. From ~rāmus~ come ~rama~, ~ramo~, ~ramaje~, ~ramificar~, ~derrame~, and ~desparramar~.
en.derribar:
Spanish ~derribar~ is formed from ~dē-~ plus ~riba~ (“bank, slope”), from Latin ~rīpa~ (“bank, shore”), reflecting a Vulgar Latin *~dērīpāre~. Through ~rīpa~ it is cognate with French ~arriver~ and English ~arrive~ (originally “to reach the shore,” from ~ad~ + ~rīpa~), and — through the derivative ~rīpāria~ — with English ~river~ and French ~rivière~.

The starting image was concrete: to throw or tumble something down a bank or slope. From that came the modern “to knock down, to demolish, to topple” — a wall, a government. The bridge from “riverbank” runs through the intermediate ~riba~ (“slope”), still plain to see in ~arriba~ (“up, upward,” literally “to the bank”) and ~ribera~ (“riverside”). From ~rīpa~ also descend ~riba~, ~ribera~, ~arriba~, ~ribereño~, and ~derribo~ (“demolition”).
en.derrocar:
Spanish ~derrocar~ combines the prefix ~de-~ with the early Medieval Latin noun ~rocca~ (“boulder, crag”), the same word that, through Old French ~roche~, gave English ~rock~ and Spanish ~roca~. That base noun is of uncertain, probably pre-Roman origin, and scholars reconstruct no secure Latin or Indo-European source for it. Italian ~rocca~ (“fortress on a crag”) keeps the height-and-stone image that made the compound so vivid.

The literal picture is topographic and violent: to ~derrocar~ was to hurl someone down from a rock or cliff, an old sense glossed “to cast headlong from a height.” From that concrete image the verb broadened to “to demolish” a building and, most enduringly, “to overthrow” a ruler or government — a monarch is still ~derrocado~ as if flung bodily from a crag. Spanish words from the same ~roca~ include ~roquedo~, ~roqueño~ and ~roquero~.
en.derrotar:
Spanish ~derrotar~ (“to defeat”) belongs to the family of ~derrota~, originally “route, course,” which came through an old verb ~derromper~ (“to break through”) from Latin ~rupta~, the feminine past participle of ~rumpere~ (“to break”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *~rewp-~ (“to break, snatch”). The same ~rupta~ gave French ~route~ and, borrowed, English ~route~, ~rout~ and ~rupture~; the Italian cognate is ~rotta~.

The word ~rupta~ named a road “broken” open through obstacles, and from it ~derrota~ came to mean a ship’s or traveller’s course. The martial sense — a “defeat,” a breaking of the ranks — is late: Corominas finds no example of ~derrotar~ meaning “to defeat” before 1683 and judges it a borrowing shaped by French ~déroute~ (“rout”), from Old French ~desroter~; that Gallicism is the favored account rather than a settled fact. From the same root Spanish keeps ~romper~, ~ruptura~, ~corromper~ and the nautical ~derrotero~.
en.desafiar:
Spanish ~desafiar~ prefixes the reversative ~des-~ to Old Spanish ~afiar~, itself from ~fiar~ (“to entrust, guarantee”), which Spanish inherited from Vulgar Latin ~fīdāre~, from Latin ~fīdere~ (“to trust”) and the noun ~fidēs~ (“faith, trust”). The ultimate source is the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰeydʰ-~ (“to trust, confide”). The very same Vulgar Latin compound *~disfīdāre~ surfaces in English ~defy~, an exact structural twin.

The logic is feudal: to pledge ~fe~ was to swear loyalty, so to ~desafiar~ was to formally withdraw that pledge — to renounce the trust binding vassal to lord — and, from there, to issue a challenge or provocation. The modern noun ~desafío~ (“challenge, duel”) preserves the confrontational charge. From the same trusting root Spanish keeps ~confiar~ (“to trust”), ~fiel~ (“faithful”) and ~fe~ itself.
en.desaliñar:
Spanish ~desaliñar~ negates ~aliñar~ with the reversative prefix ~des-~. That base verb was built with the prefix ~a-~ on Latin ~līneāre~ (“to align, set in a line”), from ~līnea~ (“line, thread”), from ~līnum~ (“flax, linen”). The noun goes back to an old European culture-word for flax, reconstructed as *~līno-~, which also gave English ~line~ and ~linen~.

~aliñar~ first meant to set things in a straight line, hence to arrange or tidy and — in the kitchen — to dress or season food, whence ~aliño~, the “dressing.” To ~desaliñar~ is to undo that order: to rumple, dishevel or leave untidy, and ~desaliñado~ describes someone unkempt. The same ~līnea~ underlies Spanish ~alinear~ (“to line up”) and ~lino~ (“flax, linen”).
en.desamparar:
Spanish ~desamparar~ is the reversative ~des-~ prefixed to ~amparar~ (“to shelter, protect”), which came from Vulgar Latin *~anteparāre~, a compound of Latin ~ante~ (“before”) and ~parāre~ (“to prepare, make ready”) — literally to make ready in advance, hence to ward off and protect. ~parāre~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~perh₃-~ (“to produce, procure”).

If ~amparar~ is to place a protective shield in front of someone, ~desamparar~ is to withdraw it — to forsake, abandon, leave defenseless. The noun ~desamparo~ names that state of helpless abandonment, while ~amparo~ (also a given name) is protection or refuge, and in law the ~recurso de amparo~ is the constitutional remedy that shields fundamental rights. From the same ~parāre~ Spanish keeps ~parar~ (“to stop”), ~preparar~ and ~reparar~.
en.desaparecer:
From ~des-~ (a privative prefix, from Latin ~dis-~, “apart, reversal”) prefixed to ~aparecer~ (“to appear”), which comes from Latin ~appārēscere~, an inchoative (“to begin to be visible”) built on ~appārēre~ (“to appear, come into view”), from ~ad-~ (“to”) plus ~pārēre~ (“to come forth, be visible, obey”). The further origin of ~pārēre~ is uncertain. Cognate with Italian ~apparire~ (and ~sparire~), French ~apparaître~ (and ~disparaître~) and Portuguese ~desaparecer~, and with English ~appear~ and ~apparent~.

The ~-ēscere~ inflection is telling: ~aparecer~ is not merely “to be visible” but “to come into visibility,” an entering; ~des-~ then reverses the motion into “to pass out of sight, vanish.” The same ~pārēre~ underlies ~parecer~ (“to seem, to appear-to-be”) — appearing and seeming from one Latin verb — and feeds a wide family: ~aparición~ (“apparition”), ~aparente~ (“apparent”), ~transparente~ (“transparent”) and ~comparecer~ (“to appear in court”).
en.desarmar:
Spanish ~desarmar~ prefixes the reversative ~des-~ to ~armar~ (“to arm, assemble”), from Latin ~armāre~ (“to equip with weapons”), a verb built on ~arma~ (“arms, weapons, tools”). ~arma~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂er-~ (“to fit, join together”) — arms being the gear one fits to the body — a root shared by English ~arm~, the limb whose very name means the joined-on part.

To ~armar~ is to fit weapons or parts together, so ~desarmar~ is to take them apart again: to disarm a person, dismantle a machine, or defuse a quarrel — even to disarm someone figuratively with charm. The noun ~desarme~ is “disarmament.” From the same root Spanish keeps ~armamento~, ~armadura~ and, through the related sense of skillful fitting, ~arte~ (“art”).
en.desarrollar:
A Spanish formation from ~des-~ (a prefix of reversal) and ~arrollar~ (“to roll up”), which is ~a-~ plus ~rollo~ (“a roll, scroll”). ~rollo~ descends from Latin ~rotulus~ (“little wheel, roll”), the diminutive of ~rota~ (“wheel”), from Proto-Indo-European *~Hret-~ (“to run, to roll”). The wheel-root has far-flung cognates: German ~Rad~ (“wheel”), Sanskrit ~rátha~ (“chariot”), and Old Irish ~roth~ (“wheel”); ~rotulus~ itself gave English ~roll~ and ~role~ through French ~rôle~.

The image is vivid and exact: to develop is literally to un-roll — ~des-~ + ~arrollar~ — as one opens a rolled scroll to reveal what is written inside. Growth, in this metaphor, is a scroll unspooling. English ~develop~ carries the very same picture by a different route (Old French ~desveloper~, “to unwrap”), so the two languages independently imagine progress as undoing a wrapping. From the same wheel-root Spanish keeps ~rollo~, ~arrollar~, ~rueda~ (“wheel,” straight from ~rota~), ~rótula~ (“kneecap”), and the borrowed ~rotación~ and ~control~ (via the roll-counter of French ~contre-rôle~).
en.desatar:
Spanish ~desatar~ is ~atar~ (“to tie”) carrying the reversing prefix ~des-~ (from Latin ~dis-~). ~Atar~ descends from Latin ~aptāre~ (“to fasten, fit”), a verb built on ~aptus~ (“fitted, joined”), the participle of ~apere~ (“to attach”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ep-~ (“to grasp, reach”). The consonant cluster simplified over time: ~aptāre~ → ~attāre~ → ~atar~. Cognate with Portuguese ~atar~.

So ~desatar~ literally undoes a fastening — to untie, unleash, or, figuratively, set loose, as in ~desatar~ una tormenta (“to unleash a storm”). Through its learned doublet the same ~aptus~ gave Spanish ~apto~, ~aptitud~, ~adaptar~, and ~inepto~ (“inept,” literally “not fitted”), while ~atar~ yields ~atadura~ and ~desatar~. English, from the same root, has ~apt~, ~adapt~, and ~attitude~.
en.desayunar:
Spanish ~desayunar~ is the prefix ~des-~ on ~ayunar~ (“to fast”), from Late Latin ~ieiūnāre~, from Latin ~ieiūnus~ (“fasting, empty, hungry”). The compound answers to a Vulgar Latin *~disieiūnāre~, “to break the fast”; the same idea gave French ~déjeuner~ and Italian ~digiunare~. The Latin adjective also reached English as ~jejune~ (“dry, insipid”) and named the jejunum, the stretch of small intestine anatomists usually found empty in dissection.

Where ~ayunar~ is to abstain from food, ~desayunar~ is to break that overnight fast — the sense narrowed from any fast-breaking to the specific morning meal, just as breakfast did in English. The noun ~ayuno~ is “fasting,” and ~desayuno~ is “breakfast.” The image stays transparent: every breakfast is literally a de-fasting.
en.desbaratar:
Spanish ~desbaratar~ joins the prefix ~des-~ to ~baratar~ (“to barter, haggle, exchange”), a deverbal relative of ~barato~ (“cheap”). The origin of ~barato~ and ~baratar~ is genuinely uncertain: Corominas and the DLE treat it as a word of disputed, likely Old Castilian coinage, and no secure Latin or foreign etymon has been established — proposals exist but none is settled. A Sicilian cognate ~sbarattari~ shows the family circulated around the Mediterranean, and English ~barter~ may belong to the same uncertain group.

If ~baratar~ was to strike a cheap, tricky bargain, then ~desbaratar~ literally undoes the deal — and from there fans out to “to wreck,” “to spoil,” “to throw into disorder,” and, in military use, “to rout” an army. The image is of a scheme falling apart. Cheapness survives in modern ~barato~, in ~baratija~ (“trinket”) and in the bargain-sale sense of ~barata~.
en.descabalgar:
Spanish ~descabalgar~ prefixes the reversative ~des-~ to ~cabalgar~ (“to ride on horseback”), which Spanish inherited from Vulgar Latin *~caballicāre~, from Latin ~caballus~. In classical Latin ~caballus~ was a workhorse or nag, set against the noble ~equus~; its own origin is uncertain — often traced to a Gaulish or wider Wanderwort for “horse,” with no settled Indo-European root — yet the humble word triumphed across Romance, giving Spanish ~caballo~, French ~cheval~ and Italian ~cavallo~.

If ~cabalgar~ is to sit and travel astride a horse, then ~descabalgar~ is to come down from it — to dismount. The verb keeps the martial, equestrian flavor of the old ~caballus~ world, the same world that produced ~cabalgata~ (“cavalcade, mounted procession”), ~caballero~ (“knight, gentleman”) and ~caballería~ (“cavalry; chivalry”).
en.descabezar:
A compound of the prefix ~des-~ (from Latin ~dis-~, marking reversal or removal) and ~cabeza~ (“head”) — literally “to un-head.” Spanish ~cabeza~ comes from Vulgar Latin ~capitia~, a neuter plural of ~capitium~ reinterpreted as a feminine singular, ultimately from Latin ~caput~ (“head”), whose deeper origin is uncertain though often linked to Proto-Indo-European *~kaput-~. Portuguese ~cabeça~ and Italian ~capo~ descend the same way, and through Latin ~caput~ the head-word is a distant cousin of English ~chief~, ~captain~ and ~chapter~.

~Descabezar~ first meant plainly “to cut off someone's head,” a word of battlefield and scaffold, and then it spread into gentler figures: to « ~descabezar~ un sueño » is to snatch the first sleep of the night, and a leaderless body is left ~descabezada~. The fertile root ~caput~ seeded a broad Spanish family — ~cabo~ (“cape; end; corporal”), ~cabecera~ (“headboard, head of the table”), ~capital~, ~caudillo~ and ~cabizbajo~ (“crestfallen”).
en.descalabrar:
An old and etymologically knotty verb of debated origin. The account favored by Corominas links it to ~calavera~ (“skull”), from Latin ~calvāria~ (“skull,” originally any bald or bare thing), itself a derivative of ~calvus~ (“bald”); ~descalabrar~ would then go back to a syncopated Vulgar Latin *~descalavārāre~, roughly “to leave without a skull,” i.e. to break someone's head. The reconstruction is not without trouble — the sound-changes it demands are part of why the etymology remains uncertain. Through ~calvus~ the verb is kin to French ~chauve~ (“bald”); the deeper Indo-European root for “bald” is itself disputed.

Beside its core sense “to wound in the head,” ~descalabrar~ took on the broader figure “to harm or damage,” and the noun ~descalabro~ came to mean a setback or heavy loss — a financial ~descalabro~ is a crash, no blood required. From the same ~calvus~ Spanish keeps ~calvo~ (“bald”), ~calva~ (“bald patch”), ~calvicie~ (“baldness”) and ~calvario~ (“Calvary; ordeal”), the last from Church Latin ~Calvāria~, the Latin name for Golgotha, “the place of the skull.”
en.descansar:
Spanish ~descansar~ is ~des-~ (“un-, reversal”) prefixed to ~cansar~ (“to tire”), so it means literally to un-tire — to rest. The verb ~cansar~ is the puzzle. The standard account, argued by Corominas, derives it from Latin ~campsāre~ (“to bend, turn, to double a cape”), a nautical borrowing of Ancient Greek ~kámptein~ (“to bend, curve”). The Romance reflexes are thin outside Ibero-Romance; Portuguese shares ~cansar~ and ~descansar~.

The semantic path is the memorable part, and it is Corominas’s reconstruction rather than a documented certainty: ~campsāre~ meant to swerve from a straight course — to double a headland, to turn aside — and from “turning aside, giving up the course” it drifted to “giving up, flagging,” hence “to tire.” Prefix ~des-~ and you reverse the flagging: ~descansar~, to recover, to rest. From the same ~cansar~ Spanish built ~cansancio~ (“tiredness”), ~descanso~ (“rest, break”), ~incansable~ (“tireless”), and ~cansino~ (“weary, plodding”).
en.descargar:
A compound of the prefix ~des-~ (“un-, reversal,” from Latin ~dis-~) and ~cargar~ (“to load”), from Vulgar Latin ~carricāre~ (“to load a wagon”), a verb built on Latin ~carrus~ (“wheeled wagon, cart”). ~Carrus~ was a Gaulish loan, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). Cognate with French ~charger~, Italian ~caricare~ and Portuguese ~carregar~; through ~carrus~ it is related to English ~charge~, ~cargo~ and ~car~.

At bottom ~descargar~ means to take the load off a cart — to ~cargar~ was to pile goods onto a ~carrus~, and ~des-~ reverses it. From that concrete image the word fanned out: to unload a ship, to fire (“discharge”) a weapon, to vent one's anger, to relieve an electric ~carga~ — and, in our century, to ~descargar~ a file from the internet, so that the newest sense of the word still rides on a Roman ox-cart. The family is large in Spanish: ~carga~, ~cargo~, ~cargamento~, ~carguero~, ~descarga~, ~recargar~, ~sobrecargar~ and ~encargar~, this last meaning “to entrust,” literally to load a task onto someone.
en.descartar:
From ~des-~ (“un-, away”) + ~carta~ (“card; letter”), from Latin ~charta~ (“sheet of papyrus, paper”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~khártēs~ (“leaf of papyrus”). Parallel formations run through Romance: Italian ~scartare~, Portuguese ~descartar~, and — built on the same ~card~ — English ~discard~.

~Descartar~ began at the card table: to ~descartar~ was to throw away unwanted playing cards (~cartas~), and only later did it broaden to discarding, ruling out, or setting aside anything at all (~descartar una posibilidad~). The Greek ~khártēs~ behind it also gave, through Latin ~charta~, a large Spanish family: ~carta~ (“letter, card”), ~cartel~ (“poster”), ~cartón~ (“cardboard”), ~cartera~ (“wallet”) and ~carpeta~ (“folder”) — and, through French, English ~chart~ and ~charter~. Fittingly, the surname of the philosopher ~Descartes~ happens to read as ~des~ + ~cartes~, though it in fact derives from a place-name, not from discarding at all.
en.descender:
From Latin ~dēscendere~ (“to climb down, to go down”), from ~dē-~ (“down from”) plus ~scandere~ (“to climb”), from Proto-Indo-European *~skend-~ (“to climb, to leap”). Cognate with French ~descendre~, Italian ~scendere~ and Portuguese ~descer~, and — through the same root — with English ~ascend~ and ~scan~.

The core verb ~scandere~ meant to climb, and Latin built a matched pair on it: ~ascendere~ to climb up, ~dēscendere~ to climb down. The same root gave ~scāla~ (“ladder, staircase”), whence Spanish ~escala~ and ~escalera~. A stranger descendant is ~scan~: to “scan” a line of verse was originally to mark its metrical feet by beating them out, as if climbing step by step through the rhythm. In Spanish the family includes ~descenso~, ~descendencia~, ~descendiente~ and ~ascender~.
en.descolgar:
Formed from ~des-~ (Latin ~dis-~, “apart, un-”) and ~colgar~ (“to hang”), so “to unhang, take down.” ~Colgar~ descends from Latin ~collocāre~ (“to place, set in position”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~locāre~ (“to place”), from ~locus~ (“place”). The same ~collocāre~ gave French ~coucher~ (“to lay down, put to bed”) and, borrowed straight from Latin, English ~collocate~ and ~couch~; Spanish itself kept a learned doublet ~colocar~ (“to place”) beside the inherited ~colgar~.

The sense narrowed from Latin's neutral “to place” to Spanish “to hang,” and ~descolgar~ is its undoing — to ~descolgar~ a picture or a phone (« ~descolgar~ el teléfono », to pick up the receiver) or, reflexively, ~descolgarse~, to let oneself down a rope, drop out of a cycling pack, or « ~descolgarse~ con » an unexpected remark. From the ~locus~ family Spanish also has ~local~, ~localizar~, ~lugar~ (the inherited reflex of ~locālis~/~locus~) and ~dislocar~.
en.desconocer:
A Spanish formation: ~des-~ (a negating and reversing prefix, from Latin ~dis-~) prefixed to ~conocer~ (“to know”). ~Conocer~ descends through Old Spanish ~conoscer~ from Latin ~cognoscere~ (“to get to know”), a compound of ~com-~ (intensive) and ~gnoscere~ / ~noscere~ (“to know”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~know~ and ~can~, and with the heirs of ~cognoscere~: Italian ~conoscere~ and French ~connaître~.

The prefix ~des-~ negates, so ~desconocer~ literally means “to not know,” but Spanish sharpened it into two everyday senses: to be unaware of or unacquainted with something, and, more pointedly, to refuse to recognize — to disown a signature, a debt, or a person one no longer acknowledges. The PIE root *~ǵneh₃-~ is one of the most fertile in the language, behind ~conocer~, ~conocimiento~, ~reconocer~, ~noticia~ and the learned ~cognición~.
en.descoser:
A compound of ~des-~ (from Latin ~dis-~, reversal) and ~coser~ (“to sew”), literally “to unsew.” ~Coser~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~cōsere~, from Latin ~cōnsuere~ (“to sew together”), formed from ~com-~ (“together”) and ~suere~ (“to sew”). ~Suere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~suō~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~syuh₁-~ (“to sew”), a very old root: it also yields English ~sew~, Sanskrit ~sū́tra~ (“thread; rule”) and — through Latin ~sūtūra~ — English ~suture~.

The meaning stayed close to Latin's, and the verb thrives in its reversal and idioms: to ~descoser~ a hem is to unpick it, while « hablar hasta ~descoserse~ » — literally to talk until one's seams come apart — means to chatter without stop. From the same ~suere~ root Spanish keeps ~costura~ (“seam, sewing”), the participle ~cosido~ and the learned borrowing ~sutura~; the everyday ~coser~ and bookish ~sutura~ are thus two reflexes of a single Latin thread.
en.descreer:
Built from ~des-~ (Latin ~dis-~, negation) and ~creer~ (“to believe”), “to disbelieve, cease believing.” ~Creer~ descends from Latin ~crēdere~ (“to believe, trust, entrust”), from Proto-Italic *~krezdō~, from a Proto-Indo-European phrase *~ḱred-dʰeh₁-~ (“to place one's heart/trust”), a compound of *~ḱ(e)rd-~ (“heart”) and *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place”). The “heart” element is the same one behind Latin ~cor~ and English ~heart~; through ~crēdere~ the family reaches English ~creed~, ~credo~, ~credit~ and ~credence~.

~Descreer~ is the verb of losing faith rather than merely doubting, and its participle ~descreído~ became a noun for an unbeliever or freethinker — a milder, more literary word than ~ateo~. The rich ~crēdere~ family runs through Spanish ~creencia~ (“belief”), ~crédulo~ (“gullible”), ~increíble~ (“incredible”), ~credencial~ and ~credo~; the sense “entrust” survives in ~acreedor~ (“creditor”) and in the very idea of ~crédito~, money advanced on trust.
en.describir:
From Latin ~dēscrībere~ (“to write down, copy off, sketch, describe”), a compound of the prefix ~dē-~ (“down, off”) and ~scrībere~ (“to write”). ~scrībere~ originally meant “to scratch, incise” — writing was cutting marks into a surface — and descends from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kreybʰ-~ (“to scratch, tear, cut”), an extension of *~(s)ker-~ (“to cut”). A striking cognate survives in Ancient Greek ~skáriphos~ (“a scratching, outline, sketch”). Note the false friend: German ~schreiben~ (“to write”) looks cognate but was actually borrowed from the Latin verb, and English ~write~ comes from a different root entirely. The learned Romance descendants include Italian ~descrivere~, French ~décrire~ and Portuguese ~descrever~.

The metaphor of scratching stayed alive across the whole family. To describe is, etymologically, to “write down” the shape of a thing — to sketch it in words. From ~scrībere~ Spanish inherited ~escribir~ (“to write”) and built a dense thicket of compounds — ~describir~, ~inscribir~, ~prescribir~, ~suscribir~, ~transcribir~ — plus nouns like ~escritura~ (“writing, deed”), ~escritor~ (“writer”) and ~escritorio~ (“desk”). From the past participle ~scrīptus~ came ~escrito~ (“written; a writing”) and ~inscripción~ (“inscription”). English drew a matching crop of borrowings from the same Latin verb — ~scribe~, ~script~, ~scripture~, ~describe~ — all still carrying, faintly, the old sense of a stylus scoring a line.
en.descuajar:
A compound of ~des-~ (Latin ~dis-~, reversal) and ~cuajar~ (“to curdle, coagulate”). ~Cuajar~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~coāglāre~, a syncopated form of Latin ~coāgulāre~ (“to curdle, thicken”), from ~coāgulum~ (“rennet, curdling agent”), which is itself ~co-~ (“together”) + a form of ~agere~ (“to drive, set in motion”). Latin ~coāgulum~ was borrowed learnedly as Spanish ~coágulo~ (“clot”), so ~cuajo~ and ~coágulo~ are an inherited-versus-bookish doublet from one Latin word.

~Descuajar~ first meant “to un-curdle, dissolve what had set,” and figuratively “to break someone's spirit.” But its dominant modern sense moved to the soil: “to uproot, tear out by the roots” (« ~descuajar~ un árbol »), as if pulling a clot free — hence ~descuajaringar~ / ~descuajeringar~, the colloquial “to break to pieces, fall apart.” The ~coāgulum~ root also yields ~cuajada~ (“curds”), ~cuajo~ (“rennet; and, in « arrancar de cuajo », the very idea of tearing out completely”) and the medical ~coagular~ and ~anticoagulante~.
en.descubrir:
From ~des-~ (a reversative prefix, from Latin ~dis-~) plus ~cubrir~ (“to cover”), which comes from Latin ~cooperīre~ (“to cover completely”), a compound of ~co-~ (intensive) and ~operīre~ (“to cover, close”). ~Operīre~ derives from Proto-Italic *~opweriō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂wer-~ (“to cover, shut”). The formation matches Old French ~descovrir~, whence English ~discover~; compare Italian ~scoprire~ and Portuguese ~descobrir~.

The morphology is beautifully transparent: to ~descubrir~ is literally to un-cover, to take the lid off — and Spanish uses it both for physically uncovering and for the mental act of discovery, exactly as English ~discover~ pairs with ~cover~. Columbus’s ~descubrimiento~ of America is the same word as lifting a cloth. From the ~cubrir~ family come ~cubierta~, ~cobertura~, ~encubrir~ and ~recubrir~, while the reversative ~des-~ productively negates hundreds of Spanish verbs.
en.desdecir:
Formed from ~des-~ (Latin ~dis-~, “apart, un-”) and ~decir~ (“to say”), literally “to unsay.” ~Decir~ descends from Latin ~dīcere~ (“to say, tell”), from Proto-Italic *~deikō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, point out”). That root of pointing also surfaces in Latin ~index~ and ~iūdex~ (“judge”), in Greek ~deíknymi~ (“I show”) and — through Germanic — in English ~teach~ and ~token~.

~Desdecir~ means “to retract, take back what one said,” and reflexively ~desdecirse~ is to go back on one's word; it also carries a subtler sense, “to be unworthy of, clash with” — a rude act « desdice de » a gentleman, ill befits him. The ~dīcere~ family is enormous in Spanish: ~dicho~ (“saying”), the many prefixed kin of ~decir~ — ~bendecir~, ~maldecir~, ~contradecir~, ~predecir~ — plus the learned ~dictar~, ~dictamen~, ~índice~ and ~edicto~.
en.desdeñar:
An old verb, in Berceo already, from Latin ~dēdignārī~ (“to scorn, reject as unworthy”), formed from ~dē-~ (“down from, away”) and ~dignārī~ (“to deem worthy”), a deponent of ~dignus~ (“worthy”). Spanish did not simply inherit the ~dē-~: speakers remodeled the prefix to ~des-~ by analogy with verbs like ~despreciar~, feeling that ~desdeñar~ meant stripping away worth. ~Dignus~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~deḱ-~ (“to take, accept”), the root behind Latin ~decēre~ (“to be fitting”) and, through French, English ~deign~ and ~disdain~.

So ~desdeñar~ is, at root, “to consider unworthy,” to reject with a lifted chin; the noun ~desdén~ (“disdain”) and adjective ~desdeñoso~ (“disdainful”) round out the set. From ~dignus~ Spanish keeps a whole worthiness family: ~digno~, ~dignidad~, ~dignatario~, ~indigno~ and the verb ~dignarse~ (“to deign”), the polite cousin of ~desdeñar~ that grants worth where ~desdeñar~ denies it; more distant kin through *~deḱ-~ include ~decente~, ~decoro~ and ~doctor~.
en.desear:
From Latin ~dēsīderāre~ (“to long for, miss, feel the want of”), traditionally analyzed as ~dē-~ + ~sīdus~ (stem ~sīder-~, “star, constellation”), and inherited by Old Spanish as ~desear~. Cognate with Italian ~desiderare~ and Portuguese ~desejar~, and — through the noun ~dēsīderium~ — with English ~desire~ (via Old French).

The star etymology is the classic account, pairing ~dēsīderāre~ with ~cōnsīderāre~ (“to observe the stars closely”): to desire would be to note a star’s absence, to long for what is no longer in sight. But this is disputed — some scholars reject the ~sīdus~ connection outright and derive the verb from a root meaning “stretch, survey,” so the celestial story, charming as it is, should be taken as one proposal, not settled fact. Secure descendants include ~deseo~, ~deseable~ and ~desiderátum~; from ~sīdus~ itself come ~sideral~ and ~considerar~.
en.desechar:
Spanish ~desechar~ is a compound of the privative prefix ~des-~ (from Latin ~dis-~) and ~echar~ (“to throw, to cast”), which descends from Late Latin ~iectāre~, itself from Latin ~iactāre~, the frequentative of ~iaciō~ (“to throw”). The chain reaches back to Proto-Indo-European *~(H)yeh₁-~ (“to throw, to let go”). Through the same Latin verb, ~echar~ is cognate with French ~jeter~ and Portuguese ~jeito~, and — via Latin ~iactāre~ borrowed into English through French — with English ~jet~ and ~jut~; the underlying ~iaciō~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~híēmi~ (“to send, to throw”).

The literal sense is transparent: to ~echar~ something away from oneself is to cast it off, and ~desechar~ settled into the meaning “to discard, to reject.” Old Spanish used it freely for casting aside objects, people, and counsel alike, and the medieval texts preserve it in the sense of spurning advice. From the same stem Spanish keeps the noun ~desecho~ (“waste, castoff”) and the modern adjective ~desechable~ (“disposable”), a throwaway word for a throwaway age. The base ~echar~ meanwhile fanned out into one of Spanish's most versatile verbs, covering everything from pouring to sprouting to dismissing.
en.desempeñar:
A Romance formation: the prefix ~des-~ (“un-, reversal,” from Latin ~dis-~) added to ~empeñar~ (“to pledge, pawn”), which comes from ~empeño~ and ultimately from the old noun ~peño~ (plural ~peños~, “a pledge”), from Latin ~pignus~ (“pledge, security, pawn”). The deeper source of ~pignus~ is uncertain; it is sometimes connected to ~pangere~ (“to fix, fasten”). Cognate formations appear in Portuguese ~empenhar~ and Italian ~impegnare~.

The literal sense came first: to ~desempeñar~ something was to redeem it — to undo a pledge and reclaim a pawned object. From there it turned figurative — to free oneself from an obligation, to make good on one's word — and finally to the modern “to discharge, carry out”: one ~desempeña~ a role, a post, or a duty. The noun ~desempeño~ now means “performance” in every sense, from a job review to an actor's delivery. From the same ~pignus~ Spanish also keeps ~empeño~ (“determination, resolve”) and, as a doublet through the Latin plural ~pignora~, the everyday word ~prenda~ (“a garment; a token of love”) — all of them, at root, something handed over as a guarantee.
en.desencantar:
Spanish ~desencantar~ layers the reversive prefix ~des-~ onto ~encantar~ (“to enchant, to cast a spell”), which comes from Latin ~incantāre~ — ~in-~ (“upon”) plus ~cantāre~ (“to sing”), so literally “to sing a charm over” someone. ~cantāre~ is the frequentative of ~canere~ (“to sing”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂n-~ (“to sing”). The same Latin verb gave French ~enchanter~ and English ~enchant~ and ~incantation~, while bare ~cantāre~ surfaces in French ~chanter~ and English ~chant~.

The magic is built into the word: a spell, in the ancient and medieval imagination, was something sung, so to ~encantar~ was to bewitch by chant. ~desencantar~ then names the undoing of that spell — to break the enchantment and, by a natural figurative turn, “to disillusion” or “to disappoint,” the sense in which it now most often lives. Spanish keeps the whole family close at hand: the noun ~encanto~ (“charm, delight”), the participle-adjective ~encantado~ (“delighted; haunted”), and the everyday ~canto~ (“song”) and ~cantar~ all spring from the same singing root.
en.desesperar:
From Latin ~dēspērāre~ (“to lose hope”), from ~dē-~ (here privative, “un-”) and ~spērāre~ (“to hope”), from ~spēs~ (“hope”), from Proto-Indo-European *~speh₁-~ (“to prosper, turn out well”). Cognate with Italian ~disperare~, French ~désespérer~ and Portuguese ~desesperar~, and — through Old French — with English ~despair~.

Etymologically it means simply “to stop hoping.” From the same ~spēs~ Spanish keeps ~esperar~ — which carries both “to hope” and “to wait” — along with ~esperanza~, ~prosperar~ and ~próspero~. A curious descendant travelled abroad: the Spanish ~desesperado~ (“hopeless, reckless one”) gave English its ~desperado~.
en.desestimar:
Spanish ~desestimar~ (“to reject, dismiss, disregard”) is transparently ~des-~ (“un-, away”) plus ~estimar~ (“to esteem, value, estimate”), which descends from Latin ~aestimāre~ (“to appraise, value, judge”); the compound answers to Latin ~dis-~ + ~aestimāre~. The origin of ~aestimāre~ within Latin is disputed. The Romans linked it to ~aes~ (“bronze, copper money”), and one traditional analysis reads it as ~aes~ plus a root *~temh₁-~ (“to cut”) — a “cutter of bronze,” i.e. one who sets a price in coin. De Vaan rejects that concretization and connects the verb instead to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eys-~ (“to seek”); the matter is unsettled, so neither story should be told as fact. From ~aestimāre~ English drew ~estimate~, ~esteem~ and — through Old French — ~aim~.

The compound simply negates the valuing: to ~desestimar~ something is to judge it not worth keeping — hence its home in the courtroom, where a judge ~desestima~ (“dismisses”) an appeal, and in everyday “to disregard.” Around it Spanish keeps the positive side of the root: ~estima~ (“regard”), ~estimación~ (“esteem, estimate”), ~inestimable~ (“invaluable”) and modern ~autoestima~ (“self-esteem”). The English branch hides a small surprise: ~aim~ came from the same verb by way of Vulgar Latin *~adaestimāre~ and Old French ~esmer~, so to aim at a target and to esteem a person are long-lost siblings, both once a matter of reckoning worth. To ~desestimar~, then, is to take that reckoning and turn it down.
en.deshacer:
A transparent Spanish compound of the prefix ~des-~ (“un-, reversal,” from Latin ~dis-~, “apart”) and ~hacer~ (“to do, make”), from Latin ~facere~ (“to do, make”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to set, put, place”). The Latin ~f-~ became a silent ~h-~ in Castilian — ~facere~ → ~hacer~, as ~farīna~ → ~harina~ — so the verb is literally “un-make.” Cognate with French ~défaire~, Italian ~disfare~ and Portuguese ~desfazer~; through the root, ~facere~ is kin to English ~do~ and ~deed~ and to Greek ~τίθημι~ (~títhēmi~, “I place”).

Since ~hacer~ is the great all-purpose verb of making, ~deshacer~ spreads across every kind of undoing: to take apart (~deshacer~ a knot), to melt or dissolve (~deshacerse~ la nieve), to defeat, and reflexively ~deshacerse~ de algo, “to get rid of something.” The prefix ~des-~ is Spanish's most productive reverser, and the same ~-hacer~ core anchors ~rehacer~ (“to redo”), ~contrahacer~ (“to counterfeit”) and ~satisfacer~ (“to satisfy,” literally “to do enough”).
en.designar:
From Latin ~dēsignāre~ (“to mark out, point out”), a compound of ~dē-~ (“off, out”) and ~signāre~ (“to mark”), from ~signum~ (“sign, mark, token”). The origin of ~signum~ is debated: it goes back to Proto-Italic *~seknom~ and, beyond that, to either Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut”) or *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). Spanish ~designar~ is a learned doublet of the inherited, popular ~diseñar~ (“to design, sketch”). English has ~designate~ and ~design~ from the same verb, French ~désigner~, and Italian ~designare~.

The core image is marking something out — and from “marking” the verb reached “to point to” and then “to appoint or name to a post,” the modern sense. ~signum~ seeded an unusually rich Spanish family: ~signo~, ~señal~, ~seña~, ~señalar~, ~asignar~, ~consignar~, ~insignia~, and the doublet pair ~designar~/~diseñar~. The prettiest surprise is ~enseñar~ (“to teach”), from Late Latin ~īnsignāre~ (“to mark in, imprint”) — teaching imagined as pressing a sign into the mind.
en.deslizar:
Spanish ~deslizar~ is of uncertain origin, and the sources hedge. Most trace it to an expressive or onomatopoeic base *~liz-~ evoking a smooth, gliding motion, prefixed with ~des-~; some scholars instead suspect Germanic influence, comparing a Frankish *~slīdan~ that would also be the source of English ~slide~. Neither account is settled, so the word is best described as probably imitative in root, perhaps colored by a Germanic form. Its clear cognate is Portuguese ~deslizar~.

Whatever its beginning, the verb has always meant “to slide, to slip,” the effortless motion of something moving over a smooth surface. From it Spanish forms the noun ~desliz~ — literally a slip, and figuratively a moral “slip” or lapse, an indiscretion — along with ~deslizamiento~ (“sliding; landslide”), the geological term for a slope giving way. The uncertainty of its own etymology suits a word about losing one's footing: even the philologists cannot quite get a grip on where it came from.
en.desmentir:
Spanish ~desmentir~ joins the prefix ~des-~ to ~mentir~ (“to lie”), inherited from Latin ~mentīrī~. That verb derives from ~mēns~ (stem ~mentis~, “mind”) plus a verbal suffix, and so from Proto-Indo-European *~méntis~ (“thought”), from the root *~men-~ (“to think”). Latin ~mentīrī~ is cognate through that root with a vast mental vocabulary; the base ~mentir~ matches French ~mentir~ and Portuguese ~mentir~ exactly.

The semantic history is pointed: the sense “to lie” arose from an earlier “to be inventive, to conjure up,” so that lying is framed as an act of the imagining mind. ~desmentir~ turns that against a falsehood — to un-lie a statement is “to deny, to contradict, to give the lie to” someone's claim. Old Spanish used it in exactly this confrontational sense, and the medieval texts preserve it. From the same PIE root *~men-~ Spanish keeps ~mente~ (“mind”), ~mental~, ~mención~, and ~comentar~ — a family in which thinking, remembering, and, at its edge, lying all meet.
en.desnudar:
Spanish ~desnudar~ comes from Latin ~disnūdāre~, an altered form of ~dēnūdāre~ (“to lay bare”), built from the prefix ~dē-~ and the adjective ~nūdus~ (“naked, bare”). ~nūdus~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~nogʷedos~ to Proto-Indo-European *~nogʷós~ (“naked”), one of the oldest and most widely inherited adjectives in the family. It is cognate with English ~naked~ and German ~nackt~, and — from the same root by different suffixes — with Ancient Greek ~gumnós~ and Sanskrit ~nagná~.

Latin ~nūdus~ carried not only “unclothed” but also “stripped, deprived, defenseless,” a range Spanish still feels. ~desnudar~ is the plain verb “to undress, to strip bare,” literal for clothing and figurative for laying anything open. Its participle gave the adjective and noun ~desnudo~ (“naked; a nude”), the artist's term for the unclothed figure. Learned Latin re-entered the language as the doublet ~denudar~ (“to denude”), and the same root yields ~nudismo~ and ~nudista~ — proof that a very old word for bareness stayed useful across every register.
en.desollar:
Spanish ~desollar~ (“to skin, to flay”) descends from Vulgar Latin *~exfollāre~, formed on Latin ~follis~ (“bellows; leather bag”) with the prefix ~ex-~ (“off, out of”). It passed through Old Spanish ~desfollar~ before the ~-f-~ was lost, and still survives dialectally as Asturian ~esfollar~. ~follis~ is probably inherited from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰolǵʰnis~, from the root *~bʰelǵʰ-~ (“to swell”), though the derivation is not certain. By that root it is cognate with Old English ~belġ~ (source of English ~belly~) and Old Irish ~bolg~ (“bag, bellows”).

The image behind the word is the leather bag: to ~desollar~ an animal is to strip off its hide as one would empty or peel a skin-bag. ~follis~ had a lively afterlife of its own — its sense of an inflated, empty windbag gave Vulgar Latin the word for a fool, whence French ~fou~ (“mad”) and English ~fool~ and ~folly~; the anatomical ~follicle~ comes from its diminutive. In Spanish the bag-sense stayed literal in ~fuelle~ (“bellows”), so the flayer and the blacksmith's bellows share a single Latin ancestor.
en.desorejar:
Spanish ~desorejar~ is a Spanish formation, not a Latin inheritance: the privative prefix ~des-~ attached to ~oreja~ (“ear”) with the verb-forming ending ~-ar~, yielding “to cut off the ears.” ~oreja~ itself comes from Latin ~ōricula~, a variant of ~auricula~ (“little ear”), the diminutive of ~auris~ (“ear”) — the diminutive, not the plain noun, being what most of Romance inherited. ~auris~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ṓws~ (“ear”), cognate with English ~ear~, Ancient Greek ~oûs~, and Lithuanian ~ausis~.

The verb belongs to a grim semantic field: cutting off ears was a judicial and battlefield punishment, and ~desorejar~ named the act, appearing in medieval Spanish for the mutilation of criminals and captives. It never became common, and today it is chiefly historical or literary. The homely ~oreja~, by contrast, thrives — in ~orejón~ (“dried apricot”; also “big-eared”) and, through the learned Latin form, in the medical ~aurícula~ (“atrium of the heart”) and ~auricular~ (“earpiece; of the ear”), which sit beside the inherited word as its Latinate cousins.
en.despedazar:
Spanish ~despedazar~ (“to tear to pieces”) is built on ~pedazo~ (“piece”) with the prefix ~des-~ and the verbal ending ~-ar~ — literally “to break into pieces.” ~pedazo~ descends from Old Spanish ~pedaço~, from Vulgar Latin ~pitaccium~, a metathesized form of Latin ~pittacium~ (“a patch, a small piece of leather; a label”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~pittákion~ (“a small tablet or label”). The word is cognate with Portuguese ~pedaço~ and Galician ~pedazo~.

The journey from a written label to a torn fragment ran through the everyday sense of a small patch or scrap; a ~pittacium~ was a little bit of something, and ~pedazo~ generalized to any “piece” at all. From it ~despedazar~ took shape for violent fragmentation — tearing prey, cloth, or a body to shreds — and the medieval texts use it for exactly such rending. Spanish keeps ~pedazo~ vigorously alive in affectionate idiom, as in “~pedazo~ de pan” for a kind-hearted soul, so the same root spans both tenderness and dismemberment.
en.despedir:
From Latin ~expetere~ (“to demand, long for, strive after”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) + ~petere~ (“to seek, ask, aim at”), from Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to fly, rush”). Vulgar Latin doubled the prefix into *~deexpetere~ (~de-~ + ~expetere~), which Spanish reduced to ~despedir~; the simple ~petere~ gave Spanish ~pedir~ (“to ask”). Cognate with Portuguese ~despedir~.

The semantic path is striking.
