The deeper origin of ~patta~ is disputed: the traditional Iberian account derives it from Latin ~pacta~, plural of ~pactum~ (“pact, agreement”) — a drawn game being a kind of settled truce — whereas en.Wiktionary instead links it to Italian ~patta~/French ~patte~ (“flap, paw”). The sources hedge, so everything beyond Italian ~impattare~ should be read as debated, not settled.

However the noun is resolved, the core notion is equality: from ~empate~ (“a tie”) the verb came to mean “to make two contestants level.” Corominas records a second, textile sense — “to splice two threads or cords so cleanly they seem one” — and a Portuguese meaning “to hinder, to hold up,” still current in Portugal. In today’s Spanish ~empatar~ belongs above all to the football pitch and the ballot box: teams and candidates ~empatan~ when neither can pull ahead. Kindred forms include ~empate~ and ~desempate~ (“tie-breaker”).
en.empeorar:
Spanish ~empeorar~ was built in the medieval period from the prefix ~en-~ (Latin ~in-~) and the adjective ~peor~ (“worse”), plus the verbal ending ~-ar~ — literally “to make worse.” ~Peor~ descends from Latin ~peior~ (“worse”), the comparative of ~malus~ (“bad”), from Proto-Italic *~pedjōs~ and, as many reconstruct it, from Proto-Indo-European *~ped-~ (“foot; to fall, stumble”) — as if the worse thing were the one that stumbles or falls short, though this deeper link is proposed rather than settled. It is cognate with Italian ~peggiore~, French ~pire~, and Portuguese ~pior~.

The idea began as a plain comparative: to ~empeorar~ is to move toward ~peor~, sliding down the scale of ~malus~. Latin’s superlative ~pessimus~ (“worst”) gave Spanish ~pésimo~ (“dreadful”) and the learned ~peyorativo~ (“pejorative”), which literally names language that makes something seem worse. The language also kept the noun ~empeoramiento~ (“worsening”) for the process itself. English borrowed the same comparative in ~pejorative~, so a Spanish speaker whose situation empeora and an English speaker talking in pejorative terms are, unknowingly, reaching for the very same Roman word for “worse.”
en.empezar:
Spanish ~empezar~ is a compound of the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and the noun ~pieza~ (“piece”) — some accounts reconstruct an intervening Vulgar Latin *~impettiāre~, though that form is only proposed, not attested. What is clear is the ~pieza~ at its core, and ~pieza~ is not Latin: it comes from Late Latin ~pettia~, borrowed from Gaulish *~pettyā~, from Proto-Celtic *~kʷezdis~. So one of Spanish's common verbs for “to begin” has a Celtic heart. Its Romance kin through ~pieza~ include French ~pièce~, Italian ~pezza~ and Portuguese ~peça~.

The image behind ~empezar~ is concrete and homely: to begin something is to break into it — to break off the first ~pieza~, to broach a whole. You start a loaf or a task by taking the first piece of it. From the same Celtic-derived ~pieza~ Spanish built ~despiezar~ (“to dismantle, to break into pieces”) and the noun ~empiece~ (“a beginning”), while ~pieza~ itself ranges from a coin to a room to a musical or theatrical piece. It is a small monument to the Gaulish substrate embedded in everyday Castilian.
en.emplear:
From Old French ~empleiier~, a variant of ~emploiier~ (whence modern French ~employer~), from Latin ~implicāre~ (“to enfold, involve, entangle”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~plek-~ (“to plait, weave”). Cognate with English ~employ~, Italian ~impiegare~ and Portuguese ~empregar~; and, as a learned twin of the very same Latin verb that entered Spanish directly, ~implicar~.

Latin ~implicāre~ literally meant to fold one thing into another, and from “to involve, engage” its Old French descendant slid toward “to put to use, occupy.” Spanish took it in that practical sense of setting things — and hands — to work, so ~emplear~ covers both « usar » and « dar trabajo a ». The bookish doublet ~implicar~ kept the abstract Latin idea of “to involve, imply,” a neat case of one etymon yielding two Spanish verbs. From the same root *~plek-~ come ~empleo~, ~aplicar~, ~explicar~, ~plegar~ and ~pliegue~, plus the everyday ~empleado~ (“employee”).
en.emprender:
From Vulgar Latin *~imprendere~ (“to take in hand, undertake”), from ~in-~ (“in, upon”) plus Latin ~prehendere~ (“to grasp, seize”), itself ~prae-~ (“before”) with ~-hendere~ (“to take hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰed-~ (“to seize”). Cognate with French ~entreprendre~, Italian ~intraprendere~ and Portuguese ~empreender~, and — through ~prehendere~ — with English ~comprehend~, ~apprehend~ and ~prehensile~; the same PIE root also yielded English ~get~.

To ~emprender~ is literally to lay hold of something and set it going — to grasp a task and begin it. Spanish spun a whole vocabulary of initiative from this root: ~empresa~ (“enterprise, company,” originally the feminine participle “thing undertaken”), ~emprendedor~ (“entrepreneur”) and ~emprendimiento~. Around them cluster the ~prehendere~ doublets that shaped the language — ~prender~ (“to seize, catch”), ~aprender~ (“to learn,” literally “to grasp”), ~comprender~, ~sorprender~ and ~desprender~ — a family whose common thread is always the hand closing on something.
en.empujar:
The favored account derives ~empujar~ (“to push”) from Late Latin ~impulsāre~, a frequentative of ~impellere~ (“to drive against, impel”), which is ~in-~ (“against”) plus ~pellere~ (“to drive, push, strike”). ~pellere~ reflects Proto-Indo-European *~pelh₂-~ (“to drive, strike”). An alternative proposal instead builds the word from ~en-~ and ~pujar~; the derivation is debated, though ~impulsāre~ is the account most etymologists prefer. Through ~pellere~ English is cousin in ~impulse~, ~compel~ and ~pulse~.

A frequentative names repeated action, and ~empujar~ does suggest shoving again and again to get something moving. Whatever the exact path, the ~pellere~ family is large in Spanish: the learned ~impulsar~ (“to propel”) and ~impulso~ (“impulse”) sit beside the inherited ~empujar~, joined by ~expulsar~ (“to expel”), ~propulsar~ (“to propel”), ~pulso~ (“pulse”) and the vivid ~empellón~ (“a hard shove”). All turn on the old sense of driving something before you.
en.enajenar:
The verb ~enajenar~ (“to alienate, to transfer property to another”) grew from the medieval adjective ~ajeno~ (“belonging to someone else”) with the frame ~en-~…~-ar~; Latin already had the parallel verb ~aliēnāre~. ~Ajeno~ comes from Latin ~aliēnus~ (“of another, foreign”), a derivative of ~alius~ (“other”), from Proto-Italic *~aljos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₂élyos~ (“other”), from the root *~h₂el-~ (“beyond, other”). The same root surfaces in Ancient Greek ~ἄλλος~ (állos, “other”) and, through Germanic, in English ~else~; English ~alien~ is itself the Latin ~aliēnus~ in borrowed dress.

At heart ~enajenar~ means “to make something another’s,” and Spanish put that to work in two directions. In law it is to transfer ownership — to place a good in the hands of ~ajeno~, someone else. Applied to the mind it yields ~enajenación~ (“derangement, taking leave of one’s senses”), the self carried off as if it belonged to another; a person may ~enajenarse~, grow estranged. From the same Latin stock Spanish also keeps the learned pair ~alienar~ and ~alienación~ (the philosopher’s “alienation”) and the science-fiction ~alienígena~. Whether in a property deed, a diagnosis, or a spaceship, the thread is constant: the state of being ~ajeno~ — other, and no longer one’s own.
en.enamorar:
~enamorar~ is a Spanish formation — the prefix ~en-~ (“to put into a state”) plus ~amor~ (“love”) plus the verbal ending ~-ar~ — literally “to put into love.” ~amor~ comes from Latin ~amor~, ~amōris~, the noun of ~amāre~ (“to love”), a verb whose deeper origin is uncertain; it is often taken for an expressive nursery word (a ~Lallwort~ of the ~am-~ babble type) rather than a securely reconstructed Indo-European root. Its Romance kin are everywhere: Spanish ~amar~, Italian ~amare~, French ~aimer~ and, borrowed into English through Latin and French, ~amateur~, ~amiable~ and ~amorous~.

Where Latin had ~amāre~, Spanish preferred the built-up ~enamorar~ for the specific event of kindling love — and above all its reflexive ~enamorarse~ (“to fall in love”), the moment one passes into the state of ~amor~. The same root branches into a warm Spanish family — ~amar~, ~amante~, ~amistad~, ~amable~, ~amoroso~, ~amado~ and ~enamorado~ — while a separate poetic descendant, ~amorío~, names a lighter, fleeting infatuation.
en.encabezar:
~Encabezar~ combines the prefix ~en-~ with ~cabeza~ (“head”) and the ending ~-ar~. ~Cabeza~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~capitia~, a reshaping of Latin ~caput~, genitive ~capitis~ (“head”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kaput-~ (“head”). It is cognate with Portuguese ~cabeça~ and French ~chef~ — and, remarkably, with English ~head~, which descends from the very same PIE root.

~Cabeza~ overtook Latin ~caput~ in everyday Spanish, and ~encabezar~ moved from “to put a head on” to “to head, lead, or top” a list, a movement, or a page — whence the noun ~encabezado~ (“heading, headline”). The ~caput~ family is vast: ~capital~, ~capítulo~ (“chapter,” a “little head”), ~cabo~ (“cape; corporal”), ~caudillo~ (“leader”), ~decapitar~ (“to behead”), and ~capitán~. French ~chef~ shows the metaphor plainly: a “head” became a “chief,” and the head of a kitchen gave English its ~chef~.
en.encajar:
From the prefix ~en-~ (“in”) and the noun ~caja~ (“box”), from Latin ~capsa~ (“box, case, chest for books”), a derivative of ~capere~ (“to take, hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp, seize”). The box-word spread across Romance: alongside Spanish ~caja~ stand Portuguese ~caixa~, Italian ~cassa~ and French ~caisse~, and through Old French it entered English as ~case~ and, via the diminutive ~capsula~, as ~capsule~.

The image behind the verb is concrete: to ~encajar~ a thing was to make it fit into its ~caja~ — its box, socket or slot — and from that snug fit grew the general senses “to fit” and “to fit together,” plus the figurative “to take” a blow or “to accept” an idea. The same root seeded a wide Spanish family — ~cajón~ (“drawer”), ~cajero~ (“cashier”) and ~encaje~ (“lace,” literally something fitted together) — and, more surprisingly, English ~cash~, which first meant “money box” before it meant the money inside.
en.encaminar:
From ~en-~ (“in, on”) and ~camino~ (“road, way”) plus the verbal suffix ~-ar~. ~Camino~ descends from Vulgar Latin ~camminus~, a word of Celtic origin — borrowed from Gaulish and traced to Proto-Celtic *~kanxsman-~ (“step, pace”); the deeper Indo-European root, perhaps one meaning “to step” or “to limp,” is less certain and is best flagged as such. The road-word is shared across the West: French ~chemin~, Italian ~cammino~, Portuguese ~caminho~ and Catalan ~camí~ are all cognates.

To ~encaminar~ someone is literally to “put them on the road,” whence the senses “to direct,” “to guide,” “to set on the way” and, reflexively, “to head toward” a goal. The Celtic road left deep tracks in Spanish: ~caminar~ (“to walk”), ~caminata~ (“a long hike”), ~caminante~ (“wayfarer”) and the pilgrim’s ~Camino~ de Santiago all descend from the same borrowed word.
en.encantar:
From Latin ~incantāre~ (“to sing over, to chant a spell upon”), a compound of ~in-~ (“on, upon”) and ~cantāre~ (“to sing”), which is the frequentative of ~canere~ (“to sing”). The root is the Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂n-~ (“to sing”). ~incantāre~ gave Italian ~incantare~, Portuguese ~encantar~, and — through Old French ~enchanter~ — English ~enchant~ and ~incantation~. From the related Latin ~carmen~ (“song, spell,” itself from ~canere~) English even draws ~charm~.

The magic here was literally sung: to ~incantāre~ was to chant a spell over someone, and Spanish ~encantar~ still means both “to bewitch” and, softened, “to delight, to charm.” The past participle ~encantado~ (“enchanted”) became the everyday courtesy for “pleased to meet you” — a small linguistic spell cast at every introduction. The noun ~encanto~ is a “charm” and ~encantador~ means “charming” (or “a sorcerer”). Alongside these stand the plain musical descendants of ~cantāre~: ~cantar~ (“to sing”), ~canto~ (“song”), ~canción~ (“song”), and ~cantante~ (“singer”). To enchant, in the end, was only ever to sing — and to sing well enough that someone fell under the spell.
en.encargar:
From ~en-~ plus ~cargar~ (“to load”), from Late Latin ~carricāre~ (“to load a wagon”), a verb built on Latin ~carrus~ (“wheeled cart, wagon”). ~carrus~ was itself borrowed from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *~karros~, and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱers-~ (“to run”) — a cart being, in essence, “the running thing.” Through ~carricāre~ it is cognate with Italian ~caricare~, French ~charger~, and Portuguese ~carregar~; and, by way of Old French, with English ~charge~ and ~cargo~, while ~carrus~ itself lies behind English ~car~.

The literal image was “to load a cart,” and ~cargar~ kept that sense of loading, carrying, and burdening. The prefixed ~encargar~ shifted figuratively from “to load a burden onto someone” to “to entrust, commission, or order.” The same family crowds modern Spanish: ~carga~ (“load”), ~cargo~ (“post, charge”), ~descargar~ (“to unload, download”), ~recargar~ (“to recharge”), ~sobrecargar~ (“to overload”), and the noun ~encargo~ (“an order, an errand”). It is a fittingly busy brood for a root that, at its Indo-European base *~ḱers-~, meant only “to run.”
en.encender:
From Latin ~incendere~ (“to set on fire, kindle”), a compound of ~in-~ with a verb root akin to ~candēre~ (“to glow, be white-hot”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kend-~ (“to shine, glow”). The inherited Romance verbs line up neatly — Portuguese ~acender~, Italian ~accendere~ — while the learned stratum lent English ~incendiary~ and, through the participle ~incensum~, the word ~incense~. From the sibling ~candēre~ came English ~candle~, ~candid~, and ~incandescent~.

Latin ~incendere~ literally made something ~candēre~, made it glow, by putting fire into it. Old Spanish softened ~in-~ to ~en-~ and reduced the stem, yielding ~encender~ — first “to kindle a flame,” later extended to switching on a lamp or a light, and figuratively to inflaming passions. The Latin root left Spanish a bright cluster: the noun ~incendio~ (“fire, blaze”), ~incendiar~, ~candela~ (“candle”), ~candente~ (“red-hot”), ~cándido~ (“naïve,” from ~candidus~ “white”), ~incienso~ (“incense”), ~candil~ (“oil lamp”), and ~encendedor~ (“lighter”).
en.encerrar:
From ~en-~ (“in”) + ~cerrar~ (“to close, shut”), literally “to shut in, enclose.” ~cerrar~ descends from Late Latin ~serāre~ (“to bolt, lock”), built on ~sera~ (“a bar, bolt, or lock for a door”). Portuguese ~cerrar~ and the Old French ~serrer~ (“to press, tighten”) preserve the same verb; the French descendant survives in ~serrure~ (“lock”) and, through a related noun, in English ~serried~ (“pressed close together, as ranks”).

Where Latin ~serāre~ meant to secure a door with its ~sera~, Spanish ~cerrar~ generalized to “close” of any kind, and the prefixed ~encerrar~ specialized to “to lock in, confine, enclose.” The most famous derivative is the noun ~encierro~ — both the general “confinement” and, specifically, the ~encierro~ of Pamplona, the running of the bulls that pens them toward the ring. Related forms from ~cerrar~ include ~cierre~ (“closure, zipper”), ~cerradura~ (“lock”) and ~cerrojo~ (“bolt”).
en.enclavar:
~Enclavar~ (“to nail, to fix in place”) is the prefix ~en-~ welded to ~clavo~ (“nail”); Latin already formed ~inclāvāre~. ~Clavo~ descends from Latin ~clāvus~ (“nail”), close kin of ~clāvis~ (“key”), both from Proto-Italic *~klāwos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~kleh₂w-~ (“nail, peg, hook” — the old instruments for barring a door). The root also gave Latin ~claudere~ (“to shut”) and Ancient Greek ~κλείς~ (kleís, “key”). Its Romance children split neatly: French ~clou~ and Italian ~chiodo~ for the nail, French ~clef~ and Italian ~chiave~ for the key.

The nail spread far beyond carpentry. ~Clāvus~ gave everyday ~clavo~ and the phrase “dar en el clavo,” to hit the nail on the head, while its sibling ~clāvis~ became Spanish ~llave~ (“key”) and the learned ~clave~ (“key, code, clef”). A small key named a bone: ~clavícula~ (“collarbone”). From French, geography borrowed ~enclave~, a territory “nailed” inside another. Most surprising is the spice: the clove, ~clavo de olor~, is a dried bud shaped like a tiny nail, and English ~clove~ itself traces back through French to Latin ~clāvus~ — so ~enclavar~ a plank and seasoning a stew reach for the same Roman nail.
en.encoger:
~Encoger~ (“to shrink, to draw in”) is the prefix ~en-~ added to ~coger~ (“to gather, to take”), from Latin ~colligere~ (“to gather together”), itself ~con-~ (“together”) plus ~legere~ (“to gather, pick, read”). ~Legere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, collect”). The root ran through much of Europe: Italian ~cogliere~ and French ~cueillir~ (“to gather”) match Spanish ~coger~, while English inherited ~collect~, ~legend~, and ~lecture~ from the same ~legere~.

The image behind ~encoger~ is a body ~coger~-ing itself together — gathering inward until it contracts. That is why one ~encoge~ a wool sweater in hot water, and why ~encogerse de hombros~ is to “shrink the shoulders,” to shrug. Figuratively an ~encogido~ person is timid, drawn in on themselves. Around ~coger~ Spanish grew a whole family of gathering verbs — ~recoger~ (“to collect”), ~acoger~ (“to welcome”), ~escoger~ (“to choose”) — plus the bookish ~colegir~ (“to infer”) and the noun ~colección~. From folding laundry to folding oneself in fear, the root keeps its ancient sense: to bring things together.
en.encomendar:
~Encomendar~ (“to entrust, to commend”) comes from Vulgar Latin *~incommendāre~, the prefix ~en-~ reinforcing Latin ~commendāre~ (“to entrust, hand over for safekeeping”). That verb is ~con-~ (“fully”) plus ~mandāre~ (“to commit, entrust”), and ~mandāre~ itself is transparent: ~manus~ (“hand”) and ~dare~ (“to give”) — to entrust is literally to place in someone’s hand. ~Dare~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). The family is broad: Italian ~raccomandare~, French ~recommander~, and English ~commend~, ~command~, and ~mandate~ all rest on the same ~mandāre~.

To ~encomendar~ was to put something in trustworthy hands, and Spanish leaned on it for both prayer and power. One would ~encomendarse~ a Dios, commending one’s soul to God before a journey or a battle. From the same verb came ~encomienda~ — in medieval Spain the estate and income granted to a military order, and in the Americas the notorious colonial grant of Indigenous labor to a conquistador, a word that still weighs heavily in the region’s history; today an ~encomienda~ is more often simply a parcel sent by post. Alongside sit ~mandar~ (“to order, to send”), ~mandato~, ~comando~, and ~recomendar~ — every one of them a way of placing a task, gently or forcefully, into another’s hand.
en.enconar:
~Enconar~ (“to inflame, to irritate a wound; to embitter”) descends, by Corominas’s well-argued account, from Latin ~inquināre~ (“to stain, to defile, to contaminate”). The Spanish form lost the medial consonant and shifted sense as the polluted wound became the inflamed one. The deeper origin of ~inquināre~ is less secure: it is usually parsed as the prefix ~in-~ over a root tied to ~caenum~ (“filth, mire”), but that analysis is proposed rather than proven, so it is best left as an educated guess. From the very same ~inquināre~ Spanish also drew, by a learned route, the noun ~inquina~ (“grudge, ill will”) and the verb ~inquinar~ (“to defile”).

The path of meaning runs from dirt to anger. To ~enconar~ a wound was first to let filth work in it until it festered; from the swollen, throbbing wound the verb reached the heart, so that today one can ~enconar~ a quarrel — inflame it, make it fester. The noun ~encono~ names exactly that: a settled, rankling resentment. What makes the story neat is the split between twin descendants of one Latin word: popular ~enconar~ took the road of the infected body, while learned ~inquina~ took the road of the poisoned mind — two words for the same slow corruption, one physical, one moral, both born of Latin ~inquināre~.
en.encontrar:
From Vulgar Latin *~incontrāre~ (“to meet, to come up against”), a verb built from Latin ~in-~ (“in, upon”) plus ~contrā~ (“against, facing”), itself from ~cum~ / ~com-~ (“with”). Old Spanish inherited it as ~encontrar~. Its Romance relatives include Italian ~incontrare~, Portuguese ~encontrar~, and French ~encontrer~ (surviving today mainly in ~rencontrer~, “to meet”); English borrowed the same formation as ~encounter~ and, more plainly, ~counter~.

The literal core is confrontational — to come face to face, even against one another — but Spanish softened the edge: ~encontrar~ is now the neutral, everyday verb both for meeting a person and for finding a thing (« no encuentro las llaves »). The reflexive ~encontrarse~ adds “to be located” and “to feel” (« me encuentro bien »). From the same stem come the noun ~encuentro~ (“a meeting, a match”), the blunt ~encontronazo~ (“a collision, a run-in”), and, through the shared ~contrā~, a whole regiment of words — ~contra~, ~contrario~, ~encontrado~ (“opposing, conflicting”), and ~contrariar~.
en.encordar:
~Encordar~ (“to string,” as an instrument or a racket) is the prefix ~en-~ joined to ~cuerda~ (“cord, string”) with the ending ~-ar~. ~Cuerda~ comes from Latin ~chorda~ (“gut, cord, the string of a lyre”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~χορδή~ (khordḗ, “gut-string”), which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰerH-~ (“gut, entrail”) — strings were once made of dried animal gut. Through that root ~cuerda~ is a distant cousin of English ~yarn~, another thread first spun from gut; and Latin ~chorda~ itself gave, by direct borrowing, English ~cord~ and ~chord~, French ~corde~, and Italian ~corda~.

From the lyre’s gut the word spread to every kind of line. Spanish ~cuerda~ names a rope, the string of a guitar, the spring of a wind-up clock (~dar cuerda~, to wind it), and — in the plural — the ~cuerdas vocales~, the vocal cords. Diminutive and derived forms branched off: ~cordón~ (“cord, lace”), ~cordel~ (“twine”), and even ~cordillera~ (“mountain range”), imagined as a long cord of peaks. To ~encordar~ a violin is to fit it with strings, but climbers also ~encordarse~, roping themselves together for safety. Across music, medicine, geography, and the mountains, the same Greek gut-string keeps binding things — quite literally — into one.
en.encubrir:
~Encubrir~ (“to conceal, to cover up”) is the prefix ~en-~ (intensifying, “over”) added to ~cubrir~ (“to cover”), from Latin ~cooperīre~ (“to cover over, bury”), a compound of the intensive ~co-~ and ~operīre~ (“to cover, to shut”). ~Operīre~ comes from Proto-Italic *~opwerjō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂wer-~ (“to cover, to shut”). The Romance descendants line up closely: French ~couvrir~, Italian ~coprire~, Portuguese ~cobrir~. English ~cover~ is the same Latin ~cooperīre~ borrowed through Old French, so the English and Spanish words are, at root, one.

Where ~cubrir~ simply covers, ~encubrir~ covers with intent — to hide a fault, a crime, a truth. Spanish law still calls the person who shelters a wrongdoer an ~encubridor~ (“accessory, harborer”). The verb sits at the center of a busy family: ~descubrir~ (“to uncover, to discover”) and its ~descubrimiento~, the everyday ~cubierta~ (“cover, deck”), and ~cobertura~ (“coverage”). The tidiest surprise lies in the root: the same PIE *~h₂wer-~ that built ~operīre~ (“to cover”) also built its opposite, ~aperīre~ (“to open”), which became Spanish ~abrir~. So ~cubrir~ and ~abrir~ — covering and opening — are, astonishingly, two faces of a single ancient root.
en.enderezar:
From Old Spanish ~derezar~ with the prefix ~en-~, from Vulgar Latin *~directiāre~, a verb built on Latin ~directus~ (“straight, set right”), the past participle of ~dīrigere~ (“to guide, set straight”) — itself ~dis-~ plus ~regere~ (“to rule, keep straight”). The ultimate source is Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, direct, rule”). Cognate with Portuguese ~endireitar~ and Catalan ~adreçar~, and — through the same Vulgar-Latin verb — with French ~dresser~ and Italian ~dirizzare~; through the root alone it ties to English ~right~ and ~direct~.

The literal sense was concrete: to make something ~derecho~ (“straight”), to stand it upright. From there it broadened to setting matters right, correcting, and directing one's steps or aim. The same root *~h₃reǵ-~ seeded a broad Spanish family, among them ~directo~, ~dirigir~, ~regir~, ~corregir~, ~regla~, ~región~ and even ~rey~ (“king,” the one who rules).
en.enervar:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~ēnervāre~ (“to weaken, to take the sinew out of”), from ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~nervus~ (“sinew, tendon; nerve”). Latin ~nervus~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European word for “sinew, tendon,” *~(s)neh₁-~, and is cognate with Greek ~neûron~ (“sinew,” later “nerve”), the source of English ~neuron~. English ~enervate~ is a direct parallel borrowing of the same Latin verb.

The image is bodily and vivid: to ~enervar~ was literally to cut or draw out the sinews, leaving a body limp — and so, figuratively, to sap strength, energy, or resolve. In modern Spanish it has drifted toward “to irritate or fray the nerves,” under the influence of ~nervioso~. From the same ~nervus~ come Spanish ~nervio~, ~nervioso~, ~enervante~ and ~inervar~ (the anatomical “to supply with nerves”).
en.enfatizar:
~Enfatizar~ is formed from the noun ~énfasis~ (“emphasis”) and the verb-forming suffix ~-izar~. ~Énfasis~ passed through Latin ~emphasis~ from Greek ~émphasis~ (“outward appearance, force of expression”), a noun from ~emphaínein~ (“to display, show in”), itself ~en-~ (“in”) plus ~phaínein~ (“to show, bring to light”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰeh₂-~ (“to shine”). Italian ~enfatizzare~ is its Romance twin, and English ~emphasize~ its direct cognate.

In Greek rhetoric ~émphasis~ named the extra meaning shown through the words — an implied force beyond the literal — so to ~enfatizar~ is, at root, to make something shine out. The Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰeh₂-~ (“to shine”) is astonishingly fertile: from ~phaínein~ and its kin Spanish inherited ~fantasma~, ~fantasía~, ~fenómeno~, ~fase~, ~epifanía~ and ~diáfano~ — a constellation of words all turning on light, appearance, and showing.
en.enfermar:
From Latin ~īnfirmāre~ (“to weaken, make feeble”), from the adjective ~īnfirmus~ (“weak, infirm”), literally ~in-~ (a negating prefix, “not”) plus ~firmus~ (“firm, strong, steady”). ~firmus~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰer-~ (“to hold, support”). Cognate with Portuguese ~enfermar~ and Italian ~infermare~, and — through ~firmus~ — with English ~firm~ and French ~ferme~.

The logic is transparent once unpacked: to fall ill is to become “un-firm,” to lose one's steadiness — hence the adjective ~enfermo~ (“sick”), which is simply ~īnfirmus~ worn down by centuries of speech. From the same ~firmus~ Spanish also drew the doublet ~firme~ and the learned ~firmar~ (“to sign,” i.e. to make fast), ~afirmar~, ~confirmar~ and ~enfermedad~.
en.enfocar:
A Spanish coinage: the prefix ~en-~ plus the noun ~foco~ plus the verb-forming ~-ar~. ~Foco~ descends from Latin ~focus~ (“hearth, fireplace”), a word of uncertain, much-debated Indo-European origin. In Vulgar Latin ~focus~ elbowed aside the classical ~ignis~ as the ordinary word for “fire,” and in that everyday sense it became Spanish ~fuego~, French ~feu~, and Italian ~fuoco~; the more learned line kept the original hearth-meaning and produced ~foco~.

The leap to optics came through burning: a lens gathers the sun’s rays to one blazing point, a tiny “hearth,” and it was Johannes Kepler who in the early 1600s borrowed ~focus~ for that point of convergence, in both lenses and the ellipse of a planet’s orbit. Spanish ~foco~ thus means both a “fireplace/light-source” and a geometric or optical “focus,” and ~enfocar~ means “to focus (a lens, a camera)” and, figuratively, “to frame or approach (a problem).” The noun ~enfoque~ (“focus; approach, angle”) is now common in essays and journalism. The hearth kept other descendants too: ~hogar~ (“home,” from Latin ~focārium~), ~fogata~, ~fogón~, and ~hoguera~.
en.enfrentar:
From ~en-~ (“in, into”) plus ~frente~ (“forehead; front”) and the verbal ending ~-ar~ — a verb built directly on the noun. ~frente~ descends from Latin ~frontem~, accusative of ~frons~ (“forehead, brow, front”), whose ultimate origin is uncertain; De Vaan finds “no plausible etymology”. The Latin noun lives on in Italian ~fronte~, French ~front~ and Portuguese ~frente~, and English ~front~ is its doublet, borrowed through Old French.

In Latin ~frons~ named the forehead and, by an easy metaphor, the foremost part of anything, including an army's front line — the sense that powers military ~frente~. Spanish keeps both meanings and even sorts them by gender: ~la frente~ is the forehead, ~el frente~ the front. To ~enfrentar~ is literally to set foreheads or fronts against each other, hence “to confront, to face”. From the same root grew ~frontera~ (“frontier”), ~afrontar~, ~confrontar~ and ~frontal~, while English gained ~frontier~ and ~confront~ along the way.
en.engañar:
From Vulgar Latin ~ingannāre~ (“to mock, deceive”), formed with intensive ~in-~ on Latin ~gannīre~. Cognate with Italian ~ingannare~, Portuguese ~enganar~, and Catalan ~enganyar~, all meaning “to deceive.” The verb is common to the Romance languages but has few clear relatives beyond them.

~gannīre~ originally named the yelping or snarling of dogs, and in popular speech came to mean idle chatter or prattle — so ~ingannāre~ was, by one account, “to take someone in with talk,” to fool with words. Corominas treats the root as an expressive, onomatopoeic formation rather than a word with a secure Indo-European pedigree, and the deeper connections proposed for it (such as a Slavic verb for “to murmur”) remain uncertain — so the vivid “barking dog” image should be read as the favored account, not settled fact. From the same base Spanish has ~engaño~ (“deceit”), ~engañoso~ (“deceptive”), and ~desengañar~ (“to undeceive, disillusion”), whose noun ~desengaño~ is a cherished word of Spanish Golden-Age moralism.
en.engendrar:
From Latin ~ingenerāre~ (“to engender, produce, implant”), from ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~generāre~ (“to beget, bring forth”), a verb from ~genus~ (“birth, origin, kind”). All of these rest on Proto-Indo-European *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to beget, give birth”). Cognate with French ~engendrer~ and Portuguese ~engendrar~, and — through the root — with English ~generate~ and ~kin~ and German ~Kind~ (“child”).

The excrescent ~-d-~ (Latin ~generāre~ → Spanish ~engendrar~) is a phonetic wedge that Spanish routinely inserts between ~n~ and ~r~. The verb kept its core sense, “to bring life into being,” while the root fanned out spectacularly: ~género~, ~generar~, ~gente~, ~genio~, ~ingenio~, ~genital~, ~gen~ and the borrowed ~generación~ all trace to *~ǵenh₁-~.
en.enjalbegar:
From Vulgar Latin *~exalbicāre~, apparently a crossing of ~exalbāre~ and ~albicāre~ (both “to whiten”), from ~ex-~ (marking the onset of a process) and ~albicāre~ (“to be white”), from ~albus~ (“white, matte white”). Latin ~albus~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂elbʰos~ (“white”), cognate with Greek ~alphós~ and, distantly, with English ~elf~. The old form was ~jalbegar~ (also ~xalbegar~), which only later took the prefix ~en-~.

The word names a humble craft: coating a wall with whitewash or lime. Corominas traces a tangled history of variants — Salamancan ~jabelgar~ shows a metathesis of the ~l~, and forms like ~axalvegar~ are attested in the sixteenth century. From the same ~albus~ Spanish keeps ~albo~ (“white,” poetic), ~alba~ (“dawn”), ~álbum~, ~albino~ and ~albura~ (“sapwood”), plus the pigment name ~albayalde~ (“white lead”).
en.enlazar:
~enlazar~ (“to link, tie together”) is ~en-~ plus the noun ~lazo~ (“loop, bow, tie”) plus a verbal ending. ~lazo~ comes from Latin ~laqueus~ (“noose, snare”); its deeper origin is uncertain — a link to ~lacere~ (“to entice”) has been proposed but is doubted, so the trail stops securely at Latin. The Romance cousins are plain: Italian ~laccio~, Portuguese ~laço~ and French ~lacet~, while English borrowed the same root twice, as ~lace~ (through Old French) and ~lasso~ (straight from Spanish ~lazo~).

The image is a snare drawn tight, then generalized to any binding: to ~enlazar~ is to loop two things together, whether ropes, ideas or people. From ~lazo~ Spanish also formed ~lazar~ and ~lacear~ (“to lasso”), the abstract ~enlace~ (“link, connection”) and its theatrical opposite ~desenlace~ (“dénouement,” literally the untying of a plot). A highway ~enlace~ is where roads are tied into one — all keeping the ancient picture of a knot that fastens.
en.enloquecer:
A derivative of the adjective ~loco~ (“mad, crazy”) with the inchoative frame ~en-~ … ~-ecer~, the suffix continuing Latin ~-ēscere~ (which marks a change of state, “to become”). So enloquecer is literally “to become ~loco~” or “to drive someone ~loco~.” The origin of ~loco~ itself, however, is genuinely disputed: it is shared in Romance only with Portuguese ~louco~, and no account is secure.

One widely repeated proposal derives ~loco~ from Arabic ~lawqa~ (feminine of ~alwaq~, “foolish, stupid”), and this is often called the likeliest guess — but Corominas rejected it and leaned instead toward an expressive or pre-Roman Hispanic base, comparing words like ~clueca~ (“broody hen”); he concluded that none of the hypotheses convinces. Whatever its source, ~loco~ anchors a clear Spanish family: ~locura~ (“madness”), ~loquear~, ~alocado~ and the very verb ~enloquecer~.
en.enmarcar:
A prefixed derivative of ~marco~ (“frame”): ~en-~ (“in, into”) plus ~marco~ plus the verbal ending ~-ar~ — “to put into a frame.” ~Marco~ comes from a Germanic word for a boundary or sign, Frankish *~marka~, from Proto-Germanic *~markō~ (“boundary, borderland”), from Proto-Indo-European *~merǵ-~ (“edge, boundary”). It is cognate with Italian ~marca~ and — through the same Germanic root — with English ~mark~, ~march~ (a borderland, as in “the Welsh Marches”), and ~margin~ (via Latin ~margō~, from the same PIE edge-root), and with German ~Mark~ (“border region”).

The thread that ties the senses together is the edge: a ~marca~ was first a border, then a boundary-sign or token set upon a thing, then any mark, and a ~marco~ the bordering edge that runs around a picture or a door — its frame. To ~enmarcar~ is thus to set an edge around something, literally a painting and figuratively a situation seen “within a frame.” The same border-root gave Spanish ~marca~ (“mark, brand”), ~marcar~ (“to mark”), ~comarca~ (“district, region”), ~margen~ (“margin, edge”), and ~marqués~ (“marquis,” originally the lord of a border march).
en.enmendar:
A twelfth-century borrowing from Latin ~ēmendāre~ (“to correct, to free from fault”), from ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~menda~ / ~mendum~ (“fault, blemish, defect”). Latin ~mendum~ has been linked to a Proto-Indo-European *~mend-~ (“physical defect, fault”), though the exact root is uncertain and disputed. English ~amend~ and ~emend~, French ~amender~ and Italian ~emendare~ all come from the same verb.

Where the learned ~ēmendāre~ entered as the semi-cultism ~enmendar~ (“to amend, revise”), the very same Latin word also came down by the fully popular road as ~remendar~ (“to mend, patch”), with its noun ~remiendo~ (“a patch”) — a neat doublet, one bookish and one homely. From ~enmendar~ Spanish drew ~enmienda~ (“amendment”), the word for a correction to a law or a text.
en.enojar:
From Old Galician-Portuguese, borrowed from Old Occitan ~enojar~, from Vulgar Latin *~inodiāre~ (“to make hateful”), from the Latin phrase ~in odiō~ (“in hatred”), built on ~odium~ (“hatred”). Cognate with Catalan ~enutjar~, Italian ~annoiare~, French ~ennuyer~ and English ~annoy~ — the same open-vowel-plus-nasal shape running through them all.

The semantic drift is one of the loveliest in Romance: the strong Latin ~odium~ softened differently in each language. English ~annoy~ weakened into mild irritation, French ~ennui~ collapsed into world-weary boredom, and Spanish ~enojo~ settled into plain anger. From the same ~odium~ Spanish keeps the learned ~odio~ (“hatred”) and ~odiar~ (“to hate”), while the noun ~enojo~ and the adjective ~enojoso~ stay beside ~enojar~.
en.enriquecer:
~enriquecer~ (“to enrich”) is built from the prefix ~en-~, the adjective ~rico~ (“rich”) and the verb-forming suffix ~-ecer~. Its heart, ~rico~, was not inherited from Latin but borrowed from Germanic — from Gothic ~reiks~ (“mighty, powerful”), reflecting Proto-Germanic *~rīkijaz~ (“royal, powerful”). That word ultimately traces to Proto-Indo-European *~h₃rḗǵs~ (“king, ruler”), the same root that gave Latin ~rēx~; Germanic itself may have taken it from Celtic *~rīxs~.

Because ~reiks~ meant power before it meant money, ~rico~ first denoted the noble and mighty and only later the merely wealthy — a nuance you can still feel when ~rico~ is used to mean “delicious.” Through the same Indo-European king-word Spanish is cousin to English ~rich~, German ~reich~ and French ~riche~, while sharing the deeper root with Latin ~rēx~. From this family Spanish keeps ~riqueza~ (“wealth”), ~ricura~ and even the name ~Ricardo~ (“strong ruler”).
en.ensayar:
From the noun ~ensayo~ plus the verb-forming suffix ~-ar~. ~Ensayo~ was inherited from Late Latin ~exagium~ (“a weighing, an assaying”), a noun built on Latin ~exigō~, ~exigere~ (“to weigh out, measure, demand”), which is ~ex-~ (“out”) plus ~agō~ (“to drive, lead, set in motion”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”). Through the same Late Latin word Spanish is cognate with French ~essai~ and, by later borrowing, with English ~essay~ and ~assay~.

In Latin an ~exagium~ was literally the act of weighing a thing on a balance, and the word entered Castilian first as the assayer's term for testing the purity of a metal. From that careful trial the sense widened to any attempt or test, and finally to the theatrical ~ensayo~ (“rehearsal”), the trial run before a performance — which is what ~ensayar~ most often means today. The same root ~agō~ seeded a broad Spanish family, among them ~exigir~ (“to demand”), ~examen~, ~exacto~, ~agente~ and ~acción~.
en.ensañar:
Of uncertain origin. Corominas holds that it goes back to Latin ~insania~ (“madness, frenzy”), through a Vulgar Latin verb *~insaniāre~ (“to drive mad, to enrage”), from which the noun ~saña~ (“blind rage, fury”) was later back-formed; ~insania~ is ~in-~ (here intensive) plus ~sānus~ (“healthy, sane”). A rival proposal instead derives ~saña~ from a Vulgar Latin *~sania~, a popular form of Latin ~sanies~ (“diseased matter, venom”). Either way the family is bound up with Latin ~sānus~, source by borrowing of English ~sane~ and ~insane~.

The reflexive ~ensañarse~ names not mere anger but a cruel relentlessness — to keep hurting someone or something already beaten, to gloat in the harm. That step from ~saña~ (“fury”) to deliberate cruelty is what colours the modern verb. If the ~insania~ account is right, the image beneath it is madness itself: rage as a kind of temporary derangement. From the same ~sānus~ Spanish keeps a wholly opposite, healing branch — ~sano~ (“healthy”), ~sanar~ (“to heal”), ~sanidad~ and ~insano~.
en.enseñar:
From Vulgar Latin *~insignāre~ (“to mark, point out”), a reshaping of Latin ~insignīre~ (“to distinguish, mark”), from ~in-~ (“on, upon”) plus ~signum~ (“sign, mark”). ~signum~ is itself of uncertain deeper origin, traced by different scholars either to Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut”) or to *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). Cognate with French ~enseigner~, Italian ~insegnare~ and Portuguese ~ensinar~; and, by way of ~signum~, with English ~sign~.

The road from “to mark” to “to teach” runs through “to point out, show”: teaching is marking knowledge onto a mind, and tellingly ~enseñar~ still means both “to teach” and “to show” — « me enseñó la casa » may be a lesson or a tour. From ~signum~ Spanish drew a large family: ~seña~, ~señal~, ~señalar~, ~diseñar~ (“to design,” literally to mark out), ~insignia~ and ~signo~ itself. And because that root is contested, the tempting gloss “to cut a mark” has to stay a maybe: the sign may be something cut — or something that lets one follow.
en.ensillar:
From ~en-~ (“in, on”) plus ~silla~ (“chair; saddle”) plus the suffix ~-ar~. ~Silla~ comes from Old Spanish ~siella~, from Latin ~sella~ (“seat, saddle”), from Proto-Italic *~sedlā~, from Proto-Indo-European *~sed-~ (“to sit”). Cognate with French ~selle~ and Italian ~sella~ (both “saddle”), and — through the same root — with English ~sit~, ~settle~ and ~sedentary~. English ~saddle~ belongs to the same “sit” family but reached English down the Germanic line, so it is a relative rather than a direct cognate.

Latin ~sella~ was a seat of any kind — a stool, a chair, the seat a rider took on a horse — and it is this last sense that lives on in the Spanish ~silla~ used for a saddle. To ~ensillar~ is therefore to put the ~silla~ on the animal, literally to set it seated for the rider. The “sit” root *~sed-~ runs deep in Spanish through learned Latin borrowings: ~sede~ (“see, seat”), ~sedimento~, ~residir~, ~presidir~ and ~sesión~.
en.entender:
From Latin ~intendere~ (“to stretch toward, direct, aim at”), formed from ~in-~ (“toward”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, extend”). It is cognate with Italian ~intendere~, Portuguese ~entender~ and French ~entendre~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~intend~; the bare root shows up in English ~tend~ and ~thin~.

The Latin phrase ~intendere animum~ meant “to direct the mind toward” something; that mental aiming narrowed from “pay attention” to “grasp, understand.” A neat contrast: French ~entendre~ took the same verb and settled on “to hear” instead. The root *~ten-~ is remarkably fertile in Spanish: besides ~atender~ (“to attend to”) and ~intención~, it yields ~tensión~, the Greek-derived ~tono~, and — unexpectedly — ~tienda~ (“shop; tent”), originally a “stretched” awning under which goods were sold.
en.enterar:
~Enterar~ derives from the adjective ~entero~ (“whole, entire”) plus ~-ar~. ~Entero~ comes from Latin ~integrum~, accusative of ~integer~ (“untouched, whole”), formed from ~in-~ (“not”) and the root of ~tangere~ (“to touch”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~teh₂g-~ (“to touch”). It is cognate with English ~integer~ and ~entire~, French ~entier~, and Italian ~intero~.

~Integer~ meant literally “untouched,” hence “whole, intact.” The verb first meant “to make whole, to complete,” and its modern sense “to inform” grew from that: to inform someone is to make their knowledge complete, to put them fully in the picture — whence reflexive ~enterarse~ (“to find out, become aware”). In parts of Latin America ~enterar~ also keeps the “make whole” idea as “to pay in full.” Relatives include ~entereza~ (“integrity, fortitude”), ~integridad~, and ~integrar~; and, from ~tangere~, ~tacto~, ~tangente~, ~contagio~, and ~intacto~.
en.enterrar:
A compound of the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”), the noun ~tierra~ (“earth, land”) and the suffix ~-ar~. ~tierra~ descends from Latin ~terra~, from Proto-Italic *~tersā~ (“dry land”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ters-~ (“dry”). By that root the earth is literally “the dry one,” named in contrast to the sea, and it is cognate with Latin ~torrēre~ (“to parch,” whence “toast”) and with English ~thirst~. Romance parallels include French ~enterrer~ and Portuguese ~enterrar~.

The literal sense is “to put into the earth,” so ~enterrar~ means “to bury,” its noun ~entierro~ being “a burial, a funeral,” and its opposite ~desenterrar~ “to unearth, dig up.” The productive ~tierra~ anchors a wide family — ~terreno~ (“terrain, plot”), ~territorio~ (“territory”), ~terrestre~ (“terrestrial”), ~subterráneo~ (“underground”), ~soterrar~ (“to bury, hide away”) and even ~aterrizar~ (“to land” an aircraft, literally to come to earth). The same ~terra~ names the ~Mediterráneo~ — the sea “in the middle of the land.”
en.entrar:
Spanish ~entrar~ comes, through Old Spanish ~entrar~, from Latin ~intrāre~ (“to go in, enter”), a verb built on ~intrā~ (“within, inside”). ~intrā~ is the feminine ablative of an adjective going back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁énteros~ (“inner”), a comparative formed from *~h₁én~ (“in”) with the contrastive suffix *~-teros~. The word thus meant, quite literally, to move into the more-inner space. English ~enter~ (borrowed through Old French ~entrer~) and Italian ~entrare~ are close relatives, as are Portuguese and Catalan ~entrar~.

The Latin sense was concrete and spatial, and Spanish ~entrar~ keeps that physical core — to enter a room, a country, a stage — while branching into countless idioms: ~entrar en razón~ (“to see reason”), ~entrar en calor~ (“to warm up”), the new year that ~entra~. From the same ~intrā~/~inter~ stock Spanish holds ~entrada~ (“entrance, ticket”), ~entrante~ (“incoming; starter course”), and ~adentro~; the sister preposition ~inter~ underlies ~interior~, ~íntimo~, and ~entre~ (“between”) itself. The comparative shape of *~h₁énteros~ — “more inward” — reminds us that Latin often located actions not just in space but along a scale of depth.
en.entregar:
From Latin ~integrāre~ (“to make whole, renew, restore”), a verb built on the adjective ~integer~ (“whole, untouched, intact”), which is itself ~in-~ (“not”) plus the root of ~tangere~ (“to touch”) — literally “untouched.” The Proto-Indo-European root is *~teh₂g-~ (“to touch, handle”). ~Entregar~ is a semi-learned descendant that underwent metathesis (~integrāre~ → ~entregar~); its fully learned doublet is ~integrar~ (“to integrate”). The pair is cognate with Portuguese ~entregar~, Italian ~integrare~ and English ~integrate~ and ~integer~.

The semantic path is unexpected. Latin ~integrāre~ meant to make something whole again, to restore it; Old Spanish ~entregar~ first meant to give back or restore what was owed, and from “to hand back” it slid to the general “to hand over, deliver” it means today. So the modern act of delivering a parcel hides an older idea of restoring something to wholeness. From the same ~tangere~ Spanish also has ~tangible~, ~tañer~ (“to play an instrument, to ring”), ~contacto~ and ~intacto~ (“untouched”), while ~integer~ lives on in ~íntegro~ (“whole, upright”) and ~entrega~ (“delivery, devotion”).
en.entremeter:
From ~entre-~ (“between, among,” from Latin ~inter~) plus ~meter~ (“to put in”), the pair reflecting Latin ~intromittere~ (“to let in, introduce”); it is attested in Spanish from around 1300. ~Meter~ descends from Latin ~mittere~ (“to send, to put”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, remove”). Cognate with French ~mettre~ and Italian ~mettere~, and — through borrowings of ~mittere~ into English — with ~mission~, ~missile~ and ~admit~.

To ~entremeter~ is literally to put a thing in among others, to insert it; and the reflexive ~entremeterse~ (with its common variant ~entrometerse~) shifted that spatial idea to a social one — to insert oneself where one is not wanted, to meddle. The same ~mittere~ gave Spanish a large working family, among them ~meter~ itself, ~someter~ (“to subject”), ~prometer~ (“to promise”), ~admitir~ and ~misión~.
en.entrenar:
Spanish ~entrenar~ is a nineteenth-century borrowing from French ~entraîner~ (“to drag along; to train”), a compound of ~en-~ (“in, into”) and ~traîner~ (“to drag, pull”). ~traîner~ descends from a Vulgar Latin *~tragināre~, a frequentative ultimately rooted in Latin ~trahere~ (“to drag, draw”) — the very verb behind ~extraer~. English ~train~ comes from the same French stock, so ~entrenar~ and ~train~ are, at bottom, the same word.

The metaphor is one of “drawing along”: a coach draws a pupil forward through discipline and repetition. French ~entraîner~ carried both a literal sense (“to drag, sweep away”) and the athletic one, and Spanish borrowed chiefly the second, specialized meaning for sport. The Proto-Indo-European source of ~trahere~ is uncertain — a root *~tragʰ-~ is often proposed, but some derive the Latin from a non-Indo-European substrate word — so the deepest step stays open. From ~entrenar~ Spanish coined ~entrenador~ (“coach, trainer”), ~entrenamiento~ (“training”), and ~entreno~.
en.entretener:
A compound of ~entre-~ (“between, among,” from Latin ~inter~) and ~tener~ (“to hold,” from Latin ~tenēre~), built on the model of Old French ~entretenir~ (“to hold together, keep up”). ~tenēre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~tenēō~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). It is cognate with Italian ~intrattenere~, Portuguese ~entreter~, and French ~entretenir~, and — through that French verb — with English ~entertain~; through the deep root it is also kin to Ancient Greek ~τείνω~ (teínō, “to stretch”) and English ~thin~.

The literal image is “to hold in between,” hence to keep something going, to maintain. From “keep occupied” the sense slid gently to “keep pleasantly occupied,” that is, to amuse — the exact same drift that turned English ~entertain~ from “to maintain” into “to divert.” Spanish still hears both: to ~entretener~ someone can mean to amuse them or, less kindly, to hold them up and make them wait, and reflexive ~entretenerse~ is to amuse oneself or to dawdle. From the same ~tener~ come ~mantener~, ~contener~, ~detener~, ~sostener~, ~obtener~, and the noun ~entretenimiento~ (“entertainment”).
en.entrevistar:
A denominal verb from the noun ~entrevista~ (“interview, meeting”), which is itself ~entre-~ (“between,” from Latin ~inter~) plus ~vista~ (“sight, view,” the past participle of ~ver~, from Latin ~vidēre~, “to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”). The compound was modeled on French ~entrevue~ (“interview”), from ~s’entrevoir~ (“to see one another, to catch a glimpse of each other”), and it is cognate through the root with English ~vision~ and ~wit~ and German ~wissen~ (“to know”).

The heart of the word is mutual sight: an ~entrevista~ is an occasion on which two parties see one another, the ~entre-~ making the seeing reciprocal. From that came the sense of a formal meeting, and then, through nineteenth-century journalism, the sense of a reporter’s questioning; ~entrevistar~ now serves equally for a job interview and a talk-show chat. The ~vidēre~ root runs deep in Spanish: besides ~ver~ and ~vista~ it gave ~visión~, ~visible~, ~evidente~, ~prever~ (“to foresee”), ~revisar~ (“to review”), and even ~vídeo~ (Latin “I see”).
en.enumerar:
From Latin ~ēnumerāre~ (“to count out, reckon up”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~numerāre~ (“to count”), itself from ~numerus~ (“number”). ~Numerus~ goes back through Proto-Italic to Proto-Indo-European *~nem-~ (“to allot, distribute; to take”). Through that root ~enumerar~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~némō~ (“to distribute, apportion”) — the source of ~nómos~ (“law”) and of the ~-nomy~ in ~economy~ and ~astronomy~ — and with Germanic verbs of taking, Gothic ~niman~ and German ~nehmen~ (“to take”). Romance carried the verb on as Italian ~enumerare~, French ~énumérer~, and Portuguese ~enumerar~.

The literal force of ~ēnumerāre~ was to “count out” — to run through items one by one until the tally is complete, which is exactly what ~enumerar~ still does when it lists things in order. The kernel idea in *~nem-~ was fair distribution: to number something was to portion it out. That seed grew a numerous Spanish family — ~número~, ~numeroso~, ~numeral~, ~innumerable~, and ~numerador~ — while the Greek branch of the same root supplies the learned ~economía~ and ~autonomía~, literally a “household-apportioning” and a “self-law.”
en.enviar:
Spanish ~enviar~ comes from Old Spanish ~enviar~, from Late Latin ~inviāre~ (“to send on a journey, dispatch”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in, on”) and ~via~ (“way, road”). To ~inviāre~ was literally to put someone or something ~in viam~ — “on the road.” ~via~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~weǵʰ-~ (“to go, transport in a vehicle”), one of the great roots of the family: it gave Latin ~vehere~ (“to carry”) and English ~way~, ~weigh~, ~wain~, and ~wagon~, plus the borrowings ~via~, ~vehicle~, and ~voyage~. French ~envoyer~ is the exact cognate — and English ~envoy~ (“a messenger”) is simply its past participle ~envoyé~ borrowed whole.

The metaphor is transparent and durable: sending is still, etymologically, a matter of setting something on its way. From ordinary dispatch Spanish extended ~enviar~ to letters, messengers, goods, and now email and messages (~enviar un correo~, “to send an email”). A quirk of stress splits its present tense — the accent falls on the ~i~ in ~envío~ and ~envías~ but not in ~enviamos~ — a hiatus Spanish marks with a written accent. The verb’s own nouns are ~envío~ (“shipment, dispatch”) and ~enviado~ (“envoy, correspondent”). From the same ~via~ Spanish also keeps ~vía~, ~viaje~, ~enviar~’s cousin ~desviar~ (“to divert”), ~obvio~ (“obvious,” literally “in the way”), and ~trivial~ (from ~trivium~, “a place where three roads meet”).
en.envolver:
From Latin ~involvere~ (“to roll into, wrap up, envelop”), from ~in-~ (“in, into”) plus ~volvere~ (“to roll, turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *~welH-~ (“to turn, roll, wind”). Cognates: Italian ~involgere~, Portuguese ~envolver~; and from ~volvere~, English ~involve~, ~evolve~ and ~revolve~, plus ~volume~ (originally a rolled scroll).

To ~involvere~ was literally to roll a thing up in a wrapping; Spanish ~envolver~ keeps the physical “to wrap” and extends it to “to involve, mix (someone) up” in an affair. Its sibling ~volver~ (“to return, turn”) comes from plain ~volvere~, and the pair ~revolver~ (“to stir up”) and ~revólver~ (the firearm, named for its rotating cylinder) share the root. Other Spanish kin: ~volumen~, ~involucrar~, ~revuelta~ and ~desenvolver~ (“to unwrap; to develop”). The same *~welH-~ also became English ~wallow~ and Greek-derived ~hélice~ (“helix”).
en.equilibrar:
From Latin ~aequilibrāre~ (“to balance evenly”), from ~aequilibris~ (“in even balance”), a compound of ~aequus~ (“equal, level”) and ~libra~ (“a balance, a pair of scales; a pound weight”). The origin of ~libra~ is uncertain: its Proto-Italic form was something like *~līðrā~, which also surfaced in Ancient Greek ~lítra~ (a unit of weight), the source of English ~litre~. ~aequus~, too, is of unknown origin. So the compound is transparent even though its parts are etymologically hazy.

The image is a two-pan scale hanging level: to ~equilibrar~ is to make the two sides weigh the same. From ~libra~ (“scales; pound”) Spanish and its neighbors drew a surprising harvest — the zodiac sign ~Libra~ (“the Scales”), the old currency names Italian ~lira~ and French ~livre~, and the pound-sterling symbol £, a stylized L for ~libra~. From ~aequus~ come ~igual~, ~igualar~, ~ecuador~, and ~equinoccio~. And the whole idea lives on in ~equilibrio~ (“balance, equilibrium”) and ~equilibrista~ (“tightrope walker, acrobat”), one who makes a living by never letting the scales tip.
en.equipar:
From French ~équiper~ (“to equip, fit out”), from Old French ~esquiper~ (“to fit out a ship, load a vessel”), a borrowing from Old Norse ~skipa~ (“to arrange, manage, fit out a ship”), a verb from ~skip~ (“ship”), from Proto-Germanic *~skipą~. It is thus a cognate of English ~ship~ and ~skipper~, German ~Schiff~, and Dutch ~schip~ — and, more distantly, of English ~equip~ itself, borrowed from the same French source.

The word began as pure seafaring vocabulary: to ~skipa~ a longship was to crew and provision it for a voyage. As the term passed through French, the nautical sense widened to “provide with whatever is needed,” and by the sixteenth century it covered outfitting a person or a household for any undertaking. Spanish borrowed it in that generalized sense, and from it come ~equipo~ (“team, kit, equipment”), ~equipaje~ (“luggage” — the things you fit out a traveler with) and ~equipamiento~. The sports “team,” the traveler’s “luggage,” and the soldier’s “gear” all trace back, remarkably, to the arranging of a Viking ship.
en.equivaler:
From Latin ~aequivalēre~ (“to be worth as much, be equivalent”), a compound of ~aequi-~ (“equally,” from ~aequus~, “level, even, equal”) and ~valēre~ (“to be strong, be well, be worth”). The verb ~valēre~ descends through Proto-Italic *~waleō~ from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂welh₁-~ (“to be strong, to rule”). Spanish shaped ~equivaler~ on its own inherited ~valer~, following the Latin pattern. It is cognate with Italian ~equivalere~ and French ~équivaloir~, and — through ~valēre~ — kin to English ~value~, ~valiant~, and ~valor~. The first element, ~aequus~, is of uncertain origin, with no secure cognate outside Latin.

The meaning has stayed remarkably stable: ~equivaler~ is for one thing to be worth, mean, or count as much as another — in value, in force, or in effect. The image is quantitative, two quantities worth the same. From ~aequus~ Spanish also drew ~igual~ (via Old Spanish ~egual~), ~ecuación~, and ~equidad~; from ~valēre~ come ~valer~, ~valor~, ~válido~, ~valiente~, and ~evaluar~. English ~equivalent~ is this very compound borrowed whole. In use the verb takes ~a~: una milla ~equivale~ a 1,6 kilómetros — “a mile equals 1.6 kilometres.”
en.equivocar:
Spanish ~equivocar~ descends from Latin ~aequivocus~ (“having equal voice, ambiguous”), a compound of ~aequus~ (“equal, level”) and ~vōx~ / ~vocāre~ (“voice; to call”), itself a loan-translation of Greek ~homṓnymos~. The ~vōx~ element goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~wekʷ-~ (“to speak, to utter”), the source also of English ~voice~ and ~vocal~; ~aequus~, by contrast, has no secure Indo-European etymology and is best left unexplained. Spanish shares the adjective with Italian ~equivoco~ and English ~equivocal~.

In late Latin ~aequivocus~ was a technical term of logic and grammar for a word carrying two meanings — the root of “equivocation.” Spanish took the next step: ~equivocar~, and especially the reflexive ~equivocarse~, moved from “to be ambiguous” to plainly “to be mistaken, to get it wrong.” The two halves seeded large families. From ~aequus~ came ~igual~, ~ecuación~, ~equidad~, ~equilibrio~ and ~adecuar~; from ~vōx~ came ~voz~, ~vocal~, ~convocar~, ~provocar~ and even ~abogado~ (from ~advocātus~, “one called to aid”).
en.errar:
From Latin ~errāre~ (“to wander; to stray; to be mistaken”), from Proto-Italic *~erzāō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁ers-~ (“to be in motion, to flow”). Cognate with German ~irren~ (“to go astray, to err”) and Gothic ~airzjan~; Italian ~errare~, French ~errer~ and Portuguese ~errar~ continue the same Latin verb, and English ~err~ and ~error~ are borrowings of it.

The Latin word held both a physical and a moral sense at once — to roam without a fixed course, and thus to depart from the right path — and Spanish ~errar~ inherited the whole span, from “to wander” to “to miss the mark” to “to make a mistake.” The wandering sense survives in ~errante~ (“wandering,” as in the knight errant) while the mistaking sense fills out ~error~, ~erróneo~, ~errata~ and ~aberración~.
en.escapar:
From Vulgar Latin *~excappāre~, literally “to get out of one's cloak,” from ~ex-~ (“out of”) plus Late Latin ~cappa~ (“cloak, hooded cape”), itself of uncertain origin. The picture is a fugitive slipping free of the cloak a pursuer has grabbed. Cognate with Italian ~scappare~, French ~échapper~ and Portuguese ~escapar~; English ~escape~ came in through Old Northern French, and English ~cape~ and ~cap~ likewise descend from ~cappa~.

The garment metaphor is the memorable part: to ~escapar~ was, at root, to wriggle out of your cape and leave it in the captor's hands — capture without the cloak. From that literal escape the verb generalized to “to flee, to get free, to avoid,” and even “to leak” (as gas or water escapes). The ~cappa~ itself clothes a wide family in Spanish — ~capa~, ~capote~ and ~capucha~ — while the verb's own offshoots include ~escape~, ~escapada~ and ~escapatoria~.
en.escarbar:
From Old Spanish ~escarvar~, from Latin ~scarīfāre~ (earlier ~scariphāre~, “to scratch, to make superficial incisions”), which Latin borrowed from Ancient Greek ~σκάριφος~ (skáriphos, “stylus; a scratched outline”). This is the derivation Corominas favours, though it is not the only one proposed: some would make ~scarīfāre~ a dialectal frequentative of Latin ~scabere~ (“to scratch”), and others posit a ~scaber~ (“rough”) derivative *~scabrāre~. Cognate with English ~scarify~.

The Greek word named the light scratching of a stylus over a surface, and the Latin verb kept that sense of scraping and superficial cutting. Old Spanish ~escarvar~ shows the pretonic ~i~ syncopated and the ~f~ voiced to ~v~; the modern spelling ~escarbar~ settled later. The everyday image is a hen or a dog raking at the ground with claws or snout, and from that comes the common ~escarbadientes~ (“toothpick,” literally a tooth-scratcher).
en.escardar:
From ~es-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out”) plus ~cardo~ (“thistle”) plus the suffix ~-ar~; the related noun ~escarda~ means both the weeding-hoe and the act of weeding. ~Cardo~ descends from Latin ~cardus~, a variant of ~carduus~ (“thistle”). Through that Latin word Spanish is cognate with English ~chard~ and ~cardoon~, both names of cultivated relatives of the thistle.

To ~escardar~ is literally to clear the thistles from a field — to weed — and from the fields the verb passed easily into figurative use, to separate the bad from the good. The same Latin thistle gave Spanish the ~cardencha~ (the teasel, once used to raise the nap on cloth) and keeps the edible ~cardo~ (“cardoon”) on the table, while the weeder's hoe is still the ~escarda~ that names the whole task.
en.escarmentar:
Of disputed origin. The verb is built on the older noun ~escarmiento~ (“exemplary punishment,” attested in the 13th century), but where that noun comes from is unsettled. Corominas takes ~escarmiento~ to be a syncope of ~escarnimiento~, a derivative of ~escarnio~ (“derision, mockery”; from the Germanic word behind Old Occitan ~escarn~), the sense passing from “mockery” through “harm inflicted on someone” to “punishment meant as a warning.” An older view instead connected the verb with ~escarmenar~ (“to card, to disentangle wool,” from Latin ~ex-~ plus ~carmināre~, “to card”); another derived it from ~escarnamiento~ (“a flaying”). The Germanic ~escarnio~ account is the one now generally preferred.

Whatever its source, the meaning settled early: to ~escarmentar~ someone is to punish them so pointedly that the lesson sticks, and — reflexively and intransitively — to ~escarmentar~ is to learn one's lesson the hard way, to be chastened by a bad experience. Spanish keeps the noun ~escarmiento~ for that stinging lesson, and the neighbouring ~escarnio~ and ~escarnecer~ (“to mock, to deride”) for the derision at the root of Corominas's account.
en.escarnecer:
Spanish ~escarnecer~ (“to mock, deride”) was formed within Castilian from the noun ~escarnio~ (“scorn, mockery”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-ecer~. ~escarnio~ descends from Old Spanish ~escarnir~ (“to taunt”), which is of Germanic origin: the sources trace it to a Frankish or Old High German *~skirnjan~ (“to mock”), akin to Old High German ~skern~ (“jest, derision”), though the exact Germanic donor is uncertain. The same Germanic word spread across Romance, giving Italian ~schernire~ (and the noun ~scherno~) and Old French ~escharnir~.

The root sense was playful mockery or jesting, which in Spanish hardened into cruel derision — to ~escarnecer~ someone is to ridicule them woundingly. Medieval texts favored the verb for public shaming and insult. From the same family Spanish keeps ~escarnio~ itself, the agent noun ~escarnecedor~ (“mocker”), and ~escarnecimiento~ (“derision”). The Germanic layer it belongs to reminds us how many words for social attitudes — pride, shame, mockery — entered Ibero-Romance from the speech of Visigothic and Frankish settlers rather than from Latin.
en.esclarecer:
~esclarecer~ (“to clarify, illuminate”) comes from Latin ~exclarescere~, the prefix ~ex-~ joined to ~clarescere~ (“to grow bright”), the inchoative of ~clareo~ (“to be bright”) from the adjective ~clarus~ (“clear, bright, famous”). ~clarus~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~klāros~ (“loud”) to Proto-Indo-European *~kelh₁-~ (“to call, shout”); the primitive image was acoustic — a clear, ringing sound — which shifted to clear light. Cognates include Italian ~chiaro~ and French ~clair~, and, through the same root, German ~hell~ (“bright”) and Latin ~clāmō~ (“to shout”).

The inchoative ~-escere~ formation means “to become clear,” and Spanish kept both the literal dawn sense (~esclarecer~, “for day to break”) and the intellectual one, “to shed light on, elucidate.” A parallel sense, “to ennoble, make illustrious,” survives in the adjective ~esclarecido~ (“distinguished”). Relatives from ~clarus~ crowd the modern lexicon: ~claro~, ~aclarar~, ~claridad~, ~declarar~, ~esclarecimiento~, and the borrowed ~clarividencia~. The verb thus links the sound of a shout, the light of dawn, and the clarity of an idea under one Indo-European root.
en.escoger:
From Latin ~excolligere~ (“to gather out, pick out”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~colligere~ (“to gather, collect”), itself ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~legere~ (“to gather, pick, read”), from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to collect, gather”). Cognate through ~legere~ with Greek ~λέγω~ (“I say, pick out”) and with English ~collect~, ~elect~, and ~legend~. The verb gave Portuguese ~escolher~ and, by a parallel formation, Italian ~scegliere~.

The image inside ~escoger~ is one of selection: to “gather out” from a heap is to pick the good and leave the rest, so ~excolligere~ narrowed neatly to “to choose.” Latin ~colligere~ also entered Spanish by the ordinary, worn road, losing syllables to become ~coger~ (“to grab, take, catch”) — so ~escoger~ and ~coger~ are doublets, the learned-ish and the everyday reflexes of one Latin verb. The wider ~legere~ family fans out through Spanish: ~recoger~ (“to gather up”), ~acoger~ (“to welcome”), ~colegir~ (“to infer”), ~elegir~ (“to elect”), ~colección~ (“collection”), and ~legible~ (“legible”).
en.esconder:
From Old Spanish ~asconder~, from Latin ~abscondere~ (“to stow away, conceal”), from ~abs-~ (“away”) plus ~condere~ (“to put together, store, hide”). ~condere~ is ~con-~ (“together”) plus a ~-dere~ from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place”). Cognate with Portuguese ~esconder~ and Italian ~nascondere~; English ~abscond~ borrows the same Latin verb.

The surprise is buried in that ~-dere~: the Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put”) that ends ~condere~ is the very same root that, through Latin ~facere~, became Spanish ~hacer~ (“to do, make”) — and, in Germanic, English ~do~. So to hide and to make are, at the deepest level, kin. In Spanish the ~a-~ of ~asconder~ opened to ~e-~, giving ~esconder~, which spun off the nouns ~escondite~ and ~escondrijo~ (“hiding place”), and the children's ~escondite~ game itself.
en.escotar:
~escotar~ (“to cut a low neckline”) is a denominative verb built on ~escote~ (“neckline, décolletage”), a word tied to ~cota~ (“tunic, coat of mail”). ~cota~ reached Spanish through Old French ~cote~ from a Frankish *~kotta~ (“coarse woolen cloth, garment”) — the same Germanic source that gave English ~coat~, French ~cotte~, and Italian ~cotta~. The exact path from the garment word to the neckline verb is debated; one proposal links the low-cut curve to the rounded lower edge of a coat of arms, so the derivation is best flagged as uncertain.

Whatever the route, the meaning settled on cutting cloth away to shape an opening, especially at the neck, giving the adjective ~escotado~ (“low-cut”). Spanish also has a homonymous ~escotar~, “to pay one's share,” from a separate ~escote~ (“shared expense”), source of the idiom pagar a escote (“to split the bill”). Through medieval armor the same clothing root lives on in the ~cota de malla~ (“coat of mail”), while the fashion sense endures every time a dress is called ~escotado~.
en.escribir:
Spanish ~escribir~ descends from Latin ~scrībere~ (“to write”), whose original sense was “to scratch, to incise.” It goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kreybʰ-~ (“to scratch, to cut”), an extension of *~(s)ker-~ (“to cut,” also behind English ~shear~). Its native cognate is Greek ~skáriphos~ (“a scratching, an outline”). Tellingly, Germanic had no inherited verb for writing and simply borrowed this one from Latin — so German ~schreiben~ and Old English ~shrive~ are early loans, not true cognates. Romance kin include Italian ~scrivere~ and French ~écrire~.

The etymology preserves the physical act: to write was to gouge marks into wax, clay or stone with a stylus long before it meant putting ink to paper. From ~scrībere~ Spanish inherited a large family: ~escritura~ (“writing; Scripture; a legal deed”), ~escritor~ (“writer”), the participle ~escrito~ (“written; a document”), and the prefixed verbs ~describir~ (“to describe”) and ~inscribir~ (“to inscribe”), plus ~manuscrito~ (“manuscript,” literally hand-written).
en.escuchar:
From Old Spanish ~ascuchar~ (also ~escuchar~), from Vulgar Latin *~ascultāre~, a metathesis of Latin ~auscultāre~ (“to listen, give ear to”). The verb was built on the stem of ~auris~ (“ear,” from *~aus-~) plus a second element from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱlew-~ (“to hear”); by another account the second piece is *~ḱel-~ (“to incline”), itself linked to *~ḱlew-~. Romance kept the word everywhere: French ~écouter~, Italian ~ascoltare~, Portuguese ~escutar~.

The sound history is memorable: Latin ~auscultāre~ shed its heavy cluster through metathesis to Vulgar Latin *~ascultāre~, and the initial ~au-~ opened to ~e-~, yielding ~escuchar~. Centuries later the medical verb ~auscultar~ (“to listen to the chest”) was borrowed afresh straight from Latin, so Spanish keeps a doublet: everyday ~escuchar~ beside learned ~auscultar~, both literally “to lend an ear.” Many speakers preserve an aspectual contrast between ~oír~ (“to hear,” passive) and ~escuchar~ (“to listen,” attentive). From the same “ear” root come ~auricular~ and, of course, ~auscultar~.
en.escudar:
~escudar~ (“to shield, protect”) is a denominative of ~escudo~ (“shield”), from Latin ~scūtum~ (“shield”). ~scūtum~ is generally traced to Proto-Indo-European *~skoy-tó-m~ (“piece of wood, board”), from the root *~skey-~ (“to cut, split”) — a shield being, at root, a split plank — though some derive it instead from *~(s)kewH-~ (“to cover, protect”), so the deep root is not fully settled. Cognates include Italian ~scudo~, Portuguese ~escudo~, French ~écu~, and Old Irish ~scíath~ (“shield”).

The verb runs the metaphor forward: to ~escudar~ is to put a shield before something, and reflexively ~escudarse~ (“to shield oneself”) commonly means to hide behind an excuse or authority. The noun ~escudo~ named not only the weapon but the heraldic coat of arms and, from the device stamped on it, several ~escudo~ coins and currencies. From the same base Spanish keeps ~escudero~ (“squire, shield-bearer”) and the diminutive ~escudete~. The image of interposing a barrier — literal in battle, figurative in speech — has kept the word vivid for a thousand years.
en.escupir:
~escupir~ (“to spit”) is traditionally derived from a Late Latin *~exconspuere~, built on ~conspuere~ (“to spit upon”), an intensive of ~spuere~ (“to spit”). ~spuere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~spujō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~(s)ptyew-~ (“to spit”), an expressive root imitating the act; it is cognate with English ~spew~ and Ancient Greek ~πτύω~ (~ptúō~). Because the initial ~esc-~ is hard to explain from ~conspuere~, Corominas judged the Spanish form to be at least partly onomatopoeic — reshaped by the very sound of spitting — so its exact descent is disputed.

Either way, the word belongs to a family of Indo-European spitting verbs whose forms seem to mime the gesture. Spanish shows the double route clearly: alongside popular ~escupir~ it kept the learned ~esputo~ (“sputum”), taken straight from Latin ~sputum~, the participle of ~spuere~. Everyday derivatives include ~escupitajo~ (“gob of spit”) and ~escupidera~ (“spittoon”). Few word-families wear their sound-symbolic origin so openly.
en.escurrir:
In its “drain” sense, ~escurrir~ descends from Latin ~excurrĕre~ (“to run out, run off”), the prefix ~ex-~ on ~currere~ (“to run”). ~currere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~korzō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). Cognates fill the Romance world — Italian ~correre~, French ~courir~, Portuguese ~correr~ — and the same root reached English through Latin and French in borrowings like ~current~, ~course~, and ~corridor~. A separate homonym ~escurrir~ (“to slip”) is instead referred to Vulgar Latin *~excorrigere~ (“to lead out”).

The path of meaning is vivid: liquid that “runs out” of a cloth or dish is liquid draining away, so ~escurrir~ came to mean to wring, drain, or let drip. Reflexive ~escurrirse~ keeps the older motion sense, “to slip or slide off.” The ~currere~ family is one of the largest in Spanish, giving ~correr~, ~corriente~, ~correo~ (“mail,” once carried at a run), ~concurrir~, ~ocurrir~, ~discurrir~, ~recurrir~, and ~escorrentía~ (“runoff”). Behind them all runs a single Indo-European idea of running.
en.esforzar:
From ~es-~ (an intensive prefix from Latin ~ex-~) and ~forzar~ (“to force”). ~forzar~ continues Vulgar Latin *~fortiāre~, from Latin ~fortis~ (“strong”), Old Latin ~forctis~. The deeper root is disputed: it is traced either to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰerǵʰ-~ (“high, lofty”) or to *~dʰerǵʰ-~ (“to be firm”), and the sources do not settle between them. Cognates crowd the Romance languages — Italian ~sforzare~, French ~efforcer~ — and English borrowed the family as ~force~, ~effort~ and ~fort~.

Built on ~fortis~, ~esforzar~ literally means to apply strength outward; in practice it lives as the reflexive ~esforzarse~ (“to strive, exert oneself”), whose noun is ~esfuerzo~ (“effort”). The same Latin adjective seeded ~fuerte~ (“strong”), ~fuerza~ (“strength”), ~forzoso~ (“unavoidable”), ~forzudo~ (“brawny”) and ~reforzar~ (“to reinforce”). Music borrowed the Italian cousin whole in ~sforzando~ — a note played with sudden force.
en.esmerar:
~esmerar~ (“to take great care, do with pains”) descends from a Vulgar Latin *~exmerāre~ (“to purify, refine”), the prefix ~ex-~ on ~merus~ (“pure, unmixed” — said above all of undiluted wine). ~merus~ is the source of Spanish ~mero~ (“mere, sheer”) and of the English adjective ~mere~; the Vulgar Latin verb also gave Portuguese ~esmerar~ and Galician ~esmerar~.

The semantic thread runs from purifying to polishing to taking pains: to refine metal or wine by removing its dross became, figuratively, to perfect one's work by removing every flaw. Hence reflexive ~esmerarse~ (“to go to great lengths, do one's best”) and the noun ~esmero~ (“meticulous care”), with the participle-adjective ~esmerado~ (“careful, painstaking”). The image of removing impurity to leave something pure survives too in ~mero~ itself. Where English says someone worked with great care, Spanish can say they acted con ~esmero~ — literally, having purified the task down to its essence.
en.espantar:
~espantar~ (“to scare, frighten”) comes from Old Spanish ~espantar~, from a Vulgar Latin *~expaventāre~ (“to terrify”), a frequentative built on Latin ~expavēre~ (“to dread”), from ~pavēre~ (“to be struck with fear, tremble”). The deeper root is uncertain: ~pavēre~ has been linked to a Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂w-~ (“to strike”) — fear as a blow to the heart — but the connection is disputed, so it is best left tentative. Romance cognates are clear, though: Italian ~spaventare~, French ~épouvanter~, Catalan and Portuguese ~espantar~.

The sense held steady at frightening or driving off in fright; ~espantar~ moscas is to shoo flies, and something ~espantoso~ is dreadful. From the same ~pavēre~ Spanish also inherited ~pavor~ (“dread”) and its family ~pávido~, ~despavorido~ (“terrified, panic-stricken”), and the learned ~pavura~. The everyday noun is ~espanto~ (“fright, dismay”), and in much of Latin America ¡qué ~espanto~! is a common cry of horror. Fear that once felt like a physical strike still echoes in the word.
en.especializar:
A modern, learned coinage: the adjective ~especial~ (“special, particular”) plus the productive verb-forming suffix ~-izar~ (ultimately from Greek ~-ίζειν~ via Latin ~-izāre~). ~especial~ descends from Latin ~speciālis~ (“of a particular kind”), from ~speciēs~ (“appearance, kind”), from ~specere~ (“to look at”), from Proto-Indo-European *~speḱ-~ (“to observe”). The Spanish verb was shaped in the 1800s under the pull of French ~spécialiser~.

Unlike verbs inherited by word of mouth over centuries, ~especializar~ was assembled from Latin parts by scholars in the modern age. The learned ~speciēs~ even has a popular twin: worn down through everyday speech, the same Latin word also became ~especia~ (“spice”). The root *~speḱ-~, “to look,” is among the most productive in the language: from it Spanish has ~especie~, ~especial~, ~espejo~ (“mirror,” from ~speculum~), ~espía~, ~espectáculo~ and ~aspecto~, while English, from the same Latin stock, has ~special~, ~species~, ~spy~ and ~spectacle~. To specialize, then, is to look ever more closely at one narrow ~especie~ of thing.
en.especificar:
~Especificar~ comes from Late Latin ~specificāre~, from ~specificus~ (“of a particular kind”), from ~speciēs~ (“kind, appearance, a seeing”) plus ~-ficāre~ (a combining form of ~facere~, “to make”). ~Speciēs~ belongs to ~specere~ (“to look at”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~speḱ-~ (“to observe”). It is cognate with English ~specify~, French ~spécifier~, and Italian ~specificare~ — and, through the root, with German ~spähen~ (“to spy, peer”).

~Speciēs~ first meant “a look, an appearance,” then “a kind” (things that look alike) — the sense biology later fixed. To ~especificar~ is thus to state the kind precisely. The seeing-root fanned out enormously: ~especie~ and its doublet ~especia~ (“spice,” originally “a particular kind” of goods), ~espejo~ (“mirror,” from ~speculum~), ~espectáculo~, ~aspecto~, ~espécimen~, ~sospechar~ (“to suspect,” to look up at), and ~perspectiva~. That a spice and a species share a word is the tidy surprise here: both are just “a kind of thing.”
en.esperar:
From Old Spanish ~esperar~, from Latin ~spērāre~ (“to hope”), a verb built on the noun ~spēs~ (“hope”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~speh₁-~ (“to thrive, prosper”). Cognate with Italian ~sperare~, French ~espérer~, and Portuguese ~esperar~, and — through the same Latin stem — with English ~prosper~, ~desperate~, and ~despair~, this last from ~dēspērāre~ (“to lose hope”).

As with ~estar~ and ~escuela~, Spanish grew a prothetic ~e-~ before the awkward ~sp-~ cluster, turning ~spērāre~ into ~esperar~. More striking is a semantic merger unusual among the big Romance languages: ~esperar~ carries both “to hope” and “to wait, expect,” so the same verb that voices optimism also names the patience it demands — context and prepositions do the sorting, as in ~esperar a~ someone (wait) versus ~esperar que~ something happen (hope).
