The root flowered into ~esperanza~ (“hope”), ~espera~ (“a wait”), and the darker ~desesperar~ and ~desesperado~ (“to despair”; “desperate”), alongside ~inesperado~ (“unexpected”).
en.espulgar:
From Vulgar Latin *~expulicāre~, from Latin ~ex-~ (“out, off”) and ~pūlex~ (stem ~pūlic-~), “flea,” a word traced to Proto-Indo-European *~plus-~. The verb has close Romance cousins in Catalan ~espuçar~, French ~épucer~, and Italian ~spulciare~, all built on the same insect.

Etymologically the verb means “to take the fleas off” someone or something; from that literal grooming it widened to the removal of lice and other vermin, and then turned figurative — to ~espulgar~ a text or an account is to pick through it minutely, item by item. The Latin flea left a small family in Spanish: ~pulga~ (“flea”), ~pulgón~ (“aphid, plant louse”), and the adjective ~pulguiento~ (“flea-ridden”). The image of stripping something clean, parasite by parasite, is what still colors the verb's careful, faintly destructive tone.
en.esquilmar:
A verb of uncertain origin, derived from the noun ~esquilmo~ (“the yield or produce of land and livestock”). Corominas proposed a Vulgar Latin base *~excymulāre~, connected to ~cumulus~ “heap” — the same root that, through ~cumulāre~, gave ~colmar~ (“to fill to the brim”) — with the modern consonant cluster arising by metathesis and reinforced by ~quilma~, a dialectal word for the sack used at harvest time. Another account traces it instead to a Latin *~exculmāre~, “to strip of stalks”; the question remains unsettled.

The verb's core sense is agricultural and slightly ruthless: to draw off everything a field, tree, or flock can give — to ~esquilmar~ the land is to work it to exhaustion. From that came the figurative modern meaning, to drain or bleed dry any source of wealth, so one can ~esquilmar~ a company, a client, or a natural resource. The related ~esquilmo~ survives as a rural term for the season's yield, especially of a flock. Whatever its exact Latin root, the verb has always carried the picture of taking so much that little is left behind — the fruit stripped from the branch, the wool from the sheep.
en.esquivar:
From Old Spanish ~esquivar~, from the adjective ~esquivo~ (“aloof, disdainful, wary”), of Germanic origin: from a Gothic *~skiuhs~ “shy, timid” (or the parallel Frankish *~skiuhan~ that reached Spanish through Old French ~eschiver~ and Occitan). Behind them stands Proto-Germanic *~skeuhwaz~ “shy, afraid.” The word is thus a cousin of English ~shy~ and ~eschew~, German ~scheu~, and Italian ~schivare~.

The adjective ~esquivo~ described a person who kept others at a distance — shy, standoffish, hard to approach — and the verb first meant to shun or spurn. From “to keep away from someone” it slid naturally to the physical sense of ducking out of the way, which now dominates: one ~esquiva~ a blow, a question, a tax, a responsibility. Modern Spanish keeps both the wary adjective ~esquivo~ and the nimble verb ~esquivar~, along with the noun ~esquive~ (“a dodge, a sidestep”). It is a rare case of a Germanic warrior-culture word for fear and avoidance surviving, softened, into an everyday verb about ducking a punch or a bill.
en.establecer:
From Old Spanish ~establecer~, from Latin ~stabilīre~ (“to make firm, to establish”), a verb from the adjective ~stabilis~ (“steady, firm”), from ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate with French ~établir~, Italian ~stabilire~, and Portuguese ~estabelecer~; English ~establish~ was borrowed through Old French ~establir~, and its unetymological -sh reflects the Old French stressed stem.

Spanish reshaped the inherited verb with the inchoative suffix ~-ecer~ (from Latin ~-ēscere~, “to become”), the same ending seen in ~crecer~ and ~conocer~ — so ~establecer~ literally colors “to make firm” with a sense of coming-to-stand. The e- at the front is the familiar Spanish prop-vowel that Latin ~st-~ always acquires (compare ~estar~, ~escuela~). All of this rests on the great PIE root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”), one of the most productive in the language: from it Spanish also has ~estable~, ~estabilidad~, ~establecimiento~, ~estado~, and ~estar~ itself.
en.estallar:
By the account of Corominas, ~estallar~ (“to burst, explode”) arose as a metathesis of an older ~astellar~ (“to shatter into splinters”), the vowels swapping to turn ~astellar~ into ~estallar~. That verb was formed on ~astilla~ (“splinter, chip”), from Late Latin ~astella~ (“little splinter”), a diminutive of ~astula~, itself a variant of Latin ~assula~ (“chip, shaving of wood”). The chain reaches back to Latin ~assis~ (“a cut, board”), attested since Plautus. The word thus belongs, at root, to the vocabulary of splitting wood rather than of fire or explosion.

The semantic leap is easy to picture: dry wood that ~estalla~ splits apart with a sharp crack, and from that violent splintering the verb generalized to any bursting — a bomb, a tire, a storm, a war, or a fit of laughter that “bursts” out. It is worth flagging that this splinter etymology is Corominas’s reconstruction, resting on the proposed metathesis ~astellar~ → ~estallar~ rather than on a directly attested older spelling. The same ~astilla~ root gives modern Spanish ~astillar~ (“to splinter”), ~astillero~ — a shipyard, once a place piled with wooden ~astillas~ — and the noun ~estallido~ (“a burst, bang, outbreak”).
en.estar:
From Latin ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Italic *~stāō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate with Italian ~stare~ and Portuguese ~estar~, and — through the same root — with English ~stand~ and ~stay~ and French ~ester~, an Old French verb now surviving only as a legal term.

Spanish inherited two verbs from Latin's copula system and split the work of “to be” between them: ~ser~ (from ~esse~, reinforced by ~sedēre~, “to sit”) carries permanent, essential being, while ~estar~ (from ~stāre~, “to stand”) carries location, state, and condition — literally, how something “stands” at a given moment. That is why someone ~es~ tall but ~está~ tired. The past participle ~estado~ (“been; state”) gave the noun ~estado~ (“state, condition,” and by extension the political “State”). The same PIE root *~steh₂-~ seeded a vast family of Spanish words, among them ~estación~, ~estable~, ~estatua~, ~constante~, ~restar~, and ~estatuto~.
en.estimar:
Spanish ~estimar~ comes from Latin ~aestimāre~ (older ~aestumāre~, “to value, to appraise, to reckon”), taken in as a learned word; Old Spanish also had the worn popular form ~asmar~ (“to reckon, judge”), long since obsolete. French ~estimer~, Italian ~stimare~, and Portuguese ~estimar~ share the source, and through French ~estimer~ English gained both ~esteem~ and ~estimate~.

The deep origin of ~aestimāre~ is disputed. It has traditionally been analyzed as ~aes~ (“copper, bronze,” hence money) plus a second element meaning “to cut,” yielding roughly *~ais-temos~, “one who cuts (i.e. mints) copper” — an appealing image of the money-valuer. But the connection is far from secure; de Vaan judges it “not very credible,” so it is best flagged as a proposal, not a fact. What is certain is the semantic core “to set a value on,” which in Spanish branched into both “to calculate” (~estimación~) and “to hold dear” (~estima~; ~estimado~, “dear” in a letter’s salutation).
en.estimular:
From Latin ~stimulāre~ (“to goad, prick, spur on”), a denominal verb from ~stimulus~ (“a goad, a pointed stick for driving cattle”). ~stimulus~ is usually traced to Proto-Indo-European *~steyg-~ (“to prick, be sharp”) — the root of Greek ~stízein~ (“to prick”) and ~stígma~, and of Latin ~īnstīgāre~ (“to goad on”) — though de Vaan cautions that the internal Latin group (~stilus~, ~stimulus~, ~stiva~) may not all belong together. Spanish ~estimular~ is a learned borrowing, with the prosthetic ~e-~ Spanish adds before initial ~s-~ plus consonant. Cognate with English ~stimulate~, Italian ~stimolare~, and French ~stimuler~.

The image underneath is agricultural and sharp: a ~stimulus~ was the literal pointed stick a driver jabbed into oxen, and to ~stimulāre~ was to jab. The metaphor moved inward — from pricking an animal's flank to pricking a person's will — so that ~estimular~ came to mean “to rouse, encourage, spur on” without any physical point at all. Spanish keeps the noun ~estímulo~ (“stimulus, incentive”) alongside the verb. Through the same PIE root ~estimular~ is distantly kin to ~instigar~ (“to instigate”), which carries the same picture of goading someone forward. English preserves the sting more vividly still: a ~stimulus~ in the lab and a ~stigma~ on the skin are, at root, both little pricks.
en.estorbar:
From Latin ~exturbāre~ “to drive out, thrust away,” from ~ex-~ (“out”) + ~turbāre~ “to throw into confusion,” itself from ~turba~ “crowd, turmoil,” a word borrowed from Greek ~túrbē~. Old Spanish had ~estorvar~; the same Latin verb underlies Portuguese ~estorvar~. Through ~turbāre~ the verb is kin to Spanish ~turbar~, ~disturbar~, and ~perturbar~, and to English ~disturb~ and ~trouble~.

The Latin verb literally meant to disperse a crowd — to drive the ~turba~ out — and Spanish narrowed that pushing-away into “to get in the way, to impede.” What began as scattering people became placing an obstacle in someone's path; to ~estorbar~ is to be the thing that hinders. The noun ~estorbo~ (“hindrance, nuisance, encumbrance”) followed. It is worth noticing how the same ~turba~ that means a disorderly mob gave both the calm-shattering ~perturbar~ and the humbler ~estorbar~ — one disturbs the mind, the other merely blocks the doorway.
en.estragar:
From the noun ~estrago~ (“havoc, devastation”), which comes from a Vulgar Latin verb *~stragāre~ built on Classical Latin ~strāges~ “overthrow, slaughter, ruin.” ~strāges~ belongs to the family of ~sternere~ “to spread out, strew, lay low,” from Proto-Indo-European *~sterh₃-~ “to spread, stretch out.” Through that root the verb is a distant kinsman of English ~strew~ and ~street~ (the latter from Latin ~strāta~, “a paved, ‘spread-out’ road”), and of Spanish ~estrato~ and ~consternar~.

Where the Latin noun named the slaughter left on a battlefield — bodies literally strewn on the ground — Spanish ~estrago~ kept the sense of massive ruin, and the verb ~estragar~ came to mean to spoil, corrupt, or lay waste. It can be physical (bad food ~estraga~ the stomach; drought ~estraga~ the crops) or moral (vice that corrupts). The plural ~estragos~ is especially alive in the idiom ~hacer estragos~, “to wreak havoc,” said of anything from a storm to a heartbreaker. The through-line from Latin to now is destruction spread wide — the same image of things scattered and flattened that sits in the PIE root.
en.estrenar:
From Latin ~strēna~ (“a good omen; a New Year's gift”), of probably Sabine origin, through a Vulgar Latin verb *~strēnāre~ that gave Old Spanish ~estrenar~. The noun survives across Romance as French ~étrenne~ and Italian ~strenna~, both a New Year's or holiday present, and within Spanish as ~estrena~ (“first use, first fruits”). The deeper Indo-European source is uncertain, so no root is claimed here.

The Latin ~strēna~ was the good-luck gift exchanged at the turn of the year. By one account the word goes back to the Roman goddess ~Strēnia~, in whose sacred grove the first auspicious twigs were gathered — but that derivation is disputed, so it is best taken as tradition rather than settled fact. What passed into Spanish is the notion of something newly received and used for the very first time: to ~estrenar~ is to wear, use, or show a thing for the first time — a new shirt, a car, and above all a play or film, whose opening night is its ~estreno~. From the same family come ~estreno~ (“premiere, debut”) and ~estrena~.
en.estructurar:
From ~estructura~ (“structure”), a learned borrowing of Latin ~structura~ (“a fitting-together, a building”), from ~struere~ (“to pile up, build, arrange”), whose past participle was ~structus~. The root goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~strew-~ (“to spread, strew”). Cognate with Italian ~struttura~ and French ~structure~, and, through the same root, with English ~strew~ and ~straw~.

The verb ~estructurar~ (“to structure, organize”) is young — a back-formation from the noun, spreading with nineteenth- and twentieth-century talk of social and grammatical “structures.” Its Latin ancestor ~struere~ pictured building as heaping and layering things into place, and that image seeded a broad family in Spanish: ~construir~ (“build with”), ~destruir~ (“un-build”), ~instruir~ (“build knowledge into”) and ~industria~, once the “diligence” of one who builds indoors.
en.estudiar:
Spanish ~estudiar~ comes from Latin ~studiāre~ (also read as a denominal from ~studium~, “zeal, application, study”), which belongs to the verb ~studeō~ (“to be eager, to apply oneself”). That verb goes back to Proto-Italic *~studēō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~(s)tewd-~ (“to push, thrust”), an extension of *~(s)tew-~ (“to push, hit”) — so its Latin sibling is ~tundō~ (“to beat, strike”). It is cognate with Italian ~studiare~, French ~étudier~ and Portuguese ~estudar~, and, as a borrowing from Old French, with English ~study~; through the deeper root it even touches English ~stub~ (“to strike, knock”).

The surprise is in that root: to study was once, at bottom, to push hard. Latin ~studeō~ meant an eager, driving zeal — a shoving of oneself toward a goal — and ~studium~ named that ardor before it ever named schoolwork. Only in late and medieval Latin did the “zeal” narrow to intellectual application, “to study.” The old heat still flickers in English ~studious~ and in Spanish ~estudioso~. The family the verb heads in Spanish is large and familiar: ~estudio~ (“study, studio”), ~estudiante~ (“student”), ~estudiantil~ (“student-related”), and ~estudioso~ (“studious; a scholar”) — every one of them descended from a word that first meant sheer eager pushing.
en.evaluar:
A relatively late borrowing (19th century) from French ~évaluer~ (“to evaluate, assess”), from Old French ~evaluer~, built on ~value~ (“value, worth”) — the feminine past participle of ~valoir~ (“to be worth”) — with the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~). The root is Latin ~valēre~ (“to be strong, be well, be worth”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂welh₁-~ (“to be strong”). Through that root ~valēre~ is cognate with English ~value~, ~valiant~, ~valid~ and ~wield~, with German ~walten~ (“to rule, govern”), and with the Romance kin Italian ~valutare~ and Portuguese ~avaliar~.

Where the native Spanish ~valorar~ and ~valuar~ descend straight from ~valēre~, ~evaluar~ arrived dressed in French clothes and at first meant to reckon a numerical value; it broadened to today's “to assess, judge the worth of.” The Latin ~valēre~ was above all about strength and health — a Roman closed a letter with ~valē~ (“be strong, farewell”) — and that vigor still shines through the family: ~valer~ (“to be worth”), ~valor~ (“value; courage”), ~valiente~ (“brave”), ~válido~, ~valía~, ~valioso~ (“valuable”), ~equivaler~ (“to be equivalent”), ~prevalecer~ (“to prevail”) and ~convalecer~ (“to convalesce,” to regain one's strength). Even the parting ~vale~ (“okay,” originally “be well”) belongs here.
en.evidenciar:
From ~evidencia~ (“evidence”), from Latin ~ēvidentia~ (“clearness, distinctness”), from ~ēvidēns~ (“clear, obvious”), from ~ē-~ (“out”) + the participle of ~vidēre~ (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”), the root behind English ~vision~ and ~evident~, Greek ~idéa~, and — via its ‘know’ sense — English ~wit~.

Latin ~ēvidēns~ literally described what “sees itself out” — what is so visible it forces itself on the eye — and ~ēvidentia~ was that quality of obvious clarity. Spanish turned the noun into a verb: ~evidenciar~ means to make something evident, to show or demonstrate it plainly, and reflexive ~evidenciarse~ is for a truth that becomes undeniable of its own accord. The same ~vidēre~ root runs through a large Spanish family: ~ver~ (“to see”), ~visión~, ~evidente~, ~prever~ (“to foresee”), ~previsión~, ~vídeo~, and ~providencia~.
en.evitar:
Spanish ~evitar~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ēvītāre~ (“to shun, avoid”), a compound of ~ē-~/~ex-~ (“out, away”) and ~vītāre~ (“to avoid, evade”). The origin of ~vītāre~ is genuinely uncertain, and the sources disagree: by one account (De Vaan) it rests on an unattested *~vītus~ (“avoiding”), linked to Proto-Indo-European *~weyh₁-~ (“to chase, pursue”); others connect it instead to *~weyk-~ (“to yield”), or to the root of ~dīvidō~ (“to divide”). None of these is settled. Its Romance kin are straightforward: French ~éviter~, Italian ~evitare~, Portuguese ~evitar~.

Whatever its deep root, ~vītāre~ already meant in Latin “to keep clear of,” and the prefix ~ē-~ (“away”) reinforces the sense of drawing back from something — so ~evitar~ has meant “to avoid, prevent, spare” throughout its Spanish life. Because the verb entered Spanish as a learned Latinism rather than by the slow mouth-worn route of inheritance, it kept its Latin shape almost unchanged, and its Spanish family is correspondingly small and transparent: chiefly the adjectives ~evitable~ (“avoidable”) and its negation ~inevitable~ (“unavoidable”), with the adverb ~inevitablemente~. The lesson of ~evitar~ is a quieter one: not every common verb comes with a tidy prehistory, and an honest etymology sometimes ends in a shrug.
en.evolucionar:
From ~evolución~ (“evolution”), from Latin ~ēvolūtiō~ (“an unrolling”), from ~ēvolvere~ (“to unroll, unfold”), from ~ē-~ (“out”) + ~volvere~ (“to roll, turn”), from Proto-Italic *~wolwō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~welH-~ (“to turn, roll, wind”), the root behind English ~volume~ and ~revolve~ and Greek ~helíssō~ (“to roll”).

The metaphor is a scroll: to ~evolvere~ was to unroll a papyrus volume and read it out, so ~ēvolūtiō~ was an “unrolling.” The biological sense — Darwinian evolution — is a nineteenth-century development layered onto that older image of something unfolding gradually into its full form, and ~evolucionar~ carries all of it: species, ideas, situations, and dance steps all ‘evolve.’ Fittingly, the Latin word for a book, ~volūmen~, meant a rolled scroll and gave Spanish ~volumen~. From the same ~volvere~ root come ~volver~ (“to return”), ~revolver~ (“to stir”), ~envolver~ (“to wrap”), ~desenvolver~, ~revolución~, and ~voluble~.
en.exagerar:
From Latin ~exaggerāre~ (“to heap up, pile on, magnify”), from ~ex-~ (“up, out”) plus ~aggerāre~ (“to heap up”), a verb built on the noun ~agger~ (“heap, mound, embankment”). ~agger~ itself derives from ~aggerere~ (“to carry to, bring together”), that is ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~gerere~ (“to carry, bear, conduct”). Spanish took the word by the learned route; compare French ~exagérer~, Italian ~esagerare~ and English ~exaggerate~.

The picture behind ~exagerar~ is a physical one: heaping earth ever higher into a mound. From “to pile up” came the figurative “to pile it on” — to overstate, to blow out of proportion — which is now the only living sense in Spanish, the literal mound left behind in Latin. The parent verb ~gerere~ (whose supine is ~gestum~) is quietly prolific: from it come ~gesto~ and ~gestión~, ~digerir~ (“to digest”), ~sugerir~ (“to suggest”), ~registro~ and ~gerundio~, the grammarian’s “gerund.”
en.exaltar:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~exaltāre~ “to raise up, lift high,” from ~ex-~ (here intensive) + ~altus~ “high, tall,” originally the past participle of ~alere~ “to nourish, make grow” — so “high” meant, at root, “grown tall” — from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂el-~ “to grow, nourish.” The same ~altus~ gave Spanish ~alto~ and ~altura~, English ~altitude~ and ~exalt~, and Italian ~esaltare~.

In Latin the verb meant simply to make something physically higher, but it was Church Latin that charged it with its enduring sense — to raise in honor, dignity, or praise, as in ~exaltar~ a saint or a virtue. Spanish inherited both: one can ~exaltar~ the merits of a hero (to extol) and, reflexively, ~exaltarse~ can mean to get worked up, to fly into a passion — emotion raised to a pitch. From the same nourishing root *~h₂el-~ Spanish also draws ~alimento~ and ~alumno~ (the one “being nourished,” hence a pupil), ~adulto~ (“grown up”), and ~enaltecer~ (“to elevate, praise”). To exalt, then, is etymologically to make grow tall.
en.examinar:
From Latin ~exāmināre~ (“to weigh, test, examine”), from ~exāmen~, which named both the tongue of a balance and a swarm of bees. ~Exāmen~ is a contraction of *~exagmen~, from ~exigere~ (“to drive out; to measure, weigh”), itself ~ex-~ (“out”) plus ~agere~ (“to drive, do”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”). Through ~agere~ the root reaches English ~act~, ~agent~, and ~agenda~; through ~exāmen~ it reaches English ~examine~ and ~exam~.

The two senses share one image: a swarm is what is driven out of the hive, and the pointer of a scale is what the weighing drives to a stop. Latin let the balance sense win for ~exāmināre~ — to read the needle, hence to weigh, assess, and finally test someone’s knowledge. Spanish then split ~exāmen~ into a doublet: the learned ~examen~ (“examination”) beside the fully inherited ~enjambre~ (“swarm”), which few speakers guess is the same word. Kin from ~exigere~ and ~agere~ include ~exigir~ (“to demand”), ~agente~, ~acto~, ~agenda~, and ~ambiguo~.
en.exceder:
From Latin ~excēdere~ (“to go out, go beyond, surpass”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~cēdere~ (“to go, withdraw, yield”). The origin of ~cēdere~ is debated: by one account it goes back, through Proto-Italic *~kezdō~, to Proto-Indo-European *~ḱyesdʰ-~ (“to drive away”), cognate with Sanskrit ~sedhati~ (“drives off”); by another it is ~ce-~ (“here”) plus *~sed-~ (“to sit”), the sense passing from “to sit” to “to go.” English borrowed the compound directly as ~exceed~ and the base as ~cede~.

The literal picture is spatial — to ~exceder~ is to step beyond a boundary — and the modern sense “to surpass, be too much” follows straight from it, giving the nouns ~exceso~ (“excess”) and ~excedente~ (“surplus”) and the adjective ~excesivo~. The base ~cēdere~ is one of Spanish's great prefix factories: ~ceder~, ~acceder~, ~conceder~, ~preceder~, ~suceder~, ~proceder~, ~retroceder~ and ~interceder~ all pivot on the same idea of going, yielding, or giving way.
en.excluir:
From Latin ~excludere~ (“to shut out, exclude”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~claudere~ (“to close, shut”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kleh₂u-~ (“hook, peg, key”). Cognate with Italian ~escludere~, French ~exclure~ and Portuguese ~excluir~, and — through ~claudere~ — with English ~close~, ~clause~ and ~conclude~; the same PIE root gave Latin ~clavis~ (“key”), source of Spanish ~llave~ and ~clave~, and Ancient Greek ~kleís~ (“key”).

The picture behind ~excluir~ is a closing door: to shut something out, to leave it on the far side of the threshold — hence “to exclude, bar, rule out.” In compounds Latin ~claudere~ regularly weakened to ~-cludere~, which is why the Spanish family wears a ~-cluir~ dress: ~incluir~ (“to shut in”), ~concluir~ (“to close off, finish”) and ~recluir~ (“to shut away”). From the closing-and-locking imagery Spanish also keeps ~exclusivo~, ~clausura~ and ~claustro~, all turning on the same act of shutting.
en.exhibir:
From Latin ~exhibēre~ (“to hold forth, present, produce, show”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~habēre~ (“to have, hold”), from Proto-Italic *~haβēō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰeh₁bʰ-~. Spanish ~exhibir~ is a learned borrowing. Through ~habēre~ it is cognate with English ~habit~, ~prohibit~ and ~inhibit~, with French ~exhiber~, and with the Spanish family ~haber~, ~hábito~, ~prohibir~ and ~inhibir~.

The sense went from “hold out” to “display, show, exhibit,” and reflexively (exhibirse) “to show off.” Here lurks one of the great false cognates. Latin ~habēre~ and English ~have~ match almost perfectly in form and meaning, yet they are not related: English ~have~ descends from PIE *~kh₂p-~ (“to grasp”), the very root of Latin ~capere~ (“to seize”) — so have's true Latin twin is grasping ~capere~, not ~habēre~ at all. As for ~habēre~'s own kin, one debated proposal links it instead to English ~give~; the sources do not treat the connection as settled. From ~habēre~ Spanish also draws ~exhibición~, ~hábil~ and ~haber~ itself.
en.exigir:
From Latin ~exigere~ (“to drive out, demand, exact, weigh precisely”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~agere~ (“to drive, lead, do”). ~agere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”), making it cognate with Ancient Greek ~ἄγω~ (ágō, “I lead”) and Sanskrit ~ajati~ (“drives”). The Latin verb descends in parallel as Italian ~esigere~, French ~exiger~ and Portuguese ~exigir~.

The core image is forceful: to ~exigere~ was to drive a debt out of someone, to exact what was owed, and Spanish ~exigir~ keeps that insistence in “to demand, to require”. A quieter branch meant “to weigh out exactly”, which is why the past participle ~exactus~ yielded ~exacto~ (“exact”), and why Latin ~examen~ (“the tongue of a balance”) gave both “swarm” and, through “a weighing”, English ~exam~. Spanish adds ~exigente~ and ~exigencia~, while ~agere~ underlies ~acto~, ~agente~ and ~ágil~; English took ~exact~, ~exigent~, ~act~ and ~agent~ from the same stock.
en.existir:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~exsistere~ (also ~existere~, “to step forth, emerge, come into being”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out, forth”) and ~sistere~ (“to stand, take a stand”), a reduplicated form of ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate with Italian ~esistere~, French ~exister~, and Portuguese ~existir~, and — through ~sistere~ and ~stāre~ — with English ~exist~, ~insist~, ~resist~, and ~consist~, and with Spanish ~estar~.

The image hidden in ~existir~ is startlingly physical: to exist is to “stand forth,” to step out of the background into visibility. Latin ~exsistere~ first meant to emerge or come into view, and only from there did it settle into the abstract “to be.” Because it is a bookish, late-arriving word — not a battered popular inheritance — it kept its Latin shape almost intact. It supplies philosophy's most famous first person, Descartes' ~existo~ in “pienso, luego ~existo~” (“I think, therefore I am”). From it Spanish built ~existencia~ (“existence”), ~existente~, ~existencial~ and ~existencialismo~, plus ~inexistente~ (“nonexistent”) and ~coexistir~ (“to coexist”).
en.expandir:
From Latin ~expandere~ (“to spread out, unfurl”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) plus ~pandere~ (“to spread, open”), from Proto-Italic *~pandō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to spread out”). ~pandere~ is cognate with Latin ~patēre~ (“to lie open”) and, further off, with Ancient Greek ~πέταλον~ (pétalon, “leaf,” a spread-out thing). The verb has Romance cousins in Italian ~espandere~, French ~épandre~, and Portuguese ~expandir~, and it was borrowed straight into English as ~expand~.

The image is simple — to open outward, to widen — and Spanish uses ~expandir~ for gases, empires, and businesses alike. The prettiest surprise hides in English: ~spawn~ is a doublet of ~expand~, reaching English through Anglo-Norman ~espaundre~ from the same ~expandere~, and it named the way a fish “spreads out” its eggs into the water — so a spreading empire and a spawning fish share one Latin verb. From the root Spanish keeps ~expansión~ and ~expansivo~, and, through the sister form ~patēre~, the adjective ~patente~ (“evident, patent”) and the Greek loan ~pétalo~ (“petal”).
en.expedir:
From Latin ~expedīre~ (“to free, disentangle, make ready”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out of”) and the root of ~pēs~, ~pedis~ (“foot”) — literally to free the feet from a snare. That root reaches back to Proto-Indo-European *~ped-~ (“foot”). Italian preserves the verb as ~spedire~ (“to send, dispatch”), and through the same Latin verb English gained ~expedite~ and ~expedient~.

The image is vivid: to ~expedir~ was to get one's feet out of the fetters, hence to clear obstacles and set something in motion — a sense that narrowed in Spanish to “to dispatch, send off” and, in official use, to “issue” a document or decree. Its exact antonym survives too: ~impedir~ (“to impede”) is ~in-~ plus the same foot-root, “to catch by the feet.” From that Indo-European foot descends a broad Spanish family, among them ~pie~, ~pedal~, ~pedestre~, ~expediente~ (“file, dossier”) and ~expedición~.
en.experimentar:
From Latin ~experīmentum~ (“a trial, test, proof”), the noun of ~experīrī~ (“to try, to put to the test”), which joins the prefix ~ex-~ to an old verb ~perīrī~ (“to attempt, to go through”). The deeper root is debated: it is traditionally linked to a Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to try, to risk, to traverse”), the family that also underlies Latin ~perīculum~ (“trial, danger”) and ~perītus~ (“experienced, skilled”) and, through Greek, English ~empirical~.

Spanish ~experimentar~ carries both branches of the meaning: “to experiment” (to test) and “to experience, to undergo” (to live through). The same Latin verb gave the pair ~experiencia~ (“experience”) and ~experimento~ (“experiment”), and the ~perīculum~ branch surfaces vividly in ~peligro~ (“danger”) — for to test and to risk were, to the Roman mind, close kin — alongside ~experto~ (“expert”) and ~pericia~ (“skill, expertise”).
en.explicar:
Spanish ~explicar~ comes from Latin ~explicāre~ (“to unfold, unroll, unravel”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). ~plicāre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to fold”). Through that root it is cognate with Greek ~plékō~ (“I plait, weave”) and German ~flechten~ (“to braid”). To explain, then, was to unfold something rolled up — to spread a folded scroll open so it could be read.

The root ~plicāre~ was extraordinarily productive. Prefixed, it gave ~aplicar~ (“to apply”), ~implicar~ (“to implicate”), ~complicar~ (“to complicate”) and ~replicar~ (“to reply”); inherited by regular sound change it became ~plegar~ (“to fold”). Its most surprising Spanish descendant is ~llegar~ (“to arrive”): from Latin ~applicāre~ (~ad-~ + ~plicāre~), which in the peninsula's seafaring usage meant to bring a ship to shore — so “to fold in to land” became simply “to arrive.” Also here: ~pliegue~ (“fold, crease”).
en.explorar:
From Latin ~explōrāre~ (“to investigate, to search out, to reconnoitre”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) plus ~plōrāre~ (“to cry out, to wail”). The ancient and much-repeated explanation is that ~explōrāre~ was a hunters’ word meaning “to set up a cry” to flush or track game — but this is uncertain: the sense of the second element is debated, and it has also been read as “to make flow.” Modern authorities call the hunting story “not unlikely” rather than proven, so it is best offered as a plausible guess, not a fact. Through ~plōrāre~ it is cognate with English ~explore~, ~deplore~, and ~implore~.

Whatever the original scene, the classical sense was already “to examine, to test, to spy out,” and Spanish kept it as ~explorar~ — to explore territory, and, in medicine, to examine a patient. The same ~plōrāre~ (“to weep”) gave Spanish the everyday ~llorar~ (“to cry”), so ~explorar~ and ~llorar~ are quiet cousins. From the verb come ~explorador~ (“explorer, scout”) and ~exploración~, and beside them the borrowed ~deplorar~ and ~implorar~.
en.explotar:
Spanish ~explotar~ in the sense “to exploit” came from French ~exploiter~, from Old French ~esploitier~, from Latin ~explicitāre~, a frequentative of ~explicāre~ (“to unfold, unroll”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) plus ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, fold”). Its French relatives include the noun ~exploit~ (“feat”), and English borrowed both ~exploit~ and the doublet family of ~apply~ and ~ply~.

Old French ~esploit~ meant a “carrying-out, achievement, profit,” and its verb meant to “accomplish” and then to “work, make profit from” — a mine, an estate. The harsher modern sense, “to exploit people,” is young: it spread in the mid-nineteenth century when utopian socialists denounced the economic order. Beware a false twin: the identical Spanish ~explotar~ meaning “to explode” is unrelated, taken from French ~exploser~. From the same ~plicāre~ root Spanish also drew ~explicar~, ~aplicar~, ~plegar~ and ~complicar~.
en.exponer:
From Latin ~exponere~ (“to set forth, put out, display”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~ponere~ (“to put, place”). ~ponere~ is traditionally parsed as ~po-~ (“away”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, leave”), though its deeper Proto-Indo-European ancestry is uncertain. Spanish ~exponer~ shares its Latin source with Italian ~esporre~ and Portuguese ~expor~.

The literal sense “to place out” ran in two directions: one displays an object and one sets forth an argument, and Spanish ~exponer~ still means both “to exhibit” and “to expound”, while reflexively ~exponerse~ is “to expose oneself” to danger. The derived noun ~exposición~ likewise covers an art “exhibition” and a reasoned “exposition”. The verb ~ponere~ seeded an enormous Spanish family — ~poner~, ~componer~, ~proponer~, ~imponer~ and the noun ~posición~ — and reached English in the learned derivatives ~expose~ and ~exponent~.
en.exportar:
~Exportar~ derives from Latin ~exportāre~ (“to carry out, carry away”), from ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~portāre~ (“to carry”), from Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to cross, pass over, lead through”). Spanish took it up in the modern commercial era alongside Italian ~esportare~ and French ~exporter~; through ~portāre~ it is cognate with English ~port~ and ~portable~, and — by native descent from *~per-~ — with English ~fare~ and ~ford~.

The image is spatial before it is economic: ~exportar~ is literally to carry out across a boundary, and only later to sell abroad — the counterpart of ~importar~, to carry in. Latin ~portāre~ seeded a broad Spanish family: ~portar~, ~transportar~, ~importar~, ~deportar~, ~soportar~ and ~aportar~, plus ~deporte~ (which reached Spanish through Old French, from the idea of carrying oneself away from work). The wider root *~per-~ also gave Latin ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbor”), whence ~puerta~ and ~puerto~.
en.expresar:
From Late Latin ~expressāre~, a frequentative of ~exprimere~ (“to press out, squeeze out”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~premere~ (“to press”), whose past participle is ~expressus~. ~premere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~premō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~pres-~ (“to press”), an extension of *~per-~ (“to strike, press”). Cognates: French ~exprimer~, Italian ~esprimere~, English ~express~; and through ~premere~, English ~press~ and ~print~.

The metaphor is physical: ~exprimere~ meant to squeeze the juice from a fruit, and from “pressing out” juice came the figurative “pressing out” of words and feelings — to express. Spanish still holds both halves as a doublet: concrete ~exprimir~ (“to squeeze a lemon”) beside abstract ~expresar~ (“to put into words”). An ~expreso~ train, and espresso coffee, are likewise “pressed,” quick. From ~premere~ Spanish also drew ~prensa~ (“press, the press”), ~imprimir~ (“to print”), ~comprimir~, and ~oprimir~.
en.expulsar:
From Latin ~expulsāre~, the frequentative of ~expellere~ (“to drive out”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) plus ~pellere~ (“to push, to drive”), whose participle is ~pulsus~; from Proto-Indo-European *~pel-~ (“to thrust, to drive”). Cognate with French ~expulser~, Italian ~espellere~ and Portuguese ~expulsar~, and — through the same root — with English ~expel~, ~compel~ and ~pulse~.

Because ~expulsāre~ was a frequentative, it framed the pushing-out as done forcibly or repeatedly — driving someone out and out. A homely descendant hides in plain sight: Spanish ~empujar~ (“to push”) comes from Vulgar Latin ~impulsāre~, the very same frequentative pattern applied to ~impellere~. From ~pellere~ and its participle ~pulsus~ Spanish also drew ~pulso~, ~pulsar~, ~impulso~, ~repeler~, ~propulsar~ and ~expulsión~.
en.extender:
From Latin ~extendere~ (“to stretch out, spread”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate with French ~étendre~, Italian ~estendere~ and English ~extend~; and, through ~tendere~, with English ~tend~ and ~tent~.

~tendere~ literally meant to pull something taut, and that image of stretching runs through the whole clan: to extend is to draw a thing out across space, time or scope. A charming relative is Spanish ~tienda~, meaning both “tent” and “shop” — a tent being cloth stretched over poles, and a market stall much the same. From the participle ~tēnsus~ come ~tensión~ and ~tenso~. The far-reaching root *~ten-~ also yields Spanish ~tender~, ~atender~, ~extensión~, ~tono~ and ~contento~, and, in English, ~tend~, ~tense~ and even ~thin~ (what is stretched grows thin).
en.extraer:
From Latin ~extrahere~ (“to draw out, pull out”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~trahere~ (“to drag, draw, pull”). In Spanish the verb was rebuilt on the pattern of ~traer~ (“to bring,” the direct descendant of ~trahere~), which is why ~extraer~ conjugates like it — ~extraigo~, ~extrajo~. It is cognate with Italian ~estrarre~ and French ~extraire~, and — through ~trahere~'s participle ~tractus~ — with English ~extract~, ~tractor~, and ~trace~.

The Proto-Indo-European source of ~trahere~ is uncertain: a root *~tragʰ-~ (“to draw, drag”) is often cited, but some scholars instead trace the Latin and Celtic forms to a non-Indo-European substrate word — so the deep root is best left open. The Latin sense was thoroughly physical, “to drag,” and ~extraer~ still means to pull something out, whether a tooth, a mineral, or a conclusion. The same root seeded a large Spanish family: ~traer~, ~atraer~, ~distraer~, ~contraer~, ~sustraer~, ~tratar~ (from ~tractāre~), and the noun ~retrato~ (“portrait”).
en.extrañar:
From Latin ~extrāneāre~ (“to treat as foreign, estrange”), from ~extrāneus~ (“external, foreign, not of one’s household”), from ~extrā~ (“outside”), ultimately from ~ex~ (“out of”). Old Spanish had ~estrañar~, later relatinized to ~extrañar~. It is cognate with Italian ~estraniare~ and French ~étranger~, and — through Old French ~estrange~ — with English ~strange~, ~stranger~, and ~estrange~; the learned English ~extraneous~ comes straight from ~extrāneus~.

The modern Peninsular sense “to miss someone” grew out of “to find strange”: what is absent feels foreign, out of place, and so one notices its lack — the very thing once seen as strange is now sorely missed. Spanish still keeps the older meaning in ~extrañar~ (“to find odd”) and in the reflexive ~extrañarse de~ (“to be surprised at”), and Latin America favors ~extrañar~ for “to miss” where Spain often uses ~echar de menos~. From ~extrā~ and ~extrāneus~ Spanish also inherited ~extraño~ (“strange; stranger”), ~extranjero~ (“foreigner”), and ~extrañeza~ (“strangeness, puzzlement”).
en.fabricar:
From Latin ~fabricāre~ (“to build, construct, forge”), from ~fabrica~ (“workshop, craft, construction”), from ~faber~ (“craftsman, smith”). The deeper origin of ~faber~ is uncertain; it is often traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeHbʰ-~ (“to fit together, be fitting”), but the reconstruction is not secure. Cognate with Italian ~fabbricare~, French ~fabriquer~, and Portuguese ~fabricar~. English ~fabricate~ and ~fabric~ come from the same Latin family, and English ~forge~ descends, through Old French ~forge~, from ~fabrica~ itself.

Latin ~fabrica~ took two roads into Spanish. As a learned borrowing it gave ~fábrica~ (“factory”), while its inherited, sound-worn descendant became ~fragua~ (“forge, smithy”) — the same word, one in Latin dress and the other showing the full erosion of popular speech, a classic doublet. From ~fragua~ comes the verb ~fraguar~, “to forge,” and figuratively “to hatch or concoct a plan.” The learned line gives ~fabricar~ (“to manufacture, make up”), ~fabricante~ (“manufacturer”), ~fabricación~ (“manufacture”), and ~fabril~ (“industrial, of factories”). Because ~fabricar~ can also mean “to fabricate” in the sense of inventing — a lie, an excuse — it carries, like its English cousin, a shadow of falsehood alongside honest making.
en.facilitar:
From the adjective ~fácil~ (“easy”) with a verb-forming suffix, ~fácil~ itself from Latin ~facilis~ (“easy, feasible”), which meant literally “do-able” — from ~facere~ (“to do, to make”) plus the ending ~-ilis~. ~Facere~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to set, put, do”). Spanish ~facilitar~ is cognate with Italian ~facilitare~, French ~faciliter~ and Portuguese ~facilitar~, and with English ~facilitate~ and ~facile~.

Because ~facilis~ was built as “(a thing) that can be done,” its Spanish descendant ~facilitar~ means precisely “to make do-able,” to smooth the way. Its antonym preserves the same logic in reverse: ~difícil~ is ~dis-~ plus ~facilis~, “not do-able.” The parent ~facere~ is one of the great root-verbs of Spanish, surviving above all as the everyday ~hacer~ — its Latin ~f-~ softened to ~h-~ — and branching into ~fábrica~, ~facultad~ and ~facilidad~, among many others.
en.fallar:
From ~falla~ (“fault, defect”), from Vulgar Latin *~fallia~, from Latin ~fallere~ (“to deceive, disappoint, fail”). Cognate with Italian ~fallire~ and French ~faillir~, and — through French — with English ~fail~, ~fault~, and ~false~.

The Latin sense was betrayal: ~fallere~ meant to trip someone up, to let them down, and Spanish ~fallar~ still lives there — a memory that ~falla~, a strength that ~falla~ has broken faith with expectation. From the same ~fallere~ Spanish drew ~falta~ (“lack, want”), ~falso~ (“false”), ~falacia~, and, most strikingly, ~fallecer~ (“to die”) — where “failing” hardened into “expiring.” Spanish also has a second, homonymous ~fallar~, “to hand down a verdict,” from the noun ~fallo~ (“ruling”), so named because a judge’s decree once opened with the first-person ~fallo~ (“I rule”); whether that judicial ~fallo~ ultimately belongs to the same ~fallere~ family is debated, and the sources treat the two verbs as separate.
en.fallecer:
From Old Spanish ~fallecer~ / ~fallir~ (“to fail, be lacking”), from Vulgar Latin *~fallescere~, an inchoative of Latin ~fallere~ (“to trip, deceive, fail”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)gʷʰh₂el-~ (“to stumble, trip”). Cognate with Greek ~σφάλλω~ (“to trip up, cause to fall”), Sanskrit ~skhalate~ (“stumbles”), and Armenian ~sxalem~ (“I stumble”). The same Latin verb gave Italian ~fallire~, French ~faillir~, and — through Old French — English ~fail~, ~false~, and ~fault~.

Latin ~fallere~ meant literally “to make someone stumble,” and from that physical image grew the figurative senses “to deceive” and “to be lacking, fall short.” Spanish took that last, gentler sense and pushed it to its limit: to ~fallecer~ was first “to run out, come to an end,” and then, as a euphemism, “to die” — the same softening impulse behind English “to pass away.” The blunter descendants of ~fallere~ survive alongside it: ~fallar~ (“to fail, miss”), ~falla~ and ~fallo~ (“fault, flaw; verdict”), ~falta~ and ~faltar~ (“lack; to be missing”), and ~falso~ (“false”). What began as a body losing its footing became, in Spanish, a life quietly running out.
en.faltar:
From Vulgar Latin *~fallitare~, a frequentative of Latin ~fallere~ (“to deceive, to trip, to fail”). The origin of ~fallere~ is uncertain, but it is often traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)gʷʰh₂el-~ (“to stumble”); on that account it is cognate with Ancient Greek ~σφάλλω~ (sphállō, “to bring down, trip up”). The same Latin verb reached English, through Old French, in ~fail~, ~fault~ and ~false~.

The semantic drift is neat: from “to deceive” to “to disappoint or come up short” and finally to “to be missing”. Spanish ~faltar~ is now the ordinary verb for something's absence — ~falta~ un ingrediente, “an ingredient is missing” — and its noun ~falta~ means “lack”, “fault”, even a sporting “foul”. The root threw off a wide family: ~falla~, ~fallar~, ~falso~ and, most strikingly, ~fallecer~ (“to die”), which began as “to fail, to expire”. English ~fallacy~ belongs here too, another child of deceiving ~fallere~.
en.favorecer:
~favorecer~ is a Spanish formation from the noun ~favor~ (“favor, goodwill”) plus the inchoative suffix ~-ecer~ (from Latin ~-ēscere~), meaning roughly “to come to favor.” The noun continues Latin ~favor~ (“goodwill, approval”), a derivative of the verb ~favēre~ (“to be well-disposed, be favorable”). The Romance sisters built the verb the same way: Italian ~favorire~, French ~favoriser~, and Portuguese ~favorecer~; English ~favor~ itself is a borrowing from the same Latin stock through Old French.

The deep origin of ~favēre~ is genuinely disputed. By one account it goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰeh₂-~ (“to shine”) or *~bʰuH-~ (“to be, become”); by another, to *~gʷʰew-~ (“to worship, heed”), which would make it a distant cognate of Old Church Slavonic ~gověti~ (“to fast, revere”). The sources hedge, so the most striking link is best left open. What is clear is the semantic arc: from a god's or a crowd's ~favor~ at the games, to social approval, to the modern “to favor, help along.” From the same family come ~favorable~, ~favorito~ (“favorite,” via Italian), ~desfavorecer~, and ~favorecedor~ (“flattering,” of clothes).
en.felicitar:
From Latin ~fēlīcitāre~ (“to make happy”), from ~fēlīx~ (stem ~fēlīc-~, “happy, fortunate, fruitful”), from Proto-Italic *~fēlwī-~ (“suckling, with young”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁(y)-~ (“to suckle, to nourish”). Cognate with French ~féliciter~, Italian ~felicitare~ and Portuguese ~felicitar~, and — through the same root — with English ~felicity~ and ~fecund~.

The startling fact is what ~fēlīx~ first meant: not “happy” but “fruitful, fertile,” said of teeming soil and nursing mothers, for the root *~dʰeh₁(y)-~ is the root of suckling. To congratulate someone is thus, at bottom, to wish them fruitfulness. The same nourishing root fed a surprising set of Latin words — ~fēcundus~, ~fēmina~ and ~fīlius~ (“son”) — living on in Spanish as ~fecundo~, ~hembra~ (from ~fēmina~) and ~hijo~ (from ~fīlius~), alongside the plainer ~feliz~, ~felicidad~ and ~felicitación~.
en.fiar:
From Vulgar Latin *~fīdāre~, a popular remodeling of Classical Latin ~fīdere~ “to trust, to confide in,” kin to the noun ~fidēs~ “faith, good faith,” from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰeydʰ-~ “to trust, confide.” It is cognate with Italian ~fidare~ and Portuguese ~fiar~, and — through ~fidēs~ — with English ~faith~ and ~fidelity~ (both borrowed via Latin), and even with English ~bide~ and ~abide~, which reached the same PIE root down the Germanic line.

The core idea is entrusting: to ~fiar~ is to hand something over on the strength of trust. From that grew the commercial sense every shopkeeper knows — ~fiar~ as selling on credit, giving goods now against a promise to pay later, so buying ~al fiado~ is buying on tick. The reflexive ~fiarse~ means to rely on someone. The root fanned out into a broad Spanish family: ~fe~ (“faith”), ~fiel~ (“faithful”), ~fidelidad~, ~confiar~ and ~confianza~, ~desafiar~ (“to challenge” — literally to withdraw one's faith), and ~fianza~ (“a bond, bail money”). Few roots have branched so widely from one idea: that things and people can be relied upon.
en.figurar:
From Latin ~figūrāre~ (“to form, to shape”), from ~figūra~ (“shape, form, figure”), a derivative of ~fingere~ (“to mold, to fashion,” especially in clay), from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeyǵʰ-~ (“to knead, to shape, to build from clay”). Through ~fingere~ the word is cognate with English ~figure~, ~feign~ and ~fiction~; through the raw root it even relates to English ~dough~.

The starting point is a potter's hands: *~dʰeyǵʰ-~ named the shaping of clay, so ~fingere~ was “to mould” and ~figūra~ the moulded shape. From “to give shape” Spanish ~figurar~ branched into “to represent, to depict,” “to appear (in a list),” and “to stand out, to cut a figure” — to ~figurar~ among the best. The clay-kneading root also, remarkably, rose as English ~dough~. Nearby Spanish relatives include ~figura~, ~figurativo~, ~figurín~, ~desfigurar~, ~configurar~ and ~transfigurar~, plus the ~fingere~ cousins ~fingir~, ~ficción~ and ~efigie~.
en.fijar:
Spanish ~fijar~ derives from the adjective ~fijo~ (“fixed”), earlier ~fixo~, from Latin ~fixus~, the past participle of ~fīgere~ (“to fasten, drive in, pierce”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeygʷ-~ (“to stick, set up”). Cognates include Italian ~fissare~, French ~fixer~, and Portuguese ~fixar~; English took ~fix~ and ~fixate~ from the same participle, and ~crucifix~ preserves ~fīgere~ literally as “fastened to a cross.”

Because ~fijar~ was reshaped from the participle rather than inherited whole, Spanish shows a telling split: the learned ~fijo~ (“fixed”) stands beside an older, popular descendant ~hito~ (“landmark, milestone”), where Latin ~f-~ became silent ~h-~ — a boundary-post is literally a “fixed” thing. From ~fīgere~ the language also draws ~fijación~ (“fixation”), ~fijeza~ (“fixity”), ~prefijo~ and ~sufijo~ (things “fastened” before and after), and ~crucifijo~ (“crucifix”). Note the distinct root of ~fingir~ and ~figura~, from ~fingere~ (“to shape”), easy to confuse but etymologically separate.
en.filtrar:
Spanish ~filtrar~ comes from the noun ~filtro~ (and its doublet ~fieltro~, “felt”), from Medieval Latin ~filtrum~ (“felt; filter”), itself borrowed from a Germanic source: Proto-West Germanic *~felt~, from Proto-Indo-European *~pel-~ (“to beat, strike”). Felt is made by beating and matting wool, and because a pad of felt made a serviceable strainer, the same word came to mean “filter.” Cognate with English ~felt~ and German ~Filz~.

A separate ~filtro~ should not be confused with this one: the “love potion” ~filtro~ of older Spanish, and the anatomical ~philtrum~ (the groove of the upper lip), descend instead from Greek ~φίλτρον~, from ~φιλεῖν~ (“to love, to kiss”) — a wholly different root. From the felt-based word Spanish built the verb ~filtrar~ (“to strain a liquid,” then figuratively “to leak information”) and a family of derivatives: ~filtración~, ~infiltrar~, ~filtrado~, and the fabric-name ~fieltro~ itself.
en.finalizar:
From Spanish ~final~ (“final”), from Latin ~fīnālis~ (“of the end or boundary”), from ~fīnis~ (“boundary, limit, end”). The deeper origin of ~fīnis~ is uncertain; it has traditionally been traced to an earlier *~fīg-sn-is~, a derivative of ~fīgere~ (“to fix, drive in, fasten”), on the idea that a boundary was originally a marker driven into the ground — though this account remains a proposal rather than settled fact. Cognate with Italian ~finalizzare~, French ~finaliser~ and Portuguese ~finalizar~, and with English ~finalize~.

The verb itself is a modern formation, ~final~ plus the suffix ~-izar~, meaning “to bring to a close.” If the ~fīgere~ hypothesis holds, the notion of an “end” began with a stake fixed into the earth to mark where one field stopped and another began — a vivid image, but one to be offered cautiously. From ~fīnis~ Spanish drew a large family: ~fin~, ~final~, ~definir~, ~confín~ (“far border”), ~finiquito~ (“settlement, final receipt”) and the literary ~finar~ (“to pass away”).
en.financiar:
From French ~financer~ (“to pay, to finance”), from Medieval Latin and Old French ~finance~ (“payment, settlement, ransom”), a noun on ~finer~ (“to pay, settle, bring to an end”), from ~fin~ (“end”), from Latin ~fīnis~ (“boundary, limit, end”). The deep origin of ~fīnis~ is uncertain; it is traditionally linked to ~fīgere~ (“to fix, drive in”), as though a boundary were a fixed marker, but the derivation is not secure. From the same French source English took ~finance~, and from ~fīnis~ the wider family ~final~, ~finish~, and ~confine~; Italian has ~finanziare~ and Portuguese ~financiar~.

The surprise is that “finance” began not with wealth but with ending: to ~finer~ was to finish a matter by paying it off, and ~finance~ first meant the settlement of a debt — even a ransom. Over the later Middle Ages “finishing a payment” swelled into the whole business of managing money, and Spanish re-borrowed the verb, through French, only in the modern era. The end-sense survives across the family: ~fin~, ~final~, ~finalizar~, the legal ~finiquito~ (“full settlement”), ~confín~, ~definir~, ~refinar~ — and the money branch ~finanzas~, ~financiero~, and ~financiación~.
en.firmar:
From Latin ~firmāre~ (“to make firm, strengthen, confirm”), from the adjective ~firmus~ (“firm, strong, stable”), from Proto-Italic *~fermos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~dʰer-mo-s~ (“holding”), from the root *~dʰer-~ (“to hold, support”). It is cognate with Italian ~firmare~ and Portuguese ~firmar~, and — with a striking shift — with French ~fermer~ (“to close”). It is kin to English ~firm~, ~confirm~, and ~affirm~, and, far afield, to Sanskrit ~dhárma~, “that which upholds.”

The path to “sign” runs through the law: to ~firmar~ a document was first to make it firm, to confirm and ratify it, and from ratifying an act came the act of subscribing one's name to it. French, meanwhile, took ~firmāre~ toward “to shut firmly,” yielding ~fermer~, “to close.” The Spanish family keeps the core sense of steadiness: ~firme~, ~firmeza~, ~confirmar~, ~afirmar~, the ~firmamento~ (the “firm” vault of heaven), and ~firma~, the signature itself.
en.fluir:
From Latin ~fluere~ (“to flow”), adapted in Spanish to the ~-ir~ conjugation. The Latin verb goes back to Proto-Italic *~flūō~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰlewH-~ (“to overflow”), perhaps an extension of *~bʰleh₁-~ (“to swell, blow”). It is cognate with Italian ~fluire~ and Portuguese ~fluir~, and, further back through the root, with Ancient Greek ~φλέω~ (phléō, “to abound”) and ~φλύω~ (phlúō, “to boil over”). A tempting cognate that is not one: English ~flow~ merely resembles ~fluere~ by accident — it descends from a different root — so the likeness is a coincidence.

~fluere~ already carried the modern range of “stream, run, pour,” and Spanish uses ~fluir~ for everything from rivers to conversation and traffic. The root seeded a large family: ~fluido~, ~flujo~, ~fluvial~, ~afluente~, ~influir~, and ~confluir~. One surprising descendant is the element ~flúor~: it was named from Latin ~fluor~ (“a flowing”) because fluorite melts easily and was long used as a flux to make ores flow in smelting — a chemical name that, at heart, still means “flowing.”
en.fomentar:
From Latin ~fomentum~ (“a warm dressing, poultice”), contracted from *~fovimentum~, from ~fovēre~ (“to warm, keep warm, cherish”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰegʷʰ-~ (“to burn, warm”). Cognate through that root with Sanskrit ~dáhati~ (“it burns”) and Lithuanian ~degti~ (“to burn”), and sharing the Latin stem with English ~foment~ and ~fomentation~.

A ~fomentum~ was literally a warm compress laid on the body, and ~fomentar~ first meant to apply such heat as a treatment. From there the sense turned figurative — to encourage a thing's growth as if by warmth — which is why today one can ~fomentar~ tourism, dialogue, or, less happily, unrest. Spanish keeps the noun ~fomento~ (“promotion, fostering”) beside the verb. The old medical picture survives faintly: to foster something is still, etymologically, to keep it warm.
en.formar:
From Latin ~formāre~ (“to shape, to fashion”), from ~forma~ (“form, shape, mold”). The deeper origin of ~forma~ is genuinely disputed: one long-standing account connects it to Ancient Greek ~morphḗ~ (“shape”) by metathesis, the swapping of sounds, but scholars object that Latin shows no trace of an intermediate stage and that the required sound changes are irregular. Others reconstruct a native Proto-Indo-European source instead. Cognate with French ~former~, Italian ~formare~, and English ~form~ and ~format~.

Whatever its ultimate root, ~forma~ was one of Latin’s most productive nouns, covering shape, beauty, and pattern alike. Spanish multiplied it into ~formación~, ~fórmula~ (a diminutive, “a little form”), ~informar~ (“to give form to,” to shape into knowledge), ~transformar~, and ~uniforme~ (“of one form”). A charming survival is ~horma~, the shoemaker’s or hatmaker’s last — the wooden mold that shapes a shoe. ~horma~ is the popular, inherited descendant of ~forma~, while ~forma~ itself is the learned borrowing: a doublet in which the down-to-earth mold and the abstract idea of “form” are the same Latin word taking two roads into Spanish.
en.formular:
~Formular~ was formed from the noun ~fórmula~, a Latin diminutive of ~forma~ (“shape, form, mold”). The origin of Latin ~forma~ is genuinely uncertain: by one long-standing but disputed account it was borrowed, perhaps through Etruscan, from Ancient Greek ~μορφή~ (“shape, figure”), the two words being near-mirror images (m-r-f beside f-r-m); other scholars reject the loan. Whatever its source, ~forma~ gave Italian ~formulare~, French ~formuler~, and English ~formula~ and ~form~.

A ~fórmula~ was, in Roman law, a small fixed ~forma~ — a set wording laid down for a contract or a legal action, a template to be filled in. From “little prescribed form” came the modern senses that ~formular~ carries: “to formulate, to draw up, to word precisely,” as one formulates a theory, a complaint, or a chemical ~fórmula~. The parent ~forma~ is one of the most productive roots in Spanish, behind ~forma~ itself, ~formar~ (“to form”), ~formato~ (“format”), ~informar~ (“to inform”), ~uniforme~ (“uniform”), ~deformar~ (“to deform”), and ~transformar~ (“to transform”).
en.fortalecer:
~Fortalecer~ was built in Old Spanish from the noun ~fortaleza~ (“fortress; strength”) with the inchoative suffix ~-ecer~ (from Latin ~-ēscere~, “to become”). ~Fortaleza~ goes back to Latin ~fortis~ (“strong”), from Old Latin ~forctis~. The deeper origin of ~fortis~ is disputed: it is traced either to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰerǵʰ-~ (“to rise, be high”) or to *~dʰerǵʰ-~ (“to hold firm, be firm”). Through ~fortis~ it is cognate with Italian ~forte~, French ~fort~, and English ~force~ and ~fort~.

The inchoative ~-ecer~ is the engine of the word: where ~fortaleza~ names strength as a state, ~fortalecer~ names the process of becoming strong — “to grow or make strong.” Latin poured ~fortis~ into a large Spanish family. From the adjective came ~fuerte~ (“strong”); from the derived noun ~fortia~ (“strength”) came ~fuerza~ and the verb ~forzar~ (“to force”); and from compounds came ~esforzarse~ (“to strive”), ~reforzar~ (“to reinforce”), and ~confortar~ (“to comfort”). Even the musical ~forte~ traces back to the same small, sturdy Latin word for strength.
en.forzar:
From Vulgar Latin *~fortiāre~ (“to use force on”), a verb built on Latin ~fortia~ (“strength,” a neuter plural of ~fortis~ reinterpreted as feminine), from ~fortis~ (“strong”), Old Latin ~forctis~, from Proto-Italic *~forktis~. The Proto-Indo-European source is disputed: the sources hesitate between *~bʰerǵʰ-~ (“to rise, be high”) and *~dʰerǵʰ-~ (“to be firm, hold fast”), and settle on neither. Cognate are French ~forcer~, Italian ~forzare~ and Portuguese ~forçar~, while English borrowed ~force~.

~fortia~ meant deeds or resources of strength, and Vulgar Latin turned it into a verb, “to bring strength to bear,” hence “to compel.” Because the deep root is contested, any single Indo-European gloss should be offered as one option among two. The stem is enormously productive in Spanish: ~fuerza~ (“force”), ~fuerte~ (“strong”), ~esforzar~ (“to strive”), ~reforzar~ (“to reinforce”) and ~fortaleza~ (“fortress; fortitude”) all trace to ~fortis~.
en.fracasar:
From Italian ~fracassare~ (“to smash, shatter, make an uproar”), taken into Spanish in the Golden Age. The make-up of the Italian word is disputed: by the traditional account it is a reshaping of Latin ~conquassāre~ (“to shatter to pieces,” from ~con-~ + ~quassāre~, “to shake violently”), with the prefix ~con-~ swapped for Italian ~fra-~ (“in the midst of,” from Latin ~īnfrā~) — but this blend is proposed rather than certain, so treat it as one hypothesis, not settled fact. Cognate with French ~fracasser~ and English ~fracas~ (a din or brawl), both from the same Italian source.

The meaning arrived transitive and violent: Corominas records ~fracasar~ first as “to shatter, break into fragments” (Cervantes has giants and fleets ~fracasados~ in the 1605 Quijote), then “to be wrecked at sea” by mid-century. From that maritime disaster — a ship dashed to splinters on the rocks — grew the now-dominant intransitive sense “to fail, come to nothing,” and the transitive use faded. The related noun ~fracaso~ (“failure”) mirrors Italian ~fracasso~ (“crash, uproar”), preserving the older idea of a resounding, catastrophic smash.
en.frenar:
From Latin ~frēnāre~ (“to bridle, curb”), a denominative of ~frēnum~ (“bridle, bit”), which goes back to Proto-Italic *~frēnom~ and, by one reconstruction, to Proto-Indo-European *~dʰer-~ (“to hold, support”). Cognate with Italian ~frenare~ and French ~freiner~, and — if that etymology holds — with Latin ~firmus~ (“firm”) and its English borrowing ~firm~.

A ~frēnum~ was the bit and bridle by which a rider checks a horse, so ~frēnāre~ meant to hold an animal back — and Spanish ~frenar~ still lives in that metaphor of restraint, whether braking a car, curbing spending, or reining in an impulse. The noun ~freno~ names both the horse's bit and the brake pedal, a nice fossil of the shift from cavalry to automobile. The same root gave Spanish ~freno~, ~frenazo~ (“a sharp braking”), ~refrenar~ (“to rein in”), ~desenfrenado~ (“unbridled, wild”), and ~enfrenar~.
en.fumar:
From Latin ~fūmāre~ (“to smoke, steam”), from ~fūmus~ (“smoke”), from Proto-Italic *~fūmos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰuh₂mós~ (“smoke”) — built on *~dʰewh₂-~ (“to smoke, raise dust”). Cognate with Italian ~fumare~, French ~fumer~ and Portuguese ~fumar~, and, through the root, with Ancient Greek ~θῡμός~ (~thȳmós~), Sanskrit ~dhūmá~ and — surprisingly — English ~dust~.

Spanish inherited the root twice over. The patrimonial noun ~humo~ (“smoke”) shows the regular Castilian change of Latin ~f-~ to ~h-~ (compare ~facere~ → ~hacer~), while the verb ~fumar~ kept its ~f-~, entering later and by a more learned route — so Spaniards make ~humo~ but ~fuman~ tobacco. The same root fans out into ~humear~ (“to give off smoke”), ~fumigar~, ~esfumar~ (“to blur, make vanish like smoke”) and even ~perfume~, literally something given off “through smoke,” from incense burned before the gods.
en.funcionar:
~funcionar~ is a denominal verb built on the noun ~función~, from Latin ~functiō~ (accusative ~functiōnem~), “a performing, execution,” from the deponent verb ~fungī~ (“to perform, discharge, carry out”), past participle ~functus~. This goes back to Proto-Italic *~fungōr~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰewg-~ (“to enjoy, make use of”), the present stem carrying a nasal infix. English borrowed ~function~; French has ~fonctionner~, Italian ~funzionare~.

In Latin ~fungī~ meant “to carry out a duty,” and ~función~ named the carrying-out itself; only in the modern age did Romance coin ~funcionar~ for machines and systems that “do their job” — which is why in Spanish an engine ~funciona~. A striking cousin: ~dēfungī~ meant “to finish, be done with,” so the one who has discharged life is the ~difunto~ (“deceased”), and death is a ~defunción~. From the “use up” sense comes ~fungible~ (goods consumed in use); everyday kin include the ~funcionario~, the civil servant who performs an office.
en.fundamentar:
A relatively modern derivative of ~fundamento~ (“foundation, basis”), from Latin ~fundāmentum~ (“foundation”), from ~fundāre~ (“to found, to lay the bottom of”), from ~fundus~ (“bottom, base, farm”). ~fundus~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰudʰmn̥~ (“bottom”). Cognate with Italian ~fondamento~ and French ~fondement~, and — through the same root — with English ~bottom~, German ~Boden~ (“ground, soil”) and Ancient Greek ~πυθμήν~ (~puthmḗn~, “bottom”).

Where ~fundar~ (the inherited verb) means to found or establish a thing, ~fundamentar~ is the abstract cousin: to give something a basis, to back a claim with reasons — to ~fundamentar~ an argument is to set it on solid ground. From ~fundus~ Spanish drew a broad family: ~fondo~ (“bottom; fund; background”), ~hondo~ (“deep,” showing the Castilian ~f-~ → ~h-~ shift), ~profundo~, ~fundación~ and ~fundamental~. The metaphor is constant — the deepest part is the part everything else stands on.
en.fundar:
From Latin ~fundāre~ (“to lay a base, to found”), a verb built on ~fundus~ (“bottom, ground, landed estate”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰudʰmn̥~ (“bottom”). It is cognate with Italian ~fondare~, French ~fonder~ and Portuguese ~fundar~; the underlying noun ~fundus~ is kin, through that root, to English ~bottom~ and German ~Boden~.

Latin ~fundāre~ meant to give a thing its ~fundus~ — its bottom — hence to establish a city, a house, or an institution on solid ground, the sense Spanish still carries. The same noun descended into Spanish twice: as the learned ~fundar~ and ~fundamento~, and as the popular ~hondo~ (“deep”), by the regular change of initial ~f-~ to ~h-~. So a firm foundation and a deep place turn out to be relatives — what is well ~fundado~ rests on the bottom of things. From the family also come ~fondo~, ~profundo~ and ~ahondar~, and, through Latin, English ~found~, ~fund~ and ~profound~.
en.fundir:
From Latin ~fundere~ (“to pour, melt, cast”), from Proto-Italic *~hundō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰew-~ (“to pour”). It is cognate with Ancient Greek ~χέω~ (“I pour”) and Gothic ~giutan~, and with the Romance reflexes Italian ~fondere~, French ~fondre~ and Portuguese ~fundir~. Curiously, Spanish inherited ~fundere~ twice: the popular, fully evolved ~hundir~ (“to sink”) survived beside the semi-learned ~fundir~.

The original sense “to pour” narrowed toward pouring molten metal, so ~fundir~ came to mean both “to melt” and “to cast” — the labor of the ~fundición~ (“foundry”). From that grew the figurative “to merge, blend,” as when two firms ~se funden~ into one. Richly prefixed, the same verb gave ~confundir~ (“to confuse,” literally “to pour together”), ~difundir~ (“to diffuse, broadcast”), ~infundir~ (“to instill”) and ~refundir~; the learned participle ~fūsus~ yielded the modern ~fusión~ and ~fusible~.
en.galardonar:
From the noun ~galardón~ (“award, prize, guerdon”), a word of Germanic origin remodeled in Romance. Its base is a Gothic *~wiþralaun~ “counter-payment, reward for a service,” compounded from ~wiþra~ “against, in return” and ~laun~ “pay, reward” — the parallel of Old High German ~widarlōn~ and Old English ~wiþerlēan~. Old Spanish ~gualardón~ shows the Germanic w- turned to gu-, and the second element was later reshaped under the pull of Latin ~dōnum~ “gift.” Behind ~laun~ lies Proto-Germanic *~launą~ “reward,” from Proto-Indo-European *~leh₂w-~ “to gain, seize as spoils” — the same root as Latin ~lucrum~ “gain,” source of English ~lucre~.

The word entered Spanish from the feudal world of service and recompense — a ~galardón~ was the reward owed to a vassal or a poet for loyalty rendered — and the verb ~galardonar~ meant to repay such service with honor or prize. Over time both narrowed to the elevated register they keep today: to ~galardonar~ is to bestow an award, and a ~galardonado~ is a laureate, a prize-winner — the word one meets at film festivals and literary ceremonies rather than in daily speech. The Germanic ~laun~ (“reward”) that hides inside it is a rare survival; most of Spanish's vocabulary of payment is Latin, which makes ~galardón~ a small monument to the Gothic and Frankish layer beneath Castilian.
en.ganar:
The origin of ~ganar~ is debated. Corominas argues it descends, with Portuguese ~ganhar~, from a Gothic *~ganan~ (“to covet, desire eagerly”), akin to Old Norse ~gana~ (“to gape, yearn”) — a Germanic family whose primitive sense was “to open the mouth.” Its meaning was then crossed with a separate Romance family from Frankish *~waidanjan~ (“to forage, harvest, gain”): Italian ~guadagnare~, French ~gagner~ and Catalan ~guanyar~. Corominas stresses that ~ganar~ is phonetically incompatible with ~guadagnare~, so it is not simply the same word — the tidy “all from *~waidanjan~” story is exactly what he rejects.

The “desire” origin ties the verb to Spanish ~ganas~ (“urge, desire,” as in ~tener ganas~), from the very same root — a satisfying link, though it rests on the debated Gothic etymology and should be flagged as such. The senses “to gain, earn, win” all grew from there. Modern kin include ~ganancia~ (“profit”), ~ganador~ (“winner”) and, strikingly, ~ganado~ (“livestock”) — literally “what has been gained,” a reminder of an age when wealth was counted in cattle.
en.garantizar:
From ~garante~ (“guarantor”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-izar~. ~garante~ was borrowed from French ~garant~ (“warrantor, defender”), of Germanic origin: from Frankish *~werēnt~, the present participle of a verb *~werjan~ (“to warrant, to vouch for”), tracing to the Proto-Germanic root *~war-~ (“to watch, to guard, to be aware”). The same Frankish word entered English by another door: kept with its Germanic w-, it became ~warrant~ and ~warranty~, while the Central-French gu- form gave ~guarantee~ — so ~garantizar~ and ~guarantee~ are, letter for letter across the w/gu alternation, the same word.

The Germanic idea behind the word is protection. A ~garante~ was originally the one who stood surety — who vouched for another and would answer for him — and Old French already used ~garant~ in this sense in the Chanson de Roland around 1080. From this Germanic stock Spanish built a whole legal and commercial family: ~garantía~ (“guarantee, warranty”), ~garante~, ~garantizar~, and ~garantizado~, all of them galicismos layered over older native vocabulary. English keeps the twin senses in its own doublet — a ~warrant~ authorizes and vouches, while a ~guarantee~ promises and secures — two faces of the single Frankish notion of standing good for something.
en.gastar:
From Latin ~vastāre~ (“to lay waste, devastate”), from ~vastus~ (“empty, desolate, waste”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁weh₂-~ (“to leave, abandon”). The Spanish form is a blend: its initial ~g-~, where Latin alone would give ~va-~, reflects reinforcement by a Western Germanic verb *~wōstijan~ (“to ruin, lay waste”) — a mixing that Corominas presents as the standard account. Along the purely Latin line the same verb gave English ~waste~ (through Old North French ~waster~) and, from ~vastus~, English ~vast~; the Germanic-tinged Romance forms are French ~gâter~ (“to spoil”), Italian ~guastare~, and Catalan and Portuguese ~gastar~.

The sense traveled from “to devastate” to “to consume, use up” and finally to “to spend” and “to wear out” — ruin softening into mere expenditure. The verb keeps that older bite in ~desgastar~ (“to wear away”) and ~malgastar~ (“to squander”), and it turns playful in the idiom ~gastar~ una broma (“to play a joke”). Early traces appear in 12th-century Mozarabic and in the Aragonese Liber Regum around 1200. From the same stock Spanish drew the noun ~gasto~ (“expense”), plus ~gastador~ and ~gastable~.
en.generalizar:
A learned formation: the adjective ~general~ + the verb-forming suffix ~-izar~ (from Greek ~-ízein~), “to make general.” ~general~ comes from Latin ~generālis~ (“belonging to a whole kind or class”), derived from ~genus~, genitive ~generis~ (“birth, race, kind, class”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to beget, give birth”). The root is enormously productive: it underlies Latin ~gignere~ (“to beget”), Greek ~génos~, and, in Germanic, English ~kin~ and ~kind~.

Latin ~generālis~ meant “pertaining to the whole genus rather than the species,” the opposite of ~speciālis~; ~generalizar~ therefore means to extend a claim from particular cases to the whole class — to reason from the specific to the general. The same PIE root *~ǵenh₁-~ seeded a vast Spanish family beyond ~general~: ~género~ (“genre, gender”), ~gente~ (“people”), ~generar~, ~genio~, ~ingenio~, ~indígena~ and ~progenitor~, all circling the idea of birth, kind, and kinship.
en.generar:
From Latin ~generāre~ (“to beget, to produce”), from ~genus~ (“birth, origin, kind”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to give birth, to beget”), one of the most fertile roots in the whole language family. Cognate with Ancient Greek ~génos~ (“race, kind”), with English ~genus~ and ~generate~, and — through Germanic — with English ~kin~ and ~kind~.

At its heart the word is about birth: to generate is to bring forth offspring, and only later, by extension, to produce anything at all — heat, electricity, income, ideas. The Latin ~genus~ meant a family or stock, which is why so much vocabulary of both kinship and classification springs from it. Spanish descendants include ~género~ (“gender, genre”), ~generación~, ~gente~ (“people,” from Latin ~gens~), ~genio~ and ~ingenio~ (the inborn talent one is “born with”), and ~degenerar~ — and, more surprisingly, ~nacer~ itself, from Latin ~nāscī~ (“to be born”), a cousin from the very same root.
en.gestionar:
A modern Spanish verb, formed from the noun ~gestión~ (“management”) plus ~-ar~. ~Gestión~ comes from Latin ~gestiō~ (“a carrying out, administration”), from ~gestus~, the past participle of ~gerere~ (“to carry, to conduct, to manage”). The deeper root of ~gerere~ is uncertain — De Vaan connects it hesitantly to ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), but the reconstruction is not secure. Through ~gerere~ and ~gestus~ the word is cognate with English ~gesture~, ~digest~ and ~register~, and with French ~gérer~ and Italian ~gestire~.

Latin ~gerere~ meant, very physically, to carry or bear — to carry on war, to carry an office, to carry oneself — and its noun ~gestiō~ was the carrying-out of a task. Spanish inherited the abstract sense: to ~gestionar~ is to carry a matter through the necessary steps, to administer it. The same “carrying” underlies some surprising relatives: ~gesto~ (a “bearing” of the body), ~gestación~ (the carrying of a child), and ~congestión~ (a carrying-together, a piling up). All belong to the wide ~gerere~ family that also gave ~gestión~, ~gerente~, ~sugerir~, ~digerir~ and ~registro~ — a lexicon of bearing, doing and managing.
en.girar:
From Latin ~gȳrāre~ (“to turn in a circle, to rotate”), from the noun ~gȳrus~ (“circle, ring, orbit”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~γῦρος~ (“ring, circle”). Because the word entered Latin from Greek, it is cognate with the English learned borrowings ~gyre~, ~gyrate~, and ~gyroscope~, and with the Greek loanword ~gyros~ — the spit-roasted meat named for the way it turns.

Latin ~gȳrāre~ meant simply to go round, and Spanish ~girar~ keeps that literal spin while adding figurative branches: a discussion ~gira~ around a topic, and, in commerce, money is “turned over” — hence ~girar~ a payment and the noun ~giro~ (“turn; money order; turn of phrase”). The same ~gȳrus~ yields ~giratorio~ (“revolving”), ~autogiro~ (the Spanish-invented aircraft, Juan de la Cierva’s ~autogiro~), and the vivid ~girasol~ (“sunflower”), literally the flower that “turns to the sun.”
en.glorificar:
From Late Latin ~glōrificāre~ (“to make glorious”), a compound of the noun ~glōria~ (“glory, renown”) and ~-ficāre~, an unstressed combining form of ~facere~ (“to make, do”). Spanish absorbed the word as a learned borrowing, a ~cultismo~, so it bypassed the popular sound-changes that reshaped inherited vocabulary and kept its Latin shape nearly intact. Italian ~glorificare~, French ~glorifier~, Portuguese ~glorificar~ and English ~glorify~ are all the same ecclesiastical coinage, carried across Europe by the Church. The base noun ~glōria~ is itself of uncertain origin: it has been proposed to descend, by dissimilation, from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know”) — the root also behind Latin ~nōscō~ (“to know”) and ~nārrō~ (“to tell”) — but that derivation is debated rather than settled.

The element ~-ficāre~ was a Latin word-factory, forming dozens of verbs meaning “to make into X,” and Spanish inherited or re-borrowed a whole shelf of them: ~santificar~ (“make holy”), ~purificar~, ~clasificar~, ~verificar~, ~edificar~ (“build up”). ~Glorificar~ began in a strictly religious register — to render praise and honour to God — and much of its Spanish life stayed liturgical; the ~Gloria~ of the Mass is the same word turned noun. In modern usage it broadened to secular praise — to glorify a hero, a brand, a war — often with a critical edge, as when someone is accused of ~glorificar~ violence. From the same ~glōria~ also come the adjective ~glorioso~ and the idiom ~estar en la gloria~ (“to be in heaven, utterly content”).
en.gobernar:
From Latin ~gubernāre~ (“to steer a ship, to direct”), itself borrowed early from Greek ~κυβερνάω~ (kybernáō, “to steer, to pilot”). The nautical image — a helmsman guiding a vessel — sat under “rule” from the start. Latin passed the verb to the Romance languages, giving French ~gouverner~, Italian ~governare~, and (through French) English ~govern~.

In Castilian the Latin b softened, giving ~gobernar~ and its family ~gobierno~, ~gobernador~, and the learned ~gubernamental~ (which preserves the original b). The Greek source has a spectacular modern echo: from ~κυβερνήτης~ (kybernḗtēs, “steersman”) Norbert Wiener coined ~cybernetics~ in 1948 — so “government” and everything “cyber-” trace back to the same Greek helmsman at the tiller.
en.golpear:
Spanish ~golpear~ is a verb derived from the noun ~golpe~ (“blow, hit”), which comes from Vulgar Latin ~colpus~, a syncopated form of Latin ~colaphus~ (“a blow with the fist, a cuff”). The Latin word was itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κόλαφος~ (~kólaphos~, “a slap, a box on the ear”). The same Vulgar Latin ~colpus~ gave Italian ~colpo~, Portuguese ~golpe~, and French ~coup~ — so Spanish ~golpe~ is a cognate of the English borrowing ~coup~.

The journey from a Greek word for a slap to a modern verb for any impact is straightforward: as ~colaphus~ lost its middle syllable in speech it became ~colpus~, and the initial ~c~ voiced to ~g~ on the way into Castilian. From ~golpe~ Spanish built ~golpear~ (“to hit, to strike, to knock”) and a spread of derivatives — ~golpazo~ (“a hard blow”), ~golpiza~ (“a beating”), and the political ~golpe de estado~ (“coup d'état”), whose agent noun ~golpista~ names one who stages a coup. The homely modern verb thus rests on a Greek fist.
en.gozar:
From ~gozo~ (“joy”), a noun from Latin ~gaudium~ (“joy, gladness”), itself bound to the Latin verb ~gaudēre~ (“to rejoice”), from Proto-Indo-European *~geh₂w-~ (“to rejoice”). Cognate with Italian ~godere~ and Portuguese ~gozar~, and — through the same root — with French ~jouir~ and, by way of Old French, the English words ~joy~, ~enjoy~ and ~rejoice~ (all from Latin ~gaudia~).

By Corominas's account ~gozar~ is an exclusively Spanish creation — popular and frequent in every period — built on the noun ~gozo~ rather than inherited ready-made from Latin. Old Aragonese kept a rival form, ~godir~, the regular popular continuation of ~gaudēre~, which the noun-based Castilian ~gozar~ eventually displaced. The sound-change is tidy: the Latin diphthong ~au~ closed to ~o~ and the group ~-di-~ regularly gave Castilian ~z~, so ~gaudium~ became ~gozo~. The sense runs from “to feel joy” to “to have the use or enjoyment of” something — one ~goza~ de buena salud. From the same family come ~gozoso~, ~regocijo~ and ~regocijar~.
en.grabar:
~grabar~ is one of Spanish's Germanic imports: it was borrowed from French ~graver~ (“to engrave”), which comes from Frankish *~graban~, from Proto-Germanic *~grabaną~ (“to dig”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰrebʰ-~ (“to dig, scratch, scrape”).
