Its Germanic cousins stay homely: English ~grave~ (“a dug pit”) and ~grub~, German ~graben~ (“to dig”), and Dutch ~graven~. The engraver's art is, at root, a kind of controlled digging into metal or stone.

From cutting lines into a plate, ~grabar~ generalized to “to engrave, carve,” then leapt to modern technology: to ~grabar~ is now “to record” sound or video — the groove of a phonograph record being, fittingly, an incised line. Figuratively an image can ~grabarse~ (“become etched”) in the memory. Kin include ~grabado~ (“engraving, print”), ~grabación~ (“a recording”), and ~grabadora~ (“recorder”). Beware the near-twin ~gravar~ (“to tax, burden”), a separate word from Latin ~gravāre~ (“to weigh down”) — same sound, unrelated root.
en.graduar:
From Medieval Latin ~graduāre~ (“to admit to a degree”), a verb built on Latin ~gradus~ (“step, pace, rung, degree”). ~gradus~ belongs to the verb ~gradī~ (“to step, walk”), from Proto-Italic *~graðus~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰredʰ-~ (“to walk, stride”). Through that root Spanish ~graduar~ is kin to English ~grade~, ~gradual~ and ~degree~, to French ~degré~ and to Italian and Portuguese ~grado~/~grau~.

The core image is the step: a ~gradus~ was a single pace or a stair-tread, and from “step” came “degree, rank, stage,” the graded steps of a scale. To ~graduar~ is thus to mark something off in steps (a thermometer, a lens) or to advance someone up the academic steps to a ~grado~. The same root yields ~grada~ (“tier, stand”), ~gradual~, ~gradiente~, ~degradar~ (“to demote,” step down) and ~ingrediente~, from ~ingredī~ “to step in.”
en.granar:
From Spanish ~grano~ (“grain, seed”), from Latin ~grānum~ (“grain, kernel”), from Proto-Italic *~grānom~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵr̥h₂nóm~ (“ripened grain”). ~Granar~ is a denominal verb: Spanish built it on its own noun ~grano~ with the suffix ~-ar~ rather than inheriting a ready-made Latin verb. The root noun has cognates everywhere — Portuguese ~grão~, Italian ~grano~, French ~grain~ — and, through the Germanic branch, English ~corn~ and ~kernel~ (historically a diminutive of ~corn~), while English also holds the learned Latin borrowing ~grain~.

To ~granar~ is what a cereal or fruit does when it forms and fills its seed — the grain sets and swells toward ripeness — and figuratively a plan or effort that ~grana~ is one that comes to fruition. The same PIE root *~ǵr̥h₂nóm~ seeded, fittingly, a large Spanish family: ~grano~, ~granero~ (“granary”), ~granizo~ (“hail,” little grains of ice), ~granada~ (“pomegranate”), from which came the ~grenade~, ~granito~ (“granite,” speckled with grains) and ~granuja~ (originally loose grape-seeds, later a “rascal, scoundrel”). Even ~granular~ and ~granja~ (“farm,” a place for stored grain) belong to the clan.
en.gritar:
From Vulgar Latin *~critāre~, a reduction of Latin ~quiritāre~ (“to wail, cry out for help”). A long-repeated account connects ~quiritāre~ to ~Quirites~, the formal name of the Roman citizens, as though to shout were “to call upon the citizens” for aid — but this is widely judged a folk etymology; Ernout–Meillet and others take ~quiritāre~ to be simply onomatopoeic (it also meant to squeal like a pig), and Corominas notes the sound-changes into Romance are not fully regular. Cognate with Italian ~gridare~, Portuguese ~gritar~, and French ~crier~, from which English borrowed ~cry~.

So the origin is debated, and the vivid image of a Roman crowd invoking their fellow ~Quirites~ should be read as a proposed story rather than settled fact. What is clear is the Romance outcome: an ordinary word for raising the voice. Spanish built a small family on it — the noun ~grito~ (“shout”), the collective ~griterío~ (“uproar, clamor”), and phrases like ~gritar~ a pleno pulmón (“to shout at the top of one’s lungs”).
en.guardar:
From Old Spanish ~guardar~, from a West Germanic verb *~wardōn~ (“to watch, keep guard”) taken into Hispano-Romance, from Proto-Germanic *~wardōn~, from Proto-Indo-European *~wer-~ (“to perceive, watch out for, heed”). Germanic initial ~w-~ was regularly reshaped as ~gu-~ in Romance. Cognate with Italian ~guardare~, French ~garder~ (and ~regarder~) and Portuguese ~guardar~. English inherited the same root twice: natively as ~ward~ (with ~warden~ and ~reward~) and, borrowed through French, as ~guard~ and ~guardian~ — a ~w-~/~gu-~ doublet of one Germanic word.

The oldest sense was “to keep watch, guard,” and Spanish widened it toward “to keep, store, put away safely,” and “to observe” a rule — ~guardar silencio~ is “to keep silent,” ~guardar las formas~ “to observe the proprieties.” The doublet is the memorable part: ~ward~ and ~guard~ are the very same Germanic word, one native to English, the other looped back in through French centuries later. From the root Spanish built ~guarda~, ~guardia~, ~guardián~, ~guardarropa~ (“wardrobe”), ~aguardar~ (“to wait for”) and ~resguardar~ (“to shelter”).
en.guerrear:
From Spanish ~guerra~ (“war”) plus the verbal suffix ~-ear~, so literally “to make war.” ~Guerra~ passed into Early Medieval Latin as ~werra~ from Frankish *~werru~ (“confusion, quarrel”), from Proto-West Germanic *~werran~ (“to confuse, bring into discord”), ultimately from a Proto-Indo-European root *~wers-~ (“to confuse, mix up”). The Romance world took the Germanic word instead of Latin ~bellum~ — perhaps because ~bellum~ had drifted too close to ~bellus~ (“pretty”) — giving Italian ~guerra~, French ~guerre~, Portuguese ~guerra~ and Occitan ~guerra~. Its Germanic siblings survive as English ~war~ and German ~wirren~ / ~verwirren~ (“to confuse, tangle”), which keep the older sense of chaos rather than organized combat.

That etymology is a quiet reminder that, to the peoples who coined the word, war was first of all confusion — the tangle and disorder of a brawl, not a tidy institution. ~Guerrear~ means to wage or carry on war, and by extension to squabble endlessly; a contrary child is said ~dar guerra~ (“to give trouble”). The family is large and everyday in Spanish: ~guerrero~ (“warrior”), ~guerrilla~ (“little war,” the diminutive), ~guerrillero~, ~posguerra~ (“post-war years”) and ~aguerrido~ (“battle-hardened”). English quietly took the diminutive back as ~guerrilla~, first for the irregular fighters of the Peninsular War, and still shares, far upstream, the same Germanic root as ~war~.
en.guiar:
Spanish ~guiar~ is of Germanic origin, though the details are debated. It is usually traced to Old Occitan ~guidar~, from Frankish *~wītan~ (“to show the way”), from Proto-Germanic *~wītaną~ (“to see, know; go”). The whole Romance family — Portuguese ~guiar~, Italian ~guidare~, French ~guider~, and, borrowed from French, English ~guide~ — reflects the same Germanic import into the Romance-speaking world.

The precise Germanic etymon is genuinely uncertain. One account points to a Frankish *~wītan~ meaning “to show a direction,” but Corominas objects that no Germanic word with exactly that sense is actually attested: Old High German ~wīzan~ meant “to impute, reproach,” and Anglo-Saxon ~wītan~ chiefly “to blame,” only rarely “to watch over.” He weighs instead a Gothic *~witan~ (“to observe, pay attention”), from which “to guide” might grow out of “watching someone's movements,” while conceding the semantic leap is a wide one — so the source should be read as proposed, not settled. From ~guiar~ Spanish formed ~guía~ (“guide, guidebook”), ~guion~ (“script, hyphen”), and ~guiaje~.
en.guisar:
From Spanish ~guisa~ (“manner, way, fashion”) plus ~-ar~; so ~guisar~ meant originally “to arrange or prepare in a certain manner,” and only later narrowed to “to cook.” ~Guisa~ came from a Germanic *~wīsa~ (“manner, way”), reaching Spanish through Gothic or by way of Old French ~guise~, and going back to Proto-Germanic *~wīsǭ~ (“manner”). It is therefore a cousin of English ~wise~ in the old sense of “way, manner” (as in ~likewise~ and ~otherwise~), of German ~Weise~ (“manner, melody”) and — reborrowed through French — of English ~guise~. Italian ~guisa~ and Portuguese ~guisa~ keep the same noun. The Proto-Germanic word is usually traced to the Indo-European root *~weyd-~ (“to see, know”) that also gave Latin ~vidēre~ (“to see”).

The jump from “manner” to “cooking” runs through the idea of preparing food the proper way — dressing, seasoning and arranging it in due form — a logic still alive in ~guiso~ (“a stew, a cooked dish”) and ~guisado~ (“stew, casserole”). Old Spanish used ~guisa~ freely for “way, manner,” a sense that now survives chiefly in the fixed phrase ~a guisa de~ (“by way of, in the manner of”). The same Germanic ~wīsa~ underlies the ~-wise~ of English adverbs such as ~clockwise~ and ~lengthwise~, each meaning “in the manner of,” so a Spanish kitchen verb and an English direction-word rest on one Gothic ancestor. From the culinary sense come the everyday ~guiso~, ~guisado~ and the agent noun ~guisandero~ (“cook”).
en.guiñar:
The origin of ~guiñar~ (“to wink”) is uncertain. It is usually classed as an expressive or imitative formation of the western Romance area, and one proposal derives it from a Late Latin ~cinnus~ (“a signal made with the eyes, a wink”), perhaps reshaped under the influence of Spanish ~ceño~ (“frown, knitted brow”). The same doubtful ~cinnus~ has been invoked for Italian ~ghignare~ (“to sneer, grin”), Old French ~guigner~ (“to peer, wink”) and Portuguese ~guinar~, but none of these connections is secure, and the whole set may simply be parallel expressive coinages rather than descendants of one word. Because the trail runs cold at the Latin level, no confident Proto-Indo-European root can be attached to it; the sources hedge, and so should we.

Whatever its source, ~guiñar~ settled firmly into Spanish as the verb for a deliberate wink — the quick closing of one eye that signals complicity, flirtation or a shared joke — and, of a light, ~guiñar~ can mean “to flicker.” The core noun is ~guiño~ (“a wink,” and figuratively “a knowing nod, an allusion”), as when a film makes ~un guiño~ to its fans. Sailors also use ~guiñar~ for a ship that yaws, swinging its head off course, and from that came the nautical noun ~guiñada~ (“a yaw, a lurch”). It is a small, human word whose etymology, appropriately enough, keeps winking at us from behind an uncertain past.
en.gustar:
Spanish ~gustar~ goes back to Latin ~gustāre~ (“to taste, sample, enjoy”). Curiously, the inherited Old Spanish form was ~gostar~; modern ~gustar~ is a later reborrowing closer to the Latin, whereas Portuguese kept the inherited ~gostar~. The Latin noun ~gustus~ (“a tasting, a flavor”) comes from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵews-~ (“to taste; to choose”). Through that root ~gustar~ is cognate with English ~choose~ and with the archaic English ~gust~ (“relish, keen enjoyment”).

The remarkable Spanish development is grammatical: ~gustar~ came to mean “to be pleasing to,” so the thing tasted becomes the subject and the taster an indirect object — hence ~me gusta~ literally says “it is pleasing to me,” not “I like it.” This “to like” sense is peculiar to Ibero-Romance; the older “to taste” survives in ~degustar~ (“to taste, sample”). From the same root come ~gusto~ (“taste, pleasure”), ~gustoso~ (“tasty; glad to”) and ~disgusto~ (“displeasure, upset”).
en.haber:
Spanish ~haber~, through Old Spanish ~aver~, descends from Latin ~habēre~ (“to have, hold”), from Proto-Italic *~habēō~, and — the root is generally traced this way, though debated — from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰh₁bʰ-~ (“to grab, take, hold”). Its Romance siblings all preserve the sense of holding or possessing: French ~avoir~, Italian ~avere~, Portuguese ~haver~, and Romanian ~avea~. English ~have~ looks and sounds like an obvious cousin, but it is a false friend: it belongs to the Germanic family and, as we will see, springs from an entirely different root, so the resemblance is pure coincidence.

Where French and Italian kept ~avoir~ and ~avere~ as the everyday verb of possession, Spanish demoted ~haber~ to a near-pure auxiliary and handed ownership to ~tener~ (from Latin ~tenēre~, “to hold”). Two roles remained: the auxiliary of the compound tenses (~he cantado~, “I have sung”) and the impersonal existential ~hay~, ~había~, ~habrá~ (“there is, there are”). The old possessive sense survives only fossilized, in the noun ~haber~ / ~haberes~ (“assets, wages”) and set phrases like ~habérselas con~. The form ~hay~ deserves its own note: it is medieval ~ha~ plus the locative clitic ~y~ (from Latin ~ibī~, “there”), exactly parallel to French ~il y a~ and Catalan ~hi ha~ — literally “it has there,” hence “there is.” From the same Latin verb Spanish also draws a learned family: ~hábito~, ~habitar~, ~exhibir~, ~prohibir~, and — via ~dēbēre~, that is ~dē-~ plus ~habēre~ — the verb ~deber~.

German ~haben~ completes the trap. It comes not from the root behind ~habēre~ but from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”) — the very root that in Latin produced ~capiō~ (“I seize”), and through it Spanish ~captar~, ~cautivo~, and ~aceptar~. So the two great “have” verbs of Western Europe are not related at all; they were pulled into the same shape by a ~Sprachbund~, the long convergence of neighboring languages, until each ended up an auxiliary: Spanish ~he comido~ mirrors German ~ich habe gegessen~. There is a final twist. Old Spanish did once share the European auxiliary split, taking “be” for verbs of motion and change — ~es nacido~ (“is born”), ~so venido~ (“is come”) — but it later leveled the system, generalizing ~haber~ to every compound tense (~ha muerto~, not older ~es muerto~). So modern Spanish, unlike French and German, no longer keeps the ~ser~/~haber~ division it once had. English quietly did the same: it once formed the perfect of verbs of motion and change with ~be~ — ~I am come~, ~he is risen~ — before ~have~ took over there too.
en.habilitar:
From Medieval Latin ~habilitāre~ (“to make able”), from Latin ~habilis~ (“handy, apt, manageable”), a verbal adjective from ~habēre~ (“to have, hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰeh₁bʰ-~ (“to grab, take, hold”). Cognate with French ~habiliter~ and ~habile~, and — through ~habilis~ — with English ~able~ and ~ability~.

~Habilis~ literally meant “easy to hold or handle,” hence apt or fit; ~habilitāre~ made that “to render fit,” and Spanish ~habilitar~ ranges from enabling a feature to legally qualifying a person or fitting out a space. The parent ~habēre~ gave Spanish ~haber~, and the root sprouted ~hábil~ (“skillful”), ~habilidad~ (“skill”), ~inhabilitar~ (“to disqualify”) and ~rehabilitar~ (“to rehabilitate”). English ~able~ shed its Latin ~h-~ long ago, but the fuller stem still shows in ~ability~ and ~rehabilitate~.
en.habitar:
From Latin ~habitāre~, the frequentative of ~habēre~ (“to have, to hold”), from Proto-Italic *~habēō~, traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰeh₁bʰ-~ (“to grab, to take”) that the sources themselves call uncertain. It is cognate with French ~habiter~, Italian ~abitare~ and Portuguese ~habitar~, while English borrowed the same Latin stem in ~habit~ and ~inhabit~.

A frequentative names a repeated or habitual action, so ~habitāre~ meant literally “to have again and again, to keep on holding” — and the thing one keeps holding and returning to is a home, whence “to dwell, to reside.” That short step from possessing to residing is the whole life of the word. Because the deep root *~gʰeh₁bʰ-~ is debated, its cognates outside Latin are offered with caution. Within Spanish the family flourished: ~habitación~ (“room”), ~habitante~ (“inhabitant”) and ~hábitat~ all descend from the verb, while the related noun ~habitus~ gave ~hábito~ (“habit; monk’s robe”) and the adjective ~habitual~.
en.hablar:
From Old Spanish ~fablar~, from Latin ~fābulārī~ (“to chat, converse”), a verb built on ~fābula~ (“story, talk”), itself from ~fārī~ (“to speak”) and the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰeh₂-~ (“to speak”). Cognate with Portuguese ~falar~ and Italian ~favellare~, and — through the same root — with Latin ~fāma~ (whence English ~fame~) and the learned English doublet ~fable~, borrowed straight from ~fābula~.

The Latin ~f~ of ~fablar~ weakened to an aspirated ~h~ in early Castilian and then fell silent, so medieval ~fablar~ became modern ~hablar~ while the letter lingered on, mute — one of the sound-changes that most sharply distinguishes Spanish from its Romance siblings. The meaning drifted too: where classical Latin used ~fābulārī~ for idle chatting, Spanish promoted it to the ordinary word for “to speak,” displacing ~loquī~. From ~fābula~ Spanish also drew the learned ~fábula~ (“fable”) and ~fabuloso~, while ~hablar~ itself seeded ~habla~ (“speech”), ~hablador~ (“chatterbox”), ~hablante~ (“speaker”), and ~hablilla~ (“rumor”).
en.hacendar:
From ~hacienda~ (“estate, landed property, farm”) plus ~-ar~. ~hacienda~ descends from Latin ~facienda~ (“things that must be done”), the neuter plural gerundive of ~facere~ (“to do, to make”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to set, to put, to make”). That root also surfaces in English ~do~ and ~fact~ and in German ~tun~.

The journey from “things to be done” to “ranch” is the charm of the word: ~facienda~ meant one's tasks and business, which in Castilian became one's affairs, then one's wealth, and finally the ~hacienda~ — the estate that both produces and embodies that wealth (in Spain, capitalized, the Treasury itself). So ~hacendar~ means “to grant property to,” and ~hacendado~ is the landholder. The huge ~facere~ family fans out through ~hacer~, ~hecho~, ~quehacer~ and ~hazaña~ (“a deed, a feat”), alongside the learned ~facción~ and ~afición~.
en.hacer:
Spanish ~hacer~ comes, through Old Spanish ~fazer~, from Latin ~facere~ (“to do, to make”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, set, place”). The same root gave the English verb ~do~ and German ~tun~, so ~hacer~ and ~do~ are true cousins under the skin. Its Romance siblings kept the Latin ~f-~: Italian ~fare~, French ~faire~, Portuguese ~fazer~. Spanish alone let that ~f-~ drift to a silent ~h-~, the regular change that turned ~facere~ into ~hacer~.

Latin ~facere~ was the great all-purpose verb of doing and making, and its progeny is enormous. Spanish keeps the past participle ~hecho~ (“done; fact”), and builds ~deshacer~ (“to undo”), ~satisfacer~ (“to satisfy,” literally “to make enough”), and ~hacienda~ (“estate, treasury”). Learned borrowings that skipped the ~f-~-to-~h-~ shift preserve the older look: ~factor~, ~efecto~ (“effect”), and ~factible~ (“feasible”) — a whole workshop of words for making.
en.halagar:
~Halagar~ (“to flatter, to please”) descends from Old Spanish ~falagar~, with the regular Castilian change of initial ~f-~ to a silent ~h-~ — the same shift that turned ~farīna~ into ~harina~ (“flour”) and ~fīlum~ into ~hilo~ (“thread”). Its deeper origin is disputed. The account favoured by Corominas derives it from Andalusi and ultimately Classical Arabic ~ḵallaqa~ (“to smooth, to polish”), with the related ~ḵālaqa~ (“to treat someone kindly, agreeably”) — flattery as a smoothing-over. Earlier authorities proposed instead Arabic ~ḥalāwa~ (“something sweet or agreeable”) or a Latin ~flagitāre~ (“to entreat, importune”), and others have floated Basque or Hebrew sources; the verb-ending ~-agar~ probably reflects the Latin suffix ~-icāre~. The competing theories remain unresolved, and the word is best labelled of uncertain, probably Arabic, origin.

The semantics stay consistent across the theories: to ~halagar~ is to smooth someone with pleasing words, to gratify and cajole — sometimes sincerely (“to delight”), sometimes with an ulterior motive (“to flatter”). Old ~falagar~ could also mean “to caress, to soothe,” a gentler physical sense preserved in dialect. The living family is small but common: the noun ~halago~ (“a piece of flattery, a compliment”), the adjective ~halagüeño~ (“flattering, promising,” as in ~una noticia halagüeña~, encouraging news) and ~halagador~ (“flattering; flatterer”). The word keeps the double edge that always shadowed flattery in Spanish — a ~halago~ can warm the heart or grease a request — fitting for a verb whose own past refuses to be pinned down.
en.hallar:
From Old Spanish ~fallar~ (“to find”), from Latin ~afflāre~ (“to blow toward, breathe on”), from ~ad-~ (“toward”) plus ~flāre~ (“to blow”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰleh₁-~ (“to blow”). The initial ~f-~ became ~h-~ in the regular Castilian shift (as ~facere~ → ~hacer~), and the ~h~ fell silent. Portuguese ~achar~ and Romanian ~afla~ (both “to find”) descend from the very same ~afflāre~.

How does “to blow toward” become “to find”? The sources agree on the etymon but debate the path; Corominas favors applying to the Latin verb the sense of a hound catching a scent — the dog winds its game and so comes upon it. That hunting image, though the preferred account, is not certain, and other Romanists proposed “to reach with one’s breath, and thus to touch.” The ~h~ of ~hallar~ itself likely arose by a metathesis of the internal ~-f-~. Spanish keeps the noun ~hallazgo~ (“a find, discovery”) beside everyday ~hallar~ (“to find, to come upon”).
en.hartar:
~Hartar~ (“to fill, to satiate, to sate to excess”) is built on the adjective ~harto~ (“full, sated; fed up”), from Latin ~fartus~ (“stuffed, crammed”), the past participle of ~farcīre~ (“to stuff, cram, fatten”). The initial Latin ~f-~ became the silent Castilian ~h-~, as in ~harina~ from ~farīna~. ~Farcīre~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~farkiō~ to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰrekʷ-~ (“to stuff, cram together”), a root that also yielded Ancient Greek ~φράσσω~ (“to fence in, block up”) and Latin ~frequēns~ (“crowded, frequent”). English ~farce~ is a close relative: it reached English through French ~farcir~ (“to stuff”), and a farce was originally comic padding stuffed into a church play. Portuguese ~farto~, Catalan ~fart~ and Galician ~farto~ are the exact Iberian cognates of ~harto~.

The metaphor at the heart of ~hartar~ is over-fullness: to stuff someone or something past satisfaction. Reflexively, ~hartarse~ is to eat one's fill, even to gorge (~hartarse de dulces~, “to stuff oneself with sweets”), and figuratively to have more than enough of anything — hence ~harto~ as “fed up” and the adverbial ~harto~ meaning “quite, very” in parts of Latin America. The sense of surfeit turned readily to weariness: ~estar harto~ is “to be sick and tired.” From the same stem come ~hartazgo~ and ~hartura~ (both “a surfeit, a bellyful”) and the verb ~hartarse~. It is a neat irony that ~farcīre~, ancestor of both a good stuffing and a light stage ~farce~, also gave Spanish its everyday word for being utterly fed up.
en.heder:
~Heder~ (“to stink, to reek”) comes from Latin ~foetēre~ (also written ~fētēre~), “to give off a foul smell.” The word shows two classic Castilian sound-changes: the initial Latin ~f-~ became a silent ~h-~, and the stressed ~ē~ diphthongized to ~-ie-~ under stress, which is why the verb is ~heder~ in the infinitive but ~hiede~ (“it stinks”) in the present. The Latin verb goes with the noun ~foetor~ (“a stench”) and the adjective ~foetidus~ (“foul-smelling”). Its history before Latin is not securely established, so no Proto-Indo-European root should be asserted with confidence. The nearest Romance cognates are Portuguese ~feder~ and Galician ~feder~, which kept the ~f-~ that Castilian dropped.

~Heder~ is a strong, old-fashioned word — much blunter than ~oler mal~ (“to smell bad”) — and it carries a whiff of the archaic and the literary, turning up in medieval and biblical registers (the raised Lazarus who ~hiede~) more than in casual speech. Its most productive relative is the noun ~hedor~ (“stench, reek”), from Latin ~foetor~, an everyday word where the verb itself has grown rare. The learned, un-Castilianized doublet ~fétido~ (“fetid, foul”) was borrowed straight from ~foetidus~ without the ~f-~-to-~h-~ change, so Spanish keeps both the popular ~heder~ and the bookish ~fétido~ side by side. English ~fetid~ comes, through the same ~foetidus~, from the very same Latin source.
en.helar:
From Latin ~gelāre~ (“to freeze”), a verb formed on the noun ~gelū~ (“frost, cold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~gel-~ (“cold”). Cognate with Italian ~gelare~, French ~geler~ and Portuguese ~gelar~, and — through the same root — with English ~cold~ and ~cool~ and the learned ~gelid~. Unlike most Spanish words in h-, whose h continues a Latin f, the h of ~helar~ marks a Latin initial g that vanished before a front vowel — the very change that turned ~germānus~ into ~hermano~.

The core sense of freezing held firm across three millennia. In Spanish the verb also took on figurative life — a scene of horror can ~helar la sangre~ (“freeze the blood”), and someone stunned is left ~helado~ (“frozen, dumbfounded”). From the same root Spanish drew a rich family: ~hielo~ (“ice”), ~helada~ (“frost”), ~helado~ (“ice cream; frozen”), ~congelar~ (“to freeze, congeal”), ~deshelar~ (“to thaw”) and the borrowed ~gelatina~ (“gelatin”).
en.henchir:
From Latin ~implēre~ (“to fill up”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~plēre~ (“to fill”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”). Through a Vulgar Latin shift to the third conjugation, *~implīre~, it passed into Old Spanish as ~enchir~; the initial f- (later h-) was borrowed by contamination with ~finchar~ (“to swell”), modern ~hinchar~. Cognate with Italian ~empire~, French ~emplir~ and Portuguese ~encher~.

The same root *~pleh₁-~ underlies the adjective ~plēnus~ (“full”), which gave Spanish ~lleno~ and the everyday verb ~llenar~ that has largely displaced ~henchir~ — now mostly literary, surviving where a heart may ~henchirse~ with pride. English relatives through Latin and Greek include ~full~, ~plenty~, ~complete~, ~plethora~ and ~implement~. Spanish keeps a few derivatives of its own: ~henchimiento~ and ~henchidura~ (“a filling”).
en.hendir:
A variant of ~hender~, from Old Spanish ~fender~, from Latin ~findere~ (“to split, cleave”), from Proto-Italic *~findō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰeyd-~ (“to split”). The regular Castilian change of Latin initial f- to a silent h- gave ~fender~ > ~hender~/~hendir~. Cognate — through the Germanic branch of the same root — with English ~bite~ and ~bit~, and, through the Latin past participle ~fissus~, with the borrowings ~fissure~ and ~fission~.

The verb kept its concrete sense of cleaving — an axe that ~hiende~ wood, a prow that ~hiende~ the waves — and extended figuratively to cutting through a crowd. From the same Latin stem Spanish inherited ~hendidura~ and ~hendedura~ (“a crack, cleft”), the colloquial ~rendija~ (“chink, slit”), and ~hendimiento~. The learned doublets ~fisura~ (“fissure”) and ~fisión~ (“fission”) entered later straight from Latin, keeping the original f-.
en.heredar:
From Latin ~hērēditāre~ (“to inherit, make an heir”), a Late Latin verb built on ~hērēs~ (stem ~hērēd-~, “heir”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰeh₁-~ (“to leave behind, be empty, forsaken”) — the heir being the one who takes over what a death left vacant. By the same root the Latin ~hērēs~ is often linked to Ancient Greek ~χῆρος~ (~khêros~, “bereft”) and ~χήρα~ (~khḗra~, “widow”). Cognate through the Latin with English ~heir~, ~heritage~ and ~inherit~ (all via Old French), French ~hériter~ and Italian ~ereditare~.

Old Spanish already had ~heredar~ and the noun ~heredad~ (“landed estate, inherited property”), reminding us that the earliest inheritances were above all land. The Latin ~h-~ fell silent in speech but survived in spelling, which is why the whole family is written with a mute ~h~: ~heredero~ (“heir”), ~herencia~ (“inheritance”), ~heredad~ and the learned ~hereditario~ (“hereditary”). The verb has kept its ancient double face — one both ~hereda~ a fortune and, less happily, ~hereda~ a grandparent's temper.
en.herir:
~herir~ comes straight from Latin ~ferīre~ (“to strike, hit, deal a blow”), with the regular Castilian shift of initial Latin ~f-~ to a silent ~h-~ — the same change that turned ~facere~ into ~hacer~ and ~farīna~ into ~harina~. ~ferīre~ is usually traced to Proto-Italic *~ferjō~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰerH-~ (“to strike, pierce”), though the verb’s deeper connections are debated, and some link it instead to *~bʰer-~ (“to cut, bore”), the root behind Latin ~forāre~ and Spanish ~horadar~. Its Romance siblings are transparent: Italian ~ferire~ and Portuguese ~ferir~, both still meaning “to wound.”

To a Roman, ~ferīre~ named the blow itself — to strike with a weapon or a hand, even to “strike” a bargain. Spanish shifted the emphasis from cause to effect: the consequence took the name of the act, and ~herir~ came to mean “to wound,” to leave a ~herida~ (“wound”). The word now cuts in every register, from a physical gash to a wounded pride — one can ~herir~ someone’s feelings. Around the same root cluster, Spanish still ~malhiere~ (wounds badly) and ~zahiere~ (rebukes cuttingly), while the noun ~herida~ and the adjective ~malherido~ keep the old sense of a body struck and marked.
en.herrar:
From Old Spanish ~ferrar~, from Late Latin ~ferrāre~ (“to fit with iron”), a verb built on Latin ~ferrum~ (“iron”); the regular shift of Latin initial f- to a silent h- yields modern ~herrar~. The origin of ~ferrum~ itself is uncertain: it was most likely borrowed from an unknown non-Indo-European substrate language, and some scholars have proposed an ultimate Semitic source (compare Hebrew ~barzel~, Akkadian ~parzillum~), perhaps reaching Latin through Etruscan — but this remains disputed. Cognate with Portuguese and Catalan ~ferrar~, French ~ferrer~ and Italian ~ferrare~.

The verb means to fit with iron: to shoe a horse, and — from the branding iron — to brand livestock. From ~ferrum~ Spanish drew a whole workshop of words: ~hierro~ (“iron”), ~herradura~ (“horseshoe”), ~herrador~ (“farrier”), ~herrero~ (“blacksmith”), ~herrería~ (“smithy”) and ~herramienta~ (“tool”), all with the native h-. Later learned borrowings kept the Latin f-: ~férreo~ (“iron, unyielding”) and ~ferretería~ (“hardware store”).
en.hervir:
From Old Spanish ~fervir~, from Latin ~fervēre~ (“to boil, be hot”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰrewh₁-~ (“to boil, seethe”). The verb passed from the Latin second conjugation to the Spanish -ir class, perhaps by analogy with ~servir~ and ~vivir~, and the regular loss of Latin initial f- as a silent h- gave modern ~hervir~. Through the same root it is cognate with English ~brew~ and ~broth~, and, through Latin, with ~ferment~ and ~fervent~.

The root evokes bubbling heat, and Spanish keeps both the literal and figurative senses — water that boils and a plaza that ~hierve~ (“swarms”) with people. Native derivatives include ~hervor~ (“boiling, ardor”), ~hervidero~ (“hotbed, throng”) and ~hirviente~ (“boiling”). Learned borrowings straight from Latin kept the f-: ~fervor~ (“fervor”), ~férvido~ (“fervid”), ~efervescente~ (“effervescent”) and ~fermento~ (“ferment”).
en.hincar:
From Old Spanish ~fincar~, from Vulgar Latin *~fīgicāre~, a frequentative built on Latin ~fīgere~ (“to fix, fasten, drive in”), from Proto-Italic *~feigʷō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeygʷ-~ (“to stick, set up”); the regular Castilian shift of initial f- to h- gave ~hincar~, and the intrusive -n- is thought to owe to influence from ~fingere~. It is a doublet of ~ficar~ and cognate with Italian ~ficcare~, French ~ficher~ and Portuguese ~fincar~.

The core sense is driving something in — a stake into the ground, a knee to the floor. To kneel is ~hincarse de rodillas~, and to apply oneself is to ~hincar los codos~ (literally “to sink one’s elbows”). From the same verb Spanish keeps ~ahínco~ (“eagerness, insistence”), ~ahincar~ and, most familiarly, ~hincapié~ in the idiom ~hacer hincapié~ (“to stress, insist on”). Through Latin ~fīgere~ English gained ~fix~, ~fixture~ and ~fibula~.
en.hinchar:
From Old Spanish ~finchar~, from Latin ~īnflāre~ (“to blow into, inflate”), a compound of ~in-~ and ~flāre~ (“to blow”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰleh₁-~ (“to blow, swell”). Through assimilation of the inner consonants and the regular Castilian loss of initial f- as a silent h-, it became ~hinchar~ — a doublet of the later learned borrowing ~inflar~. Cognate with Portuguese ~inchar~ and French ~enfler~, and, through the same root, with English ~blow~ and ~bladder~.

The sense stayed close to the source — to swell or inflate, literally and of pride. Native derivatives include ~hinchazón~ (“swelling”), ~hinchado~ (“swollen, bombastic”) and, in a striking modern turn, ~hincha~ — a sports fan — with the collective ~hinchada~ (“the fans”). From the same Latin ~flāre~ Spanish also has the learned ~inflar~ and ~inflación~, while English drew ~inflate~, ~deflate~ and ~flatulent~.
en.holgar:
From Old Spanish ~folgar~, from Vulgar Latin *~follicāre~ (“to pant, breathe hard”), from Latin ~follis~ (“bellows, leather bag”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰelǵʰ-~ (“to swell”); the regular Castilian shift of initial f- to a silent h- gave ~holgar~. The root’s idea of a swelling, air-filled bag survives in Spanish ~fuelle~ (“bellows”) and ~follículo~ (“follicle”), and — through Latin ~follis~ in its sense “windbag, empty-head” — in English ~fool~ and ~folly~, borrowed via French. It is cognate through the same root with English ~belly~ and ~bellows~.

The semantic path is vivid: from a winded animal panting to catch its breath, ~follicāre~ came to mean pausing, then resting, then enjoying leisure — so ~holgar~ is “to rest, be idle, take one’s ease.” Its most consequential descendant is ~huelga~ (“labor strike”), literally a time of rest from work, alongside ~huelgo~ (“breath”). Everyday relatives include ~holgado~ (“roomy, comfortable”), ~holgura~ (“ease, slack”), ~holgazán~ (“idler”) and the festive ~jolgorio~ (“revelry”).
en.honrar:
From Latin ~honōrāre~ (“to honor, respect”), from ~honor~ (earlier ~honōs~, “honor, esteem, public office”). The ultimate origin of Latin ~honor~ is uncertain — no secure Indo-European source is known, so the deeper root is best left open. Cognate with Italian ~onorare~, French ~honorer~, Portuguese ~honrar~, and English ~honor~ (borrowed through Old French ~honor~).

Old Spanish showed the verb as ~ondrar~ and ~onrar~, an epenthetic ~d~ slipped between the ~n~ and the ~r~ to ease the cluster before it settled as ~honrar~; the silent ~h~ is a learned restoration modeled on the Latin spelling. To a Roman, ~honor~ named not only esteem but public office — a magistracy itself was an ~honor~, and the ~cursus honōrum~ (“course of honors”) was the ladder of political posts one climbed. From the same noun Spanish holds ~honra~, ~honesto~, ~honorario~, ~honorable~, ~honroso~, and ~deshonra~.
en.horadar:
From Old Spanish ~horado~ (a hole, a perforation) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-ar~; ~horado~ descends from Latin ~forātus~, the past participle of ~forāre~ (“to bore, to pierce”), from Proto-Italic *~forāō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰerH-~ (“to pierce, strike”). The initial Latin ~f-~ became Castilian ~h-~, a hallmark sound change that also turned ~farīna~ into ~harina~. Cognate with Italian ~forare~, Portuguese ~furar~ and Catalan ~foradar~, and — through the same root — with English ~bore~.

The meaning has held remarkably steady: to make a hole by boring or tunneling through something. A Latin sibling formed with the prefix ~per-~ (“through”) gave ~perforāre~, source of the learned Spanish ~perforar~ — so the same root reaches Spanish twice, once inherited and homely in ~horadar~, once borrowed and technical in ~perforar~. Other kin include ~horado~ itself and the anatomical ~foramen~, a Latinism naming a natural opening in bone.
en.hospedar:
From Late Latin ~hospitāre~ (“to receive as a guest”), a verb built on Latin ~hospes~ (stem ~hospit-~), “host; guest; stranger”. That noun was itself a compound, ~hostis~ (“stranger, and later enemy”) plus *~pótis~ (“master, lord”) — reconstructed Proto-Indo-European *~gʰóstipotis~, literally the “lord of guests”. Its first element is PIE *~gʰóstis~ (“stranger, guest”), which also gave, through Germanic, English ~guest~, and through Latin the words ~host~ and ~hostile~.

The word carries an old ethic of hospitality in which host and guest were two faces of one relationship — the same person who lodges you was bound to protect you. Spanish kept the inherited noun ~huésped~ (which can still mean either host or guest) and built ~hospedar~, “to lodge, to put someone up”, alongside ~hospedaje~ (“lodging”). From the same ~hospit-~ stem came the learned family ~hospital~ and ~hostal~, while the enemy-branch ~hostis~ survives in ~hueste~ (“armed host, troop”).
en.hostigar:
Inherited from Old Spanish ~fostigar~, from Late Latin ~fūstīgāre~ (“to beat with a cudgel”), a compound of Latin ~fūstis~ (“stick, staff, cudgel”) and a reduced form of ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”). The word thus first meant to thrash someone with a stick. The Castilian shift of initial ~f-~ to ~h-~ produced ~hostigar~, while a later learned borrowing of the same Latin verb entered as the doublet ~fustigar~. The base noun ~fūstis~ is itself of uncertain origin. Cognate with Italian ~fustigare~.

From literal flogging the sense softened and turned figurative: to lash with words, to harass, to pester relentlessly — and in parts of Spanish America ~hostigar~ can even describe a food or drink that cloys and turns the stomach. The stick stayed visible in the learned doublet ~fustigar~, which today means “to censure harshly”, and in the noun ~fuste~ (“shaft; wooden frame; and figuratively substance or weight”). Whip, rebuke and saddle-frame all trace back to a single Latin cudgel.
en.huir:
From Latin ~fugere~ (“to flee, run away”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰeug-~ (“to flee”). The same root surfaces in Ancient Greek ~pheúgein~ (“to flee”) and in the Latin noun ~fuga~ (“flight”), and, borrowed into English from Latin, in ~fugitive~ and ~refuge~. The Romance cousins stayed close to the verb — Portuguese ~fugir~, Italian ~fuggire~, French ~fuir~.

Spanish ~huir~ is a showcase of Castilian sound change: Latin initial ~f-~ weakened to an aspirated ~h-~ and then fell silent, so ~fugere~ passed through Old Spanish ~fuir~ to today’s ~huir~, whose ~h~ is written but mute. The learned words kept the ~f~ that the popular verb lost: ~fuga~ (“flight, escape, leak”), ~fugitivo~, ~refugio~, ~fugaz~ (“fleeting”), and ~subterfugio~. The verb even rebuilt a prefixed cousin, ~rehuir~ (“to shun, avoid”), on its own now-Spanish shape.
en.hundir:
From Latin ~fundere~ (“to pour, pour out, melt, cast”), which in Old Spanish became ~fondir~ / ~hundir~ with the regular Castilian change of initial ~f-~ to ~h-~. ~fundere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰew-~ (“to pour, to libate”). It is a doublet of the learned ~fundir~ (“to melt, to cast”), reborrowed later and keeping its ~f-~. Cognate with Italian ~fondere~ and French ~fondre~, and — through the same root — with English ~found~ (“to cast metal”), German ~gießen~ (“to pour”) and Ancient Greek ~χεῖν~ (~kheîn~, “to pour”).

The sense traveled a vivid road: from “to pour out” to “to make something sink or collapse,” as if a poured-down mass were dragging everything downward. Spanish ~hundir~ now means to sink, submerge, or ruin — a ship ~se hunde~, a roof ~se hunde~, a business ~se hunde~. Its learned twin ~fundir~ keeps the metallurgical sense of melting and casting, and the two split a rich family between them: ~fundición~ (“foundry; casting”), ~difundir~ (“to diffuse”), ~confundir~ (“to pour together → to confuse”), ~infundir~ and ~refundir~. The figurative ~hundido~ (“sunken; downcast”) applies as readily to eyes as to ships.
en.hurtar:
Inherited from Old Spanish ~furtar~, from the noun ~furto~ (“theft”) plus ~-ar~; ~furto~ comes from Latin ~fūrtum~ (“theft; stolen thing”), a derivative of ~fūr~ (“thief”). The thief was, etymologically, a carrier-off: ~fūr~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”), the same root behind Latin ~ferre~ and, in Greek, ~φώρ~ (“thief”). As usual in Castilian, initial ~f-~ weakened to ~h-~, giving ~hurtar~ beside older ~furtar~.

So to steal was pictured as carrying something away on the sly. English borrowed the related adjective ~furtivus~ as ~furtive~, keeping precisely that sense of stealthy, hidden action. Spanish preserves the noun ~hurto~ (“petty theft, pilfering”) and the learned ~furtivo~ — a ~cazador furtivo~ is a poacher, a hunter who bears the game away in secret. The everyday phrase ~a hurtadillas~ (“on the sly, stealthily”) still carries the old furtive image in its bones.
en.identificar:
From Medieval Latin ~identificāre~ (“to make identical”), a compound of ~identitās~ (“sameness, identity”) and ~-ficāre~, the combining form of ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). ~identitās~ was itself a late, learned coinage from ~idem~ (“the same”). The word spread through the Romance languages as a scholarly borrowing rather than by inheritance: Italian ~identificare~, French ~identifier~, Portuguese ~identificar~, and English ~identify~ all arrived by the same learned route in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

Because ~identificar~ is a bookish, relatively modern formation, its story belongs to philosophy and law rather than to folk speech. ~idem~, “the very same,” carried the Latin idea of exact sameness, and ~-ficāre~ carried “to make,” so the verb means literally “to make one and the same” — to establish that a person and a name denote a single thing. From ~idem~ Spanish also keeps ~ídem~ (the ditto word), ~identidad~, and ~idéntico~; from ~facere~ descends a whole crowd of ~-ficar~ verbs such as ~verificar~, ~clasificar~, and ~modificar~. The reflexive ~identificarse~ (“to identify oneself” — to show one's papers, or to feel kinship with someone) is a later extension, its bureaucratic and emotional senses growing up side by side.
en.ignorar:
Spanish ~ignorar~ descends from Latin ~ignōrāre~ (“not to know, to be unaware of”), from ~ignārus~ (“not knowing”), a compound of the negative ~in-~ and ~gnārus~ (“knowing”). ~Gnārus~ belongs with the verb ~nōscere~ (“to know”), both from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know”) — one of the great Indo-European roots, cognate with Greek ~gignṓskein~ and with English ~know~ and ~ken~. Its Romance heirs include Italian ~ignorare~ and French ~ignorer~.

For most of its history ~ignorar~ meant only “to be ignorant of,” and Spanish purists long resisted the newer sense “to disregard, to snub,” which spread in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries under English ~ignore~. The root ~gnārus~ hides a surprise: it also produced ~narrāre~ (“to tell”), on the logic that one who knows a thing can recount it — so ~ignorar~ and ~narrar~ are cousins. From the same *~ǵneh₃-~ Spanish gathers ~conocer~, ~reconocer~, ~noticia~, ~notorio~ and even ~noble~, from Latin ~gnōbilis~, “knowable, well-known.”
en.igualar:
From ~igual~ (“equal”), from Latin ~aequālis~ (“equal, even”), formed with the suffix ~-ālis~ on ~aequus~ (“level, even, fair”). ~aequus~ itself is of uncertain origin, with no secure Indo-European cognates outside Latin. Cognate with Italian ~uguale~, French ~égal~ and Portuguese ~igual~, and — as a learned borrowing — with English ~equal~.

In Latin ~aequālis~ described things level or of the same measure; late and medieval Latin sharpened it toward the abstract “equal,” and the monophthongized vulgar form ~equalis~ closed its first vowel to give ~igual~. To ~igualar~ is thus to make things level or the same. From ~aequus~ Spanish draws a wide family — ~igualdad~, ~igual~, ~ecuación~, ~adecuar~ and ~equilibrio~ (with ~libra~, “balance”).
en.iluminar:
From Latin ~illūmināre~ (“to light up”), from ~in-~ plus ~lūmen~ (“light,” stem ~lūmin-~), from Proto-Indo-European *~lewk-~ (“to shine”). Cognate with French ~illuminer~, Italian ~illuminare~ and Portuguese ~iluminar~, and — through the same root — with English ~illuminate~ and ~luminous~. It shares its root with ~ilustrar~, another child of *~lewk-~.

Latin ~lūmen~ descended into Spanish twice: as the learned ~iluminar~ and, by ordinary inheritance, as ~lumbre~ (“fire, light”). The verb ~alumbrar~ shows the same double life — it means both to give light and, beautifully, to give birth, to bring a child into the light. From *~lewk-~ Spanish gathered a bright cluster: ~luz~, ~lumbrera~, ~luminoso~, ~luminaria~ and ~iluminación~. The eighteenth-century age of reason was even named for the metaphor of light itself.
en.ilustrar:
From Latin ~illūstrāre~ (“to light up, to make bright, to clarify”), from ~in-~ (here intensive) plus ~lūstrāre~ (“to illuminate, to make bright”), a verb tied to ~lūx~ (“light”), from Proto-Indo-European *~lewk-~ (“to shine, to be bright”). Cognate with French ~illustrer~, Italian ~illustrare~ and Portuguese ~ilustrar~, and — through the same root — with English ~illustrate~, ~lustre~ and ~illustrious~.

The Latin verb meant literally to shed light on something, and from there moved figuratively to “to make clear, to explain,” and later “to adorn with pictures or examples,” the sense that dominates today. The adjective ~illūstris~ (“bright, distinguished”) gave Spanish ~ilustre~ and English ~illustrious~, a close cousin of the verb. The same root *~lewk-~ lit a broad family of Spanish words: ~luz~, ~lucir~, ~lúcido~, ~lustre~ and ~ilustración~, the last of which also names the Enlightenment.
en.imaginar:
From Latin ~imāgināri~ (“to picture to oneself, imagine, fancy”), a verb formed on ~imāgō~ (“image, likeness, copy; also phantom, apparition”). ~imāgō~ was built on the stem of ~imitārī~ (“to imitate, copy”), and the pair is usually traced to Proto-Indo-European *~aim-~ (“to copy”), the root also behind Latin ~aemulus~ (“rival, emulous”). Cognate with Italian ~immaginare~, French ~imaginer~ and Portuguese ~imaginar~, and with English ~imagine~.

Before it meant a mental picture, ~imāgō~ named a very physical thing: the wax death-masks of ancestors that Roman families kept and paraded at funerals — an ~imāgō~ was a likeness of the dead, and the word also meant a ghost. From “likeness” it moved inward to “the image formed in the mind,” which is what ~imaginar~ carries today. The same family gave Spanish ~imagen~, ~imaginación~, ~imaginario~, ~imitar~ (“to imitate”) and ~émulo~ (“emulator, rival”).
en.imitar:
From Latin ~imitārī~ (“to copy, imitate”), a deponent verb, from Proto-Italic *~imā~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eym-~ (“to copy, imitate”). The same root gave two of Latin's most important nouns of likeness: ~imāgō~ (“image, likeness”) and ~aemulus~ (“a rival, one who strives to equal another”). Outside Italic the root is rare, but it surfaces in Hittite ~ḫimma-~ (“substitute, imitation”). Romance kept the verb as Italian ~imitare~, French ~imiter~, and Portuguese ~imitar~, while English borrowed both ~imitate~ and, from the noun, ~image~.

What makes ~imitar~ quietly interesting is its family: ~imitar~ (“to imitate”) and ~imagen~ (“image”) are cousins, both descended from the root idea of making a likeness — the one a copy in action, the other a copy in form. From the ~aemulus~ branch Spanish and English share ~emular~ / ~emulate~, the imitation that means to rival and outdo. The Latin verb was a frequentative, built to suggest repeated copying, and Spanish carries the whole cluster forward: ~imitación~, ~imitador~, ~imagen~, ~imaginar~, and ~imaginación~ all rest on the ancient sense of fashioning a likeness.
en.impactar:
From Latin ~impāctus~, the past participle of ~impingere~ (“to drive in, strike against”), from ~in-~ (“into, against”) plus ~pangere~ (“to fix, fasten, drive in”). ~pangere~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂ǵ-~ (“to fasten, fix in place”), through a nasal-infixed *~ph₂-n-ǵ-~. Cognate with Ancient Greek ~πήγνυμι~ (~pḗgnymi~, “to make fast”), and, through the root, with English ~pact~, ~page~ and ~propagate~.

The root idea is fixing something firmly — a ~pactum~ (“pact”) was an agreement “driven home,” and a ~pāgina~ (“page”) a surface of fastened-together sheets. ~impactar~ is a newcomer: back-formed from the noun ~impacto~ in the twentieth century, it began in ballistics — the ~impacto~ of a bullet — and only lately spread to the figurative “to make a strong impression, to shock.” Spanish relatives from the same root include ~pacto~, ~propagar~ (“to fasten cuttings into the ground”) and ~página~.
en.impartir:
Spanish ~impartir~ comes from Latin ~impartīre~ (also ~impertīre~, “to share out, to bestow”), from ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~partīre~ (“to divide, to share”), a verb on the noun ~pars~ (stem ~part-~, “a part, a share”). The Romance languages kept the compound closely — Italian ~impartire~ and Portuguese ~impartir~ — and Latin lent the word directly to English as ~impart~. The ultimate prehistory of ~pars~ is debated, so it is safest to stop at the Latin noun.

The core idea is division that gives: to ~impartir~ is to hand out a share — of knowledge, a blessing, orders, or classes. The plain ~partīre~ became Spanish ~partir~, which kept “to divide” but also grew the sense “to depart,” as one splits off and sets out. Around it cluster ~compartir~ (“to share”), ~repartir~ (“to distribute”), and, from the noun ~pars~, a broad family: ~parte~, ~partido~, ~partícula~, ~partícipe~ and ~participar~ — every one of them a way of having or handing over a portion of the whole.
en.impedir:
From Latin ~impedīre~ (“to hinder, obstruct”), literally “to shackle the feet,” from ~in-~ (“in, on”) and ~pēs~, ~pedis~ (“foot”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pṓds~ (“foot”). Cognate with Italian ~impedire~ and English ~impede~; and, through ~pēs~, with English ~foot~, ~pedal~ and ~pedestrian~ and Spanish ~pie~.

The image is wonderfully concrete: to impede someone is to snare their feet, as with a fetter — and Latin had the exact opposite, ~expedīre~, “to free the feet,” which yields Spanish ~expedito~ (“unobstructed”) and English ~expedite~. Popular Latin also coined ~impedicāre~, “to entangle,” which travelled a separate road into French ~empêcher~ (“to prevent”). From the “foot” root Spanish keeps ~pie~, ~pedal~, ~peatón~, ~expedir~ and ~impedimento~, while the same Proto-Indo-European *~pṓds~ surfaces across the family, from Greek ~poús~ to German ~Fuß~.
en.implantar:
From Latin ~implantāre~, from ~in-~ (“in, into”) plus ~plantāre~ (“to plant”), from ~planta~ (“sprout; sole of the foot”), ultimately from a nasalized Proto-Indo-European root *~plat-~ (“to spread, be flat”), though that deepest step is uncertain. The compound is shared with French ~implanter~, Italian ~impiantare~ and English ~implant~.

Literally ~implantāre~ was “to plant into,” to fix something firmly in place — and Spanish still uses ~implantar~ both concretely, of a surgical or dental ~implante~, and abstractly, of establishing a custom, a law or a system. Much of that abstract, institutional sense was reinforced by French ~implanter~ in the modern era. It sits beside its plainer siblings ~plantar~ and ~trasplantar~, the whole group rooted in the image of setting something into the ground.
en.implementar:
From ~implemento~ (“implement, tool”), and, more directly, borrowed in the twentieth century from English ~implement~ (verb, “to carry out”). The ultimate source is Late Latin ~implēmentum~ (“a filling-up”), from Latin ~implēre~ (“to fill, fulfil”), from ~in-~ (intensive) and ~plēre~ (“to fill”), from the same Proto-Indo-European root *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”) that underlies ~lleno~. It is cognate with English ~complete~ and ~supply~ and, through the root, with Spanish ~pleno~ and ~lleno~.

Curiously, Castilian never really took up the Latinism ~implemento~ on its own; the noun and the verb ~implementar~ came in from English, where ~implement~ had specialized from “a thing that fills a need, a tool” to “to put into effect.” Prescriptivists long flagged ~implementar~ as an ill-formed anglicism, but the DLE now records it. Its fill-root cousins in Spanish include ~lleno~, ~llenar~, ~pleno~, ~plenitud~ and ~completar~.
en.implicar:
From Latin ~implicāre~ (“to fold in, entangle, involve”), from ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, fold”). Cognate with — and in several cases borrowed as — English ~imply~, ~employ~, and ~implicate~, and French ~impliquer~.

The image is physical: to ~implicar~ is to fold something in so that it becomes entangled with something else — hence “to involve” and, of a statement, “to imply.” A quiet surprise is that Spanish ~emplear~ (“to employ, use”) is a doublet: the same ~plicāre~ reached it by a worn popular road through Old French, whereas the learned form was lifted straight from Latin. The fold-family is large: ~aplicar~ (“to apply”), ~explicar~ (“to explain,” to unfold), ~complicar~ (“to complicate”), ~plegar~ (“to fold”), and ~replicar~ (“to reply”).
en.imponer:
From Latin ~impōnere~ (“to set upon, lay on”), a compound of ~in-~ (“on, upon”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, place”). ~Pōnere~ was itself a contraction of the particle ~po-~ and ~sinere~ (“to let, set down”). Spanish ~imponer~ is cognate with Italian ~imporre~ and Portuguese ~impor~; French ~imposer~ and English ~impose~ belong to the family too, though both were reshaped on the participle stem ~positus~ rather than the infinitive.

The literal “place upon” quickly turned figurative: to ~imponer~ is to lay a tax, a rule, or a penalty on someone, and reflexively ~imponerse~ is to assert oneself or prevail. The participle ~impositus~ gave the popular ~impuesto~, which in Spanish is not only “imposed” but the everyday noun “tax.” The parent ~pōnere~ founded one of Spanish's largest verb families — ~poner~, ~componer~, ~disponer~, ~exponer~, ~proponer~ — each pairing a learned noun in ~-posición~ with a popular participle in ~-puesto~, as in ~composición~ beside ~compuesto~.
en.importar:
From Latin ~importāre~ (“to bring in, carry in”), a compound of the prefix ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~portāre~ (“to carry, bear”). ~portāre~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to cross over, pass through, bring across”), the same root that gave Latin ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbor”). The cognate branches are many: through Germanic the root surfaces in English ~ford~ and ~ferry~, and through Greek in ~póros~ (“passage, ford”). Within Romance the compound yields Italian ~importare~, French ~importer~ and Portuguese ~importar~.

The verb’s two modern senses both flow from “carrying in.” Commercially, to ~importar~ is to carry goods into a country — the plain, literal meaning. But Spanish ~importar~ also means “to matter, to be of concern.” The bridge is the notion of what a thing “brings in” or “carries” as its weight or value: what is entered into an account is its ~importe~ (“sum, amount”), and what carries weight is ~importante~ (“important”). From the same Latin ~portāre~ Spanish also built ~transportar~, ~exportar~, ~deporte~ (“sport,” originally “to carry oneself off, amuse”) and ~puerto~ (“port”).
en.imprimir:
From Latin ~imprimere~ (“to press into or upon”), a compound of ~in-~ (“into, upon”) and ~premere~ (“to press, squeeze”), the latter often traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to strike”). Spanish ~imprimir~ shares its ancestor with Portuguese ~imprimir~ and French ~imprimer~; through ~premere~ it is also kin to English ~press~ and ~print~, the second of which reached English through Old French ~preinte~ (“an impression”).

In Rome ~imprimere~ meant to press a stamp or seal into wax, leaving a mark — a sense Spanish still keeps when one ~imprime~ a shape onto a surface. When movable type arrived in the fifteenth century, that same pressing gave the modern meaning “to print.” The Latin past participle ~impressus~ yielded ~impresión~ and ~impreso~, and the workshop where pressing happened became the ~imprenta~ (“printing house”). The wider family of ~premere~ crowds the language: ~prensa~ (“press”), ~presión~, ~comprimir~, ~exprimir~ and ~oprimir~ all descend from the single idea of pressing.
en.impugnar:
From Latin ~impugnāre~ (“to fight against, assail, attack”), from ~in-~ (“against”) plus ~pugnāre~ (“to fight”), a verb built on ~pugnus~ (“fist”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pewǵ-~ (“to prick, punch”). Greek ~πυγμή~ (pugmḗ, “fist”) is a cognate, and Latin ~pungere~ (“to prick”) belongs to the same nest. Through Latin the root reaches English ~impugn~, ~pugnacious~, ~pungent~, and ~poignant~ (literally “pricking”), and French ~poing~ (“fist”).

To impugn was first to come at someone with fists, then to attack with words, and finally — in the legal register where Spanish ~impugnar~ now lives most — to contest, challenge, or dispute a claim, a ruling, an election result. The pugilistic image never fully faded: to impugn a witness is to strike at their credibility. The same fist gave Spanish ~puño~ (“fist,” the inherited form), ~puñal~ (“dagger”), ~pugna~ (“struggle”), ~pugnar~ (“to strive”), and the kindred ~expugnar~ (“to storm, take by force”) and ~repugnar~ (“to repel,” literally “to fight back”).
en.impulsar:
From ~impulso~ (“impulse”) + ~-ar~, on Latin ~impulsus~, the participle of ~impellere~ (“to drive against, to push forward”), from ~in-~ (“in, upon”) + ~pellere~ (“to push, to drive, to beat”). ~pellere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~pelh₂-~ (“to drive, to thrust”). Cognate with French ~impulser~ and Portuguese ~impulsar~, and — through ~pellere~ — with English ~impel~, ~impulse~, and ~pulse~.

The root sense is a forceful push, and the ~in-~ prefix aims it forward: to ~impulsar~ is to drive something ahead — a boat, a reform, a career. The participle ~pulsus~ (“driven, struck”) spawned a whole cluster about pushing and throbbing. ~pellere~ was remarkably fertile in Latin compounds, each surviving in Spanish: ~expulsar~ (“to expel,” drive out), ~repeler~ (“to repel,” drive back), ~compeler~ (“to compel,” drive together), ~propulsar~ (“to propel”), and ~pulsar~ (“to press, to pulse”). The plain noun ~pulso~ means both “pulse” and “steadiness of hand,” while everyday ~empujar~ (“to push”) reached Spanish from the same ~impellere~ through Vulgar Latin ~impulsāre~.
en.imputar:
From Latin ~imputāre~ (“to enter in an account, charge, ascribe”), a compound of the prefix ~in-~ (“in, into,” assimilated to ~im-~ before a labial) and ~putāre~ (“to reckon, settle an account,” earlier “to prune, clean”). ~putāre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~pewH-~ (“to cut, strike, cleanse”), the same root behind a whole accounting vocabulary. Spanish took ~imputar~ as a learned borrowing rather than by uninterrupted oral descent, which is why it kept the Latin shape almost intact. Cognate with Italian ~imputare~, French ~imputer~, and Portuguese ~imputar~, and — through the shared root — with English ~impute~ and ~amputate~.

The bridge from “to prune” to “to reckon” is the idea of clearing away: the verb ~putāre~ named both the pruning of a vine — cutting off the excess — and the settling of an account, cutting the tangle down to a clean figure. From that same ~putāre~ Spanish inherited a large family: ~computar~, ~disputar~, ~reputar~, ~diputar~, and ~amputar~, plus the adjective ~putativo~ (“supposed, reputed”). Modern ~imputar~ narrowed toward the legal and moral: to ~imputar~ is to charge someone with a fault or a crime, to lay it to their account — the bookkeeping metaphor still visible under the courtroom sense. English ~computer~, by the same logic, is literally a thing that reckons.
en.inaugurar:
Spanish ~inaugurar~ comes from Latin ~inaugurāre~ (“to consecrate by augury, to install after taking the auspices”), from ~in-~ and ~augurārī~ (“to act as an augur”), from the noun ~augur~, the Roman priest who read the will of the gods in the flight and cries of birds. The learned word passed into the Romance languages together — Italian ~inaugurare~, French ~inaugurer~, Portuguese ~inaugurar~ — and into English as ~inaugurate~. Beside the learned ~augurio~, Spanish also keeps the inherited, worn-down doublet ~agüero~ (“omen”).

A Roman inauguration was literally that: no magistrate took office and no temple was founded until an ~augur~ judged the bird-signs favorable, so to ~inaugurar~ was to begin a thing under good omens. The origin of ~augur~ itself is disputed. Ancient writers linked it to ~avis~ (“bird”) plus a verb of talking or doing, but many modern scholars prefer a derivation from ~augēre~ (“to increase”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ewg-~ — an augur’s rite as one of “increase” and blessing. That second account ties ~inaugurar~ to a wide family: ~aumentar~, ~autor~, ~autoridad~ and ~augusto~.
en.incentivar:
From ~incentivo~ (“incentive”) + ~-ar~, from Latin ~incentīvus~ (“that sets the tune, striking up”), from ~incinere~ (“to strike up, sound”), from ~in-~ + ~canere~ (“to sing”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂n-~ (“to sing”). Cognate — through ~canere~ — with English ~chant~, ~cant~, ~accent~, and ~incantation~, and with Spanish ~cantar~.

~incentīvus~ first meant, in music, “that which sets the tune” or strikes up a melody. In Late Latin its sense of “inciting” was reinforced by association with the unrelated ~incendere~ (“to kindle, set afire”), and it is this crossing that lends ~incentivo~ its faint charge of “kindling” someone to act — but the fiery ~incendere~ is a late contaminant, not the true source, which is the musical ~canere~. ~Incentivar~ itself is a modern verb, at home in economics (“to incentivize”). True kin, by descent through ~canere~, are ~canto~, ~cantar~, ~cantante~, and ~encantar~; ~incendio~ and ~incendiar~ merely look related.
en.incidir:
From Latin ~incidere~ (“to fall upon, fall into, happen”), from ~in-~ (“on, into”) plus ~cadere~ (“to fall”), from Proto-Italic *~kadō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱad-~ (“to fall”). Cognate with the inherited Spanish ~caer~ (“to fall”), and, through the root, with English ~cadence~, ~accident~ and ~decay~ — all built on the image of falling.

A genuine coincidence hides here: Spanish ~incidir~ answers to two different Latin verbs at once. From ~incidere~ (“to fall upon,” from ~cadere~) comes the main sense — to have a bearing on, to influence, or to fall into an error; from the look-alike ~incīdere~ (“to cut into,” from ~caedere~, “to cut”) comes the medical sense of making an incision. The “falling” root is the more fruitful: it gave ~caer~, ~accidente~ (something that “befalls”), ~coincidir~ (“to fall together”), ~occidente~ (the “falling,” setting sun) and ~decadencia~.
en.inclinar:
From Latin ~inclīnāre~ (“to bend, to lean toward”), from ~in-~ (“toward”) plus ~clīnāre~ (“to lean, to bend”). The root is Proto-Indo-European *~ḱley-~ (“to lean”), and it is unusually well populated with cognates: English ~lean~ is a direct native descendant, alongside borrowed ~incline~ and ~decline~; German has ~lehnen~ (“to lean”); Greek ~klínein~ (“to lean”) gave ~klínē~ (“bed, couch”) and ~klíma~ (“slope, zone”), sources of ~clínica~ and ~clima~.

The development runs from the body to the mind. First ~inclīnāre~ was physical — to tip, tilt or bend something from the vertical. Then it turned figurative: to be ~inclinado~ toward an opinion is to lean mentally in its direction, and an ~inclinación~ is a leaning of temperament. Spanish keeps the whole ~clīnāre~ family: ~inclinar~, ~inclinación~, ~declinar~ (“to decline, to slope down”), ~reclinar~ (“to recline”), and — through Greek — ~clima~ and ~clínica~, the latter recalling the physician who tends the patient bent over a ~klínē~, a bed.
en.incluir:
A semi-learned borrowing from Latin ~inclūdere~ (“to shut in, enclose”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~claudere~ (“to close, shut”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kleh₂u-~ (“hook, peg; to close”). Cognate with Italian ~includere~, French ~inclure~, and Portuguese ~incluir~, and — through ~claudere~ — with English ~include~, ~conclude~, ~exclude~, and ~close~, plus Latin ~clāvis~ (“key,” whence Spanish ~llave~ and ~clave~).

That ~incluir~ is only semi-learned shows in its shape: a fully popular descent would have battered the word far more, but scholars and scribes reintroduced it close to the Latin, keeping the combining form ~-clūdere~ (with the ~au~ of ~claudere~ raised to ~ū~). The literal image is spatial — to shut something inside — from which the modern “to contain, comprise, include” follows directly. The same ~claudere~ radiates through Spanish ~concluir~, ~excluir~, and ~recluir~, and ~inclūdere~ itself yields ~inclusión~, the adverb ~incluso~ (“even, including”), and ~inclusivo~ (“inclusive”).
en.incorporar:
From Latin ~incorporāre~ (“to form into a body, embody”), from ~in-~ (“into”) plus ~corpus~ (stem ~corpor-~, “body”) plus the verbal suffix ~-āre~. ~Corpus~ descends from Proto-Italic *~korpos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~krep-~ (“body, form”). Cognate with French ~incorporer~ and English ~incorporate~; the root itself is shared with English ~midriff~, from Old English ~hrif~ (“belly”).

The literal sense is “to put into a body,” to make separate things into one mass — it is the verb for folding egg whites into a batter, and the reason a company is “incorporated” into one legal body. Spanish ~incorporarse~ also means to sit or stand up, to bring the body upright. From ~corpus~ Spanish inherited ~cuerpo~ (“body”), ~corporal~, ~corpóreo~, ~corporación~, ~corpiño~ (“bodice”), and — by a French detour — ~corsé~ (“corset”).
en.incrementar:
From Latin ~incrementum~ (“growth, increase”), the noun of ~incrēscere~ (“to grow in, swell”), from ~in-~ plus ~crēscere~ (“to grow”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱreh₁-~ (“to grow, nourish”). Spanish ~incrementar~ is a fairly modern verb coined from the noun ~incremento~. Cognate with English ~increment~ and ~increase~, and, through the same root, with ~crescent~, ~create~, and ~recruit~ (originally “a fresh growth of troops”).

The Latin ~crēscere~ was an inchoative — a verb of beginning, “to start to grow” — and it seeded a wide Spanish family: ~crecer~ (“to grow”), ~creciente~ (“growing, crescent”), ~crear~ and ~criar~ (both “to create, raise,” doublets from ~creāre~), and ~concreto~ (“concrete,” literally “grown together”). Beside the everyday ~crecer~, ~incrementar~ keeps a more measured, quantitative ring — one ~incrementa~ a figure, a rate, a dose.
en.increpar:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~increpāre~ (“to rattle at, to chide, to rebuke”), formed from ~in-~ (here intensive, “at, upon”) and ~crepāre~ (“to rattle, crackle, creak, make a sharp noise”), a verb of imitative, onomatopoeic origin. Because ~increpar~ entered Spanish through the learned channel, it kept the Latin ~-cr-~ cluster intact rather than evolving it.

The base ~crepāre~ is a small etymological treasure: its ordinary inherited descendant is Spanish ~quebrar~ (“to break, to snap”) — the cracking noise became the breaking itself — while the borrowed branch gave ~crepitar~ (“to crackle”) and the noun ~quiebra~ (“bankruptcy; a business that breaks”). The same root, through ~decrepitus~, yielded ~decrépito~. So the sharp reproach of ~increpar~ shares an ancestor with a snapping twig, a crackling fire and a broken vase.
en.incumplir:
From ~in-~ (negative prefix) + ~cumplir~ (“to fulfill, carry out”). ~Cumplir~ descends from Latin ~complēre~ (“to fill up, complete, fulfill”), from ~com-~ (intensive) + ~plēre~ (“to fill”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”). Cognate with Italian ~compiere~, French ~accomplir~, and Portuguese ~cumprir~, and — through the same root — with English ~complete~, ~plenty~, and ~full~, and Latin ~plēnus~ (“full”).

The prefix ~in-~ negates, so ~incumplir~ means literally “to not fulfill”: to fail a duty, a contract, or a law. It is a relatively modern, largely juridical formation, the everyday antonym of ~cumplir~. Latin ~complēre~ meant “to fill completely,” and Spanish kept the idea of “filling out” an obligation until it is whole. From the same root *~pleh₁-~ Spanish gathered a wide family: ~lleno~, ~llenar~, ~completo~, ~cumplido~, ~complemento~, ~plenitud~, and ~pleno~.
en.incurrir:
From Latin ~incurrere~ (“to run into, run against”), a compound of the prefix ~in-~ (“into, upon”) and ~currere~ (“to run”), from Proto-Italic *~korzō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). The same root gave, through Gaulish, Latin ~carrus~ (“wagon”) and is cognate — surprisingly — with English ~horse~. Spanish inherited ~incurrir~ as a learned Latinism, and it is a sibling of the everyday ~correr~ (“to run”), which descends from the same ~currere~ by ordinary popular transmission.

In Latin, to “run into” something extended figuratively to falling into a state or consequence — one “ran into” danger, debt, or blame. Spanish preserves exactly this figurative core: one ~incurre~ en un error, en una deuda, en la ira de alguien — always running headlong into something unwanted. From the same ~currere~ Spanish built a large family: ~correr~, ~corriente~, ~corredor~, ~recorrer~, ~ocurrir~, ~currículum~ and ~socorrer~ (“to run to aid,” literally to run beneath). English ~current~, ~occur~ and ~courier~ belong to the same stream.
en.indicar:
From Latin ~indicāre~ (“to point out, show, declare”), from ~in-~ (“toward”) and ~dicāre~ (“to proclaim, dedicate”), a cousin of ~dīcere~ (“to say”); all go back to Proto-Indo-European *~deik-~ (“to show, point out”). It is cognate with Italian ~indicare~, Portuguese ~indicar~ and French ~indiquer~, and with English ~indicate~ and ~index~; through Germanic the same root gives English ~teach~ and ~token~.

Where ~dicāre~ was “to proclaim aloud,” ~indicāre~ was “to point a finger at,” and the finger is not incidental: the ~índice~ (“index finger”) is literally the pointer, and an ~índice~ in a book points you to its contents. From *~deik-~ Spanish gathers a wide family — ~indicio~ (“clue”), ~indicador~ (“indicator”), ~dedicar~ (“to dedicate,” from ~dēdicāre~) and ~predicar~ (“to preach,” from ~praedicāre~) — while Latin ~digitus~ (“finger”), from the same root, underlies ~dígito~ and English ~digit~.
en.inducir:
~inducir~ comes from Latin ~inducere~ (“to lead in, bring in, introduce, influence”), from ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~ducere~ (“to lead, draw”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to lead, draw”). It is cognate with Italian ~indurre~, French ~induire~ and Portuguese ~induzir~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~induce~ and ~induct~. The root ~ducere~ was extraordinarily productive: Spanish inherited a whole rank of ~-ducir~ verbs from its compounds — ~conducir~, ~producir~, ~reducir~, ~traducir~, ~deducir~ and ~seducir~ among them.

Latin ~inducere~ meant literally “to lead in” — to bring on, introduce, or move someone to act; Spanish ~inducir~ keeps all of that, from ~inducir a error~ (“to lead into error”) to inducing an electric current. Its most elegant afterlife is in logic, where ~inducción~ (“induction”) is the reasoning that “leads” the mind up from particular cases to a general rule — the exact mirror of ~deducción~, which leads down from the rule to the case, both of them, at root, kinds of ~ducere~ “leading.” The same root surfaces in nouns too: a ~ducto~ (“duct”) leads fluid along, and a ~duque~ (“duke”) was once, literally, a ~dux~ — a leader.
en.infectar:
Spanish ~infectar~ comes from Latin ~inficere~ (“to dip in, stain, dye, taint”), a compound of the prefix ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~facere~ (“to make, do”), whose past participle was ~infectus~. ~Facere~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to set, put, place”), so ~inficere~ meant, at bottom, “to put something into” — specifically to steep a thing in dye. The vowel of ~facere~ weakened to ~i~ in the compound, a regular Latin change. Spanish took the word in its learned, re-Latinized shape; English borrowed the same participle as ~infect~ and ~infection~, and the French line gives ~infecter~.

Its meaning darkened over time. The oldest sense was chromatic and neutral — to ~infectar~ a cloth was to dip it in dye, to tinge or stain it; from there Latin moved to the figurative “to taint, to corrupt” (a mind, a reputation) and only later to the medical “to infect with disease” that now dominates. Spanish once carried an inherited, popular form ~inficionar~ (from ~infectiōnem~), which the re-Latinized ~infectar~ eventually crowded out. The ~facere~ family is vast: through it ~infectar~ is kin to ~hacer~ (“to do, make”) and to a crowd of ~-fecto~ words — ~perfecto~, ~defecto~, ~afectar~ and ~confección~. From a root that first meant only “to put in,” Spanish drew both the dyer's vat and the sickbed.
en.influir:
From Latin ~influere~ (“to flow in”), from ~in-~ (“into”) + ~fluere~ (“to flow”). ~fluere~ has no secure Indo-European pedigree; it is often traced to a Proto-Indo-European *~bʰlewH-~ (“to overflow, swell”), perhaps an extension of *~bʰleh₁-~ (“to blow, swell”), but the reconstruction is uncertain. (Despite the resemblance, English ~flow~ is not related.) Cognate with Italian ~influire~, French ~influer~, and Portuguese ~influir~, and — through ~fluere~ — with English ~fluid~, ~fluent~, and ~influence~.

The abstract sense hides a vivid astrological past. In Medieval Latin ~influentia~ named an ethereal fluid thought to stream down from the stars and shape human character and fate — an ~influence~ was literally a “flowing-in” from the heavens. The same belief named a disease: Italian ~influenza~ (whence English ~influenza~) was an outbreak blamed on the stars' malign flow. Spanish ~influir~ began as “to flow in” and settled into “to influence, to have an effect on.” From it come ~influencia~, ~influjo~, and ~influyente~ (“influential”); and from the parent ~fluere~ a whole wet family — ~fluir~, ~fluido~, ~flujo~, ~afluente~ (“tributary”), and ~confluir~ (“to converge”).
en.informar:
From Latin ~informāre~ (“to give shape to, to form, to describe, to instruct”), a compound of ~in-~ (“into”) and ~formāre~ (“to form, to shape”), from the noun ~forma~ (“form, shape, figure”). The origin of ~forma~ is genuinely uncertain: it has long been proposed to derive from Ancient Greek ~morphḗ~ (“shape, form”) by metathesis, perhaps mediated by Etruscan, but the account is disputed and remains unproven, so the deeper source is best left open. The verb carried into Italian ~informare~, French ~informer~, and English ~inform~.

The literal sense is “to put into form,” and the abstract senses grew straight out of it: to shape the mind (“to instruct”), to shape an account (“to describe, to report”), and at last “to inform.” The very word “information” is, at root, a shaping of the mind. A charming doublet hides in the family: Spanish ~forma~ and ~horma~ (a shoemaker's “last” or mold) are the same Latin ~forma~ — one learned, one popularly inherited with ~f~ turned to ~h~. Alongside them stand ~formar~, ~fórmula~, ~formal~, ~transformar~, ~reformar~, and ~uniforme~.
en.ingresar:
From Latin ~ingressus~, participle of ~ingredī~ (“to step in, to enter”), from ~in-~ (“into”) + ~gradī~ (“to step, to walk”). ~gradī~ derives from ~gradus~ (“a step, a pace”) and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰredʰ-~ (“to walk, to stride”). Cognate with Portuguese ~ingressar~, and — through ~gradī~ — with English ~ingress~, ~progress~, ~grade~, and ~gradual~.

The image is a footstep: ~gradus~ was literally “a step,” and to ~ingredī~ was to “step into.” Spanish ~ingresar~ kept that spatial core — to enter — but specialized it in ways English splits across several words: one ~ingresa~ (is admitted) into a university or hospital, ~ingresa~ (deposits) money into a bank account, and ~ingresos~ are “income,” the money that steps in. The old ~gradus~ “step” also became a rung on a ladder of rank or measurement, giving ~grado~ (“degree”) and ~grada~ (“tier of seats”). From the same root Spanish drew a whole march of words: ~progresar~ (“to progress”), ~regresar~ (“to return”), ~agredir~ (“to attack,” literally to step toward), ~transgredir~ (“to transgress”), and ~gradual~.
en.iniciar:
From Latin ~initiāre~ (“to begin, to initiate into”), from ~initium~ (“a beginning, an entrance”), from ~inīre~ (“to go in, to enter”), which is ~in-~ (“into”) + ~īre~ (“to go”). ~īre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~eō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”), a root shared with Sanskrit ~éti~ (“he goes”) and Ancient Greek ~eîmi~ (“I will go”). Spanish borrowed the learned ~iniciar~ from Latin. Cognate with Italian ~iniziare~, French ~initier~, and Portuguese ~iniciar~.

In Rome ~initiāre~ carried a solemn charge beyond “to begin”: it meant to admit someone into the ~initium~ — the entrance, the threshold — of the mystery religions, to initiate them into secret rites. Spanish ~iniciar~ preserves both the everyday “to start” and this ceremonial “to initiate.” The going-root *~h₁ey-~ is faint in Spanish because ~īre~ was largely replaced, but it still shows in ~ir~ (whose forms mix three Latin verbs), ~inicio~, ~iniciativa~, ~éxito~ (“a going-out,” hence “success”), and ~tránsito~.
en.inscribir:
From Latin ~īnscrībere~ (“to write in or upon”), from ~in-~ (“in, on”) plus ~scrībere~ (“to write”), which originally meant “to scratch or incise,” from Proto-Indo-European *~skreybʰ-~, an extension of *~(s)ker-~ (“to cut”). Romance kept it as Italian ~inscrivere~, French ~inscrire~, and Portuguese ~inscrever~; a true cognate through the root is Greek ~σκάριφος~ (~skáriphos~, “a scratch, a sketch”). Latin ~scrībere~ was itself borrowed all across Europe, giving English ~scribe~ and ~script~ and German ~schreiben~.

The “scratch” is the giveaway: to write, for Romans, was to cut letters into wax, stone, or bark. To ~inscribir~ is to cut a name into a surface — and from carving names onto a public register came the modern civic sense: to enroll, to register, to sign up for a course, a census, or a contest. Geometry borrowed it too, for one figure drawn inside another. The family is large — ~escribir~, ~escritura~, ~inscripción~, describir, suscribir, manuscrito — every one of them still, faintly, scratching marks onto a surface.
en.insertar:
From Latin ~insertāre~, frequentative of ~inserere~ (“to insert, implant”), from ~in-~ (“into”) plus ~serere~ (“to join, bind, weave together”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ser-~ (“to bind, tie together, thread”). Cognate with French ~insérer~, Italian ~inserire~ and English ~insert~.

The root ~serere~ meant to bind things into a row or thread them together, and from *~ser-~ that image of linking runs everywhere: Latin ~series~ (“a row, chain, succession”) and ~sermō~ (“connected discourse,” source of English ~sermon~) both come from it. ~insertāre~, a frequentative, added the sense of setting something in among others. Spanish keeps the family in ~serie~, ~inserción~ and ~aserción~, all turning on the idea of things joined in sequence.
en.insistir:
From Latin ~īnsistere~ (“to stand on, set foot on; persist”), from ~in-~ (“on, upon”) and ~sistere~ (“to cause to stand, take a stand”), a reduplicated form built on ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). It is cognate with Italian ~insistere~ and French ~insister~, and — through ~sistere~ — with English ~insist~, ~assist~ and ~resist~.

To insist was, at root, to plant your feet on a spot and not move — ~in-~ (“on”) plus “to stand.” The metaphor is still legible: someone who insists takes a stand and holds it. The prolific root *~steh₂-~ gave Spanish a whole regiment of ~-sistir~ verbs — ~asistir~, ~resistir~, ~consistir~, ~persistir~, ~desistir~ and ~existir~ — alongside ~estar~ itself.
en.inspirar:
From Latin ~inspīrāre~ (“to breathe into”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~spīrāre~ (“to breathe, blow”). The deeper history of ~spīrāre~ is uncertain: De Vaan judges it probably of onomatopoeic origin, and the proposed Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)peys-~ (“to blow, breathe”) is disputed.
