Romance kept the compound in Italian ~inspirare~, French ~inspirer~, and Portuguese ~inspirar~; from the same Latin verb English inherited ~inspire~, ~spirit~, ~respire~, and ~conspire~.

The picture is first bodily and then divine: to breathe into someone, and — when a god or a Muse did the breathing — to fill them with an idea. From physical respiration the word rose to mean the sudden kindling of thought or feeling, though medicine still uses ~inspiración~ for the drawing-in of breath. Spanish keeps a whole lung of relatives from ~spīrāre~: ~espíritu~ (“spirit, breath”), ~respirar~, ~aspirar~, ~suspirar~ (“to sigh”), ~expirar~, and ~conspirar~ — literally “to breathe together.”
en.instalar:
From French ~installer~, borrowed from Medieval Latin ~installare~, a compound of Latin ~in-~ (“in”) and ~stallum~ (“stall, seat”). ~stallum~ was itself taken from a Germanic word for a standing-place or stable, Frankish *~stall~, from Proto-Germanic *~stallaz~, traceable to the Proto-Indo-European root *~stel-~ (“to put, stand”). The Germanic noun surfaces directly in English ~stall~ and German ~Stall~ (“stable”).

The medieval verb was strikingly concrete: to ~installare~ a canon or official was to seat him in his ~stallum~ — the assigned stall or choir seat that marked his office. From “to place someone in his seat” the meaning widened to “to set anything in its proper place”, and modern Spanish ~instalar~ ranges from installing a person in a post to installing plumbing or software. Spanish keeps the family in ~instalación~ and ~instalador~, while the same Germanic root gave English ~stall~, ~stallion~ and ~forestall~.
en.instar:
From Latin ~īnstāre~ (“to stand upon, press hard, urge”), a compound of ~in-~ (“on, upon”) and ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). It shares its root with Spanish ~estar~ and, in English, with ~stand~ itself; more closely, the Latin present participle ~īnstāns~ (“pressing, imminent”) gave English ~instant~ and ~instance~, and Italian keeps the learned ~instare~.

The metaphor is bodily: to ~instar~ is to “stand upon” someone — to press so close that you urge, insist and implore them to act. The most charming heir is the everyday ~instant~: from the participle ~īnstāns~, an instant is a moment “pressing upon” the present, so the very word for “now” is built from urgency. Spanish keeps the family in ~instante~, ~instancia~ (“request; instance”), ~constar~ and ~constante~ — all built on that firm Latin “standing.”
en.integrar:
From Latin ~integrāre~ (“to make whole, to renew”), from the adjective ~integer~ (“whole, untouched, intact”), from Proto-Italic *~n̥tagros~ (“untouched”): the negative prefix ~in-~ (“not”) joined to the root of ~tangere~ (“to touch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~teh₂g-~ (“to touch”). Something ~integer~ was, literally, un-touched. English borrowed the same Latin adjective as ~integer~ and ~entire~, and the root surfaces again in the borrowed ~tangent~ and ~tact~; the Italian ~integrare~ and French ~intégrer~ descend from the same verb.

Latin ~integrāre~ meant “to make whole again, to renew, to restore,” and that sense of completing and unifying carried into Spanish ~integrar~ (“to integrate, to make up, to compose”). The idea of the untouched-and-therefore-whole also gave Spanish a pair of doublets from the same ~integer~: the learned ~íntegro~ (“upright, complete”) and the inherited ~entero~ (“entire, whole”). From the “touch” root came a wide family — ~integridad~, ~integración~, and, through ~tangere~, the words ~tacto~, ~contacto~, ~intacto~, ~tangente~ and ~contagio~.
en.intentar:
From Latin ~intentāre~ (“to stretch toward, to aim at”), a frequentative of ~intendere~ (“to direct, to focus one's attention”), formed from ~in-~ (“toward”) plus ~tendere~ (“to stretch”). ~tendere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~tendō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~tend-~, a d-extension of the root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Through that root it is cognate with Ancient Greek ~teínō~, Sanskrit ~tanóti~, and English ~thin~, ~tend~, and ~tense~. Italian ~intentare~ and Portuguese ~intentar~ preserve the same compound.

The frequentative suffix once painted a repeated, insistent stretching-toward, and from that intensified aiming the sense narrowed to “to attempt, to try.” Spanish also kept a legal and rhetorical use, where ~intentar~ una demanda means “to bring a suit.” The prolific root *~ten-~ seeded a wide family in Spanish, among them ~tender~, ~tienda~ (a “tent,” and hence a “shop”), ~tensión~, ~intención~, ~atender~, ~extender~, and ~contender~.
en.interactuar:
A modern compound of the prefix ~inter-~ (“between, among”) and the verb ~actuar~ (“to act”), formed on the model of English ~interact~. ~actuar~ descends from Medieval Latin ~actuāre~, from Latin ~actus~, the past participle of ~agere~ (“to drive, do, act”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, lead”). The root is cognate with Ancient Greek ~ἄγω~ (“I lead”), Sanskrit ~ájati~ (“drives”) and Old Norse ~aka~ (“to drive”).

Where ~actuar~ means simply “to act” or “to perform,” the prefix ~inter-~ adds reciprocity: to ~interactuar~ is to act upon one another. It is a recent arrival, spreading in the twentieth century with the vocabulary of science and computing. From the same fertile root ~agere~ Spanish draws a huge family — ~acto~, ~acción~, ~actor~, ~actual~, ~actividad~, ~agente~, ~agitar~ and ~ágil~ — while ~inter-~ recurs in ~internacional~, ~intervenir~ and countless others.
en.intercambiar:
A Spanish compound of the prefix ~inter-~ (“between, mutually”) and the verb ~cambiar~ (“to change, exchange”). ~Cambiar~ descends from Late Latin ~cambiāre~ (“to barter, exchange”), a commercial term first attested in Apuleius and borrowed into Latin from Celtic (Gaulish), ultimately tied to an Indo-European notion of “bending” or “curving,” root *~(s)kamb-~. Italian ~cambiare~, French ~changer~ (source of English ~change~) and Portuguese ~cambiar~ all spring from the same Gaulish loan.

Latin already had ~mūtāre~ for “to change,” so the survival of the Celtic ~cambiāre~ specifically for commercial exchange — swapping one thing for another of equal value — is telling about trade across the ancient Gaulish frontier. The ~inter-~ prefix makes the mutuality explicit: to ~intercambiar~ is for two parties each to give and receive. From ~cambiar~ Spanish built ~cambio~, ~recambio~, ~canje~ and ~cambista~; the Romance root also surfaces in English ~exchange~ and ~interchange~.
en.interesar:
From ~interés~ (“interest”), a noun Spanish took from Latin ~interest~ (“it matters, it concerns”), the third-person form of the verb ~interesse~ (“to be between, to be present at, to concern”). That verb joins ~inter-~ (“between, among”) to ~esse~ (“to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁es-~ (“to be”), the same root behind Spanish ~ser~ and ~es~. Spanish ~interesar~ is cognate with Italian ~interessare~, French ~intéresser~ and English ~interest~, all descending from that Latin idiom for something that “lies between” the parties and therefore concerns them.

The semantic journey is a small lesson in economics and psychology alike. What “is between” people was, in Roman law, what mattered to them — a stake, a share, a concern. From that came the financial ~interés~ (the “concern” a lender holds in a loan, hence the money it earns) and, in parallel, the mental ~interés~, the attention we give to what concerns us. The reflexive ~interesarse~ (“to take an interest”) captures the second sense, while ~interesado~ can mean both “interested” and, less flatteringly, “self-interested.” Kin through ~esse~ include ~esencia~, ~ausente~, ~presente~ and ~interesante~ itself.
en.interponer:
From Latin ~interpōnere~ (“to place between, interpose”), from ~inter-~ (“between”) + ~pōnere~ (“to put, place”), itself a contraction of ~po-~ (“forth”) + ~sinere~ (“to let, leave”). Cognate with Italian ~interporre~ and Portuguese ~interpor~; English ~interpose~ and ~compose~ reached the same sense through Old French ~poser~, whose forms merged in Romance with those of ~pōnere~.

~Pōnere~ was among Latin's most productive verbs, and its ~inter-~ compound meant literally to set one thing amid others — Spanish ~interponer~ still does, whether one interposes an object, an obstacle, or a legal appeal (~interponer un recurso~). Its irregular participle ~interpuesto~ echoes Latin ~interpositus~. The parent ~pōnere~ gave Spanish ~poner~, and its prefixed children fill the dictionary: ~componer~, ~disponer~, ~exponer~, ~proponer~, ~suponer~, ~oponer~ and ~posponer~, beside the noun ~posición~ from the participle ~positus~.
en.interpretar:
From Latin ~interpretārī~ (“to explain, translate, understand”), a deponent verb from the noun ~interpres~ (genitive ~interpretis~, “a go-between, negotiator, translator”). The first element is clearly ~inter-~ (“between”); the second element, ~-pres~, is of debated origin. One account links it to ~pretium~ (“price, value”), as though the interpreter were a broker who set a price between two parties; de Vaan and others reject a direct tie to ~pretium~ and connect ~-pres~ instead to a root meaning “to speak out, make known,” comparing Ancient Greek ~φράζω~ (~phrázō~, “to point out, declare”). The safest statement is that the second half is uncertain. Romance cognates include Italian ~interpretare~, French ~interpréter~ and Portuguese ~interpretar~.

In Rome the ~interpres~ stood between two sides who could not understand each other — a translator of tongues, but also a mediator of meaning, and even an interpreter of omens who explained the will of the gods. Spanish ~interpretar~ carries all three: to translate speech, to make sense of a text or a dream, and — via the stage — to perform a role or a piece of music, since an actor or musician “interprets” the work. From the same noun come ~intérprete~ (“interpreter, performer”), ~interpretación~ and ~interpretativo~. The contested link to ~pretium~ is worth flagging precisely because it is the most memorable story — an interpreter as the one who prices the exchange between strangers — yet it is not securely established, so enjoy it as a possibility, not a fact.
en.interrumpir:
From Latin ~interrumpere~ (“to break apart, break off”), a compound of ~inter-~ (“between”) and ~rumpere~ (“to break, burst”). ~rumpere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~rewp-~ (“to break, tear”). English drew the same Latin root into ~rupture~, ~erupt~, ~corrupt~ and, of course, ~interrupt~; Spanish inherited ~rumpere~ directly as the everyday verb ~romper~ (“to break”).

To ~interrumpir~ is literally to break in between — to snap the continuity of speech, motion or a signal. Latin used ~rumpere~ for bursting and shattering of every kind, and Spanish preserves that violence: ~irrumpir~ is to burst in, ~corromper~ (“to corrupt”) is to break thoroughly and ~erupción~ is a bursting-forth. The broken participle ~roto~ and the nouns ~ruptura~ and ~rotura~ complete the family, all echoing the same Indo-European sense of tearing apart.
en.intervenir:
From Latin ~intervenīre~ (“to come between”), a compound of ~inter-~ (“between”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷenjō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to go”). It is cognate with Italian ~intervenire~, French ~intervenir~ and Portuguese ~intervir~; through ~venīre~ it is also kin to Spanish ~venir~ and, more distantly, to English ~come~, which descends from that same Indo-European verb.

In Latin ~intervenīre~ was largely literal — to come in the middle of something, to interrupt, to fall between events — and from there it grew the senses of coming to someone's aid and stepping into an affair. Spanish preserved both readings: an army ~interviene~, and so does a surgeon or a mediator. The learned prefix ~inter-~ marks “betweenness” throughout the language, while ~venīre~ seeded a large family, among them ~venir~, ~convenir~, ~avenida~, ~porvenir~, ~aventura~ and ~convento~. The last two are a small surprise: an ~aventura~ is etymologically a thing “about to come” (from ~adventūra~), and a ~convento~ a “coming together” (from ~conventus~).
en.introducir:
From Latin ~intrōdūcere~ (“to lead in, bring in”), from ~intrō~ (“inward, within”) and ~dūcere~ (“to lead, draw”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to lead, draw”). The Spanish form was refashioned on ~-ducir~ (like ~conducir~ and ~producir~), the learned outcome of ~-dūcere~. Cognate with French ~introduire~, Italian ~introdurre~ and English ~introduce~; and, through ~dūcere~, with English ~duke~, ~duct~ and ~educate~ and German ~ziehen~.

To introduce is etymologically to “lead something inward” — hence both “to insert, put in” and the social “to bring a person in” by presentation. ~dūcere~ was a leader among Latin verbs for compounding, and Spanish inherited a whole column of its offspring in ~-ducir~: ~conducir~, ~producir~, ~reducir~, ~traducir~, ~seducir~ and ~aducir~, plus nouns like ~conducto~, ~producto~ and ~duque~ (“duke,” literally “leader”). The root *~dewk-~ even surfaces in English ~tow~ and ~team~, distant Germanic cousins of the Latin verb that Spanish borrowed so freely.
en.invadir:
~Invadir~ comes from Latin ~invādere~ (“to go into, attack”), a compound of ~in-~ (“into, upon”) and ~vādere~ (“to go, advance”), from Proto-Italic *~wāðō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~weh₂dʰ-~ (“to go, advance”). Italian ~invadere~ and French ~envahir~ share the compound; through ~vādere~ the verb is cognate with English ~evade~ and, more distantly, with the Germanic ~wade~ (Old English ~wadan~), which kept the older sense of pushing forward through water.

The literal core is simply “to go in” — but forcibly, with hostile intent, so ~invadir~ has meant to overrun a territory since Roman times, later widening to invasions of privacy, of markets, of the body by disease. Latin ~vādere~ left a surprising mark on Spanish: the everyday verb ~ir~ (“to go”) borrows its present forms — ~voy~, ~vas~, ~va~, ~vamos~ — from ~vādere~. From the same source come ~evadir~, ~evasión~, ~invasión~ and the noun ~vado~ (“ford”).
en.inventar:
~inventar~ derives from Latin ~inventāre~, a frequentative built on ~inventus~, the past participle of ~invenīre~ (“to come upon, find, discover”). That verb is simply ~in-~ (“on, upon”) plus ~venīre~ (“to come”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷenjō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷem-~ (“to go, come”) — the same root that gives English ~come~, Spanish ~venir~ and, through Greek ~baínō~ (“I go”), a raft of ~-basis~ words. So ~inventar~ is a close cousin of ~convenir~, ~prevenir~, ~intervenir~ and the noun ~aventura~ (“what is about to come”).

Latin ~invenīre~ was about discovery — to “come upon” something already there, as an explorer finds a river. The creative twist came later: ~inventar~ shifted from finding what exists to devising what does not, giving both the honest “to invent” and the shadier “to make up, fabricate.” That double life persists — a scientist ~inventa~ a machine, but a liar ~inventa~ an excuse. From the same participle Spanish keeps ~invento~ and ~inventor~, the legal-commercial ~inventario~ (“inventory,” a list of what one comes upon in a place) and ~inventiva~, the faculty of dreaming things up.
en.invertir:
From Latin ~invertere~ (“to turn upside down, reverse”), from ~in-~ plus ~vertere~ (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (“to turn”) — the same root as ~divertir~. Cognate with Italian ~invertire~, Portuguese ~inverter~, and English ~invert~ and ~inverse~.

Spanish ~invertir~ carries two meanings that look unrelated: “to invert, reverse” and “to invest money.” The first is straightforward from ~invertere~ (“to turn over”). The second is disputed: the favored account holds that the financial sense is not native but a semantic loan — the “put money to work” meaning is first recorded in English around 1610 in the East India trade and probably borrows a special use of Italian ~investire~ (literally “to clothe,” from Latin ~investīre~), which also gave Spanish ~investir~ (“to invest with an office”); the two look-alikes then converged on ~invertir~. So the “reverse” sense descends cleanly from ~vertere~, while the money sense likely rode in from elsewhere. From ~vertere~ Spanish also keeps ~verter~, ~inverso~, and ~convertir~.
en.investigar:
From Latin ~investīgāre~ (“to track down, search into”), from ~in-~ (“in, into”) plus ~vestīgāre~ (“to follow a trail”), from ~vestīgium~ (“footprint, track, trace”). Cognate with Italian ~investigare~, Portuguese ~investigar~, and English ~investigate~ and ~vestige~. The origin of ~vestīgium~ itself is uncertain — perhaps from ~verrō~ (“to sweep”), perhaps ~vē-~ plus a root *~steygʰ-~ (“to stride, walk”); the sources disagree.

The picture behind the word is the hunter or tracker reading the ground: to investigate was to go step by step along the ~vestīgia~, the footprints, until the quarry was found. That physical trailing hardened into the modern sense of methodical inquiry — scientific, criminal, journalistic. Spanish keeps the concrete noun ~vestigio~ (“vestige, trace, relic”) beside the abstract family ~investigación~ (“research, investigation”) and ~investigador~ (“researcher, investigator”), all still carrying, faintly, the shape of a footprint in soft earth.
en.invitar:
From Latin ~invītāre~ (“to invite, summon, entertain, treat”). Spanish in fact inherited this verb twice: the patrimonial form is ~convidar~ (from Vulgar Latin *~convītāre~, a remodeling of the classical verb), while ~invitar~ is a later learned borrowing — a cultismo — taken directly from ~invītāre~, so the two are doublets that split the labor of inviting. In the other Romance languages the learned form gives Italian ~invitare~, French ~inviter~ and Portuguese ~invitar~; English borrowed ~invite~ from the same Latin stock by way of French.

The deeper root is genuinely debated. Some etymologists connect ~invītāre~ with ~invocāre~ (“to call upon”), treating it as a frequentative of calling someone over; de Vaan instead derives it from a Proto-Indo-European *~weyh₁-~ (“to pursue, chase after”), so that to invite would be, at root, to “go after” a guest. An older account linked it to ~velle~ (“to want”). Because the sources hedge, none of these can be stated as settled fact. What is clear is the warmth the word kept: Latin ~invītāre~ meant not only to summon but to host graciously — which is why modern Spanish ~invitar~ commonly means to pay for another’s meal or drink. From the same family Spanish keeps ~convidar~, ~convite~ (“banquet, feast”) and the adjective ~invitado~ (“guest”).
en.invocar:
From Latin ~invocāre~ (“to call upon, to appeal to”), from ~in-~ (“on, upon”) plus ~vocāre~ (“to call”), the verb of ~vōx~ (“voice”). ~vocāre~ and ~vōx~ descend from Proto-Indo-European *~wekʷ-~ (“to speak, to sound out”). Cognate with Italian ~invocare~, French ~invoquer~ and Portuguese ~invocar~, and — through the same root — with English ~invoke~, ~voice~ and ~vocation~.

The Latin verb was already what it is now — to call a name aloud so as to summon its bearer, whether a god, a law, or an authority. Spanish ~invocar~ keeps that solemn ring: one ~invoca~ a deity, a principle, or a legal article. The calling root *~wekʷ-~ runs through a large Spanish family — ~voz~, ~vocación~, ~vocablo~, ~convocar~, ~provocar~, ~evocar~ and ~abogado~ (“lawyer,” literally one “called to” a case, from ~advocātus~). It is the same root that, far upstream, gives the ~-voc-~ in English ~vocabulary~.
en.involucrar:
~involucrar~ derives from the Latin noun ~involūcrum~ (“wrapper, covering, envelope”), itself from ~involvere~ (“to roll up, wrap up”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~volvere~ (“to roll, turn”). ~volvere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~welwō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~welH-~ (“to turn, wind, roll”). Through that root ~volvere~ is kin to English ~involve~, ~revolve~, and ~volume~ (originally a rolled scroll), to Ancient Greek ~elýō~ (“I roll”), and, via Germanic, to English ~wallow~.

The image is physical: to ~involucrar~ someone is literally to “wrap them up” in a matter, to roll them into it. Spanish long used it for physically enveloping, then for entangling a person in an affair — the sense that now dominates, alongside the reflexive ~involucrarse~ (“to get involved”). The same ~volvere~ seeded a broad family: ~volver~ (“to return”), ~revolver~, ~envolver~ (“to wrap”), ~volumen~, ~revólver~ (the borrowed English name of the rotating pistol), and ~voluble~.
en.ir:
Spanish ~ir~ is, like ~ser~, a patchwork of several Latin verbs. Its infinitive and future come from Latin ~īre~ (“to go”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”), a root also visible in Greek ~eîmi~ (“I go”) and Sanskrit ~éti~. But the present tense (~voy~, ~vas~, ~va~, ~van~) comes instead from a different Latin verb, ~vādere~ (“to walk, advance”), and the preterite (~fui~, ~fue~) is borrowed wholesale from ~esse~, the perfect ~fuī~ that ~ser~ also uses.

So a single tiny verb draws on three sources — ~īre~ for the infinitive, ~vādere~ for the present, ~fuī~ for the past — one of the most thoroughly suppletive verbs in the language. The shared preterite is the memorable twist: ~fui~ means both “I went” and “I was,” the two verbs indistinguishable in that tense, context alone deciding. The ~vādere~ strand seeded further Spanish words — ~invadir~ (“to invade,” to go in), ~evadir~ (“to evade,” to go out), and ~vadear~ (“to ford”) — while ~īre~ itself left little behind but this one indispensable verb.
en.jamar:
Spanish ~jamar~, a colloquial word for “to eat” or “to scoff down,” entered the language from Caló, the Romani-derived cant of the Spanish Roma, where ~jamar~ — with its synonym ~jalar~ — meant “to eat.” The Diccionario de la lengua española traces it no further than the label “from Caló.” M. L. Wagner carried the Romani verb back to the Sanskrit root ~khā-~ (also ~khāda-~, “to eat, to chew”), but that deeper step is his proposal, not settled fact, and is best marked as such.

The word keeps low, lively company. It circulated in the old thieves’ cant and in the same street milieu that fed the slang of the River Plate; in Mexico and Honduras it surfaces as ~jambar~. Wagner explained the synonym ~jalar~ just as neatly, from a Romani form meaning “he eats,” which is why the two are usually filed together. Register is the whole flavor of the verb: warm, slangy and never formal — it belongs to the kitchen and the street, not to the state banquet.
en.jugar:
From Latin ~iocāre~, a Vulgar-Latin variant of ~iocārī~ (“to jest, to play”), from ~iocus~ (“joke, jest”), from Proto-Indo-European *~yek-~ (“to speak”). Cognate with Italian ~giocare~, French ~jouer~, and Portuguese ~jogar~, and — through the same ~iocus~ — with English ~joke~ and ~juggle~ (the latter from Latin ~ioculārī~).

The surprise is that play began as talk. ~iocus~ was originally a spoken jest — the PIE root *~yek-~ means “to speak” — so the earliest “play” was word-play, banter, a joke. Only later did Spanish broaden ~jugar~ to cover games, sport, and gambling of every kind, leaving the verbal sense to ~bromear~. The old root still shows in ~jocoso~ (“humorous, jocular”), which kept close to the original joking. Everyday relatives include ~juego~ (“game, play”), ~jugador~ (“player”), and ~juguete~ (“toy”) — the whole vocabulary of fun grown from a single spoken quip.
en.juntar:
From Vulgar Latin *~iūnctāre~, a frequentative built on ~iūnctus~ (“joined”), the past participle of Latin ~iungere~ (“to join, yoke together”), from Proto-Indo-European *~yewg-~ (“to join, yoke”). Cognate with Portuguese ~juntar~ and Italian ~giuntare~; through ~iungere~ and its root, with English ~join~, ~junction~, ~yoke~ and even ~yoga~.

The root *~yewg-~ named the yoking of oxen, and its metaphor of binding-together runs through ~juntar~ (“to join, gather, put together”) and its noun ~junta~ (“board, council, junta”), a body of people “joined” for a purpose. Latin ~iungere~ gave Spanish ~uncir~ (“to yoke”), ~junto~ (“together”), ~juntura~ and ~coyuntura~ (“joint; juncture”), and ~conjunto~ (“set, ensemble”); and from the yoke-noun ~iugum~ came ~yugo~ (“yoke”). That same root, in ~coniugāre~ (“to yoke together”), produced the very verb ~conjugar~ — the act of conjugation this app is built to teach.
en.jurar:
From Latin ~iūrāre~ (“to swear, take an oath”), a verb built directly on the noun ~iūs~ (“law, right, that which is binding”). ~Iūs~ descends from Proto-Italic *~jowos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₂yew-~, tied to a notion of what is right, ordained or binding; Sanskrit ~yós~ (“welfare, health”) and Avestan ~yaoš~ preserve a related sacral sense. To swear was, literally, to place oneself under the ~iūs~. Italian ~giurare~, French ~jurer~ and Portuguese ~jurar~ continue the same Latin verb.

Because ~iūs~ was the root of law itself, its derivatives cluster around justice and obligation. An oath binds; so does a curse, and in Spanish ~jurar~ came to cover both the solemn “to swear (an oath)” and the profane “to swear (blaspheme, curse).” The Spanish family from ~iūs~ / ~iūrāre~ includes ~jurado~ (“jury; sworn”), ~juramento~ (“oath”), ~jura~, ~perjurar~ and ~conjurar~. Through the same ~iūs~, English inherited ~jury~, ~just~, ~justice~, ~injury~ and even ~perjury~ — a whole legal vocabulary rooted in one small Latin word for “what is right.”
en.justificar:
From Late Latin ~iūstificāre~ (“to do justice, to make righteous”), joining ~iūstus~ (“just, lawful”) to ~-ficāre~, the combining form of ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). ~iūstus~ in turn derives from ~iūs~ (“law, right, that which binds”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂yew-~ (“law, rule”). Through ~iūs~ it is cognate with English ~just~, ~justice~, and ~jury~.

In Roman thought ~iūs~ named binding right, often with a sacral tinge, and ~iūstus~ was what conformed to it; ~justificar~ thus began as “to make just” before it acquired its everyday sense of “to give reasons for.” (English borrowed it for the press, too: to ~justify~ a line of type is to make its edges straight and even.) The ~iūs~ family is large in Spanish: ~justo~, ~justicia~, ~juez~ (from ~iūdex~, “one who declares the law”), ~jurar~ (“to swear”), and ~injuria~ (“insult, wrong” — literally “that which runs against right”).
en.juzgar:
~Juzgar~ comes, through Old Spanish ~judgar~, from Latin ~iūdicāre~ (“to judge”), a verb built on ~iūdex~, genitive ~iūdicis~ (“judge”) — itself a compound of ~iūs~ (“law, right”) and ~dīcere~ (“to say, pronounce”), which rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, point out”). ~Juzgar~ is cognate with English ~judge~, French ~juger~, and Italian ~giudicare~.

An ~iūdex~ was literally “the one who pronounces (dīcit) what is right (~iūs~)” — justice as an act of speech. Spanish keeps the pairing across ~juez~ (“judge”), ~juicio~ (“judgment, trial”), ~judicial~, and, from that same ~iūs~, ~justicia~ and ~jurídico~. The verbal half lives on in ~decir~ (“to say”) and ~dictar~ (“to dictate”). To judge, etymologically, was never to weigh in silence but to speak the law aloud.
en.laborar:
From Latin ~labōrāre~ (“to work, toil, take pains”), a verb derived from the noun ~labor~ (“work, toil, hardship”). ~laborar~ is the learned, later borrowing; the same ~labōrāre~ also came down by ordinary sound change as the popular Spanish ~labrar~ (“to till, to work land, to carve”), so the two are doublets. Cognate with Italian ~lavorare~, French ~labourer~ (“to plough”), Portuguese ~laborar~, and English ~labour~ (borrowed via Old French). The noun ~labor~ itself is of uncertain origin; it has sometimes been connected with ~lābī~ (“to slip, to totter”), as if labour were the strain of one bending under a load, but this link is unproven and Latinists generally leave ~labor~ etymologically obscure.

In Latin ~labor~ meant not just effort but the burden of it — hardship, distress, even suffering — and that double edge survives: to ~laborar~ is to work, but Spanish ~laboral~ means “pertaining to work,” ~labor~ is a task or needlework, and ~laborable~ marks a working day. From the same root came ~labrador~ (“farmer,” one who ~labra~ the land), ~laboratorio~, ~elaborar~, ~colaborar~, and ~laborioso~. English inherited the whole family too — ~labor~, ~laboratory~, ~elaborate~, ~collaborate~. The split between cultured ~laborar~ and earthy ~labrar~ is a neat snapshot of how Spanish often keeps two reflexes of one Latin word, one bookish and one worn smooth by centuries of speech.
en.labrar:
Inherited from Latin ~labōrāre~ (“to work, to toil, to labor”), the verb of the noun ~labor~ (“labor, toil, hardship”), whose deeper origin is uncertain. Through regular syncope ~labōrāre~ passed to Old Spanish ~lavrar~ and then ~labrar~, while a later learned borrowing gave the doublet ~laborar~. Cognate with Italian ~lavorare~, Portuguese ~lavrar~ and French ~labourer~ (“to plow”); English took the same Latin word, via French, as ~labour~.

Where Latin ~labōrāre~ meant to work at anything, Spanish ~labrar~ narrowed toward working the land — plowing and tilling — and, by extension, to working a material by hand: to carve stone, tool leather, embroider cloth, hence a ~labrador~ (“farmer”) and finely ~labrado~ (“wrought, carved”) silver. The wider root still shows in the learned family ~labor~, ~laboratorio~, ~laborioso~, ~elaborar~ and ~colaborar~, all built on the old idea of effortful work.
en.ladrar:
Inherited from Latin ~lātrāre~ (“to bark”), from Proto-Italic *~lātrom~, from the Proto-Indo-European expressive root *~leh₂-~ (“to bark, to howl”) — a sound-imitative base, so the word is in a sense a stylized rendering of a dog's voice. The same expressive root is linked to Latin ~lāmentum~ (“wailing, lament”) and to Ancient Greek ~λάσκω~ (“to shout, to ring out”).

The meaning has scarcely moved in two thousand years: dogs still ~ladran~. Spanish built the everyday noun ~ladrido~ (“a bark”) and the agent noun ~ladrador~ (“barker”), the latter fixed in the proverb ~perro ladrador, poco mordedor~ (“a barking dog seldom bites”). Figuratively ~ladrar~ can mean to rail or clamor at someone — to bark in the human sense — while the rare learned English ~latrate~ preserves the untouched Latin form for anyone wanting a fancy word for a dog's noise.
en.lamentar:
From Latin ~lāmentārī~ (“to wail, moan, mourn aloud”), from the noun ~lāmentum~ (“a wailing, lament”). This belongs to an expressive, imitative Proto-Indo-European root *~leh₂-~ (“to shout, howl, bark”) — a root that names loud cries rather than reasoned speech. Cognate with Italian ~lamentare~, French ~lamenter~, and English ~lament~; from the same root come Latin ~lātrāre~ (“to bark”) and Greek ~lȇros~ (“idle talk, nonsense”).

Latin ~lāmentum~ was the loud, ritual wailing of grief and mourning. Spanish softened it: ~lamentar~ now most often means simply “to regret, be sorry” — ~lamento que no puedas venir~ (“I'm sorry you can't come”) — while the reflexive ~lamentarse~ keeps more of the old moaning and complaining. The immediate family is small and transparent: ~lamento~ (“a lament, moan”), ~lamentable~ (“regrettable, deplorable”), and ~lamentación~ (“lamentation”), all still audibly rooted in a cry.
en.lamer:
Inherited from Latin ~lambere~ (“to lick, to lap”), from a Proto-Indo-European imitative base *~leh₂b-~ evoking licking and lip-smacking. Cognate with Ancient Greek ~λάπτω~ (“to lap, to sip”) and, through Germanic, with English ~lap~ (“to lap up”); the Romance siblings are Italian ~lambire~ and Portuguese ~lamber~. English also borrowed the Latin present participle in ~lambent~, said of a flame that seems to lick a surface.

Latin ~lambere~ meant plainly to pass the tongue over something, and Spanish ~lamer~ keeps exactly that. Around it grew a lively word-family: ~lametón~ and ~lametazo~ (“a big lick”), ~lamedura~ (“a licking”), ~relamer~ (“to lick one's lips, to relish”) and the vividly unflattering ~lameculos~ (“bootlicker, sycophant” — literally a licker of a less polite part). Poets, meanwhile, still let flames and waves ~lamer~ the things they touch.
en.lanzar:
From Old Spanish ~lançar~, from Late Latin ~lanceāre~ (“to wield or hurl a lance”), from Latin ~lancea~ (“lance, light spear”). The origin of ~lancea~ itself is disputed: the Roman writer Varro reported it as a foreign, Hispanic word, so it is often traced to a Celtic or Iberian source — but the details are uncertain and no reconstruction is secure. Cognate with Italian ~lanciare~, French ~lancer~, and — borrowed through Old French — English ~lance~ and ~launch~.

The semantic path is neat: from a specific act, “to thrust with a lance,” Latin ~lanceāre~ broadened to any forceful throwing, and Spanish ~lanzar~ now covers hurling a ball, launching a rocket, or bringing a product to market. English ~launch~ took the very same journey through French. From ~lancea~ Spanish keeps the noun ~lanza~ (“lance”), ~lance~ (“incident, cast”), ~lanzamiento~ (“throw, launch”), and ~lanzadera~ (“shuttle”).
en.lastimar:
From Late Latin ~blastēmāre~, a popular variant of Latin ~blasphēmāre~ (“to blaspheme, revile”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~βλασφημεῖν~ (blasphēmeîn), from ~βλάσφημος~ (“speaking evil”), a compound of a first element related to ~βλάπτω~ (“to harm”) and ~φήμη~ (“speech, fame”). Spanish ~lastimar~ is thus a doublet of the learned ~blasfemar~, which kept the religious sense. Cognate through the same Latin verb with French ~blâmer~ and English ~blame~, and with Italian ~bestemmiare~.

The journey from “to revile with words” to “to hurt” ran through the idea of wounding by speech: to ~lastimar~ was first to insult or grieve someone, and only later to injure the body. The noun ~lástima~ (“pity, a shame”) preserved the emotional side — what stirs compassion — while the verb kept the sense of harm. Modern derivatives include ~lastimadura~ and ~lastimoso~. The blunt religious doublet survives in ~blasfemar~ and ~blasfemia~, so one Greek word gave Spanish both a term for cursing God and an everyday word for a scraped knee.
en.lavar:
From Latin ~lavāre~ (“to wash, bathe”), from Proto-Italic *~lawāō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~lewh₃-~ (“to wash”). The root also yielded Latin ~luere~ (“to wash away”) and Greek ~loúein~ (“to bathe”). Spanish ~lavar~ is a plain popular inheritance, worn smooth by ordinary use. Cognate with Italian ~lavare~, French ~laver~, Portuguese ~lavar~, and — through the same PIE root — with English ~lather~ (from Proto-Germanic *~lauþrą~) and the borrowed ~lave~ and ~lavatory~.

*~lewh₃-~ ran everywhere water did. From ~lavāre~ and its perfect stem Spanish and its neighbours drew a wide vocabulary of washing and flooding: ~lavabo~ (“washbasin,” literally Latin “I shall wash”), ~lavandería~ (“laundry”), ~loción~, and — from the related ~dīluvium~ — ~diluvio~ (“deluge”). English ~latrine~ and ~lavish~ belong to the same current, the latter from an Old French word for a downpour. The plant name ~lavanda~ (“lavender”) has long been associated with ~lavāre~, since it scented wash-water, though its ultimate origin is disputed. The metaphor of washing away guilt is ancient and still live: ~lavar~ una afrenta means to wipe out an insult, and the modern ~lavar~ dinero — “to launder money” — cleans it in exactly the figurative sense Latin already knew.
en.leer:
From Latin ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick out, to choose, to read”), from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to collect, to gather”). Cognate with Italian ~leggere~, French ~lire~, and Portuguese ~ler~; the Greek branch, ~légō~ (“I gather, I say”), yielded ~lógos~ and the whole ~-logy~ family. Through Latin the same root gives English ~lecture~, ~legible~, ~legend~, ~collect~, and ~elect~.

The oldest sense was physical — ~legere~ meant to gather up or pick out, as one gathers firewood or picks grapes. “To read” is a metaphor grown from it: the eye gathers the scattered letters and picks out the words, one by one. Greek made the parallel leap from “gathering” to “speaking,” which is how a word for collecting became ~lógos~, “word, reason.” Spanish narrowed ~leer~ to reading alone but keeps the gathering sense in ~elegir~ (“to choose”) and ~colegir~ (“to infer, to gather”), plus the reading cluster ~lección~, ~lectura~, ~legible~, and ~leyenda~ (“legend,” literally “things to be read”).
en.lesionar:
Spanish ~lesionar~ (“to injure”) is a modern denominal verb, built by adding the verb-forming ~-ar~ to the noun ~lesión~ (“injury, lesion”). ~Lesión~ itself descends from Latin ~laesiō~ (accusative ~laesiōnem~, “a hurting, damage”), a noun on the past participle ~laesus~ of the verb ~laedō~, ~laedere~ (“to strike, hurt, wound, offend”). There the trail goes cold: ~laedō~ is of uncertain origin, with no securely established Proto-Indo-European cognates — a rare dead end for so productive a Latin verb. In its prefixed compounds the diphthong raised from ~ae~ to ~ī~, giving ~collīdere~ (“to dash together”) and ~ēlīdere~ (“to strike out”); English borrowed the whole set as ~lesion~, ~collide~ and ~elide~.

Although ~lesionar~ is recent and tilts toward the concrete — a torn ligament, the sports-page ~lesionado~ (“injured player”) — the root's older reach was moral as much as bodily, for ~laedere~ also meant “to offend.” That double edge survives in the fossil adjective ~lesa~ (feminine of ~laesus~): the legal formula ~lesa humanidad~ (“crimes against humanity”) means, literally, a wounded humanity, and ~lesa majestad~ once named an injury to the sovereign's dignity. The un-hurt counterpart endures in ~ileso~ (“unharmed,” from Latin ~illaesus~), as in ~salir ileso~ (“to come out unscathed”), while the prefixed cousins yielded ~colisión~ (“collision”) and ~elisión~ (“elision”). For a verb whose ancestry ends in a shrug, ~laedere~ bequeathed a strikingly legalistic family.
en.levantar:
From Vulgar Latin *~levantāre~, built on ~levāns~ (stem ~levant-~), the present participle of Latin ~levāre~ (“to raise, lift, lighten”), from ~levis~ (“light in weight”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light, nimble”). It is cognate with Portuguese ~levantar~ and, through ~levāre~, with French ~lever~ and Italian ~levare~; through ~levis~ it is kin to English ~light~ (not heavy) and even ~lung~, the “light” organ that floats.

The base ~levāre~ meant both “to make lighter” and “to raise up,” and the frequentative ending gave ~levantar~ its brisk sense of lifting and getting up. Two descendants preserve a vivid picture: ~Levante~, the East, is the quarter where the sun “raises itself,” and ~levadura~ (“leaven, yeast”) is what makes dough rise. The wider family includes ~elevar~, ~aliviar~ (“to lighten, relieve”), ~leve~, ~liviano~, and ~levantamiento~ (“uprising”) — all turning on the double idea of lightness and rising.
en.levar:
From Latin ~levāre~ (“to raise, lift; to lighten”), from the adjective ~levis~ (“light in weight”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light, nimble”). Cognate with Italian ~levare~, French ~lever~, and Portuguese and Galician ~levar~; and, through the same root, with English ~light~ (the opposite of heavy), ~lever~, and ~alleviate~. Spanish ~levar~ is the inherited doublet of ~llevar~ (“to carry, take”), the two having split from one verb.

Where ~llevar~ generalized to “to carry” and “to take,” ~levar~ narrowed to the sea: to ~levar~ anclas is to weigh anchor — literally to “lift” it from the seabed before sailing — and that phrase is now the verb's chief survival, archaic or nautical elsewhere. The causative ~levantar~ (“to raise, to get up”) was built on the same stem with a Romance suffix, and the family runs deep in Spanish: ~elevar~, ~aliviar~, ~leve~, ~liviano~, and ~relevar~ all trace back to ~levis~ and ~levāre~.
en.liar:
From Latin ~ligāre~ (“to bind, tie”), from Proto-Indo-European *~leyǵ-~ (“to bind”). The word appeared relatively late in Castilian and may have come partly through Old French ~lier~; the fully inherited Old Spanish outcome was ~legar~ (“to tie”), now a rare regionalism, while the semi-learned ~ligar~ is its doublet. Cognate with Italian ~legare~, French ~lier~, and Portuguese ~liar~/~ligar~, and — through the same root — with English ~ligature~, ~ally~, ~league~, and ~rely~.

The core sense stayed physical: to ~liar~ is to bundle, wrap, or roll up, as in ~liar~ un cigarrillo (“to roll a cigarette”). From “tangling things together” came the figurative colloquial senses: ~liarse~ can mean to get muddled, to get caught up in an affair, or, in Spain, to get romantically involved. The learned doublet ~ligar~ supplies the chemistry and card-game senses and the everyday “to flirt,” while the same root yields ~liga~ (“league; garter”), ~ligadura~, ~aliar~, and ~obligar~.
en.liberar:
From Latin ~līberāre~ (“to set free, release”), from the adjective ~līber~ (“free”). ~līber~ goes back, through Old Latin ~loeber~ and Proto-Italic *~louðeros~, to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁léwdʰeros~ (“belonging to the people,” hence “free”), from the root *~h₁lewdʰ-~ (“to grow, to rise; people”). The kinship is striking: the same root gave Ancient Greek ~eleútheros~ (“free”), German ~Leute~ (“people”), and Russian ~ljúdi~ (“people”). Beside Spanish stand Italian ~liberare~ and Portuguese ~libertar~/~liberar~.

The etymology carries a whole social theory: to be ~līber~ was to belong to the people, the tribe, the free community — the opposite of the outsider or the slave, who was mere property. Freedom was membership, and German ~Leute~ still preserves that older “people” sense of the root. Spanish grew a large free-family — ~libre~, ~librar~, ~libertad~, ~liberal~, ~liberto~ (“freedman”), and ~libertino~ — while English borrowed ~liberty~ and ~liberate~ from the same Latin ~līber~. One caution: the noun ~libro~ (“book”) is no relative — it comes from a homonymous ~liber~, the inner tree-bark once written on.
en.librar:
From Latin ~līberāre~ (“to set free”), from ~līber~ (“free, not a slave”), from Old Latin ~loeber~, from Proto-Italic *~louðeros~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁léwdʰeros~ (“belonging to the people”), a suffixed form of *~h₁leudʰ-~ (“people; to grow”) — the same root behind German ~Leute~ (“people”). Cognates include Italian ~liberare~, French ~livrer~ (“to deliver”), Portuguese ~livrar~ and, through Late Latin, English ~deliver~.

The semantics are quietly political: to be free was, at root, to “belong to the people” rather than to a master. Spanish inherited the verb twice — the popular ~librar~ and the learned doublet ~liberar~ — beside ~libre~ and ~libertad~. ~librar~ fans out into many senses: to free or deliver from danger, to issue or draw a payment, and colloquially to have a day off work. One tempting link is false: ~libro~ (“book”) is not from this ~līber~ at all but from a homonym meaning the inner bark of a tree, where early texts were written.
en.licenciar:
From the noun ~licencia~ (“permission, license”), from Latin ~licentia~ (“freedom, leave, permission”), an abstract noun from ~licēns~, the present participle of ~licēre~ (“to be permitted, be allowed”). The deeper origin of ~licēre~ is uncertain — it is tentatively traced to a Proto-Italic *~likēt~ and a possible Proto-Indo-European root *~leyk-~, but there are no secure cognates outside Italic beyond the Oscan ~líkítud~ (“it is permitted”). Italian ~licenziare~, French ~licencier~ and Portuguese ~licenciar~ are the Romance parallels.

~Licenciar~ means to grant leave — and granting someone leave to go is precisely how it came to mean “to discharge,” whether releasing a soldier from service (a ~licenciado~ is a discharged conscript) or, historically, dismissing an employee. The very same word ~licenciado~ is also the university degree-holder — one given license to practice — which is why in much of Latin America ~licenciado~ (~licenciada~) is a courteous title. From ~licēre~ Spanish also has ~lícito~ (“licit, lawful”) and ~licencia~; English ~license~, ~licit~, ~illicit~ and ~leisure~ (through French, “time one is permitted”) share the root.
en.liderar:
Unlike its Latinate neighbors, ~liderar~ is young: it is a denominal verb built on the noun ~líder~ (“leader”), which Spanish borrowed between the 19th and 20th centuries from English ~leader~. That noun comes from the verb ~lead~, from Old English ~lǣdan~ (“to guide”), from Proto-Germanic *~laidijaną~, a causative of *~līþaną~ (“to go, travel”), from Proto-Indo-European *~leyt-~ (“to go forth”). Cognates include German ~leiten~ (“to lead”) and Dutch ~leiden~; Spanish also took in the derivative ~liderazgo~, echoing English ~leadership~.

The word’s interest lies in its route: a Germanic root for “going” that reached Spanish not by unbroken inheritance but as a modern press-and-politics loan through English. Purists long resisted it — the Spanish Academy admitted ~líder~ only in 1970 — yet it filled a gap the language had covered with ~dirigir~, ~encabezar~, or ~acaudillar~. Today it anchors a small, fully naturalized cluster: ~líder~, the feminine ~lideresa~, the abstract ~liderazgo~, and the verb ~liderar~ itself, now unremarkable in sports pages and boardrooms alike.
en.lidiar:
From Latin ~lītigāre~ (“to dispute, go to law”), a compound of ~līs~ (genitive ~lītis~, “lawsuit, quarrel”) and ~agere~ (“to drive, do”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”). Spanish ~lidiar~ is the inherited doublet of the later borrowing ~litigar~, which kept the legal sense. Cognate through the same Latin verb with English ~litigate~ and ~litigious~, and with Italian ~litigare~ and Portuguese ~lidar~.

The courtroom sense faded and the sense of struggle stayed: to ~lidiar~ is to fight or contend or — in the classic idiom — to ~lidiar~ con algo, to cope or grapple with a nuisance. In the bullring, ~lidiar~ became the technical verb for fighting the bull through the stages of the ~lidia~ (the whole ordered combat), and the noun ~lid~ (“fight, contest”) survives in the fixed phrase ~en buena lid~ (“by fair means”). The learned ~litigar~, ~litigio~, and ~litigante~ carry the original juridical branch.
en.ligar:
From Latin ~ligāre~ (“to bind, tie”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~leyǵ-~ (“to bind”). The Latin verb passed directly into Spanish as ~ligar~ and into its sisters as Italian ~legare~, Portuguese ~ligar~, and French ~lier~. Through ~ligāre~ and its derivatives, Spanish ~ligar~ is cognate with a surprising spread of English words — ~ligature~, ~ligament~, ~ally~, ~rely~, ~liable~, and ~league~ — all built on the idea of tying.

The core sense is simply “to bind,” and Spanish ~ligar~ still means to join, tie, or alloy. But it also picked up a lively colloquial sense, “to flirt” or “to hook up,” as though binding oneself to another for the evening. The prefixed ~obligāre~ (“to bind toward, oblige”) gave ~obligar~, and ~religāre~ (“to bind fast”) is one proposed source of ~religión~, though ancient writers debated whether ~religio~ came instead from ~relegere~ (“to reread, go over again”) — a genuinely disputed point. From the same root Spanish keeps ~liga~ (“league; garter”), ~ligadura~ (“ligature”), ~ligamento~, ~aliar~ (“to ally”), and ~ligazón~ (“bond”).
en.limitar:
From Latin ~limitare~ (“to mark off, set bounds”), formed from ~limes~ (genitive ~limitis~), “a boundary, a cross-path between fields, a frontier”. ~limes~ is usually derived from ~limus~ (“sidelong, transverse”) and set beside ~limen~ (“threshold”), though the exact relationship among these words is debated. It descends in Italian ~limitare~, French ~limiter~ and Portuguese ~limitar~.

The Roman ~limes~ began as the balk or path running crosswise between plots, then hardened into something grander: the fortified ~limes~ that marked the edge of the empire, from the German frontier to Hadrian's Wall. To ~limitare~ was to trace such a boundary, and Spanish ~limitar~ still means both “to set a limit” and “to border on” a neighbour. The family includes ~límite~, ~limítrofe~ (“bordering”) and ~limitación~, and English drew ~limit~ and ~limitation~ straight from the same Latin, while the neighbouring ~limen~ surfaces in English ~liminal~.
en.limpiar:
Spanish ~limpiar~ derives from the adjective ~limpio~ (“clean”), which comes from Latin ~limpidus~ (“clear, transparent, limpid”), especially of water. The verb continues a Late Latin ~limpidāre~ (“to make clear”). Through the Latin adjective ~limpiar~ is cognate with English ~limpid~ and French ~limpide~; Italian and Portuguese, however, reached the same idea by other words (~pulire~, ~limpar~).

The origin of ~limpidus~ is uncertain and debated. It has traditionally been linked to a Proto-Indo-European root *~leh₂p-~ (“to shine”) — which would make it kin to Ancient Greek ~lámpō~ (“to shine”) and Lithuanian ~liepsna~ (“flame”) — but another line ties it to Latin ~lympha~ (“clear water”), the water-nymph word, whose own spelling was reshaped by Greek ~νύμφη~ (~nýmphē~). Because the accounts diverge, the deep root is best left open. The sense-shift is easy to follow: what is “clear” becomes what is “clean.” From ~limpio~ Spanish built ~limpiar~, ~limpieza~ (“cleaning, cleanliness”), ~limpión~, and the adjective ~límpido~ (“limpid”).
en.liquidar:
From Latin ~liquidāre~ (“to make liquid or clear”), from ~liquidus~ (“fluid, clear”), from ~liquēre~ (“to be fluid or clear”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *~wleikʷ-~ (“to flow, be moist”), though the deeper root is uncertain. Cognate with Italian ~liquidare~ and French ~liquider~, and — as a learned borrowing — with English ~liquidate~.

The core idea is “to make clear.” Applied to accounts, ~liquidar~ meant to clear or settle them; hence “to pay off,” then “to sell off cheaply,” and in slang even “to do away with, kill.” From ~liquēre~ Spanish keeps ~líquido~, ~licuar~, ~licor~, ~liquidez~ and ~prolijo~ (from ~prōlixus~, “poured forth, drawn out”).
en.llagar:
From Latin ~plagāre~ (“to wound”), from the noun ~plāga~ (“a blow, wound, stroke”), akin to Ancient Greek ~πληγή~ (plēgḗ, “blow”) and to the verb ~plangere~ (“to beat, to lament”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₂g-~ (“to strike”). Latin initial ~pl-~ palatalized in Castilian, giving inherited ~llaga~ (“sore, ulcer”) and its verb ~llagar~, whereas the learned doublet ~plaga~ kept the cluster. Cognate through the same root with English ~plague~, ~plaint~, and ~complain~, and with French ~plaie~ and Italian ~piaga~.

~plāga~ named the blow and then the mark a blow leaves, so Spanish ~llaga~ settled on the open sore or ulcer, and ~llagar~ on wounding someone all over — often figuratively, a heart ~llagado~ by grief. The learned branch divided the senses: ~plaga~ took the sense of a scourge or infestation — locusts, disease — and ~plagar~ came to mean “to fill with.” The devotional language of the five ~llagas~ of Christ kept the inherited form alive in worship.
en.llamar:
From Old Spanish ~clamar~, from Latin ~clāmāre~ (“to cry out, shout”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kelh₁-~ (“to call, shout”). Cognate with Italian ~chiamare~, French ~clamer~, and Portuguese ~chamar~, and — through the same root — with Latin ~calāre~ (“to call out”) and the English borrowings ~claim~ and ~clamor~.

The initial Latin cluster ~cl-~ palatalized to the Spanish ~ll-~ (the same shift that turned ~clāvem~ into ~llave~ and ~plēnum~ into ~lleno~), so ~clāmāre~ yielded popular ~llamar~ while a learned ~clamar~ (“to clamor, cry out”) was later re-borrowed alongside it. The sense softened from the urgency of shouting to the everyday acts of calling, summoning, and — reflexively, in ~llamarse~ — being named: one no longer cries out a name but simply ~se llama~ it. The root also gave Spanish ~clamor~, ~reclamar~ (“to claim, demand”), and ~exclamar~, plus the derivatives ~llamada~ (“call”), ~llamamiento~ (“summons”), and ~llamativo~ (“eye-catching”).
en.llegar:
From Old Spanish ~llegar~, from Latin ~plicāre~ (“to fold”) — or, by a competing account, from its compound ~applicāre~ (“to bring to, to land a ship”), the initial ~a-~ later lost. Either way the ~pl-~ hardened into Spanish ~ll-~. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to fold”). Portuguese ~chegar~ came the same way; the folding sense stayed put in the learned doublet ~plegar~ and in Italian ~piegare~ and French ~plier~; English ~ply~ and ~apply~ are relatives.

How “to fold” became “to arrive” is debated. The usual explanation is nautical — a ship reaching harbor folds its sails, or is brought folded up against the shore — fitting for the seafaring peninsula, though it remains a proposal rather than a proven fact. Strikingly, the very same Latin verb went the opposite way in Romanian ~pleca~ (“to leave, to depart”), by one account from folding up a tent to move on — so a single root yielded both “arrive” and “leave.” Spanish derivatives include ~llegada~ (“arrival”) and the doublet family of ~plegar~, ~aplicar~, ~replicar~, and ~complicar~.
en.llenar:
From ~lleno~ (“full”), from Latin ~plēnus~ (“full”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”); the Latin initial ~pl-~ regularly became Spanish ~ll-~. It is cognate with Italian ~pieno~, French ~plein~ and Portuguese ~cheio~, and, through the same root, with English ~full~ and ~plenty~ and German ~voll~.

The adjective ~plēnus~ gave the adjective ~lleno~, from which Spanish coined the verb ~llenar~, “to make full.” Beside the inherited ~ll-~ line, Spanish also borrowed the Latin ~pl-~ form learnedly, so the family runs double: popular ~lleno~, ~llenar~, ~rellenar~ alongside cultured ~pleno~, ~plenitud~ and ~pleamar~ (“high tide”). English ~fill~ itself is built on ~full~, from the very same PIE root *~pleh₁-~.
en.llevar:
From Old Spanish ~levar~, from Latin ~levāre~ (“to raise, to lift”), from the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light in weight”) — the same root that gave English its native ~light~. The Romance siblings are Italian ~levare~, French ~lever~, and Portuguese ~levar~; English also took the learned ~lever~, ~elevate~, ~alleviate~, and ~relieve~ from the same Latin stock.

The path from “to lift” to Spanish ~llevar~ (“to carry, to take, to wear”) runs through the natural chain of lifting a load, then bearing it, then bearing it away. Spanish split the work with a cousin: ~llevar~ carries something from here to there, while ~traer~ brings it toward the speaker. The plainer sense of “to raise” stayed with the doublet ~levantar~ (“to lift, to raise”), and the family also yields ~leve~ (“light, slight”), ~elevar~, ~aliviar~ (“to relieve”), ~relevar~ (“to relieve, to relay”), and ~sublevar~ (“to incite to revolt”).
en.llorar:
From Latin ~plōrāre~ (“to weep, wail, cry out”), of uncertain origin — possibly from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₃(w)-~ (“to flow”), though the link is not secure. Latin ~pl-~ regularly became Spanish ~ll-~, as in ~plēnus~ → ~lleno~ (“full”) and ~pluvia~ → ~lluvia~ (“rain”). Cognate with Portuguese ~chorar~, Catalan ~plorar~ and French ~pleurer~.

In Latin ~plōrāre~ meant to cry out aloud, and only gradually narrowed toward weeping. Its Roman compounds still live in English through French: ~deplōrāre~ (“to lament”) gave ~deplore~ and ~implōrāre~ gave ~implore~; and — by one much-repeated but uncertain account — ~explōrāre~ was first a hunters' term, “to cry out” on sighting game, before it came to mean ~explore~. Spanish keeps ~plōrāre~'s core in ~llorar~ and built ~lloro~ (“weeping”), ~llorón~ (“crybaby”), ~lloroso~ (“tearful”) and ~lloriquear~ (“to whimper”).
en.llover:
Spanish ~llover~ (“to rain”) was inherited through Vulgar Latin *~plovere~ from Classical Latin ~pluere~ (“to rain”), from Proto-Italic and ultimately the Proto-Indo-European root *~plew-~ (“to flow, to swim”). Its Romance siblings all begin from the same Latin verb: Portuguese ~chover~, Italian ~piovere~, French ~pleuvoir~ and Catalan ~ploure~. Reaching deeper, the root *~plew-~ lies behind Ancient Greek ~pléō~ (“to sail, to float”), the shared image being water in motion. (English “flow,” despite the perfect fit of sound and sense, springs from a different root and is only a look-alike.)

That initial cluster is a giveaway of the word’s age. In Castilian, Latin ~pl-~ regularly softened to ~ll-~: ~plōrāre~ became ~llorar~ (“to weep”) and ~plēnum~ became ~lleno~ (“full”), by the very same sound-law that turned the rain verb into ~llover~. The learned Latin shape stayed visible in borrowings, so beside the homely noun ~lluvia~ (“rain”) Spanish keeps the bookish ~pluvial~, and the adjective ~lluvioso~ (“rainy”) still carries the ancient image of flowing water all the way down to the weather report.
en.loar:
From Latin ~laudāre~ (“to praise, extol”), from the noun ~laus~ (genitive ~laudis~, “praise, glory”). The deeper origin of that noun is uncertain: it has been tentatively linked to a Proto-Indo-European root for “song” or “fame,” and compared with Germanic words such as English ~loud~, but the link is disputed and no secure Indo-European etymon is established. Spanish ~loar~ is the inherited form, a doublet of the later learned ~laudar~. Cognate with Portuguese ~louvar~, Galician ~loar~, and Italian ~lodare~, and — through the Latin verb — with English ~laud~, ~applaud~, and ~allow~.

In Old Spanish ~loar~ was the ordinary word for praising, but it slowly gave way to ~alabar~ (itself of debated origin) and now sounds elevated or literary — one ~loa~ a hero or a virtue in solemn registers. The related noun ~loa~ was a short laudatory prologue once recited before a play; ~loable~ (“praiseworthy”) and ~loor~ (“praise,” as in the phrase en loor de multitudes) keep the root current, beside the learned ~laudable~, ~laudatorio~, and the musical ~laude~.
en.localizar:
A modern verb formed on the adjective ~local~, from Latin ~locālis~ (“of a place”), from ~locus~ (“place, spot”). Older Latin had ~stlocus~, a word of uncertain origin; some link it to a Proto-Indo-European root *~stel-~ (“to set, place”), but that descent is debated. Cognate with Italian ~luogo~, French ~lieu~ and English ~locus~ and ~location~.

The learned ~locālis~ actually reached Spanish twice: inherited through popular speech it became ~lugar~ (“place”), while borrowed straight from Latin it gave the doublet ~local~ (“local; premises”). ~locus~ seeded a wide family — ~localidad~, ~colocar~, ~locomotora~, ~dislocar~ — and in the nineteenth century Spanish took ~localizar~ from French ~localiser~, meaning to fix a thing in its place. Fittingly for a word about location, ~locus~ still refuses to disclose its own origin.
en.lograr:
From Latin ~lucrārī~ (“to gain, to profit”), a deponent verb from the noun ~lucrum~ (“gain, profit, wealth”), from Proto-Indo-European *~leh₂w-~ (“to seize, to gain”). The same root surfaces in Germanic as Proto-Germanic *~launą~ (“reward”), giving German ~Lohn~ (“wage”) and Old English ~lēan~ (“reward”), and in Greek ~apolaúō~ (“to enjoy”). Within Romance, Spanish ~lograr~ stands beside the learned borrowing ~lucro~ and its Portuguese and Italian relatives.

The meaning traveled a satisfying road. Latin ~lucrārī~ was mercantile — to turn a profit — and Old Spanish ~lograr~ first meant “to enjoy or possess” something, to have the benefit of it. From “enjoying the gain” the verb slid to “obtaining the desired thing” and finally to today’s “to achieve, to manage to.” The word’s history is thus its own small success story: from raw profit, through enjoyment, to accomplishment. Alongside the popular ~lograr~ Spanish keeps the doublet ~logro~ (“achievement,” and formerly “usury, interest”), plus the learned ~lucro~ and ~lucrativo~, which stayed close to the original money-making sense.
en.luchar:
From Latin ~luctari~ (“to wrestle, to struggle”), attested since Plautus, from Proto-Indo-European *~lewg-~ (“to bend, to twist”). The Latin cluster ~-ct-~ palatalized to Spanish ~-ch-~, the same change that turned ~lacte~ into ~leche~ and ~pectus~ into ~pecho~. It is cognate with Italian ~lottare~, French ~lutter~ and Portuguese ~lutar~, and — through the deponent compound ~reluctari~ — with English ~reluctant~ (literally “struggling back”).

The image behind the root is a body twisting against an opponent, and ~luchar~ began as literal wrestling before broadening to any fight or striving — against an enemy, an illness, or oneself. By the traditional account the same *~lewg-~ root also yielded Latin ~luxus~ (“dislocated; excess”), whence Spanish ~lujo~ (“luxury”) and ~lujuria~ (“lust”) — the twist of a joint and the twist of indulgence sharing one ancestor. Closer to home the root gives ~lucha~, ~luchador~ and ~luchadora~.
en.lucir:
From Latin ~lūcēre~ (“to shine, be bright”), related to ~lux~ (“light”), from Proto-Indo-European *~lewk-~ (“to shine, be white”). Cognate with English ~light~, German ~Licht~, Greek ~leukós~ (“white”) and Sanskrit ~rócate~ (“shines”), and with the Latin kin ~lūna~ and ~lūmen~.

The root *~lewk-~ is a beacon across the family: Latin ~lūna~ (“moon”) is literally “the shining one,” from *~louksnā~. In Spanish it lit up ~luz~ (“light”), ~lucero~ (“bright star”), ~lúcido~ (“lucid”), ~alumbrar~ (“to illuminate”) and ~iluminar~. The verb ~lūcēre~ itself drifted from plain shining to display: to ~lucir~ is to shine in the sense of showing off — a new dress, a talent, a tan — while ~relucir~ keeps the older, literal glow.
en.madrugar:
From Old Spanish ~madurgar~, from Vulgar Latin *~mātūricāre~, a formation on Latin ~mātūrāre~ (“to hasten, to ripen”), itself from the adjective ~mātūrus~ (“ripe, timely, early”), from Proto-Indo-European *~meh₂-~ (“good, timely”). A metathesis then swapped the consonants, turning ~madurgar~ into ~madrugar~. Cognate through ~mātūrus~ with its learned doublet ~madurar~ (“to ripen”), and with English ~mature~ and ~matutinal~, French ~mûr~, and Italian ~maturo~.

The Latin idea of acting “in good time,” hence early, narrowed in Castilian to the morning: to ~madrugar~ is specifically to rise at dawn. From it grew ~madrugada~ (“the small hours, daybreak”) and ~madrugador~ (“early riser”), and the culture prized the habit — hence the proverb ~a quien madruga, Dios le ayuda~ (“God helps those who rise early”). The same ~mātūrus~ that yielded “early rising” gave, by the learned route, ~madurar~ and ~maduro~ for fruit and wisdom, so one Latin word underlies both early ripeness and the early alarm. The dawn goddess ~Mātūta~ and the adjective ~matutino~ share the root.
en.madurar:
From Latin ~mātūrāre~ (“to ripen, to make ripe; to hasten”), from the adjective ~mātūrus~ (“ripe, timely, early, mature”), from Proto-Indo-European *~meh₂-~ (“good, timely, on time”). Cognate with Portuguese and Catalan ~madurar~, Italian ~maturare~, and French ~mûrir~; and, through ~mātūrus~, with English ~mature~ and ~maturate~. The adjective is linked to ~Mātūta~, the Roman goddess of the dawn, and to ~mātūtīnus~ (“of the morning”), source of English ~matutinal~ and ~matins~.

The verb kept both faces of ~mātūrus~ — the natural “to ripen” (fruit reddening on the branch) and the figurative “to mature” (a person, a plan, an idea coming to fruition) — and Spanish still uses ~madurar~ for a peach, a decision, and a mind alike. Its inherited twin ~madrugar~ (“to rise early”) shows what the same root did on the popular route, taking the sense of doing things “in good time.” From ~mātūrus~ Spanish also has ~maduro~ (“ripe, mature”), ~madurez~ (“maturity”), and ~maduración~, while the learned ~prematuro~ (“premature”) carries the Latin adjective under a prefix.
en.magnificar:
From Latin ~magnificāre~ (“to esteem greatly, extol”), from ~magnificus~ (“great, noble, splendid”), a compound of ~magnus~ (“great, large”) and ~facere~ (“to make, do”). ~magnus~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~meǵ-~ (“great”). English inherited the same Latin verb — reshaped through French — as the cognate ~magnify~, and ~magnificent~ preserves the fuller stem; Italian has ~magnificare~ and Portuguese ~magnificar~.

The original sense was social and moral — to ~magnificar~ someone was to praise them, to make them great in esteem — before the word also took on the optical meaning “to enlarge to the sight,” as a lens does. The PIE root *~meǵ-~ is remarkably productive in Spanish: it surfaces in the learned ~magno~, ~magnate~, and ~magnitud~, and, worn down by centuries of everyday use, in ~mayor~ (from Latin ~maior~, “greater”) and ~maestro~ (from ~magister~, literally “the greater one”). The Marian antiphon ~Magníficat~ — “my soul magnifies the Lord” — is simply this same verb, frozen as a title.
en.majar:
From Vulgar Latin *~malleāre~ (“to hammer, beat”), a verb built on Latin ~malleus~ (“hammer”); through an Old Spanish ~majo~ it became modern ~majar~. Portuguese and Galician kept ~malhar~ and ~mallar~, and English ~maul~ (“to beat, mangle”) is a cognate, borrowed from the related French ~mail~. The deeper origin of ~malleus~ is disputed: it is often traced to Proto-Indo-European *~melh₂-~ (“to grind, crush”), the root also seen in Latin ~molere~ (“to grind”), though other reconstructions have been proposed.

~majar~ names the pounding of ingredients in a mortar — garlic, spices, herbs — and by extension the crushing or wearying of a person. From ~malleus~ Spanish also drew ~mazo~ and ~maza~ (“mallet, mace”) and the ~majadero~, first the pestle that performs the ~majar~ and then, figuratively, a tedious, thick-headed fool. Because the hammer’s deeper ancestry is contested, any vivid link between the smith’s ~malleus~ and the grinding root *~melh₂-~ should be read as likely rather than proven.
en.malcasar:
A transparent compound: the pejorative prefix ~mal-~ (from Latin ~male~, “badly,” the adverb of ~malus~, “bad, evil”) prefixed to ~casar~ (“to marry”). ~casar~ is denominal, from ~casa~ (“house”), which descends from Latin ~casa~ (“hut, cottage, cabin”) — so to marry was, literally, to set up a household together. Portuguese and Galician share ~casar~ with the same “house → marry” logic.

To ~malcasar~ is to marry badly or to marry someone off badly — to an ill-suited or unequal partner — and reflexively ~malcasarse~ is to make such a match oneself. The ~mal-~ prefix is one of Spanish’s liveliest, generating ~maldecir~, ~malgastar~, ~maltratar~, and ~malograr~; the ~casa~ family yields ~casamiento~ (“marriage, wedding”), ~casero~ (“landlord; homemade”), and the dismissive ~casorio~ for a hasty or ill-considered wedding. Latin ~casa~ narrowed from “humble hut” in classical usage to the ordinary word for “house,” displacing the loftier ~domus~ across most of Romance.
en.maldecir:
From Latin ~maledīcere~ (“to speak ill of, slander, curse”), a compound of ~male~ (“badly”) and ~dīcere~ (“to say, speak”). ~dīcere~ rests on Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, point out”), the same root that gave Latin ~dīcō~ its family and, through Germanic, English ~teach~ and ~token~. The exact counterpart ~benedīcere~ (“to bless”) gave Spanish ~bendecir~, so the two verbs remain mirror images.

Spanish inherited ~maledīcere~ twice over. The popular line, worn by everyday speech, produced ~maldecir~ and the noun ~maldición~ (“curse”); a later learned borrowing from the same Latin yielded ~maledicencia~ (“slander, backbiting”) — a classic doublet, one form battered by centuries of use, the other lifted straight from the books. English ~malediction~ comes from the very same ~maledīcere~. The root ~dīcere~ seeded a huge Spanish family — ~decir~, ~dicho~, ~dictar~, ~contradecir~, ~predecir~ — all ultimately pointing, as *~deyḱ-~ did, to the act of showing in words.
en.mamar:
From Latin ~mammāre~ (“to suckle, give the breast”), from ~mamma~ (“breast; teat; mother”). ~mamma~ is one of those nursery words that arise almost identically the world over from a baby’s earliest babbling — Latin itself may have reshaped it under Greek ~mámmē~ — so it has no deeper Indo-European pedigree to trace. Italian ~mammella~ and the whole European family of “mama” words spring from the same infant sound.

In Spanish ~mamar~ is what a nursing baby or animal does — to take the breast — and the noun ~mamá~ (“mum”) is the affectionate reduplication of the same syllable. Figuratively, to ~mamar~ something is to absorb it from earliest childhood, as in ~mamar~ una lengua desde la cuna. The root fed a large cluster: ~mama~ and ~mamila~, the causative ~amamantar~ (“to breastfeed”), the scornful ~mamón~ (“still suckling; sponger”), and the scientific ~mamífero~ (“mammal”) — the animals defined, exactly as the Latin sense had it, by the ~mamma~ that feeds their young. English ~mammal~ and ~mammary~ share that last root.
en.manar:
From Latin ~mānāre~ (“to flow, trickle, drip”). Its deeper origin is uncertain: it is tentatively linked to a Proto-Indo-European *~meh₂-~ (“wet, damp”), but etymologists such as de Vaan hesitate over the connection, so the pre-Latin history is best left open. Portuguese preserves the verb intact as ~manar~; note that identical-looking Catalan ~manar~ (“to command”) is a false friend, descending instead from Latin ~mandāre~.

~manar~ describes water welling up and running out — a spring, a wound, tears — and figuratively anything that issues abundantly from a source: ~manar~ leche y miel. From the same Latin verb Spanish keeps ~manantial~ (“spring, wellspring”) and the derived ~manadero~. The prefixed Latin ~ēmānāre~ (“to flow out from”) gave the learned ~emanar~ (“to emanate, issue from”), whose English cognate ~emanate~ carries the identical image of something streaming out of its origin — a metaphor for radiance and influence built, at bottom, on the picture of a quietly flowing spring.
en.mandar:
From Latin ~mandāre~ (“to entrust, to order”), a compound traditionally explained as ~manus~ (“hand”) + ~dāre~ (“to give”) — literally “to place in someone's hand.” ~dāre~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Cognate with Italian ~mandare~ (“to send”), French ~mander~, and Portuguese ~mandar~, and — through the compound — with English ~mandate~, ~command~, and ~demand~.

The literal picture — putting a task into someone's hand — explains the whole semantic spread. To hand someone a charge is to “entrust” it (the sense in English ~mandate~), and to entrust with authority shades into “to order,” which is why ~mandar~ means “to command.” But Spanish also took a second path: to put something in a messenger's hand is to “send” it, so ~mandar~ means “to send” as well — ~mandar una carta~ is to send a letter, ~mandar a alguien~ can be to order someone about. Few Spanish verbs carry so wide a range on one root. Related descendants include ~mando~ (“command, control”), ~mandato~ (“mandate”), ~mandamiento~ (“commandment”), ~comandar~ (“to command [troops]”), ~demandar~ (“to demand, to sue”), and ~encomendar~ (“to entrust”).
en.manejar:
From Italian ~maneggiare~ (“to handle, to manage, especially to handle a horse”), a denominative ultimately built on Latin ~manus~ (“hand”). Spanish borrowed it in the sixteenth century. The word is traditionally parsed as ~manus~ plus ~agere~ (“to drive by hand”), but that account is disputed: Corominas rejects it, treating ~maneggiare~ instead as a reinforced formation from ~mano~ / ~manus~, parallel to Italian ~maniglia~ (“handle”). Through the same Italian verb, Spanish ~manejar~ is cognate with English ~manage~ and French ~manège~ (“riding school”).

Its first home in Spanish was the riding school: to ~manejar~ a horse was to work it through its paces by hand and rein. From there it widened to handling tools, money, ideas and people — and in much of Latin America ~manejar~ became the ordinary verb for driving a car, where peninsular Spanish prefers ~conducir~. The Latin ~manus~ seeded a broad family, among them ~mano~, ~manejo~, ~manija~, ~maniobra~, ~manual~ and ~manuscrito~.
en.manifestar:
From Latin ~manifestare~ (“to make plain, reveal”), derived from the adjective ~manifestus~ (“caught in the act, flagrant, evident, palpable”). Its first element is clearly ~manus~ (“hand”); the second is disputed — it may descend from a Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰers-~ (“to be bold”), itself from *~dʰer-~ (“to hold”), but the analysis is uncertain and no confident sense can be assigned. Latin passed the verb to Italian ~manifestare~, French ~manifester~ and Portuguese ~manifestar~.

Whatever its build, ~manifestus~ evoked something so palpable it could almost be taken in the hand — a wrongdoer “caught red-handed”, a fact plain to all. Spanish ~manifestar~ accordingly means “to show, reveal, declare”, and reflexively ~manifestarse~ is “to demonstrate”, to make one's views public in the street. Hence the noun ~manifestación~ (“demonstration, manifestation”) and ~manifiesto~ (“manifesto”). The transparent first element ~manus~ anchors a huge Spanish family — ~mano~, ~manejar~, ~manual~ and ~mantener~ — and English borrowed the verb's own offspring in ~manifest~ and ~manifesto~.
en.manipular:
From French ~manipuler~ (“to handle, manipulate”), a late learned coinage — first in pharmacy and chemistry — from ~manipule~, from Latin ~manipulus~ (“a handful; a bundle; a maniple of soldiers”). ~Manipulus~ joins ~manus~ (“hand”) with the root of ~plēre~ (“to fill”): a handful is what fills the hand. It is cognate with Italian ~manipolare~ and Portuguese ~manipular~, and — through ~manus~ — with English ~manipulate~, ~maniple~, ~manual~, ~manufacture~, and ~maneuver~ (French ~manœuvre~, “handwork”).

The Roman ~manipulus~ began as a literal wisp of hay bound to a pole as a standard, then named the company of soldiers who followed it — a vivid jump from “handful” to “military unit.” The modern verb kept the hand at its center: to manipulate is to work something with the hands, and figuratively to handle people or facts to one’s advantage — a pejorative shade the word gained only in the nineteenth century. Spanish ~manipular~ shares the hand-family with ~mano~ (“hand”), ~manejar~ (“to handle, drive”), ~manual~ (“manual”), ~maniobra~ (“maneuver”), and ~manipulación~ (“manipulation”).
en.mantener:
From Latin ~manū~ ~tenēre~, literally “to hold in the hand,” a phrase of ~manus~ (“hand”) and ~tenēre~ (“to hold, keep”) that fused into Vulgar Latin ~manutenēre~. The second element, shared with ~tener~, goes back to Proto-Italic *~tenēō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, extend”); the first, ~manus~, comes from Proto-Italic *~manus~ and *~man-~ (“hand”). Cognate Romance descendants include Italian ~mantenere~, Portuguese ~manter~ and French ~maintenir~; English ~maintain~ is the same compound, borrowed through Old French ~maintenir~.

The image is concrete: to “hold in the hand” became to keep, support, sustain and maintain — the range Spanish ~mantener~ still spans, from ~mantener~ una promesa to ~mantener~ a la familia. Its ~tenēre~ half anchors a huge family — ~tener~, ~contener~, ~detener~, ~obtener~, ~sostener~ and ~retener~ — while ~manus~ gives ~mano~, ~manejar~, ~manual~ and ~maniobra~ (“maneuver,” from ~manū~ ~operāre~, “to work by hand”). Through the root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”) ~mantener~ is even distantly kin to ~tender~, ~tienda~ (a stretched tent-shop) and English ~tenant~ and ~tension~.
en.maquinar:
From Latin ~māchinārī~ (“to contrive, devise, plot”), the verb of ~māchina~ (“machine, device, contrivance, trick”). Latin borrowed the noun from Doric Greek ~māchaná~ (Attic ~mēkhanḗ~, “device, means, contrivance”), from ~mêkhos~ (“means, expedient”), from Proto-Indo-European *~magʰ-~ (“to be able, to have power”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~machine~ and ~machination~, and — via Germanic — with English ~may~ and ~might~ and German ~Macht~ (“power”).

The Greek ~mēkhanḗ~ was the crane that lowered a god onto the stage — the original ~deus ex machina~ — and any clever contrivance; the metaphorical leap from “build a device” to “devise a plot” was already present in Latin ~māchinārī~. So Spanish ~maquinar~ means “to scheme, plot,” while its innocent doublet ~máquina~ kept the concrete “machine.” From the same source come ~maquinaria~, ~maquinación~, ~mecánico~ and ~mecanismo~ — the engineering and the intrigue springing from one Greek word for a device.
en.maravillar:
From ~maravilla~ (“marvel, wonder”), from Late Latin ~mīrābilia~ (“wonders,” the neuter plural of ~mīrābilis~, “wonderful”), from ~mīrārī~ (“to wonder at, be amazed”), from ~mīrus~ (“wonderful, astonishing”). ~mīrus~ traces to Proto-Italic *~smeiros~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~smey-~ (“to laugh, be glad”) — the very root that, through Germanic, produced English ~smile~. So amazement and a smile are, etymologically, the same reflex.

~mīrābilia~ passed into Old Spanish as ~maravilla~, and the denominal ~maravillar~ means “to fill with wonder,” reflexively ~maravillarse~ “to marvel.” The parent verb ~mīrārī~ took a different, humbler path: as its sense drifted from “wonder at” to merely “look at,” it became everyday ~mirar~ (“to look”). The same root gave ~admirar~, ~milagro~ (from ~mīrāculum~, with the r-metathesis so typical of Spanish), and the English cognates ~marvel~ and ~miracle~ — a whole family born from the ancient idea that wonder lights up the face.
en.marcar:
Spanish ~marcar~ (“to mark”) has a debated immediate history: it is either a native formation from the noun ~marca~ (“mark, boundary”) plus the verb-ending ~-ar~, or a loan from Italian ~marcare~ (“to put a mark on”). Either way the deeper source is Germanic. The noun ~marca~ goes back, through Medieval Latin ~marca~, to Proto-Germanic *~markō~ (“boundary, borderland, region”), which entered Ibero-Romance from a Germanic tongue — Gothic or Frankish. So the root idea is not a scribble but a border. It is cognate with Italian ~marca~, German ~Mark~ and English ~mark~ and ~march~ (“borderland”).

The semantic path runs from the land inward. A ~marca~ was first a frontier district — the borderlands a ruler had to guard — which is exactly why medieval marches gave us titles like “marquis” (Spanish ~marqués~), the lord set over a ~marca~. From “boundary” the noun narrowed to the “mark” one sets to claim or delimit, and the verb ~marcar~ to the act of making such a mark — on cattle, on a page, on a scoreboard. Its Spanish kin spread across that whole span: ~marco~ (“frame”), ~marcador~ (“marker; scoreboard”), ~comarca~ (“district,” literally land within borders), ~demarcar~ (“to demarcate”) and ~marcapasos~ (“pacemaker”).
en.marchar:
Spanish ~marchar~ was borrowed from French ~marcher~ (“to walk, tread, march”), attested from the twelfth century. The ultimate origin is disputed. The favored account traces ~marcher~ to Frankish *~markōn~ (“to mark, to tread”), from Proto-Germanic *~markōną~, a verb on *~markō~ (“boundary, mark”); a rival proposal derives it instead from a Vulgar Latin *~marcāre~ (“to hammer,” from ~marcus~ “hammer”), but this is generally rejected, and the word’s confinement to French favors the Germanic source. English borrowed the French verb as ~march~; Italian has ~marciare~, Portuguese ~marchar~.

If the Germanic account is right, ~marchar~ shares a root with English ~mark~ and ~march~ (“borderland”) and with the Spanish loans ~marca~ (“mark, brand”), ~marcar~, ~comarca~ (“district”), and ~marqués~ (“marquis,” originally the warden of a border ~march~). The sense in Spanish widened from military marching to any purposeful going — a train ~marcha~, a person ~se marcha~ (“leaves”), and a machine ~marcha~ (“runs”) — plus the noun ~marcha~ (“march, pace, gear, nightlife”).
en.matar:
From Old Spanish ~matar~ (“to fell, subdue, kill”), a word shared by the Hispanic Romance languages whose ultimate origin is genuinely uncertain.
