From its participle ~passus~ that idea fanned out remarkably, giving English ~passion~ (originally the enduring of suffering, as in the Passion of Christ), the grammatical ~passive~ (the voice whose subject undergoes the action rather than performing it), and ~patient~, literally “one who endures.” Spanish ~padecer~ narrowed the sense to bearing hardship or illness: one ~padece~ a disease, a hunger, a heartbreak. Kindred Spanish words abound: ~paciencia~, ~paciente~, ~pasión~, ~pasivo~, ~compasión~ (“a suffering-with”), and the noun ~padecimiento~ (“ailment, suffering”).
en.pagar:
Spanish ~pagar~ comes from Late Latin ~pācāre~ (“to pacify, appease, satisfy”), a verb on ~pāx~ (“peace”). ~pāx~ goes back, through Proto-Italic *~pāks~, to Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂ḱ-~ (“to fasten, join”) — peace conceived as the binding-together of parties — a root shared with Latin ~pangere~ (“to fix, fasten”) and ~pacīscī~ (“to make a pact”). Its Romance reflexes include French ~payer~, Portuguese ~pagar~, Italian ~pagare~, and Catalan ~pagar~; English ~pay~ was borrowed from Old French ~paiier~.

The meaning traveled a very human road: to ~pācāre~ a creditor was to “appease” him, and appeasing a creditor means handing over money — so “pacify” slid into “pay.” The old sense still peeks through: someone ~pagado de sí mismo~ is “pleased with himself,” satisfied rather than paid. From ~pāx~ Spanish gathered ~paz~ (“peace”), ~pago~ (“payment”), ~pagador~, ~pacífico~, ~pacto~, and ~apaciguar~ (“to appease”). Most striking is ~apagar~ (“to switch off, extinguish”), from Vulgar Latin *~appācāre~: to quiet a flame is, quite literally, to make peace with it.
en.paginar:
A modern, learned formation from the noun ~página~ (“page”), which Spanish took from Latin ~pāgina~ (“page, column of writing, leaf of papyrus”). ~pāgina~ derives from ~pangere~ (“to fix, fasten, drive in”), from Proto-Italic *~pangō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂ǵ-~ (“to attach, fasten”). ~paginar~ itself is not an inherited word but was coined on the Latin stem to mean “to number the pages.” Cognate with French ~paginer~ and Italian ~paginare~; through the root, ~página~ is kin to English ~page~ and — via Latin ~pāx~ (“peace, a binding agreement”) — to English ~pact~ and Spanish ~paz~.

How a word for “fastening” came to mean “page” is debated. The usual account runs through the making of a book: separate sheets were fastened together, so a ~pāgina~ was a fixed-in leaf. Ayto and Watkins propose a more agricultural image, offered as an alternative rather than settled fact: a ~pāgina~ was first a trellis of vines fastened to stakes, whose orderly rows suggested the columns of writing on a scroll. Either way the root idea is “things fixed in ordered ranks.” From the same ~pangere~ Spanish holds ~compaginar~ (“to collate, make consistent”), and from the wider root *~peh₂ǵ-~ come ~pacto~ (“pact”) and ~paz~ (“peace”). To ~paginar~ a document is, at bottom, to fasten an order onto its pages.
en.palpar:
Spanish borrowed ~palpar~ (“to feel, to touch”) from Latin ~palpāre~ (“to stroke, to touch gently”). The verb’s deeper origin is disputed. An older tradition links it to Proto-Indo-European *~pel-~ (“to shake, to swing”) — which would make it cognate with Ancient Greek ~pállō~ (“I brandish, shake”) and with English ~feel~ (Old English ~fēlan~) — but de Vaan rejects that connection on phonetic grounds and calls ~palpāre~ of unknown origin, perhaps an onomatopoeic or reduplicated formation. Treat the *~pel-~ link as proposed, not proven.

Whatever its source, the Latin sense was the light, exploratory touch of a hand feeling its way, and Spanish keeps that squarely: to ~palpar~ is to examine by touch, as a doctor palpates an abdomen or one gropes ~a tientas~ in the dark. From the same Latin stem come the adjective ~palpable~ (“palpable, tangible”) and, through the sense of a fluttering beat, ~palpitar~ (“to throb”) and ~palpitación~. The English palpable and palpitate are the same words, borrowed independently from Latin rather than inherited.
en.paralizar:
Spanish took ~paralizar~ in the modern era from French ~paralyser~, formed on ~paralysie~, which goes back through Latin ~paralysis~ to Ancient Greek ~parálysis~ (“a loosening, disabling of the side of the body”). That noun is built from ~pará~ (“beside, aside”) and the verb ~lýein~ (“to loosen, untie, release”), from Proto-Indo-European *~lewH-~ (“to cut off, loosen, separate”). Through that root it is a distant cognate of English ~loose~, ~lose~, and the suffix ~-less~. Modern relatives include English ~paralyze~ and French ~paralyser~.

The Greek medical term described exactly what a stroke does — a “loosening” of the muscles down one side, leaving them slack and powerless. Latin borrowed it as ~paralysis~, and from it Vulgar Latin produced ~paralysia~, the source of the everyday Spanish noun ~perlesía~ (“palsy, trembling weakness”) — English ~palsy~ is the same word worn down through French. The learned form re-entered as ~parálisis~, giving the adjective ~paralítico~ and the verb ~paralizar~, whose meaning soon spread from bodies to things: traffic, negotiations, or a whole country can now be ~paralizado~. The ~lýein~ root also underlies the ~-lisis~ of ~análisis~, ~diálisis~, and ~catálisis~.
en.parar:
From Latin ~parāre~ (“to prepare, make ready”), from Proto-Italic *~parō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to grant, provide”). Cognate with Italian ~parare~, Portuguese ~parar~, and French ~parer~ (“to adorn, parry”); from the same Latin verb English drew ~prepare~ and ~apparatus~.

The Latin verb meant “to prepare, arrange,” and in Ibero-Romance it drifted from readying something toward halting and coming to rest — perhaps by way of “to set in position, hold in place.” The sources record the shift but do not fully explain it, so the intermediate step is best offered as a plausible bridge rather than a settled fact. That is why modern Spanish uses the verb for stopping a bus, warding off a blow, and ending up somewhere. The noun ~paro~ carries this to its conclusion — a work stoppage, unemployment, even a cardiac arrest — and ~parada~ names a bus stop or a military parade. From the same Latin verb Spanish also built ~preparar~, ~reparar~, ~amparar~ (“to shelter”), and the noun ~aparato~ (“apparatus, device”).
en.parecer:
From Old Spanish ~pareçer~, from Vulgar Latin *~parēscere~, an inchoative formed on Latin ~pārēre~ (“to appear, become visible, show oneself”). The inchoative suffix ~-ēscere~ marked a coming-into-view, which the ~-ecer~ ending of Spanish still carries. Cognate with Italian ~parere~, French ~paraître~, Portuguese ~parecer~, and Catalan ~parèixer~; through Latin ~appārēre~ English is kin by way of ~appear~ and ~apparent~.

Latin ~pārēre~ meant “to come into sight”; the inchoative *~parēscere~ stressed the moment of appearing, and from “to appear” Spanish ~parecer~ slid naturally into “to seem” — for what appears is not always what is. Reflexive ~parecerse~ took the further step to “to resemble,” and the noun use in ~el parecer~ means an “opinion,” literally how a thing appears to someone. The prefixed ~aparecer~ (“to appear”) and ~desaparecer~ (“to disappear”) stayed closer to the root sense, while ~comparecer~ (“to appear in court”) narrowed it to legal presence. From the same base come ~aparición~, ~apariencia~, ~parecido~, and ~aparente~.
en.parir:
From Latin ~parere~ (also ~parĕre~, “to give birth, to bring forth, to produce”), from Proto-Italic *~parjō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to bring forth, to grant, to allot”). The root shows up in Ancient Greek ~époron~ (“I gave, granted”), Sanskrit ~pṛṇā́ti~ (“grants, bestows”), and — through the Latin agent noun ~parēns~ — in English ~parent~. Sisters of ~parere~ are Italian ~parire~ and Portuguese ~parir~.

The Latin verb meant productive bringing-forth of every kind, but Spanish narrowed ~parir~ almost entirely to animal and human birth, giving it a blunt, earthy register beside the polite ~dar a luz~ (“to give to the light”). A vivid relative hides in ~víbora~ (“viper”): Latin ~vīpera~ was understood as ~vīvus~ + ~parere~, “the one that bears its young alive” — an ancient (if not strictly accurate) belief about the snake. Other kin include ~parto~ (“childbirth”), ~parturienta~, ~posparto~, and the -parous words ~vivíparo~ and ~ovíparo~. Note that ~parere~ (“give birth”) is a different verb from ~parāre~ (“prepare”), which fathered ~preparar~ and ~reparar~.
en.parlar:
From Old Spanish ~parlar~, borrowed from Gallo-Romance — Occitan and Catalan ~parlar~ and Old French ~parler~ — from Late Latin ~parabolāre~ (“to talk, speak”), a verb built on Latin ~parabola~ (“comparison, parable”), itself from Ancient Greek ~παραβολή~ (parabolḗ, “comparison”), from ~παρα-~ (para-, “beside”) plus ~βάλλω~ (bállō, “to throw”), from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷelH-~ (“to throw, reach”). Cognate with Italian ~parlare~, French ~parler~, and Portuguese ~parlar~.

The key twist is theological: in Christian Latin ~parabola~ (the Gospel parables, Jesus's comparisons) drifted from “comparison” to simply “word, speech,” crowding out ~verbum~. That shift is why Spanish ~palabra~, French ~parole~, and Italian ~parola~ all mean “word.” The derived verb ~parabolāre~ contracted to ~parlar~ / ~parler~, and Spanish borrowed the Gallo-Romance form with a tinge of idle talk — hence ~parlanchín~ (“chatterbox”) and ~parloteo~ (“prattle”). From the same ~parabola~ Spanish also keeps the learned ~parábola~ (both the story and the geometric curve), ~parlamento~ (a “speaking,” hence parliament), and the American ~parlante~ (“loudspeaker”).
en.participar:
From Latin ~participāre~ (“to share, to partake”), from the adjective ~particeps~ (“sharing, partaking”), a compound of ~pars~ (“part”) and ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”) — literally “taking a part.” ~capere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”). Cognate with French ~participer~, Italian ~partecipare~, and English ~participate~ and ~participle~.

The image behind the word is delightfully literal: to participate is to take your portion of something shared. Latin ~particeps~ was originally an everyday adjective for anyone who had a share in an affair. From ~pars~ Spanish drew a large family — ~parte~, ~partícipe~, ~participio~ (the grammatical “participle,” which likewise “shares” properties of verb and adjective), and ~partido~ (“party, match”). The other half, ~capere~, is even more prolific, giving ~caber~ (“to fit”), ~captar~, and even ~cazar~ (“to hunt,” i.e., to catch). To take part, in short, is to seize your slice.
en.partir:
Spanish ~partir~ descends from Latin ~partīre~ (also deponent ~partīrī~, “to divide, to share out”), a verb built on the noun ~pars~ (stem ~partis~, “a part, a share”). The deeper prehistory of ~pars~ is debated: it is usually linked with Latin ~pār~ (“equal”), ~portiō~ (“portion”) and ~parāre~ (“to make ready”), but the Proto-Indo-European root behind them is disputed and no single reconstruction is secure. Romance cognates are plentiful — French ~partir~, Italian ~partire~, Portuguese ~partir~ — and English ~part~ was borrowed from the same Latin stock.

~partir~ still means both “to split” and “to share,” but it also took on the sense “to depart” — to part from company, to set out (~partir de viaje~, “to leave on a trip”); French carried that branch all the way, so its ~partir~ means simply “to leave.” The noun ~pars~ underlies a broad Spanish family: ~parte~ (“part”), ~partido~ (“party; match”), ~partícula~ (“particle”), ~repartir~ (“to distribute”), ~compartir~ (“to share”) and the musical ~partitura~ (“score”).
en.pasar:
From Late Latin ~passāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~passus~ (“a step, a pace”), originally the past participle of ~pandere~ (“to spread out, to stretch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to spread”). Cognate with Italian ~passare~, French ~passer~, and Portuguese ~passar~; English ~pass~ entered through Old French rather than directly from Latin.

The image at the root is bodily: a ~passus~ was the stretch of the legs in a single stride, and by extension the Roman unit of distance measured by that stride. From “to take a step” the verb widened to “to move past, to cross, to go through,” and then to the whole sweep of senses Spanish now gives it — to happen (« ¿qué pasa? »), to spend time, to pass an exam, to hand something over. The same family seeded ~paso~ (“step”), ~pasaje~ (“passage, fare”), ~pasaporte~ (literally a warrant to ~pasar~ a port or gate), ~paseo~ (“a stroll”), and the ubiquitous ~pasado~ (“the past; passed”).
en.pasear:
A derivative of ~paso~ (“step, pace”) with the frequentative-flavored suffix ~-ear~, giving the sense of stepping about at leisure. ~paso~ comes from Latin ~passus~ (“a step, pace”), originally the past participle of ~pandere~ (“to spread, stretch out”) — a pace being the stretch opened between the feet. ~passus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~patstus~ and Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to spread”). Through French it gave English ~pace~ and ~pass~, and Italian has ~passeggiare~ (“to stroll”).

The suffix ~-ear~ often adds a sense of repeated, unhurried action, and that is exactly the difference between ~pasar~ (“to pass, go by”) and ~pasear~ (“to stroll, take a walk”) — not to cross a distance but to step along it for pleasure. Its noun is ~paseo~ (“a walk; a promenade”). From the same ~passus~ Spanish also has ~paso~, ~pasar~, ~pasaje~, ~pasillo~ (“corridor”) and ~compás~ (“a pair of compasses; a beat”), while ~pandere~ itself surfaces in ~expandir~ (“to expand”).
en.pecar:
From Old Spanish ~pecar~, from Latin ~peccāre~ (“to make a mistake, to sin”). Its deeper origin is proposed but not certain: many trace it to Proto-Italic *~petkāō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ped-~ (“to step, stumble, fall”) — the same root as ~pēs~, ~pedis~ (“foot”) — so that sinning was pictured as a misstep. Cognate with Italian ~peccare~, Portuguese ~pecar~, and Catalan ~pecar~; French ~pécher~ (“to sin”) is the parallel form, not to be confused with ~pêcher~ (“to fish”).

If the *~ped-~ etymology holds, the metaphor is a stumble off the right path — a picture Latin shared with several languages — though careful sources flag the connection as merely likely. In Latin, ~peccāre~ meant broadly “to err,” and Christian usage sharpened it toward moral “sin,” the sense Spanish inherited. The past participle noun ~peccātum~ gave Spanish ~pecado~ (“sin”), alongside ~pecador~ (“sinner”) and the adjective ~pecaminoso~ (“sinful”). The learned negative ~impecable~ (“impeccable”) is literally “incapable of erring or sinning.”
en.pechar:
In the sense given here — “to shove, to barge with the chest” — from ~pecho~ (“chest, breast”) plus ~-ar~, ~pecho~ descending from Latin ~pectus~ (“chest, breast”), a word of uncertain Indo-European origin (several roots have been proposed, none confirmed). Cognate through ~pectus~ with Italian ~petto~, Portuguese ~peito~, and Catalan ~pit~. The literal idea is to charge into someone breast-first; in the River Plate it slid into slang ~pechar~ (“to hit someone up for money, to cadge”).

Here lies a neat homonym trap. Spanish also had an archaic ~pechar~ meaning “to pay tribute or tax,” but that one comes from a different ~pecho~ (“tribute, tax”), which descends not from ~pectus~ but from Latin ~pactum~ (“agreement”), via Medieval Latin ~pactāre~ (“to settle, agree”). So two unrelated Latin words, ~pectus~ and ~pactum~, both surfaced in Spanish as ~pecho~, each spawning a verb ~pechar~. From the body-part branch Spanish also keeps ~pechuga~ (“breast of fowl”) and ~apechugar~ (“to put up with,” literally to take it on the chest).
en.pedir:
From Latin ~petere~ (“to make for, to seek, to ask, to aim at, even to attack”), from Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to fly, to rush”). The root’s flight-sense shows plainly in its cognates: Greek ~pétomai~ (“I fly”) and ~píptō~ (“I fall”), Sanskrit ~pátati~ (“flies, falls”), and — through Germanic — English ~feather~, literally “the flying thing.” In Romance, Portuguese ~pedir~ is the direct sibling; Italian and French chose other verbs for “to ask.”

The semantic heart is motion toward a target: ~petere~ first meant to rush at or make for something, which is why the one verb could mean both “to attack” and “to request” — to ask is to launch yourself at what you want. Spanish wore the sound down to the humble ~pedir~, but the vigorous original survives in a crowd of learned relatives: ~petición~ (“petition, request”), ~competir~ (“to compete,” to seek alongside), ~apetito~ (“appetite,” a seeking-toward), ~ímpetu~ (“impetus, a rushing upon”), ~repetir~ (“to seek again”), and ~perpetuo~ (“continually rushing onward”). English shares the set through ~petition~, ~compete~, ~appetite~, and ~impetus~.
en.pegar:
From Latin ~picāre~ (“to coat with pitch”), from ~pix~, genitive ~picis~ (“pitch, tar”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pik-~. A genuine cognate is Greek ~πίσσα~ (~píssa~, “pitch”); English ~pitch~ comes from the very same Latin ~pix~, borrowed into Old English. Romance kept the verb as Portuguese ~pegar~ (“to stick; to catch”) and Italian ~appiccare~.

The first meaning was concrete: pitch is glue, so ~picāre~ meant to join, stick, or fasten one thing to another — and ~pegar~ still means “to glue, to stick.” The sense “to hit,” the everyday modern one, came later; by Corominas's account it grew out of “to press close up against” → “to set upon” → “to land blows,” and the blow-dealing ~pegar~ is well attested by the age of the Quixote. The adhesive root lives on in ~pegamento~ (“glue”), ~pegajoso~ (“sticky”), ~pez~ (“pitch” itself), and — best of all — ~despegar~, “to unstick,” which is also the Spanish word for an airplane's takeoff.
en.pelar:
From Latin ~pilāre~ (“to deprive of hair”), a verb derived from ~pilus~ (“a hair”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pil-~ (“hair”). Cognate with Italian ~pelare~, French ~peler~, and Portuguese ~pelar~, and — through ~pilus~ — with English ~pile~ (the soft nap of a fabric or carpet).

The original job was to strip hair or feathers; from there Spanish ~pelar~ generalized to “to peel” skin and fruit, and figuratively to fleece someone of their money (~pelar a alguien~). The idiom ~duro de pelar~ (“hard to peel”) is Spanish for a tough nut to crack. From the same ~pilus~ Spanish keeps a hairy family: ~pelo~ (“hair”), ~peluca~ (“wig”), ~peluquero~ (“hairdresser, barber”), and the learned ~depilar~ (“to depilate”). English preserves the root more faintly — a fabric's ~pile~ and a ~depilatory~ cream both go back to ~pilus~ — which is why the humble hair sits, etymologically, behind both a peeled orange and a plush carpet.
en.pelear:
A Spanish derivative of ~pelo~ (“hair”) plus the verbal suffix ~-ear~. ~pelo~ descends from Latin ~pilus~ (“a hair”), of disputed deeper origin but often linked to a Proto-Indo-European base *~pilo-~ (“hair”). Cognate through ~pilus~ with Italian ~pelo~ and French ~poil~, and with the borrowed English ~pile~ (the raised nap of a fabric) and ~plush~.

This is the famous etymology where fighting begins with hair: the traditional account, given in the standard dictionaries, derives ~pelear~ from ~pelo~ on the image of two combatants grabbing and pulling each other's hair — literally “to come to hairs.” From that vivid picture the verb generalized to fighting and quarreling of every kind, physical or verbal, and reflexive ~pelearse~ covers falling out with a friend. The same ~pelo~ gave Spanish ~peludo~ (“hairy”), ~pelaje~ (“coat, fur”), ~peluca~ (“wig”), ~pelusa~, and ~peluquero~ (“barber, hairdresser”).
en.peligrar:
From ~peligro~ (“danger”) plus ~-ar~. ~peligro~ comes, as a semi-learned word, from Old Spanish ~periglo~, from Latin ~perīculum~ (“a trial, attempt; hence danger”), built on the same root as ~experīrī~ (“to try”) and ~perītus~ (“experienced”), from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to go through, attempt, risk”). Cognate through ~perīculum~ with Italian ~pericolo~, French ~péril~, and English ~peril~.

The Latin idea is that a trial or attempt is inherently risky, so ~perīculum~ slid from “test” to “danger,” and the verb ~peligrar~ means “to be at risk.” The path from ~periglo~ to ~peligro~ shows a classic Spanish swap of the two liquids, r and l trading places (dissimilation). From the same root Spanish keeps ~peligroso~ (“dangerous”), and the learned ~experto~ (“expert”) and ~pericia~ (“skill, expertise”), while English adds ~experience~ and ~experiment~ — so the words for danger and for hard-won expertise both grow from one root meaning to venture something and see what happens.
en.penar:
From ~pena~ (“penalty; sorrow”) plus ~-ar~. ~pena~ descends from Latin ~poena~ (“penalty, punishment”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~ποινή~ (poinḗ, “blood-money, penalty”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kʷey-~ (“to pay, atone”). Cognate with Italian ~pena~, French ~peine~, and — through Old French — English ~pain~; the same root yields English ~penal~ and even ~pine~ (“to waste away”).

The Greek ~ποινή~ was the compensation paid for a killing, a fine to make amends; Latin ~poena~ widened it to “punishment,” then to “torment, suffering,” and Spanish ~penar~ keeps both threads — transitive “to punish, impose a penalty” and intransitive “to suffer, to be in torment” (as one might ~penar~ for love). The noun ~pena~ meanwhile softened toward “sorrow, pity,” as in the exclamation of regret. From the same source Spanish keeps ~penal~ (“penal; prison”), ~penoso~ (“arduous, distressing”), ~penalidad~ (“hardship”), and the borrowed ~penalti~ (the soccer penalty), while English ~pain~ preserves the old punitive edge in the phrase “on pain of death.”
en.penetrar:
From Latin ~penetrāre~ (“to enter, pierce, penetrate”), a verb connected to ~penitus~ (“deep within, inmost”) and to ~penus~ (“the innermost store of a household, provisions”). De Vaan reconstructs an extended stem *~pen-et-~ underlying ~penes~, ~penitus~, and ~penetrō~, and links the family, more tentatively, to Proto-Indo-European *~penos~ (“food, provisions”), also seen in Lithuanian ~penėti~ (“to feed”). Cognate with Italian ~penetrare~ and French ~pénétrer~, and — as a learned borrowing — English ~penetrate~.

The intriguing thread is the link to food and home. ~penus~ named the innermost storeroom, and the ~Penātēs~, Rome's household gods, watched over that pantry at the heart of the house. By one account (Stüber's), the sense developed from “what one feeds with” (food) to “the place where one feeds” (the inner home) to “innermost” — so that to ~penetrar~ is, etymologically, to reach the deepest, most guarded interior. That derivation is a proposal, not settled fact, and the Indo-European food-connection is offered only tentatively in the sources. In modern Spanish the root lives on in ~penetración~, ~penetrante~, ~impenetrable~, and the mythological ~penates~.
en.pensar:
From Old Spanish ~pensar~, from Latin ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh, ponder”), the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to hang”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull, stretch”). Cognate with Italian ~pensare~, French ~penser~, and Portuguese ~pensar~, and — through the same stem — with English ~pensive~, ~ponder~, and ~pension~; Spanish keeps a doublet in ~pesar~ (“to weigh; to grieve”).

The heart of this word is a metaphor so old it feels literal: to think is to weigh one thing against another. Latin ~pēnsāre~ meant to weigh out repeatedly, hence to ponder, to balance one option against the next — and Spanish ~pensar~ still does exactly that. The same ~pēnsāre~ took a different turn in French ~panser~ (“to dress a wound, tend a horse”), from the sense “to attend to,” a nice reminder of how far one root can wander. From it Spanish drew ~pensamiento~ (“thought”), ~pensador~ (“thinker”), ~pensativo~ (“pensive”), and ~pensión~ (“pension”), while the popular doublet ~pesar~ gave the noun ~peso~ (“weight; the currency”).
en.percibir:
From Latin ~percipere~ (“to seize, take in, perceive”), a compound of ~per-~ (“thoroughly”) and ~capere~ (“to take, grasp”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”). It is cognate with Italian ~percepire~, French ~percevoir~ and Portuguese ~perceber~, and — through the same ~capere~ — with English ~capture~ and ~capable~.

Latin ~percipere~ meant literally “to take hold of thoroughly,” and that physical grasping was extended to the mind: to seize something with the senses or the intellect is to perceive it. Spanish kept both threads — one perceives a sound and also perceives (collects) a salary, ~percibir~ un sueldo. The same root *~keh₂p-~ seeded a large family in Spanish, among them ~recibir~, ~concebir~, ~capaz~, ~captar~ and ~caber~.
en.perder:
From Latin ~perdere~ (“to lose, to ruin, to squander”), a compound of the prefix ~per-~ (here “thoroughly, to destruction”) and an element ~-dere~. That second element is traditionally identified with ~dare~ (“to give,” from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~), which would make ~perdere~ a “giving away through and through”; but many etymologists now trace the ~-dere~ of such compounds instead to PIE *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to place”), and the point remains debated. Either way the Romance descent is uniform: Italian ~perdere~, French ~perdre~, Portuguese ~perder~, and Romanian ~pierde~.

Whatever the deep root, the Latin sense was strong — not mild misplacement but thorough undoing: ~perdere~ could mean to destroy, to bring to ruin, as well as to lose. Spanish softened it to everyday “losing,” yet the darker charge survives in ~perdición~ (“perdition, ruin”) and in phrases like ~echar a perder~ (“to spoil, to wreck”). If the older ~dare~ analysis is right, to lose is to “give something away completely,” an oddly generous image for misfortune; if the *~dʰeh₁-~ analysis is right, it is rather to “put something clean out of reach.” From the verb Spanish keeps ~pérdida~ (“loss”), ~perdido~ (“lost”), and ~perdición~.
en.perdonar:
Spanish ~perdonar~ (“to forgive, pardon”) comes from Late Latin ~perdōnāre~, a compound of the intensive prefix ~per-~ (“thoroughly, completely”) and ~dōnāre~ (“to give, grant”), from ~dōnum~ (“gift”), from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Its Romance line is broad: Italian ~perdonare~, French ~pardonner~ and Portuguese ~perdoar~; English ~pardon~ was borrowed from the Old French form.

Forgiveness is imagined here as a kind of giving — to ~perdōnāre~ a debt is to “give it away completely,” to release the claim. Strikingly, the Germanic words are built the very same way: English ~forgive~ and German ~vergeben~ pair a “for-/ver-” intensive with “give,” exactly mirroring ~per-~ + ~dōnāre~. Which side copied which is debated — the Latin compound may be calqued on Germanic *~fragebaną~, or the reverse — so the parallel is best presented as an open question rather than a settled loan. From the same *~deh₃-~ Spanish keeps ~dar~ (“to give”), ~donar~ (“to donate”), ~don~ (“gift”) and ~dádiva~ (“gift, present”).
en.perecer:
From Old Spanish ~perir~, later reshaped with the inchoative suffix ~-ecer~ into ~perecer~, from Latin ~perīre~ (“to perish, pass away”), a compound of ~per-~ (here intensive, “to destruction”) plus ~īre~ (“to go”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”). Cognate with French ~périr~, Italian ~perire~, Portuguese ~perecer~, and — through Old French — English ~perish~.

Literally ~perīre~ is “to go all the way through, to pass away,” with ~per-~ carrying the same destructive force it has in ~perdere~ (“to destroy”). Old Spanish kept the plain ~perir~, but Castilian preferred to recast such verbs with ~-ecer~ (as in nacer, crecer), giving ~perecer~. The buried root ~īre~ (“to go”) is among the oldest Indo-European verbs and lies behind Spanish ~ir~ itself. From that same root Spanish draws the learned ~tránsito~ (“transit”) and ~éxito~ (literally an “exit,” which came to mean “success”); ~perecer~ leaves the everyday adjective ~perecedero~ (“perishable”), stamped on foods with a short shelf life.
en.perjudicar:
From Latin ~praeiūdicāre~ (“to prejudge, to decide beforehand — often to someone’s detriment”), from ~prae-~ (“before”) plus ~iūdicāre~ (“to judge”), a verb from ~iūdex~ (“judge”), which compounds ~iūs~ (“law, right”) with the root of ~dīcere~ (“to say, declare”), from Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, point out”). Cognates: French ~préjudicier~, English ~prejudice~ and ~prejudicial~; through ~iūdicāre~, English ~judge~ and ~judicial~.

The word literally means “to prejudge”: a ~praeiūdicium~ was a prior ruling or precedent, and a judgment fixed in advance readily became one that worked against a party — whence Spanish “to harm, to damage.” Tellingly, ~perjuicio~ (“damage, detriment”) and ~prejuicio~ (“prejudice, preconception”) are doublets, both from ~praeiūdicium~ but split in sense. The family includes ~juez~, ~juzgar~, ~juicio~, ~judicial~ and ~jurídico~; and from ~dīcere~ come ~decir~, ~dictar~ and ~dicho~.
en.perjurar:
From Latin ~periūrāre~ (“to swear falsely, to break an oath”), a compound of ~per-~ (here “to ill effect”) plus ~iūrāre~ (“to swear”), a verb formed from the noun ~iūs~, ~iūris~ (“law, right, that which is binding”), from Proto-Italic *~jowos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂yew-~ (“right, law; vital force”). Cognate with French ~parjurer~, Portuguese ~perjurar~, and — through Old French — English ~perjure~.

Spanish ~perjurar~ carries two senses that its ~per-~ neatly splits: the formal “to perjure oneself, to swear falsely,” and a colloquial intensive “to swear up and down,” as in the pairing ~juró y perjuró~ (“he swore and swore again”). The root noun ~iūs~ seeded a vast legal family in Spanish — ~jurar~ (“to swear”), ~jurado~ (“jury”), ~juez~ (“judge”), and ~injuria~ (“insult, injury”) — while English draws ~jury~, ~justice~, and ~injury~ from the very same ~iūs~. So a courtroom's oath, its jurors, and its judge all trace back to one Latin word for what is binding and right.
en.permanecer:
From Latin ~permanēre~ (“to remain, to hold out to the end”), from ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) + ~manēre~ (“to stay, to remain”); Spanish reshaped it with the inchoative suffix ~-ecer~. ~manēre~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to stay, to remain, to abide”). Cognate with Italian ~permanere~ and Portuguese ~permanecer~, and — through ~manēre~ — with English ~permanent~, ~remain~ (from Latin ~remanēre~), and ~mansion~; French ~permanent~ shares the same source.

The prefix ~per-~ adds thoroughness — to remain not just briefly but all the way through — so ~permanecer~ is a more emphatic “to stay” than plain quedarse. The bare root ~manēre~ meant simply “to stay,” and its participle ~mansiō~ (“a staying, a lodging, a stopping-place on a journey”) traveled far: it became French ~maison~ (“house”) and English ~mansion~. Spanish drew a rich crop from the same root: ~permanente~ (“permanent”), ~mansión~ (“mansion”), ~remanente~ (“remainder”), ~inmanente~ (“immanent”), and even ~menaje~ (“household goods”), which reached Spanish through Old French ~ménage~ from Vulgar Latin *~mansionaticum~ — the belongings of a household.
en.permitir:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~permittere~ (“to let through, give up, allow”), from ~per-~ (“through”) plus ~mittere~ (“to send, let go, release”); ~mittere~ is of uncertain further origin, with no secure Proto-Indo-European etymology. Cognate with Italian ~permettere~, French ~permettre~, and Portuguese ~permitir~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~permit~. The base ~mittere~ underlies a huge Romance and English family.

In Latin ~mittere~ first meant “to send,” and ~permittere~ literally “to send through” — to let something pass — from which grew the idea of granting passage, yielding, and finally “allowing.” Because Spanish took ~permitir~ from written Latin rather than through gradual sound-change, it kept the Latin shape almost intact, unlike its inherited cousin ~meter~ (“to put in”), which descends from the very same ~mittere~ by the popular route. That double inheritance — learned and popular — makes ~mittere~ one of the most productive Latin verbs in Spanish: ~permiso~, ~mensaje~ and ~mensajero~ (from ~missus~), ~misión~, ~remitir~, ~admitir~, ~cometer~, ~prometer~, ~someter~, and ~transmitir~ all spring from it.
en.perseguir:
Spanish ~perseguir~ comes from Latin ~persequī~ (“to follow persistently, to pursue, to prosecute”), from the intensive prefix ~per-~ (“thoroughly”) and ~sequī~ (“to follow”). ~Sequī~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), a root richly represented across the family — Greek ~hépomai~, Latin ~secundus~, and, through Latin, English ~sequence~, ~pursue~ and ~prosecute~. Its Romance reflexes include Italian ~perseguire~ and Portuguese ~perseguir~.

The Latin verb already gathered the meanings Spanish keeps: ~perseguir~ is at once to chase, to hound, and to persecute, with the noun ~persecución~ close behind. From the plain ~sequī~ Spanish inherited ~seguir~ and its many prefixed forms — ~conseguir~, ~proseguir~, ~perseguir~ — plus ~secuencia~ and ~consecuente~. The same root hides in unexpected places: ~segundo~, the “following” number, in ~séquito~, the retinue that follows a lord, and in ~ejecutar~, from Latin ~exsequī~, literally “to follow out” to the end.
en.perseverar:
From Latin ~perseverāre~ (“to persist, hold firm”), from ~persevērus~ (“very strict, earnest”), itself the intensive prefix ~per-~ (“thoroughly”) joined to ~sevērus~ (“stern, severe, grave”). Cognate with Italian ~perseverare~, French ~persévérer~, and Portuguese ~perseverar~; English ~persevere~ was borrowed through Old French, and through the shared adjective English ~severe~ belongs to the same family.

The underlying picture is moral: to keep at something with unbending seriousness, to stay ~sevērus~ toward one's own purpose. The deeper Indo-European root of ~sevērus~ is uncertain, so its earliest sense is best left open rather than guessed. In modern Spanish the root lives on in ~perseverancia~ (“perseverance”) and, through the base adjective, in ~severo~ (“severe”) and ~severidad~ (“severity, strictness”).
en.personalizar:
A modern verb built with ~-izar~ on ~personal~, from ~persona~, from Latin ~persōna~ (“actor's mask; character; person”). Latin most likely borrowed it from Etruscan ~phersu~ (“mask”); the old textbook derivation from ~per-~ plus ~sonāre~ (“to sound through” the mask) is a folk etymology, not the true source. Cognate with French ~personne~, Italian ~persona~ and English ~person~ and ~parson~.

Even the Etruscan trail is not fully lit: ~phersu~ is often connected to Greek ~prósōpon~ (“face, mask”), but that link is disputed and phonetically awkward, so it is best left as proposed rather than proven. What is clear is the arc of meaning — from the mask an actor wore, to the dramatic role, to the human being behind it. Spanish grew from it ~persona~, ~personaje~ (“character”), ~personal~, ~personalidad~ and, recently, ~personalizar~ (“to personalize”): to fit a thing to one particular person, one specific mask.
en.pertenecer:
From Latin ~pertinēre~ (“to reach to, concern, belong”), reshaped in Hispano-Romance with the inchoative suffix ~-ecer~ (from Latin ~-ēscere~), probably through a Vulgar Latin *~pertinēscere~. ~pertinēre~ is ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) plus ~tenēre~ (“to hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate with Portuguese ~pertencer~; and, through ~tenēre~, with French ~appartenir~ and English ~pertinent~.

The image behind ~pertinēre~ is of a holding that “reaches all the way through” to something — hence “to concern” and then “to belong.” Latin favored the plain verb; Spanish and Portuguese preferred the inchoative dress in ~-ecer~, the same suffix that turns nouns and adjectives into “becoming” verbs (compare ~florecer~ and ~envejecer~). From ~tenēre~ Spanish inherited a large clan: ~tener~ itself, ~contener~, ~retener~, ~mantener~, ~sostener~ and the adjective ~pertinente~, all sharing the root idea of holding and, further back, of stretching taut.
en.pesar:
From Latin ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh carefully”), the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to hang, to weigh, to pay”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)pen-~ (“to draw, stretch, spin”). Cognate with French ~peser~, Italian ~pesare~, and Portuguese ~pesar~, and — through the same root — with English ~pension~ and ~pendant~, both of which recall the old link between weighing and paying.

Roman merchants weighed coins to check their value, and ~pēnsāre~ carried that sense of careful assessment. Spanish inherited the verb twice: the popular line gave ~pesar~ (“to weigh”), while a more learned development gave ~pensar~ (“to think”) — literally, to weigh ideas in the mind. The two are doublets, one physical and one mental. ~pesar~ also came to name sorrow (~a pesar de~, “in spite of”; the noun ~pesar~, “grief”), as though sadness were a weight pressing down. The same family yielded ~peso~ (“weight,” and the currency), ~pesado~ (“heavy”), ~compensar~, and ~dispensar~.
en.picar:
~picar~ has no tidy Latin pedigree: it is generally traced to a Vulgar Latin *~piccare~ of expressive, onomatopoeic origin — a root *~pikk-~ imitating the sharp little tap of a beak or point striking a surface. Rather than descending from a single classical etymon, it surfaces across Romance almost in parallel: Italian ~piccare~, French ~piquer~, Portuguese and Catalan ~picar~. The related noun ~pico~ (“beak, point, peak”) belongs to the same expressive family. Through French ~piquer~, English gained ~pique~; the words ~pike~ and ~peck~ are often linked to the same sound-symbolic cluster, though that connection is not certain.

From the base sense “to strike with something pointed,” ~picar~ fanned out into one of Spanish's most versatile verbs: a bee or nettle ~pica~ (“stings”), a bird ~pica~ (“pecks”), one ~pica~ carne (“minces meat”) or ~pica~ a stone, and chili ~pica~ on the tongue — whence ~picante~ (“spicy, hot”). Figuratively it is to needle or to entice: curiosity ~se pica~. The expressive root seeded a crowded family — ~pico~, ~picadura~ (“sting, bite”), ~picador~ (the lancer in the bullring), ~picadillo~ (“mince”), ~picazón~ (“itch”) and the noun ~pique~ (“pique, resentment”). Even the roguish ~pícaro~ is very probably from ~picar~, though Corominas flags that link as uncertain.
en.pillar:
Spanish ~pillar~, in its colloquial sense “to catch, nab” and its older sense “to plunder,” was taken from Italian ~pigliare~ (“to take, seize”), a verb of disputed origin. The favored account, following Corominas, derives it from a Vulgar Latin *~piliāre~ linked to ~compilāre~ (“to plunder, snatch up”); by this hypothesis ~pillar~ would be a distant cousin of the learned ~compilar~ (“to compile”). Rival explanations exist and should not be laundered into fact: one traces ~pigliare~ to ~pilum~ (“javelin”), another to a Late Latin *~pileāre~ from ~pīleus~, the freedman's cap, as if “to set free.” Cognate with French ~piller~ and Catalan ~pillar~; English ~pillage~ was borrowed from the French.

Whatever its root, the word carried a martial charge — the ~pillaje~ (“pillage”) of a sacked town — before Spanish softened it into everyday “to grab, to catch,” as in catching a cold or a bus. The same stem gives ~pillo~ (“rascal”) and ~pillería~. Because the ultimate etymon is unsettled, the tidy line that ~pillar~ and ~compilar~ are kin remains, honestly, only the leading guess rather than a proven fact.
en.pintar:
From Vulgar Latin *~pinctāre~, a verb built on ~pictus~, the past participle of Latin ~pingere~ (“to paint, to embroider, to tattoo”). ~pingere~ shows a nasal-infix present of Proto-Indo-European *~peyḱ-~ (“to mark, to color, to paint”), whence Ancient Greek ~poikílos~ (“many-colored, dappled”), Proto-Germanic *~faihaz~ (“spotted”), and Sanskrit ~piṅkté~ (“paints, tinges”). Romance kept the nasal ~n~ of the present stem: beside Spanish ~pintar~ stands Portuguese ~pintar~, while French ~peindre~ and Italian ~dipingere~ come more directly from ~pingere~.

Latin ~pingere~ meant marking a surface with color of any kind — painting a wall, embroidering cloth, even tattooing skin. Spanish ~pintar~ generalized to “to paint” and, figuratively, to how things “look” (~tener buena pinta~, to have a good appearance). From the participle ~pictus~ and its Vulgar-Latin reflexes come ~pintura~, ~pintor~, ~pinta~, and ~pinto~ (“spotted,” a horse-coat term English borrowed straight from Spanish). The learned branch kept the original ~c~: ~pigmento~ (from ~pigmentum~) and ~pictórico~, plus English “picture” and “pigment.” One root, two textures — the earthy ~pintar~ and the bookish ~pigmento~.
en.pisar:
From Vulgar Latin *~pinsāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~pinsere~ (also ~pīnsāre~, “to pound, crush, grind”), from Proto-Indo-European *~peis-~ (“to crush, pound”). Cognate with Italian ~pigiare~ and ~pestare~, and — through the same root — with English ~pestle~ and ~piston~. In Latin the verb named the pounding of grain into meal.

From “pound, crush” the sense broadened to treading and trampling, and so to today's “to step on, tread.” From the Latin participle ~pistus~ came Italian ~pista~ (“trail, track”), which Spanish borrowed back as ~pista~ — literally the path beaten flat by trampling feet. The same family includes ~pisón~ and ~apisonar~ (“rammer; to tamp down”), ~pisada~ (“footstep”), ~piso~ (“floor, flat”), and ~pisotear~ (“to stamp on”). By one much-debated proposal, even Italian ~pizza~ traces to this crushing-and-pressing root — but the true origin of ~pizza~ is genuinely contested, with rival Greek and Germanic accounts, so the tie is best left as a hypothesis rather than a fact.
en.placer:
From Latin ~placēre~ (“to please, to be agreeable”), related to ~plācāre~ (“to appease, placate”) and ~placidus~ (“calm, gentle”). The deeper root is debated: the traditional link to Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₂k-~ (“flat, calm”) has been questioned, and Michiel de Vaan instead proposes a root *~pleHk-~ tied to pleasing or assent, with Tocharian B ~plāk-~ (“to please”) as its closest relative. Whatever the source, the verb thrived in Romance: Italian ~piacere~, French ~plaire~, Portuguese ~prazer~, and Romanian ~plăcea~.

In Spanish ~placer~ survives both as the verb “to please” and as the noun ~placer~ (“pleasure”). Its most striking relic is a strong preterite: alongside the regular ~plació~, older and literary Spanish said ~plugo~ and ~pluguieron~ (“it/they pleased”), from Latin ~placuit~, forms that still surface in fixed phrases like ~pluguiera a Dios~ (“would to God”). The root seeded a rich family: ~plácido~, ~placentero~, ~complacer~, ~aplacar~ (from ~plācāre~), and even ~placebo~, Latin for “I shall please,” once the opening word of a sung office of vespers and later medicine's name for a pleasing but inert remedy.
en.planear:
From ~plano~ (“flat surface; plan”), from Latin ~plānus~ (“flat, level”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₂-~ (“flat”). Cognate with Italian ~piano~, French ~plan~, and Portuguese ~plano~, and — through the same root — with English ~plain~, ~plane~, and ~floor~.

The verb was built on the noun: to ~planear~ is to lay out a project the way a draftsman lays lines on a flat sheet — a ~plano~ (“map, blueprint”). Spanish also uses ~planear~ for the gliding of a bird or an aircraft that rides the air without beating its wings, a sense shaped by French ~planer~; the image is the same flat plane, now traced through the sky. From the same root *~pleh₂-~ Spanish drew ~llano~ (“plain, level”), ~llanura~, ~explanar~, ~plana~, and ~planicie~, while the learned doublet ~plano~ kept the Latin ~pl-~ that popular ~llano~ softened to ~ll-~.
en.planificar:
A late, learned borrowing from French ~planifier~ (“to plan”), formed from ~plan~ plus the suffix ~-ifier~ (“to make”). French ~plan~ descends from Latin ~plānum~ (“flat surface, level ground”), the neuter of ~plānus~ (“flat, level”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₂-~ (“flat, to spread”). Cognate with English ~plan~ and ~plain~, and — through the same root — with Spanish ~llano~ and ~plaza~.

Latin ~plānus~ described flat ground; a ~plānum~ was a level surface, and from “a drawing on a flat surface” French ~plan~ came to mean a scheme or design. ~planificar~ entered Spanish only in the twentieth century, riding the vogue for economic ~planificación~ (“central planning”), and it still carries a systematic, large-scale flavor that plain ~planear~ lacks. From the same root *~pleh₂-~ Spanish drew ~plano~, ~llano~ (its inherited, sound-changed twin), ~llanura~, ~plancha~, and ~plaza~ (from ~platea~, a broad flat space).
en.plantar:
From Latin ~plantāre~ (“to plant”), from ~planta~, which in Latin meant “the sole of the foot” (and also a shoot or cutting), perhaps from a nasalized form of a Proto-Indo-European root *~plat-~ (“to spread, be flat”), though the deeper connection is uncertain. The verb passed intact into the Romance languages: Italian ~piantare~, French ~planter~, Portuguese ~plantar~; English ~plant~ is itself an early borrowing of Latin ~planta~.

The tie between “sole of the foot” and “plant” is the entry's curiosity. By one proposed account, ~plantāre~ first meant to press a cutting into the soil with the sole of the foot — but the botanical ~planta~ may instead be a separate word, and the sources hedge, so the foot-story is best offered as a plausible guess rather than fact. Either way Spanish reaped a rich harvest from ~planta~: ~plantación~, ~plantilla~ (“insole,” and by extension a “roster” or “template”), ~implantar~, ~trasplantar~ and ~plantear~ (“to pose a question,” as if setting it in the ground).
en.plantear:
From ~planta~ (“sole of the foot; plant; ground plan”), from Latin ~planta~, itself of disputed deeper origin: one account traces it to Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₂-~ (“flat”), another to *~pleh₂k-~ (“to strike”); the sources do not settle the question. ~Plantear~ is built on ~plantar~ (“to plant, to set firmly”), from Latin ~plantāre~. Cognates of ~planta~ include Italian ~pianta~, French ~plante~ and English ~plant~, all Latin borrowings or inheritances.

The chain of sense is vivid but the endpoint is figurative: from the ~planta~ (“sole”) one gets ~plantar~ (“to set on the ground, to plant”), then ~plantear~ for laying out the ground plan of a building — and finally the modern abstract sense, “to set out, to pose” a problem, a question, a hypothesis. When you ~planteas~ a doubt, you are, etymologically, staking it out on the ground like a foundation. Kin words include ~planta~, ~plantar~, ~plantación~, ~plantilla~, ~implantar~ and ~trasplantar~. (The very deep origin of ~planta~ remains, as noted, unsettled.)
en.plasmar:
From Latin ~plasmāre~ (“to mold, to shape”), a borrowing of Ancient Greek ~πλάσσειν~ (~plássein~, “to mold, to form”), related to ~πλάσμα~ (~plásma~, “something molded”). The Greek verb is generally traced to Proto-Indo-European *~pleth₂-~ (“to spread out, to flatten”), the idea being of spreading and pressing soft matter into shape. Cognate with Italian ~plasmare~ and, as a learned borrowing, with English ~plasma~ and the suffix ~-plasm~ in ~protoplasm~.

~plasmar~ entered Spanish as a learned word and kept the sculptor's sense — to give material form to something — before broadening to the modern figurative “to embody, to capture, to set down,” as when an artist ~plasma~ an idea on canvas. The Greek stem is unusually productive in modern scientific vocabulary: from it Spanish has ~plasma~ (blood plasma, and the physicist's ionized gas), ~plástico~, ~plasticidad~, ~emplasto~ (“a poultice”) and ~protoplasma~. The blood sense was coined only in the 19th century, when a physiologist saw the fluid as the “mold” in which blood cells take shape.
en.plegar:
From Latin ~plicāre~ (“to fold, bend”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to fold”), an extension of *~pel-~ (“to fold, wrap”). Italian ~piegare~, French ~plier~, and Portuguese ~pregar~ (in the sense “to fold”) descend from the same verb; through the same root English has ~ply~, ~pleat~, and ~plait~.

The Latin verb was extraordinarily productive: in Spanish, alongside the direct ~plegar~, its prefixed compounds gave ~aplicar~, ~explicar~, ~implicar~, ~replicar~, and ~complicar~, all built on the idea of things folded together or apart. The noun ~pliegue~ (“fold, crease”) and the reflexive ~plegarse~ (“to yield, give in”) show the metaphor still at work — to fold is to bend, and to bend is to submit. A learned doublet, ~plicar~, never took hold, but the folk form ~llegar~ (“to arrive”) is widely traced to the same ~plicāre~, by way of furling sails on reaching port.
en.poblar:
From Latin ~populāre~ (“to people, to fill with inhabitants”), a verb built on ~populus~ (“people, populace”), whose own origin is uncertain: it goes back to Proto-Italic *~poplos~, apparently meaning “army,” which has been derived either from Etruscan or from the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”) — neither certain. Spanish ~poblar~ answers to Italian ~popolare~, Portuguese ~povoar~ and French ~peupler~; from ~populus~ English draws ~people~ and ~popular~.

With the regular Spanish diphthong the stressed ó became ue, so ~populus~ surfaces in the noun ~pueblo~ (“town; a people”) and the verb ~poblar~ (“to settle, populate”). Tellingly, the same Latin ~populāre~ also meant “to ravage, lay waste” — what an army does to a countryside — a sense preserved in ~despoblar~ (“to depopulate, empty out”), so that peopling and unpeopling spring from one word. The family fills a page: ~población~, ~popular~, ~público~, ~pueblerino~ and, in English, ~people~ itself, arriving through Old French ~peuple~.
en.podar:
From Latin ~putāre~ (“to clean, to prune,” and also “to reckon, to think”), from the adjective ~putus~ (“clean, pure”). The Proto-Indo-European source is uncertain; the original sense was probably something like “to cut off,” but the sources flag the root as unsettled, so it is safer not to fix it. Italian ~potare~ and Portuguese ~podar~ share the inheritance.

Remarkably, ~podar~ and a crowd of abstract Spanish verbs are the same word: the Roman farmer's ~putāre~, “to prune, to clean up,” slid into “to settle accounts, to reckon,” so its prefixed compounds gave ~computar~, ~disputar~, ~imputar~, and ~reputar~ — to compute or dispute is, at root, to prune a tally into shape. Spanish kept the concrete branch as ~podar~, with derivatives like ~poda~ (“pruning”), ~podadera~ (“pruning hook”), and ~podador~ (“pruner”), while the learned ~putativo~ (“putative, supposed”) preserves the mental sense.
en.poder:
Spanish ~poder~ descends from a Vulgar Latin verb *~potēre~, a regularized reshaping of Classical Latin ~posse~ (“to be able”). ~posse~ was itself a contraction of ~potis~ (“able, powerful”) plus ~esse~ (“to be”) — “to be able” quite literally “to be capable.” The Proto-Indo-European root is *~poti-~ (“powerful, master”). The reshaped infinitive spread across Romance: Italian ~potere~, French ~pouvoir~, and Portuguese ~poder~.

Like several verbs of ability, ~poder~ doubles as a noun — ~el poder~, “power” itself, the thing one has the capacity to wield. The root's sense of capability and dominance fans out across the vocabulary: ~poderoso~ (“powerful”), ~poderío~ (“might”), ~potente~ and ~potencia~ (“potent,” “power”), ~posible~ (“possible,” what one is able to do), and ~potestad~ (“authority”). Even the English ~potent~ and ~possible~ belong to the same family, borrowed from the same Latin stock.
en.poner:
From Latin ~pōnere~ (“to put, to place, to set down”), earlier *~posinere~, analyzed as the prefix ~po-~ (“away, off”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, to leave”) — so to “put” was first to “set aside, to let stand.” From Proto-Italic *~posinō~. Its Romance offspring include Portuguese ~pôr~, Italian ~porre~, and French ~pondre~, which narrowed touchingly to mean “to lay eggs.” English holds the root through the learned forms ~position~, ~component~, ~deposit~, and ~compound~.

Because a bird “puts” its eggs in the nest, French preserved the most literal descendant of all; Spanish keeps that sense too in ~poner un huevo~ (“to lay an egg”), alongside every other kind of placing. ~poner~ is also famously irregular — its past participle is ~puesto~, its preterite ~puse~ — and it swarms with prefixes: ~componer~ (“to compose”), ~disponer~ (“to arrange”), ~proponer~ (“to propose”), ~suponer~ (“to suppose”), and ~exponer~ (“to expose”). From the participle ~puesto~ come the nouns ~posición~, ~postura~, and ~puesto~ (“post, stall, position”).
en.porfiar:
From the noun ~porfía~ (“stubborn insistence, dispute”) plus the verb ending ~-ar~; ~porfía~ itself descends from Latin ~perfidia~ (“faithlessness, treachery, breach of faith”), from ~perfidus~ (“treacherous”), literally ~per-~ (“through, beyond”) + ~fidēs~ (“faith, trust”) — one who goes beyond, or against, good faith.

The semantic journey is the memorable part: what began as “treachery” in Latin softened, in Spanish, into dogged, quarrelsome persistence — the ~perfidia~ of refusing to yield an argument. The shift from moral betrayal to sheer obstinacy is striking, though the sources present the descent from ~perfidia~ soberly, without a colorful anecdote to explain the bridge, so none should be invented. The same ~fidēs~ underlies a large Spanish family: ~fe~ (“faith”), ~fiel~ (“faithful”), ~fiar~ (“to entrust”), ~confiar~ (“to trust”), and the learned ~pérfido~ (“perfidious”).
en.portar:
From Latin ~portāre~ (“to carry, bear”), a verb of the everyday language, from Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to lead, pass over, cross”). Cognate with Italian ~portare~, French ~porter~, and Portuguese ~portar~. From the very same root Latin also built ~porta~ (“gate, passage”) and ~portus~ (“harbor, entrance”), and — far along the Germanic branch — English ~fare~ and ~ford~.

Where Latin ~portāre~ was the ordinary word for carrying, Spanish ~portar~ stayed comparatively formal (“to carry, bear”), while its reflexive ~portarse~ came to mean “to behave (oneself).” The productive descendants are the prefixed compounds: ~importar~, ~exportar~, ~transportar~, ~soportar~, ~deportar~, ~aportar~, and ~comportar~. The adjective ~portātilis~ gave ~portátil~ (“portable”), and the sister nouns ~porta~ and ~portus~ came down by inheritance as ~puerta~ (“door”) and ~puerto~ (“port”) — all of them, at bottom, about passing through.
en.posar:
Spanish ~posar~ descends from Late Latin ~pausāre~ (“to halt, rest, cease”), a verb built on the noun ~pausa~ (“a stop, pause”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~παῦσις~ (~paûsis~, “a ceasing”), from the verb ~παύειν~ (~paúein~, “to stop, make cease”). In everyday Spanish ~posar~ keeps close to that meaning — “to rest, to lodge, to alight,” a bird ~posa~ on a branch — and gave the noun ~posada~ (“inn,” a resting place) and ~reposar~ (“to repose”), from Latin ~repausāre~. The Romance story then takes a famous twist, because ~pausāre~ collided with the unrelated Latin ~pōnere~ (“to place”): cognate French ~poser~ and Italian ~posare~ took the form of ~pausāre~ but absorbed the “put, place” sense of ~pōnere~.

That crossover loops back into Spanish: ~posar~ in the sense “to pose” — to hold still for a painter or a camera — is a nineteenth-century borrowing from French ~poser~, so the modeling ~posar~ and the resting ~posar~ are the same ancient verb returning by two doors. The quiet sense of settling also survives in ~posarse~ (of dust or sediment coming to rest) and in the noun ~poso~ (“dregs, lees,” what settles at the bottom). English shares the whole inheritance through French, taking both ~pause~ and ~pose~. It is fitting that a verb meaning “to stop” should have produced words for an inn, a coffee's dregs, and a photographer's held breath — every one of them a small pause made solid.
en.poseer:
From Latin ~possidēre~ (“to have and hold, own, be master of”), most likely a compound of ~potis~ (“able, powerful, master,” from Proto-Indo-European *~poti-~ “powerful; lord”) and ~sedēre~ (“to sit,” from *~sed-~ “to sit”). Cognate with French ~posséder~, Italian ~possedere~, and — as a borrowing — English ~possess~.

The metaphor is vivid and legal: to ~possidēre~ was to sit as master over a thing, and the verb began in Roman law as a term for occupying land. Spanish ~poseer~ kept that sense of holding and owning. From the ~potis~ half the language also drew ~poder~ (“power; to be able”), while the ~sedēre~ half seeded ~sede~ (“seat, headquarters”). Everyday relatives include ~posesión~ (“possession”) and ~poseedor~ (“possessor, holder”).
en.posibilitar:
Spanish ~posibilitar~ was built at home from the adjective ~posible~ plus the verb-forming suffix ~-itar~. ~posible~ comes from Latin ~possibilis~ (“that can be done”), from ~posse~ (“to be able”), itself a fusion of ~potis~ (“able, powerful, master”) and ~esse~ (“to be”). ~potis~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~pótis~ (“master, lord”), and ~esse~ to *~h₁es-~ (“to be”). The adjective is shared across Romance: Italian ~possibile~, French ~possible~, Portuguese ~possível~, and English ~possible~.

The literal force of ~posse~ was “to be master of” something — capability imagined as ownership or power — so ~posibilitar~ means to make a thing masterable, to enable it. The ancestor ~potis~ has strikingly wide kin: Sanskrit ~páti~ (“lord, husband”), Greek ~pósis~, and, through Greek, English ~despot~. In Spanish the same root seeded ~poder~, ~potente~, ~potencia~ and ~potestad~, a cluster all circling the idea of being able.
en.posicionar:
A relatively recent denominal verb: the noun ~posición~ + ~-ar~, “to place, position.” ~posición~ comes from Latin ~positiō~, genitive ~positiōnis~ (“a placing”), from ~positus~, the past participle of ~pōnere~ (“to put, place, set”). The etymology of ~pōnere~ itself is disputed: it is traditionally analyzed as ~po-~ (an old preverb, “away”) + ~sinere~ (“to let, leave”), but some now derive it instead from a Proto-Indo-European *~tḱey-~ (“to settle, dwell”) — so its deepest root is unsettled.

Whatever its origin, ~pōnere~ became one of Latin’s most productive verbs, and ~posición~ passed through learned Latin rather than by ordinary sound-change. ~posicionar~ is newer still — a twentieth-century verb, much used in marketing (“to position a brand”) and reflexively, ~posicionarse~ (“to take a stance”). The ~pōnere~ family in Spanish is huge: ~poner~, ~componer~, ~disponer~, ~exponer~, ~oponer~, ~proponer~, ~suponer~, plus ~posición~, ~postura~, ~puesto~ and ~positivo~.
en.posponer:
From Latin ~postpōnere~ (“to place after, esteem less”), from ~post-~ (“after, behind”) + ~pōnere~ (“to put, place”). ~pōnere~ itself is a compound of the old prefix ~po-~ (“off, away”) and ~sinere~ (“to leave, let, allow”). Cognate compounds appear across Romance: Italian ~posporre~, French ~postposer~, Portuguese ~pospor~.

Spanish reshaped ~pōnere~ into ~poner~, and every prefixed compound followed the same pattern, giving ~componer~, ~disponer~, ~exponer~, ~imponer~, ~proponer~, and ~suponer~ alongside ~posponer~. The core sense stayed physical — to set one thing behind another — before drifting to the temporal “to postpone” and the evaluative “to value less.” Through Latin ~pōnere~ English shares ~position~, ~compose~, and ~postpone~ (the last straight from ~postpōnere~), and the family reaches nouns like ~posición~ and ~compostura~ in Spanish.
en.postular:
~postular~ comes from Latin ~postulare~ (“to ask, demand, claim, require”), most likely built on a participial form *~posk-to-~ of the verb ~poscere~ (“to ask urgently, demand”) — a derivation the sources give as probable rather than certain. ~poscere~ itself goes back to Proto-Italic *~poskō~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~preḱ-~ (“to ask, entreat”). Spanish ~postular~ is cognate with French ~postuler~, Italian ~postulare~ and English ~postulate~.

In classical Latin ~postulare~ was to put forward a claim — in law, to request a formal hearing; in the Church, to nominate someone to an office. Both senses survive: a scientist ~postula~ a hypothesis (lays it down as a starting claim), while a candidate ~postula~ for a post, and a novice entering a religious order is a ~postulante~. What is laid down is a ~postulado~ (“postulate, axiom”). The deeper root *~preḱ-~ (“to ask”) is quietly devout: it also gave Latin ~precari~ (“to pray”), and through it Spanish ~plegaria~ (“prayer”), ~precario~ (“precarious” — held only by request) and ~imprecar~ (“to curse”), plus English ~pray~ and ~deprecate~.
en.potenciar:
From ~potencia~ (“power, might”), from Latin ~potentia~, from ~potēns~ (“powerful, able”), the present participle of ~posse~ (“to be able”), itself a contraction of ~potis~ (“able, master”) + ~esse~ (“to be”). Cognate with Italian ~potenziare~ and French ~potentialiser~; the underlying ~potēns~ is shared with English ~potent~ and ~possible~ and, through French, ~power~.

The kernel is ~potis~, from Proto-Indo-European *~pótis~ (“master, lord, husband”), the same word that surfaces in Latin ~hospes~ (“host, guest”) and, via Greek ~δεσπότης~ (~despótēs~), in Spanish ~déspota~. ~Potenciar~ is a young, abstract coinage — to raise something to a higher power, to amplify it — and it wears its mathematics openly: a ~potencia~ is also an exponent. From the same source Spanish holds ~poder~ (the popular descendant of ~posse~), ~poderoso~, ~potente~, ~posible~, ~potestad~, and ~omnipotente~.
en.practicar:
From Late and Medieval Latin ~practicāre~ (“to do, perform, practice”), from Late Latin ~practicus~ (“practical, active”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~πρακτικός~ (~praktikós~, “fit for action, effective”), from ~πράσσω~ (~prássō~, “to do, act, achieve,” earlier “to pass through, traverse”). Spanish probably received the verb by way of Old French ~pratiquer~. Kindred Romance forms include Italian ~praticare~ and Portuguese ~praticar~, and the borrowed English ~practice~ and ~practical~ belong to the same Greek stock.

The related Greek noun ~πρᾶξις~ (~prâxis~, “action, deed”) captures the core idea: practice is knowledge put into action, as opposed to bare theory — a contrast Spanish keeps in the pair ~teoría~ / ~práctica~. The verb ranges from “to practice, rehearse” to “to carry out”: ~practicar una operación~ is to perform an operation, ~practicar un agujero~ to make a hole. From the same stock Spanish has ~práctica~ (“practice”), ~práctico~ (“practical,” and as a noun a harbor pilot), ~pragmático~ and ~praxis~. That last word, unchanged from the Greek, keeps the ancient sense of a deed actually done.
en.preciar:
From Latin ~pretiāre~ (“to value, to price”), a denominative from ~pretium~ (“price, worth, value, reward”), from Proto-Italic *~pretjom~; the noun is linked to Proto-Indo-European *~preti-~ (“in return, against”), related to the root *~per-~ (“forward, before”). Italian ~prezzare~ and Portuguese ~prezar~ are the same verb.

Spanish inherited ~pretium~ as ~precio~ (“price”) and ~pretiāre~ as ~preciar~ (“to value, to prize”), which in daily use yields to its own compounds ~apreciar~ (“to appreciate”) and ~despreciar~ (“to despise”) — literally to price up or price down. From ~pretium~ came also ~precioso~ (“precious”) and ~apreciación~. The same Latin noun traveled through Old French into English as three separate words that still show their kinship: ~price~, ~prize~, and ~praise~ — the last from praising a thing by naming its worth.
en.precisar:
From the adjective ~preciso~ (“precise”) plus ~-ar~. ~Preciso~ comes from Latin ~praecīsus~ (“cut off, shortened, clipped”), the past participle of ~praecīdere~ (“to cut off in front”), from ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~caedere~ (“to cut, to strike”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kh₂eyd-~ (“to strike, to hew”). It is cognate with French ~préciser~ and, through ~caedere~, with English ~precise~, ~concise~, ~decide~ and even ~scissors~.

Something ~preciso~ is, at root, something cut short — trimmed of all excess — so precision is a kind of cutting away, and to ~precisar~ a thing is to pare it to its exact outline, to state it with nothing superfluous. Spanish then took a second, striking step: because what is cut to the essential is what one cannot do without, ~preciso~ also came to mean “necessary,” and ~precisar~ acquired the everyday sense “to need.” The cutting root ~caedere~ runs through many relatives: ~conciso~ (“cut short”), ~decidir~ (to “cut off” deliberation and choose), ~incisión~, ~inciso~ and the grim ~homicidio~.
en.predecir:
From Latin ~praedīcere~ (“to foretell, predict”), from ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) + ~dīcere~ (“to say, tell”), from Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, point out”). Spanish rebuilt it on its own ~decir~ (from ~dīcere~), so the modern verb is ~pre-~ + ~decir~. Italian ~predire~, French ~prédire~, and Portuguese ~predizer~ are the same formation.

The literal core is “to say beforehand.” English ~predict~ comes from the participle ~praedictus~, and English ~diction~, ~dictate~, and ~dictionary~ all trace to ~dīcere~. In Spanish the root *~deyḱ-~ is enormously fertile: besides ~decir~ and ~predecir~ it yields ~bendecir~, ~maldecir~, ~contradecir~, and the noun ~predicción~. Note the near-twin ~predicar~ (“to preach”): it looks related but comes from a different Latin verb, ~praedicāre~, so the two are cousins rather than the same word.
en.predicar:
From Latin ~praedicāre~ (“to proclaim publicly, to preach”), from ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) + ~dicāre~ (“to proclaim, dedicate”). ~dicāre~ shares the Proto-Indo-European root *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, point out”) with its close relative ~dīcere~, but is a distinct verb of dedicating and declaring. Italian ~predicare~ and Portuguese ~pregar~ (“to preach”) continue it.

The standout fact: English ~preach~ is this same ~praedicāre~, worn down through Old French ~prêchier~ / ~prëechier~ — so a Spanish priest who ~predica~ and an English one who preaches are doing the etymologically identical thing. The learned ~predicar~ kept the Latin shape in Spanish, beside ~predicador~ (“preacher”), ~predicación~, and ~predicamento~. From the same ~dicāre~ come ~dedicar~ (“to dedicate”), ~indicar~ (“to indicate”), and ~abdicar~ (“to abdicate”).
en.preferir:
From Latin ~praeferre~ (“to carry before, set before, prefer”), from ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, bear”). Cognate with French ~préférer~, Italian ~preferire~ and English ~prefer~; and, through the very old verb ~ferre~, with English ~bear~ and German ~gebären~.

To ~preferir~ is, etymologically, to “carry one thing in front of” the rest — to hold it forward as the better choice, a vivid spatial metaphor frozen inside the word. Latin ~ferre~ was one of the great suppletive verbs, borrowing its perfect from ~tulī~ and its participle from ~lātus~, and it seeded a huge Spanish family through its compounds: ~ofrecer~, ~conferir~, ~diferir~, ~referir~, ~transferir~ and ~sufrir~, plus nouns like ~oferta~ and ~referencia~. The root *~bʰer-~ is among the most widespread in Indo-European, surviving in English ~bear~ and ~birth~.
en.preguntar:
Spanish ~preguntar~ comes from a Vulgar Latin *~praecontāre~ (or *~praecunctāre~), a reshaping of Classical Latin ~percontārī~ (“to question, inquire”). ~percontārī~ was built from ~per-~ (“through”) and, by the traditional account, ~contus~ (“a long pole,” borrowed from Greek ~kontós~): it was originally a sailors’ word meaning to sound the depth of water with a pole — and, by an old and vivid metaphor, to probe or sound out a person with questions. In Vulgar Latin the prefix ~per-~ was refashioned as ~prae-~ (~pre-~), perhaps under the influence of ~cunctārī~ (“to hesitate, delay”). Portuguese ~perguntar~ keeps the original ~per-~; Spanish generalized ~pre-~.

The pole is the memorable image, but it should be flagged: the derivation of ~percontārī~ from ~contus~ (“pole”) is the traditional explanation and is plausible, yet not beyond dispute, so the seafaring picture is best offered as the received story rather than proven fact. What is certain is that the sense narrowed cleanly to “to ask,” and that Spanish generalized the ~pre-~ form across the board. From it come the noun ~pregunta~ (“question”), ~preguntón~ (“inquisitive; a busybody”), and the reflexive ~preguntarse~ (“to wonder, ask oneself”). A useful pair to keep straight: ~preguntar~ is “to ask a question,” while ~pedir~ (from Latin ~petere~) is “to ask for, request” — Spanish, unlike English, never lets one verb do both jobs.
en.premiar:
Spanish ~premiar~ (“to reward, give a prize”) comes from the noun ~premio~ (“prize, reward”) plus ~-ar~. ~premio~ descends from Latin ~praemium~ (“prize, reward, spoils”), a compound of ~prae-~ (“before, ahead”) and ~emere~ (“to take, obtain; buy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁em-~ (“to take, distribute”). English ~premium~ is the very same Latin noun borrowed whole; Italian ~premiare~ and Portuguese ~premiar~ match the Spanish verb.

The literal sense of ~praemium~ is striking: “what one takes ahead of the others” — originally the choice share of the booty, the pick seized before the spoils were divided. From reward-as-loot it softened to reward-as-prize, and ~premiar~ is simply to bestow that prize. The root verb ~emere~ meant “to take” before it meant “to buy,” and it seeded a large Spanish family through its compounds — ~ejemplo~ (“example,” from ~exemplum~, “what is taken out”), ~eximir~ (“to exempt”), ~redimir~ (“to redeem”) and ~prima~ (“premium, bonus”).
en.prendar:
From the noun ~prenda~ (“pledge, security; garment; jewel”) Spanish built the verb ~prendar~; the noun descends from Latin ~pignora~, plural of ~pignus~ (“pledge, pawn”), and the verb continues Latin ~pignorāre~ (“to give as a pledge”) through an older Spanish ~pendrar~. The origin of ~pignus~ is disputed: some trace it to Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂ǵ-~ (“to fasten, to fix”) — a pledge being something fixed as security — while others prefer *~peyǵ-~. A close Romance cognate is Portuguese ~penhor~ (“pledge”).

The semantic path runs from law to love. To ~prendar~ was first to seize goods as a pledge; from holding a person as one might hold a pledge came the figurative sense “to captivate, to win someone's heart,” and the reflexive ~prendarse~ means “to fall in love.” The same Latin root seeded a family of Spanish words for pledging and pawning: ~prenda~ (now the everyday word for “garment”), ~empeñar~ (“to pawn, to pledge”), ~empeño~ (“pledge; determination”), and the learned ~pignorar~ (“to pledge as collateral”).
en.prender:
From Latin ~prēndere~, the syncopated everyday form of ~prehendere~ (“to grasp, to seize”), a compound of the prefix ~prae-~ (“before”) and a lost verb *~hendere~ (“to take”). This goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~gʰend-~ (“to seize, to take”), which also gave — through Germanic — English ~get~ and, in Ancient Greek, ~χανδάνω~ (khandánō, “to hold, to contain”), a distant cousin. Romance kept the verb well: French ~prendre~ and Italian ~prendere~ both mean “to take.”

Spanish ~prender~ spread across a wide field of meaning: “to seize, to arrest,” “to catch fire, to light,” “to pin or fasten,” and in the Americas “to switch on.” Its participle ~preso~ (“prisoner”) and the noun ~prisión~ (“prison”) descend from the Latin participle ~prehēnsus~. The same ~prehendere~, differently prefixed, underlies a whole cluster of Spanish verbs of grasping — mental and physical: ~aprender~ (“to learn,” i.e. to grasp with the mind), ~comprender~ (“to understand”), ~emprender~ (“to undertake”), and ~sorprender~ (“to surprise”).
en.preocupar:
From Latin ~praeoccupāre~ (“to seize beforehand, take possession of in advance”), a compound of ~prae-~ (“before”) and ~occupāre~ (“to seize, occupy”), itself ~ob-~ (“toward, over”) plus a verb built on ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kap-~ (“to grasp”). Cognate with Italian ~preoccupare~ and French ~préoccuper~; English took the same root through ~occupy~ and ~capture~.

The mental sense is a metaphor of premature seizure: to ~preocupar~ is literally to “occupy beforehand,” as a worry takes hold of the mind before the feared thing arrives. Latin ~praeoccupāre~ was concrete — to seize a hill or a town ahead of the enemy — but Spanish specialized the reflexive ~preocuparse~ for the anxiety that grabs one first. From ~capere~ comes a huge family: ~ocupar~, ~capturar~, ~capaz~, ~recibir~, ~concebir~, and ~caber~ itself, all turning on the idea of taking hold.
en.preparar:
From Latin ~praeparāre~ (“to make ready beforehand”), from ~prae-~ (“before”) + ~parāre~ (“to make ready, provide”), from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to provide, grant”). Cognate with Italian ~preparare~, French ~préparer~, Portuguese ~preparar~ and English ~prepare~; through the root, with Latin ~parere~ (“to give birth, bring forth”) and Sanskrit ~pṛṇā́ti~ (“to grant, bestow”).

The simple verb ~parāre~ meant “to make ready,” and its offspring fanned out across Spanish: ~parar~ (“to stop”), ~preparación~, ~preparativo~, ~aparato~ (“apparatus”), ~reparar~, ~separar~ and ~amparar~ (“to shelter”). Through the closely related ~parere~ (“to bear young”) come ~parir~ and ~parto~ (“childbirth”). The root’s basic idea is provision: to prepare is to have things furnished in advance, ready to hand.
en.presentar:
From Latin ~praesentāre~ (“to place before, show, offer”), the verb of ~praesēns~ (“present, at hand”), the present participle of ~praeesse~ (“to be before, be at hand”), from ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) plus ~esse~ (“to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁es-~ (“to be”). Cognate with Italian ~presentare~, French ~présenter~, Portuguese ~apresentar~, and English ~present~ and ~represent~.

The core image is spatial: ~prae-~ “before” plus ~esse~ “to be,” so ~praesēns~ described whatever “is before you,” present in place and in time. From ~praesentāre~, “to set before someone,” Spanish ~presentar~ branched into introducing a person, showing a document, staging a show, and lodging a complaint — every sense a variation on putting something in front of an audience. The adjective and noun ~presente~ carries both meanings the Latin fused: the present moment and a present, a gift “placed before” the receiver. From the same ~prae-~ + ~esse~ come ~presencia~, ~presentación~, ~presentador~, and ~presentimiento~ (“foreboding,” a feeling that “is there beforehand”).
en.preservar:
From Late Latin ~praeservāre~ (“to guard beforehand”), from ~prae-~ (“before”) plus ~servāre~ (“to keep, guard, watch over”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ser-~ (“to protect”). Cognate with French ~préserver~, Italian ~preservare~ and Portuguese ~preservar~, and, through the same root, with English ~observe~, ~conserve~ and ~reserve~.

A worthwhile warning: the ~servāre~ of “keep, guard” has nothing to do with the near-identical ~servīre~ (“to serve”) or ~servus~ (“slave”) — a different root, which gave ~servir~ and ~siervo~. From the “guard” verb Spanish built ~conservar~ (“keep together, safe”), ~observar~ (“watch over, notice”) and ~reservar~ (“keep back”). ~preservar~ adds ~prae-~, “beforehand”: to preserve is to guard something in advance against harm or decay, which is why we speak of preservatives that keep food from spoiling.
en.presidir:
From Latin ~praesidēre~ (“to sit before, to guard, to preside”), a compound of ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sed-~ (“to sit”). It is a famously wide root: ~sedēre~ gives English ~sedentary~, ~reside~, and ~session~, while the Germanic branch of the same *~sed-~ gives English ~sit~ and ~seat~. The Romance line kept the compound — Italian ~presiedere~, Portuguese ~presidir~, French ~présider~.

To ~presidir~ is to sit before or above an assembly — the seat of authority at the head of the table — hence to chair, to lead, to preside. From the related noun ~praesidium~ (“a guard, garrison, protection”) Spanish drew ~presidio~, which slid from “fortified garrison” to “penal settlement” to today’s plain “prison” — a striking drift for a word about protection. Kin abound: ~presidente~, ~presidencia~, ~sede~ (“seat, see, headquarters”), ~residir~, ~sedentario~, ~sesión~, and ~asiduo~ (“assiduous,” one who sits at a task).
en.presionar:
A modern verb from the noun ~presión~ plus ~-ar~. ~presión~ comes from Latin ~pressiō~ (accusative ~pressiōnem~, “a pressing”), from ~pressus~, the past participle of ~premere~ (“to press, squeeze”), from Proto-Italic *~pres-~, of uncertain deeper Indo-European ancestry — the present stem was perhaps reshaped on the model of ~tremere~ (“to tremble”). English ~press~ and ~print~ reached English from the same Latin verb by way of French ~presser~; the Italian reflex is ~premere~.

Spanish coined ~prensar~ (“to press, compress”) directly, so ~presionar~ is the latecomer, built on the abstract noun rather than on the participle. From ~premere~ radiates a large family: ~prensa~ (“press; the media”), ~oprimir~, ~comprimir~, ~exprimir~, ~expresar~, ~imprimir~, and ~apremiar~ (“to press, urge”). The concrete act of squeezing became the abstract ~presión~ one exerts on a person, and ~presionar~ now means to pressure or lean on someone — the metaphor of a weight pressing down made fully social.
en.prestar:
From Latin ~praestāre~ (“to stand before, to excel, to furnish, to provide”), a compound of ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — the very root of ~estar~. Cognates include Italian ~prestare~, French ~prêter~ and Portuguese ~prestar~, all inheriting the same “furnish” sense.

The path from “standing before” to “lending” runs through the sense “to make available, to furnish”: what you ~prestas~ you place at another’s disposal. Latin ~praestāre~ already meant “to guarantee, to supply,” and Romance narrowed that to lending. Spanish preserves both threads — you can ~prestar~ money (lend) but also ~prestar~ attention or a service (furnish). From it come ~préstamo~ (“loan”), ~prestación~ (“benefit, service”), ~prestamista~ (“lender”) and ~empréstito~ (“public loan”). Note that ~prestigio~, despite the look, belongs to a different Latin word.
en.presumir:
From Latin ~praesūmere~ (“to take in advance, anticipate”), from ~prae-~ (“before”) and ~sūmere~ (“to take up, take”). ~Sūmere~ itself is a compound of ~sub-~ (“up from under”) and ~emere~ (“to take, buy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁em-~ (“to take, distribute”). The prefixed verb is cognate with English ~presume~ and, through ~sūmere~, with ~assume~, ~consume~ and ~resume~; Romance keeps it in Italian ~presumere~ and French ~présumer~.

Latin ~praesūmere~ meant to take something for granted ahead of proof — the sense preserved in “to presume.” But Spanish grew a second, very human branch: to ~presumir~ came to mean “to show off, to be vain,” and a ~presumido~ is a conceited person — as if someone who presumes too much of themselves ends up preening. Both senses live on today, beside the noun ~presunción~ (“presumption; conceit”) and cousins like ~asumir~, ~consumir~ and ~resumir~.
en.pretender:
From Latin ~praetendere~ (“to stretch forth, hold out before, put forward as a reason”), a compound of ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch, extend”). ~tendere~ rests on Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, extend”), a root that also thinned things out: from its extension *~tenh₂u-~ (“stretched thin”) come Latin ~tenuis~ (“thin”) and English ~thin~. Through the same root ~pretender~ is cognate with Greek ~teínō~ (“I stretch”) and with English ~tend~, ~tension~, and ~tent~ (a stretched cloth). Italian ~pretendere~ and French ~prétendre~ are its direct Romance kin.
