In Spanish the family clusters around the noun ~robo~ (“theft”), the booty-born ~ropa~, and the compound ~guardarropa~ (“wardrobe”).
en.rodar:
Spanish ~rodar~ comes from Latin ~rotāre~ (“to turn, whirl”), a verb formed from the noun ~rota~ (“wheel”). ~rota~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~Hroth₂o-~, from the root *~ret-~ (“to run, roll”). It has cognates far outside Latin: German ~Rad~ (“wheel”), Sanskrit ~ratha~ (“chariot”), Old Irish ~roth~ and Welsh ~rhod~. Within Romance the verb is echoed by Italian ~rotare~ and Portuguese ~rodar~.

~rodar~ kept the physical sense of turning like a wheel — a stone, a car, an actor rolling through a film shoot (~rodar una película~, “to shoot a film”). The old noun ~rota~ left an unusually rich Spanish family. Beyond obvious relatives like ~rueda~ (“wheel”) and ~rotar~ (“to rotate”), it hides inside ~redondo~ (“round,” from ~rotundus~), ~rodear~ (“to surround”) and ~alrededor~ (“around”). The most charming descendant is ~rodilla~ (“knee”), from Vulgar Latin ~rotella~ (“little wheel”) — the joint named for the way the leg pivots on it.
en.rodear:
A Spanish formation from the noun ~rueda~ (“wheel”) plus the verbal suffix ~-ear~, so at root “to wheel around” something. ~rueda~ itself comes from Latin ~rota~ (“wheel”), from Proto-Indo-European *~Hroth₂o-~ (“wheel”), a derivative of *~ret-~ (“to run, to roll”). The word is widespread: cognate with German ~Rad~ (“wheel”) and Sanskrit ~rátha~ (“chariot”), while Latin ~rotundus~ yielded Spanish ~redondo~ (“round”) and English ~rotate~.

To ~rodear~ is to trace a circle about a thing — to surround, or to take the long way round. The noun ~rodeo~ names exactly that “going around”: a roundabout route, an evasion, or the cattle roundup in which riders circle the herd — the sense English borrowed wholesale as ~rodeo~. The wheel-root spun off a wide Spanish family besides: ~rodar~ (“to roll”), ~rotar~, ~rodillo~ (“roller”), and ~rótula~ (“kneecap”).
en.rodrigar:
The verb ~rodrigar~ — “to stake plants,” that is, to prop them up — is built directly on the noun ~rodrigón~, a cane or stake driven in beside a plant to hold its stems upright. The origin of ~rodrigón~ itself is genuinely disputed. It is tempting to link it to the personal name ~Rodrigo~, but Corominas judged that resemblance to be largely accidental, at most a secondary influence, not the source. The competing accounts are Latin: a derivation from ~rīdica~ (“vine-prop”), perhaps crossed with ~rudis~ / ~rudicula~ to yield a Vulgar Latin *~rŭdica~; a Germanic compound *~rodirakjo~ has also been floated. None is settled, and the phonetics trouble every version, so the honest verdict is “of uncertain origin.”

Whatever its root, ~rodrigón~ took on a charming figurative life: besides the garden stake, it came to mean an elderly manservant who escorted ladies about — a human “prop” at a lady’s side. The verb ~rodrigar~ stays firmly horticultural, naming the springtime chore of staking vines and young plants; a gardener ~rodriga~ the tomatoes so they will not sprawl on the ground. The word-family is small and rustic — essentially ~rodrigón~ and ~rodrigar~ — a reminder that even a humble vineyard tool can leave the dictionaries frankly unsure of where it came from.
en.rogar:
From Latin ~rogare~ (“to ask, beg, request”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, stretch out”) — the underlying image being of stretching out the hand to ask. Cognate with Italian ~rogare~ and Portuguese ~rogar~, and — through the same root — with English ~interrogate~ and ~arrogant~, and even ~right~ and German ~recht~ (“straight; law”).

In Roman public life ~rogare~ was a technical verb: to put a proposal before the assembly, a ~rogatio~ — which is why so many of its Spanish descendants are legal and political: ~derogar~ (“to repeal”), ~abrogar~, ~subrogar~, and ~prerrogativa~ (“prerogative”). Ordinary ~rogar~ leaned toward entreaty — to beg, plead, and pray — and gave the noun ~ruego~ (“plea”) and the religious ~rogativa~ (public prayers, once chiefly for rain). The idiom ~hacerse de rogar~ (“to play hard to get,” literally to make oneself be begged) keeps the old force alive, as does the formal ~se ruega no fumar~ (“you are kindly asked not to smoke”).
en.romper:
Spanish ~romper~ descends directly from Latin ~rumpere~ (“to break, burst”), inherited through Vulgar Latin with regular loss of the nasal before the plosive. The Latin verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~Hrewp-~ (“to break”), its present formed with a nasal infix. It is cognate with Italian ~rompere~, French ~rompre~, and Portuguese ~romper~, and — through the same root — with Sanskrit ~lumpáti~ (“breaks”) and, more distantly, with the English words below.

Latin ~rumpere~ was extraordinarily productive in prefixed compounds, and English borrowed the lot from its participle ~ruptus~: ~rupture~, ~erupt~, ~corrupt~, ~interrupt~, ~abrupt~, and ~disrupt~. Spanish kept a parallel learned family beside the everyday ~romper~: ~ruptura~ (“rupture”), ~corromper~ (“to corrupt”), ~interrumpir~ (“to interrupt”), and ~irrumpir~ (“to burst in”). A pleasant survival is ~rompeolas~ (“breakwater”), literally “it breaks waves,” preserving the raw physical force of the original verb.
en.rumiar:
From Latin ~rūmigāre~ (“to chew the cud”), a verb formed on the noun ~rūmen~ (“gullet; the first stomach of a ruminant”) with the denominative element ~-igāre~, which contains ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”). It descended regularly into Old Spanish as ~rumiar~. It is cognate with Portuguese ~ruminar~ and with the learned Spanish doublet ~ruminar~, while the bare stem survives in the anatomical Latinism ~rumen~ shared across European languages.

Latin already held both senses — the literal grinding of cud and, figuratively, turning a thought over and over — and Spanish kept the metaphor intact, so to ~rumiar~ a grievance is to chew on it in the mind. The book-learned ~ruminar~ arrived later and sounds more clinical, whereas ~rumiar~ stayed homely and everyday. From the same ~rūmen~ Spanish also draws ~rumiante~ (“ruminant”) and the noun ~rumia~ (“the act of ruminating”), so that a whole vocabulary of cattle and of brooding grows from one word for a cow's stomach.
en.saber:
From Vulgar Latin *~sapēre~, a reshaping of Latin ~sapere~ (“to taste; to have good sense, to be wise”), from Proto-Italic *~sapjō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~seh₁p-~ (“to taste, to perceive”). The verb runs straight across Romance as Italian ~sapere~, French ~savoir~, and Portuguese ~saber~; English carries the same root in the borrowings ~sapient~, ~savor~, ~insipid~ (“without taste”), and ~sage~ (“wise”).

The metaphor inside the word is that of the palate: to know is to have tasted, to have discernment — the tongue standing in for the mind. Latin already ran both senses side by side, and Spanish kept the double life, since ~saber~ still means both “to know” and “to taste” (« esta sopa sabe a ajo », “this soup tastes of garlic”). From the same root grew ~sabio~ (“wise; a sage”), ~sabor~ (“flavor”), ~sabroso~ (“tasty”), ~sabiduría~ (“wisdom”), and the adjective ~sabihondo~ (“know-it-all”). Spanish neatly distinguishes ~saber~ (to know a fact) from ~conocer~ (to be acquainted with).
en.sacar:
Modern Spanish ~sacar~ descends from Old Spanish ~sacar~, but its ultimate origin is genuinely disputed. By the account Corominas favors, it comes from Gothic ~sakan~ (“to quarrel, dispute, accuse at law”), a Germanic legal term: to ~sacar~ would first have meant to obtain something by winning a lawsuit, and only later to extract or take out in general. A competing account instead links it to Medieval Latin ~saccāre~ and to ~saccus~ (“sack”) — from Greek ~sákkos~, itself a Semitic loan — imagining the act of pulling goods out of a bag. The earliest Castilian traces are Latinized forms like ~saccāre~ in tenth-century documents. Portuguese ~sacar~ (“to draw out; to draw a weapon or withdraw money”) matches the Spanish form closely, and the two languages share the ambiguity of the source.

Because the origin is unsettled, the vivid legal image — winning by litigation — should be taken as a hypothesis, not a fact. What is clear is the semantic breadth Spanish gave the verb: to take out, extract, withdraw, obtain, and figuratively to deduce (~sacar en claro~) or to snap a photo (~sacar una foto~). From it Spanish built ~sacacorchos~ (“corkscrew”), ~sacapuntas~ (“pencil sharpener”), the noun ~saca~ (“large sack; withdrawal”), and the compound ~entresacar~ (“to pick out, thin out”). The related ~sonsacar~ (“to draw information out of someone, to wheedle”) preserves almost perfectly the notion of extracting something someone would rather keep — whichever of the two etymologies proves right.
en.sacrificar:
From Latin ~sacrificāre~ (“to perform a sacrifice; to make sacred”), a compound of ~sacer~ (“sacred, holy”) and ~facere~ (“to make, do”) — literally “to make holy.” ~sacer~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~sakros~; its deeper Indo-European root is debated, so it is safest to stop there. ~facere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, make”). Cognate with Italian ~sacrificare~, French ~sacrifier~, and English ~sacrifice~, all built on the same Latin compound.

The verb kept its literal Roman sense: a ~sacrificium~ was an act that rendered something ~sacer~, handing it over from the human world to the divine, whether an animal offering or a libation. From “making sacred” the meaning broadened to the modern “to give something up for a higher purpose” — the emotional and figurative sacrifice of time, comfort, or self. The same Latin ~sacer~ seeded a large Spanish family beyond ~sacrificar~: ~sagrado~ and its learned doublet ~sacro~, ~consagrar~ (“to consecrate”), ~sacerdote~ (“priest,” literally one who performs sacred acts), and ~sacramento~. The ~facere~ half, meanwhile, hides inside hundreds of Spanish verbs in ~-ficar~ and ~-facer~, from ~edificar~ to ~satisfacer~.
en.sacudir:
From Latin ~succutere~ (“to shake from below, to jolt”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under, up from under”) and ~quatere~ (“to shake”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *~kʷeh₁t-~ (“to shake”). In Old Spanish it appears as ~sacodir~, an outcome of an earlier ~socodir~ reshaped by vowel dissimilation, before settling as modern ~sacudir~. It is cognate with French ~secouer~ and Portuguese ~sacudir~, and — through ~quatere~ — with English ~percussion~ and ~concussion~.

The physical core, a sharp shaking or striking, still governs every use: one can ~sacudir~ a rug, ~sacudir~ dust from a coat, or ~sacudir~ off laziness, the figurative sense growing straight out of the literal jolt. The verb keeps a living present-tense vowel change inherited from Latin. From the same family Spanish has ~sacudida~ (“a shake, a jolt”) and the augmentative ~sacudón~ (“a violent shake”), while the learned root ~quatere~ also seeded ~percutir~ and ~discutir~ — literally to strike through and to shake apart — showing how a verb of physical shaking spread into speech about hitting and arguing.
en.salar:
Spanish ~salar~ (“to salt”) is a straightforward derivative of the noun ~sal~ (“salt”), from Latin ~sāl~, from Proto-Indo-European *~seh₂l-~ (“salt”). The same root surfaces in Italian ~sale~, French ~sel~ and — on the Germanic branch — English ~salt~ and German ~Salz~.

Roman soldiers drew a ~salarium~, an allowance tied to salt, which handed English its ~salary~ and Spanish its ~salario~ — the ordinary word for a wage still carries a grain of the ancient seasoning. To ~salar~ was to preserve and flavour food with salt, a craft as old as trade itself. The same root seasons a whole pantry of Spanish words: ~salsa~ (“sauce,” literally salted), ~ensalada~ (“salad,” once salted greens), ~salmuera~ (“brine”), ~salino~ and ~salchicha~ (“sausage”).
en.salgar:
Spanish ~salgar~ descends from Latin ~sāl~ (“salt”), most likely through a Vulgar Latin verb *~salicāre~, and traces back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~séh₂ls~ (“salt”). The Latin noun survives across Romance as Italian ~sale~, French ~sel~, Portuguese ~sal~ and Spanish ~sal~, while the same ancient root surfaces in English ~salt~, German ~Salz~ and Ancient Greek ~háls~ (“salt, sea”).

Where many languages simply say “to give salt,” Spanish coined a dedicated verb: ~salgar~ means to give salt to livestock, a herder’s chore of setting salt out for cattle and sheep. Salt was so central to daily life that it seeded a wide family of Spanish words — ~sal~ itself, ~salario~ (from Latin ~salārium~, traditionally explained as a soldier’s salt allowance, though that “paid in salt” story is now doubted), ~salsa~, ~ensalada~ and ~salazón~, the salting of fish and meat. The next time you order a ~salsa~ or collect a ~salario~, you are speaking the same root a herder invokes when he goes to ~salgar~ the flock.
en.salir:
From Latin ~salīre~ (“to jump, leap, spring”), from Proto-Italic *~saljō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~sel-~ (“to spring, jump”). The same root gave Ancient Greek ~hállomai~ (“to leap”) and, most likely, Sanskrit ~sárati~ (“flows, runs”). Through Latin and French, ~salīre~ furnished English ~salient~ and ~sally~, while its frequentative ~saltāre~ (“to leap repeatedly, dance”) gave Spanish ~saltar~ and Italian ~saltare~.

The leap became a departure. In Vulgar Latin ~salīre~ drifted from “to jump” toward “to jump out, spring forth,” and Old Spanish ~salir~ settled into the everyday “to go out, leave, exit” it has today — a spring of water still ~sale~ from the ground, keeping the old image alive. Its relatives cluster around leaping and springing: ~salto~ (“a jump”), ~saltar~, ~sobresalir~ (“to stand out,” literally to “leap above”), ~salida~ (“exit, departure”) and ~asaltar~ (“to assault,” to leap upon). English ~assault~ and ~somersault~ leap from the very same Latin verb.
en.saltar:
From Latin ~saltāre~ (“to dance, leap”), the frequentative of ~salīre~ (“to jump, spring”), from Proto-Italic *~saliō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~sel-~ (“to jump”). Cognate with Italian ~saltare~, French ~sauter~ and Portuguese ~saltar~, and — through ~salīre~ — with English ~salient~, ~sally~ and the ~-sault~ of ~assault~ and ~somersault~.

Because ~saltāre~ was the “leap again and again” of a dancer, Latin used it for dancing as well as jumping; Spanish took the leaping sense and let the noun ~baile~ carry dancing. A ~somersault~ hides the etymology neatly: it is “a leap over,” from ~suprā~ (“over”) + ~saltus~ (“a jump”). From the same root Spanish gathers ~salto~, ~saltamontes~ (literally “leap-hills”), ~sobresaltar~ and ~resaltar~.
en.saltear:
From Spanish ~salto~ (“a leap”) plus the verbal suffix ~-ear~; ~salto~ comes from Latin ~saltus~, a noun to ~salīre~ (“to leap”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sel-~ (“to jump”). The frequentative Latin ~saltāre~ (“to keep leaping, to dance”) lies in the same nest. It is cognate with Italian ~saltare~ and French ~sauter~, and — through ~salīre~ — with English ~assault~, ~result~, and ~somersault~.

The idea of repeated leaping fanned out into strikingly different senses. A highwayman who pounced on travelers was said to ~saltear~, giving ~salteador~ (“bandit”); to skip over parts of a task is likewise to ~saltear~. The cooking sense, ~saltear~ (“to sauté”), is a calque of French ~sauter~, where food is tossed — made to jump — in the pan; it does not mean to salt, a common trap for English speakers. From the same *~sel-~ Spanish also holds ~saltar~, ~salto~, ~asaltar~, and ~sobresaltar~ (“to startle”), a whole family of sudden movement.
en.saludar:
From Latin ~salūtāre~ (“to greet, to wish health to”), a verb built on ~salūs~ (genitive ~salūtis~, “health, safety, well-being”). ~Salūs~ belongs with ~salvus~ (“safe, sound, whole”) and traces to Proto-Indo-European *~solh₂-~ (“whole, entire”), the root that also gave Greek ~hólos~ (“whole,” as in “holistic”) and, through Latin, English ~salute~ and ~salutary~. Sister forms appear across Romance: Italian ~salutare~, French ~saluer~ and Portuguese ~saudar~.

The meaning is a small kindness fossilized in grammar: to greet someone was to wish them ~salūs~ — health and wholeness. Spanish ~saludar~ kept exactly that, and the derived noun ~salud~ serves at once as the toast raised to someone's health and the word murmured after a sneeze, each a miniature blessing. From the same root *~solh₂-~ Spanish also holds ~saludable~, ~salubre~, ~salvar~ (“to save,” to make whole and safe) and ~salvo~ (“safe, excepted”). To greet, at root, is to hope the other stays in one piece.
en.salvar:
From Late Latin ~salvāre~ (“to save, make safe”), a verb built on Latin ~salvus~ (“safe, whole, unharmed”), from Proto-Indo-European *~solh₂-~ (“whole, every”). Cognate with Italian ~salvare~, French ~sauver~, and Portuguese ~salvar~. English ~save~ and ~safe~ both descend, through Old French, from ~salvus~, as does ~salvage~; and through the same PIE root the Latin adjective is cognate with Ancient Greek ~hólos~ (“whole”), source of the ~holo-~ in “holograph.”

The root idea is wholeness: to save is to keep something entire and unharmed. Latin ~salvus~ gave the greeting ~salvē~ (“be well, hail”), and the interjection survives in Spanish ~salve~. Christianity gave ~salvar~ its theological weight — ~salvación~ (“salvation”), ~Salvador~ (“Savior”) — beside the everyday senses of rescuing and the computing sense of saving a file. The family is wide: ~salvo~ (“safe; except”), ~a salvo~ (“in safety”), ~salvavidas~ (“lifeguard, life preserver”), ~salvoconducto~ (“safe-conduct”), and ~salvaguardar~ (“to safeguard”). The noun ~salud~ (“health”), from the related ~salūs~, springs from the same idea of being whole and sound.
en.sanar:
From Old Spanish ~sanar~, from Latin ~sānāre~ (“to heal, to cure”), a verb built on the adjective ~sānus~ (“healthy, sound”), whose deeper origin is uncertain and not securely traced to any Proto-Indo-European root. It is cognate with Italian ~sanare~ and Portuguese ~sanar~, and — through ~sānus~ — with English ~sane~, ~sanity~, and ~sanitary~.

In Latin ~sānāre~ was transitive, «to make well», and Spanish keeps that but also lets ~sanar~ turn intransitive, so a wound itself can ~sanar~ (“heal up”). The bodily sense reaches easily into the moral and social — one may ~sanar~ an economy or a grievance — the way English speaks of healing a rift. From the same ~sānus~ Spanish draws a large family: ~sano~ (“healthy”), ~sanidad~ (“public health”), ~sanación~ (“healing”), ~sanatorio~ (“sanatorium”), and the negated ~insano~ (“unhealthy, insane”), so that the single Latin word for «sound» underlies both medicine and the vocabulary of madness.
en.sancionar:
Spanish ~sancionar~ derives from the noun ~sanción~ plus ~-ar~. ~sanción~ comes from Latin ~sanctiō~ (“a making binding, ordinance”), from the verb ~sancīre~ (“to make sacred, ratify, decree”), which is built on ~sanctus~ (“holy, sacred”) and belongs with ~sacer~ (“consecrated, holy”). All trace to Proto-Indo-European *~seh₂k-~ (“to sanctify, make a treaty”). The same root gives English ~saint~, ~sacred~ and ~sanction~, Italian ~sanzionare~ and French ~sanctionner~.

The original idea was religious: to ~sancīre~ a law was to make it sacred and therefore inviolable, hedged by divine penalty. That double edge survives as a striking quirk — ~sancionar~ is an auto-antonym, meaning both “to approve, ratify” (a law is sanctioned) and “to penalize” (an offender is sanctioned), exactly like English ~sanction~. The penalty half preserves the old sense that breaking a sacred rule invites punishment. From the same *~seh₂k-~ Spanish keeps a visibly religious cluster — ~santo~ (“saint, holy”), ~sagrado~ (“sacred”), ~santificar~ (“to sanctify”) and ~sagrar~ (“to consecrate”).
en.sangrar:
From Old Spanish ~sangrar~, from Latin ~sanguināre~ (“to bleed”), a verb on ~sanguis~ (stem ~sanguin-~, “blood”). The ancestry of ~sanguis~ itself is debated; it is often linked to the Proto-Indo-European word for blood, *~h₁ésh₂r̥~, but the connection is uncertain. It is cognate with Portuguese and Galician ~sangrar~, and — through ~sanguis~ — with English ~sanguine~ and French ~sang~.

The everyday Spanish noun ~sangre~ (“blood”) descends from the same ~sanguis~ by regular sound change, and ~sangrar~ follows it from the literal loss of blood into figurative drains: to ~sangrar~ someone can mean to bleed them of money. In printing, ~sangrar~ came to mean “to indent,” and the noun ~sangría~ names both an old blood-letting and, by the image of red wine drawn off like blood, the familiar drink. Other kin include ~sangriento~ (“bloody”), ~desangrar~ (“to bleed dry”), and the learned ~sanguíneo~ (“sanguine, of the blood”), a whole family rooted in one Latin word for blood.
en.santiguar:
From Latin ~sanctificāre~ (“to make holy, to sanctify”), a compound of ~sanctus~ (“holy”) and ~facere~ (“to make”); ~sanctus~ derives from ~sancīre~ (“to consecrate, to make binding”), from Proto-Indo-European *~seh₂k-~ (“to sanctify, to make a pact”). Through ordinary popular wear ~sanctificāre~ contracted to ~santiguar~, while the same Latin verb, taken later from books, gave the learned doublet ~santificar~. It is cognate — through ~sanctus~ — with English ~saint~ and ~sanctify~.

The learned ~santificar~ keeps the broad sense “to make holy,” but the inherited ~santiguar~ narrowed to a single concrete rite: to bless by tracing the cross, and reflexively ~santiguarse~, “to cross oneself.” The gesture stands so vividly for shock that ~santiguarse~ can mean to be aghast. From the same ~sanctus~ Spanish holds ~santo~ (“saint; holy”), ~santidad~ (“holiness”), ~santuario~ (“sanctuary”), and ~santiguamiento~ (the act of crossing oneself), a devotional family grown from one root meaning to set apart as sacred.
en.satisfacer:
From Latin ~satisfacere~ (“to do enough, satisfy”), a compound of ~satis~ (“enough”) and ~facere~ (“to do, make”). ~satis~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~seh₂-~ (“to satiate, be full”) and ~facere~ to *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, do”). Cognate with Italian ~soddisfare~, French ~satisfaire~, and Portuguese ~satisfazer~; English took ~satisfy~ through Old French. Surprisingly, English ~sad~ belongs to the same *~seh₂-~ family — its original sense was “sated, full” — while ~facere~ shares its root with English ~do~.

The compound is transparent: to satisfy a debt, a creditor, or a hunger is to do (~facere~) enough (~satis~) to meet it. Roman law used ~satisfacere~ for discharging an obligation, and that legal weight survives in the modern range of ~satisfacer~ — to satisfy a person, a requirement, or a curiosity. Like ~hacer~, it conjugates irregularly (~satisfago~, ~satisfizo~, ~satisfaré~). Its family includes ~satisfacción~, ~satisfactorio~, and the past participle ~satisfecho~ (“satisfied, content”). From ~satis~ alone Spanish also drew ~saciar~ (“to sate”) and ~saturar~ (“to saturate”), and the archaic ~asaz~ (“enough”), from ~ad~ ~satis~.
en.secar:
From Latin ~siccāre~ (“to dry, drain”), from the adjective ~siccus~ (“dry”). The deeper history is debated: ~siccus~ is generally traced to Proto-Italic *~siskʷos~ and, more tentatively, to a Proto-Indo-European root reconstructed variously as *~seyk-~ or *~seikʷ-~ (“to dry up, flow out”) — the sources disagree, so the exact Indo-European etymon is best called uncertain. Cognate with Italian ~seccare~, French ~sécher~, and Portuguese ~secar~; the learned English ~desiccate~ keeps the ~siccus~ root intact.

The adjective ~siccus~ came into Spanish as ~seco~ (“dry”), and from ~seco~ the everyday verb ~secar~ was formed. Around them clusters a dry little family: ~sequía~ (“drought”), ~desecar~ (“to drain, dry out”), ~secano~ (“unirrigated land”), ~sequedad~ (“dryness”), and ~resecar~ (“to parch”). A pleasing survival is the wine sense: a ~seco~ wine is a dry one, and the very same Latin adjective, by way of French ~sec~, gives English ~sec~ on a label of dry champagne — one adjective for parched fields and for a crisp glass alike.
en.secuestrar:
From Latin ~sequestrāre~ (“to place in safekeeping, sequester”), from ~sequester~ (“a trustee, a neutral depositary”), a form tied to the preposition ~secus~ (“alongside, otherwise”) and ultimately to ~sequī~ (“to follow”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). Cognate with Italian ~sequestrare~, French ~séquestrer~ and Portuguese ~sequestrar~, and — through the same stem — with English ~sequester~.

In Roman law ~sequestrāre~ meant to place a disputed object in the hands of an impartial third party until a court decided who owned it; the ~sequester~ was that trusted go-between. Spanish preserved this strictly legal sense for centuries — to impound or attach property — and the violent modern meaning “to seize a person and demand a ransom” is a late arrival, recorded by the Academy only in 1884. From the same root ~sequī~ Spanish also drew ~secuaz~ (“follower”), ~séquito~ (“retinue”), ~consecuente~ and ~secta~ — a whole family built on the idea of following.
en.segar:
From Latin ~secāre~ (“to cut”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut”). It passed regularly into Old Spanish as ~segar~, narrowing toward the field sense “to reap, to mow.” It is cognate with Italian ~segare~ and Portuguese and Catalan ~segar~, and — through *~sek-~ — with English ~saw~ (the tool), ~scythe~, ~section~, and ~segment~.

Where Latin ~secāre~ meant any cutting, Spanish ~segar~ specialized to the swing of the blade through standing grain or grass, and from that comes the vivid figurative ~segar~ (“to cut short”), as a life or a hope is mowed down. The harvest itself is the noun ~siega~, and the reaper is the ~segador~. The learned side of *~sek-~ gave Spanish ~sección~, ~segmento~, ~secante~, and ~disecar~ (“to dissect”), so that the humble verb for mowing a meadow shares its deepest root with the vocabulary of surgery and geometry.
en.seguir:
From Vulgar Latin *~sequēre~, a reshaping of the Latin deponent ~sequī~ (“to follow”), from Proto-Italic *~sekʷōr~, from Proto-Indo-European *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). The root is deep and wide: cognate with Sanskrit ~sácate~, Ancient Greek ~hépomai~ (“I follow”), and, in the Romance line, Italian ~seguire~, French ~suivre~, and Portuguese ~seguir~. English draws on the same root through Latin borrowings like ~sequence~, ~sequel~, ~second~, and ~pursue~.

Beyond plain “to follow,” Spanish ~seguir~ took on “to continue, to keep on” — « sigo esperando », “I’m still waiting” — so the verb tracks both a person and an action through time. The prefixed compounds are especially productive: ~conseguir~ (“to obtain,” literally to follow through to the end), ~perseguir~ (“to pursue, to persecute”), ~proseguir~ (“to carry on”), and ~subsiguiente~ (“subsequent”). From the same PIE root, through other Latin stems, Spanish also inherited ~secuencia~, ~consecuencia~, ~séquito~ (“retinue”), and ~ejecutar~ (“to execute”).
en.seleccionar:
From the noun ~selección~ (“selection”), a learned borrowing of Latin ~sēlēctiō~ (“a picking out, choice”), the action noun of ~sēligere~ (“to pick out, select”). ~sēligere~ is itself a compound of ~sē-~ (“apart, aside”) and ~legere~ (“to gather, collect,” later “to read”). ~legere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, collect”). The root’s most famous cognate is Ancient Greek ~légō~ (“I gather; I say”) and its offspring ~lógos~ (“word, reason”). The verb ~seleccionar~ itself is a modern denominal — Spanish built it from ~selección~ rather than inheriting it whole — paralleled by Italian ~selezionare~, French ~sélectionner~ and Portuguese ~selecionar~.

The heart of the word is ~legere~’s gathering: to select is to gather items apart from the rest, picking out the chosen few. That gathering-and-choosing sense radiates widely. From ~legere~ Spanish holds ~leer~ (“to read,” gathering letters with the eye), ~elegir~ (“to choose”), ~colegir~ (“to infer, gather”), ~colección~ (“collection”), ~elección~ (“election”), ~lector~ (“reader”) and ~legible~ (“legible”). The same root, through Latin ~intellegere~ (“to discern, gather between”) and ~dīligere~ (“to single out, esteem”), gave ~inteligente~ and ~diligente~. And through Greek ~lógos~ it seeded the whole family of ~-logía~ sciences. To ~seleccionar~ a team, then, is to do in the stadium what a reader does on the page: gather the best and set them apart.
en.sellar:
From ~sello~ (“seal, stamp”) + ~-ar~; ~sello~ derives from Latin ~sigillum~ (“a small figure, statuette; seal, signet”), the diminutive of ~signum~ (“sign, mark, token, military standard”). A ~sello~ is thus, at root, a “little sign.” The deeper origin of ~signum~ is uncertain. Cognate developments include Italian ~sigillo~, French ~sceller~, and Portuguese ~selar~; English ~seal~ (through Old French ~seel~) and the learned ~sigil~ come from the same ~sigillum~, while through ~signum~ the word is kin to English ~sign~, ~signal~, and ~ensign~.

To ~sellar~ began as pressing a ~sello~ into wax or clay to authenticate a document — the mark of the signet ring — and then radiated outward: to stamp, to affix a postage ~sello~, and figuratively to close something up tight or fix it beyond change, as in ~sellar~ un pacto (“to seal a pact”) or labios ~sellados~ (“sealed lips”). From ~signum~ Spanish grew a large family: ~signo~, ~señal~ and ~señalar~, ~seña~, ~diseñar~, ~designar~, ~asignar~, and ~insignia~. The humble postage stamp and the solemn sealed covenant are, etymologically, the same “little sign” pressed onto a surface.
en.sembrar:
From Latin ~sēmināre~ (“to sow, to plant”), the verb of ~sēmen~ (“seed”), from Proto-Indo-European *~seh₁-~ (“to sow, to scatter seed”). Old Spanish ~sembrar~ shows the regular Vulgar Latin shift of ~-mn-~ to ~-mbr-~ (just as ~homine(m)~ became ~hombre~). Cognate with Italian ~seminare~, French ~semer~ and Portuguese ~semear~, and — through the same root — with English ~seed~, ~sow~ and ~semen~, and Latin's own ~satiō~ (“a sowing”).

The metaphor was there from the start: to ~sembrar~ has meant, since antiquity, both to scatter grain in a furrow and to scatter anything that will later spring up — discord, doubt, hope. Spanish is rich in the literal family: ~semilla~ (“seed”), ~siembra~ (“the sowing; the sown field”), ~sembrado~, ~semen~ and the learned ~seminario~ (“seminary,” a seed-bed for training). The proverb about the one who ~siembra~ winds and reaps storms keeps the figurative sense alive in daily speech.
en.semejar:
From Vulgar Latin *~similiāre~ (“to be like”), a verb built on Latin ~similis~ (“like, similar”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sem-~ (“one; together, as one”). It came down to Old Spanish as ~semejar~ and is a near-doublet of the learned ~simular~. It is cognate with Portuguese ~semelhar~ and Italian ~somigliare~, and — through French ~sembler~ — with English ~resemble~; the same *~sem-~ underlies English ~same~ and ~similar~.

The root idea of oneness became the idea of matching: things that ~semejar~ are, so to speak, of one kind. Beside plain ~semejar~ (“to resemble”) Spanish uses the reflexive ~asemejarse~ and the very common ~parecerse~ for the same notion. From ~similis~ and its kin come ~semejante~ (“similar; fellow human being”), ~semejanza~ (“resemblance”), ~símil~ (“simile”), and ~semblante~ (“face, look”), while *~sem-~ also fed ~ensamblar~ (“to assemble”) and ~sencillo~ (“simple”) — a wide family spun from the single thought of sameness.
en.sentar:
From Vulgar Latin *~sedentāre~, a verb built on ~sedēns~ (genitive ~sedentis~), the present participle of Latin ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sed-~ (“to sit”). That root is one of the most widespread in the family: it gave English ~sit~ and ~seat~ (via Old English ~sittan~), German ~sitzen~, and the Latin ~sedēre~ that also partly underlies Spanish ~ser~. Portuguese ~sentar~ and Italian ~sedere~ are Romance kin.

Spanish turned the participle into a fresh verb: *~sedentāre~ meant “to cause to be sitting,” which is exactly what ~sentar~ does — you ~sientas~ a guest at the table. The same “sit” root produced a large and varied family: ~sede~ (“seat, see”), ~sesión~ (“a sitting”), ~sedimento~ (what settles), ~sedentario~, ~asentar~, ~presidir~ (“to sit in front of”) and ~residir~. Even ~silla~ (“chair”) descends, through ~sella~, from this root.
en.sentenciar:
From the noun ~sentencia~ (“sentence, judgment”), from Latin ~sententia~ (“opinion, judgment, verdict”), from ~sentīre~ (“to feel, perceive, be of the opinion”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sent-~ (“to head for, to sense a direction”). That root's path from going to sensing is preserved on the Germanic side, where it yielded English ~send~ (“to cause to go”), while the Latin branch turned inward to feeling — so ~sentenciar~ and English ~send~ are, remarkably, cousins. English also borrowed the Latin side heavily, as ~sentence~, ~sense~, and ~sentiment~; Romance kept the verb as Italian ~sentenziare~, French ~sentencier~, and Portuguese ~sentenciar~.

The semantic drift is a small drama of the courtroom. ~Sententia~ began as an “opinion,” what one feels or thinks; a judge's opinion became a formal verdict; and pronouncing that verdict became ~sentenciar~ — “to sentence, to pass judgment.” The same noun, on another branch, gave English the grammatical ~sentence~ and the adjective ~sententious~ (“fond of terse maxims”). The root verb ~sentīre~ anchors a broad Spanish family of feeling and perceiving: ~sentir~, ~sentido~, ~sentimiento~, ~consentir~, ~presentir~, ~disentir~, and the learned ~sensato~ and ~sensible~ all flow from the same ancient sense of heading toward and perceiving.
en.sentir:
From Latin ~sentīre~ (“to feel, perceive, be of an opinion”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sent-~, reconstructed with the sense “to head for, go, find one’s way.” It is cognate with Italian ~sentire~, Portuguese ~sentir~ and French ~sentir~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~sense~, ~sentiment~ and ~scent~; through Germanic the root also gives English ~send~ and German ~Sinn~ (“sense, mind”) and ~senden~ (“to send”).

The semantic leap from “to go” to “to feel” is striking: to perceive was, on this reconstruction, to “find one’s way” mentally toward a thing — to discern it. Latin ~sentīre~ already spanned bodily sensation, emotion and judgment, a breadth Spanish ~sentir~ keeps (“to feel” and “to be sorry”). From the same stem come ~sentido~ (“sense, meaning”), ~sentimiento~ (“feeling”), ~sensación~ (via ~sēnsus~), ~consentir~ (“to consent”), ~presentir~ (“to have a foreboding”) and ~sensato~ (“sensible”).
en.separar:
Spanish ~separar~ comes from Latin ~sēparāre~ (“to pull apart, divide”), a compound of ~sē-~ (“apart, aside”) and ~parāre~ (“to make ready, prepare”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to produce, procure”). Cognates include Italian ~separare~, French ~séparer~, and Portuguese ~separar~; and from ~parāre~ alone come Spanish ~parar~ and ~preparar~ and English ~prepare~.

The image behind ~sēparāre~ is homely: to “make ready apart,” to arrange things each on its own side. From Latin, French produced a second, popularized descendant, ~sevrer~ (“to wean”), and English borrowed its Frenchified doublet ~sever~ (“to cut off”), so ~separate~ and ~sever~ are ultimately the same word wearing different clothes. English ~several~ (“distinct,” then “more than one”) belongs to the family too. Spanish descendants cluster thickly: ~separación~ (“separation”), ~inseparable~ (“inseparable”), ~separata~ (“offprint”), and the noun ~separo~ used in Mexico for a holding cell.
en.ser:
Spanish ~ser~ descends, in its commonest forms, from Latin ~esse~ (“to be”), which reaches back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁es-~ (“to be”). That root also gave Italian ~essere~, French ~être~, and the English verb itself — ~is~ and ~am~ — as well as German ~ist~. From the Latin present ~esse~ Spanish keeps ~soy~, ~es~, and ~son~; but the paradigm is famously stitched together, and several of its everyday forms descend not from ~esse~ at all.

The present indicative (~soy~, ~eres~, ~es~, ~somos~, ~sois~, ~son~) and the imperfect (~era~, from Latin ~eram~) continue ~esse~ — though ~eres~ is a curiosity, descending from the Latin future ~eris~ (“you will be”), pressed into a present to keep it distinct from ~es~. A second donor, ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from *~sed-~, supplied the infinitive ~ser~ itself (through Old Spanish ~seer~), the future and conditional (~seré~, ~sería~), the present subjunctive (~sea~), and the imperative (~sé~) — so the very name of the verb means, etymologically, “to sit.” A third donor, the Latin perfect ~fuī~, from *~bʰuH-~ (“to become, grow”), gave the preterite (~fui~, ~fuiste~, ~fue~) — forms shared identically with ~ir~ (“to go”), so that ~fui~ means both “I was” and “I went,” context alone deciding.

From the ~esse~ / *~h₁es-~ side comes a wide family of learned words: ~ente~, ~esencia~, ~presente~, ~ausente~, and ~interés~. From ~sedēre~ (“to sit”) comes another cluster built on the idea of sitting or settling: ~sede~ (“seat, see”), ~sentar~, ~sesión~, and ~residir~. The suppletion that looks so chaotic in the paradigm is, in the vocabulary, two tidy word-families braided into one verb.
en.seriar:
Spanish ~seriar~ (“to arrange in a series; to mass-produce”) is built on ~serie~ (“series”), a learned borrowing from Latin ~seriēs~ (“a row, a chain, a succession”). That noun comes from the verb ~serere~ (“to join, to link, to string together”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ser-~ (“to line up, to bind in a row”). English took the noun directly as ~series~ and ~serial~, and the same Latin verb underlies English ~sermon~ — literally a “stringing-together” of words. Deeper still, the root shows in Ancient Greek ~eírō~ (“to fasten in rows, to string together”).

To ~seriar~ is to put things in a line — and, in the industrial age, to make them one after another off a production line, so that ~seriar~ came to mean serial manufacture and ~seriado~ describes anything made in series. The threading metaphor runs through the family: to ~insertar~ is to “string in,” to ~disertar~ (“to discourse”) is to string arguments in a row, to ~desertar~ is to unstring oneself from the ranks, and an ~aserción~ (“assertion”) is a claim joined firmly on. From a TV ~serie~ to a factory’s serial output, all of it is threaded on the same ancient string.
en.servir:
From Latin ~servīre~ (“to be a slave, to serve”), derived from ~servus~ (“slave, servant”). There the trail grows faint: the origin of ~servus~ is uncertain. It is usually traced to Proto-Italic *~serwos~ and compared with Umbrian ~seritu~, and it has sometimes been proposed as an Etruscan borrowing, but no account is secure, so the deeper root is best left open. The verb passed intact into Italian ~servire~, French ~servir~, and Portuguese ~servir~.

In Rome ~servīre~ meant literally to live in bondage; as that social reality faded, the word softened into today's neutral senses of waiting on someone, serving food, and — in ~servir~ para algo — simply being useful. A caution for the curious: Latin ~servāre~ (“to keep, to guard”), the source of ~conservar~ and ~observar~, springs from a different root and is not a relative, despite the resemblance. The genuine family of ~servus~ includes ~siervo~, ~servicio~, ~servil~, ~servidumbre~, and ~servidor~; its present participle ~servientem~ gave both Spanish ~sirviente~ and, by a long detour through French, English ~sergeant~.
en.señalar:
A denominative from ~señal~ (“sign, mark, signal”), which comes from Late Latin ~signālis~ (“of a sign”), from Latin ~signum~ (“mark, sign, military standard”). The root of ~signum~ is genuinely disputed: one account derives it from Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut”), making a sign “something cut or carved”; another from *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow,” as in Latin ~sequī~), making it “the standard the troops follow.” The forms are cognate with Italian ~segnalare~, French ~signaler~ and English ~signal~ and ~sign~.

From ~signālis~ Spanish built the noun ~señal~ and then the verb ~señalar~, “to mark” and hence “to point out, indicate.” Because the deeper origin is unsettled, the vivid “a sign is something carved” reading should be offered only as one contested hypothesis, not as fact. The same ~signum~ radiates through Spanish: ~seña~ (“gesture, sign”), ~signo~, ~diseñar~ (“to design,” via Italian) and, most surprisingly, ~enseñar~ (“to teach”), from Latin ~īnsignāre~, literally “to mark in, imprint.”
en.significar:
Spanish ~significar~ was borrowed from Latin ~significāre~ (“to make a sign, to indicate”), a transparent compound of ~signum~ (“sign, mark, token”) and ~-ficāre~, the combining form of ~facere~ (“to make, do,” from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~, “to put, place”). So the word means, literally, “to make a sign.” The deeper root of ~signum~ itself is disputed: it is traced to Proto-Italic *~seknom~ and thence either to Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut”) or to *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), and the sources do not settle between them. It is cognate with Italian ~significare~, French ~signifier~ and English ~signify~.

If ~signum~ began as a “cut” mark or a “follow” token, both readings suit a sign — a notch scored into a surface, or the trail one follows. From “to make a sign” the verb moved naturally to “to be a sign of,” that is “to mean”; a word ~significa~ something the way a symptom signifies a disease. The ~signum~ family is one of the richest in Spanish. Popular descent gave ~seña~ (“sign”), ~señal~ (“signal”) and ~señalar~ (“to point out”); learned borrowing gave ~signo~, ~significado~ (“meaning”), ~insignia~, and — through ~dēsignāre~ — ~diseñar~ (“to design”). All of them are still, at heart, about setting down a mark that stands for something else.
en.silbar:
From Latin ~sībilāre~ (“to whistle, to hiss”), a frequentative of ~sībilus~ (“a hissing, a whistling”), a word of imitative origin ultimately traced to Proto-Indo-European *~sweysd-~ (“to whistle, hiss”). In Old Spanish the verb appeared as ~silvar~ and ~siblar~; syncope of the short vowel and metathesis of the liquid produced modern ~silbar~. A more expressive Vulgar Latin variant of the same root gave ~chiflar~ (“to whistle”). It is cognate with the learned English ~sibilate~ and with Portuguese ~silvar~.

The sense stayed remarkably stable for two millennia, from the hiss of a snake or the wind to the sharp whistle of a person or a referee. Spanish also gave it a theatrical use: to ~silbar~ a play or a bullfighter is to whistle it down — to jeer. The imitative stem stayed productive, yielding the noun ~silbato~ (“whistle,” the instrument), ~silbido~ (“a whistle, a whistling sound”), and the technical ~sibilante~ (“sibilant”), a linguist's term for hissing consonants.
en.simplificar:
From Medieval Latin ~simplificāre~ (“to make simple”), a compound of ~simplus~/~simplex~ (“simple, single”) and ~facere~ (“to make, do”). ~Simplex~ is itself ~sem-~ (“one, single”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sem-~ (“one, together”), plus ~-plex~ (“-fold”), from *~pleḱ-~ (“to fold, plait”) — literally “one-fold,” the opposite of ~duplex~ (“two-fold”) and ~complex~ (“folded together”). ~Facere~ descends from *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, make”). Through these roots ~simplificar~ is cognate with English ~-fold~, ~ply~, and ~plait~, with Greek ~plékō~ (“to weave”), and with English ~do~ and ~fact~.

The metaphor buried in ~simplificar~ is textile: what is ~simplex~ is folded only once, a single ply, while what is ~complex~ has been folded together and ~duplex~ folded in two. To simplify, then, is to reduce the folds. Latin ~simplus~ reached Spanish along two roads at once, giving a classic doublet: the learned, borrowed ~simple~ and the inherited, popularly worn-down ~sencillo~ (from Vulgar Latin *~simpliciellus~) — the same Latin word arriving twice, once through scholars and once through centuries of everyday speech. Around them cluster ~simpleza~, ~simplicidad~, and ~simplón~, all turning on the idea of the single fold.
en.situar:
From Late Latin ~situāre~ (“to place, locate, set in position”), formed on Latin ~situs~ (“site, position, situation”), which is the past participle of the verb ~sinere~ (“to let, allow; to set down, lay”). De Vaan traces ~sinere~ to a Proto-Indo-European root *~tḱey-~ (“to settle, build”), the same root behind Sanskrit ~kṣéti~ (“he dwells”). Because ~situs~ passed into the Romance languages and into learned Latin borrowings alike, its offspring are widespread: English ~site~ and ~situate~, French ~site~, Italian ~sito~, and Portuguese ~sítio~ all stand beside Spanish ~sitio~.

The chain hides a quiet irony: ~sinere~ meant “to let be, leave alone,” so a ~situs~ was first a place where something had simply been left — and one old sense of Latin ~situs~ was precisely the “neglect, mold, decay” that settles on a thing left untouched. Medieval clerks turned the noun back into the verb ~situāre~, “to give a thing its place,” and Spanish inherited it as ~situar~. From the same noun Spanish keeps ~sitio~ (“place; also a military siege,” a spot one occupies and holds) and ~situación~ (“situation”), while the reflexive ~situarse~ means to find or position oneself. What began as land left to itself became the vocabulary of putting things deliberately in their place.
en.sobar:
Spanish ~sobar~ (“to knead, to rub, to fondle”) is of disputed origin, marked uncertain in the standard dictionaries. Corominas proposed that it descends from a Vulgar Latin ~subagere~, a remaking of Classical Latin ~subigere~ (“to work from below, to knead, to subdue”) under the influence of the simplex ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”); regular loss of the intervocalic velar and the opening of the vowel of ~sub-~ would yield ~sobar~. A competing proposal derives it instead from Latin ~subāre~ (“to be in heat”), which would explain the amorous nuance. It is cognate with Portuguese ~sovar~.

The medieval record is telling: in Old Spanish, from the eleventh century, ~sobar~ most often meant “to beat, to thrash,” a sense that fits the “work from below, subdue” reading of ~subagere~. Only later did the gentler senses of “to knead” and “to massage” — and the colloquial “to fondle, to grope” — come to the fore. Its derivatives are few and homely: ~sobo~ and ~sobadura~ (“a rubbing, a kneading”) and the adjective ~sobado~ (“well-worn, trite”).
en.sobrar:
~sobrar~ comes from Latin ~superare~ (“to rise above, surpass, be in excess”), a verb built directly on the preposition and preverb ~super~ (“above, over”), from Proto-Indo-European *~uper~ (“over, above”). The learned doublet ~superar~ (“to overcome, surpass”) was borrowed straight from the same Latin verb centuries later, so Spanish carries both the inherited and the bookish descendant side by side. It is cognate with Portuguese ~sobrar~ and Italian ~superare~, and — through the same root — with English ~over~ and the prefix ~super-~, and with Greek ~hyper~.

The Latin verb meant “to go over the top” — to climb higher, to overcome, and hence to be more than enough. Spanish kept the last shade: what ~sobra~ is what remains once need is met, so ~sobrar~ is “to be left over” and, of a person, “to be one too many” — the pointed ~aquí sobras~ (“you are not wanted here”). The noun ~sobra~ gives ~las sobras~ (“leftovers”) and the handy phrase ~de sobra~ (“more than enough; only too well”). From the same ~super~ come ~soberano~, ~sobrepasar~, the prefix ~sobre-~ and, through Latin ~superbia~, the deadly sin ~soberbia~ (“pride”) — pride being, quite literally, an excess.
en.sobrevivir:
From ~sobre-~ (“over, beyond,” from Latin ~super~) plus ~vivir~ (“to live,” from Latin ~vīvere~), a calque of Latin ~supervivere~ (“to outlive”). ~vīvere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~gʷeyh₃-~ (“to live”). Cognate with Portuguese ~sobreviver~, French ~survivre~ and Italian ~sopravvivere~, and — through ~vīvere~ — with English ~vital~, ~vivid~ and ~revive~; the same PIE root gave Ancient Greek ~bíos~ (“life”) and, in Germanic, the archaic English ~quick~ (“living, alive”).

The literal sense is spatial-turned-temporal: to live beyond a limit — beyond a disaster, an era, or another person — hence “to outlive, survive, endure.” The prefix ~super~ (“over”) itself descends from PIE *~uper~, kin to English ~over~ and Greek ~hyper~. Spanish draws deeply on the ~vīvere~ branch: ~vida~, ~vívido~, ~vital~, ~convivir~, ~revivir~ and ~víveres~ (“provisions”), while ~sobrevivir~ yields ~superviviente~ and ~supervivencia~ — all circling the plain fact of staying alive.
en.socavar:
From Old Spanish ~socavar~, probably from a Vulgar Latin *~subcavāre~ / *~succavāre~, from Latin ~sub-~ (“under”) plus ~cavāre~ (“to hollow out, to excavate”). The verb ~cavāre~ is denominal from the adjective ~cavus~ (“hollow, concave”), from Proto-Italic *~kawāō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱówHwos~ (“hollow, cavity”). By surface analysis it reads as ~so-~ (“under”) plus ~cavar~ (“to dig”). It is cognate with Portuguese ~socavar~, and — through ~cavus~ — with English ~cave~ and ~excavate~ and Italian ~cavo~.

The compound was always concrete and then figurative: to hollow out earth from beneath something — a river ~socava~ its bank, water ~socava~ the foundations of a wall — and then, by natural extension, to undermine an argument, a reputation, or someone's authority. The ~cavus~ family is unusually rich in Spanish: the simplex ~cavar~ (“to dig”), the nouns ~socavón~ (“a sinkhole, a cave-in”), ~socava~ and ~socavación~, and, from the learned line, ~cavidad~ (“cavity”), ~caverna~ (“cavern”), and ~excavar~ (“to excavate”).
en.soler:
Spanish ~soler~ was inherited through Old Spanish ~soler~ from Latin ~solēre~ (“to be accustomed, to be wont”). Its deeper origin is disputed. One tradition (Walde-Hoffmann, Pokorny) reconstructs Proto-Italic *~sweðēō~ and a Proto-Indo-European *~swé-dʰh₁-~, literally “to set as one's own,” from *~swé~ (“self”) plus *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place”); on this account ~solēre~ would be close kin to ~sodālis~ (“companion”) and ~suēscō~ (“to grow accustomed”). De Vaan rejects that derivation on sound grounds — a following ~ē~ should have blocked the shift *~swe-~ > ~so-~ — and looks instead toward *~sel-~ / ~solum~ (“ground, base”). The safe statement is that ~solēre~ is old and its ultimate root unsettled. It is cognate with Italian ~solere~ and Catalan ~soler~, and with the now-archaic Portuguese ~soer~.

In Spanish ~soler~ became a pure habit-marker, an auxiliary that adds “usually” to whatever verb follows: ~suele~ llover (“it usually rains”), ~solíamos~ caminar (“we used to walk”). Fittingly for a verb about the customary, it is itself defective, living almost entirely in the present and the imperfect — one rarely meets it in the future or the preterite, because a one-off habit is a contradiction. The “custom” sense is preserved beautifully in a common relative: ~insólito~ (“unusual, extraordinary”), from Latin ~insolitus~, literally “un-accustomed” — what does not usually happen. Beside it stand the rarer ~sólito~ (“customary”) and ~desueto~ / ~desuetud~ (“disused, desuetude”). Thus a single Latin verb of habit gave Spanish both its everyday word for “to usually do” and its bookish word for what breaks all habit.
en.solicitar:
Spanish ~solicitar~ comes from Latin ~sollicitāre~ (“to disturb, stir up, agitate”), a verb built on the adjective ~sollicitus~ (“thoroughly moved, anxious, worried”). That adjective is transparent: ~sollus~ (“whole, entire”) plus ~citus~ (“set in motion, roused”), the past participle of ~ciēre~ (“to move, stir”). ~sollus~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~solh₂-~ (“whole”), the root behind Greek ~hólos~ (“whole,” as in ~holo-~) and Latin ~salvus~ (“safe”); ~ciēre~ reflects *~keyh₁-~ (“to set in motion”). English borrowed the family directly: ~solicit~, ~solicitous~, and ~solicitude~ all sit beside the Spanish verb.

The literal Latin sense was physical agitation — to shake something thoroughly, to trouble it entirely. From “to disturb, importune” the meaning softened into “to entreat, petition,” and Spanish ~solicitar~ now spans a polite request (~solicitar una beca~, “to apply for a scholarship”), a formal application, and the still-charged ~solicitar a alguien~ (“to court or proposition someone”), where the old sense of stirring another person up survives. The past participle gave ~solícito~ (“attentive, obliging”) and the noun ~solicitud~ (“request; application; solicitude”). Through the same root *~solh₂-~ Spanish also holds ~sólido~, ~salvo~, ~salud~, and ~católico~ (from Greek ~katholikós~, “universal, on the whole”).
en.soltar:
From Vulgar Latin *~soltāre~, a verb built on ~suelto~ (“loose, released”), which descends from ~solŭtus~, a Vulgar Latin variant of Classical ~solūtus~ (“loosened, freed”), the past participle of ~solvere~ (“to loosen, release, dissolve”). ~solvere~ joins the separative prefix ~se-~ to ~luere~ (“to loosen”), from Proto-Indo-European *~lewH-~ (“to cut apart, loosen”). It is cognate with Portuguese ~soltar~; through ~solvere~ it is kin to English ~solve~, ~dissolve~ and ~solution~; and through the PIE root, to Ancient Greek ~λύω~ (“I loosen”) and ~λύσις~ (“a loosening”), the ancestor of analysis and dialysis.

Latin had no simple verb *soltāre; Spanish minted its own from the participle-turned-adjective ~suelto~, so the sense stayed close to “to let loose”: to release, untie, set free, and figuratively to blurt out (soltar una carcajada, to burst out laughing). From the same ~solvere~ family come ~absolver~, ~disolver~, ~resolver~, ~soltura~ and ~solución~. The adjective ~soltero~ (“unmarried, single”) is traditionally attached to this family — the single person as one who is “unbound” — but it may instead descend from Latin ~solitarius~ (“solitary, alone”); the two forms clearly influenced each other, and the sources do not fully settle the matter.
en.solucionar:
A modern verb built on the noun ~solución~ (“solution”), from Latin ~solutio~ (“a loosening, dissolving”), from ~solvere~ (“to loosen, release, dissolve”), itself ~se-~ (“apart”) plus ~luere~ (“to loosen, wash”), from Proto-Indo-European *~lewh₃-~ (“to wash, loosen”). Cognate through Latin with English ~solve~, ~dissolve~ and ~absolute~, and with French ~solution~.

Latin ~solvere~ combined the separative ~se-~ with ~luere~, so to solve was literally to loosen or untie a bind. Its past participle ~solutus~ gave Spanish ~suelto~ (“loose”) and a learned family: ~soluble~, ~solvente~, ~absolver~, ~disolver~ and ~resolver~. The noun ~solución~ held both senses at once — a substance dissolved in liquid, and a knotty problem untied — and only in the modern era did Spanish coin the everyday verb ~solucionar~ from it, beside the older ~resolver~.
en.someter:
From Latin ~submittere~ (“to place under, lower, let down; to subject”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, let go”). It is thus a close sibling of ~committere~ above, built on the same ~mittere~, which traces through Proto-Italic *~meitō~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange”), an extension of *~mey-~ (“to change”). Spanish ~someter~ is the inherited reflex; alongside it the language kept learned forms from the participle ~submissus~. Romance cognates include French ~soumettre~ and Italian ~sottomettere~ / ~sommettere~, and English ~submit~ comes from the same ~submittere~.

The literal picture is spatial: to “send under” is to bring beneath one’s power — hence ~someter~ “to subdue, subject, put down (a revolt),” and reflexively ~someterse~ “to submit, yield, give in.” The verb keeps a useful ambiguity English splits between “subdue” (imposing from above) and “submit” (yielding from below), the difference lying only in who does the sending-under. From the participle ~submissus~ came the learned pair ~sumiso~ (“submissive, meek”) and ~sumisión~ (“submission, obedience”), which sit beside ~sometimiento~ (“subjection”) built on the verb. It is a nice symmetry of Latin word-building that ~sub-~ + ~mittere~ (“send under”) and ~com-~ + ~mittere~ (“send together”) should have travelled into Spanish as the near-rhyming ~someter~ and ~cometer~, two prefixes turning one humble verb of “sending” to opposite ends.
en.sonar:
~sonar~ descends from Latin ~sonāre~ (“to make a sound, resound”), a verb from the noun ~sonus~ (“sound, noise”). ~sonus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~swonos~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~swenh₂-~ (“to sound, resound”). The most charming cognate is English ~swan~: from Proto-Germanic *~swanaz~, literally “the sounding one, the singing bird.” Sanskrit ~svan~ (“to sound”) and Russian ~zvon~ (“chime, ring”) belong to the same family, and English ~sound~ itself is a borrowing of ~sonus~ through Old French.

Spanish kept the plain sense — bells, instruments, and phones all ~sonar~ — plus idiomatic branches: a name that ~suena~ is one that “rings a bell,” and ~sonarse~ (“to blow one's nose”) trades on the noise. From ~sonus~ and ~sonāre~ spring a large family: ~sonido~ (“sound”), ~sonoro~, ~son~ (“tune,” as in the Cuban dance), ~sonata~ (via Italian), ~resonar~, ~consonante~, and ~sonajero~ (“baby's rattle”).
en.sonreír:
From Latin ~subrīdēre~, from ~sub-~ (“under, slightly”) plus ~rīdēre~ (“to laugh”), whose own origin the sources leave uncertain. The prefix ~sub-~ regularly surfaced in Spanish as ~son-~ before r, giving ~sonreír~ beside plain ~reír~ (“to laugh”). It is cognate with Italian ~sorridere~, French ~sourire~ and Portuguese ~sorrir~; through ~rīdēre~ English shares ~risible~, ~ridicule~ and ~deride~.

The compound is quietly literal: a smile is an “under-laugh,” mirth kept below the full voice of laughter. Because ~rīdēre~ is of unknown origin — some have proposed it is imitative, but the sources do not settle the matter — no confident Indo-European root can be attached here. Within Spanish the same stem yielded the noun ~sonrisa~ (“smile”) beside ~risa~ (“laughter”), plus ~ridículo~, ~irrisorio~ and the participial adjective ~sonriente~ (“smiling”).
en.sopesar:
From Old Spanish ~sopesar~ (mid-thirteenth century), by surface analysis ~so-~ (“sub-, under”) plus ~pesar~ (“to weigh”). The base ~pesar~ descends from Latin ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh carefully, to ponder”), a frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to hang”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull, to stretch, to spin”). It is cognate with Portuguese ~sopesar~, Italian ~soppesare~, and French ~soupeser~, all built on the same “weigh from below” image. Through ~pēnsāre~ it is also a doublet-relative of ~pensar~ (“to think”).

The prefix ~so-~ here is not really “under” but attenuative: to ~sopesar~ is to lift something in the hand to gauge its weight, and hence, figuratively, to weigh up options, evidence, or consequences before deciding. It preserves neatly the old metaphor by which physical weighing became mental judging — the very shift that split ~pesar~ (“to weigh”; also “to cause sorrow”) from its learned doublet ~pensar~ (“to think”). The same root feeds a broad family: ~peso~ (“weight”), ~pesado~ (“heavy”), ~pensión~, ~compensar~, and ~pensativo~ (“thoughtful”).
en.soportar:
From Latin ~supportāre~ (“to carry up, convey, bring”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“up from under”) and ~portāre~ (“to carry”), from Proto-Italic *~portāō~ and ultimately the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to carry across, pass over”). The same verb reached the other Romance languages as French ~supporter~, Italian ~sopportare~, and Portuguese ~suportar~, and English borrowed it, through Old French, as ~support~.

The literal Latin sense was to shoulder a load and carry it upward; from bearing physical weight the verb slid to bearing hardship, and Spanish ~soportar~ now means chiefly “to endure, put up with, tolerate.” This makes it a classic false friend of English ~support~: « no lo puedo ~soportar~ » means “I can’t stand it,” not “I can’t support it.” Spanish keeps the load-bearing sense too — a beam can ~soportar~ a roof — and the noun ~soporte~ means a “stand, bracket, support.” From the same ~portāre~ come a whole convoy of verbs: ~aportar~, ~transportar~, ~importar~, ~exportar~, and ~deportar~.
en.sorprender:
Spanish ~sorprender~ came in from French ~surprendre~ (“to overtake, catch unawares”), a compound of ~sur-~ (“over, upon,” from Latin ~super~) and ~prendre~ (“to take”). ~prendre~ continues Latin ~prehendere~ (“to seize, grasp, catch”), itself ~prae-~ (“before”) plus a verbal element ~-hendere~. That ~-hendere~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵʰend-~ (“to seize, take”), whose scattered kin include Greek ~khandánein~ (“to hold, contain”), Old Norse ~geta~ (“to get, obtain”), and, through Germanic, English ~get~ itself. Because Spanish reshaped the French word on the pattern of its own inherited ~prender~ (“to seize, catch; to catch fire”), the family is doubly present in the language — one branch borrowed, one branch inherited.

The metaphor is vivid and physical: to surprise someone is to “take” them from “over” or “above,” catching them before they can react — the same military image that lets ~sorprender~ mean “to take by surprise, ambush.” From the astonishment sense grew the noun ~sorpresa~ (“a surprise”) and the adjective ~sorprendente~ (“surprising, astonishing”). The inherited ~prender~ side of the family is one of the richest in Spanish: ~prisión~ (“prison”) and ~preso~/~presa~ (“prisoner; prey”) for the “seizing,” ~aprender~ (“to learn,” to “grasp” knowledge), ~comprender~ (“to understand,” to grasp fully), ~emprender~ (“to undertake”), and ~prenda~ (“a garment; a pledge”). English ~prehensile~ and ~comprehend~ preserve the fuller Latin ~-hendere~ that French and Spanish wore away.
en.sortear:
From ~suerte~ (“luck, lot, fortune”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-ear~, or directly from Latin ~sortem~, the accusative of ~sors~ (“a lot; one's lot, fate, fortune”). Latin ~sors~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~sortis~ (“a joining”) and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ser-~ (“to bind, to line up, to arrange in a row”) — the same root behind ~seriēs~ (“series”) and ~sermō~ (“speech”). It is cognate with Italian ~sorte~ and French ~sort~, and — through Old French — with English ~sort~.

The connecting idea is drawing lots: Latin ~sors~ named the token — a chip, a pebble, a slip — cast to let chance or the gods decide, so the word bundled together “lot,” “chance,” and “fate.” From that ~sortear~ took two threads of meaning: to decide something by lot — to raffle or draw — and, by a nice twist, to dodge or get around an obstacle, as if slipping past it by luck. From the same base come ~suerte~, ~sorteo~ (“a draw, a raffle”), ~sortija~ (“a ring”), ~sortilegio~ (“a spell, sorcery”), and ~consorte~ (“consort, spouse”).
en.sosegar:
From Old Spanish ~sessegar~, from a Vulgar Latin *~sessicāre~, a frequentative built on ~sessus~, the past participle of Latin ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sed-~ (“to sit”). The idea is one of settling down, of coming to rest as one does when sitting. It is cognate with Portuguese ~sossegar~ and Galician ~sosegar~, and — through the same PIE root — with English ~sit~ and ~settle~ and the many offspring of Latin ~sedēre~.

The semantic path ran from “to sit” to “to settle, to make still,” and so to “to calm.” In Spanish ~sosegar~ means to quiet, to soothe, to bring to tranquility, and reflexively ~sosegarse~ is to calm down, to settle oneself. Its chief derivative is the noble noun ~sosiego~ (“calm, serenity, repose”), a favorite of Golden Age prose. The wider ~sedēre~ family is vast in Spanish: ~sede~ (“seat, see”), ~sedimento~, ~residir~, ~presidir~, and ~sesión~ (“session”), literally a “sitting.”
en.sospechar:
From Old Spanish ~sospechar~, from Latin ~suspectāre~ (“to look up at, mistrust”), the frequentative of ~suspicere~ (“to look up, look askance at, suspect”), itself ~sub-~ (“under, from below”) plus ~specere~ (“to look, watch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~spek-~ (“to observe”). Cognate with English ~suspect~ (a learned borrowing from the same Latin), French ~suspecter~ and Italian ~sospettare~.

The verb literally pictures someone glancing up from below — a wary, sidelong look for signs of hidden wrongdoing — and that guarded gaze became the abstract sense of mistrust. The Spanish form shows two textbook Castilian sound changes: initial ~sub-~ weakened to ~so-~, and the Latin cluster ~-ct-~ became ~-ch-~, exactly as in ~noctem~ → ~noche~ and ~octo~ → ~ocho~. The same Proto-Indo-European root *~spek-~ seeded a vast Spanish family, among them ~aspecto~, ~espectáculo~, ~inspeccionar~, ~espejo~ (“mirror,” from ~speculum~) and ~espiar~.
en.sostener:
From Latin ~sustinēre~ (“to hold up, support, endure”), from ~sus-~ (a form of ~sub-~, “under, up from under”) plus ~tenēre~ (“to hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate with Italian ~sostenere~, French ~soutenir~, and — through Old French — English ~sustain~.

The image is physical: to hold a thing up from below, and from there to support, maintain, and endure. Spanish ~sostener~ still spans all of these — the same ~sostener~ holds a weight, an argument, or a conversation. The ~tenēre~ core, from *~ten-~ “to stretch,” is one of the most fertile in Spanish, giving ~tener~ (“to have”), ~mantener~ (“to maintain”), ~contener~ (“to contain”), ~detener~ (“to stop”), the noun ~sostén~ (“support”), and — from the “stretched” sense — ~tenso~ and ~tenaz~.
en.soterrar:
From ~tierra~ (“earth, land”), or possibly directly from a Late Latin ~subterrāre~, from Latin ~sub-~ (“under”) plus ~terra~ (“earth, ground, land”); by surface analysis it reads as ~so-~ (“under”) plus an old ~terrar~ (“to earth”). The base ~terra~ is of debated deeper origin, often connected with a Proto-Indo-European root *~ters-~ (“dry”), the notion being dry land as opposed to the sea. It is cognate with Portuguese ~soterrar~ and shares its root with English ~terrace~ and ~terrestrial~.

The compound means to put under the earth: to bury, literally, and by extension to hide away or suppress — a scandal can be ~soterrado~, buried out of sight. In modern engineering ~soterrar~ is the ordinary word for putting cables, pipes, or railways underground. It sits in a large field of Spanish words for earth and burial: ~tierra~, ~enterrar~ (“to bury”), ~desenterrar~ (“to unearth”), ~entierro~ (“burial”), ~subterráneo~ (“underground”), and ~terreno~ (“terrain, plot of land”).
en.soñar:
From Latin ~somniāre~ (“to dream”), from ~somnium~ (“dream”), a derivative of ~somnus~ (“sleep”); both trace to Proto-Indo-European *~swépnos~ (“sleep, dream”) beside the root *~swep-~ (“to sleep”). Cognate with Portuguese ~sonhar~, Italian ~sognare~ and French ~songer~, and — through the same root — with Latin-borrowed English ~somnolent~ and ~insomnia~, Ancient Greek ~hýpnos~ (“sleep”) and even the archaic English ~sweven~ (“a dream”).

Latin distinguished ~somnus~ (“sleep”) from ~somnium~ (“the dream one has while sleeping”), but Castilian let them merge: the single noun ~sueño~ carries both “sleep” and “dream,” so tener ~sueño~ is to be sleepy while tener un ~sueño~ is to have a vision. The verb ~soñar~ followed the dream branch, from literal night-dreaming to the figurative “to long for, imagine” — one ~sueña~ con un mundo mejor. The family is wide: ~soñoliento~, ~ensueño~, ~ensoñación~, ~sonámbulo~ and the learned ~insomnio~ all descend from the same root.
en.subir:
From Latin ~subīre~ (“to go under; to come up, approach; to undergo”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under, up from below”) and ~īre~ (“to go”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”). The Romance descendants split in meaning: Portuguese ~subir~ climbs like Spanish, while Italian ~subire~ means “to undergo, to suffer,” keeping the older “come under” sense.

The paradox is that a verb built on ~sub-~ (“under”) means “to go up.” The bridge is the idea of coming up from underneath, approaching from below — Latin ~subīre~ could mean both “to go under” and “to steal up on.” Spanish generalized the upward reading, so today one ~sube~ a staircase or a price. The same ~sub-~-plus-~īre~ formation gave ~súbito~ (“sudden” — literally “having come up unawares”), and ~īre~ itself seeded ~éxito~ (“success,” a “going out”), ~tránsito~ and ~ambiente~.
en.subrayar:
~subrayar~ is not inherited whole from Latin but built inside Spanish, a parasynthetic compound of ~sub-~ (“under”), the noun ~raya~ (“line, stroke”) and the verb ending ~-ar~ — to “under-line.” ~raya~ descends from Late Latin ~radia~, a feminine formed on ~radius~ (“rod, spoke, ray of light”), in which the ~-di-~ before a vowel palatalized into a Spanish y. The same ~radius~ was borrowed straight into English as ~radius~ and, softened through French, gave English ~ray~.

Latin ~radius~ first named a pointed rod, then the spokes of a wheel and the rays of the sun — all things springing out from a center — and Spanish ~raya~ inherited the plainest of these: a drawn line or stroke. To ~subrayar~ is thus to set a line beneath a word for emphasis, matching English underline and French souligner stroke for stroke. From the same radiant family come ~rayo~ (“ray, lightning bolt”), ~radio~, ~irradiar~, ~radiante~ and the verb ~rayar~ (“to scratch, to rule lines”).
en.suceder:
From Latin ~succēdere~ (“to go under, come up from below, follow after, take the place of”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under, up from below”) and ~cēdere~ (“to go, move, withdraw, yield”). ~cēdere~ comes through Proto-Italic *~kesd-o-~ (“to go away, withdraw”) from a Proto-Indo-European root *~ked-~ (“to go, yield”). Through it ~suceder~ is cognate with a whole rank of English verbs built on ~cēdere~ — ~cede~, ~concede~, ~proceed~, ~recede~, and ~succeed~ itself — and with ~cease~, from the related ~cessāre~. Italian ~succedere~ and French ~succéder~ are its Romance doubles.

The literal picture is of one thing moving up into the place another has vacated — which is why ~succēdere~ meant at once “to follow after” and “to take over from.” Spanish kept the ‘follow/inherit’ thread in ~sucesor~ (“successor”) and ~sucesión~, but its most common modern sense drifted further: because what follows in time is what next occurs, ~suceder~ came to mean simply “to happen.” Hence the noun ~suceso~ — not a ‘success’ (that false friend trips English speakers) but an “event, occurrence.” The same ~cēdere~ root threads through ~ceder~ (“to yield”), ~exceder~ (“to exceed”), ~proceder~ (“to proceed”), and ~acceder~ (“to accede”). To ask ¿qué ~sucede~? is to ask what is coming up next from below.
en.sudar:
Inherited from Latin ~sūdāre~ (“to sweat”), a denominative from ~sūdor~ (“sweat”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sweyd-~ (“to sweat”). This is one of the oldest and best-attested Indo-European roots for a bodily function, and its cognates are strikingly transparent: English ~sweat~ (Old English ~swāt~), German ~schwitzen~, Ancient Greek ~ἱδρώς~ (~hidrṓs~), and Sanskrit ~svedate~. Spanish kept the verb almost unchanged from Latin ~sūdāre~.

The meaning has stayed literal — to perspire — while Spanish grew a lively figurative crop around effort and hardship: ~sudar~ la gota gorda is to sweat buckets, to work extremely hard, and ~sudar~ tinta (“to sweat ink”) means to slave over something. The root's descendants in Spanish include ~sudor~ (“sweat”), ~sudoración~ (“sweating, perspiration”), ~sudadera~ (“sweatshirt”), and the somber ~sudario~ (“shroud, sudarium”), the cloth that wiped a sweating brow — famously the Shroud of Turin, the ~Santo Sudario~.
en.sufrir:
From Old Spanish ~sofrir~, from Vulgar Latin *~sufferīre~ (a re-conjugated form), from Latin ~sufferre~ (“to bear up under, endure”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, bear”). Romance kept the compound: French ~souffrir~, Italian ~soffrire~, Portuguese ~sofrer~; English borrowed ~suffer~ through Anglo-Norman, while the same root *~bʰer-~ gives inherited English ~bear~.

The image is bodily: ~sufferre~ joins ~sub-~ (“under”) to ~ferre~ (“carry”), so to suffer is to bear a load from beneath, to hold up under weight; the sense drifted from “endure, tolerate” to “undergo pain,” though Spanish ~sufrir~ still keeps the older “put up with.” ~ferre~ was one of Latin's great verb-forges, yielding Spanish ~referir~, ~transferir~, ~preferir~, and even ~ofrecer~ (from ~offerre~), plus the adjective ~fértil~ (“bearing, fruitful”). Through *~bʰer-~ it is a cousin of English ~bear~.
en.sugerir:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~suggerere~ (“to bring up from below, to supply, to prompt”), from ~sub-~ (“under, up from under”) plus ~gerere~ (“to carry, to bear, to conduct”). The deeper origin of ~gerere~ is uncertain; De Vaan tentatively links it to the root of ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), but the reconstruction is disputed. Spanish took the verb from written Latin, so it is cognate with the equally learned Italian ~suggerire~, French ~suggérer~ and Portuguese ~sugerir~, and — through ~gerere~ — with English ~suggest~, ~gesture~ and ~digest~.

Picture a servant carrying supplies up from a cellar: ~suggerere~ first meant to furnish or supply from below, and only then to put a thought quietly into another's mind — to ~sugerir~ is, etymologically, to slip an idea up under someone's notice. That undertone of prompting survives in the theatre, where the ~suggeritore~ (Italian for the offstage prompter) whispers forgotten lines. The Latin root ~gerere~, “to carry on, to manage,” proved enormously fertile in Spanish: from it and its participle ~gestus~ come ~gesto~, ~gestión~, ~gestionar~, ~sugestión~, ~digerir~, ~registro~ and ~gerente~, a whole vocabulary of bearing, doing and managing.
en.sujetar:
A semi-learned borrowing from Latin ~subiectāre~ (“to place under, bring near”), the frequentative of ~subicere~ (“to throw under, place under”), from ~sub-~ (“under”) + ~iacere~ (“to throw”), from Proto-Indo-European *~yeh₁-~ (“to throw, let go”). Cognate with English ~subject~, ~inject~, ~project~, and ~jet~, and with Spanish ~sujeto~ (its own learned doublet).

Latin ~iacere~ meant “to throw”; ~subicere~, “to throw or set underneath,” gave both the grammar-and-logic term ~sujeto~ (“subject”) and, through the frequentative ~subiectāre~, the everyday ~sujetar~ (“to hold, fasten, keep in place”) — literally to keep something “thrown under” control. The half-learned path shows in the form; full popular wear would have reduced ~iacere~ far more. From ~iacere~ and its compounds Spanish also holds ~echar~ (the fully popular descendant, “to throw”), ~inyectar~, ~proyecto~, ~adyacente~, and ~sujeción~.
en.sumar:
Spanish ~sumar~ (“to add, sum up”) was borrowed from Medieval Latin ~summāre~ (“to add up”), from Latin ~summa~ (“sum, total, the whole”), the feminine of the adjective ~summus~ (“highest, topmost”), a superlative connected with ~super~ (“above”) and, ultimately, Proto-Indo-European *~upér~ / *~upo~ (“over, up from under”). It is cognate with Italian ~sommare~, French ~sommer~ and Portuguese ~somar~, and — through Latin borrowings — with English ~sum~, ~summit~ and ~summary~.

Why should “the highest” mean “a total”? By the usual account, the connection is a habit of Roman reckoning: numbers were added in a column and the result written at the top, so the ~summa~ — the “topmost” line — was the whole added up. Whether the Romans really summed from the bottom is not certain, but the metaphor of the total as the “high point” is old and vivid; a ~summa~ was also the crowning “sum” of a subject, as in the medieval ~Summa~ of theology. From ~summus~ Spanish keeps ~sumo~ (“utmost,” as in ~sumo sacerdote~, “high priest”) and ~sumamente~ (“extremely”), while from the verb come ~suma~ (“sum, addition”), ~sumando~ (“addend”) and ~sumario~ (“summary”).
en.sumergir:
From Latin ~submergere~ (“to plunge under, sink”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~mergere~ (“to dip, plunge”). ~mergere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~mesg-~ (“to dip, submerge”), a root also behind Sanskrit ~majjati~ (“sinks, dives”) and Lithuanian ~mazgóti~ (“to wash”). Cognate with Italian ~sommergere~, French ~submerger~ and Portuguese ~submergir~, and with the English borrowings ~merge~, ~emerge~ and ~immerse~.

~sumergir~ is the learned, bookish form; the same Latin verb also came down a rustic road to name a bird — the ~somormujo~ (“grebe”), a diver that stays under water an uncannily long time, from a Vulgar Latin ~mergulus~ (“little diver”). The core ~mergere~ splits neatly by prefix: dip under and you ~sumergir~; rise back out and you ~emerger~. From the family Spanish keeps ~inmersión~, ~sumersión~, ~emergencia~ and the everyday ~emerger~ — every one of them a motion into or out of water.
en.suministrar:
From Latin ~subministrāre~ (“to furnish, supply, provide”), from ~sub-~ (“from below, up to”) plus ~ministrāre~ (“to serve, wait on”), a verb from ~minister~ (“servant, attendant”). ~Minister~ was built on ~minus~ (“less”) on the model of ~magister~ (“master,” from ~magis~, “more”), from Proto-Indo-European *~mei-~ (“small, less”). Cognates: Italian ~somministrare~ and Portuguese ~subministrar~; through ~ministrāre~, English ~minister~ and ~administer~.

A ~minister~ was the “lesser” member of a household, the counterpart of the ~magister~ or “greater” one; ~ministrāre~ meant to attend and serve, and ~sub-~ added the image of handing something up from below — hence “to supply.” Spanish kept the practical sense “to provide goods or resources.” From the family come ~ministro~, ~ministerio~, ~administrar~ and ~menester~; from ~minus~, ~menos~, ~menguar~ and ~minúsculo~. A tasty relative is Italian ~minestra~ (“soup,” literally something “served up”).
en.sumir:
From Old Spanish ~somir~, from Latin ~sūmere~ (“to take up, take, consume”), a compound of the prefix ~sub-~ (“up from below”) and ~emere~ (“to take, to buy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁em-~ (“to take, distribute”). It is thus a close relative of Spanish ~consumir~, ~asumir~, ~presumir~ and ~resumir~, all built on that same ~emere~.

Latin ~sūmere~ meant “to take up” or “to consume”; Spanish narrowed and darkened the sense to “to submerge, to plunge, to sink.” Used reflexively, ~sumirse~ describes being plunged into grief, poverty or thought, and a hollow that caves inward is said to be ~sumido~. The verb kept one strikingly liturgical use: in the Catholic Mass, ~sumir~ is for the priest to “consume” the consecrated bread and wine — the old take-and-consume sense of ~sūmere~ preserved almost intact. From the same family comes ~sumidero~ (“drain, sinkhole”).
en.superar:
From Latin ~superāre~ (“to rise above, overcome, surpass”), a verb built on ~super~ (“above, over”), from Proto-Indo-European *~upér~ (“over, above”). The same root surfaces in Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~, and — through Germanic — English ~over~. Spanish took ~superar~ as a learned borrowing straight from Latin, keeping ~super~ intact where popular speech wore it down: the fully inherited descendant of the same word is the everyday preposition ~sobre~ (“on, above”), and from Vulgar Latin *~superānus~ came ~soberano~ (“sovereign”). Italian ~superare~ and Portuguese ~superar~ are its direct cousins.

Latin ~superāre~ already meant both to physically top something and to get the better of a rival, and modern Spanish keeps both threads: one ~supera~ an obstacle, a record, or an opponent. From ~super~ the language drew a wide learned family — ~superior~, ~superficie~ (“surface,” literally the face on top), and the vice-name ~soberbia~ (“pride,” from Latin ~superbia~, the fault of setting oneself above others). The living prefix ~super-~ that turns any word into a heightened version of itself is that same Latin element, still doing what it did in Rome.
en.supervisar:
