From Latin ~supervidēre~ (“to oversee, inspect”), from ~super~ (“over”) and ~vidēre~ (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”). The modern Spanish verb was shaped by, and largely taken through, English ~supervise~, which itself drew on the Medieval Latin participle ~supervīsus~. Cognate — through the deeper root — with English ~wit~ and ~wise~ and German ~wissen~ (“to know”).

The sense is transparent: to look from above, to oversee the work of others. From ~vidēre~ Spanish keeps a large family — ~ver~ (“to see”), ~visión~, ~vista~, ~revisar~, ~prever~ and ~evidente~ — all rooted in seeing.
en.suplir:
From Latin ~supplēre~ (“to fill up, complete”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“up from below”) and ~plēre~ (“to fill”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”). The same root gives English ~supply~ and ~supplement~ as well as ~complete~ and ~plenty~, and French ~suppléer~.

The Latin idea was “to fill up what is lacking,” and Spanish ~suplir~ still turns on that gap: to ~suplir~ is to make up for an absence — to stand in for a missing person, cover a shortfall, or eke out scarce means. From the same verb come ~suplente~ (“substitute, stand-in”) and ~suplencia~ (“temporary replacement”), and the noun ~suplemento~ (“supplement”). The wider *~pleh₁-~ family is enormous in Spanish, including ~pleno~, ~lleno~, ~cumplir~, ~completar~ and ~repleto~ — all, at bottom, about fullness.
en.suponer:
Spanish ~suponer~ comes from Latin ~suppōnere~ (“to place under, to substitute”), from ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, to place”). ~pōnere~ itself is a contraction of an older ~po-~ (“off, away”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, to leave”), so “to place” was originally “to set down and leave.” Because Spanish inherited ~pōnere~ as the everyday ~poner~, the compound was reshaped on it. Cognate Romance verbs include French ~supposer~ and Italian ~supporre~.

From “to place under” came the mental sense: to suppose is to lay a proposition down as a foundation to reason from — quite literally to place it beneath an argument. The Latin verb's past participle ~positus~ gave Spanish ~puesto~ (“placed; a post, position”) and spread through a large prefixed family built on ~poner~: ~componer~ (“to compose”), ~proponer~ (“to propose”), ~disponer~ (“to arrange”), ~exponer~ (“to expose”) and ~imponer~ (“to impose”), plus the nouns ~posición~ (“position”) and ~apuesta~ (“a bet,” something put down).
en.suprimir:
From Latin ~supprimere~ (“to press down, hold down, suppress”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under, down”) and ~premere~ (“to press”). ~premere~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~premō~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to strike, press”). Spanish took the word by the learned route, so the consonant cluster survived rather than eroding; compare French ~supprimer~, Italian ~sopprimere~ and English ~suppress~, all from the same Latin verb, and — more distantly, through ~premere~ itself — English ~press~ and ~print~.

The literal Latin sense was physical, to press or weigh something down, and the figurative one, to put down a revolt, a feeling, or a fact, followed naturally: to suppress is to keep a thing pressed beneath the surface. ~premere~ was extraordinarily productive in Spanish, and its many prefixed descendants still carry the image of pressure: ~imprimir~ (“to print,” press onto a page), ~exprimir~ (“to squeeze out”), ~comprimir~, ~oprimir~, ~deprimir~ and ~expresar~, alongside the nouns ~presión~ and ~prensa~ (“press”).
en.surgir:
From Latin ~surgere~ (“to rise, spring up”), a worn-down form of ~surrigere~, itself ~subrigere~, from ~sub-~ (“up from below”) and ~regere~ (“to keep straight, guide”); the ultimate root is Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, direct”). It is cognate with Italian ~sorgere~ and Portuguese ~surgir~, and — through the same root — with English ~surge~ and ~source~, the latter from a French reflex of the same Latin verb.

In Spanish the word arrived first as a sailor's term. According to Corominas, ~surgir~ meant “to ride at anchor, put into harbour” — from the Latin picture of a ship “standing upright,” at rest in port (~navis surgit in portu~), much as ~estar~ (“to stand”) came to mean “to be somewhere.” Only later did the nautical sense broaden into today's “to arise, emerge, well up.” The verb left ~resurgir~ and ~insurgente~ in the language, while its Latin root ~regere~ seeded a large family — ~regir~, ~región~, ~dirigir~, ~corregir~ and ~recto~.
en.suscitar:
From Latin ~suscitāre~ (“to raise up, rouse, stir up”), a compound of ~sus-~ (a reduced form of ~subs-~/~sub~, “up from under”) and ~citāre~ (“to set in motion, summon”), the frequentative of ~ciēre~ (“to move, stir”). ~Ciēre~ comes from Proto-Indo-European *~keyh₂-~ (“to set in motion”), the root that, through Ancient Greek ~kīnéō~ (“to move”), also underlies ~kinetic~ and ~cinema~. Romance kept the verb intact: Italian ~suscitare~, French ~susciter~, Portuguese ~suscitar~, and English has the rare ~suscitate~ and the everyday ~resuscitate~.

Latin ~suscitāre~ meant to make something rise up from below — to rouse a sleeper, raise the dead, stir a fire back to life. Spanish narrowed the physical sense into a figurative one: ~suscitar~ now means “to provoke, arouse, give rise to,” as a remark ~suscita~ debate or a discovery ~suscita~ interest — you raise up a reaction where there was none. Its close relative ~resucitar~ (“to resuscitate, bring back to life”) keeps the older, literal charge. The base ~citāre~ seeded a whole Spanish family of summoning and stirring: ~citar~, ~excitar~, ~incitar~, ~recitar~, and ~solicitar~ all trace to the same root.
en.suscribir:
From Latin ~subscrībere~ (“to write underneath, to sign at the foot of a document”), from ~sub-~ (“under”) plus ~scrībere~ (“to write, to incise”), from Proto-Indo-European *~skreybʰ-~ (“to scratch, to incise”), an extension of the root *~(s)ker-~ (“to cut”). Because writing began as scratching marks into a surface, ~scrībere~ is cognate with English ~scribe~, ~describe~, and ~subscribe~ itself, and, more remotely, with ~shrive~.

The literal sense — signing one’s name beneath a text — is the seed of every modern meaning. To ~suscribir~ a document is to endorse it with your signature; from “signing on” came the sense of committing to pay for something in advance, giving ~suscripción~ (“subscription”). Figuratively one can ~suscribir~ an opinion, i.e. put one’s name to it. From the same ~scrībere~ Spanish inherited ~escribir~ (“to write”) and built ~describir~, ~inscribir~, and ~manuscrito~ — the whole literate vocabulary springing from the humble act of scratching a line.
en.suspender:
~Suspender~ descends from Latin ~suspendere~ (“to hang up”), from ~sub-~ (“up from under”) plus ~pendere~ (“to hang; to weigh”). ~Pendere~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull, stretch, spin”). It is cognate with English ~suspend~, French ~suspendre~, and Italian ~sospendere~.

~Pendere~ meant both “to hang” and “to weigh,” because the Romans weighed by hanging goods from a balance — and since debts were paid by weighing out metal, it also meant “to pay.” Its frequentative ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh carefully”) split into ~pesar~ (“to weigh”) and ~pensar~ (“to think,” i.e., to weigh in the mind). The hanging sense left ~depender~ (“to depend, hang from”), ~suspenso~ (both “suspense” and a failing grade — the student left dangling), ~péndulo~, ~pensión~, and ~apéndice~. To suspend something is still, quite literally, to leave it hanging.
en.sustentar:
From Latin ~sustentāre~ (“to hold up, to support”), the frequentative of ~sustinēre~, from ~sub-~ (“up from below”) plus ~tenēre~ (“to hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate with French ~soutenir~, Italian ~sostenere~ and Portuguese ~sustentar~, and — through the same root — with English ~sustain~, ~tenant~ and ~tenor~.

Being a frequentative, ~sustentāre~ carried the nuance of holding up again and again, keeping something aloft over time — fitting for a verb that now means to nourish, maintain and support. Latin ~tenēre~ (“to hold”) and its sibling ~tendere~ (“to stretch”) both grew from *~ten-~, and Spanish inherited a dense thicket: ~tener~, ~sostener~, ~mantener~, ~contener~, ~retener~, ~tenso~ and ~tienda~ (a “tent,” literally something stretched taut). The verb also yields ~sustento~ (“sustenance”) and ~sustentable~.
en.sustituir:
From Latin ~substituere~ (“to put in the place of, to set under”), from ~sub-~ (“under”) plus ~statuere~ (“to set up, to establish”), a verb built on ~status~ and ultimately on ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate with Italian ~sostituire~ and French ~substituer~, and, through ~statuere~, with English ~substitute~, ~statute~ and ~constitute~.

The literal sense is spatial: to “set one thing under or in the place of” another. Older Spanish wrote ~substituir~, faithful to the Latin b; the modern spelling ~sustituir~ simply drops the awkward consonant cluster, as Spanish tends to. It shares its ~statuere~ core with ~estatuir~, ~estatuto~, ~constituir~, ~instituir~, ~restituir~ and ~destituir~; and behind them all stands the same great root *~steh₂-~ that gives everyday ~estar~ and ~estado~ — the very family of the verb “to be” standing in place.
en.tachar:
From the noun ~tacha~ (“fault, flaw, blemish”) plus the verbal suffix ~-ar~. The origin of ~tacha~ itself is disputed: it descends from a Medieval Latin ~tacca~ (“mark, spot”) — shared with French ~tache~, Catalan ~taca~ and Italian ~tacca~ — but the source of that word is contested. Corominas favours a Germanic root ~taikn~ (“sign, token,” akin to English ~token~); others propose instead a Vulgar Latin *~tagicāre~, from Latin ~tangere~ (“to touch”), the idea being of touching-and-marking.

Whatever its root, Spanish built the verb on the sense of a blemish: to ~tachar~ was first to accuse someone of a fault or find them wanting, and only later to “cross out” — to strike a mark through written words. Both senses survive: a judge may ~tachar~ a witness, and a student ~tacha~ a wrong answer. From the same noun come ~tachón~ (“crossing-out; stud”), ~tachadura~ (“deletion”) and the adjective ~intachable~ (“irreproachable,” literally without blemish).
en.tajar:
Inherited from Late Latin ~tāliāre~ (“to cut, split”), a verb derived from Latin ~tālea~ (“a cutting, slip, or rod taken from a plant”). Cognate with Italian ~tagliare~, French ~tailler~, Portuguese ~talhar~ and Catalan ~tallar~; through French ~tailler~ English also gained ~tailor~, ~detail~ and ~retail~.

The metaphor began in the garden — a ~tālea~ was a shoot cut for grafting — and generalised to cutting of every kind. Spanish ~tajar~ means “to slice, to chop,” and its noun ~tajo~ names both a cut and, by extension, a steep gorge (as in the river Tajo, the Tagus) and a stint of hard work. A slice of food is a ~tajada~; something categorical is ~tajante~ (“sharp, emphatic,” literally cutting); and to shortcut is to ~atajar~. Spanish kept a learned doublet too: ~tallar~ (“to carve, to sculpt”), which took the same ~tāliāre~ down a different phonetic road.
en.tantear:
A Spanish formation: the quantity word ~tanto~ (“so much, so many”) plus the frequentative verbal suffix ~-ear~. ~Tanto~ descends from Latin ~tantus~ (“so great, so much”), a correlative demonstrative paired with ~quantus~ (“how much”).

The suffix ~-ear~ builds verbs of repeated, tentative action, and that nuance shaped the meaning: to ~tantear~ is literally to keep taking the measure of something — hence to feel one's way in the dark, to size up or sound out a person, and to estimate a quantity roughly. In sport and games ~tantear~ is to keep score, since each point is a ~tanto~; the score itself is the ~tanteo~. The trial-and-error flavour is the constant: a painter ~tantea~ the light, a negotiator ~tantea~ the ground before committing. From the same root come ~tanto~, ~tanteo~ and ~tanteador~ (“scoreboard, scorer”).
en.tapar:
~tapar~ (“to cover, cap, plug”) is a verb built on the noun ~tapa~ (“lid, cover”), which Spanish took from a Germanic word *~tappa~ meaning “plug, bung.” The same Germanic source produced a family of spigot-and-plug words across the north: English ~tap~ (the beer-barrel kind), Dutch ~tap~ and German ~Zapfen~ (“plug, cone”). From ~tapa~ Spanish also formed ~tapón~ (“stopper, cork”) and ~tapadera~ (“lid”).

To ~tapar~ is to put a lid on something — to close, block or conceal. The most famous story attached to the word is that of the culinary ~tapa~, the bar snack said to have begun as a slice of bread or ham used to cover a wine glass against flies and dust; charming as it is, this is a popular tradition rather than a documented etymology, so it is best told as such. What is secure is the Germanic root and its Spanish offspring: ~destapar~ (“to uncover”), ~taparse~ (“to cover oneself”) and ~tapabocas~ (“face mask,” literally mouth-cover).
en.tardar:
From Latin ~tardāre~ (“to delay, be slow”), from ~tardus~ (“slow, sluggish, late”). The origin of ~tardus~ is uncertain; one reconstruction traces it to Proto-Indo-European *~terh₂-~ (“to cross over, pass through”) by way of *~tr̥h₂-do-~ (“drawn out, slow to get through”), but close cognates meaning “slow” are lacking, and an Etruscan source has occasionally been proposed. Romance cognates are Italian ~tardare~, French ~tarder~, and Portuguese ~tardar~; English has ~tardy~ (through Old French ~tardif~) and ~retard~.

If the Indo-European reconstruction holds — and it is offered only tentatively — the idea beneath ~tardus~ is of something “drawn out,” slow to cross to its end; but with no close relatives meaning “slow,” that story stays a hypothesis. In Spanish the verb slid naturally from “to be slow” to “to take (time),” as in ~¿cuánto tardas?~ (“how long will you take?”). The same root gave the everyday ~tarde~ (“afternoon; late”), plus ~tardío~ (“late-ripening”), ~tardanza~, ~retardar~, and the zoologist’s ~tardígrado~ — literally a “slow-stepper.”
en.tañer:
Inherited from Latin ~tangere~ (“to touch”), a nasal-infix present from Proto-Italic *~tangō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~teh₂g-~ (“to touch”). The same root, through Latin, gave English ~tangent~, ~contact~, ~tangible~ and ~tact~, so that a plucked lute-string and a mathematical ~tangent~ are distant cousins.

Old Spanish ~tañer~ kept the plain sense “to touch” (still archaically a synonym of ~tocar~), but it specialised toward touching that produces sound: to ~tañer~ is to play a musical instrument — a bell, a guitar, a harp — or to toll. The sound it makes is a ~tañido~. Spanish later re-borrowed the Latin verb in learned form as ~tangir~, a doublet of ~tañer~, and the whole ~tangere~ family is well populated: ~tangente~, ~contacto~, ~tacto~, ~tangible~ and even ~contaminar~ (from Latin ~contāmināre~, “to touch or spoil by contact”).
en.tejer:
Inherited from Old Spanish ~texer~, from Latin ~texere~ (“to weave, to plait, to build”), from Proto-Italic *~teksō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~teḱs-~ (“to weave, to fabricate”). The root's reach is remarkable: it also yielded Greek ~tékhnē~ (“craft, art”), and so English ~technique~ stands beside ~text~, ~textile~ and ~texture~, all things woven. Romance cousins include Italian ~tessere~, French ~tisser~ and Portuguese ~tecer~.

The metaphor of weaving runs straight through the word. Latin ~texere~ meant both to weave cloth and to construct — a Roman could ~texere~ a wall or a speech. Spanish ~tejer~ covers weaving and knitting alike, and figuratively one ~teje~ intrigues, alliances or a plot. The product is the ~tejido~ (“fabric, tissue”); the craftsperson a ~tejedor~. From the same Latin verb Spanish drew the learned doublets ~texto~ (“text”) and ~textil~ (“textile”), plus ~contexto~ and ~tesitura~.
en.temer:
From Latin ~timēre~ (“to fear”), first person ~timeō~ — a verb Latin itself could not explain, flagged “of uncertain origin.” One proposal ties it to the Proto-Indo-European root *~temH-~ (“dark”), alongside ~tenebrae~ (“shadows”), as if fear were the instinct of one groping blindly in the dark; the connection is semantically appealing but phonetically difficult, and remains disputed. Spanish inherited it directly as ~temer~, cognate with Italian ~temere~ and Portuguese ~temer~.

The meaning has scarcely shifted in two thousand years: to fear is still to fear. Latin ~timor~ (“dread”) and ~timidus~ (“fearful”) descended into Spanish as ~temor~ and ~tímido~, and the same pair entered English as the borrowings ~timid~ and ~timorous~. From ~timidus~ Latin built ~intimidāre~, giving Spanish ~intimidar~ (“to intimidate”). Other members of the family include ~temeroso~ (“fearful”) and ~atemorizar~ (“to frighten”). Note that the vivid image of fear-as-darkness rests on the contested ~temH-~ hypothesis, not on settled ground.
en.tender:
From Old Spanish ~tender~, from Latin ~tendere~ (“to stretch, extend, spread out”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, draw”). Romance cognates include French ~tendre~ and Portuguese ~tender~; through the root it is kin to Greek ~τείνω~ (~teínō~, “I stretch”) and German ~dehnen~ (“to stretch”), and English borrowed the family as tend, extend, and tension.

The core image is a taut line: ~tender~ is to spread a cloth, hang the washing, extend a hand, lay down a cable — anything drawn out to its full length. The most charming descendant is ~tienda~: a stretched awning became a market stall and then, by extension, a “shop,” while a ~tienda~ de campaña keeps the literal “stretched” tent. From the same root Spanish also has ~tendencia~ (a “stretching toward,” an inclination), ~tendón~ (the body's own taut cord), and ~extender~. To stretch a rope and to have a tendency, then, are the same gesture seen at different scales.
en.tener:
Spanish ~tener~ comes from Latin ~tenēre~ (“to hold, keep, grasp”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”) — holding conceived as keeping something taut in the hand. Its Romance cousins keep the shape: Italian ~tenere~, French ~tenir~, and Portuguese ~ter~. Through the same root, Latin also formed ~tendere~ (“to stretch”) and ~tenuis~ (“thin”), and the root even surfaces in the English ~thin~.

In Latin ~tenēre~ meant simply to hold; Spanish then handed it a much bigger job. As ~haber~ retreated into an auxiliary, ~tener~ stepped in as the ordinary verb of possession — the everyday “I have” of ~tengo hambre~ (“I hold hunger”) and ~tener casa~. The idea of holding fast runs through its descendants: ~contener~ (“to contain”), ~obtener~ (“to obtain”), ~mantener~ (“to maintain”), and the adjective ~tenaz~ (“tenacious”), along with ~teniente~ (“lieutenant,” literally one who holds a place).
en.terminar:
From Latin ~termināre~ (“to bound, to limit”), from ~terminus~ (“boundary, limit, end-marker”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ter-~ (“peg, boundary marker”), seen in the extended form *~ter-men-~. Cognate with Ancient Greek ~térma~ (“goal”) and ~térmōn~ (“border”), and with English ~term~ and ~terminal~.

For the Romans a ~terminus~ was a very concrete thing: a boundary stone set between fields. It was sacred enough to have its own god, ~Terminus~, the deity of boundary markers, honored each February at a festival called the ~Terminalia~. To ~terminar~ something, then, is etymologically to set its limit — to mark where it ends. From the same root Spanish built ~término~ (“term, end”), ~terminal~, ~determinar~ (“to bound thoroughly, to decide”), and ~exterminar~ (“to drive beyond the boundary, to destroy”).
en.testimoniar:
A learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~testimōniāre~ (“to bear witness”), from Latin ~testimōnium~ (“testimony”), from ~testis~ (“witness”). The oldest layer is the vivid part: ~testis~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~tri-st-~, from *~tréyes~ (“three”) and *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — a witness was pictured as the third person standing by, the neutral bystander between two disputing parties.

Because it is a bookish borrowing, ~testimoniar~ kept its Latin shape almost unchanged: it means “to testify, to give witness,” whether in a courtroom or, more loosely, to attest to something (grief may ~testimoniar~ a person's love). The everyday inherited word for a witness, ~testigo~, comes from the same ~testis~, as does the popular ~atestiguar~ (“to attest”). The ~testis~ family is large in English too — ~testify~, ~testament~, ~protest~, ~contest~ and ~detest~ — mirrored in Spanish ~testamento~, ~protestar~ and ~contestar~.
en.timar:
~timar~ (“to swindle, to con”) is of uncertain origin, and the dictionaries decline to settle it. Corominas calls the etymology obscure; the Real Academia simply marks it « of uncertain origin ». Two accounts have been proposed and neither is secure: by one, it goes back to Hispano-Arabic ~tamm~ (“to complete, to finish”), with a shift from finishing off to deceiving; by another, it is a borrowing from Galician-Portuguese ~teimar~ (“to persist, to be stubborn”). Because the source is disputed, no deeper Indo-European or Semitic chain can be claimed with confidence.

Whatever its root, ~timar~ surfaced in Spanish only in the late nineteenth century: the Academy admitted it in 1899 in the sense “to take by trickery.” Curiously, the reflexive ~timarse~ was accepted in 1925 with an unrelated-sounding meaning — of sweethearts, to exchange meaningful glances or flirt with the eyes. From the verb come the everyday noun ~timo~ (“a scam, a rip-off”) and ~timador~ (“a swindler”), both thoroughly colloquial and still very much alive in peninsular Spanish.
en.tintar:
From Vulgar Latin *~tinctāre~, a frequentative built on the participial stem of Latin ~tingere~ (“to dip, moisten, dye”), whose participle ~tīnctus~ (“dipped, tinged”) supplied the stem. ~tingere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~teng-~ (“to soak, dip, make wet”), cognate with Ancient Greek ~téngō~ (“to wet”) and, through the same root, with English ~tinge~ and ~taint~ (borrowed via French) and ~dunk~.

The core image is dipping something into a liquid to color it, and Spanish preserved the sense narrowly as “to dye, to tint.” Alongside ~tintar~, Spanish inherited the same Latin verb directly as ~teñir~, so the two are doublets drawing on one source. From the participle came the noun family ~tinta~ (“ink”), ~tinte~ (“dye”), ~tinto~ (as in ~vino tinto~, literally “dyed wine,” i.e. red) and ~tintura~; the dry-cleaner's ~tintorería~ belongs here too.
en.tirar:
From Old Spanish ~tirar~, from Vulgar Latin *~tīrāre~, of genuinely uncertain origin — one of the murkiest cases in all of Romance etymology. It is cognate with Italian ~tirare~, French ~tirer~, and Portuguese ~tirar~, all built on the core sense “to pull, to draw.” The verb is old and pan-Romance, yet no one has traced it securely back to classical Latin, and lexicographers have often set it aside as insoluble. Two accounts compete. By one, the word descends from a Germanic source; by the other, favored by Corominas, it arose in Latin military slang from the Parthian word for “arrow” — reconstructed as roughly ~tir~, as in the Iranian dialects — the Parthians being Rome's great archer-enemies on the eastern frontier. Both remain proposals, and the honest verdict is that the origin is disputed.

In Spanish, ~tirar~ spread across a remarkable range of meanings — “to throw,” “to pull,” “to shoot,” “to pull down,” “to print” a run of copies, even “to last” — a semantic breadth that itself hints at an original sense of forceful drawing or launching. If Corominas is right that the arrow lies at its root, the modern sense “to throw” would faintly preserve the flight of a Parthian shaft; but because that etymology is only proposed, this is a suggestive story rather than a proven one. Whatever its source, the verb became one of the most productive in the language, yielding ~tiro~ (“shot”), ~tirada~ (“print run; stretch”), ~tirador~ (“shooter; handle”), ~estirar~ (“to stretch”), and ~retirar~ (“to withdraw”).
en.titular:
From ~título~ (“title, heading”) plus ~-ar~, or directly from Latin ~titulāre~, from ~titulus~ (“inscription, label, heading, title”), a word of unknown origin. Cognate with Italian ~titolo~ and its verb ~titolare~, French ~titre~, and English ~title~ and ~titular~.

In Rome a ~titulus~ was the placard or inscription set over a thing — a heading, a label, a mark of rank — and from that grew both “title of a book” and “title of office.” Spanish ~titular~ therefore means “to entitle, to head” and, as a noun, “the holder, the incumbent.” A quieter descendant is the accent-and-tilde mark ~tilde~: it comes from the same ~titulus~ by metathesis, once a stroke written over a letter to abbreviate it, whence also the verb ~tildar~ (“to brand, to label someone as”). Related forms include ~subtítulo~ and, of course, ~título~ itself.
en.tiznar:
A denominal verb from the noun ~tizón~ (“firebrand, half-burnt stick”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-ar~. ~tizón~ descends from Latin ~tītiō~ (accusative ~tītiōnem~, “firebrand”), and it is a doublet of the shorter ~tizo~. Wiktionary files the Latin word under the Proto-Indo-European root *~teyh₁-~, though that deeper connection is uncertain and best treated as tentative. Portuguese ~tição~ is the parallel Romance reflex.

To ~tiznar~ is to blacken or smudge something with soot or charcoal — the mark a firebrand leaves — and by extension to stain a reputation. The soot itself is ~tizne~, and to poke a fire back to life is ~atizar~, another descendant of ~tizón~; figuratively ~atizar~ also means to stir up or stoke a quarrel or the passions. The family clusters tightly around the hearth and the half-burnt log.
en.tocar:
Spanish ~tocar~ descends from Vulgar Latin *~toccāre~ (also *~tuccāre~), “to knock, strike, rap,” whose ultimate origin is uncertain — the sources call it “of Germanic or onomatopoeic origin” and do not decide between the two. The likeliest account is imitative: *~tocc~ as a spoken echo of a sharp tap or knock, the same sound-symbolism that shaped a whole Romance family. It is cognate with Italian ~toccare~, French ~toucher~ and Portuguese ~tocar~, and — borrowed from Old French ~tochier~ — with English ~touch~. There is no secure Indo-European root to reach for here; if the word is onomatopoeic, it never had one.

The development is a small drama of the senses. From “to knock” the verb spread to “to touch” in general, and then — because you strike or pluck an instrument to make it sound — to “to play” music: in Spanish one and the same ~tocar~ covers touching a surface and playing the guitar, and to ~tocar~ a bell is to ring it. Idiom pushed it further still, into “to fall to one's lot” (~me toca a mí~, “it's my turn”). The family it heads is homely and wide: ~toque~ (“a touch; a ringing”), ~tocador~ (“dressing table; player”), ~tocadiscos~ (“record player”), ~tocante~ (“concerning”) and the phrase ~tocar fondo~ (“to hit rock bottom”).
en.tomar:
The origin of ~tomar~ is genuinely uncertain — es.Wiktionary and the DLE label it « de origen incierto ». It appears very early in Spanish (already in the medieval Poema de mio Cid) and has a close counterpart in Portuguese ~tomar~, but no agreed Latin ancestor. Two hypotheses compete. Corominas proposed an aphaeresis from Latin ~autumāre~ (“to assert a claim, affirm”), the initial ~au-~ having worn away, though the meaning fits awkwardly. Another account, associated with Walsh, derives it instead from an alteration of ~domāre~ (“to tame, subdue”), noting that early ~tomar~ worked much like ~apropiar~ (“to appropriate, take possession”). The matter remains debated, and any single story should be taken as a proposal, not settled fact.

Whatever its source, ~tomar~ established itself as one of the most versatile verbs in Spanish, spreading from “to seize, take hold of” into a vast web of senses: to take a road, take a decision, take medicine, and — famously in Spain and much of Latin America — to drink (~tomar algo~, “to have a drink”). This last is a native extension of “take into the body,” not a separate root. Reflexive ~tomarse~ intensifies it (~tomarse un café~, ~tomarse su tiempo~). Because its etymology is unsettled, ~tomar~ has left a smaller word-family than the great Latin verbs, but it did yield the nouns ~toma~ (“a taking; a dose; a film take”) and ~tomadura~, and the compound ~tomavistas~ (“a movie camera,” literally a “view-taker”). Its very obscurity is a reminder that even the commonest words can guard a hidden past.
en.topar:
Of onomatopoeic origin, imitating the dull sound of two objects knocking together — the sources agree it is expressive rather than inherited from a specific Latin word. Portuguese ~topar~ is the same formation. Because the root is imitative, there is no Latin etymon or Proto-Indo-European reconstruction to point to; the word was, in effect, coined from the noise of the collision itself.

The base sense is “to bump into, to knock against, to run up against,” and from there Spanish extended it to “to meet by chance” (~toparse con alguien~, “to run into someone”) and, in the River Plate region, to the gambler's “to accept a bet, to call.” The blow itself is a ~tope~ (also “buffer, stop, limit”), a head-butt is a ~topetazo~, and to butt with the head is ~topetar~ — the whole cluster still ringing with the original thud.
en.torcer:
From Vulgar Latin *~torcĕre~, a re-formed version of Classical Latin ~torquēre~ (“to twist, wind, wring”), from Proto-Italic *~torkʷeō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~terkʷ-~ (“to twist”). Cognate with Italian ~torcere~, Portuguese ~torcer~ and French ~tordre~; through the Latin verb, English borrowed ~torture~, ~torment~ and ~torque~, and even ~nasturtium~ (literally “nose-twister,” for the plant's pungency).

The physical sense of twisting or wringing broadened readily into the figurative — to ~torcer~ can be to sprain, to distort, to pervert justice, or to lose one's moral straightness. That last metaphor produced ~tuerto~ (“one-eyed; a wrong done”), the stiff-necked ~tortícolis~, the winding ~tortuoso~ and, from a Vulgar Latin *~intorticāre~ (“to twist together”), the ~antorcha~ (“torch”), once a bundle of twisted fibers. Add ~retorcer~ (“to wring”) and the learned ~torsión~ and ~contorsión~, and the whole family keeps turning back on itself.
en.tornar:
Spanish ~tornar~ comes from Latin ~tornāre~ (“to turn on a lathe, round off”), a verb drawn from the noun ~tornus~ (“lathe, turner’s tool”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~tórnos~ (“compass, lathe”). The Greek word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~terh₁-~ (“to rub, to turn by twisting”). ~tornar~ is cognate with Italian ~tornare~, French ~tourner~ and Portuguese ~tornar~, and — through the same root — with English ~turn~ and ~tour~.

Latin ~tornāre~ meant to shape wood or metal by spinning it against a blade; from that literal “turning” Romance widened the verb to plain rotation and then to “turning back,” which is why Spanish ~tornar~ means “to return, to give back, to turn (into).” The everyday reflexive ~tornarse~ means “to become.” Its derived and prefixed kin fill the workshop and beyond: ~torno~ (“lathe, winch”), ~tornillo~ (“screw”), ~torneo~ (“tournament,” originally a wheeling of horsemen), ~retornar~, ~entornar~ (“to half-close a door”), and ~contorno~ (“outline,” what you get by turning all the way around something).
en.tornear:
A denominal verb from ~torno~ (“lathe”) plus the suffix ~-ear~. ~torno~ comes from Latin ~tornus~ (“lathe, turner's tool”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~tórnos~ (“compass, lathe”), from Proto-Indo-European *~terh₁-~ (“to rub, bore, turn”). English ~turn~ travels from the same Latin source (via ~tornāre~), as do ~tour~, ~contour~ and ~attorney~, and — sharing the deeper root — the very ~tournament~ that ~tornear~ once also named.

The two great senses run in parallel: to ~tornear~ is to shape wood or metal on a lathe, spinning the piece against a fixed tool, and — in medieval usage — to fight in a tourney, wheeling the horses in circles. Spanish drew from ~torno~ a wide family: ~tornar~ (“to return”), ~tornillo~ (“screw”), ~torniquete~ (“tourniquet, turnstile”), ~contorno~ (“contour”), ~entorno~ (“surroundings”), ~retornar~ and the noun ~torneo~ (“tournament”) itself.
en.trabajar:
From Old Spanish ~trabajar~ (“to toil, torment”), most often traced to a Vulgar Latin *~tripaliāre~ (“to torture”), from Late Latin ~tripalium~, a frame of three stakes (~tri-~ + ~pālus~, “stake”) used to restrain or torment. Cognate with French ~travailler~, Portuguese ~trabalhar~, Catalan ~treballar~, and Italian ~travagliare~, and with the noun French ~travail~ that gave English ~travail~ and, remarkably, ~travel~.

The oft-repeated tale is vivid — a word for “work” born from an engine of torture — but it should be told with the hedge the sources give it: while the DLE and Corominas do derive ~trabajar~ from ~tripalium~, the exact form of the Vulgar Latin verb and the precise semantic path from “torture” to “labor” remain debated, and some scholars are skeptical of the whole chain. What is clear is the drift attested in the Old Spanish records: from “to torment, suffer,” through “to strive, exert oneself,” to the neutral modern “to work.” English ~travel~ preserves the older bite, journeying once being an ordeal. The verb gave Spanish ~trabajo~ (“work”), ~trabajador~ (“worker”), and ~trabajoso~ (“laborious, arduous”).
en.trabar:
From the noun ~traba~ (“tie, bond, hobble, obstacle”), which descends from Latin ~trabs~ (accusative ~trabem~, “beam, timber”), from Proto-Italic *~trabs~, from Proto-Indo-European *~treb-~ (“dwelling, wooden beam”). Cognate through that root with English ~thorp~ (the “-thorpe” of village names) and ~troop~, German ~Dorf~ and Dutch ~dorp~ (“village”), and Lithuanian ~troba~ (“building”); the Latin ~taberna~ (“hut, shop”) belongs to the same family.

A beam is what holds a structure together, and so ~trabar~ came to mean “to join, to fasten, to lock together” — and then “to obstruct, to seize up,” since a jammed mechanism is one whose parts have locked. It also means to strike up: ~trabar amistad~ is “to strike up a friendship,” ~trabar conversación~ “to strike up a conversation.” The related nouns include ~traba~ (“hobble, hindrance”), ~trabazón~ (“bond, cohesion”) and ~trabilla~ (“belt loop”); to free something jammed is to ~destrabar~ it.
en.traducir:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~trādūcere~ (“to lead across, transfer”), from ~trans-~ (“across”) plus ~dūcere~ (“to lead, draw”), from Proto-Indo-European *~deuk-~ (“to lead”). Romance reflexes include Italian ~tradurre~, French ~traduire~, and Portuguese ~traduzir~; through the same ~dūcere~ root, German keeps the native cognate ~ziehen~ (“to pull, draw”).

Classical ~trādūcere~ had nothing to do with language — it meant to lead across, to transfer, even to parade someone in disgrace. The modern sense is a Renaissance coinage: by the usual account the humanist Leonardo Bruni, reading a passage in Aulus Gellius around 1400–1404, took ~trādūcere~ to mean “to carry a text over from one tongue into another.” The usage spread through the Italian humanists and reached Spanish by the mid-fifteenth century, displacing the older ~trasladar~ and ~romanzar~ (“to put into Romance”). From the same ~dūcere~ Spanish also has ~conducir~ and ~producir~, and from ~trādūcere~ itself the agent noun ~traductor~ and the act, ~traducción~ — the translator still, etymologically, ferrying meaning across a border.
en.traer:
From Old Spanish ~traer~ (also ~traher~), from Latin ~trahere~ (“to draw, to drag, to pull”). ~trahere~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~tragʰ-~ (“to draw, to drag”). Its Romance reflexes are striking: Italian ~trarre~, Portuguese ~trazer~, and French ~traire~, which — from the sense of “drawing out” — narrowed all the way down to “to milk” a cow. Through Latin loans, ~trahere~ also underlies English ~tract~, ~tractor~, ~trace~, and ~train~.

The core Latin sense was physical: to pull, to haul, to drag toward oneself. Spanish ~traer~ kept exactly that pull — to bring is to draw a thing toward the speaker — and built out an unusually neat family of prefixed verbs, each a different direction of pulling: ~atraer~ (“to attract”), ~contraer~ (“to contract, to draw together”), ~distraer~ (“to distract, to draw away”), ~extraer~ (“to extract”), ~retraer~ (“to retract”), and ~sustraer~ (“to subtract, to withdraw”). The frequentative ~tractāre~ (“to handle, to drag about repeatedly”) gave ~tratar~ (“to treat, to deal with”) and ~tratado~ (“treatise, treaty”), while the participle ~tractus~ left ~retrato~ (“portrait” — a face “drawn” from life) and ~tracción~. Nearly every “draw” in Spanish pulls back to ~trahere~.
en.tragar:
From Vulgar Latin *~tragāre~, of disputed ultimate origin. One account connects it to Doric Greek ~trágō~ (Attic ~trṓgō~, “to gnaw, eat”); another, proposed by Coromines, derives it from Latin ~dracō~ (“dragon, serpent”) by way of an attested ~tracō~ (“underground cavern”) — the notion being “that which swallows things up.” The sources do not settle the question, and the Greek and the ~dracō~ accounts are best kept as rival proposals. Portuguese and Galician ~tragar~ and Catalan ~dragar~ are the Romance kin.

Whatever its source, ~tragar~ settled on the plain meaning “to swallow,” and Spanish leaned hard on the figurative: to ~tragar~ is also to swallow an insult, to put up with someone, or to believe something gullibly (~no me lo trago~, “I don't buy it”). The family is vivid: a big eater is a ~tragón~, the gullet a ~tragadero~, a skylight a ~tragaluz~ (“light-swallower”) and a slot machine a ~tragaperras~ (“coin-swallower”).
en.tramitar:
From the noun ~trámite~ (“step, formality, procedure”), from Latin ~trāmes~ (“crosspath, byway,” genitive ~trāmitis~), traditionally analyzed as ~trans-~ (“across”) plus the root of ~meāre~ (“to go, pass”), from Proto-Indo-European *~mei-~ (“to change, go, move”) — though the internal make-up of the word is not fully transparent. Cognates through ~meāre~: Spanish ~permear~, English ~permeate~ and ~meatus~ (an anatomical “passage”).

A ~trāmes~ was a shortcut or side-path cutting across a field; figuratively it became a “course” one follows, and then the bureaucratic “steps” of a procedure — so ~tramitar~ is, almost literally, “to move something along its path.” The verb is a modern coinage (there was no such Latin *~tramitāre~). From the same ~meāre~ Spanish also has ~permear~, and around ~trámite~ cluster ~tramitación~ and ~tramitador~. Fitting for paperwork, the word began life as a humble track running across the fields.
en.transcurrir:
~transcurrir~ comes from Latin ~trānscurrere~ (“to run across, run past”), a compound of ~trāns-~ (“across, beyond”) and ~currere~ (“to run”). ~currere~ rests on Proto-Italic *~korzō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱers-~ (“to run”), which also produced Latin ~currus~ (“chariot”) and, through Gaulish, the ~car~ of English. By that root ~transcurrir~ is cousin to Spanish ~correr~, Italian ~correre~ and French ~courir~, and to a legion of English borrowings — ~current~, ~course~, ~cursor~, ~career~ and ~courier~.

In Latin ~trānscurrere~ was bodily motion — to run across a field or hurry past a place. Spanish kept a faint literal echo but handed the verb almost entirely to time: today ~transcurrir~ means “to elapse, to pass,” the way hours or years run across us while we stand still — ~transcurrió~ una hora, an hour went by. It is the quiet, intransitive cousin of racing ~correr~. The same ~currere~ root floods Spanish with motion words: ~corriente~, ~correo~, ~corredor~, ~curso~, ~recorrer~, ~ocurrir~, ~concurrir~ and ~discurrir~, each tracing some kind of running — of water, mail, roads, thought or events.
en.transferir:
From Latin ~transferre~ (“to carry across, transfer”), from ~trans-~ (“across”) plus ~ferre~ (“to bear, carry”), from Proto-Italic *~ferō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, bear”) — one of the oldest and most widespread of all roots. It is cognate with Italian ~trasferire~, French ~transférer~, Portuguese ~transferir~, and English ~transfer~, and — through the root — with English ~bear~, Ancient Greek ~φέρω~ (phérō, “I carry”), and Sanskrit ~bharati~ (“bears”).

~transferir~ came into Spanish as a learned borrowing, keeping the Latin sense of moving something across — property, funds, a meaning, a football player. Latin ~ferre~ was famously irregular: it borrowed its perfect and participle from a different verb, giving the participle ~lātus~ (as in ~translātus~). That quirk is why Spanish has two descendants of one verb — bookish ~transferir~ and everyday ~trasladar~ (“to move, relocate”), the latter from ~lātus~ — so “transferring” and “moving house” are, at root, one Latin word. The ~ferre~ family is large: ~referir~, ~preferir~, ~diferir~, ~conferir~, ~inferir~, and the noun ~transferencia~.
en.transformar:
From Latin ~transformare~ (“to change in shape”), a compound of ~trans-~ (“across, over”) and ~formare~ (“to form, to shape”), from the noun ~forma~ (“form, shape, figure”), a word of disputed origin. Spanish took it as a learned borrowing. It is cognate with English ~transform~, Italian ~trasformare~, French ~transformer~ and Portuguese ~transformar~, all continuing the same classical compound.

The literal sense is to carry a form across into another, and Latin poets already used it for metamorphosis, the bodily changes of myth. Spanish keeps both the physical sense — matter that ~transforma~ into energy — and the figurative, an experience that transforms a person. The base ~forma~ is unusually productive: from it and its relatives come ~formar~, ~formación~, ~fórmula~, ~formal~, ~deformar~ and ~reformar~, a whole vocabulary of shaping.
en.transitar:
From Latin ~transitāre~, a frequentative of ~transīre~ (“to go across, pass over”), itself ~trans-~ (“across”) plus ~īre~ (“to go”). The verb ~īre~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~ey-~ (“to go”), among the oldest and most widespread roots in the family. Italian keeps ~transitare~, and English took the participle-stem into ~transit~ and ~transient~.

A frequentative verb names repeated or habitual action, so ~transitāre~ suggested going back and forth — exactly what ~transitar~ still means: to pass along a route, the everyday word for moving through traffic. The root *~ey-~ is astonishingly productive in Spanish, hiding inside ~ir~ (“to go”) itself, ~tránsito~, ~transición~, ~itinerario~, ~ambición~ (“a going around” to canvass votes) and even ~éxito~ (“success,” from ~exitus~, “a going out”).
en.transmitir:
From Latin ~transmittere~ (“to send across, to convey”), a compound of ~trans-~ (“across, beyond”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, to let go”). ~mittere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~meitō~; its deeper origin is uncertain, but it is often traced to Proto-Indo-European *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, to remove”), an extension of the root *~mey-~ (“to change”). Spanish took ~transmitir~ as a learned borrowing rather than by unbroken popular descent. It is cognate with Italian ~trasmettere~, French ~transmettre~, Portuguese ~transmitir~, and English ~transmit~, all resting on the same Latin verb.

The literal image in ~transmittere~ is of sending something over or beyond a boundary — across a river, a frontier, a distance — and Spanish ~transmitir~ still carries it: one transmits a disease, a signal, an inheritance, a piece of news, passing it from one point or generation to the next. The rise of radio and television gave the verb its now-dominant broadcasting sense. Because ~mittere~ was extraordinarily prolific in Latin compounds, it seeded a large Spanish family sharing the notion of sending or letting go: ~admitir~, ~emitir~, ~permitir~, ~remitir~, ~someter~, ~mensaje~, and ~misión~.
en.transportar:
From Latin ~transportāre~ (“to carry across, convey over”), a compound of ~trans-~ (“across, beyond”) and ~portāre~ (“to carry, bear”). ~portāre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to carry over, pass through”), a root tied to notions of passage and crossing. Spanish ~transportar~ is a learned formation that kept the Latin shape; the fully popular outcome of ~portāre~ is ~portar~ (“to carry, behave”). Cognate with Italian ~trasportare~, French ~transporter~, Portuguese ~transportar~, and English ~transport~, all built on the same ~portāre~.

The root *~per-~ is one of the great travellers of Indo-European, underlying words for carrying, passing, and the ways one goes — Latin ~portus~ (“harbor,” a place of passage) and ~porta~ (“gate”) belong to the same family. From ~portāre~ Spanish grew a large set of prefixed verbs: ~importar~, ~exportar~, ~deportar~, ~soportar~, ~reportar~, ~aportar~, and ~comportar~, each adding a direction or a manner to the plain act of carrying. ~transportar~ took the “across” sense and, beyond moving goods and people, gained a figurative reach — a piece of music can ~transportar~ a listener, carry them somewhere else entirely. English ~transport~ shares that double life of freight and rapture.
en.trascender:
From Latin ~trānscendere~ (“to climb over, step across, surpass”), a compound of ~trāns-~ (“across, beyond”) and ~scandere~ (“to climb”), from Proto-Indo-European *~skend-~ (“to leap, climb up”). Spanish also spells it ~transcender~, though the ~n~-less ~trascender~ prevails. Cognate through ~scandere~ with English ~ascend~, ~descend~ and ~scan~, French ~scander~ and Italian ~scandire~.

The literal Latin idea is climbing up and over a wall — going beyond a boundary — and Spanish keeps both the down-to-earth and the lofty ends of that arc: news can ~trascender~ (“leak out, become known,” i.e. cross the wall of privacy), while in philosophy something ~trasciende~ ordinary experience. From ~scandere~ and its relatives Spanish gathers ~ascender~, ~descender~, ~escala~ and ~escalera~ (from ~scāla~, “ladder,” literally a thing for climbing), and the metrical ~escandir~ (“to scan verse,” counting feet as if climbing steps).
en.trasladar:
From Latin ~trānslātāre~, a frequentative built on ~trānslātus~ (“carried across”), which served as the suppletive past participle of ~trānsferre~ (“to carry over, transfer”). The compound is ~trāns-~ (“across, beyond”) plus ~lātus~, an old participle meaning “borne, carried” that belonged not to ~ferō~ but to the unrelated verb ~tollō~ (“to lift, raise”); ~lātus~ goes back to *~tlātos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~telh₂-~ (“to bear, carry, endure”). Through that root ~lātus~ is cognate with English ~tolerate~ and ~extol~, and the family shows up in Portuguese ~trasladar~ and Italian ~traslatare~.

The image beneath ~trasladar~ is purely physical — to lift something and carry it across — and Spanish keeps that literal weight: one ~traslada~ an office, a prisoner, a body, or a holiday to another date. Because ~trānslātus~ also meant “carried over” in a figurative sense, the same Latin stem gave ~traslado~ (“transfer, removal”) and ~traslación~ / ~translación~ (the Earth's orbital motion, and also figurative or metaphorical language — a meaning literally “carried across”). English ~translate~ is the very same word: where Spanish carried bodies from place to place, English carried meaning between tongues.
en.trasnochar:
A parasynthetic verb from ~tras-~ (a variant of ~trans-~, “across, through, beyond”) plus ~noche~ (“night”), formally matching a Vulgar Latin *~trānsnoctāre~ (~trāns~ + ~nox~, genitive ~noctis~). ~noche~ descends from Latin ~noctem~, from Proto-Indo-European *~nókʷts~ (“night”), one of the most stable words in the family — cognate with English ~night~, German ~Nacht~, French ~nuit~ and Italian ~notte~.

The literal sense is “to pass across the night,” i.e. to stay up all night or go without sleep, and figuratively ~trasnochado~ means “stale, hackneyed” — something left out overnight and gone off. The night-word seeds a large family in Spanish: ~nocturno~ (“nocturnal”), ~anochecer~ (“to grow dark”), ~medianoche~ (“midnight”), the sleep-walking ~noctámbulo~, the formal ~pernoctar~ (“to spend the night”) and even ~equinoccio~ (“equinox,” the “equal night”).
en.traspasar:
Spanish ~traspasar~ compounds the prefix ~tras-~ (from Latin ~trans-~, “across, beyond”) with ~pasar~ (“to pass”), which descends from Vulgar Latin *~passāre~, a verb coined on Latin ~passus~ (“a step, a pace”), the past participle of ~pandere~ (“to spread, stretch open”). The chain reaches Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to spread”). The same trans-plus-pass compound travelled widely: English took in ~trespass~ and French kept ~trépasser~ — literally « to pass beyond », which in French came to mean “to die.”

The core image of « passing across » fanned out into several senses: to cross or go through, to run through or pierce (a blade that ~traspasa~ a body), and — the dominant modern meaning — to hand over, to transfer a lease, a business, or a right. Spanish keeps the noun ~traspaso~ (“transfer, conveyance”) for that very transaction. Through its base ~pasar~ the word belongs to a broad family, among them ~paso~, ~pasaje~, ~pasear~ and ~pasaporte~, and it is cognate with English ~pass~ and ~pace~.
en.trasponer:
Spanish ~trasponer~ (also ~transponer~) continues Latin ~transpōnere~ (“to place across, transfer”), a compound of ~trans-~ (“across”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, place”). ~pōnere~ is traditionally analysed as ~po-~ (a reduced prefix) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, set down”). The Romance descendants and learned borrowings run in parallel: French ~transposer~, Italian ~trasporre~ and English ~transpose~ all render the same « put across ».

The verb keeps two live senses. Transitively it means to transpose — to shift something from one place, order, or musical key to another. Intransitively, and as the reflexive ~trasponerse~, it means to slip behind something and drop out of sight: the sun ~traspone~ the ridge, and a drowsy person ~se traspone~ into a doze. The shared root ~pōnere~ underlies a vast Spanish family — ~poner~, ~componer~, ~disponer~, ~exponer~, ~suponer~ — and the nouns in ~-posición~ like ~posición~ and ~composición~.
en.trastornar:
Spanish ~trastornar~ prefixes ~tras-~ (from Latin ~trans-~, “across, over”) to ~tornar~ (“to turn, return”), which comes from Latin ~tornāre~ (“to turn on a lathe, round off”), a verb built on ~tornus~ (“lathe”). That noun was borrowed from Ancient Greek ~τόρνος~ (~tórnos~, “compass, lathe”), and the family is usually traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~terh₁-~ (“to rub, turn”). Through the same base Spanish ~tornar~ is cognate with English ~turn~ and French ~tourner~.

The literal notion of « turning something over » slid naturally into figurative disorder: to overturn or upset, to disrupt plans, to unsettle the stomach, and — most vividly — to derange the mind, so that a ~trastornado~ person is one whose reason has been « turned upside down ». Spanish preserves the noun ~trastorno~ (“disorder, disturbance,” including a clinical “disorder”). The root ~tornar~ also yielded ~torno~ (“lathe, winch”), ~torneo~ (“tournament”), ~retornar~ and ~contorno~.
en.tratar:
From Latin ~tractāre~ (“to drag about, handle, manage, deal with”), the frequentative of ~trahere~ (“to draw, drag, pull”), which is perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰregʰ-~ (“to draw, pull”), though ~trahere~’s deeper origin is uncertain. Cognate with Italian ~trattare~, French ~traiter~, and Portuguese ~tratar~; through the same Latin verb English acquired ~treat~, ~treaty~, and ~tract~, and through ~trahere~’s participle ~tractus~, English ~trace~, ~trait~, and ~portray~.

A frequentative names repeated or intensive action, so ~tractāre~ was “to keep dragging or handling,” and from physical handling grew the ideas of managing an affair, dealing with people, and discussing a subject — the whole spread of Spanish ~tratar~. To ~tratar a alguien~ is to treat someone (well or badly); ~tratar de~ means both “to try to” and “to be about”; and ~tratarse de~ means “to be a question of.” The inherited verb ~traer~ (“to bring”) descends from the very same ~trahere~ by the popular route, a doublet of learned ~tratar~. From this root also flow ~trato~, ~tratado~, ~tratamiento~, ~retrato~, ~contrato~, ~atraer~, and ~tracción~.
en.trazar:
From Vulgar Latin *~tractiāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~tractus~ (“a dragging, a drawing”), the participle of ~trahere~ (“to drag, draw, pull”). The ultimate origin of ~trahere~ is genuinely unclear: some derive it from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰragʰ-~, others (following de Vaan) suspect a non-Indo-European substrate word shared with Celtic, and a tempting link to English ~draw~ is judged phonetically impossible. Through the participle ~tractus~ it is kin to Italian ~tracciare~, French ~tracer~ and the English trio ~trace~, ~track~ and ~trait~.

The image is of dragging a point to leave a line, so ~trazar~ means “to draw, sketch, outline, plot” — one ~traza~ a route or a plan. The noun ~traza~ means “design, layout, appearance,” ~trazo~ is “a stroke of the pen,” and ~trazado~ is “a route or layout.” The parent ~trahere~ also gave Spanish ~traer~ (“to bring”) and its prefixed swarm ~atraer~, ~contraer~, ~distraer~, ~extraer~ and ~sustraer~ — every one a kind of pulling.
en.trillar:
Spanish ~trillar~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~triblāre~, a syncopated form of Latin ~tribulāre~, itself built on the noun ~tribulum~ — the studded wooden threshing-sledge dragged over cut grain to beat the kernels loose. ~tribulum~ derives from ~terere~ (“to rub, wear away”), from Proto-Indo-European *~terh₁-~ (“to rub, turn”) — the same root that gave ~tornar~ and English ~turn~. The verb is cognate with Portuguese ~trilhar~ and Galician ~trillar~, and is a learned doublet of ~tribular~.

The threshing image proved fertile. Spanish keeps concrete senses — to thresh grain, and by extension to beat, wear out, or trudge a path over and over (hence ~trillado~, “trite, hackneyed,” a « well-trodden » idea). Most striking is a cousin word: because the ~tribulum~ crushed and battered the harvest, its Latin relatives gave ~tribulación~ and English ~tribulation~ — affliction imagined as a soul being threshed. From the same field come ~trilla~ (“threshing”) and ~trillo~ (“threshing sledge”).
en.triunfar:
Spanish ~triunfar~ comes from Latin ~triumphāre~ (“to celebrate a triumph”), from the noun ~triumphus~. By the traditional account, ~triumphus~ reached Latin — probably through Etruscan — from Greek ~θρίαμβος~ (thríambos), a hymn sung in honor of Dionysus, itself borrowed from some pre-Greek language. Cognate with Italian ~trionfare~, French ~triompher~, Portuguese ~triunfar~, and English ~triumph~.

In Rome, a ~triumphus~ was the lavish procession voted to a victorious general, who rode through the city to the Capitol; from that pageant of victory the word broadened to any great success. Even the card-game term English ~trump~ is a worn-down form of ~triumph~. Spanish keeps a rich family: the noun ~triunfo~, the adjectives ~triunfal~ and ~triunfante~, and — as in English — ~triunfo~ as the winning suit at cards.
en.trocar:
Spanish ~trocar~ (“to barter, exchange”) is of uncertain origin. It continues a Medieval Latin ~trocāre~ spread across western Romance, but what lies beneath is disputed: a frequent proposal derives it from a Frankish *~trokōn~, though this is far from settled and other accounts leave the ultimate etymon unresolved. The cognate set is clear, however — Portuguese, Galician, Catalan and Occitan all have ~trocar~, French has ~troquer~, and English borrowed the mercantile ~truck~ (“to barter,” as in « to have no truck with »).

The core sense has always been reciprocal substitution — to give one thing and take another in its place. From it Spanish draws the everyday noun ~trueque~ (“barter, swap”) and the phrase ~a trueque de~ (“in exchange for”). The verb also grew a figurative sense, « to change one thing into another », so that fortune ~trueca~ joy into grief; like other verbs in ~-ocar~ it diphthongises under stress (~trueco~, ~truecas~). Because the deeper origin remains unsettled, the neat Frankish account is best held as a hypothesis, not a fact.
en.trotar:
Spanish ~trotar~ is a Romance borrowing, taken from Old French ~troter~ (or Italian ~trottare~), which go back to Medieval Latin ~trottāre~. That verb was not native Latin at all but a loan from Frankish *~trottōn~ (“to run, go”), a Germanic word tied to Proto-Germanic *~trudōną~ (“to tread, step”). Through that Germanic root ~trotar~ is a distant cousin of German ~treten~ and English ~tread~. The mount, not the rider, gave the word its life.

A trot is the horse's brisk two-beat gait between walk and gallop, and the verb kept close to the stable: to trot, to move at a jog, and figuratively to bustle about — someone always ~trotando~ from errand to errand. Spanish coined the noun ~trote~ (“trot,” and colloquially “hard work, hassle,” as in ~de mucho trote~, “hard-wearing”) and the noun ~trotamundos~ (“globetrotter”). French ~trotter~ likewise gave the ~trottoir~, the “pavement” one trots along.
en.trovar:
Spanish ~trovar~ was inherited (via Old Spanish ~trobar~) from Old Occitan ~trobar~, the verb of the troubadours, from Vulgar Latin *~tropāre~. That form was built on Latin ~tropus~ (“a figure of speech, a trope”), itself from Ancient Greek ~τρόπος~ (~trópos~, “a turn, a way”): to ~tropāre~ was to « compose in tropes », to invent melodies and verses. Its Romance kin are famous — French ~trouver~ and Italian ~trovare~, both meaning “to find,” and the noun ~trovador~ (“troubadour”). A minority view has proposed instead an Arabic source, but the Romance derivation is the standard account.

The split between “to find” and “to compose” is the memorable part. In Gallo-Romance the sense settled on discovering, chancing upon — hence French ~trouver~ and the English ~trove~ in « treasure trove » (from Old French ~trové~). In Ibero-Romance ~trovar~ kept the artistic sense: to make verses, to sing them, to court in rhyme. The word still evokes the medieval ~trovador~ who wandered ~trovando~; Spanish also has the noun ~trova~ (“a sung poem”). Both branches ultimately picture the poet « turning » language into figures.
en.ubicar:
From Latin ~ubi~ (“where”), through a Late/Medieval Latin verb *~ubicāre~ and the noun ~ubicātiō~ (“a locating, position”). ~ubi~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European interrogative-relative stem *~kʷo-~ (as in ~quis~, “who”) and is parallel to Latin ~ibi~ (“there”). Unlike most Spanish verbs, ~ubicar~ was not inherited from spoken Latin but built on a Latin adverb — a learned coinage, long especially current in American Spanish.

To ubicar is, literally, to answer the question “where?” — to fix a thing’s place. From the same ~ubi~, plus the enclitic ~-que~, Latin formed ~ubīque~ (“everywhere”), which gave Spanish ~ubicuo~ (“ubiquitous”) and ~ubicuidad~; ~ubicuidad~ began life as a theological term for God’s presence everywhere. English ~ubiquitous~ descends from the same ~ubīque~, and everyday ~ubicación~ shares the verb’s root. The homely adverb “where” thus underlies a small, learned family.
en.ultimar:
From Late Latin ~ultimāre~ (“to come to an end, to be the last”), formed on ~ultimus~ (“last, farthest, most distant”), which is the superlative of ~ulter~ (“beyond”), from Proto-Italic *~olteros~ and ultimately the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂el-~ (“beyond, other”). Spanish ~ultimar~ has siblings in Italian ~ultimare~ and Portuguese ~ultimar~, and ~ultimus~ passed into English as ~ultimate~ and ~ultimatum~. That deep root *~h₂el-~ also branched into Latin ~alius~ and ~alter~ (“other”) and into English ~else~ and ~other~.

Since ~ultimus~ meant “the last,” ~ultimāre~ meant to bring a thing to its last point — hence Spanish ~ultimar~ (“to finalize, conclude, put the finishing touches to”). In parts of Spanish America it took a grim turn, coming to mean “to finish someone off, to kill” — the ultimate act. The family gathers the endpoints of things: ~último~ (“last”), ~penúltimo~ (“next to last”), ~ultimátum~ (the “last word” of a negotiation) and, from ~ulter~ by another path, ~ultra~ (“beyond”) with its many modern compounds.
en.unificar:
From Late Latin ~unificāre~, a compound of Latin ~unus~ (“one”) and ~facere~ (“to make”) — literally “to make one.” ~unus~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~óynos~ (“one, single”), while ~facere~ goes back to *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to set, put, make”). Cognate in the Romance family with Italian ~unificare~, French ~unifier~ and Portuguese ~unificar~; and, through the two roots, with English ~one~ (from *~óynos~) and English ~do~ (from *~dʰeh₁-~).

The learned suffix ~-ificar~ (from ~facere~) is a workshop for verbs meaning “to make into”: beside ~unificar~ stand ~clarificar~, ~purificar~, ~verificar~ and ~identificar~. From ~unus~ alone Spanish built a numerous family — ~uno~, ~unidad~, ~unión~, ~único~, ~universo~ (“turned into one”) and ~reunir~. The tidy irony is that a verb meaning “to make one” is itself a fusion of two separate Latin words welded together by the ~-ificar~ suffix.
en.unir:
From Latin ~ūnīre~ (“to unite, join into one”), derived from ~ūnus~ (“one”). ~ūnus~ comes from Old Latin ~oinos~, from Proto-Italic *~oinos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~óynos~ (“one, single”). The same root gave English ~one~, ~an~ and ~only~, German ~ein~, and Greek ~oínē~ (the “one” on a die). Among cognate Romance forms are Italian ~unire~, Portuguese ~unir~ and French ~unir~; English ~unite~ is a learned borrowing of the same Latin verb.

The Latin verb was built straightforwardly from the numeral: to ~unir~ is to make things ~ūnus~, one. Because the notion of oneness is so basic, its descendants spread everywhere in Spanish — ~uno~, ~unión~, ~unidad~, ~único~, ~universo~ (literally “turned into one”), ~reunir~ and ~unánime~ (“of one mind”). Even the humble ~onza~ and English ~ounce~ trace back to ~ūnus~ through ~uncia~, a “single” twelfth part. Few roots pack so much of a language’s vocabulary into one small word for “one.”
en.untar:
Spanish ~untar~ descends from Late Latin ~unctāre~, a frequentative formed on the past participle ~unctus~ of Latin ~unguere~ (also ~ungere~, “to anoint, smear with grease”). The chain runs back through Proto-Italic *~ongʷō~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃engʷ-~ (“to anoint, salve”). English borrowed the same root repeatedly through Latin: ~unguent~, ~ointment~ and ~anoint~ all mean essentially « to smear with oil », and ~unctuous~ preserves the participle ~unctus~ intact.

The literal sense — to coat with grease, ointment, or any thick substance — has stayed put for two millennia: you can ~untar~ butter on bread or oil on a pan. But Spanish also grew a pointed idiom, ~untar la mano~ (“to grease the palm”), meaning to bribe, so that ~untar~ can quietly mean “to buy off.” From the same root come the noun ~unto~ (“grease, fat”), ~ungir~ (“to anoint,” in the religious sense), ~ungüento~ (“ointment, unguent”) and ~unción~ (“unction”), the last two straight from ~unctus~.
en.urdir:
From Latin ~ōrdīrī~ (“to lay the warp, to begin weaving”), through a Vulgar Latin variant ~ōrdīre~ that fed the Romance verbs, inherited into Old Spanish. The deeper origin is uncertain: sources list it among Latin words of unknown etymology, and although it has long been compared with ~ōrdō~ (“row, series, order”), that link is proposed rather than proven. Cognate with Portuguese ~urdir~, Italian ~ordire~ and French ~ourdir~, all keeping the weaver's sense.

The starting point was wholly concrete: to ~urdir~ was to stretch the lengthwise warp threads on a loom before weaving could begin. From that preparatory, behind-the-scenes labor the verb drifted to the figurative “to contrive, to plot, to scheme” — one quietly assembles the hidden framework of an intrigue just as a weaver assembles the warp. Spanish keeps the textile noun ~urdimbre~ (“warp; underlying scheme”) alongside the verb, and pairs it in idiom with ~tramar~ (from ~trama~, “weft”), so that a plot is something one both warps and wefts into being.
en.usar:
From Vulgar Latin ~ūsāre~, a frequentative built on ~ūsus~, the past participle of Latin ~ūtī~ (“to use, employ, make use of”). The deeper origin of ~ūtī~ is uncertain: it has been tentatively linked to Proto-Indo-European *~h₃eyt-~ (“to take along, fetch”), but the connection is disputed and far from secure. Cognate Romance descendants include Italian ~usare~, Portuguese ~usar~ and French ~user~; English ~use~ came through Old French ~user~ from the same Vulgar Latin verb.

Latin already used ~ūtī~ very broadly — to employ, enjoy, or associate with something — and the frequentative ~ūsāre~ simply meant to do so habitually, which is why Spanish ~usar~ covers everyday “using” of every kind. The participial stem ~ūsus~ is the productive one in Spanish: ~uso~, ~usar~, ~usado~, ~usuario~, ~usual~ and ~abusar~ (“to misuse”) all grow from it, as do the learned ~útil~ (“useful”) and ~utilizar~ from the related adjective ~ūtilis~. Even English ~utensil~ shares that adjective — a thing fit to be used.
en.utilizar:
A relatively modern formation, from the adjective ~útil~ (“useful”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-izar~, and closely paralleling French ~utiliser~ (whence it likely took its impulse in the nineteenth century). ~útil~ descends from Latin ~ūtilis~ (“useful, serviceable”), from ~ūtī~ (“to use, make use of”), a verb of uncertain origin with no secure Proto-Indo-European etymology. Cognate through Latin with Italian ~utilizzare~, Portuguese ~utilizar~, and English ~utilize~ and ~utility~.

The chain is short but instructive: from ~ūtī~ “to use” Latin built the adjective ~ūtilis~ “usable,” Spanish inherited it as ~útil~, and only later did the language forge a verb from the adjective with ~-izar~, giving a slightly bookish ~utilizar~ beside the older, plainer ~usar~ (from Latin ~ūsāre~, itself a frequentative of ~ūtī~ through its participle ~ūsus~). The two coexist, ~utilizar~ often carrying a shade of “to put to use, make instrumental use of.” From the same ~ūtī~ come ~útil~, ~utilidad~, ~inútil~, ~utensilio~, ~uso~, ~usar~, and ~usual~, and the borrowed ~utilitario~ (“utilitarian”).
en.vagar:
From Latin ~vagārī~ (deponent ~vagor~, “to wander, to roam, to rove”), a denominative of the adjective ~vagus~ (“wandering, unfixed, inconstant”). The deeper origin of ~vagus~ is uncertain and no secure Proto-Indo-European root is agreed. Cognate with Italian ~vagare~, French ~vaguer~ and Portuguese ~vagar~; through the same Latin adjective, English borrowed ~vague~ and ~vagary~.

The core image never really left: aimless, unfixed movement across space. Spanish keeps the literal “to roam,” but ~vagar~ also acquired a quieter sense of unhurried, purposeless drift, and as a noun it can mean leisure or idle time — the freedom of one who has nowhere he must be. The adjective ~vagus~ was enormously productive: from it Spanish has ~vago~ (“vague; also a loafer”), ~vagabundo~ (“vagabond”), ~divagar~ (“to digress,” literally to wander apart), ~vaguedad~ (“vagueness”) and the learned ~extravagante~ — from Latin ~extra~ + ~vagārī~, someone or something “wandering outside” the ordinary bounds.
en.valer:
From Latin ~valēre~ (“to be strong, be healthy, be worth”), from Proto-Indo-European *~welh₁-~ (“to be strong, to rule”). It is cognate with Italian ~valere~, French ~valoir~, and Portuguese ~valer~; through the same root it is kin to the Latin-derived English ~value~, ~valid~, and ~prevail~, and to the Germanic ~wield~, which kept the “rule, be powerful” side of the root.

In Latin ~valēre~ ran from “to be physically strong” to “to be well” to “to be worth,” and Spanish ~valer~ inherited the whole span. The imperative ~valē~ (“be well!”) served the Romans as a parting word, and its descendant survives in the colloquial Spanish ~vale~ — an all-purpose “OK, agreed” heard across Spain. The root seeded a broad family: ~valor~ (“worth, courage”), ~válido~, ~valiente~ and ~valentía~, ~equivaler~, ~evaluar~, and ~prevalecer~. Even the proper name ~Valerio~ traces back to this same idea of strength and worth.
en.validar:
Spanish ~validar~ (“to validate”) comes from Late Latin ~validāre~ (“to make valid, to strengthen”), from the adjective ~validus~ (“strong, sound”), itself from the verb ~valēre~ (“to be strong, to be worth”). The root is Proto-Indo-European *~h₂welh₁-~ (“to be strong, to rule”). English drew richly from the same well — ~valid~, ~value~, and (by one account of the root’s reach into Germanic) even ~wield~ — while Slavic shows it in names built on “rule,” such as ~Vladimir~ (“great ruler”). Spanish’s own everyday ~válido~ sits right beside the verb.

The thread running through the whole family is worth and strength. To ~validar~ something is to certify that it holds good — that it is ~válido~ — and the same root gives Spanish ~valer~ (“to be worth”), ~valor~ (“worth, courage”), ~valiente~ (“brave”), ~prevalecer~ (“to prevail”) and ~convalecer~ (“to convalesce,” to regain strength). Even the noun ~valía~ (“worth”) and the legal ~validez~ (“validity”) belong here. So a validated document and a valiant heart share a pedigree: both are, at root, things strong enough to hold.
en.valorar:
From ~valor~ (“worth, value”), from Late Latin ~valor~, a noun built on Latin ~valēre~ (“to be strong, to be worth”). ~valēre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~walēō~ and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂welh₁-~ (“to rule, to be strong”). Cognate with Italian ~valere~ and Portuguese ~valer~, and — through the same root — with English ~value~ and ~valiant~ and the given name ~Valerie~.

The root's core idea is strength, and Spanish kept both branches of it: to be worth something and to be physically able. ~valer~ still means “to be worth,” while the derived ~valorar~ specialized as “to appraise, to assign a value” and, more recently, “to esteem, to appreciate.” A person of ~valor~ shows courage — strength of character — while an object of ~valor~ has monetary worth; the two senses share one Latin heart. The same root seeded a broad family of Spanish words: ~valiente~ (“brave”), ~válido~ (“valid”), ~valía~ (“worth”), ~equivaler~ (“to be equivalent”), ~prevalecer~ (“to prevail”), and ~convalecer~ (“to convalesce,” literally to grow strong again). Even the everyday interjection ~¡vale!~ (“okay!”) is the same verb, meaning literally “it is worth, it holds.”
en.variar:
From Latin ~variāre~ (“to diversify, change, make various”), from the adjective ~varius~ (“variegated, spotted, of different kinds”). The origin of ~varius~ is unknown. De Vaan records a tentative link to a Proto-Italic *~wasios~ shared with ~vafer~ (“crafty, sly”), and separately weighs — and rejects as unconvincing — a derivation from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁weh₂-~ said to lie behind ~vārus~ (“bent, bow-legged”), ~vānus~ (“empty”), and ~vāstus~ (“vast”). No proposal has cognates outside Italic to anchor it, so the deep root is genuinely open. What is clear is the near end of the chain: Spanish ~variar~, French ~varier~, Italian ~variare~, and English ~vary~ all rest transparently on ~variāre~.

The oldest sense of ~varius~ was visual — “mottled, many-colored, dappled,” a coat or a marble of mixed hues — and from “displaying different colors” the notion generalized to “differing, changing,” which is what ~variar~ carries today: to vary, change, or differ. The Spanish family is large and plain: ~variedad~ (“variety”), ~varios~ (“several, various”), ~variable~, ~variación~, ~variante~, and ~invariable~. English shares the whole learned set — ~variety~, ~various~, ~variation~ — and the medical ~varicose~, from Latin ~varix~ (“a dilated vein”), is often linked to this same cluster, though that connection, like the root itself, is not firmly established. A word for endless change turns out to have an endlessly uncertain past.
en.vedar:
From Latin ~vetāre~ (first-person ~vetō~, “I forbid”), inherited through Old Spanish. The origin of ~vetāre~ is uncertain; it has been tentatively linked to Welsh ~gwadu~ (“to deny”), but the connection is not secure and is best treated as a proposal. Cognate with Portuguese ~vedar~, Italian ~vietare~ and Old French ~veer~.

In Rome the bare form ~vetō~ (“I forbid”) was the tribune's formula for blocking a magistrate's act or a decree of the Senate — the direct ancestor of the modern ~veto~, which Spanish much later re-borrowed straight from Latin as a learned noun, standing beside the inherited ~vedar~. The everyday verb kept the plain sense “to prohibit, to bar,” and put down roots in hunting and land law: a ~vedado~ is a preserve or closed ground where entry or hunting is forbidden, and ~veda~ is the closed season itself. Thus a single Latin verb handed Spanish both the humble gamekeeper's ~vedado~ and the grand parliamentary ~veto~.
en.velar:
From Latin ~vigilāre~ (“to keep watch, stay awake”), from the adjective ~vigil~ (“awake, watchful”), from Proto-Indo-European *~weǵ-~ (“to be lively, vigorous, awake”). ~velar~ is the inherited, popularly evolved form — the intervocalic ~-g-~ dropped and the ~-i-~ opened to ~-e-~ — while Spanish also keeps a learned twin, ~vigilar~ (“to watch, guard”), reborrowed later from the same Latin verb. Cognate with French ~veiller~ and Portuguese ~velar~, and — through the same root — with English ~wake~, ~watch~, and ~vigil~. (Do not confuse this ~velar~ with its homonym ~velar~ “to veil,” which comes from Latin ~vēlum~, “sail, cloth,” an unrelated word.)

Latin ~vigilāre~ meant to stay awake and keep the night watch. Spanish ~velar~ preserved the wakeful sense — to sit up through the night, especially over a sick person or a corpse — which is why the tending of the dead is a ~velatorio~ or ~velorio~ (“wake”), and why ~desvelar~ means both “to keep awake” and “to unveil, reveal.” The learned twin ~vigilar~ took the guarding, surveilling sense. The rest of the family keeps the same alert glow: ~vigilia~ (“vigil, wakefulness”), ~vigilante~ (“watchman”), and ~vigor~ (“vigour”). To watch over someone, then, is literally to stay awake for them.
en.vencer:
From Latin ~vincere~ (“to conquer, defeat”), from Proto-Italic *~winkō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~weyk-~ (“to fight, conquer, overpower”). Cognate with Italian ~vincere~, French ~vaincre~ and Portuguese ~vencer~, and — through Latin — with English ~victor~, ~convince~, ~evince~ and ~invincible~. The Old Irish ~fichid~ (“fights”) springs from the same root.

Latin ~vincere~ ranged from winning battles to winning arguments, and Spanish ~vencer~ kept both, adding a quieter sense: a debt or deadline ~vence~ when it “falls due,” as if time had overcome it. From the same root come ~victoria~, ~vencedor~, ~invencible~, ~convencer~ and ~vencimiento~. A ~convicto~ is, etymologically, one thoroughly ~vencido~ in court.
en.vender:
From Latin ~vēndere~, a fusion of the phrase ~vēnum dare~ (“to give for sale”), from ~vēnum~ (“sale, that which is for sale”) plus ~dare~ (“to give”). ~vēnum~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~wes-~ (“to buy, sell”), and ~dare~ to *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Romance kept the compound intact: Italian ~vendere~, French ~vendre~, Portuguese ~vender~.

Latin welded a two-word phrase — “give for sale” — into a single verb, whose passive twin ~vēneō~ meant “to be sold,” literally “to go to sale.” What ~vender~ carries is a deep commercial vocabulary: the ~vēnum~ element (“price, sale”) is cognate with Ancient Greek ~ὦνος~ (“price”) and Sanskrit ~vasná~ (“price”), showing how old the idea of a fixed price is. From it Spanish keeps ~venta~ (“sale”), ~vendedor~, and ~venal~ (“that can be bought, corruptible”), while ~dare~ seeds another vast family, beginning with ~dar~ (“to give”).
en.vendimiar:
From Latin ~vindēmiāre~ (“to gather grapes”), a denominative of ~vindēmia~ (“grape harvest, vintage”). That noun is a compound of ~vīnum~ (“wine”) — from Proto-Italic *~wīnom~, from Proto-Indo-European *~wóyh₁nom~ — and ~dēmere~ (“to take away, to remove”), itself ~dē-~ plus ~emere~ (“to take,” from PIE *~h₁em-~). The word therefore means, quite literally, the taking-away of the wine from the vine. Cognate with Italian ~vendemmiare~, French ~vendanger~ and Portuguese ~vindimar~.

Spanish kept the harvest verb and its noun ~vendimia~ (“the grape harvest and its season”), the yearly gathering that turns fruit into wine. From ~vīnum~ Spanish also has ~vino~, ~viña~ (“vineyard”) and ~vinagre~ (“vinegar,” wine gone sour); from the ~emere~ family it inherited learned words such as ~redimir~ (“to redeem”) and ~ejemplo~ (“example,” via ~eximere~, “to take out”). Through French, the same ~vindēmia~ even reached English as ~vintage~ — first the yield of a single grape harvest, only later a byword for anything of enduring, well-aged quality.
en.vengar:
From Old Spanish ~vengar~, from Latin ~vindicāre~ (“to lay legal claim to; to protect; to avenge, punish”), from ~vindex~ (“claimant, protector, avenger”). Cognate with French ~venger~, Italian ~vendicare~, and Portuguese ~vingar~; the learned doublet ~vindicar~ and the compound ~reivindicar~ were later borrowed straight from the Latin, and English has ~avenge~, ~revenge~, ~vengeance~, and ~vindicate~ from the same source.

The formation of ~vindex~ is debated: it is traditionally parsed as ~vim~ (accusative of ~vīs~, “force”) plus ~dīcere~ (“to declare”), on the model of ~iūdex~ (“judge”), giving roughly “one who asserts authority” — but that segmentation is only proposed, and the word's ultimate origin is uncertain. In Roman law ~vindicāre~ first meant to assert a formal claim over a thing or person, then to shield them, and finally to right a wrong by punishment — the path from “to claim” to “to avenge.” Spanish kept the popular ~vengar~ (with ~venganza~, “revenge”) beside the learned ~vindicar~, ~vindicta~, and ~reivindicar~ (“to vindicate, demand back”).
en.venir:
From Latin ~venīre~ (“to come”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷeniō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to come, go, step”). This is one of the great Indo-European roots: it gave English ~come~ (through Germanic), Ancient Greek ~baínō~ (“to walk, step”) and Sanskrit ~gácchati~ (“goes”). Cognate Romance verbs include Italian ~venire~, Portuguese ~vir~ and French ~venir~; English ~venue~ is Old French ~venue~, literally “a coming.”

The Latin sense “to come” passed intact into Spanish ~venir~, and the verb’s prefixed compounds became a workshop of vocabulary in both Latin and Spanish. From ~venīre~ Spanish draws ~venida~ (“arrival”), ~porvenir~ (“future,” literally “what is to come”), ~convenir~ (“to suit, agree” — to “come together”), ~intervenir~, ~prevenir~ (“to prevent,” to “come before”) and ~aventura~ (“adventure,” from ~adventūra~, “things about to come”). Through Latin the same root reaches English ~advent~, ~convene~, ~invent~ and ~revenue~ — a striking spread from one small word for “to come.”
en.ver:
Spanish ~ver~ comes, through Old Spanish ~veer~, from Latin ~vidēre~ (“to see”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~weyd-~, which meant both “to see” and “to know” — for the ancients, to have seen a thing was to know it. That double sense survives in the Germanic cousins: English ~wit~ and ~wise~, and German ~wissen~ (“to know”), all from the same root, as is Greek ~idéa~ (“form, idea”). The Romance reflexes stayed on the “see” side: French ~voir~, Italian ~vedere~.

Latin ~vidēre~ kept mainly the visual sense, and Spanish inherited it whole, down to the irregular participle ~visto~ (“seen”). The root spreads through a family of looking and seeming: ~vista~ (“sight, view”), ~visión~ (“vision”), ~evidente~ (“evident,” what is plainly seen), ~prever~ (“to foresee”), ~revisar~ (“to review”), and ~aviso~ (“notice, warning”). Modern ~vídeo~ — Latin for “I see” — joins the same ancient family, the newest branch on a very old root of seeing.
en.verificar:
